MLT.name: Malta
MLT.summary:
Malta decriminalised same-sex conduct on 29 January 1973. On 15 April 2014 parliament approved a constitutional amendment naming gender identity as a protected ground, the first European state to do so, and introduced civil unions in the same sitting; same-sex marriage has been legal since 2017. Transgender Europe was among the first non-governmental organisations to welcome gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

Statutory discrimination protections extend to sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and hate-crime provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity offences. Legal gender recognition requires no surgery, nonbinary identity is recognised, and a December 2016 amendment allows minors aged 16 and over to change their legal gender without a court application or parental approval.

Malta was the first EU country to ban conversion therapy. The Affirmation of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression Act passed its final reading unanimously on 6 December 2016, after Civil Liberties Minister Helena Dalli first tabled a bill targeting minors in December 2015; the Malta Chamber of Psychologists and related professional associations backed the measure. The Gender Identity, Gender Expression and Sex Characteristics Act of 2015 was the world's first law to ban sterilising or invasive surgery on intersex infants.

Rules governing everyday access are settled rather than contested: same-sex marriage since 2017, full joint adoption since 2014, open military service, protected bathroom access, a ban on conversion therapy, and a full ban on intersex infant surgery. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender.

Border treatment of LGBTI arrivals is documented in one live litigation. An LGBTI asylum seeker was detained on arrival in Malta in April 2023 and received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024. On 30 July 2025 the International Commission of Jurists and partner organisations filed observations in M.S. v. Malta at the European Court of Human Rights, raising non-refoulement, detention conditions and the requirement of an individualised assessment before detention under Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Violence indicators are comparatively favourable but reporting is not. Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical and sexual victimisation on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity expression in the EU27, while LGBTIQ+ people still report a comparatively high share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

Prison is the documented weak point. On 29 May 2018 the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each — €4,000 for breach of rights and €1,000 for damage to personal dignity — after the authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, used the men's showers and often went without washing, and endured insults and continuous sexual abuse and violence. The court found that the authorities had knowingly and repeatedly placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were described as hostile, so they remained in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay, and the Aditus Foundation represented the seven women.

Practice in custody continues to lag the statute. A 2024 University of Malta dissertation by Oriana Vidal, drawing on interviews with four current and former transgender and gender-diverse inmates of the Correctional Service Agency across a 25-year cohort, records that after the 2013 gender-law reform the Agency permitted transfers to the female section, replacing an earlier practice of segregating such inmates in a separate dormitory. Participants now hold individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers using masculine birth names, along with gaps in gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare, and conclude that Agency practice, policies and procedures lag the national gender-identity law. The dissertation also identifies gaps in healthcare, legislation and staff knowledge, and problems after release.
MLT.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2018 Corradino award changed Correctional Service Agency practice is not sourced here. The 2024 dissertation reports ongoing misgendering and clothing and healthcare gaps, but the inventory contains no post-judgment inspection, no agency policy revision, and no compliance review tied to the ruling.

The dissertation rests on four interviews across a 25-year cohort at one corrections agency, and the underlying 2018 award covers seven claimants. Both are specific findings rather than a count of current conditions in custody.

M.S. v. Malta was still at the observation stage as of 30 July 2025; the inventory contains no judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, so the outcome of the claim and any resulting change in detention practice at the border remain unresolved.

Police reporting rates are described only as 'significantly low' in the academic source. The inventory carries no figure for complaints of hate-motivated violence, no prosecutorial outcomes, and no data disaggregating incidents against transgender people specifically.

Equaldex's public-attitude percentage and workplace-concealment ranking are platform and survey data of unstated methodology; the inventory does not establish their sampling, date or comparability with the ILGA-Europe scoring.

sources.title: The lived experiences of transgender inmates at Malta's Correctional Service Agency (Oriana Vidal, University of Malta, 2024)
sources.summary: University of Malta master's dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of Malta's Correctional Service Agency (CSA), a cohort spanning the last 25 years. It records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform CSA practice allowed TGD inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and conclude that CSA practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report (Agius, Malta Today) of seven TGD inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

ISL.name: Iceland
ISL.summary:
Iceland ranks first of 121 jurisdictions surveyed by Equaldex as a good place for gay and lesbian people, at 93 per cent. The same source records that same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women, same-sex marriage is recognised, gender change carries no restrictions, non-binary identity is recognised, discrimination is illegal with hate-crime protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity, bathroom access is protected, conversion therapy is banned, and intersex infant surgery is fully banned.

Legal gender recognition operates on a self-determination basis under the 2019 reform, which took effect on 1 January 2020 and was implemented in January 2021. Minors may change their legal gender with parental consent, an X third-gender marker is available, and medical interventions on intersex children are prohibited except where health-related. The statute replaced an earlier law that was already regarded as among the most progressive in Europe, and activists including the chair of Trans Ísland continue to map the practical difficulties that remain.

Discrimination protection rests on the 1996 Penal Code amendments, which made it an offence to publicly attack a person or group through mockery, defamation, abuse or threats because of their sexual orientation, and on a 2014 amendment that added gender identity as a prohibited ground. Discrimination in education has been unlawful since 2008. The Equality Complaints Committee, operated through Ísland.is, is the official complaints mechanism for equality complaints, and Outright International reports that LGBTI organisations can register while noting acknowledged gaps in protection.

Police-recorded potential hate crimes rose to 16 cases in 2023, three times the previous year, with 11 recorded in 2024 and 7 in the current year. Samtökin 78 has called for stronger hate-crime legislation as recorded incidents climb. The national emergency service, 112.is, describes hate crime as an umbrella term for offences committed from prejudice or hatred, publishes guidance for victims and perpetrators, and sets out reporting routes for abuse against queer people, whom it notes are more likely to be victims of violence.

Relationship recognition has accumulated in stages. Registered partnerships from 1996 already granted same-sex couples many of the rights, responsibilities and benefits of marriage, including the ability to adopt stepchildren; stepchild adoption by a partner was permitted from 2000; and on 27 June 2006 same-sex couples gained equal access to joint adoption of children alongside public IVF insemination treatment. The 2010 same-sex marriage vote passed unanimously, 49 to 0. The conversion therapy ban followed in 2023 on a 53 to 0 vote with 3 abstentions.

GOV.UK travel advice for Iceland states that same-sex sexual activity is legal and same-sex relationships are recognised in law, and sets out dedicated LGBT+ guidance for British visitors.
ISL.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory, a travel information page for trans and non-binary visitors and two international hate-crime monitoring pages for Iceland, returned no usable finding and support none of the claims above.

Outright International states that Iceland's laws are progressive with acknowledged gaps in protection, but does not identify which protections are incomplete. The nature and extent of those gaps remain unresolved in this record.

The current-year hate-crime figure of 7 cases is a partial-year count and is not comparable to the full-year totals for 2023 and 2024.

A substantial share of the historical and statutory detail, including Penal Code section 178, the 1996 and 2014 amendments, the adoption and partnership dates and the vote counts, derives from an encyclopaedic country coverage rather than primary legislation, and has not been independently corroborated here.

Whether Icelandic border and document checks accept a foreign-issued X or non-binary marker, and how such documents are handled at screening, is not addressed by any source in the inventory and remains unresolved.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Iceland's 1996 Penal Code amendments made it illegal to publicly attack a person or group with mockery, defamation, abuse or threats because of their sexual orientation, and a 2014 amendment added gender identity to anti-discrimination grounds. Public expression is visibly supported: Reykjavík Pride drew about 100,000 people in 2015 (roughly 30% of the population), and in 2016 President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson became the first president to attend a gay pride parade. The country has a visible gay scene of bars and cafés in Reykjavík, though elsewhere the sparse population means there is almost no gay scene (Akureyri has no gay bars). Wikipedia country coverage: Stepchild adoption (a person adopting their partner's biological child) has been permitted since 2000, and on 27 June 2006 same-sex couples gained equal access to joint adoption of children alongside public IVF insemination treatment. Registered partnerships from 1996 already granted same-sex couples many of the same rights, responsibilities and benefits as marriage, including the ability to adopt stepchildren. A 2000 Gallup poll found 53% of Icelanders supported lesbian and gay adoption rights, with 35% against. Wikipedia country coverage: Section 178 of the Penal Code criminalized same-sex relations between 1869 and 1940, and public antipathy towards LGBT people remained high until the 1980s: some of the earliest Icelanders to come out publicly, Hörður Torfason and Anna Kristjánsdottir, initially faced public discrimination and ridicule. State hostility has since reversed — the 1996 anti-discrimination amendments, the 2010 unanimous (49–0) same-sex marriage vote, and the 2023 conversion therapy ban (53–0, 3 abstentions) mark the shift. One lingering restriction was the blood donation ban on men who have sex with men, challenged by a lawsuit in 2014, relaxed to a 4-month deferral in September 2021, and lifted entirely from September 2026. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2008 it has been illegal to discriminate against people on the basis of their sexual orientation in education. Since 2016 the town of Hafnarfjörður has included information about same-sex relationships in its eighth-grade (ages 14–15) sex education lessons, and the Queer Student Association of Iceland runs social activities and field trips for University of Iceland students. On gender, the 2019 self-determination law (effective 1 January 2020, implemented January 2021) lets minors change their legal gender with parental consent, adds an 'X' third-gender option, and bans medical interventions on intersex children against their will except for health-related reasons. The age of consent was set at 14 in 1992 and raised to 15 in 2007, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

ISL.blindLocalsOnly:
Since 2008 it has been illegal to discriminate against people on the basis of their sexual orientation in education. From 2016 one municipality has included information about same-sex relationships in its eighth-grade sex education lessons, covering ages 14 and 15, and a queer student group runs social activities and field trips for students at the national university.

Blood donation eligibility is a resident-facing health rule: the four-month deferral applied from September 2021 and the restriction was lifted entirely from September 2026.

An international LGBTI organisation records that LGBTI organisations can register in the country, and the national Equality Complaints Committee is the standing institutional route for equality complaints.
ISL.tangentialFactors:
Section 178 of the Penal Code criminalised same-sex relations between 1869 and 1940, and public antipathy towards LGBT people stayed high until the 1980s, when some of the first Icelanders to come out publicly, Hörður Torfason and Anna Kristjánsdottir, faced discrimination and ridicule. State policy has since reversed through the 1996 anti-discrimination amendments, the 2010 marriage vote and the 2023 conversion therapy ban.

Public expression of support is visible. Reykjavík Pride drew about 100,000 people in 2015, and in 2016 President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson became the first head of state to attend a gay pride parade. A gay scene of bars and cafés exists in Reykjavík, but the sparse population elsewhere means there is almost no scene outside the capital, and Akureyri has no gay bars.

A blood donation restriction on men who have sex with men was challenged by a lawsuit in 2014, relaxed to a four-month deferral in September 2021 and lifted entirely from September 2026.

The age of consent was set at 14 in 1992 and raised to 15 in 2007, applied regardless of gender or sexual orientation. A 2000 Gallup poll found 53 per cent of Icelanders supported lesbian and gay adoption rights against 35 per cent opposed.

ESP.name: Spain
ESP.summary:
Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023 and titled the organic law on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGTBI rights, governs legal gender recognition in Spain. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry. This administrative self-identification route replaced the previous requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is available from age 12 under conditions, and the statute regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

The same statute bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expands assisted-reproduction rules, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and adds anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Spain joined Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay among the states offering recognition by simple declaration.

Gender expression appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance of Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023, so a crime motivated by gender identity or expression is charged through general offences with the discrimination aggravation instead of a free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 separately reformed offences against sexual freedom in Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

That machinery is being applied in practice. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In January 2026 the Observatorio de delitos de odio reported a Valencia case in which a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them: the sole adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Protection is not uniform across Spain. In 2023 the newly elected regional government of Madrid repealed that region's non-discrimination law, repealed the local conversion therapy ban insofar as it applies to trans people, removed penalties for conversion therapy and repealed several trans legal recognitions.

Facility access rests on legal gender self-determination under the current framework, according to reporting of 9 July 2026, which contrasts Spain with the United Kingdom's move toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under the EHRC statutory code, where restrictions apply case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change requires no surgery or sterilisation. Official and industry framing is favourable: UK foreign travel advice describes Spain as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers with active communities and social venues, and a travel operator guide rates the country safe and welcoming, especially Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, while noting that attitudes outside the large cities can be more conservative.
ESP.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state whether Article 43 can be used by a person present in Spain on a short stay whose civil registry entry is held abroad, nor whether recognition obtained abroad is registered under the same route. This is unresolved here.

Processing times, fees and documentary requirements before the Civil Registry are not sourced in this inventory, and neither is whether an appointment or in-person appearance is required.

Whether facility access for trans people is settled by statute, by regional regulation or only by case-by-case administrative practice is not established by the single 2026 report cited; that report describes the general framework and a contrast with another country rather than Spanish case law.

The three violence data series in the inventory conflict and cover different territories and periods, so the current national direction of anti-trans violence is not resolvable from these sources. No post-2023 national incident dataset is present.

Only two enforcement outcomes are documented, both at instance level, one a misdemeanour fine and one a six-month custodial sentence against a juvenile gang's adult member; the inventory contains no appellate decisions and no data on how often the Article 22.4 aggravation is pleaded or upheld nationally.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Spain has a long history of state and political hostility toward LGBTQ people, alongside pockets of present-day backlash. Under Franco's dictatorship (1936-1975), thousands of gay men and women were jailed, held in camps or confined to mental institutions; some were sent to special prisons called galerías de invertidos, and vagrancy laws were applied arbitrarily to suspected dissidents on the basis of actual or perceived homosexuality. Trans people were prosecuted under public scandal offences and municipal legislation until the end of the 1980s. In 2023 a newly elected far-right government in the Madrid region repealed that region's non-discrimination law, repealed the local conversion therapy ban insofar as it applies to trans people, removed penalties for conversion therapy, and repealed several trans legal recognitions. In 2013 Interior Minister Jorge Fernández Díaz stated that same-sex marriage endangered the survival of the human species and opposed equal legal protection for such marriages. Public opinion is overwhelmingly accepting, with 88% acceptance recorded in a 2013 Pew poll, the highest of 39 countries. Violence statistics conflict: the Secretary of State for Security reported a 4% decrease in 2018, while the Observatorio Madrileño reported a 7% increase and Catalonia's Observatori contra l'Homofòbia a 30% increase in early 2019.

ESP.tangentialFactors:
Public attitudes predate the 2023 statute by a long margin. A 23-country survey of December 2016 ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the countries polled, the only one where a majority backed unrestricted legal gender designation change, with restroom support above 70 percent and 25 percent of respondents saying they knew a trans person. A 2013 Pew poll recorded 88 percent acceptance of homosexuality, the highest of the 39 countries surveyed.

The historical baseline runs the other way. Under the dictatorship of 1936 to 1975 thousands of gay men and women were jailed, held in camps or confined to mental institutions, with special prisons for those so classified and vagrancy laws applied arbitrarily on the basis of actual or perceived homosexuality. Trans people were prosecuted under public scandal offences and municipal legislation until the end of the 1980s. In 2013 an interior minister stated that same-sex marriage endangered the survival of the human species and opposed equal legal protection for such marriages.

Violence statistics do not agree with one another. The Secretary of State for Security reported a 4 percent decrease in reported incidents in 2018, while the Observatorio Madrileño recorded a 7 percent increase and the Observatori contra l'Homofòbia in Catalonia a 30 percent increase in early 2019. Discrepancies of this size make national trend claims unsafe to read from any single series.

Spain's tourism promotion names eight flagship LGBTQ+ destinations: Madrid (Chueca), Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cadiz, the Canary Islands (Maspalomas Pride), Sitges and Torremolinos (La Nogalera), supported by a Destinations for Diversity certification for open and discrimination-free spaces. Tourist hubs carry a visibly different social climate from smaller towns, and a visitor's exposure varies accordingly.

NLD.name: Netherlands
NLD.summary:
Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited. Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, following passage by the House of Representatives in 2018 (127 votes to 23) and the Senate on 12 March 2019 (64 to 11), after the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Since February 2023, sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution.

Since 1 July 2025, a discriminatory motive is codified in Dutch law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, operating alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. Dutch legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P), which is the framework behind published hate-crime statistics.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is rising. Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, with reports concerning transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399). The COC described the figures as extremely worrying and noted only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination in the same year. Official Dutch government figures state that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

During WorldPride Amsterdam 2026, more than 70 people reported discrimination through the RITA platform in the opening period, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants; RITA warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. Mayor Femke Halsema told the council that Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride, with police, enforcer and organiser agreements to act fast; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, and the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. Legal gender recognition has otherwise been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilisation imposed by the 1984-85 laws.

Transgender detainees occupy an unregulated space in Dutch law. No law, regulation or official policy governs their placement: the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the municipal records (BRP) together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, and physical or mental health. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection, Robine van der Meer and later Minister Weerwind, in a letter of 21 February 2024 that this absence of rules is worrying and undesirable, noting international research documenting human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence against transgender detainees, the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees, and the relevance of CPT standards. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing before transfer to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; and rulings by the Limburg court (17 October 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and The Hague appeals court (29 June 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asked the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity; the DIZ said it was drafting guidelines, unpublished at the time.

Access to care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrPreP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.

Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Equaldex records the Netherlands as recognising non-binary gender, protecting bathroom access, and prohibiting discrimination in employment and housing on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, while noting that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.
NLD.outOfScopeNotes:

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage of the Netherlands: gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, after the House passed the bill 127-23 in 2018 and the Senate 64-11 on 12 March 2019, following earlier cases in which the Dutch Institute for Human Rights treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender'. Since February 2023 sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution. Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Legal gender recognition has been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilization imposed by the 1984-85 laws. Care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrEP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices, projected to save €33 million in HIV treatment costs; assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple; the 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organizations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16; in July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate; conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was ultimately banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026. Youth and education: a 2018 Statistics Netherlands survey found 11.4% of LGBTQ youth faced online bullying and harassment, more than double the rate for heterosexual young people, and a 2020 Movisie estimate put homeless LGBTQ youth at 900-2,000, three times the rate for heterosexual youth, with rejection at home a stated cause. The government-financed religious-school 'single fact construction' loophole that let schools fire staff, as in a 2005 case of a teacher in a same-sex relationship, was closed by bills passed in 2014 (House 141-9) and 2015 (Senate 72-3), effective 1 July 2015, so LGBTQ students and teachers cannot be fired over sexual orientation. The age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1971, ending the 1911 Article 248bis rule that set 21 for same-sex activity. Acceptance among adolescents is falling: the Utrecht University/Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys dropped from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025.

Visa requirements for the country depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited. Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, following passage by the national legislature in 2018 (127 votes to 23) and the upper chamber on 12 March 2019 (64 to 11), after the national human rights institute had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Since February 2023, sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution.

Since 1 July 2025, a discriminatory motive is codified in law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, operating alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. Legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the national police Centre of Expertise Discrimination, which is the framework behind published hate-crime statistics.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is rising. Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, with reports concerning transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399). The national LGBT federation described the figures as extremely worrying and noted only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination in the same year. Official government figures state that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

During a major 2026 Pride event in the capital, more than 70 people reported discrimination through a national reporting platform in the opening period, mostly festival-goers leaving a music festival and Pride Walk participants; the platform operator warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. The capital broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during the Pride to cover a central church, a museum, the city archive, hotels and a central reporting location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. The mayor told the council that the city will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during the Pride, with police, enforcer and organiser agreements to act fast; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

Legal gender change still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, and the self-identification bill was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. Legal gender recognition has otherwise been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilisation imposed by the 1984-85 laws.

Transgender detainees occupy an unregulated space in law. No law, regulation or official policy governs their placement: the penitentiary framework only separates male and female detainees, and the national Prison Service confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in municipal records together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, and physical or mental health. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing before transfer to such a facility; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to a women's prison, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; and two court rulings treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple. The 2016 health ministry guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the national health board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.

Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Comparative data records the country as recognising non-binary gender, protecting bathroom access, and prohibiting discrimination in employment and housing on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, while noting that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. USA.name: United States
USA.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The order also mandated that federal agencies use "sex" rather than "gender," required removal of materials that promote what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces.

The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The X marker had been available since 2022. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992; the Human Rights Campaign records that the policy remains challenged in federal courts. The ACLU sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. On 5 February 2025 an executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. Separately, the Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Facilities rules vary sharply by state. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory, and some states make trans use of facilities a criminal offence in certain circumstances; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law; civil-rights attorneys described it as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents at state level are also being closed. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures, with further targeting bills pending. Equality-map research shows the conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state.

Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.

Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Care access is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation, and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and in October 2025 proposed health-department rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.
USA.outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of Executive Order 14168's facilities clause as applied to a foreign visitor in privately operated venues is not resolved in the sources; the order bars access to government-funded single-sex facilities, and the practical reach in hotels, restaurants and retail is not stated.

Whether a foreign visitor's own national passport carrying an X marker or a marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth will be accepted for entry, or will trigger secondary screening, is not directly addressed in the inventory. The sources document US-issued passport policy and foreign travel advisories, not port-of-entry treatment of third-country documents.

The "SWS25" visa marking and the fraud-based permanent ban are reported in connection with the sports-related State Department announcement of February 2025; whether the marking or the fraud finding extends to non-athlete visa categories is not stated in the sources.

The Queer Compass guide's advice to check recent violence reports before travel is a general instruction; the inventory contains no consolidated national figure for anti-trans hate crimes or their year-on-year direction, so the level of street violence risk is not sourced here.

Several federal measures are recorded as blocked or enjoined in court without a per-order status table; which specific orders remain in force as of the latest source date is not resolved in this inventory.

sources.title: Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration
sources.summary: Wikipedia survey: EO 14168 (sex-as-binary, documents, facilities clause, care-funding halt), EO 14183 (military ban), EO 14187 (care for minors), EO 14190 (schools), EO 14201 (sports), January 2025 federal funding freeze; several orders blocked or enjoined in court. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates: their hair would be cut short, they would be taken off hormone medication, and instead put into psychiatric therapy and given psychiatric drugs. Imprisoned transgender individuals reported being denied access to care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced labor programs, with guards justifying it with statements like "If you wanna be a man, I'll treat you like a man"; those who refused faced punishments including beatings and solitary confinement, and many also reported severe sexual abuse. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): In December 2025 Attorney General Pam Bondi instructed the FBI to begin offering cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called "radical gender ideology," describing such activists as "domestic terrorist groups." In May 2026 the White House's "United States Counterterrorism Strategy" stated that national counterterrorism activities would "prioritize the rapid identification and neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." The source text also reports beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse against transgender people in ICE custody, and notes that advocates have compared the administration's actions to the early stages of genocide. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): Executive Order 14168 (January 20, 2025) redefined sex for the federal government as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). On the same day Trump rescinded Executive Order 13988, which had sought to protect LGBTQ rights in federal prisons and prevent discrimination. Other measures include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers providing gender-affirming care to transgender youth; the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): The source text states that during the second Trump presidency the US government has taken actions to persecute transgender people, accompanied by anti-transgender rhetoric and misinformation often to dehumanize and scapegoat them. Anti-transgender campaigning was a large part of the 2024 Trump campaign, with spending on anti-transgender advertising exceeding spending on housing, immigration, or the economy; Trump repeatedly made false claims that schools were performing "gender-affirming surgeries on children without their parents' consent," claims conservative groups called "valid" while acknowledging they were untrue. Censorship measures include a January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT" in health agencies, removal of words from federal websites including the Stonewall National Monument site, and revocation of scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): Executive Order 14190 (January 29, 2025), "Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling," directs law enforcement to investigate schools for promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers who facilitate a transgender minor's social transition — including using preferred names or pronouns — potentially as sexual exploitation of a minor and/or practicing medicine without a license, with federal funding revoked for violating schools. Executive Order 14187 (January 28, 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the DOJ subpoenaed "over 20" hospitals for full records of patients under 19 including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialized LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; in August 2025 it threatened to pull federal funding from sex education programs mentioning transgender people (11 states and 2 territories complied by November 2025); and in October 2025 proposed HHS rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, with gender-affirming care for children already banned in 27 states. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): In January 2025 a list of "forbidden terms" was distributed within government health-related agencies instructing employees to avoid words including "gender," "transgender," or "LGBT," and such words were widely removed from federal agency websites including the National Park Service Stonewall National Monument site. Executive Order 14168 mandated federal agencies use "sex" instead of "gender," remove materials that "promote gender ideology," and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces. Executive Order 14190 additionally directs law enforcement to criminally prosecute educators who refer to a student using preferred name and pronouns or describe a student as "non-binary," and the counterterrorism strategy frames "radically pro-transgender" ideology as a security threat.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: United States: same-sex marriage is recognized nationwide under Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015), and the Respect for Marriage Act of December 2022 repealed DOMA and required all states to recognize existing same-sex marriages; DOMA had barred federal recognition of same-sex unions until it was ruled unconstitutional in 2013. Recognition still varies: same-sex marriages are not licensed or recognized in American Samoa, status differs across sovereign Native American tribal nations, and adoption remains state-dependent, with some states allowing same-sex couple adoption and others banning all unmarried couples. Berkeley, California became the first jurisdiction to recognize same-sex unions in 1984 through domestic partnership health benefits for city employees, California passed the first state domestic partnership law in 1999, and Vermont was the first state to legalize civil unions. Expression has been both suppressed and asserted: during the reservation era, Christian missionaries and federal agencies forced Native American LGBTQ people into prescribed dress and grooming, such as making males cut their hair and females wear dresses, while both Native and non-Native LGBTQ people lived in hiding because homosexuality was a criminal offense. William Dorsey Swann, born enslaved in Maryland, organized drag balls in Washington, D.C. in the 1880s and 1890s and was arrested repeatedly, including the first documented case of arrests for female impersonation on April 12, 1888. The military's Don't Ask, Don't Tell policy (1990s-2011) explicitly barred soldiers from coming out, and gender expression-related bullying contributed to a wave of teenage and young adult suicides in 2009-2010 that prompted the It Gets Better Project. Gallup found 7.6% of U.S. adults identified as LGBTQ or another non-heterosexual orientation in 2024, rising to 22.3% among Gen Z (born 1997-2012) and 9.8% among Millennials, versus 1.1% of the Silent Generation. Visibility grew through media: Ellen was cancelled in 1998 after its star came out, while Will & Grace premiered that same year and is credited with helping increase public acceptance, and Gay Straight Alliance clubs are linked to greater safety, inclusion, wellbeing and educational attainment for LGBTQ students. The FBI reports bias against sexual orientation has consistently accounted for between one-seventh and one-fifth of single-bias reported hate incidents this century, 37 states still lacked anti-bias statutes for gender-identity crimes as of 2019, and the Transgender Day of Remembrance is held annually for transgender murder victims.

USA.comparisons: Compared to the UK (0.66): the US shares bathroom-law enforcement and border hostility but adds foreign-government traveler warnings and documented foreign-visitor detention, which the UK lacks. Different risk profiles converging at the same score.
USA.blindSummary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the country. An executive order signed in January 2025 redefined sex for national purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the national justice department to "correct the misapplication" of a 2020 supreme-court employment ruling. The foreign ministry stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The supreme court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a foreign-ministry policy in place since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The national civil-liberties union has sued the foreign ministry on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and a legal-advocacy organisation maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with national records.

Screening at checkpoints carries an outing risk: transport-security screening procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Multiple foreign governments have responded. In April 2025 several countries were reported to have issued advisories about trans people travelling to the country over identity-document and data rules; in March 2025 at least eight countries in the region were reported to have adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of sub-national units. A policy-research tally counts sub-unit bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine sub-units and one state/province, with outright bans on facility use per gender identity in additional sub-units; 29 sub-units, four state/provinces and the national capital district have no such ban, and some sub-units make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at a sub-unit statehouse in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that sub-unit's bathroom-restriction law.

Sub-unit document rules are tightening. In February 2026 one sub-unit enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other sub-units, with further targeting bills pending in sub-unit legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged one sub-unit as the latest "Do Not Travel" state/province for trans people, bringing the total to four sub-units so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while national policies drove nationwide trends.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the foreign ministry announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

National custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the national prison service adopted policies from one sub-unit mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication, and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the prison service stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the national justice department instructed the national law-enforcement agency to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained for visitors needing it. An executive order of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the national justice department subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the national government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the crisis helpline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar public health insurance reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 sub-units. Several of these national measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

USA.tangentialFactors:
The federal posture differs from state practice in ways a visitor may notice at different points of a trip. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia impose no state-level ban on trans people using facilities consistent with their gender identity, while nine states and one territory restrict such use in schools and some government buildings; the practical environment therefore varies sharply by itinerary. Kansas's February 2026 law is described by rights groups as a template, and a July 2026 assessment flagged four states as "Do Not Travel" for trans people, suggesting the sub-national picture is moving in one direction rather than stabilising.

Foreign governments treat the United States as a changed destination. Advisories issued in early 2025 by multiple countries, and adjusted travel guidelines from at least eight European states, place the US in a category where allied governments formally warn their own trans citizens. That is unusual for a destination of comparable diplomatic standing and is a reasonable proxy for how seriously document and data rules are taken abroad.

Several federal measures remain contested in court. The passport sex-marker restrictions were allowed to proceed by the Supreme Court in November 2025, but the Wikipedia survey records that a number of the executive orders have been blocked or enjoined, and the ACLU suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs is pending. The legal position is therefore active rather than settled, and a visitor's experience may differ from a reading of any single order.

BRA.name: Brazil
BRA.summary:
Same-sex marriage has been legal throughout Brazil since 2013, the age of consent does not vary with sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework applies nationwide. The Supreme Federal Court ruled in 2018 that legal gender recognition does not require surgery. Following the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism.

Courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

Passports and identity cards carry an unspecified or X marker under ICAO standards; the marker has been mandatory on state-issued ID cards since 11 January 2024. A 2025 Superior Court of Justice decision permitting a neutral gender entry on the civil registry binds only the plaintiff but sets a precedent for others.

Entry and family formation are governed by nationwide equality: Brazil was the first country in Latin America to recognise same-sex unions for immigration benefits, beginning with a 25 November 2003 Curitiba judgment granting permanent residency to the British partner of gay activist Toni Reis and followed a week later by National Immigration Council Administrative Resolution No. 3, which granted temporary or permanent visas to partners without distinction of sex. Implementation was initially slow, with consulates not promptly instructed; a Florianópolis judge separately barred immigration authorities from deporting an Italian woman partnered with a Brazilian lesbian. Spousal-visa equality now forms part of the entry framework.

The public health system provides sex reassignment surgery free of charge as a constitutional right, per a 2007 ruling by the 4th Regional Federal Court, with roughly 250 such procedures performed between 2000 and 2007 at three university hospitals. Access is constrained in practice: the Health Ministry delegated qualification decisions to local officials, and long queues and poorly equipped public facilities push those who can afford it toward private care. Surgery within the public system requires patients to be at least 21, to carry no personality-disorder diagnosis, and to undergo at least two years of psychological evaluation. In July 2026 the 3rd Panel of the Superior Court of Justice ruled that private health plans must cover facial feminization surgery; in March 2024 the Supreme Court extended five-day paid paternity leave to the non-pregnant mothers of lesbian couples.

Gender-affirming care for minors has been prohibited by the Federal Council of Medicine since April 2025, alongside a reduction of the minimum age for gender-affirming surgery from 25 to 21. LGBTQ+ advocates filed a Direct Action of Unconstitutionality at the Supreme Court. The Federal Court of Acre blocked the resolution on 25 July 2025, restoring care for minors, but on 2 October 2025 a federal judge overturned that block and reinstated the ban, leaving continuity of medication for young people and travel between states for care as a live problem.

Conversion therapy has been forbidden by the Federal Psychology Council since 1999, although a Brasília federal judge approved it in September 2017 before reversing course that December; the Supreme Court ultimately banned the practice, and in 2019 Justice Cármen Lúcia issued an injunction overturning the judge's decisions. In May 2020 the Supreme Federal Court struck down as unconstitutional the 12-month abstinence requirement imposed on gay and bisexual men seeking to donate blood.

Violence persists alongside the statutory protections. Grupo Gay da Bahia reported 343 LGBTQ murders in 2016, 387 in 2017 and 420 in 2018; those figures are contested, with critics calling the methodology unscientific because it counts all media-reported murders of LGBTQ people irrespective of motive, and scholars noting that international comparisons are distorted by differences in documentation capacity. In January 2019 openly gay representative Jean Wyllys left Brazil after death threats and was replaced in February by David Miranda. In October 2024 nearly 1,000 transgender candidates ran in municipal elections across every state amid threats and intimidation, with the number of trans officeholders having tripled since the previous cycle. An investigation published in May 2024 documented drink-spiking robberies targeting LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo nightlife as the city prepared for a Pride event drawing large numbers of visitors.

Lower courts pushed the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, incorporating trans people into the violence-against-women protection framework. Education is also contested: in June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that public and private schools must combat discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, sexist bullying against cisgender and transgender girls, and homotransphobic bullying; since 2020 the Court has overturned state and municipal laws banning gender and sexuality courses in schools, and since 2023 it has overturned laws banning gender-neutral language in schools.

Custody and detention are governed by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; on arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, who must be told about available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and asked whether they prefer a female, male or specific unit and, within it, the general population or specific wings or cells. The declared preference is recorded, later changes of placement are possible with transfers prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat, LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Legislative and political hostility accompanies this machinery. Senator Marcelo Crivella attacked the pending federal anti-discrimination bill on the ground that homosexuals would receive a protection that should have gone to women, the elderly and children, while conservative senators framed the law as an aggression on religious freedom. The Catholic Church and radical evangelical groups have been identified as sources of rising intolerance.
BRA.outOfScopeNotes:
The current operative status of the April 2025 Federal Council of Medicine prohibition on gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in the sources: the July 2025 block by the Federal Court of Acre and the October 2025 reversal reinstating the ban are both dated, but no later ruling in the inventory settles the question, and the Direct Action of Unconstitutionality filed at the Supreme Court has no recorded outcome here.

Whether the 2025 Superior Court of Justice decision on a neutral civil-registry gender entry has been applied beyond the single plaintiff, and whether the X marker has in practice been issued by all state document-issuing bodies since 11 January 2024, are not sourced. The reach of the 2019 Supreme Court ruling into administrative and private-sector settings beyond the nightclub case cited here is also not documented in the inventory.

Government advisories covering Brazil contain no trans-specific finding, so the risk picture for a trans visitor rests on the criminal-law, care-access, documentation and violence material assembled here rather than on official travel guidance. The historical material on early twentieth-century Rio homosexual subculture is outside the visitor-relevant scope, as is the administrative delay in cable-ing instructions to consulates after Administrative Resolution No. 3 beyond its illustrative value for entry practice.

sources.summary:
Overview: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013; legal gender change without surgery has been allowed since 2018 under a Supreme Federal Court ruling; the age of consent is equal regardless of orientation; and a federal anti-discrimination framework applies.

Brazil was the first country in Latin America to recognize same-sex unions for immigration benefits. On 25 November 2003 Judge Ana Carolina Morozowski of the 5th Civil Court of Curitiba granted permanent residency to the British partner of gay activist Toni Reis, and a week later the National Immigration Council issued Administrative Resolution No. 3 granting temporary or permanent visas to partners without distinction of sex. The government was slow to cable consulates, leaving binational same-sex couples confused about how to apply; Immigration Equality and the Brazilian Rainbow Group met officials at the New York consulate in February 2004 to press for clarity. A Florianópolis judge also barred immigration authorities from deporting an Italian woman partnered with a Brazilian lesbian.

Identity documents reflect gender. Passports and ID cards allow an unspecified or X marker under ICAO standards, mandatory for state-issued ID cards since 11 January 2024, and a 2025 Superior Court of Justice decision permitting a neutral gender on the civil registry affects only the plaintiff but sets a precedent.

The public health system (SUS) provides sex reassignment surgery free of charge as a basic constitutional right, per a 2007 ruling by the 4th Regional Federal Court, and roughly 250 such surgeries were performed between 2000 and 2007 at three university hospitals. Access is constrained in practice: the Health Ministry left qualification decisions to local officials, and long lines and poorly equipped public facilities push those who can afford it toward private hospitals and clinics. Partners in registered stable unions are recognized as dependents on health plans and insurers. In July 2026 the 3rd Panel of the Superior Court of Justice ruled that health insurance plans must cover facial feminization surgeries, and in March 2024 the Supreme Court extended five-day paid paternity leave to the non-pregnant mothers of lesbian couples.

Gender-affirming care for minors was banned by the Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) in April 2025, alongside a reduction of the minimum age for gender-affirming surgery from 25 to 21; LGBTQ+ advocates filed a Direct Action of Unconstitutionality at the Supreme Court. The Federal Court of Acre blocked the resolution on 25 July 2025, restoring care for minors nationwide, but on 2 October 2025 Federal Judge Flávio Dino overturned that block and reinstated the ban, leaving youth medication continuity and cross-state travel a live issue. Adult access to surgery within the public system requires patients to be at least 21, diagnosed with no personality disorder, and to undergo at least two years of psychological evaluation.

Conversion therapy has been forbidden by the Federal Psychology Council since 1999, though a Brasília federal judge approved it in September 2017 before reversing course in December 2017; the Supreme Court ultimately banned it, and in 2019 Justice Cármen Lúcia issued an injunction overturning the judge's decisions. Blood donation restrictions on gay and bisexual men, requiring 12 months without same-sex activity, were struck down as unconstitutional by the Federal Supreme Court in May 2020.

Hostility is documented both in violence and in legislative opposition. Senator Marcelo Crivella attacked the pending federal anti-discrimination bill, arguing homosexuals would receive a protection that 'should have been given to women, the elderly and children,' while conservative senators framed the law as an aggression on religious freedom. In January 2019 openly gay representative Jean Wyllys left Brazil after death threats, replaced in February by David Miranda. Grupo Gay da Bahia reported 343 LGBTQ murders in 2016, 387 in 2017 and 420 in 2018, and the figures are disputed: Veja columnist Reinaldo de Azevedo called the GGB methodology 'unscientific' because it counts all media-reported murders of LGBTQ people regardless of motive, and scholars note that international comparisons are flawed because figures reflect documentation capacity rather than crime totals. The Catholic Church and radical evangelical groups have been identified as sources of rising intolerance, and a 2007 incident saw a judge brought before São Paulo's Justice Council for calling soccer a 'virile, masculine sport and not a homosexual one.'

Education is a direct battleground. In June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that public and private schools must fight discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, sexist bullying against cisgender and transgender girls, and homotransphobic bullying. Since 2020 the Court has been overturning state and municipal laws banning gender and sexuality courses in schools, and since 2023 it has been overturning laws banning gender-neutral language in schools. Youth-specific risks include the April 2025 CFM ban on gender-affirming care for minors and labour exploitation: in the central, north and northeastern regions, transgender people from extremely poor families sometimes begin sex work as early as age 12 after expulsion from home, and travestis commonly work the streets as young as 16 or 17 in southern and southeastern regions and major capitals. On the more favorable side, the 2004 government initiative Brasil Sem Homophobia was designed to protect LGBTQ students, and a 2010 Rio de Janeiro State University and University of Campinas survey found that 95% of homosexual youth had revealed their orientation by age 18, many by 16, compared with after 21 for the 1980s generation.

Expat legal guide (updated 5 Apr 2026): same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules apply nationwide, forming the entry and family framework for a trans visitor or partner.

sources.title: Resolução CNJ n. 348 de 13/10/2020 (alterada pela Resolução n. 366/2021) — diretrizes para o tratamento da população LGBTI custodiada ou privada de liberdade (Conselho Nacional de Justiça)
sources.summary: Brazil's National Council of Justice (CNJ) Resolution 348 of 13 Oct 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 Jan 2021, is the national framework for where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed: a person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing (Art. 4º); on arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person is consulted about their preference (Art. 7º), and the judge must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it general population or specific wings/cells (Art. 8º); the declared preference is recorded and a later change of placement is possible, with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat (Art. 9º). LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited (Art. 11, VI–VII). The resolution entered into force after publication (120 days, extended to 180 days by Res. 366/2021).
