RUS.name: Russia
RUS.summary:
Russia prohibits legal gender recognition outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria.

For many transgender Russians emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly. Reporting published in June 2024 profiles people caught in limbo between leaving and staying, and analysis from August 2024 describes the court-driven purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex". The provisions reach speech that justifies gender transition.

Enforcement has grown sharply. More than 180 cases were brought under the propaganda provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines. Cases under these statutes have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

The post-designation crackdown was immediate. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, and does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The state does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community.

Entry and onward-protection context carries an explicit warning for LGBT travellers. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

A 2024 law additionally bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule that bears on foreign visitors in the country.
RUS.outOfScopeNotes:
The 101 extremism-related convictions reported by Human Rights Watch in June 2025 cover participation in or display of symbols of the designated LGBT movement; the inventory does not separate how many of those charges concerned transgender people specifically, and no trans-specific conviction count is sourced.

Whether any administrative or clinical framework exists for trans people to obtain cross-sex hormone therapy without surgery, other than the documented coerced administration at a conversion centre near Novosibirsk, is not addressed by the inventory.

The enforcement figures for the propaganda statutes come from two sources using different windows (2023 alone, and the two years to mid-2025); the sources do not state whether the 2023 case total is counted under the pre-2022 or post-2022 version of the provisions.

The precise commencement date and implementing procedure of the 2024 ban on adoption by citizens or permanent residents of countries allowing gender transitions is unresolved in the inventory, as is whether the US Level 4 advisory's LGBT-specific wording has been revised since the advisory was last checked.

Conditions in the autonomous republic of Chechnya are referenced only through the UK Home Office asylum standard; no independent reporting on current enforcement there appears in the inventory.

Display of rainbow symbols has drawn extremism-related charges since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation, and the state does not record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, leaving victims without an official recognition of motive in sentencing.

Fines under the propaganda statutes fund the state: roughly 26 million rubles were imposed in 2023, and over 60 million rubles accrued to the budget across the two years to mid-2025.
RUS.blindSummary:
The country prohibits legal gender recognition outright. The law signed by the country's president in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria.

For many transgender residents of the country emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly. Reporting published in June 2024 profiles people caught in limbo between leaving and staying, and analysis from August 2024 describes the court-driven purge and mass emigration of LGBT citizens.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex". The provisions reach speech that justifies gender transition.

Enforcement has grown sharply. More than 180 cases were brought under the propaganda provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines. Cases under these statutes have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million in local currency (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the supreme court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. A global human-rights organisation recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them three of the country's largest, were outlawed as extremist.

The post-designation crackdown was immediate. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in the capital; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre in the country's interior and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.

The country provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, and does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The state does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community.

Entry and onward-protection context carries an explicit warning for LGBT travellers. A foreign government's travel advisory for the country is at its highest level, do not travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers. A second foreign government's asylum authority, in its country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025), affirms that LGBT+ people in the country, including an autonomous state/province within it, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for that country's asylum claims.

A 2024 law additionally bans adoption of the country's children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule that bears on foreign visitors.

RUS.tangentialFactors:
No recognition of same-sex relationships exists: neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions are permitted, and same-sex couples are ineligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. In July 2020 voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in Fedotova and Others v. Russia (2021) that Russia's refusal to offer any legal recognition to same-sex relationships violated human rights; Russia left that court in 2022. The same court fined Russia in 2010 for systematically refusing permits for pride parades, and Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally.

Public opinion provides the social backdrop to enforcement. A 2022 survey found 74% of Russians said homosexuality should not be accepted by society, up from 60% in 2002, and a September 2021 survey put support for equal rights for gays and lesbians at 33%.

Reporting on the scale of the fallout is consistent across outlets: an independent outlet described arrests, club raids and extremism charges as the defining features of LGBTQ life in 2025, and commentary from August 2024 characterised the court decision as driving the community into exile.

SAU.name: Saudi Arabia
SAU.summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous jurisdictions for a transgender person who is identified. The kingdom has no codified penal code. Judges apply an uncodified interpretation of sharia drawn from the Quran and the Sunnah, so penalties for same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity are unpredictable and range from fines and flogging through lengthy or indeterminate imprisonment to death in the most severe cases.

Deviation from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence, not merely incidental conduct attached to another charge. In October 2021, five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media, showing that cross-dressing enforcement is active and reaches online expression as well as conduct in public.

No legal gender recognition is available, same-sex relationships carry no legal status, and no discrimination protections exist. LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country, so there is no formal protection machinery a trans visitor could turn to.

Enforcement has proved lethal. Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman known as Meeno, died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others at Azizia prison in Riyadh. Activists from her home country reported that she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes, aggravating a chronic heart condition; Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack, and her family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account.

Prosecution reaches travellers for expression published before they enter the country. Amnesty International documented a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 August 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for social media posts written before his arrival.

Entry and exit visa paperwork does not ask about sexual orientation, but it does record nationality, sex, religion and marital status. Work-visa applicants must pass an HIV test on arrival and before permit renewal, and foreign applicants found to be infected are deported; deportation is also available as a penalty for homosexuality itself. Since tourist visas were introduced in 2019, a Public Decency Law has fined public displays of affection and immodest clothing, giving enforcement officers a further basis for action against gender-nonconforming visitors.

Official assurances of welcome carry no legal effect. A May 2023 update to the Saudi Tourism Authority's FAQ page stated that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, are welcome, and VisitSaudi states that privacy will be respected, while homosexuality remains illegal and enforcement continues. The UK government advises that legal action is uncommon but recommends that couples avoid public affection, and warns that trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care because trans status is not recognised.

Access to care is unreliable. The government has designated several hospitals to treat people with AIDS and HIV, but other hospitals often refuse care or treat patients without compassion, and condoms were until recently rarely available outside certain hospitals and medical supply stores.

A closed 2005 trial in Jeddah of dozens of Saudi men arrested at a party described as a gay wedding produced sentences totalling 14,200 lashes and up to two years in prison, handed down without defence lawyers. A Human Rights Watch researcher described prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct as flagrant human rights violations, and the case shows the severity Saudi courts have imposed.

Official hostility is expressed outside the courts as well. In June 2022, officials in Riyadh seized rainbow-coloured products in a crackdown framed as curbing the promotion of homosexuality. In September 2013, Gulf states discussed a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners, which officials later downplayed as a mere proposal.
SAU.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory establishes how Saudi authorities handle a change of sex marker on a passport or national identity document, or whether border officers screen travellers on gender presentation. This remains unresolved rather than absent.

The inventory documents individual enforcement cases and historical sentences but supplies no sentencing statistics for gender-nonconformity charges, so the frequency of prosecution relative to the severity of penalties cannot be stated.

Whether the May 2023 tourism-authority welcome statement has any operational effect on visa issuance or border decisions is not sourced, and the status of the 2013 proposal to test and ban gay foreigners remains, as officials described it, a proposal that was never confirmed as policy.

AFG.name: Afghanistan
AFG.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban presents the most extreme risk to a transgender visitor of any jurisdiction documented here. The EUAA COI Report of February 2026 finds no legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity either before or after the 2021 takeover, and records Amnesty International's position that same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Criminalisation runs in two layers. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, updated 19 January 2026, states that Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on sodomy and inciting sodomy carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the Code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity. The Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law of 31 July 2024 adds a preventive surveillance duty. Its Article 22 obliges regime overseers to intervene against listed evils including lesbianism and homosexuality "even if with one's own spouse", placing same-sex conduct under continuous moral supervision alongside adultery and gambling.

Enforcement is documented as systematic and violent. Human Rights Watch and OutRight, reporting 26 January 2022 on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans, found Taliban members and their supporters attacking, threatening and expelling LGBT people from their homes, with family, neighbour and partner abuse surging after the takeover. OutRight's own report of 14 February 2023, based on 22 interviews with LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country, found security officials pursuing gay men and trans women more systematically than in the early months of rule, using physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed such punishments on social media. CNN reported in November 2024 first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody as the crackdown intensified.

Public corporal punishment has expanded. UN human-rights experts condemned the Taliban's use of it in an OHCHR press release of March 2026, recording at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double the 2024 figure, and warning that women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for moral crimes including adultery, illicit relationships and sodomy.

Marriage and partnership recognition are absent in both eras. Under the Islamic Republic the 1971 Law of Marriages required a legal marriage between two Muslim adults of the opposite sex, with Article 41 directing that gaps be resolved through Islamic law principles, and the 1949 Law on Marriages, Weddings and Circumcision likewise framed marriage as between a Muslim man and a woman; no same-sex marriage, civil union or domestic partnership was recognised. Under Taliban rule since 2021, same-sex relationships and marriages are not recognised at all.

A JURIST feature of 8 November 2024, drawing on the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees, reports systematic persecution after August 2021, notes that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework, and identifies visibly transgender individuals as facing the gravest risks including exploitation and violence. DW's feature of 2 October 2021 profiles a trans man and a gay friend hiding in Kabul, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave, and documents street attacks on men coded as gay, who changed their clothing and confined themselves indoors.
AFG.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa screening are not addressed by the available sources. No source in this inventory describes passport checks, questioning at airports or land borders, or any screening that could disclose a visitor's gender identity or trans status on arrival, so entry-side exposure remains unresolved.

Rules on gender markers in identity documents, and whether a foreign passport bearing a marker inconsistent with the holder's presentation would attract attention at inspection, are likewise not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved.

The practical application of the death penalty for same-sex activity since 2021 is unresolved. The Human Dignity Trust profile establishes that the Sharia-reference clause permits it and Amnesty International is cited for the position that same-sex relations are punishable by death, but no source in this inventory records a completed execution for that offence under the current authorities; the OHCHR figures for 2025 record floggings rather than executions.

Enforcement data post-dating March 2026, and any reporting on how the morality-law surveillance duty in Article 22 is applied to foreign nationals or visitors as distinct from residents, is not covered by these sources.

Consular protection, the availability of emergency exit routes, and whether any government advises against travel on the basis of LGBTIQ status are outside the inventory and remain unverified.

Under the Islamic Republic, the 1971 Law of Marriages required a legal marriage to be between two Muslim adults of the opposite sex, with Article 41 directing that gaps in the law be resolved by Islamic law principles, so no same-sex marriage, civil union or domestic partnership was recognized; the 1949 Law on Marriages, Weddings and Circumcision likewise framed marriage as between a Muslim man and woman. Under Taliban rule post-2021, same-sex relationships and marriages are not recognized at all. Article 430 of the criminal code made it an 'Instigation of Delinquency' for an adult to promote or assist a minor in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution, a provision that can criminalize any adult including a caregiver or partner involved with a same-sex partner or family, and Article 427 increased punishment where the victim was under 18. Article 398 offered lesser punishment for vigilante honor killings that can target minors found engaging in homosexuality, and Article 373 imposes fines or murder-equivalent penalties for spreading a 'dangerous disease'. Persons convicted of homosexuality were generally sentenced to prison in the cities under the Islamic Republic.

No law addressed discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and political parties were prohibited from advocating anything opposing Islamic morality. The 2017 U.S. State Department report found that LGBTI community members 'did not have access to certain health services' and could be fired from jobs because of sexual orientation, and that organizations protecting LGBTI freedom 'remained underground because they could not legally register with the government', a status the 2020 report confirmed.

Care access is constrained by law, stigma and limited infrastructure. Before 2003 little or no HIV-AIDS education or treatment existed; the 2008 official count was 504 people living with HIV-AIDS, though the true figure was suspected to be in the thousands. The first HIV-AIDS treatment center opened in Kabul in 2009 with more clinics promised, access to anti-retroviral drugs is 'at best limited', and the 2020 report states that the government only permits condom distribution to married couples, excluding same-sex couples, while noting stigma against people living with HIV. Low literacy, weak infrastructure and social taboos impede comprehensive public health education.

Youth are a documented target. Bacha bazi involves teenage boys kidnapped, dressed in women's clothing, made to dance in competitions and forced into sexual acts; militia members without access to women kidnap boys to be humiliated and raped, other boys become prostitutes regardless of sexual orientation, and the practice was prevalent in big cities and reported in 2007 as still common in northern Afghanistan. US-backed Northern Alliance warlords kidnapped, trafficked and raped young boys after 2001, yet neither the U.S. Department of Defense nor the Afghan government acted despite awareness. President Hamid Karzai signed an agreement to ban the practice and a law prohibited Afghan soldiers from having their 'ashna' ('friend') live with them, but it was rarely enforced and police were reportedly complicit. When the Taliban came to power in 1996 they banned bacha bazi alongside homosexuality, both carrying the death penalty, and under the Islamic Republic young victims were often charged rather than the adult perpetrators. Article 430 can deter adults from seeking care for minors by treating any adult who promotes or assists minors in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution as committing 'Instigation of Delinquency'.

Education access is hampered by low literacy, weak infrastructure, taboos, abstinence-only sex education programs, censorship provisions including Article 32 of the 2002 Press Law prohibiting 'incitement to depravity' and Article 27(D) of the 1973 Postal Law barring material 'repugnant to public decency', and a 2009 memoir about growing up gay in Afghanistan, Hamid Zaher's It Is Your Enemy Who Is Dock-Tailed, which cannot be distributed within the country. A 2011 survey found young men displaying rainbow symbols unaware of their meaning and quickly removing them, and the 2017 and 2020 State Department reports noted that awareness of sexual orientation or gender identity remained limited and homosexuality was widely seen as taboo.

On 23 January 2025, ICC Prosecutor Karim Ahmad Khan requested arrest warrants against Taliban leaders Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani for persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ community, the first time the court has recognized crimes against the LGBTQ community.

A regional asylum body's COI Report of February 2026 finds no legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity either before or after the 2021 change of government, and records a human rights organisation's position that same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Criminalisation runs in two layers. A penal-law charity's country profile, updated 19 January 2026, states that the country criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on sodomy and inciting sodomy carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the Code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity. GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.summary:
The United Kingdom's post-April 2025 regime now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The code is the daily, nationwide consequence of the ruling: trans visitors use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The litigation had already aired the competing arguments: on 5 February 2026 the Court of Session was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard and For Women Scotland pressed its challenge to the policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

Searching and strip-searching policy has been rewritten on the same principle. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, adopting as an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth; the prior policy had permitted trans women staff to intimately search women holding a gender recognition certificate, and Sex Matters welcomed the change. On 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance under which searches in custody and stop-and-search involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, with efforts made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request where lived gender differs.

Gender recognition documents carry their own entry consequences. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. The Women and Equalities Minister, Kemi Badenoch, called the changes long overdue, while Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Within the UK, a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents; if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated, and transgender people seeking a certificate have historically been required to divorce or annul first.

Access to gender-affirming care is restricted for minors. NHS England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, a suspension renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and due to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead. The Cass Review of April 2024 also led NHS England to close the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. Bell v Tavistock (December 2020) had found that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers; that judgment was overturned on appeal in September 2021.

Restrictions reach schools and sport. The Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010.

On 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people. Northern Ireland, which sits on different equality legislation, is still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling.

Whether the For Women Scotland ruling of 19 June 2026 has been appealed, and what guidance replaced the struck-down Scottish Prison Service custody policy, are not sourced here. Northern Ireland's assessment of the Supreme Court ruling's impact was still described as ongoing in August 2026, with no outcome recorded.

On 17 April 2025 a national transport police force amended its strip-searching policy after the highest court's ruling, adopting as an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth; the prior policy had permitted trans women staff to intimately search women holding a gender recognition certificate, and a gender-critical campaign group welcomed the change. On 25 June 2025 the national police service published interim guidance under which searches in custody and stop-and-search involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, with efforts made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request where lived gender differs.

Gender recognition documents carry their own entry consequences. In December 2023 the national government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 foreign jurisdictions and sub-national authorities, including several countries in the region and one state/province in the region, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under national law to change their gender in the country. The equalities minister called the changes long overdue, while the shadow equalities minister warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded several allied countries. Within the country, a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents; if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated, and transgender people seeking a certificate have historically been required to divorce or annul first.

Access to gender-affirming care is restricted for minors. The national health service said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, a suspension renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and due to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the health service had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since a national clinical review, with some families turning to black-market or foreign hormones instead. That review also led to the closure of the national children's gender identity service in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. A 2020 appellate ruling had found that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers; it was overturned on appeal in September 2021.

Restrictions reach schools and sport. A private girls' school trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the national rugby governing bodies implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Transgender youth are otherwise covered by the national equality act of 2010.

On 18 August 2026 international human rights experts warned that revisions to the national equality act risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people. One of the country's provinces, which sits on different equality legislation, is still assessing the impact of the highest court's ruling.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.summary:
Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony (KFN) reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

How the exception is applied in practice is unsettled, and the outcome has gone both ways. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia, DW reported on 16 July 2026 that she had been transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, while critics characterised the gender change as an abuse of the self-determination law. In the earlier Penelope Frank case, covered by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Legal gender recognition itself is straightforward on paper. The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, took effect on 1 November 2024 and allows transgender, intersex and non-binary adults to change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice, replacing the Transsexuals Act of 1980, whose surgery and sterilisation requirements the Federal Constitutional Court struck down in January 2011. Since 1 January 2019 a 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status, and in April 2019 it was clarified as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024 in which, according to her account reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she provided the publication a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected spaces has been contested in the leisure sector since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a public debate about registered trans women's access, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women after the new law followed months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused. Trans people in custody in Berlin have an official information page from the Berlin prison service setting out rules and contacts across the city's facilities.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection. Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

A victim-support infrastructure exists. The German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

The Rhineland-Palatinate amendment drew no press coverage that could be located. The outcome of BASHKKA's complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment is not stated in the reporting.

Also unresolved: whether the bill to equalise birth-certificate recognition for non-biological mothers in married lesbian couples, pending in the Bundestag after the October 2018 ruling, was ever enacted. The concealment figure from the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2013 survey is now over a decade old and no comparable recent national measurement appears in the inventory. sources.summary:
Paragraph 175 of the German Empire's Penal Code recriminalized same-sex sexual activity between men in 1871. Nazi Germany extended these laws during World War II, resulting in convictions multiplying to about 8,000 per year and 5,000–15,000 suspected offenders interned in concentration camps. East Germany decriminalized in 1968 and West Germany in 1969. In 2002 the government overturned Nazi-era convictions, and in 2017 the Bundestag unanimously passed a bill to pardon around 50,000 men convicted after the war, with compensation of €3,000 per conviction plus €1,500 per year of jail time; a compensation scheme was implemented in September 2021.

Transgender people have been allowed to change their legal gender since 1980 under the Transsexuals Act, which originally required genital surgery and sterilization. In January 2011 the Federal Constitutional Court ruled those requirements unconstitutional. Effective 1 November 2024, the Self-Determination Act, passed April 2024 by 374–251, allows adults to change gender by self-determination with three months' notice and applies to transgender, intersex and nonbinary adults. Since 1 January 2019 an intersex 'divers' option has been available on birth certificates, passports and driver's licenses under the Third Gender Act, though a doctor's statement confirming intersex status is required, which LGBT groups criticized; in April 2019 the option was clarified as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is illegal in health services throughout Germany under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force 18 August 2006, and in education under the same act. Since May 2020 Germany has had a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors, making it the fifth country to do so, with penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to conversion therapy. Regarding blood donation, men who have sex with men were previously banned; a one-year deferral took effect in summer 2017, was reduced to four months in September 2021, and an individual risk-based assessment replaced the deferral from 1 April 2023. The German Medical Association is against explicit legalisation of assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and directs members not to perform such procedures, though this directive is not legally binding.

Same-sex couples have been legally recognized since 2001 through registered life partnerships, providing rights in inheritance, alimony, health insurance, immigration, hospital and jail visitations, and name change. Same-sex marriage became legal on 1 October 2017 after the Bundestag passed the bill on 30 June 2017 by 393–226, granting full marital and adoption rights. Same-sex stepchild adoption became legal in 2005 and expanded to 'successive adoption' in 2013. A Federal Court of Justice ruling in October 2018 held that the non-biological mother in a married lesbian couple is not automatically recognized on a child's birth certificate and must adopt, unlike heterosexual couples where the non-biological father is automatically recognized; a bill to rectify this inequality, initiated by the Greens in June 2018, was pending in the Bundestag.

In May 2019 the Federal Minister of Family Affairs recommended that teachers use gender-neutral forms, such as 'parent 1 and parent 2' instead of 'mother and father'. The age of consent was equalized at 14 years in East Germany in 1989 and in unified Germany in 1994. According to the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2013 survey, two-thirds of 20,000 German LGBT respondents concealed their sexual orientation at school and in public life.

JPN.name: Japan
JPN.summary:
Most travellers to Japan report little direct hostility or discrimination in ordinary contact, particularly in major tourist destinations, so the day-to-day risk posture for a transgender visitor is low. LGBTQ visibility remains limited, social attitudes are often reserved, and legal equality still lags behind that of other developed countries.

The statutory framework is the Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity, enacted by the National Diet in June 2023 after months of debate. The official translation defines gender identity, obliges the government to publish the annual implementation status of its understanding-promotion policies, and sets out the national basic plan. Parliament passed the text in watered-down form after a sustained political contest over transgender issues.

No national anti-discrimination statute stands alongside that Act, and no statutory guarantee against violence on grounds of gender identity exists. Full marriage equality is likewise absent. Judicial decisions, rather than legislation, have carried the substantive protections: in July 2023 the Supreme Court held that the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry violated public-service law by barring a transgender woman from the women's restroom at her workplace. She had challenged the restriction in 2015, and a Tokyo district court ruled for her in 2019 on the basis of her important legal interest in living by her self-identified gender, awarding damages. A separate court ruling found it unconstitutional to require surgery as a condition of changing the gender entry on legal documents, striking the sterilising-surgery requirement.

For a foreign visitor, document handling runs through the intersection of Japanese law and the law of their own nationality. A foreign national changes registered gender with the authorities of their country of nationality and then reports the change to the Immigration Services Agency for the residence card. Because recognition turns on the person's nationality, the process can break down at ward level; a 2018 case involving a United States national, Elin McCready, saw Tokyo ward offices refuse recognition of her gender change. Visitors carrying a passport that does not match their presentation should expect document checks to expose the discrepancy.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal. It was criminalised only briefly in the early Meiji period, from 1872 (a source elsewhere dates this to 1873), and repealed by the Penal Code of 1880, in force from 1882; another account dates the criminalised period to 1873-1881. Age of consent has been set at 16 years since June 2023 and applies equally to same-sex and opposite-sex relations. Same-sex marriages performed abroad are not legally recognised, and a bi-national same-sex couple cannot obtain a visa for the foreign partner on the basis of the relationship, although the Ministry of Justice applies a general rule of granting the discretionary designated-activities visa to same-sex married spouses. Since March 2009 Japanese nationals have been permitted to marry same-sex partners abroad, with the Justice Ministry instructing local authorities to issue the required single-status certificates.

Bathhouses are the main practical friction point. Onsen, sento and super-sento require undressing in gendered facilities, and the sector has no general policy for transgender bathers; guides for gender-diverse travellers describe the environment as daunting and instead point to LGBTQ-friendly venues, private-bath options and co-ed facilities, alongside etiquette rules. First-person accounts published in 2023 set out what a trans traveller can expect and where venue norms vary.
JPN.outOfScopeNotes:
Two points remain unresolved. The court that delivered the ruling striking the surgery requirement for legal gender-marker changes is identified in the available material only as a Japanese court, with no date, level or named party beyond the case reference, and no confirmation that the registry practice of the Legal Affairs Bureau has since been revised.

No source in the current inventory addresses hate-crime law, hate-speech prosecution as it applies to gender identity, access to gender-affirming healthcare for visitors, or rules on gendered security screening at airports. Whether any prefecture besides Gifu has issued a written policy on housing trans prisoners is not sourced. The 2009 CEDAW shadow report predates the promotion Act by fourteen years and should not be read as a current description of employment or health-care discrimination. Sources differ on the start of the brief criminalisation period, giving 1872 and 1873, and on its end, giving 1880 and 1881; the Penal Code of 1880, in force 1882, is the point at which repeal took effect. The outcome of the 2018 ward-office refusal to recognise a foreign national's gender change is not recorded.

sources.title: Prison warned over treatment of transgender inmate | The Asahi Shimbun
sources.summary: Asahi Shimbun (9 Sep 2023): Gifu's Kasamatsu Prison — a women's prison — holds an inmate who is listed as female on her family register but identifies as a man (diagnosed with gender identity disorder). The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded the prison allow him male clothes and a male hairstyle; after years with no policy change, the bar association issued a formal 'warning' to the prison in Sep 2023. The case shows Japan places convicted trans inmates in facilities matching their registered (family-register) sex rather than their gender identity, while treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level.

sources.title: Japan Should End Abusive Detention Conditions for Transgender People | Human Rights Watch
sources.summary: HRW (11 Jun 2025): Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention and charged with assault; he was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment (until a doctor recommended it), mocked for his transgender identity in interrogations, and only allowed to shower away from other detained men after requests. HRW frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face. For the prison-housing axis, it documents that a trans man's custodial placement followed his male legal sex, with accommodations (hormones, segregated showers) granted only grudgingly.

JPN.localsOnly:
Custodial placement follows the family register. A September 2023 report from the Asahi Shimbun documented an inmate at Kasamatsu Prison in Gifu Prefecture, a women's prison, who is listed as female on the family register but identifies as a man and has been diagnosed with gender identity disorder. The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association sought permission for male clothing and a male hairstyle; after years without a policy change, the association issued a formal warning to the prison. The case shows that convicted trans people are held in facilities matching registered sex rather than gender identity, and that treatment conditions inside are contested at prefecture level rather than settled by national rule.

Pre-trial detention has produced documented abuse. In June 2025 an international human-rights organisation reported on Tomoya Asanuma, a transgender activist arrested in March 2024 and held for more than 100 days before trial on an assault charge. He was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment until a doctor recommended it, mocked for his transgender identity during interrogations, and permitted to shower away from other detained men only after repeated requests. The organisation frames this within its broader criticism of Japan's pre-trial detention practices and the legal limbo trans people face, and records that his custodial accommodations were granted grudgingly.

For residents rather than visitors, protection depends heavily on employer policy and on court action brought individually. The government's obligation under the promotion Act is to publish annual implementation status and to operate the national basic plan, which creates reporting duties rather than enforceable individual rights. Changes to the gender entry on a Japanese national's documents proceed through the domestic legal process; the surgery requirement has been held unconstitutional by a court, but the statutory text and local-registration practice were not confirmed as amended in the sources available here.

JPN.tangentialFactors:
The 2023 statute was contested from the start. Kyodo News reported that the understanding-promotion law was enacted after months of debate but with its text weakened amid a culture-war argument focused on transgender issues, so the statute's framing of gender identity is politically fragile even where it is in force.

An international human-rights organisation assessed the July 2023 Supreme Court restroom decision as a victory for transgender employees, and a legal-practice guide characterises the period as one of significant progress, citing the promotion law, two pro-transgender Supreme Court decisions and one gay-friendly Supreme Court decision, while noting that marriage equality and violence-protection guarantees remain absent.

Older baseline material remains relevant to how institutions behave. A 2009 shadow report to the CEDAW committee described the situation of lesbian, bisexual and transgender people in Japan as one of invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation, with discrimination reported across education, employment, housing and health care and little governmental attention. It is a dated account, but it indicates how thin the institutional infrastructure of protection was when the current framework began to be built.

Comparatively, Japan sits well behind other developed countries on formal equality: consensual same-sex relations have long been lawful and public hostility to visitors is uncommon, yet the country has no anti-discrimination statute, no hate-crime provision on gender identity and no marriage recognition for couples married abroad.

THA.name: Thailand
THA.summary:
The Immigration Bureau runs 'Welcome Pride by Immigration', launched on 5 August 2024, which addresses the concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports do not match their current appearance or gender and eases immigration scrutiny on arrival. It is the one entry-side accommodation a trans visitor can rely on before landing.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 22 January 2025, after the bill passed its final Senate reading in June 2024, making Thailand the first country in Southeast Asia to do so; the statute uses gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms. Couples who married after that date gain access to property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims from which they were previously excluded.

Legal gender recognition remains absent. There is no mechanism to change the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID card or passport, and official title prefixes are fixed to the sex recorded at birth, so a trans woman's documents may still carry a male honorific. The Name Act 1962 offers only a partial workaround through first-name change, and even that leaves final discretion with officials. A 2021 Human Rights Watch report, 'People Can't Be Fit into Boxes', documented the absence of any route to documentation reflecting gender identity and found that anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced. Anti-discrimination law has existed since 2015. At a 2025 'Pride in Action' forum at Lido Connect, advocates urged the government to expedite a gender-recognition law after marriage equality, confirming that recognition legislation was still pending.

Thai law carries no hate-crime designation. In April 2025 a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya after she refused his request for sex; the perpetrator was named in domestic reporting as 42-year-old Fu Tongyung. The community described the killing as a hate crime, but bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties and no collection of bias-crime data, and LGBTQ+ groups subsequently called for new hate-crime protections. The gap is an accountability problem a trans visitor should weigh when assessing how a violent incident involving them would be classified.

Detention carries documented risk. The Department of Corrections states that LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police in 2017 and expecting to be held with men because her documents still carried the title 'Mr.', was instead placed in the separated wing. The pattern is uneven: trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request, where officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and where she was harassed at intake and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility; activists insisted placement should be an option rather than an obligation and warned that segregation could encourage exclusion. Reporting from 2016 also noted that transgender women outside such units usually face a choice between men's cells and solitary confinement.
THA.outOfScopeNotes:
The current legislative status of a gender-recognition law is unresolved. Sources through June 2026 confirm that no mechanism exists and that advocates were pressing for a bill in 2025, but the inventory does not establish whether a draft has been introduced, passed or stalled.

The fate of the Min Buri LGBT prison pilot is unresolved. The programme was announced in 2016 and discussed in 2017 reporting as a possible world-first facility; no source in the inventory states whether it remains operating, was expanded, or was discontinued.

No source establishes how the April 2025 Pattaya killing was ultimately charged or what sentence followed, so the practical consequences of the absence of a hate-crime designation in that case cannot be stated here.

The inventory contains no measurement of whether 'Welcome Pride by Immigration' has changed actual treatment of trans travellers at immigration checkpoints, beyond the programme's stated purpose. Airline and boarding-side documentation rules for trans passengers are not sourced either.

Enforcement data for the 2015 anti-discrimination law, including complaint volumes and outcomes, is not available in this inventory; the only finding on enforcement is Human Rights Watch's 2021 conclusion that protections are not fully enforced.

Bangkok Post 'Pride in Action' forum (Lido Connect, 2025): advocates urge the government to expedite a gender-recognition law following marriage-equality, with public education framed as part of expanding rights protection — legal gender recognition is still pending post-SSM.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Nov 2025): when a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya in April, the community called it a hate crime but Thai law has no hate-crime designation — bias-motivated violence is handled as ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties or data collection; documents the accountability gap.

LegalClarity (June 2026): marriage equality since January 2025 and anti-discrimination law since 2015, yet no mechanism to change the sex marker on birth certificate, national ID or passport (title prefixes locked to sex at birth; Name Act 1962 partial workaround) — precise current documentation-status read.

G.A.M. Legal Alliance (Thai firm) analysis of the post-same-sex-marriage landscape: marriage equality closes practical gaps for couples — exclusion from property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims — the concrete before/after of the January 2025 change.

GlobalGayz archive (2007-10): index of Thai LGBT news of the era — the National Human Rights Commission's role, constitutional-charter gay-rights campaigns, Phuket acceptance/rejection accounts, and the 'Please call me Miss' debate on trans legal title — historical baseline showing how long recognition questions have been live.

sources.title: Thailand Separates LGBTQ Inmates, Considers Segregated Prison (NBC News/AP)
sources.summary: NBC News/AP (29 Jan 2017): the Thai Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993; at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police and expecting to be 'thrown in prison with all the men because I still have the title of Mr.,' was instead held in the separated wing. The government was also discussing what could be the world's first exclusively-LGBTQ prison facility (the Min Buri pilot), while accepting that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary. Of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities.

sources.title: Exclusion or protection? Activists skeptical about LGBT prison (Coconuts Bangkok)
sources.summary: Coconuts Bangkok (30 Aug 2016): trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; prison officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility to prevent abuse of trans inmates, after Pattaya men's prison had already begun separating trans prisoners from cis men following reports of abuse. DOC figures: ~4,448 of ~300,000 prisoners identified as LGBT, 34 of them transgender. Activists welcomed the pilot but feared it 'could encourage exclusion' and insisted placement 'should be an option, not an obligation.'

THA.tangentialFactors:
The government has pursued positioning Thailand as an LGBTQ+ tourism hub, an effort analysed by Fulcrum/ISEAS in June 2025 against the backdrop of Bangkok Pride on 4 June 2025 and marriage equality. The stated motives range from genuine commitment to economic opportunism, and the strategy shapes how welcoming institutions are pitched to visitors without changing the underlying legal position.

Social climate runs ahead of the legal framework. Reporting from NZZ in May 2025 found that the conservative government introduced progressive measures including free hormone treatments with little public opposition, and that trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than is typical in the West. Visitors should not read that social tolerance as legal protection, since documentation rules and the absence of hate-crime penalties are unchanged.

Recognition questions have been contested in Thailand for decades. A GlobalGayz archive from October 2007 indexes campaigns around the National Human Rights Commission, constitutional-charter gay-rights petitions, accounts of acceptance and rejection in Phuket, and the 'Please call me Miss' debate over trans legal titles, showing that the title-prefix issue now blocking marker changes has been live since at least the mid-2000s.

Anti-discrimination law dates from 2015 but is not fully enforced, and no hate-crime statute exists to enhance penalties for bias-motivated assaults or to generate bias-crime statistics. Advocacy for a gender-recognition law intensified after marriage equality took effect, most visibly at the 2025 'Pride in Action' forum.

The gap is an accountability problem a trans visitor should weigh when assessing how a violent incident involving them would be classified.

Detention carries documented risk. The national corrections department states that LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and at a remand prison in that seaside city transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; of roughly 300,000 prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities. A trans woman stopped by police in 2017 and expecting to be held with men because her documents still carried a male title was instead placed in the separated wing. The pattern is uneven: a trans activist arrested in June 2015 while protesting the military government was sent to a men's prison against her request, where officials told her that under the country's law 'she remains a man' and no document can identify a trans woman as female, and where she was harassed at intake and ordered to expose her body. The corrections department then announced a pilot using a prison in a major city as an LGBT facility; activists insisted placement should be an option rather than an obligation and warned that segregation could encourage exclusion. Reporting from 2016 also noted that transgender women outside such units usually face a choice between men's cells and solitary confinement.
THA.blindOutOfScope:
The current legislative status of a gender-recognition law is unresolved. Sources through June 2026 confirm that no mechanism exists and that advocates were pressing for a bill in 2025, but the inventory does not establish whether a draft has been introduced, passed or stalled.

The fate of the major-city LGBT prison pilot is unresolved. The programme was announced in 2016 and discussed in 2017 reporting as a possible world-first facility; no source in the inventory states whether it remains operating, was expanded, or was discontinued.

No source establishes how the April 2025 seaside-city killing was ultimately charged or what sentence followed, so the practical consequences of the absence of a hate-crime designation in that case cannot be stated here.

The inventory contains no measurement of whether the immigration welcome programme has changed actual treatment of trans travellers at immigration checkpoints, beyond the programme's stated purpose. Airline and boarding-side documentation rules for trans passengers are not sourced either.

Enforcement data for the 2015 anti-discrimination law, including complaint volumes and outcomes, is not available in this inventory; the only finding on enforcement is a 2021 human-rights organisation's conclusion that protections are not fully enforced.
blindSourceSummaries: The nation has no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, and no document of the nation can identify a trans woman as female; the 2015 gender-equality act is weakly enforced and there is no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime — the 2025 murder of a trans woman in a resort city highlighted the gap.

Same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025; the border authority runs a dedicated initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender; gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The prison authority told press (2017) that LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993 and that at one remand prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; a trans activist detained in June 2015 while protesting the junta was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility, told that under the nation's law 'she remains a man'.

The prison authority announced a pilot using a prison in the capital as an LGBT facility, reported in 2016-17 as a possible world-first exclusively-LGBTQ prison; authority counts at the time recorded roughly 4,448 LGBT-identified prisoners among about 300,000 (34 transgender), with a 2017 figure of more than 6,000 registered as sexual minorities.

No current official placement rule or national special-unit or solitary-practice rule for trans prisoners is documented; whether a detained foreign visitor would be routed like the documented resident cases is not established.
THA.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents cannot obtain a legal gender change: no route exists to amend the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID or passport, and title prefixes remain tied to the sex recorded at birth. A 1962 name statute permits name changes but leaves officials with discretionary power, and a 2021 human-rights report found that even affirmative measures do not guarantee recognition of gender identity.

Anti-discrimination law dates from 2015 but is not fully enforced, and no hate-crime statute exists to enhance penalties for bias-motivated assaults or to generate bias-crime statistics. Advocacy for a gender-recognition law intensified after marriage equality took effect, most visibly at a 2025 Pride forum.

For residents in custody, placement follows the documentation problem directly: officials have told detained trans women that no document can identify them as female, and a 2016 account records a trans protester being held in a men's prison and harassed during intake. The national corrections department has reported separating LGBT prisoners nationwide since 1993, ran a pilot at a major-city prison announced after abuse reports at a seaside facility, and registered more than 6,000 sexual-minority prisoners out of roughly 300,000 in 2017 reporting; activists welcomed the pilot while demanding that placement remain voluntary.

The government funds free hormone treatment, introduced under the conservative administration with little public opposition, and domestic reporting describes trans people reaching senior corporate positions at rates unusual compared with other countries.
THA.blindTangential:
The government has pursued positioning the country as an LGBTQ+ tourism hub, an effort analysed by a regional think tank in June 2025 against the backdrop of a major Pride event on 4 June 2025 and marriage equality. The stated motives range from genuine commitment to economic opportunism, and the strategy shapes how welcoming institutions are pitched to visitors without changing the underlying legal position.

Social climate runs ahead of the legal framework. Reporting from a newspaper in the region in May 2025 found that the conservative government introduced progressive measures including free hormone treatments with little public opposition, and that trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than is typical elsewhere in the region. Visitors should not read that social tolerance as legal protection, since documentation rules and the absence of hate-crime penalties are unchanged.

Recognition questions have been contested for decades. An archive from October 2007 indexes campaigns around the national human-rights body, constitutional charter gay-rights petitions, accounts of acceptance and rejection in a southern resort province, and a debate over trans legal titles, showing that the title-prefix issue now blocking marker changes has been live since at least the mid-2000s.

MEX.name: Mexico
MEX.summary:
Legal gender recognition remains unfinished and uneven across Mexico. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, and called on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them. The same dispatch warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

The barriers are documented concretely. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. That report set these findings against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Formal rights and their enforcement diverge. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Killings of trans people continue and have drawn public protest. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide. The law is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital.

Regional oversight bodies have pressed the authorities. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.
MEX.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no source on how trans prisoners are housed in Mexico, whether placement follows birth sex or lived identity, and whether special units or segregation are used; this remains unresolved here rather than answered.

The extent of variation between states in legal gender recognition procedures is asserted by Human Rights Watch but not quantified in the sources, and the inventory does not identify which specific states lack a procedure. Whether the Paola Buenrostro law has been applied or has produced prosecutions since its approval in July 2024 is likewise not sourced.

No statute criminalising trans expression, cross-dressing or gender-nonconforming presentation appears anywhere in the inventory; the absence of such a source is recorded as unresolved rather than as a finding that no such provision exists. The sources also do not address entry or visa screening, marker requirements on passports, or whether documents are inspected at ports of entry.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ people in prison' article, Mexico section, records one Mexico-specific policy: in July 2007, through the efforts of the National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the Mexico City prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate, applying to all Mexico City prisons. sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Mexico's Wikipedia coverage describes no current statutory criminalisation of homosexuality, citing only historical executions in 1658 and the 1901 Dance of the Forty-One; street prostitution is recorded as illegal in jurisdictions including Mexico City. Same-sex marriage took effect in Mexico City on 4 March 2010, and Coahuila approved civil unions in January 2007. Pride parades have run annually in Mexico City since 1979 (over 1,000 people in 1979, 350,000 at the XXXI edition) and in Guadalajara since 1996, alongside events in over a dozen other cities. The coverage describes a norm of "sexual silence" in which gay men and lesbians conceal their orientation and lead double lives. Police are recorded as corrupt and prone to extortion, and transvestites as subject to police abuse. Government operatives have targeted Zona Rosa nightclubs since 2007 on drug, prostitution and safety grounds, which LGBT groups denounced as homophobic, and some Zona Rosa sites of cohabitation lack safety measures such as emergency exits. Mexican youth are reported committed to psychiatric clinics after coming out to their families, with some 16% rejected by family and a greater percentage physically attacked by relatives. A UAM study found 27% of LGBTQ respondents suffering mental disorders and risk of alcoholism, some 40% with thoughts of suicide and 25% having attempted it. The National Center for the Prevention and Control of HIV/AIDS is listed as an official resource, and Pride events include consciousness-raising about AIDS and HIV, highlighting youth-specific vulnerability in accessing safe care.

Same-sex marriage took effect in Mexico City on 4 March 2010 after the capital pioneered the reform in 2009; Coahuila approved civil unions in January 2007 on a 20-13 vote, becoming the third jurisdiction in Latin America to do so after Mexico City and Buenos Aires, while barring adoption and custody for those couples.

Pride parades have run annually in Mexico City since 1979 and in Guadalajara since 1996, alongside events in more than a dozen other cities, and the capital's Zona Rosa district functions as a gay hub with Pride events and hotels, bars and tours marketed as LGBT-friendly. Travel guidance aimed at LGBTQIA+ visitors advises caution outside such tourist hubs, and Oaxaca is noted for the indigenous muxé third-gender tradition.

Violence risk sits alongside the general security picture: high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping are the stated basis for a high-degree-of-caution advisory covering Mexico, which the sources do not tie specifically to gender identity.
