BRN.name: Brunei
BRN.summary:
Section 198 of Brunei's Syariah Penal Code creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa", qualified in the statute by acting "without reasonable excuse" or "for immoral purposes". Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons in the country including tourists, and travel agents are briefed to that effect.

Human Rights Watch's #OUTLAWED survey places Brunei among at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex; Malaysia has a state-sharia analogue.

Brunei does not permit a person to change their name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. A trans visitor should therefore expect to cross the border on a passport whose sex marker and name cannot be aligned with presentation, under a statute that criminalises mismatched presentation.

Enforcement of the cross-dressing provision is documented but thin. The US State Department's 2017 report on human rights practices records no known convictions under the provision that year, while noting that morality provisions including cross-dressing were among those actually enforced under the code and that the sharia implementing regulations had not yet been issued. On 11 March 2015 a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing.

Official conduct toward LGBT people is adverse in ways a visitor may encounter directly. LGBTI individuals reported intimidation by police, including threats to disclose their sexuality, interference with access to government employment, and barriers to graduation from government academic institutions. Members of the community also reported that the government monitored their activities and communications.

Events on LGBT topics were subject to restrictions on assembly and expression, with the government reportedly refusing to issue permits for them. LGBTI respondents separately reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and access to services.

The statutory severity is high. If evidentiary standards under the Syariah Penal Code Order are not met, the maximum penalty for sex between men is seven years' imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping; for unmarried men, one year in prison or 100 lashes; and sex between women is punishable by any two of forty lashes of caning, up to ten years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000. Anyone convicted of "tarnishing the image of Islam" may also be heavily punished.
BRN.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory could not be retrieved at research time: the hosted text of Brunei's Penal Code, including the Syariah Penal Code provisions, returned HTTP 403, as did an SSRN paper on the sharia penal code. The precise current wording of Section 198 is therefore taken from secondary description rather than the statute itself, and the qualified phrases "without reasonable excuse" and "for immoral purposes" are not independently verified against the primary text.

Whether the sharia implementing regulations referenced as unissued in the 2017 US State Department report have since been promulgated is unresolved in the available sources; the same report's cross-dressing enforcement picture predates the 2019 stage-3 commencement by two years.

Unresolved: whether Section 198 has been charged against foreign nationals since 2015, and whether Brunei's immigration authorities screen or annotate passports on gender grounds. Neither point is sourced in the inventory. The claim that official guidance binds tourists rests on guidance material cited in the record, not on a published enforcement case.

Whether the execution moratorium would hold if a stoning sentence were pronounced against a non-Muslim is not addressed by the sources; they state only that the moratorium covers the new code and that no execution has been carried out since 1957.

Freshness check 2026-09-27: still in force, 2019 moratorium on executions intact.

The France24 piece (April 2019) covers the fear gripping Brunei's gay community after the Sharia penal code came into force.

HRW called it 'barbaric'; the UN High Commissioner urged Brunei to halt it.
The SSRN paper relates to Brunei's Sharia penal code; it could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403).

HRW '#OUTLAWED' global map: at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise gender expression; Brunei is one of at least two, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise 'posing as' or 'imitating' a person of a different sex, the trans-specific offence for this jurisdiction, with a state-sharia analogue in Malaysia.

US State Dept 2017 report: the Syariah Penal Code bans men dressing as women or women dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse', with no known convictions in 2017; 'liwat' between men carries death by stoning if implemented, and the report records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services. sources.summary: Brunei does not allow a person to change their name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. On 11 March 2015, a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing. The SPC also prohibits men from dressing as women or women from dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse' or 'for immoral purposes', with no known convictions reported in 2017. LGBTI individuals reported intimidation by police, including threats to make their sexuality public, to hamper their ability to obtain a government job, or to bar graduation from government academic institutions. State-imposed corporal punishment is prescribed: under the SPCO, if evidentiary standards are not met, the maximum penalty for sex between men is seven years imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping; for unmarried men, one year in prison or 100 lashes; and sex between women is punishable by any two of forty lashes of caning, up to 10 years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000. Bruneian society tends to associate homosexuality with 'effeminate men'. Members of the LGBTI community reported that the government monitored their activities and communications, and events on LGBTI topics were subject to restrictions on assembly and expression, with the government reportedly refusing to issue permits for such events. Media outlets described the Sharia provisions as 'medieval' and 'uncivilized', and the UN urged Brunei to review its laws when the move to Sharia law was announced. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as 'the country that has the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in Southeast Asia', and anyone convicted of 'tarnishing the image of Islam' may be heavily punished.

BRN.tangentialFactors:
Stage 3 of the Syariah Penal Code took effect on 3 April 2019, introducing death by stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, and 40 strokes of the cane for lesbian sex. The stoning penalties extend to anal sex and adultery and, by the account of the UK House of Commons Library, to abortion; homosexuality was already an offence carrying up to ten years under the prior law.

The code applies in the main to Muslims, who make up roughly two-thirds of a population reported at between 420,000 and 450,000. The head of state stated that the capital-punishment moratorium covers the new sharia penal code, and the moratorium on executions has held; Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957. Freshness checks in September 2026 indicate the 2019 moratorium remains intact.

The code drew condemnation from the UN High Commissioner, who urged Brunei to halt it, from Human Rights Watch, which called it barbaric, and from international media, which described the sharia provisions as medieval and uncivilized. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as the country with the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in its region.

Bruneian society tends to associate homosexuality with effeminate men, a cultural association that raises the profile of gender-nonconforming presentation independently of the statute. BRN.blindSummary:
Section 198 of the country's Syariah Penal Code creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa", qualified in the statute by acting "without reasonable excuse" or "for immoral purposes". Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons in the country including tourists, and travel agents are briefed to that effect.

An international human rights organisation's global survey places the country among at least two, with a neighbouring jurisdiction, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex; a nearby jurisdiction has a national-sharia analogue.

The country does not permit a person to change their name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. A trans visitor should therefore expect to cross the border on a passport whose sex marker and name cannot be aligned with presentation, under a statute that criminalises mismatched presentation.

Enforcement of the cross-dressing provision is documented but thin. A foreign government's 2017 human rights report records no known convictions under the provision that year, while noting that morality provisions including cross-dressing were among those actually enforced under the code and that the sharia implementing regulations had not yet been issued. On 11 March 2015 a civil servant was fined 1,000 in local currency under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing.

Official conduct toward LGBT people is adverse in ways a visitor may encounter directly. LGBTI individuals reported intimidation by police, including threats to disclose their sexuality, interference with access to government employment, and barriers to graduation from government academic institutions. Members of the community also reported that the government monitored their activities and communications.

Events on LGBT topics were subject to restrictions on assembly and expression, with the government reportedly refusing to issue permits for them. LGBTI respondents separately reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and access to services.

The statutory severity is high. If evidentiary standards under the Syariah Penal Code Order are not met, the maximum penalty for sex between men is seven years' imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping; for unmarried men, one year in prison or 100 lashes; and sex between women is punishable by any two of forty lashes of caning, up to ten years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to 40,000 in local currency. Anyone convicted of "tarnishing the image of Islam" may also be heavily punished.

PRT.name: Portugal
PRT.summary:
Portugal remains among the safer European destinations for transgender visitors, standing under the national framework of the Portuguese Republic. Homosexuality is legal, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, gender-affirming care is lawful, and legal gender and name change currently runs under the 2018 self-determination law, which allows self-declaration from age 16 without a medical requirement. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, conversion therapy has been banned since 2024, surgical intervention on intersex infants is prohibited, and access to facilities matching a person's gender is protected.

The Penal Code treats sexual orientation and gender identity as explicit grounds for aggravated offending. Under Articles 132, 144 and 145, an offence determined by hatred on those grounds is aggravated, with aggravated assault punishable by up to four years, and organising discrimination on those grounds carrying one to eight years' imprisonment.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map 2026 places Portugal 12th at 67%, down one place, with no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban. A new draft bill threatens legal gender recognition based on self-determination and the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children.

On 20 March 2026 the Portuguese Parliament approved bills from PSD, Chega and CDS-PP that reverse the gender-identity law, the first legislative vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition. The proposals passed 124 to 79 and were referred to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees, directly targeting the 2018 self-identification law. At first reading Parliament backed reintroducing a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the 2018 reform.

IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal issued a joint statement warning that the three bills debated on 19 March and voted on 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans and intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition, and that if adopted Portugal would lose at least four Rainbow Map places, dropping below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France. The psychologists' order and trans groups called the rollback a 'retrocesso'; socialists invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta, a trans woman killed by youths in Porto, against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Hundreds protested outside the Assembly against the bills.

A separate set of three draft bills given preliminary approval on 20 March 2026 by a 151-79 vote would ban the inclusion of 'gender ideology' in school curricula. Committee-stage analysis by the Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality warns the bills worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties.

Justice Ministry data show legal sex and name changes climbing back toward the two-years-prior high-water mark, most in Lisbon, even as Parliament advances bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 law scrapped. European Parliament written question E-001183/2026 questions the Commission on the repeal process for the 2018 gender self-determination law and its health-and-safety impact on trans people.

The Provedoria da Justica, Portugal's Ombudsman, has requested constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C, which establishes the crime of acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression, questioning the hate-speech provision itself. Portugal's Parliament formally adopted 17 May as the National Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia in 2015.
PRT.outOfScopeNotes:
The three roll-back bills had completed first reading and committee referral as of the latest sourced reporting (March to August 2026); whether they have been enacted into law, and in what final form, is unresolved in the available sources.

The precise scope of the proposed mandatory medical opinion, including which practitioners could certify and whether a waiting period or sterilisation-type condition attaches, is not specified in the inventory and remains unresolved.

ILGA-Europe's projected loss of at least four Rainbow Map places assumes full adoption of the bills; the actual 2027 Rainbow Map score under any enacted or amended version is not sourced.

The outcome of the Provedoria da Justica's request for constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Enforcement practice for the Penal Code's aggravated-offence provisions and Article 176-C in reported cases against trans victims is not documented in the inventory.

IRL.name: Ireland
IRL.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Ireland rests on the Gender Recognition Act 2015 (No. 25 of 2015), commenced on 4 September 2015 by S.I. 369/2015 and amended by statutory instrument through 2026. Adults change their legal gender by self-declaration, with no psychological evaluation and no medical requirement, and Equaldex records gender change as legal with no restrictions. Nonbinary identities are not recognised in Irish law, so a visitor whose documents carry an X marker will not be able to obtain an equivalent domestic marker.

Since 31 December 2024 the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 has been in force, expressly covering sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; it was preceded by the Cabinet's October 2022 decision to add gender identity to the protected grounds of the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989, where a first offence carries up to a €1,000 fine or six months' imprisonment and an indictable conviction up to €10,000 or two years. Garda reports of hate crimes rose 15% in 2025, with racism and xenophobia the most common recorded motives.

Protective legislation sits alongside documented hostility. A University College Dublin study published on 3 July 2025 found that discrimination against sexual and gender minorities in Ireland has increased, despite the statutory framework. Belong To LGBTQ+ Youth Ireland maintains an anonymous online hate-crime reporting form alongside rights information and links to Equal Status Acts protections, which is the route most often recommended to young people reporting an incident.

Healthcare is the sharpest practical obstacle for a trans visitor planning a stay. A November 2022 Transgender Europe study put the wait for a first gender-affirming healthcare appointment in Ireland at 2.5 to 10 years, with a single public provider that was severely understaffed; patients were reportedly refused care for reasons including receiving social welfare, holding an ADHD diagnosis, or answering intimate screening questions in the wrong manner. Reporting by The Journal in April 2025 records years-long waiting lists for multidisciplinary gender-care assessment pushing some trans people towards underground or unsupervised options, while the HSE defends its multidisciplinary model of care. Gender-affirming care is legal but restricted for minors, and visitors should assume that continuity of an existing hormone prescription must be arranged privately in advance.

Public expression is open. Dublin Pride drew an estimated 60,000 people in 2018, and visible scenes operate in Dublin, Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford alongside the Outhouse LGBTQ+ Centre and the city's gay and gay-friendly venues. Local authority tolerance is not uniform: in April 2019 Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Council cancelled a drag storytime event, first calling it not age-appropriate and then citing the volume of homophobic abuse received on social media.

Three protection gaps remain. Employment and housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only, without gender identity. Conversion therapy is not banned, and neither is intersex infant surgery. A proposed amendment to the Gender Recognition Act 2015 that would limit the effect of a Gender Recognition Certificate for the purposes of imprisonment had passed its first legislative stage as of late 2025, which bears directly on any trans person entering the prison system.

Ireland is one of only 11 European countries permitting gender recognition through self-determination without a psychological evaluation requirement, a point activists have marked while pressing the outstanding gaps in trans rights and healthcare. GCN's anniversary coverage and a Guardian retrospective of 23 December 2025, marking a decade since the Act, both carry first-person accounts of self-declaration and updated documents and treat the statute as a break with Ireland's Catholic past. Entry and visa rules, including any document presentation at the border, are not covered by the sources reviewed here.
IRL.outOfScopeNotes:
The Garda hate-crime statistics page for 2025 returned no usable finding during research, so the 15% increase reported for 2025 rests on Irish Times reporting of 14 August 2026 rather than on the primary statistical table. The breakdown of that increase by gender identity as a motive is not available from the sources reviewed.

The diaspora support guidance on returning to Ireland for LGBTIQ+ people returned no usable finding, so advice aimed specifically at returning residents could not be verified.

The Telegraph article of September 2024 on hate-speech law and the trans debate was paywalled and unread; whether any legislative retreat actually occurred is unresolved here, and the claim should not be relied on.

Entry, visa and border document rules for trans visitors, including how a passport or identity card with an amended gender marker is handled at Dublin airport, are not addressed by any source in this inventory and remain unsourced. Similarly, sub-national variation in policing or service access beyond the Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown example is not covered.

The status of the pending Gender Recognition Act amendment after its first legislative stage in late 2025 is unresolved; no source in this inventory records its later progression or defeat.

sources.summary:
Ireland forbids incitement to hatred based on sexual orientation under the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989, with penalties up to a €1,000 fine or 6 months' imprisonment on first offence, rising to €10,000 or 2 years on indictment; gender identity was formally added to protected grounds by the Cabinet in October 2022. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024, described as the toughest and broadest hate crime legislation in Europe, has been in force since 31 December 2024 and explicitly covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

Open expression is visible: Dublin Pride drew an estimated 60,000 people in 2018, alongside the Dublin Gay Theatre Festival, the GAZE International LGBT Film Festival and gay-friendly venues nationwide. Community facilities include the Outhouse LGBTQ+ Centre, gay and gay-friendly pubs, restaurants, clubs, bars and saunas, with visible LGBT scenes in Dublin, Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford. In April 2019 Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Council cancelled Glitter Hole's Drag Storytime, first calling it "not age-appropriate" and then citing a high level of homophobic abuse on social media.

Health facilities are a serious gap: a November 2022 Transgender Europe study found wait times for a first gender-affirming healthcare appointment in Ireland of 2.5 to 10 years, with only one public trans health provider, which was severely understaffed. Patients there were reportedly denied care for reasons including being on social welfare, having an ADHD diagnosis, or not answering "highly sexualized questions" in "the right way", pushing many to the private sector or self-administered hormone therapy. A free PrEP programme through community pharmacies was established by the Department of Health in November 2019.

The Irish state itself was the historical source of hostility: male homosexual acts were criminalised under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 and Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885 until decriminalisation in 1993, and in Norris v. Attorney General (1983) the Chief Justice invoked the "Christian nature of [the Irish] State" to uphold those laws. On 19 June 2018 Taoiseach Leo Varadkar and Justice Minister Charles Flanagan issued formal public apologies to the LGBT community for state-caused suffering and criminal convictions. Residual state hostility persists in policy: Section 81E(5) of the Pensions Act 1990 bars pensioners who retired more than a year before the 2010 civil partnership law from claiming a survivor's pension for their civil partner, and Labour Minister Brendan Howlin defended refusing equal pension opt-in rights to gay men, a stance condemned by the Irish Examiner on 24 June 2015. In the courts, Judge McKechnie in Foy's case reproached the government for inaction and said Ireland was "very much isolated" among Council of Europe members on transgender recognition.

Sex education in Ireland has been described by students and teachers as "archaic", "inadequate", "biased" and "largely religious based", with reports of non-virgin students being humiliated and LGBT issues never mentioned. The Provision of Objective Sex Education Bill 2018, which would have covered consent, contraceptives, abortion, LGBT issues and sexuality, passed second reading in the Dáil in April 2018 but lapsed with the dissolution of the Oireachtas in 2020. Many LGBT youth still experience bullying, and before the 1970s LGBT individuals would mostly stay in the closet, move to England, or commit suicide. A November 2019 report by Minister Regina Doherty recommended extending self-declaration gender recognition to 16- and 17-year-olds with parental consent, and Senator Fintan Warfield's March 2018 bill to ban conversion therapy (which explicitly would not ban supportive practices for questioning LGBT youth) remained stalled in the Seanad as of April 2022 despite a coalition pledge to ban it.

IRL.blindSummary:
Legal gender recognition in the country rests on the gender recognition statute of 2015 (No. 25 of 2015), commenced on 4 September 2015 and amended by statutory instrument through 2026. Adults change their legal gender by self-declaration, with no psychological evaluation and no medical requirement, and independent equality data records gender change as legal with no restrictions. Nonbinary identities are not recognised in national law, so a visitor whose documents carry an X marker will not be able to obtain an equivalent domestic marker.

Since 31 December 2024 a national hate-offences statute has been in force, expressly covering sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; it was preceded by an October 2022 cabinet decision to add gender identity to the protected grounds of the older incitement-to-hatred statute, where a first offence carries up to a €1,000 fine or six months' imprisonment and an indictable conviction up to €10,000 or two years. Reports of hate crimes to the national police service rose 15% in 2025, with racism and xenophobia the most common recorded motives.

Protective legislation sits alongside documented hostility. A study by a national university, published on 3 July 2025, found that discrimination against sexual and gender minorities in the country has increased despite the statutory framework. An LGBTQ+ youth organisation maintains an anonymous online hate-crime reporting form alongside rights information and links to equal-status protections, which is the route most often recommended to young people reporting an incident.

Healthcare is the sharpest practical obstacle for a trans visitor planning a stay. A November 2022 study by a trans-health monitoring body in the region put the wait for a first gender-affirming healthcare appointment in the country at 2.5 to 10 years, with a single public provider that was severely understaffed; patients were reportedly refused care for reasons including receiving social welfare, holding an ADHD diagnosis, or answering intimate screening questions in the wrong manner. Reporting by a national newspaper in April 2025 records years-long waiting lists for multidisciplinary gender-care assessment pushing some trans people towards underground or unsupervised options, while the national health service defends its multidisciplinary model of care. Gender-affirming care is legal but restricted for minors, and visitors should assume that continuity of an existing hormone prescription must be arranged privately in advance.

Public expression is open. A national Pride march drew an estimated 60,000 attendees in 2018, and visible scenes operate in five major cities alongside an LGBTQ+ community centre and the cities' gay and gay-friendly venues. Local authority tolerance is not uniform: in April 2019 one county council cancelled a drag storytime event, first calling it not age-appropriate and then citing the volume of homophobic abuse received on social media.

Three protection gaps remain. Employment and housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only, without gender identity. Conversion therapy is not banned, and neither is intersex infant surgery. A proposed amendment to the gender recognition statute of 2015 that would limit the effect of a gender recognition certificate for the purposes of imprisonment had passed its first legislative stage as of late 2025, which bears directly on any trans person entering the prison system.

The country is one of only 11 countries in one region permitting gender recognition through self-determination without a psychological evaluation requirement, a point activists have marked while pressing the outstanding gaps in trans rights and healthcare. BEL.name: Belgium
BEL.summary:
Belgium prohibits discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics. Same-sex marriage and adoption are legal, and legal name and gender-marker change rests on self-determination.

Under the Law of 25 June 2017, in force since 1 January 2018, transgender people change their registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, with no medical conditions attached. The Federal Justice Department records that the Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019 and that, pending replacement provisions, applications continue to be handled under the existing procedure.

For minors, the rules are narrower: those aged 12 to 16 may change a first name only, while 16 and 17-year-olds may apply for a sex-marker change with parental consent plus a psychological opinion confirming that the decision is freely made.

The official Brussels-Capital Region guidance on changing the sex marker on an identity card still lists a medical certificate attesting to a sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision, among the requirements. The same page states the change is free of charge, takes three to six weeks, requires a valid identity document, and is applied for in person at the commune, with a digital route available. This regional guidance does not match the federal self-declaration procedure, and the sources do not resolve which requirement a visitor's application would actually encounter.

Conversion practices were banned on 20 July 2023, with penalties of eight days to two years' imprisonment and fines of 208 to 2,400 euros. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, although a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for non-consensual interventions.

Violence against LGBTQI people is rising despite the country's progressive legal framework. Equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men reported increasing violence and intimidation in May 2025, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases Unia handled in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is a dating-app trap: victims are lured by fake profiles to isolated locations and then ambushed, robbed, humiliated or assaulted. An RTBF investigation published in February 2025 found police had recorded an alarming number of such incidents, many unreported through fear or shame. In May 2025 a case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went before the Brussels Criminal Court.

Belgian legislation does not define hate crimes and provides no code to record them as such; conduct that breaches non-discrimination law but constitutes a criminal offence is prosecuted under general provisions instead. The one conviction officially qualified as hate-motivated on sexual-orientation grounds was the 22 December 2014 jury conviction of four people for the homophobic murder of Ihsane Jarfi.

Same-sex couples have held equal adoption rights since 2006 and lesbian couples can access IVF. Until 1 January 2015 the Civil Code automatically recognised the husband of a biological mother as father while a mother's female partner had to complete an adoption procedure; a bill approved in 2014 corrected this.

Recorded harassment remains widespread: a 2019 study found 90% of LGBT people in Brussels had suffered verbal or psychological harassment, and a 2018 human rights body count recorded 125 homophobic discrimination cases, including 17 physical attacks, 42 public insults, 17 housing cases and 31 online attacks.

Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases handled by a national equality body in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is dating-app traps: victims lured through fake profiles to isolated meetings, then ambushed, beaten, robbed or humiliated. A case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went before a criminal court in the capital in May 2025, and police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported because of fear or shame.

Conversion practices were banned on 20 July 2023, with penalties of eight days to two years' imprisonment and fines of 208 to 2400 euros. The country's first femicide law, adopted in 2023, covers all gender-based homicide.

Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, although a court in the capital held a hospital accountable for nonconsensual interventions.

Same-sex couples have held equal adoption rights since 2006 and lesbian couples can access IVF. Since 1 January 2015 a mother's female partner is recognised as co-mother without an adoption procedure, ending an inequality that had required one while the husband of a biological mother was automatically recognised as father.

The 2017 law was framed by the justice minister as placing self-determination at the centre: a purely administrative procedure with all medical conditions, including sterilisation and surgery, scrapped, alongside a reflection period and public-order safeguards.

FRA.name: France
FRA.summary:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The national preventive mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
French law decriminalised sodomy in the Penal Code of 1791. A 1960 ordinance (the Mirguet amendment, article 330, 2nd alinea) doubled penalties for indecent exposure when homosexual in nature and remained in force until 1980. The Vichy government's 1942 article 334 set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, equalised at 15 in 1982 under Mitterrand. In Alsace and Lorraine, LGBTQ people were persecuted and interned in concentration camps after the 1940 Nazi annexation, and were also persecuted under the Vichy regime despite no laws criminalising homosexuality. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 before 1980, still awaiting a Senate vote. Conversion therapy was banned effective 1 February 2022, punishable by two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine.

A 31 December 2004 amendment made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment. Civil liberty groups including Reporters Without Borders criticised it as a serious infringement on free speech, while the Chirac government cited rising anti-gay violence. MP Christian Vanneste of Chirac's own UMP party became the first person convicted under the law in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Homosexuality and cross-dressing were historically treated as immoral and LGBTQ people faced legal harassment under public morality and order laws. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and LGBT people may serve openly in the French Armed Forces.

French law contains no visa, asylum or border-entry provision specific to LGBTQ people. The nearest entry-related finding concerns citizenship of children born abroad: France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens until 2015, leaving many in legal limbo, and the Court of Cassation ruled in December 2019 that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France.

A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare in France: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent and self-determination model. Transsexualism is covered under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979, but French trans rights organisations said the 2010 decree removing gender identity disorder as a diagnosis changed nothing in practice. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and a "primarily social problem" and advised extreme caution, though this did not change actual practice. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state coverage for women under 43, the MSM blood donation deferral was removed entirely on 16 March 2022, and intersex people retain significant gaps in protection from non-consensual medical interventions.

The December 2004 law amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with penalties increased when a physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. A report released on 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against around 1,380 in 2018; in October 2018 President Macron denounced the violence as "unworthy of France" and promised unspecified "concrete measures". Transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison in 2017. Overseas, Mayotte sees frequent reports of family rejection, harassment and discrimination, and a 2006 Lifou Island proposal for a "family code" envisaged eviction or lynching of LGBTQ people; it was not approved.

In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all forms of gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender-affirming care, which called such care a "health scandal" and youth transness a "social contagion"; the resulting bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, provoking large-scale protests, but is opposed by the Macron government and has had no update since 23 July 2024. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the interministerial body fighting anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory, which had called gender-affirming healthcare "mutilation"; one committee member resigned and the president stepped away. The Académie Nationale de Médecine's "epidemic-like" framing of trans people seeking care is a further state-actor hostility marker. Historically the National Assembly voted 293–222 against same-sex marriage in June 2011, and conservative outrage greeted the use of "parent 1" and "parent 2" on French school enrolment forms reported in February 2019.

In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos made fighting discrimination including homophobia one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009, and in January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign Tous égaux, tous alliés, which gives students reporting services and a helpline and requires all French schools to provide guidance about LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions must use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. Youth are the direct target of the pending under-18 medical transition ban (Senate, May 2024), while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for medical care of trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 alongside calcium and vitamin D. The Vichy-era discriminatory age of consent (21 for homosexual relations versus 15 heterosexual) was equalised at 15 in 1982, and the association Le Refuge estimated 3–4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy before the 2022 ban.

A 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 77% of the French population believed homosexuality should be accepted, one of the highest of 39 countries polled, with 81% acceptance among 18–29 year-olds; the 2019 Eurobarometer found 79% backed same-sex marriage across Europe and 85% believed LGBT people should have equal rights, and the 2023 Eurobarometer found 79% and 84% respectively. Gabriel Attal was one of the few openly gay heads of government in the world during his January–September 2024 premiership, and Paris Mayor Bertrand Delanoë came out publicly in 1998 before his 2001 election. Paris Pride drew 500,000 people in 2019, the city's third-largest event after the marathon and Techno Parade, and pride events now run in dozens of cities nationwide, with Le Marais, Quartier Pigalle and Bois de Boulogne hosting a thriving LGBTQ nightlife. Acceptance is markedly lower overseas: a 2014 study found about 20% of overseas residents saw homosexuality as a sexuality like any other against 77% in metropolitan France, with Mayotte particularly taboo and the first same-sex marriages in Saint Martin and French Polynesia triggering public demonstrations.

CHE.name: Switzerland
CHE.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland rests on self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality may change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar. No surgical requirement, no medical diagnosis and no court proceeding applies to the route. In the first months after introduction about 350 people had used it, according to SWI swissinfo reporting of 7 August 2022.

The treatment of minors is contested between the chambers of the Federal Assembly. The National Council suppressed the requirement for guardian consent for 12 to 18-year-olds, while the Council of States set 16 as the age below which guardian consent is needed. The wording finally in force is not resolved by the available sources.

Same-sex marriage has been in force since 1 July 2022 under the Marriage for All reform, which also opened adoption and assisted reproduction to same-sex couples; 64.1% of voters approved the reform in referendum.

On hate speech, since 1 July 2020 public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is punishable under Art. 261bis of the Swiss Criminal Code. Switzerland has no general hate-crime provision: bias-motivated offences are addressed through anti-discrimination provisions. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report records that Swiss police do not record bias motivation and that national recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other offences.

Reported anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crime is at a sustained level and rising. Monitoring by the LGBTIQ Helpline indicates roughly six anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crimes reported per week, 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030, built on three pillars: support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence. Implementation is coordinated by the Federal Office for Gender Equality.

Placement of transgender detainees is governed cantonally. There is no federal provision on trans placement in detention, no Federal Supreme Court case law on the subject, and no trans-specific units or federal solitary-confinement practice for trans prisoners. The canton of Basel-Stadt added gender identity to its detention law (JVG), adopted by the Grand Council on 13 November 2019: §2 separates female and male detainees while stating that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, and allows the prison directorate to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority.

Employment is governed by Art. 328ff. of the Code of Obligations, which requires employers to protect employees' personal dignity, concretised for trans people by the Equality Act (GLG). Trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any change to official documents.

AUT.name: Austria
AUT.summary:
The statutory baseline in Austria is permissive. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971, marriage equality has applied since 2017, and same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2016. The Equal Treatment Act has covered employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2004, and recent amendments have broadened its use of "gender" to encompass gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics; gender identity and intersex status are not listed separately but are treated as covered under that term. By January 2017 every federal state had extended anti-discrimination protection to goods and services, Lower Austria being the last to do so.

Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1 January 2016, and offences committed on that ground are treated as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The 1993 Security Police Act obliges police to avoid actions that could be perceived as biased on grounds of sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition is possible without mandatory medical procedures. After the Constitutional Court ruled in June 2018 that gender identity must be accurately reflected in official documents, an "X" marker became available on passports and a "divers" entry on birth certificates; the Interior Ministry restricted "divers" to people holding a medical panel certificate of intersexuality, and intersex people may choose "diverse", "inter" or no designation. Changing legal gender and name does not require prior sex-reassignment surgery but is conditional on submitting a psychiatric opinion.

Detention carries a defined framework. A Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report published in 2025, produced within an EU-funded project, sets out the legal rules governing LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons and their situation and rights in detention, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection. The Justice Ministry answered parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 in May and June 2025 on the official rules for housing transgender people in penal institutions; that answer is the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained, and it is published in German.

Violence risk is documented and recent. In March 2025 police uncovered a neo-Nazi network that used fake dating profiles to lure gay and bisexual men to ambushes by masked assailants, who filmed the attacks and shared them. Austrian police arrested 15 people aged 14 to 26 over a wave of hate attacks in which at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured via fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed and falsely accused of being paedophiles; investigators believe the real victim count is much higher. Official figures for 2025 record 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives, with 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence, and police data acknowledges under-recording. Across the reporting year homophobic offences rose while transphobic incidents declined.

Political conditions are unsettled. The far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) won the most votes in the September 2024 national election, its first such result since the Second World War, on 29.2% of the vote, prompting concern about the consequences of an FPÖ-led government for LGBTQ people. New Ministry of Education rules restrict outside sex-education providers, a Vienna petition for queer sauna time slots was rejected, and the national Ombud has issued guidance on gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people.

Access to care is supported by professional bodies but partly gated. Puberty blockers for youth experiencing gender dysphoria have been endorsed by the Austrian Society of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics, and public health insurance payment for sex-change treatment is bound on submission of psychiatric opinions. Lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF treatments. In 2018 the ultra-conservative association TeenSTAR was found offering minors conversion therapy classes teaching that sexual orientation was changeable; the Education Directorate Salzburg banned TeenSTAR workshops pending review, the association was banned in April 2019, and Parliament passed a resolution on 2 July 2019 calling for a legal ban on conversion therapy on minors, with all parties voting in favour at the final vote.

Open service and public life are established. LGBT people serve openly in the Austrian Armed Forces, and since 2014 transgender people have been allowed to serve openly. Advocacy operates openly through HOSI Wien, founded 1979, HOSI Salzburg, ALGF and Afro Rainbow Austria, with community infrastructure in Vienna, Linz, Innsbruck, Salzburg and Graz and an annual Vienna Gay Pride and Regenbogenparade. Public opinion as of 2023 showed 65% support for same-sex marriage and 66% agreeing nothing is wrong with a same-sex relationship.
AUT.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory, a Graz election item and the Amnesty International Austria report, yielded no substantive Austria-specific finding and contribute nothing to this record.

Whether the conversion-therapy ban called for by the National Council resolution of 2 July 2019 has since been enacted is unresolved in the available material; only the resolution, the April 2019 ban on the association and the Salzburg education ban are sourced.

The currency of the psychiatric-opinion requirement for legal gender change and for insurance coverage of sex-change treatment is not independently dated in the inventory, and the Justice Ministry answer on housing transgender detainees is available only in German.

Police hate-crime data for 2025 is acknowledged by its own reporting to under-record incidents, and the inventory does not break the 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence down by transgender status, so the scale of trans-specific violence relative to homophobic violence is unresolved beyond the direction of travel noted for the reporting year.

In 2018 an ultra-conservative association was found offering minors conversion therapy classes teaching that sexual orientation was changeable; a regional education authority banned its workshops pending review, the association was banned in April 2019, and the national parliament passed a resolution on 2 July 2019 calling for a legal ban on conversion therapy on minors, with all parties voting in favour at the final vote.

Open service and public life are established. LGBT people serve openly in the armed forces, and since 2014 transgender people have been allowed to serve openly. Advocacy operates openly through organisations founded in the capital in 1979 and in other cities, with community infrastructure across several cities and an annual Pride parade and rainbow parade in the capital. Public opinion as of 2023 showed 65% support for same-sex marriage and 66% agreeing nothing is wrong with a same-sex relationship.

ITA.name: Italy
ITA.summary:
Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and Italy has had an equal age of consent for homosexual and heterosexual acts since before the 20th century.

Italy's position on sexual orientation and gender identity rests on court rulings and sectoral statutes rather than a single comprehensive law. No Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, and ILGA-Europe's 2021 report noted the absence of nationwide protection covering goods and services, leaving transgender people exposed to discrimination in housing, education and health care. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, implementing EU Directive 2000/78/EC; the exemptions for police, armed forces and rescue services were removed by Law no. 101 of 2008. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that firing a trans professor amounted to sex discrimination.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued during 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, which is consistent with the pattern recorded by monitors rather than with isolated incidents.

The most serious traveller-specific finding is the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania. ANSA reports that the convictions for the assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, a court outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors rather than impunity for it.

Violence by state agents has also been prosecuted. In July 2024 a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton.

Official hostility shapes the environment around that violence. The Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year, and a cardinal publicly described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment in Italy.

The courts have moved in the opposite direction on several points. In March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time, physical and psychological harm resulting from homophobic mistreatment.

Legal gender recognition has been available since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country worldwide to allow it, and since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, first recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 but declined to add a non-binary registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary; the same judgment struck down the requirement of judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered Italian identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the previous wording discriminatory.

Cross-dressing is legal. The fascist penal code of the 1920s–1940s banned it and police targeted trans people, and in 2006 a police officer was reportedly dismissed for cross-dressing in public while off duty.

Italy recognises persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and the EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU, and Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including those persecuted on those grounds.

Whether the detention findings from the Ludwig Boltzmann report and the Frontiers in Psychiatry analysis extend to short-term visitors held in custody is not stated by either source and is unresolved.

Access to Italian health services for a non-resident trans visitor, including continuity of hormone therapy, is not covered by the sources, which describe the National Health Service scheme without addressing eligibility for visitors.

The Intrepid Travel page presents Italy as an LGBTQIA+ destination for its travellers but carries no safety finding specific to Italy, and so supports no assessment either way.

Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, which implements EU Directive 2000/78/EC; the exemptions for police, armed forces and rescue services were removed by Law no. 101 of 2008. No other nationwide law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and no Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, so transgender people may face discrimination in goods and services, housing, education and health care; ILGA-Europe's 2021 report notes the absence of nationwide protection for goods and services. Regional statutes cover Tuscany (2004), Liguria (2009), Marche (2010), Sicily (2015), Piedmont (2016), Umbria (2017), Emilia-Romagna (2019), Campania (2020) and Apulia (2024). Legal gender change has been possible since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country worldwide to allow it; since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered Italian identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the previous wording discriminatory. POL.name: Poland
POL.summary:
Detention is the clearest documented threat to a trans visitor in Poland. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court had placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and her file recorded a history of violence and sexual assault, meaning she was held in a facility where those risks were live. She was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it.

Trans prisoners have won on the same issue in court. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages, while rejecting the parallel Article 3 claim. The judgment establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and can be won, though it does not prevent the denial from occurring first.

Entry rules are straightforward for short stays: Global Affairs Canada records visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, while listing sexual orientation among the reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status. The advisory therefore treats identity-based harassment as an existing condition of travel rather than a remote possibility.

Protection on paper has widened. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, and a March draft amendment to the Penal Code raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence; it passed the Government Legislation Centre in May but the government postponed approval, with a second bill introduced in late October. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. Whether the higher penalties are in force by the time of travel is not settled in these sources.

The wider record shows an official climate that has moved in both directions. HRW's World Report 2025 describes LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government as slow and insufficient: in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the Ziobro directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September the ECtHR ruled that Poland's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum in violation of their rights, calling for a recognition framework. Earlier hostility is documented in statements and enforcement: President Andrzej Duda said in the 2020 election campaign that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism'; municipalities and four voivodeships declared LGBT-free zones after 2015; ILGA-Europe's 2020 report ranked Poland worst among EU countries; and on 7 August 2020 some 47 people were arrested during the Rainbow Night mass arrest, drawing criticism from the Polish Ombudsman.

Public violence has been recorded at events a visitor might attend. In August 2019 LGBT community members said they felt unsafe amid rising violence, including attacks on the first Equality March in Białystok and a foiled bombing attempt at a march in Lublin. A Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 heard its organiser describe 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' as enemies of Poland.
POL.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in these sources: how Polish authorities treat a foreign visitor's passport or identity document carrying a gender marker that differs from the visitor's presentation, and whether Border Guard or airport screening creates an outing risk. The document analysis in the inventory addresses Polish citizens only.

Unresolved: whether the March 2024 Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence was ultimately enacted. The inventory records passage through the Government Legislation Centre in May, postponement of approval, and a second bill in late October, but no final promulgation.

Unresolved: current enforcement of the 2004 workplace discrimination protections and the 2024 response-team guidelines in practice; the sources describe their adoption, not their results.

The 2007 proposal to punish the promotion of homosexuality in schools, involving dismissal, fines or prison for teachers and students and banning LGBT organisations, belongs to an earlier government and is not evidence of current law. Historical criminal provisions, including occupation-era Paragraph 175 penalties and the pre-1932 sodomy sentences, likewise do not describe present-day Poland, where homosexuality has been legal since 1932.

Evidence Polish detention practice can endanger trans detainees' health until challenged.

TGEU (16 Jul 2024): on 11 July the ECtHR found Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 (and rejected Article 3) by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy; damages of EUR 8,000 ordered. Directly relevant precedent: trans prisoners in Poland can litigate medication denial and win.

Amnesty International report 'A Thousand Cuts' (2025): documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against Poland's LGBTI community on X, including LGBT-free-zone legacy (2019-23), lack of legal inclusion, and X's policy reversals (misgendering/deadnaming rule removed Apr 2023, reinstated 2024). sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: homosexuality was decriminalised in independent Poland in 1932 but criminalised under partition — Congress Poland 1818, Austria 1852, Prussia 1871, Russia 1845, penalised by forced resettlement to Siberia — and recriminalised from 1939 under the German occupation. Polish men in same-sex relationships were punished under Article 175, especially in annexed areas, and the General Government's criminal police could deport them or impose the death penalty; camp prisoners under Paragraph 175 were classified 'political prisoners' with red triangles. Two earlier sodomy sentences were carried out: Wojciech Skwarski of Poznań, burned at the stake in 1561 on a sentence that also counted theft and murder, and Agnieszka Kuśnierczanka in 1642, publicly beaten and exiled; the 1925 Suwałki case sentenced Stefan Góralski and Marjan Kuleszyński to three months under paragraph 516 of the 1903 Russian Penal Code. Post-war, the 1948 law set the age of consent at 15 for all sexual acts and otherwise left the liberal interwar law intact; Operation Hyacinth of 15 November 1985 registered around 11,000 suspected gay men in a national database, and 'pink files' were still held by the Institute of National Remembrance as of 2005 despite activists' requests to destroy them. A 1 January 2004 law barred workplace discrimination on sexual orientation; on 8 July 2024 the Tusk government added a registered-partnership bill (no joint adoption) to the Sejm agenda after its October 2024 presentation by Equality Minister Katarzyna Kotula. Open discussion of homosexuality stayed taboo outside literary circles: the Second Republic magazine Wiadomości Literackie and figures such as Tadeusz Boy-Żeleński and Irena Krzywicka broke taboos on contraception and homosexuality, founding the Liga Reformy Obyczajów in 1935, and 1933 produced three novels with openly lesbian themes including The Well of Loneliness with Krzywicka's preface. Communist authorities censored information about the Kinsey Report, while a 1985 Polityka article 'Jesteśmy inni' triggered a national discussion and Selerowicz's conspiratorial 1983–84 meetings produced the samizdat bulletin Etap; press came-outs followed with actor Marek Barbasiewicz in Kobieta i Życie (September 1992) and Izabela Filipiak in Viva (1998). Media has also carried hostility: the right-wing Gazeta Polska distributed 'LGBT-free zone' stickers, later reworded 'LGBT Ideology-Free Zone' after a court ordered distribution halted; President Andrzej Duda stated in the 2020 election that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism'; Lech Kaczyński opposed official Pride in 2004–05. Cultural visibility includes the 1987 Polish premiere of Larry Kramer's The Normal Heart in Poznań with a 4 May 1989 TVP broadcast, Karolina Breguła's 2023 'Let Them See Us' billboard campaign, frequently vandalised, and Lambda's Queer Museum in Warsaw, opened 6 December 2024 as the first of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe. Café Fiolka at Puławska 257 in Warsaw, the first official gay club, opened 7 October 1990 and closed in 1992 after repeated vandalism; earlier police targeted cruising spots, with Warsaw's 6th Sanitary-Moral Brigade, joined by the female 1st Brigade in 1925, hunting cruising areas in 1927 and arresting mostly working-class men identifying as 'ciota'. Health and support infrastructure developed around the AIDS crisis: the Ministry of Health established a Plenipotentiary for AIDS and a ten-person expert team in 1985, a year before Poland's first recorded AIDS case; Lambda was registered by the Warsaw Voivodeship Court on 23 February 1990 to spread tolerance and prevent HIV; and the Kochaj, nie zabijaj campaign began in spring 1990. Organisations include Campaign Against Homophobia (2001), the Polish Feminist Lesbian Archive OLA-Archiwum (registered 1998, publishing Furia Pierwsza), the Trans-Fuzja foundation co-founded by MP Anna Grodzka, and Razem for Polish LGBT immigrants in New York (1995). Medical services are documented from the first sex reassignment surgery in 1963 at Szpital Kolejowy in Międzylesie, infrequent for some twenty years, and the first recorded transgender meeting on 10 December 1985 at Warsaw's Department of Sexology. Homophobia is described as a common public attitude driven by Catholic Church influence and widespread social conservatism, with the Church later 'a factor in making homosexuality something scandalous in many social circles' and influencing the 1988 blocking of the Warsaw Gay Movement's legal registration. After 2015, several municipalities and four voivodeships declared 'LGBT-free zones', partly in response to mayor Rafał Trzaskowski's pro-LGBT declaration; in August 2019 LGBT community members said they felt unsafe amid a rise in violence including attacks on the first Białystok Equality March and a foiled bombing attempt at a Lublin march; at a Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 the organizer called 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' enemies of Poland. ILGA-Europe's 2020 report ranked Poland worst among EU countries, and on 7 August 2020 47 people were arrested in the Rainbow Night mass arrest, some peacefully protesting activist Margot's arrest, drawing criticism from the Polish Ombudsman; 50 ambassadors and representatives wrote an open letter on 27 September 2020 affirming that 'Human Rights are not an ideology'. Visibility milestones run from the first Equality Parade in Warsaw in 2001 (over 300 attendees), through banned 2004–05 Prides — the 11 June 2005 march drew about 2,500 in civil disobedience with several brief arrests and a 600–1,000-person 2004 Freedom Veche — to the 2011 election of Poland's first out LGBT MPs, Robert Biedroń and Anna Grodzka; questioned villagers in the 1925 Suwałki case reported no 'abnormality' and accepted the two men in their community.

The registered-partnership bill was added to the Sejm agenda on 8 July 2024 after its presentation in October 2023 by Equality Minister Katarzyna Kotula; it provides no joint adoption. A separate 1 January 2004 law bars workplace discrimination on sexual orientation.

POL.blindSummary:
Detention is the clearest documented threat to a trans visitor. On 13 March 2024 an association for legal intervention reported that a regional court had placed a transgender foreign woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and her file recorded a history of violence and sexual assault, meaning she was held where those risks were live. She was released only after NGO intervention prompted the border-guard commander to order it.

Trans prisoners have won on the same issue in court. On 11 July 2024 the regional human rights court found that prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages, while rejecting the parallel Article 3 claim. The judgment establishes that medication denial in custody is litigable and can be won, though it does not prevent the denial from occurring first.

Entry rules are straightforward for short stays: a foreign government travel advisory records visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, while listing sexual orientation among the reported motives for harassment, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status. The advisory therefore treats identity-based harassment as an existing condition of travel rather than a remote possibility.

Protection on paper has widened. The deputy justice minister announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, and a March draft amendment to the criminal code raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence; it passed the government's legislation centre in May but approval was postponed, with a second bill introduced in late October. The prosecutor general established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. Whether the higher penalties are in force by the time of travel is not settled in these sources.

The wider record shows an official climate that has moved in both directions. A human rights organisation's 2025 report describes LGBT-rights reform by the sitting government as slow and insufficient: in June 2024 the justice minister revoked a predecessor's directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September the regional human rights court ruled that the country's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum in violation of their rights, calling for a recognition framework. Earlier hostility is documented in statements and enforcement: the head of state said in the 2020 election campaign that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism'; subnational units declared LGBT-free zones after 2015; a regional rights body ranked the country worst among one group of states in 2020; and on 7 August 2020 some 47 people were arrested during a mass arrest, drawing criticism from the national ombudsman.

Public violence has been recorded at events a visitor might attend. In August 2019 LGBT community members said they felt unsafe amid rising violence, including attacks on a first equality march in one city and a foiled bombing attempt at a march in another. A rally on 11 November 2021 heard its organiser describe 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' as enemies of the country.

Historical criminal provisions, including occupation-era paragraph 175 penalties and pre-1932 sodomy sentences, likewise do not describe present-day law, where homosexuality has been legal since 1932.
