HUN.name: Hungary
HUN.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Hungary is prohibited. Administrative refusal was already routine from 2018, and in May 2020 the Orbán government, ruling by emergency decree during the COVID-19 pandemic, pushed through a bill barring passports and identity cards from reflecting an acquired gender, including for people already legally recognised. The same bill redefined the word nem (sex) in the civil code as immutable biological sex. A trans visitor should therefore expect to enter and be documented under the marker assigned at birth, with no domestic route to correcting it.

A layer of supranational litigation runs against that domestic position. On 13 March 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in C-247/23 (Deldits), on a reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration case, that Article 16 of the GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data once it has changed and no longer satisfies the accuracy principle of Article 5(1)(d). In September 2024 the Court's Advocate General had called on Hungarian authorities to correct the gender marker of a transgender refugee in the national registries. How far either instrument reaches a visitor's short-term documents is not established by these sources.

In April 2026 the Court of Justice found that Hungary's 2021 child-protection law, including the ban on gender change for people under 18, discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents and breached EU rules on several levels. The court held the law in breach of Article 2 of the treaty establishing the Union, an unprecedented finding against the bloc's founding values. Judgment came nine days after Hungarians voted in the 12 April 2026 election.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1961, and nothing in the entry regime conditions admission on sexual orientation or gender identity. One procedural protection does apply: in January 2018 the Court of Justice held that asylum seekers may not be subjected by authorities to psychological tests in order to determine their sexual orientation. LGBT people nevertheless continue to face discrimination and demonisation in public life, which shapes the street-level environment a visitor meets.

The 12 April 2026 election ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán's government, with Péter Magyar's Tisza party winning 138 seats. Analysts describe the outcome as a return to the democratic baseline rather than a repeal of the legal architecture built under the previous government, and Tisza has published no LGBTQ+ programme. Reform of the anti-LGBTQ statutes would require a two-thirds majority in parliament, and Tisza's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Magyar has raised questions about the pace of change. In September 2026 the new prime minister announced an intention to repeal the constitutional ban on adoption by same-sex couples.

Assembly has already reopened. The 31st Budapest Pride drew tens of thousands of marchers in June 2026, the first held since Orbán was voted out, against the backdrop of the anti-LGBT laws adopted during his rule. Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik named the restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent issue for the community. Contemporaneous reporting records cautious optimism among activists that changes will be made.
HUN.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Court of Justice's rectification ruling in C-247/23 has been implemented by the Hungarian register authority, and whether it can be invoked by a visitor rather than a resident or asylum applicant, is unresolved in the available sources. No source establishes whether the April 2026 judgment on the 2021 child-protection law has produced any change to domestic practice on gender markers, and no source confirms whether the under-18 gender-change ban remains in force pending compliance.

The inventory does not address hate-crime or hate-speech statutes covering gender identity, sentencing outcomes for violence against trans people, or any police guidance on stop-and-search or ID checks of gender-nonconforming travellers. Reporting requirements at entry, including any biometric or sex-field screening at the border, are likewise not sourced. Budapest Pride's assembly permissions for future years and any conditions attached to them are not documented beyond the June 2026 march.

The scale of the anti-LGBTQ legislative package as a whole, the parliamentary arithmetic for a two-thirds majority after the April 2026 election, and the Tisza party's actual legislative intentions on legal gender recognition are unresolved: analysts describe the election as a restoration of the democratic baseline rather than a repeal of the existing legal architecture, and no LGBTQ+ programme from Tisza has been published.

After the previous party lost power in the April 2026 election ending 16 years of rule, a Pride spokesperson named restoration of the right to assembly as 'the most urgent issue' and said anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority; the winning party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights raises questions about the pace of change.

A national report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees, part of a regional project on strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ people in detention — the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in detention amid the current legal and political climate.

A world report says LGBT people continue to face discrimination and demonization; a 2020 law bans legal gender change for transgender and intersex people, and in September 2024 a court advocate general called on national authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in national registries.

A judgment on a reference from a national court in an immigration case: data-protection rules require the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data where it has changed and no longer complies with the accuracy principle — the operative authority for updating gender markers on official records.

A 2020 news report: while ruling by emergency decree during a pandemic, the government pushed a bill barring passports and ID cards from reflecting a person's acquired gender — even for those already legally recognised — the decree-level rollback that made legal gender recognition explicitly illegal in 2020.
HUN.blindLocalsOnly:
Family law for residents differs sharply from the document regime. Unregistered cohabitation has been recognised since 1996 for any couple including same-sex couples, conferring specified rights, with inheritance available only by testament and a widow's pension after ten years. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have existed since 1 July 2009 and carry the same rights as marriage except adoption, assisted reproduction and the taking of a surname. Same-sex marriage was banned by the constitution in force from 1 January 2012.

Adoption is the contested front for residents. Same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly, stepchild adoption is restricted to married different-sex couples, and a December 2020 constitutional amendment further barred adoption by same-sex couples while restricting single-parent adoption. Female couples in a registered partnership have no access to IVF or donor insemination. The new prime minister announced in September 2026 an intention to repeal the ban on adoption by same-sex couples, but no repeal has been sourced here.

Residents retain no domestic route to changing legal sex, so the mismatch between identity papers and lived presentation is a standing condition of ordinary administration rather than a transitional problem. The rectification obligation recognised by the supranational court in case C-247/23 concerns records held under the regional data-protection regulation and its application to resident registries remains governed by the national register authority.
HUN.tangentialFactors:
Official hostility toward LGBT people was a governing instrument for much of the previous era and forms the backdrop to the current legal position. In May 2020 the National Assembly rejected the Istanbul Convention in a resolution attacking its measures as promoting destructive gender ideologies and illegal migration; in October 2020 Orbán stated that gays are to leave our children alone. In April 2026 the Court of Justice found the 2021 child-protection law had discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents, which frames how the domestic rhetoric was received at EU level.

Defamation proceedings over that rhetoric ran their full course. After a 2021 children's book published by the Labrisz Lesbian Association, the governing party launched a smear campaign conflating homosexuality with pedophilia, and the government-linked media group Mediaworks published an article calling Labrisz pedophiles without proof. Labrisz won at first instance, but in November 2022 the Curia ruled the article had not violated its right to good reputation; the case went to the Constitutional Court. The pattern indicates weak practical recourse against anti-LGBTQ incitement in the domestic courts during that period.

Adjacent advocacy has focused on detention conditions: a 2025 national report on LGBTIQ detainees, produced by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society under an EU-funded project on the rights of LGBTIQ detainees, documents the situation of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention amid the current legal and political climate. Prospects for reform sit alongside this, since anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority and the new governing party has so far kept its position unclear.

GRC.name: Greece
GRC.summary:
Law 5089/2024 legalised same-sex marriage in Greece in February 2024, making the country the first with a majority Orthodox Christian population to do so. The same law added sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics (SOGIESC) as equal-treatment grounds across goods and services, education, healthcare, housing and social protection. Civil unions have been available since 2015, adoption and foster care by same-sex couples are permitted, and the age of consent is 15 for everyone.

Legal gender change has been available on a self-declaration basis since 2017. TGEU's Trans Rights Index and Map 2025 records Greece meeting 21 of its 32 indicators, with identified gaps including age restrictions on changes of forename, the absence of a national action plan on trans rights, and no legal recognition of trans or non-binary parenthood.

Conversion practices have been banned for minors and intersex genital mutilation criminalised since 2022. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity has been prohibited since 2023, and Greece's hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity. ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map placed Greece 7th in its 2025 ranking.

Violence against trans people remains documented. In March 2024 a mob of approximately 150 people attacked two transgender people in Thessaloniki; 21 people were arrested, 11 of them minors, and a masked attack on counter-protesters followed. In July 2025 the Crete Court of Appeal convicted three French tourists over a 2017 attack.

Police conduct toward visibly trans people has been the subject of an adverse judgment: in Koutra and Katzaki v. Greece (application 459/16, 2017) the European Court of Human Rights found that officers stopped and mistreated transgender sex workers and their lawyer in Athens in 2013, and that complaints against the officers were discontinued.

The same court condemned Greece in 2025 for detaining an LGBTI Iranian refugee pending deportation, finding a violation of Article 3. A criminal case has been opened over an online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people.

Self-reported experience in the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights LGBTIQ survey III (2024) shows constrained everyday conduct: 63% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner against an EU-27 figure of 53%, 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault against 29% EU-wide, and only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ against 51% across the EU.

Official and institutional hostility persists alongside the statutory framework. The Orthodox Church officially opposed marriage equality, and transphobic comments were directed at Greek Eurovision contestants in 2024.

The UK Foreign Office updated its travel advice for LGBTQ+ travellers to Greece in April 2024, noting that same-sex relations are legal, civil unions have existed since 2015, marriage has been available since February 2024, the age of consent is 15 for all, and legal gender change is possible, while advising travellers to remain alert.
GRC.outOfScopeNotes:
The content of the age restrictions on changes of forename identified as a gap by TGEU is not sourced here; the index records the gap but the underlying statutory provision is not quoted.

Whether the 2021 route for transferring trans prisoners to women's facilities has since been codified, extended to other facilities, or applied beyond the four named detainees is unresolved in the available sources.

The enforcement record for the 2023 employment-discrimination ban and for the hate-crime and hate-speech provisions covering gender identity is not documented in the inventory; no conviction data is available.

The outcome or current status of the criminal case opened over the online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people is unresolved.

Compliance with the 2025 European Court of Human Rights judgment on the detention of an LGBTI Iranian refugee, including any policy change on detention pending deportation, is not sourced.

Non-binary legal recognition is not addressed in any source; TGEU's reference to unrecognised trans and non-binary parenthood is the only indication, and no statutory position can be stated.

The Orthodox Church's formal opposition to marriage equality and the transphobic commentary around Eurovision are institutional and media signals of the reception a visibly trans visitor may encounter, independent of the legal position.

The legislative trajectory runs from a Justice Ministry working group on cohabiting same-sex couples pledged in 2008, through civil unions in 2015, to marriage equality in 2024; the pace of statutory change has outstripped documented change in street-level conditions.

CZE.name: Czechia
CZE.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Czechia has been rebuilt on a non-surgical basis. On 24 April 2024 the Czech Constitutional Court, in judgment PL. US 52/23, struck down the requirement that an official sex change be conditional on surgery including sterilisation, holding that conditioning recognition on disabling reproductive function was unconstitutional. The legislature was given until June 2025 to act; Reuters reported in June 2025 that the surgery requirement had been dropped, and in July 2025 the Czech Health Ministry announced that trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment in order to change their legal gender.

The European Court of Human Rights confirmed that direction in T.H. v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 33037/22, judgment 12 September 2025), finding a violation of Article 8. The Court held the surgical and sterilisation condition for official sex change, and the related civil-registry treatment, incompatible with private-life rights, framing Convention-guaranteed gender recognition through self-determination; Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe intervened as third parties.

Detention and prison placement remain a documented, unresolved risk. In March 2023 the Supreme Administrative Court rebuked the Prague Municipal Court for 'sarcastic moral lectures' toward an HIV-positive trans man in transition and ruled that authorities must first assess whether detainees are 'potentially vulnerable persons' before placement, though administrative practice remains inconsistent. In November 2025 the Supreme Court demanded that the national prison concept explicitly address the needs of people in or after transition, citing the Constitutional Court ruling; the human-rights commissioner is pressing for a binding regulation while the Justice Ministry maintains that the existing framework suffices, with consultation ongoing.

Official hostility is a live factor. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 records that after the Constitutional Court repealed the surgical prerequisite, the Justice Minister publicly stated his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth' and other politicians issued transphobic statements; the far-right SPD circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists'. The government has approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, pending in Parliament, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status. Earlier, on 27 June 2021, President Miloš Zeman described sex-reassignment surgery as 'committing a crime for inflicting self-harm' and said 'these transgenders truly disgust me'.

Discrimination and harassment are widespread. The 'Being LGBTQ+ in Czechia' survey reported in the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 found 43% discriminated or harassed in the past five years, over a third within twelve months, with the highest rates among trans and non-binary respondents, and 51% targeted by insults, assault or threats in five years; politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% in 2018 to 71% in 2023, with 63% attributing rising intolerance to politicians. In June 2023 a group disrupted Brno Pride drag story-time with homophobic slurs.

Enforcement of bias-crime law is modest. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report records 94 hate crimes recorded by police in 2024, 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, with LGBTI-motivated incidents included in the bias breakdown; Criminal Code amendments move from the 'hostility model' to a discriminatory-selection model, but ODIHR notes recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes.

Entry and asylum: the new Asylum Law includes SOGI grounds with an opposite-gender interview option. Anti-discrimination protection under the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in education, employment, housing and access to goods and services. Blood donation opened to all citizens regardless of partner gender on 1 July 2024, replacing the previous ban on people with a same-sex partner, though people reporting anal sex with a new partner in the past four months are still excluded. Since 2001 Czechia has granted 'persons living in a common household' hospital and prison visitation rights similar to married couples, alongside inheritance and succession rights in housing.

Same-sex marriage remains unresolved: a cross-party bill introduced by 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs to replace registered partnerships was backed by the caretaker government in June 2018 and cleared parliamentary committees on 29 June 2023, while a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage moved to second reading with support from SPD, ODS, KDU-ČSL and ANO.

Facilities and social climate: Prague and Brno rate highest for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, with formal nondiscrimination policies and queer districts in Vinohrady and Žižkov, while harassment risk concentrates in rural areas and late-night settings. Prague Pride has run annually since 2012, and the Mezipatra film festival has run in Brno every November since 2000. An April 2023 Ostrava Regional Court ordered re-issued certificates and a diploma for a trans graduate. School-curriculum LGBTI content has prompted organised parental opt-out campaigns. Acceptance is markedly higher among younger Czechs: 84% of 18–29-year-olds in a 2013 Pew survey thought homosexuality should be accepted, versus 72% of those over 50.
CZE.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the pending Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to sexual orientation and gender identity is unresolved as to parliamentary passage; the inventory records government approval and that it remains pending in Parliament.

Whether the Justice Ministry will issue the binding prison-placement regulation sought by the human-rights commissioner is unresolved; the inventory records an ongoing consultation with the Ministry maintaining that the existing framework suffices.

The outcome of the same-sex marriage bill and of the competing constitutional ban proposal is unresolved; the inventory records committee passage in June 2023 and second reading for the ban, with no final vote recorded.

Whether the July 2025 Health Ministry announcement has been fully implemented in civil-registry practice across all registries is not sourced here; the inventory records the announcement and the ECHR judgment but no implementation audit.

The UK Foreign Office travel advice page for Czechia records no trans-specific safety finding; this is an absence in that source, not a finding of safety.

sources.summary: Czechia: same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1962, following research by Kurt Freund concluding that homosexual orientation cannot be altered; homosexual prostitution was decriminalised in 1990, and the age of consent was equalised in 1990 at 15, having previously been 18 for homosexuals. In May 2024 the Constitutional Court ruled that forced surgery and sterilisation of transgender individuals is unconstitutional and gave the government until June 2025 to change the laws; in July 2025 the Health Ministry announced that trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment to change their legal gender. State rhetoric also framed trans bodies as criminal: on 27 June 2021 President Miloš Zeman said sex-reassignment surgery means 'you are committing a crime for inflicting self-harm' and that 'these transgenders truly disgust me.' Public expression is legal and visible but carries social risk. The first Prague Pride parade was held in August 2011 with mayoral support and drew negative responses from religious conservative groups and the far-right; it has run annually since 2012, and since 2014 organisers have barred pedophile promotional activity at Pride venues. Brno has hosted the Mezipatra gay and lesbian film festival every November since 2000, and a Prague City Council-produced gay guide and map appeared in late 2010. In the 2012 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey of 93,000 LGBTQ people, only one in five Czech respondents was open about their orientation to all colleagues or classmates, 71% were selectively open at work or school, and 52% of gay men and 30% of lesbian women avoided holding hands in public outside gay neighbourhoods for fear of assault, threat or harassment; only one in five was open to all classmates, indicating school-level concealment. Facilities are concentrated in the capital: Prague has a large, well-developed gay nightlife scene centred on the Vinohrady district with at least 20 bars and clubs and 4 saunas, while gay venues are much more sparsely spread in other Czech towns, and the city acts as a magnet for the country's gay youth. Since 2001 the Czech Republic has granted 'persons living in a common household' hospital and prison visitation rights similar to married heterosexual couples, alongside inheritance and succession rights in housing. Blood donation opened to all citizens regardless of partner gender on 1 July 2024, replacing the previous ban on people with a same-gender partner, though people reporting anal sex with a new partner in the past four months are still excluded. Anti-discrimination protection under the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in education as well as employment, housing and access to goods and services. Acceptance is markedly higher among younger Czechs: a 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 84% of 18–29-year-olds thought homosexuality should be accepted, versus 72% of those over 50, and a January 2020 Median poll showed younger respondents overwhelmingly supporting same-sex marriage while those aged 55 and above were mostly opposed.

CZE.localsOnly:
Residents benefit directly from the non-surgical recognition regime: since the July 2025 Health Ministry announcement, no surgery or hormone treatment is required to change legal gender, and the Constitutional Court's June 2025 deadline for legislative action has passed with the requirement dropped.

The 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, housing and access to goods and services, giving residents a domestic cause of action independent of the ECHR ruling.

Residents in registered partnerships or common households have hospital and prison visitation rights and inheritance and succession rights in housing since 2001; blood donation eligibility was equalised on 1 July 2024, though a four-month deferral for anal sex with a new partner remains.

Prison placement for trans people is governed by an unsettled framework: the Supreme Court has demanded the national prison concept address transition-related needs, the human-rights commissioner is seeking a binding regulation, and the Justice Ministry maintains the existing framework suffices, with consultation ongoing.

A Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity has been approved by the government and is pending in Parliament; a Constitutional Court ruling meanwhile weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status.

Same-sex marriage is not yet law: the cross-party bill to replace registered partnerships cleared committees in June 2023 but has not passed, and a constitutional ban proposal advanced to second reading.
CZE.blindSummary:
Legal gender recognition in the country has been rebuilt on a non-surgical basis. On 24 April 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment PL. US 52/23, struck down the requirement that an official sex change be conditional on surgery including sterilisation, holding that conditioning recognition on disabling reproductive function was unconstitutional. The legislature was given until June 2025 to act; a news agency reported in June 2025 that the surgery requirement had been dropped, and in July 2025 the Health Ministry announced that trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment in order to change their legal gender.

The regional human rights court confirmed that direction in a case against the country (Application no. 33037/22, judgment 12 September 2025), finding a violation of Article 8. The Court held the surgical and sterilisation condition for official sex change, and the related civil-registry treatment, incompatible with private-life rights, framing Convention-guaranteed gender recognition through self-determination; two international NGOs intervened as third parties.

Detention and prison placement remain a documented, unresolved risk. In March 2023 the supreme administrative court rebuked a municipal court for 'sarcastic moral lectures' toward an HIV-positive trans man in transition and ruled that authorities must first assess whether detainees are 'potentially vulnerable persons' before placement, though administrative practice remains inconsistent. In November 2025 the supreme court demanded that the national prison concept explicitly address the needs of people in or after transition, citing the Constitutional Court ruling; the human-rights commissioner is pressing for a binding regulation while the justice ministry maintains that the existing framework suffices, with consultation ongoing.

Official hostility is a live factor. An annual regional review records that after the Constitutional Court repealed the surgical prerequisite, the justice minister publicly stated his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth' and other politicians issued transphobic statements; a far-right party circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists'. The government has approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, pending in Parliament, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status. Earlier, in June 2021, the head of state described sex-reassignment surgery as 'committing a crime for inflicting self-harm' and said 'these transgenders truly disgust me'.

Discrimination and harassment are widespread. A national LGBTQ survey reported in the same review found 43% discriminated or harassed in the past five years, over a third within twelve months, with the highest rates among trans and non-binary respondents, and 51% targeted by insults, assault or threats in five years; politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% in 2018 to 71% in 2023, with 63% attributing rising intolerance to politicians. In June 2023 a group disrupted a Pride drag story-time in one city with homophobic slurs.

Enforcement of bias-crime law is modest. A regional hate crime monitoring body recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, with LGBTI-motivated incidents included in the bias breakdown; Criminal Code amendments move from a 'hostility model' to a discriminatory-selection model, but the monitoring body notes recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes.

Entry and asylum: the new Asylum Law includes SOGI grounds with an opposite-gender interview option. Anti-discrimination protection under the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in education, employment, housing and access to goods and services. Blood donation opened to all citizens regardless of partner gender on 1 July 2024, replacing the previous ban on people with a same-sex partner, though people reporting anal sex with a new partner in the past four months are still excluded. Since 2001 the country has granted 'persons living in a common household' hospital and prison visitation rights similar to married couples, alongside inheritance and succession rights in housing.

Same-sex marriage remains unresolved: a cross-party bill introduced by 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs to replace registered partnerships was backed by the caretaker government in June 2018 and cleared parliamentary committees on 29 June 2023, while a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage moved to second reading with support from several governing and opposition parties.

Facilities and social climate: the two largest cities rate highest for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, with formal nondiscrimination policies and queer districts, while harassment risk concentrates in rural areas and late-night settings. The capital's Pride parade has run annually since 2012, and a queer film festival has run in the second city every November since 2000. An April 2023 regional court ordered re-issued certificates and a diploma for a trans graduate. School-curriculum LGBTI content has prompted organised parental opt-out campaigns. Acceptance is markedly higher among younger residents: 84% of 18–29-year-olds in a 2013 survey thought homosexuality should be accepted, versus 72% of those over 50.

SVN.name: Slovenia
SVN.summary:
Slovenia is regarded as among the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe on LGBTIQ rights. Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, legal gender recognition is available, LGBTI organisations can be registered, and comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation approved on 21 April 2016 and promulgated on 9 May 2016 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, building on anti-discrimination rules in force since 2003 that bar sexual-orientation discrimination in education.

Legal gender recognition does not depend on medical treatment. In 2024 the Health Ministry officially confirmed to the Interdisciplinary Council for Gender Recognition that medical treatment is not required, and formally asked the Interior Ministry to amend the relevant Civil Registry Act sub-article.

On 29 October 2022 the Ministry of the Interior announced that the local-jurisdiction step in the gender-change procedure had been abolished on the recommendation of the Advocate of the Principle of Equality. The stated effect is that transgender people are no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of their transgender identity in their local environment.

The anti-discrimination framework is poorly enforced. The 2016 law and the earlier rules are described as vague, open to interpretation and very rarely enforced, and an ENACT national report of January 2025 documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework.

Public visibility carries a documented violence risk. At the Ljubljana Pride Parade on 17 June 2023, which drew roughly 3,500 participants, attendees faced threats, violence, insults, flag burnings and property destruction. In June 2023 a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted near the Pride route, marchers had eggs thrown at them and rainbow flags were burned on video. Police received a report of an unidentified suspect who physically assaulted two people, causing minor injuries, and were investigating attacks, theft and public-order disturbances.

Recorded incident totals remain low relative to the reported level of harm. In 2023 the organisation Legebitra documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and TransAkcija documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents. The US State Department's 2023 report on Slovenia found that no laws criminalise consensual same-sex conduct and that there were no reports of state-condoned violence, but that authorities recorded violence incidents without tracking case numbers, while local NGOs called violence against LGBTQI+ persons prevalent and under-reported.

Official reaction to the 2023 Pride attacks was delayed and uneven. LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference about attacks and rising hate; the Prime Minister took three days to react, making a statement on 20 June, while the opposition leader Janez Janša and two ministers stayed silent. Condemnations did come from the Human Rights Ombudsman, the president of the National Assembly and the President, Nataša Pirc Musar, who attended the march.

Support for victims is largely civil-society provided. The ENACT report records that civil society supplies counselling, advocacy and safe spaces for LGBTI hate-crime victims, but that LGBTI persons using generic victim-support services face heteronormative hurdles.

On partner recognition, a law passed in 2006 legalised same-sex marriage but restricted the ceremony to the two partners plus a local community registration official, with no friends or relatives; gay and lesbian organisations welcomed it as a concrete step while criticising it as insufficient. Parliament adopted a gay-marriage law in March 2015, but a conservative challenge put it to a referendum that was later lost, four days after Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to 'support the family'.
SVN.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state the current procedural requirements for legal gender recognition in Slovenia: the filing route, the competent body, processing times, required documents and any fee are not covered by this inventory, and only the removal of the local-jurisdiction step and the position on medical treatment are sourced.

Whether the Interior Ministry has completed the requested amendment to the Civil Registry Act sub-article following the Health Ministry's 2024 request is unresolved in these sources; the request itself is sourced, the outcome is not.

The present legal status of the 2006 same-sex marriage legislation after the 2015 referendum is unresolved here. The inventory records the 2006 law, the March 2015 parliamentary adoption and the lost referendum, but no source states which regime governs partnership recognition currently.

The FandM Global Barometers country page for Slovenia records no substantive finding, so it contributes nothing to the assessment of entry, screening or document rules for trans visitors.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules, passport or travel-document gender markers, airport or border screening, or access to healthcare for visitors; any statements about those questions would be unsourced.

sources.summary: Expression rights are exercised publicly but contested. During and after the march attendees faced threats, violence, insults, flag burnings and property destruction. Police received a report of an unidentified suspect who physically assaulted two people, causing minor injuries, and were investigating attacks, theft and public-order disturbances. A Pride Parade Association representative said there had not been such hostility for years. Condemnations came from the Human Rights Ombudsman, the National Assembly president, the president and, on 20 June, the prime minister, while opposition leader Janez Janša and two ministers stayed silent. Expression of LGBTI identity is exercised publicly and contested in the open. Documentation of incidents is fragmented across NGOs rather than state recording systems, with bias-motivated speech and direct incidents counted separately by different organisations, and the state recording violence without case numbers.

Residents seeking legal gender recognition are no longer subject to the local-jurisdiction step of the procedure, abolished with effect from the interior ministry notice of 29 October 2022 on the recommendation of the equality ombudsman, which removes the requirement to process the change before one's own local community.

The health ministry's 2024 position, communicated to the interdisciplinary council for gender recognition, is that medical treatment is not required for legal gender recognition, and it has asked the interior ministry to amend the corresponding civil registry law sub-article.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression is prohibited under the anti-discrimination law promulgated on 9 May 2016, with sexual-orientation protection in education dating to 2003, but residents relying on these provisions face a law described as vague, open to interpretation and very rarely enforced.

Residents who experience bias-motivated violence are more likely to be served by civil-society organisations than by generic victim-support mechanisms: a January 2025 research report records that LGBTI people using mainstream victim services encounter heteronormative hurdles, while LGBTI groups provide counselling, advocacy and safe spaces.

Incident reporting is carried out by NGOs, including an LGBTI organisation and a trans advocacy group that recorded 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and 25 direct bias-motivated incidents respectively in 2023, and local NGOs describe anti-LGBTIQ+ violence as prevalent and under-reported.
SVN.blindTangential:
The country's standing as one of the more progressive jurisdictions in the region sits alongside a visible and organised opposition. Members of the youth wing of an opposition party used biblical arguments at the June 2023 Pride parade, and social media posts associated with them carried anti-LGBTIQ+ sentiment. A Pride parade association representative said there had not been such hostility for years.

Expression of LGBTI identity is exercised publicly and contested in the open. The 17 June 2023 march in the capital ran under the slogan 'Več skupnosti, en boj' and was attended by the head of state; anti-LGBTI mobilisation has included a referendum challenge to marriage legislation and interventions from senior religious figures ahead of the December 2015 vote.

The pattern of institutional response is a recurring factor: condemnations issued by the ombudsman, the presiding officer of the parliament and the head of state, a three-day delay before the prime minister spoke, and continued silence from the opposition leader and two ministers.

Documentation of incidents is fragmented across NGOs rather than national recording systems, with bias-motivated speech and direct incidents counted separately by different organisations, and the national government recording violence without case numbers.

SRB.name: Serbia
SRB.summary:
Serbia does not criminalise consensual same-sex activity or transgender identity. Male homosexual intercourse was decriminalised in 1994 through an amendment to article 110 of the Criminal Code, and since 1 January 2006 the current Criminal Code has set an equal age of consent of 14 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. Article 62 of the 2006 Constitution defines marriage as entered into on the free consent of a man and a woman, and same-sex couples receive no legal recognition of any kind.

Police conduct is the sharpest documented exposure for a visitor. In February 2024 Serbian authorities opened an investigation into allegations that officers assaulted, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during an apartment raid in Belgrade, and no sanction against officers has been reported. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records that intolerance and violence against LGBT people remained significant concerns during 2024, and describes the state response to the July and August protests, including activist arrests and smear campaigns, as evidence of rule-of-law weaknesses. The United States State Department's 2018 human rights report listed crimes including violence targeting LGBTI individuals among the country's human rights issues.

Recorded hostility is persistent. About 105 incidents motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity were registered in 2024, and the civil-society association Da se zna! presented the eighth annual hate-crime report, 'Transphobia and Homophobia in Serbia 2024', on 2 September 2025 as the standing incident register for that year.

Custodial treatment is a live concern for anyone detained. The Association for the Prevention of Torture, acting through the national preventive mechanism, has recommended that the Penal and Correctional Institution in Padinska Skela in Belgrade allow transgender women at intake to choose a female officer for searches and body inspection rather than a male or combined search.

Trans-specific healthcare is uneven. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 reports shortages of a specific testosterone preparation during 2024, and hormone replacement therapy is not financed by health insurance, although gender-confirming surgery has been partially covered since 2012 at up to 65 per cent of costs, with the patient paying the remainder.

The community infrastructure a visitor might rely on is under pressure. The Pride Info Centre in Belgrade was attacked in January and announced its closure in September 2025, having suffered more than 20 attacks since 2018 without any being properly sanctioned. ILGA-Europe also documents a publication's analysis of 70 instances of politicians' hate speech between April 2023 and April 2024, and a survey finding that three-quarters of trans and non-binary respondents fear job interviews because of anticipated discrimination.

Protection machinery exists on paper. The Anti-Discrimination Act adopted on 26 March 2009 prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and transgender status in all areas, with 2021 amendments adding sex characteristics, and a Penal Code hate crime provision covering sexual orientation and gender identity was adopted on 24 December 2012, with the first conviction in 2018. Enforcement of both is weak: Amnesty International found in 2014 that authorities had failed to protect LGBT people and organisations from verbal, social media and physical attacks.

Public events illustrate the same pattern of violence followed by state protection. Belgrade Pride was first held in 2001 and ended in extreme violence; events planned for Belgrade in 2004 and 2009 and Novi Sad in 2007 were cancelled because police could not guarantee safety, and the 2010 Belgrade Pride drew around 6,000 anti-gay protesters and ended in riot. Belgrade Pride has been held annually since 2014 apart from 2020, when it moved online. EuroPride in September 2022 was initially banned on security grounds and opposed by President Aleksandar Vučić, then proceeded on 17 September along a shortened route under heavy police protection, with organisers reporting close to 10,000 attendees.

No source addresses entry or visa screening. Whether passport-gender presentation mismatches trigger secondary examination at Serbian border control, or any administrative practice around them, is not sourced.

The outcome of the February 2024 investigation into the Belgrade apartment raid is unresolved: sources describe the interior ministry probe as opened, and no finding, charge or sanction is reported.

Whether the Association for the Prevention of Torture's recommendation on searches of transgender women at Padinska Skela has been implemented, and how far it applies to other detention facilities, is not stated in the inventory.

The scope, dates and geographic reach of the reported testosterone supply shortage are not specified beyond its appearance in ILGA-Europe's review covering 2024. Attitudinal figures cited from 2018 and 2021 may not reflect current opinion.

sources.summary: Serbia decriminalised same-sex activity in stages: the 1860 Kaznitelni zakon (Penalty Act) of the Principality punished intercourse 'against the order of nature' between males with 6 months to 4 years' imprisonment and did not mention lesbian sexuality; the 1929 Yugoslav Criminal Code banned 'lewdness against the order of nature' between heterosexuals and homosexuals alike; the SFRY narrowed the offence in 1959 to homosexual anal intercourse with the maximum cut from 2 to 1 year. Same-sex intercourse was legalised in Vojvodina in 1977 but male homosexuality was re-criminalised when Vojvodina was reincorporated into Serbia's legal system in 1990. Male homosexual intercourse was officially decriminalised in 1994 by amending article 110 (act against order of nature), though a new subsection 4 then banned male same-sex acts for males aged 14 to 18 with up to one year's prison; an equal age of consent of 14 regardless of sexual orientation or gender took effect on 1 January 2006 under the current Criminal Code. Public expression of LGBT identity has repeatedly been suppressed: the first Belgrade Gay Pride in 2001 ended in extreme violence, and Pride events in Belgrade (2004, 2009) and Novi Sad (2007) were cancelled because police could not guarantee safety against violent opponents. The 2010 Belgrade Pride went ahead with about a thousand participants but was met by the Belgrade anti-gay riot, attended by 6,000 anti-gay protesters and extreme nationalist group members; Amnesty International noted in May 2014 that public authorities had repeatedly banned pride parades on the basis of violent threats from homophobic groups and had failed to protect LGBTQ individuals and organisations from verbal, social media and physical attacks. Belgrade Pride successfully took place in September 2014 and has been held annually since, except in 2020 when it moved online for COVID-19, with local mayors and some ministers attending. EuroPride in September 2022 was initially banned by authorities on security grounds and opposed by President Vučić, but proceeded on 17 September along a shortened route under heavy police protection, with organisers reporting almost 10,000 attendees; Novi Sad held its first gay pride rally on 17 May 2019. Serbia had no legal protections specifically aimed at LGBTQ rights until 2002, when the Broadcasting Act barred broadcasters from spreading information encouraging discrimination, hate and violence based on sexual orientation and the Information Act of 2003 added comparable media duties; the Radiodiffusion Agency never effectively acted against offenders. In 2005 the Labor Act banned sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, the Act on Higher Education guaranteed equal rights regardless of sexual orientation in higher education institutions, and on 5 July 2011 Parliament approved a youth act prohibiting discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation and regulating local-government measures for young people. On 26 March 2009 Parliament approved the unified Anti-Discrimination Act, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and transgender status in all areas, with 2021 amendments adding sex characteristics, making Serbia one of the first Western Balkan countries to do so. A Penal Code hate crime provision covering sexual orientation and gender identity was adopted on 24 December 2012, with the first conviction in 2018; enforcement remains weak, and Amnesty International noted in 2014 that authorities had failed to protect LGBTQ individuals and organisations from discrimination including verbal and social media threats and physical attacks. Sex change surgeries have been partially covered by Serbia's statewide basic medical insurance since a Health Insurance Act change approved on 28 July 2011 (effective 2012), with government-financed insurance covering up to 65% of surgery costs and the patient paying the remainder; hormone replacement therapy is not financed by health insurance. Belgrade was described by The New York Times in 2012 as a hub for sex reassignment surgery because prices were far lower than in neighbouring and Western countries. Access remains poor in the eyes of those affected: a reported 90% of LGBT individuals in Serbia say medical institutions are not adequately responding to their needs, and Jovanka Todorović of Gayten-LGBT said about 80% of Serbian transgender people are not willing to undergo surgery. The Ministry of Health barred people with a 'history of homosexual relations during the last five years' from donating reproductive cells for artificial insemination or IVF in early 2019, removing the provision on 23 April 2021; official medical textbooks circulated classifying homosexuality under 'sexual deviations and disorders' until the Serbian Medical Society confirmed in a 2008 letter to Labris that same-sex orientation is not a disease, homosexuality having been removed from the official disease list in 1997 with ICD-10. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Map ranked Serbia 29th of 49 European countries with a 34% score, down from 27th in 2024. Same-sex couples have never been recognised by law, and the Serbian Constitution adopted in November 2006 effectively bans same-sex marriage through Article 62, which defines marriage as entered into based on the free consent of a man and a woman; civil unions and domestic partnerships are neither explicitly mentioned nor prohibited. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couples cannot legally adopt. Plans to legalise domestic partnerships by amending the Civil Code were announced in June 2019, covering joint property and alimony but not inheritance, adoption or surrogacy; in July 2019 a Novi Sad lesbian couple, Jelena Dubović and Sunčica Kopunović, were turned away when they tried to register a civil partnership and sued, with legal experts doubting they would win. Minister Gordana Čomić announced in November 2020 that a same-sex partnership law would reach parliament in the first half of 2021, and a draft went to public consultation in February 2021, but President Vučić said in May 2021 he would not sign it as unconstitutional, the bill stalled without a vote, and he reaffirmed in August 2023 he would sign no such law in his term. In September 2024 the Green-Left Front submitted a new Draft Law on Civil Partnership covering maintenance, inheritance and health and social insurance, still unscheduled for a vote as of 2026; the 2023 ECHR Grand Chamber ruling in Fedotova and Others v. Russia holds that Council of Europe states including Serbia have a positive obligation to provide some form of legal recognition for same-sex couples. Public opinion is split: 2021 Civil Rights Defenders data shows 26% support for same-sex marriage but 80% believing LGBTI+ persons should have at least some of the rights in a same-sex union law, second-highest in the Western Balkans after Montenegro, with 2018 data cited by the U.S. State Department showing 70% opposing an LGBT person inheriting a deceased partner's property. Attitudes toward LGBT young people and parenting remain hostile: 2018 data cited in the U.S. State Department human rights report found 48% of parents would seek medical treatment for their LGBT child and 90% opposed child adoption by an LGBT person, while a 2022 World Values Survey found 65% of Serbians disagreed that homosexual couples are as good parents as other couples. Support is markedly higher among younger (18 to 29) and university-educated respondents in Belgrade and Vojvodina, and 2021 Civil Rights Defenders data records a general improvement in attitudes toward LGBTI+ issues over the preceding five years, though 57% still believe homosexuality is a disease.

HRV.name: Croatia
HRV.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal in Croatia since 1977, and open military service is available. Hate-crime legislation covers sexual orientation and gender identity, and the Penal Code equalised the age of consent at 14 in 1998 and raised it to 15 with effect from 1 January 2013. Registered life partnerships have existed since 2014, but a 2013 constitutional referendum barred same-sex marriage. Same-sex couples have obtained family rights only through litigation: the Constitutional Court ruled on 7 February 2020 that excluding same-sex couples from foster care was unconstitutional and discriminatory, Mladen Kožić and Ivo Šegota became Croatia's first same-sex foster parents in September 2020 after a three-year battle, and full adoption rights were confirmed by a final court ruling in 2022.

Legal gender recognition rests on a 2013 legislative amendment that allows a gender marker to be registered without altering sex characteristics. A 2026 analysis in a Croatian legal journal works through the Criminal Procedure Act, the Police Powers Act, the Customs Act and the law governing prison sentences to set out how police, customs and court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming people, and records case studies of the difficulties that arise in practice.

Formal protection outpaces enforcement. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report recorded minority representatives saying that anti-discrimination provisions in employment, housing, education and health are not consistently enforced, NGOs reporting uneven judicial handling of discrimination cases and limited access to justice, with victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial, and hate-crime investigations judged inadequate. A 2018 Zagreb Pride documentation report on Croatia's implementation of Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 compiled hate-crime data and case studies alongside findings on under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crime, hate speech, freedom of assembly, employment discrimination, legal gender recognition and partnership recognition. A European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination, published in 2024 for the 2023 reporting period, covers transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives including sexual orientation and gender identity grounds.

Hostility is documented in official and public settings. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 records that a session of the Croatian Parliament on 'Gender Ideology' featured speakers spreading misinformation with no LGBTI organisations invited, that the first Pula Pride march faced disruption the day before, and that a Zadar prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking arising from a 2018 incident. The 2018 Zagreb Pride report further documented hate-speech case studies and constraints on freedom of assembly.

For visitors, a commercial country guide assesses Croatia as widely accepting of LGBTQIA+ travellers but notes that public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in less-populated cities and that gay venues are virtually non-existent outside the capital, with new venues appearing in several coastal and regional towns. Community infrastructure includes three LGBT centres, in the capital, in Split (opened 24 May 2014) and in Rijeka (opened 16 October 2014 as LGBTIQ+ Druga Rijeka), alongside Pride marches in Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac and Pula and the Balkans Trans Inter March.
HRV.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced: no source in the inventory addresses visa rules, passport gender markers, or entry and border screening procedures for transgender travellers, so what a trans visitor faces on arrival at Croatian passport control is unknown here. The Wikipedia overview is explicit that it says nothing about these matters.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no incident-level reporting on violence against transgender people in Croatia with dates and outcomes; the hate-crime material cited is aggregate or from 2018-era monitoring, and enforcement findings date from the 2021 reporting year.

EST.name: Estonia
EST.summary:
Estonia decriminalises same-sex relations nationwide and has permitted marriage equality since June 2023, the first Baltic state to reach that point, with joint adoption included. Opposition filed more than 700 amendments to block the bill and every one failed.

Legal gender recognition remains medicalised. A psychiatric diagnosis and physiological alteration are required, and no nonbinary identity is recognised. Advocacy continues for recognition based on self-determination, and the national action plan adopted in 2025 commits the state to updating the legal framework so that gender identity and expression are protected.

Anti-discrimination coverage is uneven. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, while housing protections are recorded by one source as covering sexual orientation only and by another as extending to gender identity. Conversion therapy is not banned. Access to facilities corresponding to a person's gender identity is recorded as protected.

Hate-speech and hate-crime legislation does not include gender identity, and no hate-crime protection on that ground is recorded. Advocacy for explicit hate-speech and hate-crime laws continues.

The reported social climate is comparatively open but guarded. In the 2024 EU rights-agency survey, 62% of LGBTIQ respondents avoided holding hands with a same-sex partner against an EU-27 figure of 53%, 40% avoided certain locations for fear of assault against 29%, and 38% were open about being LGBTIQ against 51%. Discrimination at work was reported by 12%, below the EU average of 19%.

No murders of gender-identity minorities are known in the recorded period.

The date of the action plan is given generally as 2025 in one source and as December in another; both refer to the same instrument, but the exact approval date is unresolved here.

The 2018 TGEU and ILGA-Europe compliance report on Estonia's implementation of Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 covers hate crimes and data collection, safety of LGBT people deprived of liberty, hate speech, association, expression, transgender-specific health and private life, employment, education, housing, sports and asylum; its individual findings are not itemised in the available inventory and remain unverified for this record.

The absence of a conversion-therapy ban and the protected status of bathroom access rest on a single comparative database and are not corroborated by a second source. The concealment ranking and survey percentages from that database are undated.

Recognition arrived through litigation as much as legislation. Implementation gaps in the 2014 cohabitation act forced court challenges: in 2016 an appeal court ordered a county government to register a same-sex marriage concluded abroad, and courts repeatedly found unequal treatment unconstitutional before the half-law arrangement ended with marriage equality in 2023.

LTU.name: Lithuania
LTU.summary:
Lithuania imposes no LGBT-specific entry, visa or residence screening. A trans visitor may enter and move about the country without facing any question about gender identity at the border.

The country offers no working route to legal gender recognition. Article 5.1 of the Lithuanian Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to change gender through medical intervention, but no implementing legislation has ever been adopted. The Lithuanian Gay League describes the resulting gap as 18 years of legal limbo; LRT and an earlier LGL report count 17. The two counts refer to the same condition: a statutory right with no procedure behind it.

The courts declined to close that gap twice in 2025. In August the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case concerning the amendment of civil-status gender documents and referred to the Constitutional Court the question of whether the relevant provisions comply with the Constitution. In September the Constitutional Court declined to examine the request, leaving the absence of legal provisions for changing gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents intact.

The practical consequence for a visitor is that documents are read as issued. A foreign passport or identity document carrying a gender marker inconsistent with the holder's presentation will not be matched against any Lithuanian process of recognition, because no such process exists for residents either. The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson's 2024 national review records both the absence of a legal framework and the absence of a strategic approach to trans rights in the country.

Protection machinery for gender-based violence is thin. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records a systemic lack of targeted support for LGBTI hate-crime victims. Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code explicitly bans public instigation of violence against LGBT people, and a 2010 preliminary investigation found that 160 of roughly 180 hate-speech instances, most of them online, concerned the LGBT community; perpetrators were usually fined and computers were occasionally confiscated.

Public assembly carries a documented record of police failure. In April 2024 the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police had failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly, citing an inadequate response to hostile provocators at an LGL assembly, and recommended measures to ensure effective assembly rights. Pride events have been repeatedly obstructed: permission refused in 2007, a court halt in 2010 overturned one day before Baltic Pride proceeded amid heavy policing and violence with 12 protesters arrested, and the 2013 march allowed only after litigation through all judicial instances, ending with 28 arrests. Attendance has since risen to roughly 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and around 5,000 in 2023.

Partner recognition exists in partial form. Marriage is limited to opposite-sex couples under Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code. On 17 April 2025 the Constitutional Court ruled that the absence of legal regulation of partnership institutions, including for same-sex couples, contradicts the Constitution and granted same-sex couples the right to register partnerships through the courts until the Seimas adopts a comprehensive law. Since January 2019 the Constitutional Court has required that foreign same-sex spouses be granted residence permits, following the 2018 European Court of Justice ruling in Coman and Others.

Harassment in employment is well documented. Reporting in May 2025 set out trans people's accounts of open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse at work, with experts describing systemic labour-market discrimination.

Official hostility has an explicit legislative history. In 2013 the Seimas considered five separate anti-gay and anti-trans bills, among them a ban on gender reassignment on the stated basis that gender is determined genetically from conception, a same-sex adoption ban, fines of up to €1,800 for organisers of events denigrating constitutional moral values, and legalisation of anti-gay speech; the bills did not pass. The Law on the Protection of Minors passed in 2009 by an 87-6 override of President Adamkus's veto banned information on homosexuality accessible to minors; Amnesty International called it a huge step backwards. On 18 December 2024 the Constitutional Court struck down the anti-LGBT provisions of that law as violating Article 25, freedom of speech, and in January 2023 the ECHR Grand Chamber had ruled that the 2014 ban on a children's book depicting same-sex relationships violated Article 10.

Sources differ on the length of the legal gender recognition gap, counting it as 18 years in September 2025 and 17 years in August 2025. The discrepancy is not reconciled in the available material; both describe the same unimplemented Civil Code provision.

No source in the inventory addresses how Lithuanian authorities treat a foreign passport carrying a non-binary or otherwise amended gender marker at the border or in daily document checks. That question remains unresolved here.

Whether any trans person has yet obtained a court-ordered partnership registration under the April 2025 ruling is not sourced, nor is the timeline for the Seimas to enact a registered-partnership statute.

The inventory contains no figures specific to trans people on hate-crime reporting, prosecution outcomes or police complaint procedures; the available hate-speech data dates from 2010 and is not broken down by gender identity.

Healthcare barriers are listed as a heading of the 2024 national review, but the specific findings of that section are not reproduced in the summary document available here.

sources.summary: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal in Lithuania since 1993, two years after the end of Soviet occupation; it had been criminal during the interwar period and under Soviet rule. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 2003 to meet EU accession criteria, then raised to 16 on 2 July 2010 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, a rule that applies equally to gay and straight youth. Public instigation of violence against LGBT people is explicitly banned under Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code; a 2010 preliminary investigation found 160 of roughly 180 hate-speech instances, mostly online, concerned the LGBT community, with perpetrators usually fined and computers occasionally confiscated. Two attempts to criminalise 'public propagation of homosexual relations' with fines of 2,000–10,000 litas were made, in 2011 unanimously rejected by Parliament and in 2013 also rejected. Lithuania's most prominent expression restrictions targeted minors: a 16 June 2009 amendment to the Law on the Protection of Minors banned the 'propaganda of homosexual, bisexual or polygamous relations' for under-18s; the presidential veto was overturned by Parliament, but on 22 December 2009 the anti-LGBT clauses were replaced with a broader ban on information promoting conceptions of marriage or family other than those in the Constitution. That provision was used to restrict a Vilnius Pride 2013 advertisement to night-time broadcast with an adult-content logo over a T-shirt reading 'For the diversity of families', and in 2014 the children's book 'Gintarinė širdis' was age-labelled and then banned by the Ministry of Culture because two stories involved same-sex relationships; the ECHR Grand Chamber ruled in January 2023 that this violated Article 10. On 18 December 2024 the Constitutional Court struck down the anti-LGBT provisions as violating Article 25, freedom of speech. Article 39.1 of the Public Information Act, amended 30 September 2010, briefly barred messages that 'depict or promote a sexual orientation'; this was described as a translation error and removed on 16 June 2011, with sexual orientation added as a protected ground. Pride events have been repeatedly obstructed: Vilnius City Council refused permission in 2007 citing security; Baltic Pride 2010 was halted by a court shortly before it began, overturned one day prior, then held amid heavy policing and violence with 12 protesters arrested; the 2013 march required litigation through all judicial instances to be allowed on Gedimino Avenue, about 500 participants and 28 arrests including MP Petras Gražulis. Participation has since grown, to around 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and around 5,000 in 2023. In 2014 all major TV stations refused a pro-tolerance LGBT video clip over fears of breaching the Minors law. In January 2019 the Lithuanian Constitutional Court ruled that foreign same-sex spouses must be granted residence permits, following the 2018 European Court of Justice ruling in Coman and Others. LVA.name: Latvia
LVA.summary:
Latvia has no dedicated statute on legal gender recognition, and in June 2025 coalition members of the Saeima said trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet." No targeted legislation has been adopted for transgender or nonbinary Latvians, and nonbinary identity is not recognised. Latvian law does not define "sex change": on the available account, an identity-document change has been granted on presentation of a medical certificate, and in 2008 the Supreme Court held that authorities should have granted recognition to a transgender person refused one in 2004 after partial sex change. A 2009 Saeima proposal that would have required sterilisation as a condition of changing legal gender was rejected.

One trans immigrant told LSM that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples, codified in November 2023, have been in force since 1 July 2024. They carry rights similar to marriage apart from adoption and inheritance, they do not constitute marriage, and same-sex couples cannot marry; a 2006 constitutional amendment defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman.

Adoption rules restrict couples: any person over 25 may adopt, but persons not married to each other may not adopt the same child, so in unmarried couples only one partner may adopt. In April 2023 the Saeima amended the Law on the Protection of the Children's Rights to bar foreign same-sex couples from adopting Latvian children. A 2020 court ruling in favour of parental leave rights for same-sex couples led to a Justice Ministry draft civil union law in 2022, and lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment.

Male homosexuality was decriminalised in 1992 and female homosexuality was never criminalised; the age of consent was equalised at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation in 1999. No source documents criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, or any legal restriction on access to sex-segregated facilities.

The principal institutional failure concerns hate-crime enforcement. In Hanovs v. Latvia, decided unanimously on 18 July 2024, the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after a 2020 homophobic attack on a gay couple in Riga: the aggressor admitted anti-gay slurs, no criminal charges were brought, and the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter disposed of with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

After the judgment the Prosecutor General reopened criminal proceedings in the Hanovs case. In Daugavpils the Prosecutor General likewise ordered an investigation reopened after police closed the case against two people who had been attacked. An administrative court overturned a denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker, and homophobic posts by former MEP Mamikins were investigated.

The Labour Code has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in the workplace since September 2006, a protection a president refused to sign the bill without. No source records a corresponding protection on the basis of gender identity.
LVA.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the availability of legal gender recognition. One account holds that identity change is possible in Latvia on the basis of a medical certificate, supported by a 2008 Supreme Court ruling and the absence of any statutory definition of "sex change," while reporting from June 2025 states that transgender and nonbinary Latvians lack any procedure and have no targeted legislation. Whether a usable procedure exists for a given applicant, and on what terms, remains unresolved on this inventory.

Entry, visa and border-document rules applicable to transgender or nonbinary travellers, including any screening of gender markers against passports, are not addressed by any source reviewed here. The same is true of access to sex-segregated facilities, of which the sources record no restriction; absence of sourcing is not evidence that no restriction exists.

No source documents hate-crime sentencing outcomes or penalties beyond the lenient fine imposed in the case that reached the European Court of Human Rights, and no source states whether gender identity is a recognised aggravating or protected characteristic in Latvian criminal law.

The account of gender recognition rests substantially on a secondary reference work rather than on Latvian statute text, and the description of the 2004 refusal and 2008 Supreme Court ruling has not been checked against the judgment itself.

LVA.localsOnly:
The LGBT scene is concentrated in Riga. Outside the capital the sparse population means there are no bars, clubs, stores or libraries of the kind established since democratisation, so social and community space for residents in regional areas is effectively absent.

Residents face an adoption structure in which only one partner in an unmarried couple may adopt a child, and a 2020 court ruling on parental leave for same-sex couples fed a Justice Ministry draft civil union law in 2022 that has not displaced the registered-partnership route.

The Ombudsman's 2018 call for a partnership law rested on the observation that about half of Latvian children are born out of wedlock and should enjoy legal protections regardless of their parents' status.

Workplace discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited since the September 2006 Labour Code amendments, which President Vaira Vīķe-Freiberga declined to sign until that protection was included. No equivalent gender-identity protection appears in the sources.

Healthcare: lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment, and surgical gender affirmation is available; legal identity change has been pursued through the courts with a medical certificate rather than through an administrative procedure.
LVA.blindSummary:
The country has no dedicated statute on legal gender recognition, and in June 2025 coalition members of the national parliament said trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet." No targeted legislation has been adopted for transgender or nonbinary residents of the country, and nonbinary identity is not recognised. National law does not define "sex change": on the available account, an identity-document change has been granted on presentation of a medical certificate, and in 2008 the highest court held that authorities should have granted recognition to a transgender person refused one in 2004 after partial sex change. A 2009 parliamentary proposal that would have required sterilisation as a condition of changing legal gender was rejected.

One trans immigrant told a national broadcaster that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples, codified in November 2023, have been in force since 1 July 2024. They carry rights similar to marriage apart from adoption and inheritance, they do not constitute marriage, and same-sex couples cannot marry; a 2006 constitutional amendment defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman.

Adoption rules restrict couples: any person over 25 may adopt, but persons not married to each other may not adopt the same child, so in unmarried couples only one partner may adopt. In April 2023 the national parliament amended the Law on the Protection of the Children's Rights to bar foreign same-sex couples from adopting the country's children. A 2020 court ruling in favour of parental leave rights for same-sex couples led to a justice ministry draft civil union law in 2022, and lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment.

Male homosexuality was decriminalised in 1992 and female homosexuality was never criminalised; the age of consent was equalised at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation in 1999. No source documents criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, or any legal restriction on access to sex-segregated facilities.

The principal institutional failure concerns hate-crime enforcement. In a case decided unanimously on 18 July 2024, a regional human rights court found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after a 2020 homophobic attack on a gay couple in the capital: the aggressor admitted anti-gay slurs, no criminal charges were brought, and the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter disposed of with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

After the judgment the Prosecutor General reopened criminal proceedings in that case. In a regional city the Prosecutor General likewise ordered an investigation reopened after police closed the case against two people who had been attacked. An administrative court overturned a denial of asylum to an LGBTI seeker from another country, and homophobic posts by a former member of the regional parliament were investigated.

The Labour Code has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in the workplace since September 2006, a protection a president refused to sign the bill without. No source records a corresponding protection on the basis of gender identity.
LVA.blindOutOfScope:
The sources conflict on the availability of legal gender recognition. One account holds that identity change is possible in the country on the basis of a medical certificate, supported by a 2008 highest-court ruling and the absence of any statutory definition of "sex change," while reporting from June 2025 states that transgender and nonbinary people lack any procedure and have no targeted legislation. Whether a usable procedure exists for a given applicant, and on what terms, remains unresolved on this inventory.

Entry, visa and border-document rules applicable to transgender or nonbinary travellers, including any screening of gender markers against passports, are not addressed by any source reviewed here. The same is true of access to sex-segregated facilities, of which the sources record no restriction; absence of sourcing is not evidence that no restriction exists.

No source documents hate-crime sentencing outcomes or penalties beyond the lenient fine imposed in the case that reached the regional human rights court, and no source states whether gender identity is a recognised aggravating or protected characteristic in national criminal law.

The account of gender recognition rests substantially on a secondary reference work rather than on statute text, and the description of the 2004 refusal and 2008 highest-court ruling has not been checked against the judgment itself.
