An analysis of the ruling clarifies the positive obligations of nations in homophobic-attack cases — thorough investigation and punishment of hate crimes, sending a message of zero tolerance; it notes the troubling pattern of regional nations failing to protect LGBTI+ persons and to investigate effectively.

LVA.tangentialFactors:
Latvia ranked 24th of 27 European Union countries in ILGA-Europe's 2023 assessment of LGBT rights protection, placing it in the lower tier of the union rather than outside its protections.

Strasbourg Observers' analysis of Hanovs v. Latvia treats the judgment as a further clarification of states' positive obligations: authorities must thoroughly investigate and punish hate crimes as a signal of zero tolerance, and the commentary places Latvia within a troubling pattern of states in one part of Europe failing to protect LGBTI people and to investigate effectively.

Religious and political hostility has been voiced publicly. In 2007 the Archbishop of Riga, Cardinal Jānis Pujats, described homosexuality as "total corruption in the sexual arena" and "an unnatural form of prostitution," demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage, and called for crowds of 40,000 to 50,000 to counter Pride, which he framed as a foreign-inspired action.

Public assembly has nonetheless proceeded. Around 8,000 people marched in Baltic Pride 2018 in Riga, an annual event rotating among Baltic capitals and organised by Mozaika under the motto "See Diversity! See Freedom!" In 2023 Latvia became the first European Union country to elect an openly gay head of state.

A 2006 constitutional amendment defining marriage as a union between a man and a woman is framed in terms of the family structure in which Latvian children are raised, which is the constitutional grounding for excluding same-sex marriage.

TUR.name: Turkey
TUR.summary:
Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, and the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. For a trans visitor, that requirement intersects with identity checks on the street: in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee's account captures the practical position: nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded, and officers were already applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a draft legislative package then before the government would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague provisions protecting 'the family' and 'public morals'. The Erdoğan government has repeatedly used that framing to legitimise stigmatisation, and the reform sits within a broader authoritarian drift. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions — 256 taken on the record and 43 off it — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Hostility of this scale is best read as state policy rather than residual prejudice.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. Comparable asymmetry recurs in custody: on 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Event attendance carries its own exposure: monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
TUR.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the draft legislative package reported by Human Rights Watch in October 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved in the available sources; the inventory establishes its existence and its framing, not its current status. Similarly, the passage date and final text of the 12th judicial reform package are not sourced beyond the statement that provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill.

The Istanbul detainees' reference to 'the new law' that officers were already enforcing is not identified in the source and cannot be matched to a specific instrument; it is reported here as their characterisation rather than as a confirmed statutory change. The legal status of General Information Gathering checks remains contested, with experts citing European Convention on Human Rights Article 5 but no reported judicial ruling supplied.

Several population-level and sourcing details are drawn from a Wikipedia compilation rather than primary documentation, including the surgery and marker requirements, the polling figures, the CHP bill and the 2013 draft talks. These are plausible and internally consistent but were not independently verified against the underlying sources. The 2008 Human Rights Watch material is historical and predates the 2018 legal changes; it should not be read as current law. Accounts of the Sincan prison death derive from rights-group and lawyer testimony reported through Kaos GL and have not been corroborated by an official investigation, which the sources say had not begun in the first two days after the death.

sources.title: LGBTQI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches (Kaos GL), reporting the Prison Insider 'Country Profile' on Turkey (with CİSST data)
sources.summary: Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Turkey has no visa, entry or border rules specific to LGBTQ travelers; the available material concerns people already in the country. LGBT individuals are among the most vulnerable asylum seekers and refugees in Turkey, and their access to rights and services is limited by anti-LGBTQ sentiment among state actors and the general public.

Sex reassignment surgery is available in Turkey's major cities (Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir and Antalya) and the minimum age for the procedure is 18. To change the gender marker on an identity card, the procedure must be conducted at a state hospital. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors needing continued medication must arrange and pay for it privately.

Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection regarding gender identity in Turkish law. The EU Commission's 2025 annual report wrote that legal protection of LGBTIQ persons is insufficient and not aligned with the EU acquis, and that authorities were granting official permissions for demonstrations promoting exclusion and discrimination. Bills to introduce such protections have been repeatedly proposed (CHP, February 2015) and constitutional protection agreed in 2013 draft talks, but the drafts were cancelled; KAOS GL has a case pending since 2023 alleging ineffective remedies against discrimination such as Pride bans. The government considered legislation criminalizing public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years' imprisonment, though it was not included in the 2026 judicial package.

Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as joint parents. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, which made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, but these carry no legal marital status. Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, so individuals who have legally changed their registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender; LGBT marriage for non-trans people remains legally impossible.

Youth opinion is more accepting: a 2020 Pew Research Center survey found acceptance of homosexuality higher among youth (34%) and educated respondents (41%) than the 25% national figure, and Kadir Has University polling showed support for equal rights rising from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020. Student organizing exists: the Lesbian and Gay Inter-University Organization (LEGATO) formed in 1996 with groups at several universities by 2014, yet in May 2019 police broke up a student Pride march at Middle East Technical University, arresting at least 25 students. Minors are a stated focus of the crackdown: Erdoğan's May 2025 "Decade of Family and Population" declaration (starting 2026) attacked the LGBTQ movement as a threat to children, and the September 2026 "My Family is Safe" raids against LGBTQ+ and HIV support organizations were framed as protecting children, with 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses under investigation. In April 2026 the İzmir group Genç LGBTI+ was ordered to dissolve with eleven founders put on trial, and RTÜK's stated goal includes "protecting children, youth and the family structure," backing fines against Amazon Prime Video, Disney+, HBO Max, Netflix and Mubi for LGBTQ+ content. For trans youth, the minimum age for sex reassignment surgery is 18 and the procedure must be performed at a state hospital to change an identity-card gender marker.

A national LGBT organisation (7 May 2024), reporting a prison-monitoring organisation's country profile prepared with a penal-system civil-society association and using international data: LGBTI+ prisoners in the country's prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. According to the penal-system association's observations, there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that the prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. Documents that trans and LGBTI+ prisoners are managed through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.
TUR.blindLocalsOnly:
Same-sex relationships carry no legal recognition: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as joint parents. Marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than on trans status, so someone who has legally changed their registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender, while marriage between two non-trans people of the same sex remains impossible. The 12th judicial reform package removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people from the bill, which made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, but these carry no legal marital status.

Sex reassignment surgery is available in several large cities at a minimum age of 18, and a gender-marker change on an identity card requires the procedure to be performed at a state hospital. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by public healthcare and must be paid for privately.

Discrimination has no statutory remedy. Bills to introduce protection were proposed by the main opposition party in February 2015 and constitutional protection was agreed in 2013 draft talks before the drafts were cancelled, and an LGBTI+ rights group has had a case pending since 2023 alleging ineffective remedies against discrimination such as Pride bans. The government considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years' imprisonment; that provision was not included in the 2026 judicial package.

Organisational space has narrowed sharply. In April 2026 a city-based LGBTI+ group was ordered to dissolve with eleven founders put on trial, and the September 2026 raids framed as child protection targeted LGBTQ+ and HIV support organisations across the country. LGBT individuals are among the most vulnerable asylum seekers and refugees in the country, and their access to rights and services is limited by anti-LGBTQ sentiment among state actors and the public.

Prison conditions for LGBTI+ inmates are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement: a country prison profile prepared with a penal-system reform association using international LGBTI+ body data records arbitrary body and strip searches, solitary confinement with restricted healthcare, frequent transfers that disrupt visits, ineffective complaints that can invite further violence, and an administration built on a binary, heteronormative model with no staff training. The prison death case confirms placement by registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison.
TUR.tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 2008 report 'We Need a Law for Liberation', built from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented a long-standing history of beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people in Turkey. It predates the legal changes of 2018 and should not be read as a description of current law, but it establishes continuity with the pattern the 2025 data quantify.

The child-protection framing is the organising rhetoric of the current crackdown. Erdoğan's May 2025 'Decade of Family and Population' declaration, taking effect in 2026, cast the LGBTQ movement as a threat to children, and the September 2026 'My Family is Safe' raids on LGBTQ+ and HIV support organisations were presented in the same terms, placing 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses under investigation. The broadcast regulator's stated goals include protecting children, youth and the family structure, and it has fined Amazon Prime Video, Disney+, HBO Max, Netflix and Mubi over LGBTQ+ content.

Public opinion runs noticeably ahead of the state. A 2020 Pew Research Center survey found acceptance of homosexuality at 34% among youth and 41% among educated respondents against a 25% national figure, and Kadir Has University polling put support for equal rights at 45% in 2020, up from 33% in 2016. Student organising has existed since the Lesbian and Gay Inter-University Organization formed in 1996, though police broke up a student Pride march at Middle East Technical University in May 2019 and arrested at least 25 students.

The institutional drift in healthcare is worth flagging alongside the entry picture: after a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular added 'gender reassignment' to the official reasons for medical-board reports, hospitals were barred from using the 'other' option and instructed to issue e-reports, a change contested as an online 'LGBT opening' and which risks profiling trans patients.

DNK.name: Denmark
DNK.summary:
Denmark has permitted legal gender recognition by self-declaration since 1 September 2014. A person changes their registered sex by submitting a stated request and observing a six-month reflection period, without medical evaluation or psychiatric diagnosis. It was the first jurisdiction in Europe to adopt this model, and it is the reference point cited in contemporary reporting on the country's trans legal framework.

Danish passports are issued with an 'X' sex descriptor, so non-binary people can hold a travel document that asserts neither a male nor a female marker.

Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is prohibited. The Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment and services. The 1996 Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market listed sexual orientation but did not name gender identity or expression; a 2015 ruling in a case brought by a trans woman against her former employer held that gender identity and gender expression are covered by that law. Hate-crime provisions introduced through 2004 amendments to the Penal Code add penalties for offences motivated by sexual orientation.

In September 2024 the Danish Supreme Court held that serving a sentence in a men's prison department does not violate the human rights of a trans inmate. That judgment is the leading domestic authority on where trans prisoners are placed in custody, and a trans visitor or resident facing detention should expect placement to follow sex assigned at birth rather than gender identity.

Violence against trans people is documented. In July 2024 a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen. Hate speech targeting sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics recurs annually. In its 2023 review the UN Committee Against Torture found that some trans people, some queer, trans, intersex, Black, Indigenous and people of colour, and some migrants report being denied access to spaces and services and being subjected to threats. The same review recorded that anti-trans discourse intensified while parliament debated lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition, and it urged Denmark to provide psychosocial counselling and to remedy intersex practices.

Denmark has a record of granting protection to trans asylum claimants. In February 2013 a Guatemalan trans woman became the first transgender person granted asylum in the country, refused return on the basis of her gender identity after citing police attacks and threats linked to her trans activism.

In practice, access to gender-affirming healthcare is still gated. Patients seeking hormone therapy report being required to present in ways that conform to stereotypical gender roles, including trans men being expected to give 'male' answers in clinical settings.
DNK.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not establish whether the hate-crime penalty enhancements introduced through the 2004 Penal Code amendments extend to offences motivated by gender identity or gender expression; the provisions cited name sexual orientation only. Whether a trans-motivated attack would attract an enhanced penalty is therefore unresolved here.

The status of the conversion-therapy prohibition bill revived in August 2026 is unresolved; the sources record the revival but not a vote or enactment.

Whether the multi-parent family plan announced in August 2024 has been legislated is not sourced.

The sources record the UN Committee Against Torture's recommendations on psychosocial counselling and on remedy for intersex practices, but not whether Denmark has implemented them.

The sources do not say whether the parliamentary debate on lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition produced a legislative change, or what the current minimum age is.

Healthcare gatekeeping for hormone therapy is described through patient reports rather than through clinical protocol documents; the formal criteria applied by Danish gender clinics are not sourced here.

NOR.name: Norway
NOR.summary:
Norwegian law contains no offence targeting trans people. In November 2020 the Storting amended the Penal Code so that hate speech under Paragraph 135a covers bisexual and transgender people as well as sexual orientation; the amendment took effect in 2020 and Reuters reported it as an extension of criminal liability to anti-trans hate speech. The hate-crime framework recorded by OSCE/ODIHR defines hate crimes as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability, and any offence so motivated is recorded under that framework.

Legal gender recognition runs on self-declaration with no medical-intervention requirement. Under the Gender Recognition Act as set out on the official helsenorge.no health-rights page, the change of legal gender is decided at the tax office on the basis of the individual's own perception of their gender identity: from age 16 on the person's own application, between 6 and 16 with parental consent, and below 6 only for documented congenital differences of sex development. A 2017 regulation governs the document change for citizens resident abroad.

Gender-affirming healthcare does not follow the same self-declaration route. Access still requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the National Treatment Centre for Gender Incongruence (NTCGI) at Oslo University Hospital, where only about a quarter of referred patients are admitted to treatment and those disqualified have no alternative options. A 2023 report found non-binary people still without treatment despite a 2020 guideline calling for equal access. For minors, 2020 guidelines recommend puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 following interdisciplinary assessment.

Reported hate crime is rising while clearance falls. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records an 18% increase in reported hate crimes in 2023, with the largest rises in offences motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, and antisemitism. NRK reported record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate dropped from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims told police they have little trust in the authorities, while a dedicated hate-crime group continues to encourage reporting. Official figures undercount by a wide margin: the HATECYCLE study at the University of Oslo surveyed more than 3,000 LGBTQI people and found that only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police, citing mistrust, procedural obstacles, fear of personal costs, and dismissive treatment by officers where reporting did occur.

Violence remains the principal offset to that legal position. A gunman killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022; the perpetrator, Zaniar Matapour, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years, the strictest penalty available. The same review period recorded a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime and online threats against a drag bingo event. The Police Security Service (PST) reported a significant decline in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, while warning that hate speech and intimidation risks persist, particularly during Pride, and that most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than to act.

Discrimination protection is long-standing and explicit as to gender identity. Norway was the first country to enact LGBT anti-discrimination law, amending Paragraph 349a of the Penal Code in 1981 to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation in goods and services and at public gatherings; employment discrimination on sexual grounds has been banned since 1998, and since 2013 Section 5 of the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination on the grounds of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression prohibits discrimination based on gender identity and expression. Norway is among the few countries explicitly protecting intersex people from discrimination. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 January 2009 with full rights including religious weddings, adoption and assisted reproduction, building on a registered partnership law from 1993 and recognition of unregistered same-sex cohabitation since 1991 for limited rights such as next-of-kin medical decisions; in 2024 Norway was ranked the best country in the world for same-sex couples to marry legally.
NOR.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses entry or visa rules, airport or border screening that could expose a traveller's gender history, gender markers on passports or other identity documents, or facilities and bathroom access. Those questions are unresolved for this record rather than answered in the negative.

The 2017 regulation covering citizens resident abroad is referenced on the official health-rights page but its procedural detail, including whether non-citizens can use the same route, is not sourced here. Likewise the reported treatment gap for non-binary patients rests on a 2023 report and has not been verified against a later official statement.

Official hate-crime counts are known to be a substantial undercount: the 8% reporting rate in the HATECYCLE study and the fall in clearance to 45% both indicate that recorded figures understate incidence, so year-on-year comparisons should be read as movements in reporting rather than in underlying violence. The PST threat assessment covers events and individuals generally and is not broken down by trans-specific risk.

NOR.blindSummary:
The country's law contains no offence targeting trans people. In November 2020 the national parliament amended the Penal Code so that hate speech under Paragraph 135a covers bisexual and transgender people as well as sexual orientation; the amendment took effect in 2020 and was reported as an extension of criminal liability to anti-trans hate speech. The hate-crime framework recorded by an international hate-crime monitoring body defines hate crimes as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability, and any offence so motivated is recorded under that framework.

Legal gender recognition runs on self-declaration with no medical-intervention requirement. Under the Gender Recognition Act as set out on the official national health-rights page, the change of legal gender is decided at the tax office on the basis of the individual's own perception of their gender identity: from age 16 on the person's own application, between 6 and 16 with parental consent, and below 6 only for documented congenital differences of sex development. A 2017 regulation governs the document change for citizens resident abroad.

Gender-affirming healthcare does not follow the same self-declaration route. Access still requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the national treatment centre for gender incongruence at the country's main university hospital, where only about a quarter of referred patients are admitted to treatment and those disqualified have no alternative options. A 2023 report found non-binary people still without treatment despite a 2020 guideline calling for equal access. For minors, 2020 guidelines recommend puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 following interdisciplinary assessment.

Reported hate crime is rising while clearance falls. A regional LGBTI rights organisation's annual review records an 18% increase in reported hate crimes in 2023, with the largest rises in offences motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, and antisemitism. A national broadcaster reported record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate dropped from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims told police they have little trust in the authorities, while a dedicated hate-crime group continues to encourage reporting. Official figures undercount by a wide margin: a university extremism research centre surveyed more than 3,000 LGBTQI people and found that only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police, citing mistrust, procedural obstacles, fear of personal costs, and dismissive treatment by officers where reporting did occur.

Violence remains the principal offset to that legal position. A gunman killed two people at a capital-city Pride event in 2022; the perpetrator, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years, the strictest penalty available. The same review period recorded a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime and online threats against a drag bingo event. The national security service reported a significant decline in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, while warning that hate speech and intimidation risks persist, particularly during Pride, and that most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than to act.

Discrimination protection is long-standing and explicit as to gender identity. The country was the first to enact LGBT anti-discrimination law, amending Paragraph 349a of the Penal Code in 1981 to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation in goods and services and at public gatherings; employment discrimination on sexual grounds has been banned since 1998, and since 2013 Section 5 of the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination on the grounds of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression prohibits discrimination based on gender identity and expression. It is among the few countries explicitly protecting intersex people from discrimination. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 January 2009 with full rights including religious weddings, adoption and assisted reproduction, building on a registered partnership law from 1993 and recognition of unregistered same-sex cohabitation since 1991 for limited rights such as next-of-kin medical decisions; in 2024 the country was ranked the best in the world for same-sex couples to marry legally.

SWE.name: Sweden
SWE.summary:
Sweden's parliament approved new acts on legal gender recognition and on medical procedures performed on genitalia in April 2024, as recorded by a Library of Congress global legal monitor entry of that month.

The Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025. TGEU reports that it simplifies the procedure for changing legal gender but falls short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining, so a person seeking to update legal documents may still be required to satisfy medical conditions.

As adopted in April 2024 by a Riksdag vote of 234 to 94 and effective from 1 July 2025, the minimum age for legal gender change without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis was lowered from 18 to 16, on the basis of a doctor or psychologist statement together with approval from the National Board of Health and Welfare, and with guardian approval required for 16- and 17-year-olds. Genital surgery is limited to those aged 18 and over, and gonad removal to those aged 23 and over absent exceptional reason.

Sweden's main national board decided on 28 January 2017 that transgender people would no longer be classified as mentally ill, the depathologisation step that governs diagnostic status for trans residents.

Transgender identity and expression have been covered by Swedish hate speech legislation since 1 January 2019, and were added to hate crime legislation on 1 July 2018; sexual orientation had been added to hate crime provisions in 2010. Brå, the National Council for Crime Prevention, publishes the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending through report 2024:13, a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences in which police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives.

Facility access is the clearest documented everyday friction. SVT reported in October 2025 that the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their changing rooms.

Access to gender-affirming care for minors is restricted. In March 2021 the Karolinska Institute stopped providing puberty blockers or gender-affirming hormone therapy to children and teenagers under 16, and to 16- to 18-year-olds outside approved clinical trials. On 22 February 2022 the National Board of Health and Welfare stated that puberty blockers should be used only in exceptional cases supported by what it called uncertain science; this is guidance rather than a statutory ban. In 2021 the Board reduced the number of gender-affirming clinics from seven to three. Misinformation that Sweden had banned gender-affirming care for minors nevertheless circulated on social media and was cited by politicians in the United States to justify outright bans. Nationwide Board data released in 2026 showed that trans children prescribed puberty blockers had increased slightly since the 2022 guidance.

Legal gender change was long conditional: until 2013 it required sterilisation and sex reassignment surgery. Those requirements were ruled unconstitutional in January 2013 and removed by the Riksdag in July 2013, and a law passed in March 2018 provided compensation of 225,000 SEK each to roughly 600 to 700 people subjected to forced sterilisation.

Organised opposition to trans rights is a documented feature of the political environment. Anti-gender campaigns mobilise around the pejorative concept of gender ideology, with actors including the far-right Sweden Democrats and the Christian Democrats, who oppose trans-rights legal reforms while framing that opposition as protecting women's rights and Swedish values, alongside gender-critical radical feminist groups such as the Swedish Women's Lobby. Scholars document what they describe as insidious de-democratisation and report growing political violence and intimidation against trans advocates, feminist scholars and racialised activists, including online harassment, threats and public vilification.

Sweden does not criminalise consensual same-sex relations, which have been legal since 1944, and a 2019 Spartacus Gay Travel Index reported by Newsweek ranked Canada, Portugal and Sweden as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations.
SWE.outOfScopeNotes:
No visa or entry rules for LGBTQ travellers are sourced for Sweden; the nearest material found is the 1978 state inquiry's refugee-status suggestion, and current asylum criteria are not documented in this inventory.

The date of declassification of transgender status as an illness is given inconsistently in the source coverage, as 2017 in one place and 2009 in another; the 28 January 2017 decision reported by TT/The Local is the item used here, and the 2009 reference remains unresolved.

Whether the pending conversion-practices bill described in the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 has been enacted is not established by the inventory.

The scope of the Medley changing-room restriction beyond that chain, and any parallel policy at other leisure facilities, is not documented.

Brå's dataset records only offences in which police identified an LGBTQI-related motive, so it does not measure unreported or unpolicereported hostility.

FIN.name: Finland
FIN.summary:
Finland does not criminalise trans people, and the sources reviewed record no trans-specific violence against a visitor: no assault, mob attack or police-brutality case involving a trans traveller appears in the material. The hate-crime figures below are national aggregates, not an incident series involving visitors.

Police recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences, the highest total ever logged, with defamation and the most common types being defamation and assault. The Police University College reports the sexual-orientation and gender-identity-or-expression category rising across six reported years, from 72 cases to 241. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 gives the same headline total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes, a 13% increase since 2023, and identifies sexual orientation and gender identity as recurrent motives, present in 12% of cases.

The Criminal Code contains no hate-crime offence. Motive is captured only in police reports, so sexual-orientation and gender-identity-motivated incidents are counted as reported suspicions rather than as charges. A visitor has no separate legal exposure: there is no sodomy-style offence, no public-order offence keyed to gender expression, and no law requiring a trans person to disclose status to police.

Legal gender recognition operates under the 2023 statute: applicants must be 18, down from a proposed 15 with guardian permission, observe a 30-day reflection period, and may change the registered marker only once per year. The former requirement to be sterilised or otherwise infertile and to hold a mental-disorder diagnosis applied until April 2023 and no longer binds. Finland was one of three countries in a six-country Investigate Europe investigation that wrote infertility requirements explicitly into law; the last such requirement in that group was phased out at the end of June 2025, and the people subjected to the earlier regime form a documented legacy cohort.

Conversion practices have moved into the courts and Parliament. Finland's first conversion-practices case was prosecuted as assault, with convictions in March, and Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices by 125-49 in March, though a full statutory ban remained pending.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since 1 March 2017, and a 2018 amendment to the Maternity Act recognised both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of birth rather than through later second-parent adoption. Discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, and on gender identity and expression since 2005, is prohibited under Section 8(1) of the Discrimination Act, whether the discrimination is based on fact or assumption; the Act on Equality between Women and Men also covers gender identity, and Parliament extended it in 2014 to employment, goods and services, education and health services.

Gender-affirming care for minors is delivered through the country's two centralised gender identity units. The Council for Choices in Health Care revised its clinical recommendations for gender dysphoria under age 25 in 2020, prioritising psychosocial therapy over medical transition; because these are recommendations rather than mandates, puberty blockers remain available case by case and cross-sex hormones can be considered where identity is of a permanent nature causing severe dysphoria. A Seta survey found over 40% of trans respondents entirely unable to access the care they needed, most reporting extended waiting times, which is the most concrete indicator of what a trans visitor needing unscheduled care should expect.

Which calendar year the record total belongs to is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

Signature counts for the 'Tahdon2013' initiative are given as over 162,000 in one source and over 166,000 in another. The discrepancy is unresolved and does not affect the outcome.

Whether Parliament has since enacted a full statutory ban on conversion practices, as opposed to endorsing the initiative 125-49, is not resolved in the sources; the Annual Review states a full ban remained pending.

No source in the inventory documents a trans visitor to Finland being refused entry, questioned about trans status at the border, denied a marker correction on Finnish documents, or refused service. Absence of such a record here reflects the sources reviewed, not a verified negative finding.

Statistics on hate-motivated violence against trans people specifically, as distinct from the combined sexual-orientation and gender-identity category, are not available in this inventory.

sources.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity has been legal for men and women since 1971; 'promotion' of homosexuality was decriminalised and the age of consent equalised at 16 in 1999, homosexuality was declassified as an illness in 1981, and transvestism in 2011. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation became a criminal offence in 1995 and on gender identity in 2005. Until April 2023, trans people seeking legal gender recognition had to be sterilised or otherwise infertile and hold a mental disorder diagnosis.

The 'Tahdon2013' citizens' initiative gathered over 166,000 signatures in 2013 and became the first initiative passed by Parliament, which legalised same-sex marriage in December 2014 by 101–90. The Constitution allows citizens' initiatives carrying 50,000 valid signatures to be put to Parliament. Registered partnerships, available from 2002 to 1 March 2017, gave same-sex couples the rights of married couples except adoption and joint surname, and gave immigration rights to a foreign same-sex partner. Stepchild adoption became legal in 2009, and joint adoption with same-sex marriage took effect on 1 March 2017. Surrogacy remains illegal for all couples. An April 2019 law passed 122–42 gave lesbian couples full maternity pay and parentage rights without intra-family adoption.

Public visibility rests on a 2010 gay rights panel on state broadcaster Yle TV2, the first public gay demonstration in 1981, and Pride parades in numerous cities, with an estimated 100,000 attending 2018 Helsinki Pride. A gay scene of bars, clubs and cafés operates in Helsinki, and support organisations run nationwide: Seta (founded 1974), Trasek for trans and intersex rights, and Rainbow Families.

Gender-affirming care for minors is delivered through the country's two centralised gender identity units. TWN.name: Taiwan
TWN.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Taiwan remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national ID. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining an ID matching their presentation, which makes every ID-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, a potential site of distress and discrimination. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands.

In August 2024 a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change her ID marker without surgery or a psychological evaluation, with the supporting rights group indicating an appeal was likely. No tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction access occurred during 2025. Pending changes to conscription criteria could actively harm trans people subject to military service.

Hostility is organised rather than incidental. Anti-gender movement activity rose through 2024 and 2025, with organisations promoting the anti-trans policy positions of the United States and the Taiwan Solidarity Party calling for a 'two genders' position.

Facilities are a documented friction point. The Ministry of Environment committed NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms from 623 to 1,246 by 2029, and 17% of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents who reported discrimination said it occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms. A November 2025 audit by an LGBTQ+ rights group found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.

Statutory protection exists on several fronts. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, and employment discrimination has been prohibited since the 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment. The Long-Term Care Services Act of January 2017 carries an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 of 24 May 2017 held that the constitutional grounds of discrimination are illustrative rather than exhaustive, bringing sexual orientation within the right to equality.

A Ministry of Health and Welfare letter of 22 February 2018 effectively banned conversion therapy, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.
TWN.outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the appeal flagged after the August 2024 Taipei court ruling on ID marker change is unresolved in the available sources; no later judgment is sourced.

The scope, timing and content of the pending conscription-criteria changes referenced for 2025 are not specified in the sources, and their effect on trans draftees is unverified.

Whether the 2008 executive order has been amended, and whether any legislative bill to replace the surgical requirement has been tabled, is not sourced here.

A source page dedicated to Taiwan's transgender rights laws, protections and gaps was unavailable at research time (HTTP 404), so gaps in the legal framework are documented only through the other sources.

No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, complaint-handling outcomes under the employment and education statutes, or detention and policing practice toward trans people.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Historically, a 1740 Qing decree criminalised voluntary homosexual intercourse between adults (punishable by a month in prison and 100 heavy blows), while the Republic of China's provisional criminal code abolished explicit prohibitions on 'consenting ji jian' around 1912 and sodomy was decriminalised when the ROC took over Taiwan after World War II under the 1935 criminal code. During martial law, LGBT people were harassed and detained under general public order laws (Temporary Provisions against the Communist Rebellion), repealed in 1991. Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression is open and expanding: the first Taiwan Pride was held in Taipei on 1 November 2003 with over 1,000 attendees, growing to about 80,000 by 2015, 137,000 in 2018 and 170,000 by 2019, with pride events also held in Kaohsiung (since 2010) and Taichung (20,000 in 2016). LGBTQ representation in literature and film — from Pai Hsien-yung's novel Crystal Boys in the 1970s to Ang Lee's Brokeback Mountain (2005) and Zero Chou's Spider Lilies (2007 Berlin Teddy Award winner) — is described as instrumental in raising public awareness. In 2022 Taiwan withdrew from hosting WorldPride 2025 over the disputed name 'WorldPride Kaohsiung,' which the public and government considered offensive, and the event moved to Washington, D.C. in June 2025. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples can legally adopt, and since May 2023 legislation has granted full adoption rights, replacing the partial (stepchild-only) adoption rights in place since 2019. Until 2023 they could only adopt the biological child of their partner; a January 2022 court order had already allowed a same-sex couple to adopt before the legislature codified full rights. Taiwan law also permits single individuals, including individual LGBT people, to adopt depending on circumstances, while the Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, specifically excluding same-sex female couples and single women. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004 (fine of NT$100,000 for schools discriminating in admission, instruction or assessment). Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000. The Long-Term Care Services Act (January 2017) contains an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 (24 May 2017) held that the Constitution's Article 7 grounds of discrimination are 'illustrative, rather than exhaustive,' so sexual orientation is protected by the right to equality. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in education has been banned since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, with sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties added in June 2011. In November 2018 voters passed a referendum question to ban LGBT-inclusive sex education in schools (Question 11) and rejected the pro-inclusion Question 15; Education Minister Yeh Jiunn-rong said LGBT content would be reviewed against the result, and an earlier Ministry of Education curriculum reform (announced March 2010, effective 2011) had already been watered down to 'respecting diverse sexual orientations' after anti-LGBT opposition. Youth-relevant health measures include the 22 February 2018 Ministry of Health and Welfare letter effectively banning conversion therapy, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.

TWN.localsOnly:

The Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, specifically excluding same-sex female couples and single women. TWN.blindSummary:
Legal gender recognition in the country remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national ID. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining an ID matching their presentation, which makes every ID-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, a potential site of distress and discrimination. The national health ministry has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands.

In August 2024 a court in the largest city denied a transgender woman's request to change her ID marker without surgery or a psychological evaluation, with the supporting rights group indicating an appeal was likely. No tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction access occurred during 2025. Pending changes to conscription criteria could actively harm trans people subject to military service.

Hostility is organised rather than incidental. Anti-gender movement activity rose through 2024 and 2025, with organisations promoting the anti-trans policy positions of a government in another region and a regionalist party calling for a 'two genders' position.

Facilities are a documented friction point. The environment ministry committed 280 million in local currency over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms from 623 to 1,246 by 2029, and 17% of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents who reported discrimination said it occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms. A November 2025 audit by an LGBTQ+ rights group found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.

Statutory protection exists on several fronts. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since a gender equity education act of June 2004, and employment discrimination has been prohibited since 2007–08 amendments to national employment statutes. The long-term care statute of January 2017 carries an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and a constitutional court interpretation of 24 May 2017 held that the constitutional grounds of discrimination are illustrative rather than exhaustive, bringing sexual orientation within the right to equality.

A national health ministry letter of 22 February 2018 effectively banned conversion therapy, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the child and youth welfare statute.

Whether the 2008 executive order has been amended, and whether any legislative bill to replace the surgical requirement has been tabled, is not sourced here.

A source page dedicated to the country's transgender rights laws, protections and gaps was unavailable at research time (HTTP 404), so gaps in the legal framework are documented only through the other sources.

No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, complaint-handling outcomes under the employment and education statutes, or detention and policing practice toward trans people.

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.summary:
Criminalising law in South Korea applies almost entirely to the military. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, but Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment. The Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted: in 2017 the military ran what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, criminally charging 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

A trans soldier's case marks the sharpest documented harm. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register; an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is documented as a live problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot flagged from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
KOR.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory describes how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system. There is no stated birth-sex versus identity placement rule, no account of special units, and no documentation of solitary or segregation practice for trans detainees. Any placement question in that setting is unresolved here and would need prison-service regulations or oversight-body reports.

A Library of Congress global legal monitor entry on a South Korean Supreme Court decision permitting a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register could not be retrieved for this compilation; the substance of that decision is carried from other sources, but the Library's framing of it is unverified.

The inventory contains nothing on entry, visa screening, border questioning, or airport document inspection as they might affect a trans visitor, including any practice of sex markers on passports being checked against presentation. Nor does it address recognition of foreign legal gender changes, non-binary legal status (which appears only as a survey category), or access to gender-affirming medication for short-term visitors.

LGBTI organisations may register, but registration has required litigation. Trans teenagers manage restroom access by avoidance, leaving school early or holding it in, with no legal mandate requiring schools to accommodate them.

IND.name: India
IND.summary:
India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity; the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. CHN.name: China
CHN.summary:
China is authoritarian without criminalising trans identity: there is no criminal offence attaching to being transgender, no law restricting bathroom use by gender identity, and courts have awarded compensation to a trans claimant. Against that, the legal framework offers no anti-discrimination protection, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. A visitor should expect a state that does not prosecute trans people but does not protect them either.

The most directly visitor-relevant evidence concerns the border. In May 2025 the Thai trans YouTuber Nisamanee 'Nut' Lertvorapong alleged that Chinese immigration officials laughed at, mocked and questioned her during a family trip, posting video to Instagram with the statement that no one should be treated differently on the basis of gender. A visibly trans traveller should anticipate intrusive or humiliating handling by immigration officers, with no complaint mechanism on offer.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable in China, and gender-affirming surgery for adults requires parental consent, with proof of parental death where that applies; disagreements are pushed back into the family to resolve. This is a practical barrier for trans residents and for anyone staying long enough to need medical care.

Trans-specific violence and coercive treatment are documented. A New York Times investigation in December 2024 set out transgender 'conversion' practices in the country, and in November 2024 the 28-year-old performance artist Ling'er won a record monetary payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment under family pressure — the first successful legal challenge to such treatment by a trans person in China. She said she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights. The case shows both that the medical system has permitted forced commitment and electroshock, and that a court will now hear a claim.

Public expression is tightly constrained. Around Pride month in 2026 platforms scrubbed prominent LGBT social media accounts, foreign films and events with LGBT themes, which Human Rights Watch read as evidence of a deteriorating rights situation and deepening repression of expression and association. Displaying rainbow flags or accessories is no longer permitted even inside venues, and in August 2023 officials removed an LGBTQ+ anthem titled 'Rainbow'. The broadcast regulator SAPPRFT's 2016 guideline banning depictions of 'abnormal sexual behaviour', including same-sex romance, established the censorship baseline that has since extended from television to social platforms.

Foreign gender-nonconforming performers meet the same squeeze: a Zurich drag artist on tour found the space for queer subcultures shrinking first-hand in August 2026, and the cancellation of nationwide shows by the transgender dancer Jin Xing in early 2025 led observers inside the country to fear a wider crackdown. Visible queerness by a visitor, performer or resident carries a real risk of cancellation, refusal or removal rather than prosecution.
CHN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening of trans travellers, including whether officials inspect passport gender markers or ask transition-related questions at the border beyond the reported treatment of Nisamanee Lertvorapong. That question is unresolved here.

There is no sourced material on bathroom or facility access for visitors, on hate-crime or hate-speech protection for trans people, or on whether any anti-discrimination remedy exists outside the civil claim Ling'er brought. These are not established either way by the available sources.

Whether the parental-consent requirement for gender-affirming surgery applies to foreign patients treated in China, and whether it affects short-stay visitors needing emergency care, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Enforcement is reported at national and platform level; variation between provinces and cities, and the practical treatment of trans residents by police outside documented cases, are not covered by the inventory.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D6, D7, D9, D12, D13.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Beijing currently provides dependent residency status to the same-sex partners of legal residents, such as expats — the only entry/residence-related recognition noted for same-sex partners in the source. Separately, the Chinese government requires parents adopting children from China to be in heterosexual marriages, and adoption of Chinese children by foreign same-sex couples and homosexual individuals is prohibited by the Chinese authorities. No other visa, entry, or border provisions for LGBTQ travelers appear in the text. Wikipedia country coverage: Healthcare and community facilities remain hostile: psychiatric facilities and psychiatry textbooks across the country still de facto treat homosexuality as a mental disorder and continue to offer conversion therapy, because the 2001 declassification by the Chinese Society of Psychiatry was never reflected in National Health and Family Planning Commission regulations. Gender-affirming care is limited by a conservative environment; in December 2022 Chinese authorities banned online sale of estradiol and androgen blockers even with valid prescriptions, forcing in-person purchase. As of 2025 there are 7 medical centers treating transgender youth, 3 of which offer puberty suppression, with the first such clinic opened in 2021 at the Children's Hospital of Fudan University in Shanghai. LGBTQ social venues have also been closed or forced to shut: Shanghai Pride cancelled all activities in 2020 and has not resumed, and the Roxie, one of the country's last lesbian bars (Shanghai), was forced to close in 2024. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt, and households headed by such couples are ineligible for the legal protections available to heterosexual couples; foreign same-sex couples and homosexual individuals are barred from adopting Chinese children. Since the October 2017 National People's Congress amendment allowing adults to appoint guardians by mutual agreement (yìdìng jiānhù), some same-sex couples have used this 'legal guardianship' route for limited protections, but face outright refusal or discriminatory conditions — one Hunan notary office held a six-hour meeting on whether approval would 'disrupt public disorder or morality', a Guangzhou office demanded a 100,000 yuan deposit not required of heterosexual applicants, and a 2021 China Notary Association report says some notary employees were disciplined for providing voluntary guardianship services to same-sex couples. On 12 April 2021 the Shenyang Intermediate People's Court ruled that a 79-year-old woman could not sue her female partner of 50 years over 294,000 yuan because their relationship is not recognized as a marriage. Wikipedia country coverage: Chinese law contains no explicit anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, and hate crime laws do not cover sexual orientation or gender identity. Physical attacks are documented: days before the International Day Against Homophobia in 2018, two women wearing rainbow badges were attacked and beaten by security guards in Beijing, and the security company dismissed the three guards involved shortly thereafter. During the Cultural Revolution homosexuals were regarded as 'disgraceful' and 'undesirable' and heavily persecuted, with individuals such as Zhu Zhenhua publicly humiliated in 1983 for 'hooliganism and sodomy' and Chen Baoping sentenced to nine years in 1962. Under Xi Jinping, LGBTQ rights activists face greater scrutiny under mass surveillance, authors of boys' love works are routinely arrested and criminally prosecuted (one woman received 10 years 6 months for a gay-themed novel), and in 2025 China voted against renewing the UN Independent Expert on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity mandate. Wikipedia country coverage: The Marriage Law of the PRC, adopted 10 September 1980, defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, so same-sex couples cannot marry. The first mainland same-sex marriage lawsuit — Sun Wenlin against the Furong District Bureau of Civil Affairs, filed December 2015 — was rejected by the Changsha court on 13 April 2016, though Sun and Hu Mingliang held a private wedding ceremony on 17 May 2016. The 2017 guardianship-agreement reform gives same-sex couples only partial, unevenly applied protections, and a 2021 Shenyang court refused to recognize a 50-year same-sex partnership in a property dispute. Beijing does provide dependent residency status to same-sex partners of legal residents such as expats; public support is rising, with a July 2024 William Institute poll finding 52% of Chinese agree same-sex couples should be able to marry (43% in a May 2021 Ipsos poll). Wikipedia country coverage: Education is a major pressure point: a 2016 UNDP survey found less than five percent of LGBT people are fully out at school, work, or in their religious community, and about fifteen percent are out to their families. In July 2021, LGBT accounts run by university students on WeChat — including Purple (Tsinghua), Colorsworld (Peking), Zhihe (Fudan) and Rainbow of Jin (19 Tianjin universities) — were deleted for violating account regulations, and a campaign marking the International Day Against Homophobia on school campuses was forbidden by public officials in 2018. Qiu Bai's five lawsuits against the Ministry of Education over homophobic teaching materials all failed, ending with a 2 March 2017 Beijing High Court rejection, and in 2021 a Jiangsu court upheld calling homosexuality a mental disorder in a 2013 university textbook as 'perceptual differences' rather than factual error — that textbook is used by a number of Chinese universities. A Peking University survey found trans female students face strong discrimination across sex-segregated enrollment, uniforms, bathrooms, dormitories, PE exams and conscription, all tied to legal gender marker; for trans youth specifically, the minimum age for sex reassignment surgery was lowered to 18 (from 20), Shanxi Province has allowed minors to apply for gender-marker change since 2014 with a guardian's ID, the 2022 Chinese expert consensus recommends puberty blockers for transgender youth, and as of 2025 seven medical centers treat transgender youth with three offering puberty suppression. A September–October 2016 Varkey Foundation survey found 54% of 18–21-year-olds in China supported same-sex marriage.
