MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under both federal and state law. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, for any person regardless of gender or whether the act is consensual and private; the maximum penalty is 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871. These provisions are not confined to Malaysian citizens and are used against foreign nationals.

Section 377D of the Penal Code adds a charge of "gross indecency", an undefined offence carrying up to two years, which remains a discretionary prosecutorial tool. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but that discretion is not a legal protection and has been withdrawn at moments of political pressure.

Every one of the 13 states, together with the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", alongside offences of liwat and musahaqah. Penalties reach three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences apply only to Muslims; non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone. State Islamic religious departments carry out enforcement, and the enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the line between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

Arbitrary arrest of transgender people is documented over decades, including repeated arrests of individual women more than twenty times, a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014, and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention. In July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons; the International Commission of Jurists demanded the order be revoked.

Violence against transgender women is lethal and largely unpunished. A trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months. Reporting on those killings is obstructed: investigators' working phrase, "the deceased can't speak for herself", reflects a process in which police mistreatment and impunity go unexamined.

Queue-free criminal exposure now extends to social venues. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among the arrestees were suspended from their posts. A magistrate rejected the police request to extend remand on the ground that no case had been made out under 377B, yet release was delayed and more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister said the provisions would be revisited; within days police raided another sauna in Penang. Earlier venue raids include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and 11 shopping malls in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches.

Identity documents remain controlled by the state. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and is unaffected by reassignment surgery; the edict was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is historical: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors. The nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay, and a warning to gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable, and no political party pursues LGBTQ legal reform; Mahathir told the Cambridge Union in June 2019 that Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Custodial and institutional alternatives to prison are prescribed by the same Sharia enactments: sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months, and may order cross-dressing and other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states, extended to a year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment.

Legal challenges have failed to remove the framework. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence, not on the substance, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised.
MYS.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Home Minister's 2 December 2025 statement that the section 377 provisions would be revisited has produced any legislative or charging-policy change is not established by the sources available here; the only sourced follow-up is a further police raid in Penang days later.

The sources do not state whether any current visa, arrival-card or immigration screening question asks about gender identity or transition status, or whether passport gender markers mismatching presentation trigger secondary screening. No explicit visa rule for transgender visitors is documented.

No youth-specific health-care access or medication-carrying finding for Malaysia appears in the sources reviewed; the entry on health care is general and adult.

The Human Dignity Trust profile lists active litigation in Malaysia without itemising the cases, their status or their likely timelines; the state of play beyond the February 2021 and February 2024 Federal Court decisions is unresolved here.

Whether the 1982 fatwa has since been gazetted is stated in one source as never having been gazetted, but no independent verification of its current administrative status is present in the inventory.

Human Rights Watch (24 September 2014) 'I'm Scared to Be a Woman': since the 1980s every one of Malaysia's 13 states has passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all 13 bar Muslim men from 'dressing as women' and three also bar 'women posing as men' — enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. Documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over 20 times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the Registration Department (a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery), and prison terms of four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Artist pressure has also affected entry: in July 2023 The 1975 was forced to cut short its Good Vibes Festival set after Matty Healy criticised the country's anti-LGBTQ laws and kissed a bandmate, with Healy saying he had not researched the country before booking. Adoption is not restricted on orientation or gender-identity grounds: under the Adoption Act 1952 and the Registration of Adoption Act 1952 a single person may adopt regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.
MYS.blindLocalsOnly:
State/provincial Sharia offences reach Muslim residents only, but for them the enforcement machinery is close at hand: state/provincial Islamic religious departments arrest, and sharia courts can impose imprisonment, caning and fines, or commit a person to an approved home or a religious rehabilitation institution for months at a time.

The 1982 religious committee edict, though never gazetted and therefore not legally binding, is applied in practice. It bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex, holds that sex is fixed at birth, and underpins routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the national Registration Department. That department recognised a transgender woman's female status once, in 1975; no comparable successful case has been documented since.

Conversion therapy is practised regularly and is openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders. Transgender residents report discriminatory denial of health care and employment alongside physical and sexual assault in custody, with prison terms served in male wards where sexual violence is documented.

The national blood centre prohibits homosexual and bisexual people from donating blood, in a policy that is gender-neutral in wording. Adoption is not restricted on orientation or gender-identity grounds: under national adoption legislation a single person may adopt regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.summary:
Sex between men ceased to be a criminal offence in Singapore when Parliament repealed Section 377A on 29 November 2022, in the same sitting as a constitutional amendment reserving to Parliament rather than the judiciary the power to define marriage. Same-sex relations are legal for men and women, and Reuters reported in June 2023 that the LGBT community felt safer in the wake of the repeal.

No form of same-sex relationship is recognised. Singapore recognises neither marriage, civil union nor domestic partnership between same-sex partners, and the Women's Charter precedent that a marriage not between a woman and a man is void leaves only heterosexual marriages recognised. Same-sex couples are consequently excluded from the healthcare benefits, inheritance rights and social security benefits available to married couples. In December 2018 a gay Singaporean man won a landmark appeal to adopt his son, fathered through surrogacy in the United States; in January 2019 Social and Family Development Minister Desmond Lee stated that the government does not support the formation of family units with children of homosexual parents through processes such as adoption and would seek to strengthen adoption laws. That commitment has not been made into law, and same-sex couples do not generally have their adoption of children recognised.

Legal gender recognition is available but difficult. The MPSC report of February 2025 identifies the process as carrying prohibitive cost because genital surgery is a precondition, and names discrimination, abuse and restrictions facing transgender students, employment-sector discrimination, and discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings that discourages transgender people from seeking care as the community's key challenges to health and well-being.

Statutory protection remains partial. The Workplace Fairness Legislation gives Singapore its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but gender identity and expression are not protected grounds, so LGBTQ+ workers remain outside its scope. Outright International's overview of Singapore, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTI organisations still cannot register, a structural gap that survives decriminalisation.

Expression remains regulated. A clause of the radio broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden lifestyles prompted calls for review in July 2025, with a former radio DJ and actor arguing that the grouping has no place in a post-377A Singapore. The media regulator limits the promotion or glamorisation of the homosexual lifestyle on television and radio, imposing higher age ratings (NC16, M18, R21) on productions depicting same-sex sexual activity; in 2019 the rapper Joshua Su withdrew from a TEDx radio talk after being asked not to make sensitive comments about his sexuality. Public-order provisions still reach conduct: Section 294 of the Penal Code covers obscene acts in public places with a maximum of three months' imprisonment, a fine or both, and gay men were charged with soliciting in 11 cases between 1990 and 1994, with fines of $200 to $500.

Toilet access is unsettled in practice. Yale-NUS College and Tembusu College of the National University of Singapore provide gender-neutral toilets for their students, but during Wikimania 2023 at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre (16 to 19 August 2023) the temporary conversion of a female toilet to a gender-neutral one drew public backlash, including threats of a boycott of the venue and petitions against the change. Pink Dot SG and the non-profit group Oogachaga responded that gender-neutral toilets complement gendered toilets rather than replace them.

The Singapore Prison Service reported on 15 November 2023 that 10 transgender inmates were then behind bars and that no cases of assault against them had been recorded, a rare official datum on trans prisoners. On health care, Health Minister Gan Kim Yong wrote in May 2020 that the Ministry of Health expects doctors to practise evidence-based best practice and to respect patients' preferences and circumstances including sexual orientation, with complaints to the Singapore Medical Council as the recourse, though no such complaint had been received from self-declared LGBTQ patients in the preceding three years. In January 2006 the Ministry of Community Development, Youth and Sports granted S$100,000 to Liberty League, an ex-gay conversion-therapy organisation; activists pressured the group into returning the grant and it has been defunct since 2014.
SGP.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the January 2019 undertaking by Social and Family Development Minister Desmond Lee to strengthen adoption laws has been drafted, tabled or enacted is unresolved in the available sources; the inventory records the statement and notes that it has not been made into law.

The outcome of the July 2025 calls for review of the radio broadcast code clause grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest is not sourced, so whether the clause stands or has been amended is unresolved.

The Fun and Abusive Global Barometers index values for Singapore are described but not enumerated in the inventory, so no de jure or lived-experience score can be quoted here. The cost figures for legal gender recognition are characterised as prohibitive in the MPSC report without a stated amount, and no post-2022 fee schedule is sourced.

The Singapore Medical Council complaint data cited by the Ministry of Health covers the three years to May 2020 only; no later complaint figures for LGBTQ patients are available, and the inventory does not source any enforcement action under Section 294 of the Penal Code after the 2022 repeal.

IRN.name: Iran
IRN.summary:
Iran is among the most restrictive environments in the world for a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to the death penalty, and the UK Home Office country report (CPIN, version 5.0, December 2025) records that the code carries no discrimination protections of any kind and that convictions are frequently brought on the pretext of more severe charges. Outright International confirms that same-sex relations are illegal nationwide for both sexes, and Human Rights Watch documented two men executed for homosexual conduct on 21 November 2005, the enforcement backdrop against which any visitor is assessed.

Recognition of trans status exists but is conditional. A 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini permits gender-reassignment surgery, which may be state-subsidised after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder", and Article 20, Clause 14 allows a person who has had sex reassignment surgery to change name and gender on the birth certificate by court order, with corrected identity documents reportedly issued efficiently and transparently. The Home Office report sets the limits: recognition follows only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; the surgery available is invasive and often sub-standard; and an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution.

Identity documents can themselves expose a holder. New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders; 6Rang warned that this disclosure identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination.

State pressure operates in public space as well as in paperwork. Tehran authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid busy areas, an official advisory restricting trans visibility, and the 2017 US State Department report noted that security forces raided houses and monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons.

Custodial violence against trans detainees is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted rape in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility in an open letter published by HRANA.

Raids on private gatherings produce mass arrests and threats of execution. An IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province on 13 April 2017 involved agents reportedly firing weapons and electric Tasers; those arrested were taken to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan, where they were led into the prison yard and told they would be executed. In February 2008 police in Isfahan raided a party and arrested 30 men, held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity, and in January 2008 Hamzeh Chavi (18) and Loghman Hamzehpour (19) were arrested in Sardasht on sodomy and mohārebe charges.

Judicial outcomes remain lethal. Two youths were reportedly hanged in north-eastern Iran in 2006 for "sex crimes"; in 2022 two gay men in Maragheh received death sentences for "sodomy by force", a charge stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy, later commuted to life in prison. The death penalty is legal from 18 for adults and from 15 for murder, and the 2017 US State Department report raised concerns about LGBTI minors. In May 2021 Ali Monfared, aged 20, was murdered allegedly by relatives.

6Rang documented forced anal or sodomy tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct, part of the evidentiary practice attached to these prosecutions.

The medical regime is coercive as well as permissive. The state funds gender-reassignment surgery while placing pressure on Iranian trans people to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty; surgery is invasive and often sub-standard and is framed publicly as protection. Two 2024–2025 media investigations describe foreign patients travelling for the same subsidised procedures while local transitions are effectively forced.

There is no same-sex marriage or civil union recognition and no legislation addressing discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The government does not allow any political party or organisation to endorse LGBTQ rights, leaving that role to exiled groups.

Displacement is systematic rather than incidental. A 6Rang submission to the UN Independent Expert on SOGI (February 2025), "They See Us as Criminals", surveyed 25 LGBTIQ+ people who fled Iran, 96% of them from ethnic minorities, documenting the persecution driving departure; a further 6Rang submission to Iran's Universal Periodic Review at the 48th session (January–February 2025) catalogued human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.
IRN.outOfScopeNotes:
Several document-level specifics rest on a single compiled reference rather than primary legislation in this inventory: the numbering of Article 20, Clause 14 and Article 215, the wording of the military identity card exemption subsection, and 6Rang's warning about that subsection are not corroborated by a statutory text here and remain unresolved.

The Home Office report's statement that recognition requires sterilisation is not tied to a named provision in the inventory; the legal basis and current enforceability of the sterilisation condition are unresolved.

The cash grant and loan figures date from the mid-2000s and are given in the conversion used by the source; whether those amounts remain in force, and at what real value after inflation, is not sourced.

The RFE/RL report of Tehran authorities warning transgender people away from busy areas carries no date in the inventory, so the currency of that advisory is unresolved.

The scale of trans medical tourism to Iran is asserted by two media reports without patient numbers or revenue figures in this inventory.

Whether courts currently grant Article 20 name and gender changes without surgery, and how quickly, is described only as "reportedly efficient" in secondary sourcing; no case-level verification is available here.

sources.summary: Under Article 20, Clause 14, a person who has had sex reassignment surgery may legally change name and gender on birth certification by court order, and corrected identity documents have reportedly been issued efficiently and transparently. Supporters of reassignment also invoke Article 215 of the civil code, covering acts serving a 'rational benefit', though approval by a doctor is required. New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders, a disclosure 6Rang warned identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognized, and no legislation addresses discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Because the government does not allow any political party or organization to endorse LGBTQ rights, that role has fallen to exiled groups such as the Green Party of Iran, the Worker Communist Party of Iran, the Worker's Way, the Glorious Frontiers Party, and the Constitutionalist Party of Iran. Mullah Taha, an Iranian Shia gay cleric, was forced to flee Iran in 2016 after conducting same-sex marriages, and gay Iranian couples report being afraid to be seen together in public while traditional families strongly influence who and when their children marry. The law sets the death penalty as legal for those above 18, and for murder, at the age of 15, and the 2017 US State Department report noted concerns about LGBTI minors. Documented cases involving young people include the January 2008 arrest of Hamzeh Chavi (18) and Loghman Hamzehpour (19) in Sardasht on sodomy and mohārebe charges, the reported 2006 hanging of two youths in north-eastern Iran for 'sex crimes', the 2022 case of two gay men in Maragheh whose death sentences for 'sodomy by force', a charge stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy, were later commuted to life in prison, and the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared allegedly by relatives. The 2017 report described an April 13, 2017 IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province in which agents reportedly fired weapons and used electric Tasers; the Canadian nonprofit Iranian Railroad for Queer Refugees reported that those arrested were taken to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan, where they were led to the prison yard and told they would be executed. In February 2008, police in Isfahan raided a party and arrested 30 men who were held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity. Since the mid-2000s the government has provided transgender persons grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for gender reassignment surgery, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover such surgery; HIV/AIDS medication is given free of charge to all Iranian citizens and several clinics offer free testing and counselling. Many LGBTQ Iranians seek UNHCR refugee status to be resettled in Australia, Canada, or the United States, and some middle-class Iranians have received education in Western nations. Outcomes have been mixed: the UNHCR rejected a plea in 2001 from an Iranian man who had entered the country illegally and was later convicted of killing his boyfriend; Japan rejected an Iranian gay man's asylum claim in 2005, and Sweden rejected a similar appeal that same year; LGBTQ activist Zahra Seddiqi Hamedani was reported to be living in Cologne, Germany in December 2023. The Netherlands stopped deporting gay men back to Iran temporarily in 2006: in March 2006 Dutch Immigration Minister Rita Verdonk stated there was 'no question of executions or death sentences based solely on the fact that a defendant is gay,' but after internal and external pressure she reversed course in October 2006 and announced Iranian LGBTs would not be deported. The United Kingdom drew criticism for continued deportations, with news reports documenting gay Iranians who committed suicide when faced with deportation, though campaign-backed cases such as Kiana Firouz and Mehdi Kazemi ended in asylum grants. The 2017 report also noted that security forces raided houses and monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, and 6Rang documented forced 'anal' or 'sodomy' tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct. On education, the government approved a booklet explaining condoms and distributed it to high school students and ran comprehensive HIV/AIDS education by the late 1990s, but no educational campaign for LGBTQ people has been allowed to exist; Kaveh Khoshnood noted that without acknowledging homosexuality's existence, no programs for LGBTQ people can be developed. Youth-facing cultural resources include the 2015 graphic novel Yousef and Farhad, published in English and Persian by OutRight Action International, and Maryam Keshavarz's 2011 film Circumstances about changing Iranian youth mores on sex and dating.

IRN.tangentialFactors:
The asylum landscape for people leaving Iran is mixed and inconsistent, which bears on any trans visitor facing removal. The UNHCR rejected a 2001 request from an Iranian man who had entered a country illegally and was later convicted of killing his boyfriend; Japan rejected an Iranian gay man's asylum claim in 2005 and Sweden rejected a similar appeal the same year. The Netherlands halted deportations of gay men to Iran temporarily in March 2006, when the Dutch Immigration Minister stated there was "no question of executions or death sentences based solely on the fact that a defendant is gay", then reversed under pressure and confirmed in October 2006 that Iranian LGBTs would not be deported. The United Kingdom drew criticism for continued deportations, with news reports documenting gay Iranians who took their own lives when faced with removal, while campaign-backed cases including Kiana Firouz and Mehdi Kazemi ended in grants. LGBTQ activist Zahra Seddiqi Hamedani was reported living in Cologne, Germany in December 2023.

Advocacy capacity inside the country is nil by design, so documentation of conditions comes from external bodies: 6Rang, Outright International, HRANA, Human Rights Watch and foreign government reporting each supply independent accounts that broadly agree on criminalisation and enforcement, and differ mainly in emphasis rather than finding.

Iran's conditional tolerance has an external dimension that distorts the picture for outsiders: trans medical tourism is reported to be growing, with foreign patients accessing state-subsidised surgery that local trans people receive only under pressure to conform to a binary transition and accept invasive, often sub-standard procedures.

Ethnicity compounds exposure. The 6Rang survey of 25 displaced LGBTIQ+ people found 96% came from ethnic minorities, indicating that persecution is not evenly distributed across the population.
IRN.localsOnly:
Residents who complete the surgical and legal process receive concrete state support. Since the mid-2000s the government has provided transgender persons grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for gender reassignment surgery, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover such surgery.

The legal route to corrected documents runs through Article 20, Clause 14, which permits a person who has had sex reassignment surgery to change name and gender on birth certification by court order, with corrected identity documents reportedly issued efficiently and transparently. Supporters of reassignment also invoke Article 215 of the civil code, covering acts serving a "rational benefit", subject to approval by a doctor.

HIV and sexual-health services are generally accessible to residents: HIV/AIDS medication is given free of charge to all Iranian citizens and several clinics offer free testing and counselling. The government approved a booklet explaining condoms for distribution to high school students and ran comprehensive HIV/AIDS education by the late 1990s, but no educational campaign for LGBTQ people has been allowed to exist; Kaveh Khoshnood has noted that without acknowledging homosexuality's existence, no programmes for LGBTQ people can be developed.

Political organising around these issues is impossible domestically. Because the government does not allow any political party or organisation to endorse LGBTQ rights, that role has fallen to exiled groups such as the Green Party of Iran, the Worker Communist Party of Iran, the Worker's Way, the Glorious Frontiers Party and the Constitutionalist Party of Iran.

Family authority governs marriage in practice as well as law: traditional families strongly influence who and when their children marry, gay Iranian couples report being afraid to be seen together in public, and Mullah Taha, an Iranian Shia gay cleric, was forced to flee in 2016 after conducting same-sex marriages.
IRN.blindSummary:
The state is among the most severe environments in the world for a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The national penal code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to the death penalty, and an international human-rights organisation has recorded executions carried out for homosexual conduct, most recently documenting two men put to death in November 2005. The parent nation's asylum office reports in its national country assessment that convictions are also brought under more severe charges used as a pretext, and that the code contains no discrimination protections of any kind.

The jurisdiction's position is bifurcated. Transsexuality is legally recognised under a 1987 religious ruling by the country's founding supreme leader, and gender-reassignment surgery is permitted and may be publicly subsidised after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder." Recognition of a person's acquired gender, however, comes only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process. Surgery is described by the parent nation's asylum office as invasive and frequently carried out to a sub-standard level.

For a trans visitor the practical consequence is that legal recognition does not travel with you. a LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is assessed by the parent nation's asylum office as likely to face persecution, and the same assessment places trans people who have not completed the surgical and legal pathway under immorality and indecency provisions carrying imprisonment, fines and corporal punishment.

Custodial violence is documented. a trans rights activist imprisoned in the country recounted in an open letter published by a domestic human-rights group being raped while held in a national intelligence detention facility. Public space is also restricted by administrative pressure: the municipal authorities of the capital issued a public warning instructing transgender people to avoid "busy" areas, an official advisory that narrows where gender-nonconforming people may appear.

Coercion shapes the recognition system itself. Reporting in 2025 describes pressure on residents to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty, with state/province funding for surgery presented as protection while functioning as the price of tolerance. The same international human-rights organisation's country analysis frames the arrangement as publicly funded surgery purchased at the cost of dignity. At the same time, foreign patients travel to the country for the subsidised procedure, and trans medical tourism has grown into a visible industry.

Documented persecution is systematic rather than incidental. a national LGBTIQ+ organisation's February 2025 submission to the national-level UN expert on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression surveyed 25 people who had fled the state and found 96% of them from ethnic minorities, describing forces driving displacement. The same organisation's submission to the state's universal periodic review, filed for the January–February 2025 session, separately catalogued human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, including violence and legal discrimination.
IRN.blindOutOfScope:
The current status and terms of the capital's advisory warning transgender people to avoid busy areas are not resolved here: the inventory confirms the warning was issued but does not establish whether it remains formally in force or how it is enforced.

The outcome of the imprisoned activist's criminal case and her custody location at the time of the human-rights group's publication are not sourced in this inventory; the account of the assault in a national intelligence detention facility is documented, the subsequent proceedings are not.

No source in this inventory addresses passport or visa screening of gender markers for entry into the state, airport treatment of trans travellers, or the availability of names and pronouns in official documents. Any statement about entry screening would be unsourced.

Figures specific to executions or imprisonments of trans people as distinct from same-sex conduct are not available here; the inventory supports execution records for homosexual conduct and imprisonment under immorality provisions for people without recognised surgery, but not a combined count.

The extent to which state/province-subsidised surgery meets clinical standards rests on the parent nation's asylum office characterising procedures as invasive and often sub-standard; no independent clinical audit is present in the inventory.

Whether the universal periodic review and national-level UN expert submissions produced any change in law or practice by the date of this record is unresolved; the inventory documents the filings, not their effect.

IRN.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents must obtain a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder" before surgery can proceed, after which the state may subsidise the cost of the operation. Full legal recognition of a person's acquired gender depends on completing that surgery, undergoing sterilisation and passing through a lengthy legal process; until every step is finished, the prior legal status continues to apply.

The pathway is not free choice. National reporting describes forced or strongly coerced transitions for citizens, where pressure to conform to a binary male/female outcome replaces the option of living outside that framework, and where refusal carries legal penalty. state/province funding for surgery is presented publicly as protection while operating as the condition of tolerance.

Residents who live openly as LGBT+ without recognised surgery are treated under immorality and indecency provisions, with imprisonment, fines and lashing available as penalties, and charges may be brought under more severe provisions as a pretext. There are no statutory discrimination protections covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans people face restrictions on movement and assembly in practice as well as in law: the municipal authorities of the capital publicly instructed transgender residents to stay out of busy areas. Detention carries documented risk of sexual violence, as the account of an imprisoned activist raped in a national intelligence facility demonstrates.

Displacement is a common outcome. a February 2025 survey of 25 people who left the country found 96% were from ethnic minorities, and the submission to the universal periodic review documents the pattern of persecution, violence and legal discrimination that drives people out.
IRN.blindTangential:
The state is a regional outlier in two directions at once: it combines one of the world's harshest criminal regimes for same-sex conduct with formal state/province recognition and public funding for gender-affirming surgery, an arrangement found in almost no neighbouring jurisdiction. Visitors comparing the destination with others in the national neighbourhood should not read the availability of surgery as an indicator of general safety.

The medical-tourism trade is a point of contrast between visitors and residents. Foreign patients arrive for subsidised, low-cost procedures that residents are pushed toward under penalty, so clinics catering to international clients coexist with domestic pressure to complete a binary transition. National reporting in 2025 on the boom is the clearest documentation of that split.

Persecution documented against LGBTIQ+ people overlaps substantially with ethnic and minority status: 96% of the 25 people surveyed for the February 2025 submission to the national-level UN expert were from ethnic minorities, which suggests that a trans visitor perceived as belonging to a minority group faces an added layer of exposure.

The enforcement backdrop includes state/province execution for same-sex conduct, recorded over two decades, and periodic spikes in official statements against LGBT people. The submission to the state's universal periodic review indicates that the international review mechanism is an active channel for this documentation, though it does not itself change conditions on the ground.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.summary:
Israel does not criminalise consensual same-sex acts, and its statutory framework combines anti-discrimination protections with publicly funded transition healthcare. Legal gender recognition has run through the courts: sex reassignment was first legally recognised in 1986, and on 27 July 2025 the High Court of Justice blocked a fast-track attempt to reverse a gender change, holding that the 2021 certificate "remains valid." As of 2025, registration of a person's previous name has been abolished for transgender people, removing the old-name traceability that previously followed a document change.

Border screening is the sharpest visitor-specific exposure. A first-person account published by Haaretz on 3 May 2023 documents a transgender traveller subjected to gender-identity humiliation at an Israeli airport, with security personnel insisting "if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male." Later that month the Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing the searching of transgender people, a protocol change issued after complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees and travellers.

Violence against LGBT people rose during 2025 according to official data cited by the Jerusalem Post, and Ynet reported anti-LGBTQ violence reaching a record high, with organised ambushes in which victims were lured through dating apps. Haaretz reported in February 2025 that inflammatory rhetoric from the United States was feeding into the local climate, with trans Israelis describing heightened fear.

Custody is the weakest point in the protection machinery. A law-journal study records that the state response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability has been isolation and segregation, keeping trans inmates apart from the general prison population rather than housing them in facilities matching their gender identity. An October 2019 precedent-setting case cut the other way: after a petition by ACRI, an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and move her from a male prison to a female one. She was initially held in a separate wing of the women's prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition seeking her placement with the general population.

Recognition of partners has advanced through the courts and by executive instruction. In December 2004 the Tel Aviv District Court ruled that the government had acted illegally in trying to deport the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule barring deportation of foreign nationals married to Israeli citizens to common-law and same-sex couples. In March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted residency to a gay Palestinian man from Jenin to live with his partner of eight years in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to extend the same citizenship rights to same-sex couples as to opposite-sex couples, replacing a prior position under which same-sex spouses waited up to seven years and typically received only permanent residency.

On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued an executive directive banning licensed medical professionals, including psychologists, social workers and Ministry of Health-licensed therapists, from conducting conversion therapy. The directive does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset; the governing coalition defeated a bill to ban conversion therapy on 24 February 2016 and, the same day, defeated a bill to train health professionals on gender and sexual orientation issues.

Family formation remains restricted in part. A July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples; the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the ban violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022. Between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded, against more than a thousand heterosexual couples, until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure, and the Knesset voted in July 2018 to keep single men and same-sex couples out of surrogacy.

Same-sex marriage is not legislated: a Channel 10 survey reported by the Times of Israel found majority public support for it while half of MKs declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.

Public expression has expanded alongside sustained violence. Israel's first LGBT pride march was held on 17 September 1977, Tel Aviv's first Pride parade followed in 1993 and Eilat Pride began in 2001. Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned the ban; the 2005 march was attacked by Yishai Schlissel, who stabbed three people and received a ten-year sentence, and after his 2015 release he stabbed six marchers, killing teenage girl Shira Banki. On 1 August 2009 an armed attacker killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv. The 2018 Aguda-organized LGBTQ strike drew over 100,000 to a Tel Aviv rally, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022. The 2025 Tel Aviv Pride, scheduled for 13 June, was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets; in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset.

Tel Aviv functions as a regional queer hub, and Israel is widely regarded as the most progressive destination in its part of the world for trans visitors, supported by community infrastructure that includes the Municipal LGBT Community Center opened in 2008 and the Jerusalem Open House.
ISR.outOfScopeNotes:
One source, a legal-analysis page on trans rights in Israel covering laws, protections and gaps, returned HTTP 404 at research time; none of its claims have been used and its contents remain unverified here.

The state of legal gender recognition is not settled across the sources used. Outright International's 12 March 2026 profile states that there is no legal gender recognition and that LGBTI organisations cannot register, while court decisions from 1986, 2021 and July 2025 and the 2025 abolition of previous-name registration point the other way. Which description is current, and whether the registration restriction applies to some or all organisations, is unresolved in this inventory.

The 2023 Israel Police regulation on searching transgender people is documented as adopted, but whether it is applied uniformly at airports and checkpoints is not sourced here, as is its relationship to the airport treatment recorded in the May 2023 account.

The 2025 rise and record high in anti-LGBTQ violence are attributed to official data through newspaper reports; the underlying figures, their definitions and whether they break out trans victims are not independently available in this inventory.

Public-opinion and legislative positions on same-sex marriage rest on a single reported survey, and the Knesset's current stance on legislating marriage equality is not sourced.

Whether publicly funded transition healthcare is available to visitors rather than to residents covered by national insurance is not addressed by any source in this inventory.

ISR.tangentialFactors:
Trans healthcare in Israel was historically denied rather than merely unregulated: in 1954 Attorney General Haim Cohn blocked Rina Natan's sex reassignment surgery, and statutory recognition of sex reassignment did not arrive until 1986. The present access regime sits on that history rather than on a long-standing entitlement.

Criminalisation itself is a colonial inheritance. Under the British Mandate, official questionnaires documented "unnatural" sexual expression and the mandate power pushed criminalisation into Palestinian schools and society, a policy carried into the Israeli state; in 1943 the Acre district court tried Mustafa Naif, aged 16, on a sodomy charge carrying up to ten years' imprisonment, though he was convicted of perjury instead. The offence has since been repealed, so this bears on the origin of the regime rather than on present visitor exposure.

The volatility of public-space safety is illustrated by the pattern around Jerusalem Pride rather than by any single incident, and by the fact that the 2025 Tel Aviv parade was cancelled for military rather than safety reasons. A central Jerusalem square is to be renamed "Tolerance Square" in memory of Shira Banki, and in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality hung Pride flags inscribed "equality in life" along the parade route.

Comparatively, Israel's position rests on judicial and ministerial acts more than on legislation: the conversion-therapy restriction, the same-sex citizenship instruction and much of the gender-recognition framework are directives or rulings that a future Knesset or minister could alter. That distinction separates it from jurisdictions where equivalent protections are statutory.
ISR.localsOnly:
Transgender prisoners are managed by isolation as the default practice, kept apart from the general prison population rather than placed according to gender identity. Placement by gender, where it has been ordered, has come through litigation and has included separate-wing conditions inside the destination prison.

Access to hormone-replacement therapy inside the prison system is available on court order rather than as an established entitlement, on the record of the 2019 ACRI petition.

Conversion therapy is prohibited only for licensed professionals under a 14 February 2022 Health Ministry directive. Rabbis, clergy and alternative practitioners fall outside its scope, and the ban has not been enacted in statute, so it remains reversible by a change of minister.

Family formation rules apply to residents as well as visitors' long-term counterparts: surrogacy access for single men and same-sex couples was restored only after the 2020 and 2021 court rulings taking effect on 12 January 2022, and adoption by same-sex couples was rare until the August 2017 reversal.

Residents' own accounts recorded in February 2025 describe heightened fear among trans Israelis attributed to imported political rhetoric from the United States, indicating that the domestic climate moves with external discourse.

An international LGBTI rights organisation's country profile, last updated 12 March 2026, records no legal gender recognition in the criminal and civil code and states that LGBTI organisations cannot register, alongside no criminalisation and some legal protections.

The 2023 national police regulation on searching transgender people is documented as adopted, but whether it is applied uniformly at airports and checkpoints is not sourced here, as is its relationship to the airport treatment recorded in the May 2023 account.

The 2025 rise and record high in anti-LGBTQ violence are attributed to official data through newspaper reports; the underlying figures, their definitions and whether they break out trans victims are not independently available in this inventory.

Public-opinion and legislative positions on same-sex marriage rest on a single reported survey, and the national parliament's current stance on legislating marriage equality is not sourced.

Whether publicly funded transition healthcare is available to visitors rather than to residents covered by national insurance is not addressed by any source in this inventory.
blindSourceSummaries: Court-based legal gender recognition with dead-name removal from IDs (2025) and publicly funded transition healthcare exist; the main international airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition.

An October 2019 court ruling ordered the prison service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one, after she was initially placed in a separate wing of the women's prison; a civil-rights organisation petitioned for the ruling and prepared a further petition to have her housed with the general population, whose outcome is unreported.

A 2015 academic law-journal article documents the nation's response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability as isolating and segregating trans inmates apart from the rest of the prison population rather than placing them in facilities matching their gender identity.

Violence reporting (2025): 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people 'bearing the brunt'; anti-trans rhetoric from a foreign political leader is reportedly inflaming the local climate.
No statute or prison-service regulation on trans-prisoner placement is documented; whether case-by-case judicial relief would extend to a detained foreign visitor is not established.
ISR.blindLocalsOnly:
Transgender prisoners are managed by isolation as the default practice, kept apart from the general prison population rather than placed according to gender identity. Placement by gender, where it has been ordered, has come through litigation and has included separate-wing conditions inside the destination prison.

Access to hormone-replacement therapy inside the prison system is available on court order rather than as an established entitlement, on the record of the 2019 civil-liberties petition.

Conversion therapy is prohibited only for licensed professionals under a February 2022 health ministry directive. Clergy and alternative practitioners fall outside its scope, and the ban has not been enacted in statute, so it remains reversible by a change of minister.

Family formation rules apply to residents as well as to the long-term counterparts of visitors: surrogacy access for single men and same-sex couples was restored only after court rulings taking effect in January 2022, and adoption by same-sex couples was rare until the August 2017 reversal.

Residents' own accounts recorded in February 2025 describe heightened fear among trans residents attributed to imported political rhetoric from a major allied country, indicating that the domestic climate moves with external discourse.

An international LGBTI rights organisation's country profile, last updated in March 2026, records no legal gender recognition in the criminal and civil code and states that LGBTI organisations cannot register, alongside no criminalisation and some legal protections.
ISR.blindTangential:
Trans healthcare in the country was historically denied rather than merely unregulated: in 1954 the national justice department blocked a woman's sex reassignment surgery, and statutory recognition of sex reassignment did not arrive until 1986. The present access regime sits on that history rather than on a long-standing entitlement.

Criminalisation itself is a historic-era inheritance. Under the mandate administration, official questionnaires documented "unnatural" sexual expression and the administering power pushed criminalisation into local schools and society, a policy carried into the successor polity; in 1943 a district court tried a 16-year-old on a sodomy charge carrying up to ten years' imprisonment, though he was convicted of perjury instead. The offence has since been repealed, so this bears on the origin of the regime rather than on present visitor exposure.

The volatility of public-space safety is illustrated by the pattern around one city's Pride rather than by any single incident, and by the fact that the 2025 parade in the principal city was cancelled for military rather than safety reasons. A central square in the historic capital is to be renamed "Tolerance Square" in memory of the teenage victim, and in 2026 the municipality there hung Pride flags inscribed "equality in life" along the parade route.

Comparatively, the country's position rests on judicial and ministerial acts more than on legislation: the conversion-therapy restriction, the same-sex citizenship instruction and much of the gender-recognition framework are directives or rulings that a future parliament or minister could alter. That distinction separates it from jurisdictions where equivalent protections are statutory.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.summary:
Argentina's Law 26.743 remains one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. It was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and described them as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, who was stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is not applied in the case as it now stands.
ARG.outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the court challenge to the February 2025 decree on minors is unresolved in the sources available here; whether the decree has been suspended, upheld or struck down is not established.

The 227 hate crimes recorded for 2025 come from a single monitoring body, the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio. Its geographic coverage, reporting methodology and the proportion of incidents that resulted in criminal charges are not sourced here.

No sourced information in this inventory addresses entry or visa screening, passport or identity-document markers for transgender travellers, or access to gender-affirming care for adults. Those areas are not covered rather than confirmed as unproblematic.

A Buenos Aires safety guide updated on 28 May 2026 offers a first-person account of walking in the capital at all hours, aimed at gay visitors. It contains no trans-specific legal finding and is not treated as evidence of conditions nationwide.

Whether the prison-housing decree has been implemented, and how it is applied in practice by the prison authority, is not sourced.

ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.summary:
The United Arab Emirates screens gender identity against travel documents at the point of entry, and the practice has produced documented refusals over at least a decade. In 2025 two Israeli trans women were held for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, and denied entry with their passports confiscated.

In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport after authorities declined to recognise her gender as legitimate, and her passport was confiscated. In March 2022 the Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe contest, was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand ahead of her Expo 2020 appearance; her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), which carries a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed. The same statute also reaches unmarried different-sex couples. Prosecution depends on a complaint basis: under Article 409(5) no action may be brought except on complaint by the spouse or guardian of the complainant, who may withdraw it at any time.

Article 412(2) punishes men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space with imprisonment of up to one year and a fine of up to AED 10,000. It replaced a broader previous ban on clothing 'inappropriate for one's sex', narrowing but not removing exposure for gender-nonconforming presentation in sex-restricted settings.

Legal mechanisms explicitly acknowledge and penalise nonconformity with traditional gender roles, and transgender expression or unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion. There is no legal gender recognition in the UAE, and sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances.

Detention carries documented risks specific to gender expression. Detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people, and involuntary medical and psychological treatments, including hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatments, have occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. Reports of mistreatment in detention include beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation.

Arrests for cross-dressing and gender nonconformity are on the record. In December 2013 two Brazilian trans women who called police about prejudice they had witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. In 2005 a raid on an Abu Dhabi desert resort netted 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding'; 12 were found guilty, 11 receiving five-year sentences and one receiving a year, with initial reports that some were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences.

A Brazilian trans woman detained in the UAE since September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, has accused her consulate of negligence, a case illustrating the exposure of trans foreigners to prolonged custody with uncertain consular support.

No UAE law or policy provides protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Same-sex marriage is not recognised. Officials have publicly declared that there is 'no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE'.
ARE.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether consular authorities can secure release or fair treatment for a detained trans national is unresolved in the sources; the Brazilian detainee's allegation of consulate negligence is an accusation, not a finding, and no outcome for her case is recorded here.

No source in the inventory states how UAE border officers treat a passport whose gender marker has been changed, as distinct from one where presentation and marker diverge; the documented denials involve female markers with male sex recorded at birth and a male marker with female presentation, and the general rule applied is not published.

Enforcement frequency of Article 412(2) is not sourced: the inventory supplies the penalty text and the prior broader clothing provision, but no case counts or sentences handed down under it.

The dates of the Cairo 52 legal review and the currency of individual reported incidents are not specified beyond those given; several underlying reports date from 2005 to 2013 and may not reflect current enforcement practice.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organizations operate openly anywhere in the UAE; in Dubai no formal LGBTQ organizations or nightclubs exist, and a nightclub that sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes toward homosexuality and varied gender expression, together with the likelihood of state repression, prevent the establishment of such organizations or community education. Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances, and detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people. Involuntary medical and psychological treatments, including hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatments, have occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation. No protections exist under any UAE law or policy against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), carrying a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed. Under Article 409(5), no action may be brought except upon a complaint by the spouse or guardian of the complainant, who may withdraw it at any time; because civil guardianship ends at age 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male conduct between adults, so federal prosecution is not possible, whereas for female-female relations an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative may qualify as guardian under the Islamic wali concept and a married woman's husband as spouse, so prosecution remains possible where such a complainant exists. Under Article 412(2), men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space may be imprisoned for up to one year and fined up to AED 10,000, replacing a broader previous ban on clothing 'inappropriate for one's sex'. The UAE does not recognise same-sex marriage. Censorship targets youth-facing material and LGBTQ content: the country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex'; the Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag; the Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation in 2022, with an edition withdrawn over dialogue using the Arabic word مثلي (mithli); Amazon blocked 150 search terms including 'lgbtq', 'pride' and 'closeted gay' on its UAE site in June 2023 under threat of penalties, removing listings including Roxane Gay's Bad Feminist. Officials have publicly declared there is 'no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE', and the band Steps refused a Dubai show in June 2023 over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality. Reports of mistreatment in detention, including beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture, have been consequences of suspected or established same-sex conduct. Police raids and arrests for same-sex conduct and cross-dressing include the 2005 Abu Dhabi desert resort raid on 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding', of whom 12 were found guilty, 11 receiving five-year sentences and one receiving a year, with initial reports that some were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences; a 2012 raid breaking up a gay party of 30 men in Dubai; and two Indian men arrested that year for consensual sex in a public toilet who received six months each plus deportation. In December 2013, two Brazilian transgender women who called police about prejudice they witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. Gigi Gorgeous was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport in August 2016 because authorities did not recognise her gender as legitimate, and her passport was confiscated. In July 2007 in Dubai, a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy was kidnapped and raped, was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country, though he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation; a 17-year-old acquaintance was implicated in luring him, and the family accused UAE authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention. Youth are directly criminalised and vulnerable, and the UAE ranked 85th with a score of 37 on PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index.

The Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag. The country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex', which constrains the information a visitor can reach from inside the country.

Commercial and cultural pressure follows the same pattern. Amazon blocked 150 search terms including 'lgbtq', 'pride' and 'closeted gay' on its UAE site in June 2023 under threat of penalties, removing listings including Roxane Gay's Bad Feminist, and the band Steps refused a Dubai show in June 2023 over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality.

The legal regime has been applied to victims as well as suspects. In July 2007 in Dubai a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy was kidnapped and raped, was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country; he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation, and his family accused UAE authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention.

Criminal liability attaches regardless of age, so minors travelling with families are not outside the exposure. A 2012 raid broke up a gay party of 30 men in Dubai, and two Indian men arrested that year for consensual sex in a public toilet received six months each plus deportation.

Comparative indices place the country low on measured LGBTI wellbeing: it ranked 85th with a score of 37 on PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index, a figure now a decade old.

blindSourceSummaries: News report (2025): two trans women describe being detained for hours at the airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched their female passport records, mocked by staff, and denied entry with passports confiscated — a direct visitor-experience account of gender-document screening at entry.

News report (Mar 21, 2022): a foreign trans model was stopped at immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported before a scheduled appearance because her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

News report (Apr 2023): a foreign trans woman detained in the country since September 2022 — arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test — accused the consulate of negligence; a documented case of a trans foreigner in prolonged custody.

Legal review of the country: it employs various legal mechanisms that explicitly acknowledge and penalise nonconformity with traditional gender roles; transgender expression and unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion — the legal-framework basis for visitor risk.

Country overview by an international human-rights organisation (last updated Mar 12, 2026): a new national criminal code enacted in early 2022 criminalised consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment (one provision also covers unmarried different-sex couples); charges require a complaint basis; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register.
News report (Aug 9, 2016): a trans media personality was denied entry and detained at the airport — an early high-profile case of a trans visitor refused entry on identity grounds.
ARE.blindTangential:
Censorship extends to trans-specific content. The national media regulator banned an animated film in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned a superhero sequel in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag. The country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex', which constrains the information a visitor can reach from inside the country.

Commercial and cultural pressure follows the same pattern. A major online retailer blocked 150 search terms including 'lgbtq', 'pride' and 'closeted gay' on its national site in June 2023 under threat of penalties, removing listings including a feminist essay collection, and a pop group refused a show in the country in June 2023 over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality.

The legal regime has been applied to victims as well as suspects. In July 2007 a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy was kidnapped and raped, was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country; he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation, and his family accused national authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention.

Criminal liability attaches regardless of age, so minors travelling with families are not outside the exposure. A 2012 raid broke up a party of 30 men, and two foreign men arrested that year for consensual sex in a public toilet received six months each plus deportation.

Comparative indices place the country low on measured LGBTI wellbeing: it ranked 85th with a score of 37 on a 2015 regional happiness index, a figure now a decade old.
ARE.localsOnly:
No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organisation operates openly anywhere in the UAE. In Dubai no formal LGBTQ organisations or nightclubs exist, and a nightclub that sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes toward homosexuality and varied gender expression, together with the likelihood of state repression, prevent the establishment of such organisations or community education. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Article 409(5) shapes who can be prosecuted. Because civil guardianship ends at age 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male conduct between adults, so federal prosecution is not possible in that configuration; for female-female relations an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative may qualify as guardian under the Islamic wali concept and a married woman's husband as spouse, so prosecution remains possible where such a complainant exists.

Residents have no legal route to have their gender recognised, and no non-discrimination remedy exists in law on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics.

The Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation in 2022, with an edition withdrawn over dialogue using the Arabic word مثلي (mithli), part of a domestic censorship regime that reaches youth-facing material.
