ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which also hears hate-speech and harassment complaints. Sexual-orientation grounds were written into constitutional protection in 1996, and the Civil Union Act of 2006 provides for same-sex marriage.

Criminalisation ended definitively in the 1990s. Sodomy and the common-law 'unnatural sexual offence' were struck down by the Constitutional Court in the National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality judgment of 1998, applied retroactively to 27 April 1994; the residual disparity that kept the age of consent at 19 for homosexual acts was equalised at a gender-neutral 16 by the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act of 2007, and the Constitutional Court confirmed the old disparity unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008, again retroactive to 1994. A visitor engages no consensual-conduct offence on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation.

The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act, signed into law in May 2024, explicitly names sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics as protected grounds, with hate speech requiring a 'clear intention' to be harmful, incite harm or promote hatred. Human Rights Watch and other legal commentators warned before enactment that the wording is vague and burdens free expression; the protection is nonetheless now a statutory offence framework rather than only a sentencing consideration, as it was before PEPUDA.

Legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which allows amendment of sex status in the population registry and the issue of identity documents and passports reflecting gender identity. The statute requires medical or surgical treatment, including hormone replacement therapy; sex reassignment surgery is not required. Identity documents remain strictly binary, so non-binary people cannot be recognised, and the medical requirements are criticised as pathologising and as locking people out of recognition altogether. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans for gender-neutral identification on South African ID cards, with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents, but officials confirmed the change would take a few years as it passes through consultation to legislation.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled for a transgender inmate, Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena, against the Department of Correctional Services in case 2024/070075. The court held that refusing to provide prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care in custody, and ordered the Department to provide gender-affirming hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, to implement required accommodations, and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling as an affirmation of the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities. Lawyers for Human Rights, which represented the inmate, had earlier in 2025 been litigating a transgender prisoner's conditions of detention while rights organisations questioned whether the Department's standard operating procedure was being implemented in practice; the judgment converts those obligations into binding equality-court remedies.

Mismatched documents remain a daily hazard. An analysis published in January 2026 by Mikhail Petersen of Gender Dynamix describes trans people facing humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for 'fraud' when presenting identity documents that do not match their presentation, and argues that legal gender recognition should be a right grounded in dignity. Gender Dynamix's 2024 report records a trans woman turned away from filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID, with police mocking her. Ordinary administrative tasks therefore carry an outing and refusal risk even though the underlying legal framework is protective.

Facilities access is contested rather than settled. A 2024 academic analysis in PER/PELJ, 'Did the CPA Shut the Bathroom Door?', examines whether gender-segregated bathrooms excluding transgender and non-binary people constitute unfair discrimination under the Promotion of Equality Act read with section 9 of the Constitution, and concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access. A trans visitor should expect facility rules to vary by venue and institution rather than to rest on a single settled national rule.

Gender-affirming care is lawful and available but unevenly distributed. Hormone therapy can be accessed from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. Private care is concentrated in the major cities and public systems face long waits, which forces rural patients to travel to urban centres; in December 2024 LGBT activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long treatment delays for trans healthcare.

Violence against visibly trans people remains the principal physical risk. On 26 December 2024 the 23-year-old trans woman Aobakwe Mahlobo was attacked without provocation at a tavern in Tshwane, sustaining severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's December 2024 rights watch recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders in that month alone. Lesbians and trans people have been murdered, beaten and subjected to 'corrective rape', including among pupils, and activists have accused police of negligent handling of cases, including nine allegedly related murders of gay men between 2010 and 2013, with impunity condemned by ActionAid. Protection machinery exists — a Department of Justice National Task Team from 2011, a National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities from April 2014 with a rapid response team for unsolved cases, a Justice Ministry programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence launched in the 2010s, and the 2024 Hate Crimes Act — but enforcement records remain uneven.

Partner and family recognition is broad: the Civil Union Act has been in force since 2006, and court decisions extending to same-sex couples cover immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits, and joint adoption.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
South African law and public-opinion context relevant to trans and LGBT visitors.

Criminal law history: Sex between men was a common-law crime of 'sodomy' and 'unnatural sexual offence' inherited from Roman-Dutch law. Under the National Party (1948-1994) homosexuality carried up to seven years in prison, used to break up gay events and harass activists (e.g. the January 1966 Forest Town raid), and a 1969 amendment to the Immorality Act barred men from erotic conduct with more than two people present. Male same-sex conduct was legalised in 1994 (female same-sex conduct was never illegal), and in 1998 the Constitutional Court confirmed in National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality v Minister of Justice that sodomy and 'unnatural sexual act' offences were unconstitutional, applying retroactively to 27 April 1994. A residual Sexual Offences provision kept the age of consent at 19 for homosexual acts versus 16 for heterosexual acts until the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act equalised it at 16 in gender-neutral terms in 2007 (the inequality was declared unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008, retroactive to 1994). As of a 2017 ILGA poll, 24% of South Africans still said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals, while 57% disagreed.

Hate-crime and equality law: The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (2000) prohibits hate speech and harassment on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds and set up Equality Courts; before this, South Africa had no statutory hate-crime penalty regime and courts treated homophobic hatred only as an aggravating sentencing factor. The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Bill was passed by the National Assembly in March 2023 and the National Council in November 2023 and signed into law by President Ramaphosa in May 2024, its hate-speech wording tightened after 2016 public consultation so that it requires a 'clear intention' to be harmful, incite harm or promote hatred on grounds including gender or gender identity and sexual orientation. Human Rights Watch and other legal experts warned the bill is vague, threatens freedom of expression, and has been likened to the Suppression of Communism Act, 1950. The Department of Justice's National Task Team (2011) and National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities (April 2014) addressed sex- and gender-based violence, with a rapid response team for unsolved cases.

Legal gender recognition and documents: The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act lets a person change their sex status in the population registry and obtain identity documents and passports indicating their gender identity, requiring medical or surgical treatment such as hormone replacement therapy (sex reassignment surgery is not required); hormone therapy is available from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans to introduce gender-neutral identification on South African ID cards — the first African country to do so — with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents, though the head of policy confirmed changes will take a few years as they move through consultation to legislation. Court decisions extending to same-sex couples before and after the Civil Union Act include immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption. South Africa ranks among the world's best in the 2025 Spartacus Gay Travel Index and Equaldex LGBT Equality Index, and the official South African Tourism site offers in-depth travel tips for gay travellers.

Screening: The source text contains no provisions on border checks, entry screening or security screening of travellers. The only screening-type policy described is blood donation: until 2014 the South African National Blood Service required men who have sex with men to abstain from sex for six months before donating, replaced by a gender-neutral rule barring any donor with a new sexual partner in the last six months or more than one partner.

Youth: Homosexual acts were gated at 19 versus 16 for heterosexual acts until the 2007 Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act set a uniform 16 in gender-neutral terms (inequality declared unconstitutional in Geldenhuys, 2008, retroactive to 1994). South Africa has no specific anti-bullying law, though the Protection from Harassment Act 17 of 2011 and Child Justice Act 75 of 2008 cover homophobic harassment and youth offenders; per the Department of Basic Education, South African pupils are the 'most bullied kids in the world' — a 2015 TIMSS survey found 44% of Grade 5 pupils (age 10-11) bullied weekly and 34% monthly, the highest of 38 countries, 48% of public-school pupils bullied weekly, and Grade 9 pupils (14-15) third-most bullied at 17% weekly and 47% monthly. A bill introduced in 2021 would ban conversion therapy on children — still not prohibited under the Children's Act 38 of 2005 — after three teens aged 15-19 died at a conversion therapy camp whose owners were convicted of murder and child abuse in February 2015. Transgender minors access hormone therapy from 16 and surgery from 18 (or younger with parental consent), with private care mostly urban and public systems facing long waits, forcing rural youth to travel to major cities; a non-binary teenager, Zade de Kock, petitioned Home Affairs over being forced to use inaccurate gender markers throughout his schooling. Active LGBT student organisations exist at Wits, UCT, Stellenbosch, UJ and UWC.

Visibility and public opinion: The first Lesbian and Gay Pride march was held in Johannesburg on 13 October 1990 (about 800 people), and Pride is now held annually in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Durban, Pretoria and Soweto, with smaller cities including Bloemfontein, Polokwane, Port Elizabeth, Mbombela, East London, Pietermaritzburg and Knysna hosting LGBT events — Knysna's Pink Loerie Mardi Gras draws visitors nationwide. Cape Town is called one of the world's friendliest LGBTQ+ cities, with the De Waterkant gay village, a permanent rainbow crosswalk and the Pink Lane. Public opinion is mixed but comparatively favourable: the 2015 Progressive Prudes study found 55% would accept a gay family member and 51% that gay people should have the same human rights; Afrobarometer (2016) put South Africa second in Africa at 67% comfortable with a same-sex couple next door versus a 21% Africa-wide average; ILGA (2017) found 67% back equal rights for gay and lesbian people and 72% for transgender people; and an Ipsos poll in May 2021 found 71% support some legal recognition for same-sex couples, 18% having attended a same-sex wedding. Violence remains a gap: lesbians have been murdered, beaten and subjected to 'corrective rape' (including among pupils), activists accuse police of negligent handling including nine allegedly related murders of gay men between 2010 and 2013, and ActionAid has condemned impunity; in 2012 Contralesa petitioned to remove LGBT rights from the Constitution, but the ANC parliamentary caucus rejected it.

ZAF.tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of state recognition runs back more than a decade: Justice Minister Jeff Radebe launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence citing the Constitution's equality clause, an early government framing of LGBTI violence as a policy problem that preceded the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024.

South Africa's statutory package compares with the small group of jurisdictions combining constitutional sexual-orientation protections, statutory gender recognition, marriage equality and an operative equality court; the divergence between that package and enforcement is the pattern the Mokoena litigation and the Frere Hospital memorandum illustrate.

The prison ruling is a data point within a wider correctional pattern rather than an isolated finding: a standard operating procedure existed, implementation was contested by practitioners, and a court then ordered the Department of Correctional Services to comply with its own rules.

Academic and civil-society debate continues over whether legal gender recognition should be reframed as a right grounded in dignity rather than a medical procedure, and over the exclusion of non-binary identities from a binary marker system.
ZAF.localsOnly:

Only two sex markers are available on official documents, so non-binary residents have no route to a matching marker through the existing statute, and reform toward self-determination has been proposed but is not yet law.

Residents who present with documents that do not align with their appearance report being refused service and threatened with arrest for fraud, and Gender Dynamix's 2024 report records police mocking a trans woman who sought to open a domestic-violence case.

Residents in correctional facilities are covered by the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure for transgender inmates and, since the Equality Court judgment of 14 November 2025, by court orders requiring hormone treatment at state expense, gender-expressive clothing and the delivery of prescribed care.

Township residents, particularly Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people, bear a disproportionate share of the recorded violence, and community organisations reported five LGBTQIA+ murders in December 2024 alone.

Public healthcare for trans residents is available but unevenly delivered, with documented treatment delays of up to a year prompting direct action against a provincial hospital in the Eastern Cape.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. sources.summary:
Indonesia censors expression deemed to promote homosexuality: the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction criminalizes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations (up to 7 years prison), and in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned TV/radio programs making LGBTQ behavior appear 'normal.' The government has banned websites and apps containing 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words (including Grindr), shut down the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni, and in 2025 a new bill was being discussed to explicitly prohibit online content presenting 'lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behavior.' In October 2025, President Prabowo Subianto declared the spread of LGBTQ culture a 'non-military national threat' in a presidential decree, placing it alongside separatism and terrorism.

Transgender Indonesians can change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. Since June 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung, and Papua, because many were undocumented, especially where families disapproved, leaving them without access to work or social services. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognized, with no third gender or X option, and transgender Indonesians have their gender at birth printed unless they have already obtained court recognition.

Since 2018, the Jakarta Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) 'socially dysfunctional,' regularly conducted raids against them, and taken detained trans individuals to city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres where they are incarcerated alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their 'offence'; officials stated this is meant as a deterrent against being transgender. Conversion therapy is widely practiced and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, including corrective rape from family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on setting up safe houses and evacuation plans, and the Yayasan Srikandi Sejati organization provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic; Yogyakarta has the only madrasa for transgender people in the world.

As of 2019, no specific law exists to protect Indonesian citizens from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Theoretically, protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground is guaranteed in the Constitution and Human Rights Law (No. 39/1999), and the Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer declaring LGBTQ persons need not apply after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights. A police brigadier (TT) was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him; his lawsuit was rejected by the Semarang State Administrative Court in May 2019 on procedural grounds. The police have issued a circular since 2015 to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and Regulation of the Head of National Police Number 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.

PAK.name: Pakistan
PAK.summary:
Pakistan's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognises self-perceived gender identity and prohibits discrimination in education, employment, healthcare, housing and access to goods and services. The 2020 Rules under the Act added a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents, and a 2010 Supreme Court order had already directed free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people.

Those statutory protections sit under an active constitutional challenge. On 19 May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court, delivering a reserved verdict across 12 shariat petitions, ruled that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act, covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. The struck sections remained in force pending appeals, and the UK Home Office country-policy note of November 2025 records that transgender and intersex people remain protected under the 2018 Act while describing the 2023 declaration and the litigation around it as unresolved.

Amnesty International responded to the verdict on 19 May 2023 as a blow to the rights of an already beleaguered group, and had warned the government two days earlier not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards. A further retrograde proposal surfaced later: Senator Mushtaq Ahmad has put forward a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control transgender people's official gender identity, an active legislative push against self-identification.

Lethal violence against transgender women is documented and recurring. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range in Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there within a week. On 21 September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi. In February 2026 reporting, activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana survived three bullets fired through a Karachi door at night, and the account describes a wave of violence that has left transgender Pakistanis afraid to go out.

Custody and police handling are a specific danger. Justice Project Pakistan's policy brief finds that the 2018 Act's advances have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice, and identifies implementation failure rather than absence of law as the central problem, with recommendations directed at custody and police safeguards. Local reporting from October 2025 documents the same gap at street level: rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals, street harassment, and suspicion or ridicule at police stations.

Healthcare access is a documented failure point. In 2016 the 23-year-old transgender activist Alisha was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to take her to the men's or the women's ward; men in the hospital taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was HIV-positive. Some transgender women administer hormones and silicone under unsupervised and unhygienic conditions because sex-reassignment surgery is rarely available in Pakistan, and the 2018 Act's healthcare non-discrimination clause is routinely not honoured in practice.

Open expression carries personal risk. Pakistani media censor LGBTQ-related news: the government blocked Queerpk.com in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times left a blank space where a photograph accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code provisions reinforce this, banning 'obscene' publications and public acts and designating an assembly of five or more persons an unlawful assembly where the common object is to commit any offence, so public gathering carries legal exposure as well as risk from non-state actors such as Islamist and terrorist groups.

No legal recognition exists for same-sex partnerships. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity, Article 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family and oppose obscenity, and Article 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council; Article 496 of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. A small clerical body in Lahore, Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat, declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016, but that declaration has no civil effect and the Federal Shariat Court's 2023 ruling cuts the other way.
PAK.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 'X' marker issued under the 2020 Rules is accepted at international border posts, by airlines, or by foreign missions issuing visas is not sourced in the inventory and remains unresolved here. No information is available on airport or immigration screening practices that could disclose a trans visitor's status on arrival.

The current status of the appeals against the Federal Shariat Court's 19 May 2023 ruling is not sourced beyond the November 2025 UK Home Office note describing ongoing legal disputes. Which sections of the 2018 Act are operative in practice, as distinct from on the statute book, is not resolved by these sources.

No source in the inventory addresses whether Pakistan has hate-crime sentencing enhancement covering gender identity, or any complaints mechanism available to a foreign national. Reporting requirements for trans visitors are likewise not sourced.

The precise scope of section 377 as applied, and whether a trans woman's relationships are assessed under it by sex assigned at birth or by recognised gender, is described in the sources as unclear.

A 2016 article by a young Pakistani man in the UK-based Gay Star News had his surname omitted for his security.

In 2010 the Supreme Court ordered provision of free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people, and the 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act prohibits discrimination in healthcare, education, employment, housing and access to goods and services, though the source notes locals often deny trans people basic education and healthcare. The HIV epidemic began in Pakistan in 1987; government estimates (2004) put nearly 3,000 people living with HIV while critics suggest 70,000 to 80,000 and UNAIDS reports possibly up to 210,000, and a 2009 survey found male and transgender sex workers at high risk, with prostitutes lacking access to condoms and little public health education provided.

Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition. Article 496 of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. Same-sex couples can live together only in secret; the source notes the LGBTQ community can socialise, organise, date and, in rare cases, live together as couples, if done mostly in secret, and in 2005 a tribal council in the Khyber region ordered a man who married a fellow tribesman to leave the area or face death. PAK.localsOnly:
Residents live with the statutory framework daily: the 2018 Act prohibits discrimination in healthcare, education, employment, housing and access to goods and services, and the 2020 Rules allow an 'X' marker on administrative documents, yet local reporting documents denial of basic education and healthcare to transgender people notwithstanding those clauses.

Sex-reassignment surgery is rarely available in Pakistan because of cost, limited training and social taboos, so many transgender women obtain hormones and silicone injections through unregulated providers without proper equipment or supervision. The 2020 Rules under the Act added a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents, and a 2010 Supreme Court order had already directed free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people.

Those statutory protections sit under an active constitutional challenge. On 19 May 2023 a national court with constitutional and religious-review jurisdiction, delivering a reserved verdict across 12 petitions, ruled that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act, covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of religious principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. The struck sections remained in force pending appeals, and a November 2025 country-policy note from a foreign government records that transgender and intersex people remain protected under the 2018 Act while describing the 2023 declaration and the litigation around it as unresolved.

An international human rights organisation responded to the verdict on 19 May 2023 as a blow to the rights of an already beleaguered group, and had warned the government two days earlier not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards. A further retrograde proposal surfaced later: a member of the national upper house has put forward a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control transgender people's official gender identity, an active legislative push against self-identification.

Lethal violence against transgender women is documented and recurring. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range in the country's largest city, the second deadly attack on the community there within a week. On 21 September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead on a roadside highway in a southern locality of that city. In February 2026 reporting, activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana survived three bullets fired through a door at night, and the account describes a wave of violence that has left transgender citizens afraid to go out.

Custody and police handling are a specific danger. A national legal-aid and research organisation's policy brief finds that the 2018 Act's advances have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice, and identifies implementation failure rather than absence of law as the central problem, with recommendations directed at custody and police safeguards. Local reporting from October 2025 documents the same gap at street level: rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals, street harassment, and suspicion or ridicule at police stations.

Healthcare access is a documented failure point. In 2016 the 23-year-old transgender activist Alisha was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at a public hospital in a north-western city while staff argued over whether to take her to the men's or the women's ward; men in the hospital taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was HIV-positive. No legal recognition exists for same-sex partnerships. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity, one article pledges to protect marriage and the family and oppose obscenity, and another requires all laws to be compatible with the state religion as defined by a government-appointed religious council; an article of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.summary:
The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, which allies planned to endorse to the 20th Congress on 28 July. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, since 2000, without passage. The protections that do exist form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces, including Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, and in 32 cities and municipalities, alongside sectoral statutes. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment; the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; she called the attack traumatic, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill.

Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex pairings are used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. There is no gender-matched placement. Official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation: the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.

Local ordinances restrict presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.

Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.

The proposed recognition bill would open X and non-binary markers, including for minors with consent, and its drafter states that the absence of a recognition process drives social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence.

Community organisations that formed from the 2000s onwards concentrate on sexual health, particularly HIV, psychosocial support and spiritual needs, alongside counselling and therapy services used to help people leave dangerous and hostile environments. Since gender-diverse people experience a higher rate of suicidal ideation or attempts, these services carry weight beyond their numbers.

Registered LGBTQ couples in the country's largest city can exercise medical and health decisions for each other through a care card introduced in June 2023, first in government-owned hospitals. The armed forces have accepted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender on the birth certificate.
PHL.tangentialFactors:
The assessment gap between LGBTQ+ travellers as a whole and trans travellers in Manila, 69 against 62, indicates that risk in the Philippines attaches more to visible gender non-conformity than to sexual orientation as such. The same assessment rates HIV-positive travellers higher at 81, which suggests the acute exposure for trans visitors lies in presentation and documentation rather than in health-status screening.

The absence of a national anti-discrimination statute leaves protection dependent on where a visitor is. Eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities have SOGIE ordinances, so the practical coverage of the Safe Spaces Act and local ordinances varies sharply between the capital and provincial areas. Local bans on cross-dressing, in Marawi since 2004 and Kabacan since 2019, are the clearest example of how far that patchwork can run in the restrictive direction.

Academic and human-rights reporting connects the legal vacuum to harm. A 2017 international human-rights report, 'Just Let Us Be', documented bullying and discrimination against LGBT students across Philippine schools at a time when the law offered few remedies. Reporting notes a higher rate of suicidal ideation or attempts among LGBTQ Filipinos, and documents hate crimes and forced conversion therapy carried out by family members against LGBTQ teenagers in a major religious denomination, backed by that church's central establishment.

The institutional response to detainees illustrates two divergent practices. Manila City Jail leaves protection to inmate hierarchies and forced informal pairings, while BJMP-Davao segregates LGBT detainees into a separate annex as it does for other vulnerable groups. Neither model provides gender-matched placement or recognition of legal gender.

CHL.name: Chile
CHL.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Chile rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents; those under 14 cannot use the law, though the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and the ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Transphobic violence remains documented. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The 2012 anti-discrimination law (Zamudio Law) protects against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. A bill criminalizing incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020. Article 373 of the Penal Code, covering offenses to morals and good customs, was historically used by police to harass homosexuals even for holding hands in public; a 2015 Movilh report noted that for the first time in seven years no police abuses against LGBT people were reported, credited to the Carabineros Human Rights Department. The Migration and Immigration Law, enacted 11 April 2021, bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that unrecognized asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk because of, among other grounds, sexual orientation or gender identity. A Ministry of Education circular of April 2017, Rights of girls, boys and trans students in the field of education, requires schools nationwide to provide bathroom and shower facilities that respect the gender identity of trans students, alongside guarantees of social name use and gender-conforming uniforms, and non-compliance is sanctionable. A 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centers in Chile to call and register transgender people by their social name. Since 2009 the National Organization of Gendarmeries has ended disciplinary sanctions against inmates that prevented them from dressing according to their gender identity. Since 2013, sex reassignment surgeries and hormone therapy have been funded by Chile's public health system (Fondo Nacional de Salud). In June 2024 the Ministry of Health's Circular 7 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court (7-3) annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law that had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) via the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run program continues providing support in medical centers. The Gender Identity Support Program Crece con Orgullo has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17. The Gender Identity Law 21.120 (effective 27 December 2019) lets those over 18 change name and sex by request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while 14-to-18-year-olds must go before family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and under-14s cannot use the law but are recognized as transgender. In April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the over 14 years old wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, though the ruling applies only to that case. Education protections include the 2009 General Law of Education, the 2011 School Violence Law requiring Good School Coexistence Committees, the 2013 Superintendence of Education handbook ordering non-discriminatory treatment, the 2015-2018 National School Coexistence Policy incorporating the International Day Against Homosexuality and Transphobia into the 2016 School Calendar, the School Inclusion law effective March 2016, and the April 2017 ministerial circular on trans students' rights. Law 21,430 (published 15 March 2022) is the first regulation explicitly protecting LGBTIQA+ children and adolescents, including non-discrimination on sex characteristics and the right to develop gender identity, and obliges state bodies to create programs on sexual rights and diversity. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report (56-30-6), a non-binding recommendation proposing to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors, and repeal Circular 812 protecting gender identity in schools.

COL.name: Colombia
COL.summary:
Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. More than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
COL.outOfScopeNotes:
A comprehensive trans law was under consideration in the sources reviewed, and its current status is unresolved here: the inventory does not confirm whether it has been enacted, amended or stalled, nor what it would change for document markers, healthcare access or hate-crime sentencing.

Hate-crime charging in the specific cases cited is not sourced. The Millerey investigation was ordered by the president in April 2025, but no charging decision, conviction or sentence appears in the inventory, and the same is true for the Caquetá and Guajira threat campaigns. Whether the flyers and kill lists have led to arrests or protective measures is unresolved.

Kill figures come from sources with different scopes and periods and are not directly comparable: 40-plus transgender women in 2023, 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025 recorded by the Attorney General's Office. The inventory does not establish a single current rate, nor whether any figure is contested by the government.

Implementation of the "trans" and "non-binary" markers on national identification documents from November 2025 is stated without detail on which documents carry them, whether regional registries apply them uniformly, or how they are treated at border control. Whether a foreign passport's gender marker affects entry decisions is not sourced. The conversion therapy bills' precise legislative stage as of the latest source is likewise unresolved.

sources.summary:
Wikipedia country coverage on Colombia states that consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in 1981, that law reforms in the 1990s equalized the age of consent at 14 for homosexual and heterosexual sex, and that Judgment C-507 of 1999 declared unconstitutional the military prohibition on 'homosexual acts'. Congress passed a law in 2011 penalizing discrimination based on sexual orientation with one to three years' imprisonment plus fines. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed: the 'Inconvertibles' bill of Congressperson Mauricio Toro, introduced 10 May 2022, had failed by 2024, and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposed the similar bill 'Quiérele siempre' in 2025.

The coverage records the Constitutional Court's repeated protection of public expression of same-sex affection. In 1994 the Court disapproved the National Council of Television's refusal to air a commercial featuring a same-sex couple. Judgment T-268 of 2000 permitted a gay pride parade the Mayor of Neiva had blocked. Judgment T-301 of 2004 ordered Santa Marta police to stop harassing homosexuals at the city boardwalk. Judgment T-314 of 2011 held the Tequendama Hotel's refusal of access to homosexuals at two events as discriminatory. Judgment T-909 of 2011 ordered Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali to take a course so as not to repress homosexuals expressing affection in public. As of 2020 military culture still discouraged discussion of same-sex attraction under a 'se puede ser, pero no demostrar' (you can exist, but not show off) norm.

In March 2016 the first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

The coverage states that access to public and commercial facilities has been protected by court order, citing judgment T-314 of 2011 on the Tequendama Hotel, judgment T-909 of 2011 on Cosmocentro mall's guardianship officials and security firm, and judgment T-301 of 2004 on Santa Marta police at the boardwalk. The 2016 Ministry of Interior presidential decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup. A May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Bogotá and Medellín have thriving gay neighbourhoods, bars and counselling and legal advice centres.

The Constitutional Court extended social security (health insurance) benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008, so same-sex couples now enjoy the main benefits heterosexual couples have under the same terms. In 2012 the Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation and ordered the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to rewrite donation regulations so they assess risk by sexual behaviour rather than orientation. The 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilization as a prerequisite for other physical changes. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025.

Colombian society remains generally conservative despite supportive media coverage, including gay characters in programmes such as the prime-time soap opera Dr Mata and a lesbian scene in A corazón abierto. A bloc of conservative senators defeated the civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007. The country's Inspector General asked the Constitutional Court in 2015 to invalidate all same-sex marriages approved in Colombia. By 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress, and a Congress committee shelved it 20 to 12 in May 2017. An Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% against 47% opposed, and adoption at 36% in favour against 62% opposed, while 2016 polls showed 37% to 40% support for marriage and only 22% for adoption. That referendum drive targeted exactly these rights for children of same-sex couples.

The coverage states that in 1998 the Constitutional Court ruled that public school teachers cannot be fired for revealing their sexual orientation and that private religious schools cannot ban gay students from enrolling. After student Sergio Urrego committed suicide in August 2014 following discrimination by his teachers, the Constitutional Court ruled for his family and ordered the Ministry of Education to review, within a year, the manuals of coexistence of all schools nationwide so that they contain no articles discriminating against children by sexual orientation or gender identity, meaning schools across the country cannot discriminate against students on those grounds. Youth-relevant family policy has also shifted: since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers.

COL.blindSummary:
The country's formal legal framework is among the most developed in its region. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans citizens change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended the change described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. In April 2025 a video went viral showing a 32-year-old trans woman flailing in a creek near a major city, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned. Her mother said: "They killed her for being who she was." The president ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the national prosecution service recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised. In one northern department, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In a southern department, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; a trans salon owner was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. Killings of queer citizens continued after that case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 a transitional justice court indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; a UN human rights body noted concern. In May 2025 a UN-appointed independent expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple cities of the country, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in March 2016, and the national registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as different-sex spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Court judgments of 2004 and 2011 protect entry to a city boardwalk, a hotel and a shopping centre against harassment and refusal of access. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. A 2016 interior ministry decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

The investigation into the April 2025 killing was ordered by the president, but no charging decision, conviction or sentence appears in the inventory, and the same is true for the southern and northern department threat campaigns. Whether the flyers and kill lists have led to arrests or protective measures is unresolved.

Implementation of the "trans" and "non-binary" markers on national identification documents from November 2025 is stated without detail on which documents carry them, whether regional registries apply them uniformly, or how they are treated at border control. NGA.name: Nigeria
NGA.summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the law reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (October 2016), in the report 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe', documents that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and records police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is explicit and current. Sahara Reporters (August 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria, relays warnings of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Trans visitors face lethal violence with official misgendering and subsequent impunity. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. Six months later, in February 2025, The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

Police use the law against people for how they appear. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

A decade-outcome assessment of the statute exists. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024), marking ten years of the SSMPA, finds the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.

Enforcement takes the form of mass arrests at social venues. Wikipedia's country coverage records that men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011; that 100-plus party-goers were arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure: the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned.

Cross-dressing has been proposed as a discrete offence. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

Imprisonment of a prominent transgender woman raised placement questions that remain unresolved. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting discretionary placement. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.
NGA.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Bobrisky was assigned to a male or a female section of Kirikiri prison is not recorded in the available source; press coverage raised the question of placement without resolving it, and the October 2024 panel addressed only the lawfulness of the prison classification, not the section.

The inventory does not indicate whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing reported by Reuters have been enacted, so their current legal status is unresolved here.

No enacted general legislation protecting against discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity is sourced; the education ministry's school policy is administrative rather than statutory, and its practical enforcement is not documented in these materials.

Entry, visa and gender-marker document rules for visitors are not covered by any source in this inventory and remain not sourced.

Several of the arrest totals and biographical details are drawn from tertiary reference coverage rather than primary court records, and the charge and sentence dates for Bobrisky are reported without a linked judgment.

No enacted general legislation protecting against discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity is sourced; the education ministry's school policy is administrative rather than statutory, and its practical enforcement is not documented in these materials.

Entry, visa and gender-marker document rules for visitors are not covered by any source in this inventory and remain not sourced.

Several of the arrest totals and biographical details are drawn from tertiary reference coverage rather than primary court records, and the charge and sentence dates are reported without a linked judgment.
blindSourceSummaries: An August 2024 news report: the beaten body of a transgender social-media personality was found on a highway hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and ordered an investigation — a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

A February 2025 report: six months after the killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; the country has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the 2014 prohibition law reinforced historic-era criminalisation — impunity documented.

An August 2026 report of a foreign government's travel advisory office: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under religious law in 12 state/province.

A March 2025 report: police abuse of people perceived as gay under a law described by those affected as 'weaponised', including a man struck in the mouth with a police weapon and freed only after paying almost half of the bribe demanded for 'looking gay'.

An August 2024 report marking a decade of the prohibition law: the law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; people report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed.
An April 2024 report: luring gangs attract LGBTQ+ people via dating and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

A June 2025 official assessment: same-sex conduct between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; religious law in 12 state/province criminalises same-sex acts, with male same-sex activity carrying the death penalty.

An October 2016 human-rights report: the prohibition law reaches far beyond marriage — it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of same-sex amorous relationship, and gay organisations, with punishments of 10-14 years' prison; documents police torture and arbitrary arrests under it.

An encyclopedic biography of the country's most prominent transgender woman documents the only trans-imprisonment case: pleaded guilty on 5 April 2024, sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, served the term in a maximum-security facility, released on 5 August 2024; press coverage at sentencing openly asked which section she would be kept in, reflecting discretionary placement, and the biography does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section; an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that the maximum-security placement violated the national correctional-service statute because she was a first-time offender.
A report not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying piece covers transgender people fearing proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.
NGA.blindTangential:
The Constitution, section 17(3)(d), nominally guarantees adequate medical and health care to all citizens, yet a 2015 survey by a local LGBTQ organisation found that only 30% of citizens agree LGBTQ persons should receive education, healthcare and housing. The gap between the written guarantee and measured public opinion shapes how safely a visitor can expect to be treated in institutional settings.

The national education ministry maintains a policy on safety, security and violence-free schools in all schools of the country that prohibits discrimination explicitly including on 'sexual orientation'. No enacted legislation protects against discrimination generally, and no political party endorses LGBTQ rights, so the school policy sits without a statutory counterpart elsewhere in public life.

Religious institutions are a principal driver of the environment. Mainstream religious interpretations are said to drive stigmatisation of LGBTQ students, and religious institutions play a crucial role in education, which is relevant to how public-facing hostility is framed.

The 2008 publication of church members' names and addresses in four newspapers shows that press exposure of individuals has previously produced threats, beatings and stonings, an earlier pattern that predates the 2014 statute.

KEN.name: Kenya
KEN.summary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in Kenya under the colonial-era Penal Code, carrying imprisonment of up to 14 years, and the provision is applied regardless of the nationality of those involved. No Kenyan statute governs gender identity, and there is no codified pathway for legal gender recognition; intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender, according to the UK Home Office country policy and information note of February 2025.

Legal gender recognition is obstructed in practice. Evidence before the Milimani High Court in Nairobi, in a decision delivered on 20 May 2026 by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, showed that 94 per cent of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans had been refused by civil registration offices, with some applicants spending close to four years' wages on document corrections that failed. Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.

Courts have ordered state action. On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court directed the Kenyan government to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act, after finding that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections; the petition was brought by a trans Kenyan subjected to non-consensual medical procedures and a court-ordered 'gender determination' while incarcerated.

Police harassment is routine for trans people. Twenty-six interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi described detention on pretexts such as being drunk and disorderly, on-the-spot extortion demands of 5,000 shillings, and the practice of using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through public life safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Violence against LGBT people is documented and sometimes lethal. In December 2024 a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's 'Lives on the Line' report of September 2025, produced with more than 14 community organisations, is the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering October 2023 to September 2024; it explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16 of 2019 that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

LGBTI civil-society groups may register and operate, but only within a restrictive civic space. The Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled in 2018 that forced anal testing was unconstitutional, with compensation awarded in 2024, and the Supreme Court upheld freedom of association in 2023, allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; a petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination remains before the courts. Societal discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is widespread and has caused loss of employment and education.
KEN.outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement data on prosecutions under the Penal Code's same-sex conduct provision are not sourced in this inventory; the record establishes the offence and its maximum penalty, not how often it is used against visitors or residents.

Whether the Transgender Protection Rights Act directed by the Eldoret High Court on 12 August 2025 has been enacted, and in what form, is unresolved here.

The practical effect of the Milimani High Court's 20 May 2026 decision on civil registration offices, including whether refusals of document corrections have declined, is not sourced.

The scope of intersex third-gender recognition in practice, including which documents carry the marker and whether it extends to non-intersex trans people, is not established by these sources.

Only the killing of an LGBTQ activist and the resulting 50-year sentence are documented; broader patterns of anti-trans homicide with dates and outcomes are not itemised in this inventory.
