ROU.name: Romania
ROU.summary:
Romania decriminalised same-sex relations and the practice is legal nationwide. Outright International's country overview records that Government Ordinance 137/2000 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex and sexual orientation, while institutional follow-through on that protection is limited. There is no marriage and no civil-partnership regime: the 2018 referendum to amend the constitution failed on low turnout, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017. LGBTI organisations can register and operate.

Legal gender recognition exists and is court-based. In the Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi case, the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate reflecting the trans man's UK-recognised identity, and the Bucharest Tribunal rejected the appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates, making the decision definitive in March 2026. ACCEPT Romania announced the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility and urges others who have changed their documents in another European Union member state to pursue transcription in Romania.

The legal anchor is the Court of Justice of the European Union's ruling of October 2024, reported by Reuters, that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition of a UK gender recognition certificate in Romania. The ruling builds on the position that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition.

A Council of Europe thematic review of January 2023, 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania', documents the national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering the legal and policy framework, applicable European Court of Human Rights case-law and international standards.

Official hostility intensified during 2025. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 records that anti-LGBTI rhetoric rose through the presidential campaign: candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February, Prime Minister Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes, and a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements. The National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint.

The ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report, whose Romania chapter was authored by ACCEPT, found that eight of nine country submissions reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, and cites the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.

Public visibility carries visible risk. AP reported in June 2025 that tens of thousands marched on the twentieth anniversary of the Bucharest Pride march amid rising right-wing hostility toward LGBTQ+ Romanians.

The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024, covering 2023, records that the National Council for Combating Discrimination investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials.
ROU.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source anything on entry or visa screening, border questioning of gender markers, detention or prison placement rules, or access to gender-affirming healthcare for visitors. Those areas remain unresolved here and should not be read as cleared.

No conviction or penalty figures for hate-motivated violence against LGBTI people are available in this inventory. The Council of Europe thematic review of January 2023 is a national implementation report covering frameworks and case-law, and its enforcement outcomes are not sourced.

Whether the transcription route affirmed in the Mirzarafie-Ahi judgment extends to gender recognition issued outside the European Union, including non-EU certificates, is not addressed by the sources and remains unresolved.

The FRA-commissioned study dates from February 2008 and describes the protection architecture as it stood then; its currency against present practice is not sourced.

A regional rights network's annual review (covering 2023): the national equality body investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; a 2023 survey found 51% of residents agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a counter-response from more than 50 organisations.

A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (a 2018 constitutional referendum to ban them failed on low turnout; church leadership has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBT organisations can register.

A regional human-rights body's thematic review (Jan 2023): a national report on hate crimes and other hate-motivated incidents against LGBTI people — implementation of a 2010 recommendation covering legal and policy frameworks, applicable case-law from the regional human-rights court and international standards.

A rights network's submission to the regional bloc's annual rule-of-law report (2025), with a local rights group authoring the national chapter: of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the national election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
A news outlet (Jun 2025): a gay pride march turned 20 as LGBTQ+ residents faced growing hostility — tens of thousands marched on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

A regional body-commissioned legal study (Feb 2008) by two legal academics: maps how national law implemented the regional bloc's 2000 employment directive and free-movement rules for LGBT partners — national anti-discrimination concepts, national equality-body enforcement powers and civil-society complaints; a dated baseline for the national protection architecture.
ROU.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents can bring discrimination complaints to the national anti-discrimination council, which holds enforcement powers and receives NGO complaints, as set out in the study of the employment directive's implementation.

Legal gender recognition for residents runs through national courts rather than an administrative procedure, and the Mirzarafie-Ahi judgment establishes transcription of another union member's recognition decision as a route available to those who have already changed documents abroad.

A civil-partnership bill has been pending since 2017 and is opposed by the majority church; a 2018 constitutional-ban referendum failed on low turnout, leaving the constitutional text unchanged.

LGBTI organisations can register as legal entities, and the national LGBTI rights organisation litigates and complains to regulators on their behalf, as in the complaint that produced the audiovisual regulator's warning to the television channel.
ROU.blindTangential:
Public opinion runs ahead of the legal framework: a public-opinion survey conducted in 2023 found that 51% of residents agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition, even though no partnership statute exists.

Draft education legislation in early 2024 carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew protests from 13 religious groups and a counter-response from more than 50 organisations, indicating the political cost attached to equality language in legislation.

A rights-agency-commissioned legal study of February 2008 maps how national law implemented the union's employment equal-treatment directive and free-movement rules for LGBT partners, including national anti-discrimination concepts, the anti-discrimination council's enforcement powers and NGO complaints. It is a dated baseline for the protection architecture rather than a current assessment.

BGD.name: Bangladesh
BGD.summary:
Bangladesh is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024, in protests known locally as the Monsoon Revolution, is the inflection point: hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground afterwards, and trans people who had previously lived visibly now do so in hiding.

The current national incident baseline comes from JMBF, whose annual report published in April 2026 documents 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across the country in 2025. The documented conduct includes murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. JMBF describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend it has recorded since 2022.

Lethal violence against visible trans people is ongoing and recent. On 3 February 2025 the prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district. Five unidentified individuals are accused. Shila was widely known for humanitarian work, which makes the killing a direct measure of the risk attached to visibility.

Police contact is the most likely point of danger, and it is usually extortion-driven rather than prosecutorial. After hijras refused police demands for money in Gomdondi Phultala on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack. On 17 September 2025, police arrested twelve hijras who were collecting money from vehicles carrying expatriates, a traditional livelihood, in Narayanganj.

Policing of visibly trans people reaches transit hubs. In April 2024, five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, according to JMBF. An airport perimeter is therefore an actively policed site for trans people, not a neutral arrival point.

The legal baseline is the Penal Code 1860, which criminalises intercourse against the order of nature with a penalty of up to life imprisonment. Outright International, updated 12 March 2026, records that the provision is rarely enforced through prosecution but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ. A UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, issued September 2023 and updated April 2026, states that the scope of Section 377 remains ambiguous: it is unclear whether lesbianism falls within it, with ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report reading female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere treating the provision as relevant to all genders. Any visitor's conduct sits inside that ambiguity.

Formal recognition exists and does not translate into safety. Hijra are legally recognised as a third gender, with gender-marker change permitted, and Bangladesh has held LGBTIQ and hijra pride events since recognition was extended in 2013 and 2014. The gap between that status and the violence recorded in 2025 is the central finding of the Global Press Journal reporting, which profiles a trans subject who now lives in hiding.

Hostility tolerated by the state is documented at asylum-grade evidentiary standard. A UK Upper Tribunal decision, PA/07096/2017, relies on Home Office country material recording Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under Section 377 and under Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues. A Washington Blade assessment dated 5 August 2025, one year after the ouster, reaches the same conclusion in security terms: the LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.
BGD.outOfScopeNotes:
The reach of Section 377 toward lesbian conduct is unresolved in the sources. The UK Home Office country policy note, updated April 2026, records that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within the provision, and notes that ILGA's 2019 report is internally inconsistent on the point. No source resolves it.

Whether gender-marker change and third-gender registration remain administratively available in practice after August 2024 is not sourced. The sources confirm the legal provisions stand; none documents the current administrative process or any refusal to process applications.

The outcome for the five unidentified individuals accused in the killing of Shila on 3 February 2025 is unresolved. No source records an arrest, charge or trial result.

Nothing in the source inventory addresses entry or visa screening, border questioning of trans travellers, or whether foreign passport gender markers are recognised on arrival. Any statement on document screening at entry would be unsupported.

The extent to which the post-2024 government has changed official policy toward LGBTIQ people, as distinct from the security environment described by advocacy groups and journalists, is not sourced beyond the assessments cited here.

BGD.tangentialFactors:
The contradiction between status and safety is the defining comparison inside the country. A rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021, and hijra pride events have been held in public, at a time when formal third-gender recognition was already a decade old. Both facts are drawn on by the same reporting that documents trans people going into hiding after 2024, so visibility gains of the previous decade should not be read as a current safety indicator.

The direction of travel since 2022 is documented rather than impressionistic: JMBF's own annual counts show a rising violation trend across four reporting years, with 2025 the sharpest single increase. Enforcement is concentrated on extortion, fabricated charges and arbitrary arrest rather than on conviction, which means the exposure a visitor faces is discretionary police action at street level.

The two external assessments date differently and should be read together. The UK Home Office country policy note was issued in September 2023, before the August 2024 change of government, and was updated in April 2026; the Washington Blade security assessment and the Global Press Journal field reporting both post-date the ouster and describe a worse environment than the legal note alone would suggest.

Comparable countries in the region also recognise third-gender categories in law, so legal recognition should not be treated as a proxy for regional safety either. The distinguishing feature here is the documented combination of a rarely enforced but broadly usable penal provision, an extortion economy organised around visibly trans people, and Islamist mobilisation that the state has not checked since 2024.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Vietnam and has not been criminalised in Vietnamese history; the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The 1812 Gia Long Code, Article 332, criminalised prostitution and illicit sexual activity such as extra-marital sex, and in rare cases prosecutions could be brought against homosexual conduct under those labels, but pre-colonial enforcement was inconsistent enough that little to no state action is recorded.

Article 37 of the 2015 Civil Code recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender. The amendment was passed by the National Assembly on 24 November 2015 by 282 votes to 84 and took effect in January 2017, allowing people who have undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex; a November 2015 milestone separately allowed people who had changed gender to apply for a change of civil status. Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, which forced transgender people to travel to Thailand for the procedure. The implementing bill has never been enacted, so the statutory right has no operative procedure.

Under the Law on Citizen Identification, in force from 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their identity card when undergoing gender transition, but must present confirmation documents, and the change's legal effect depends on passage of a Gender Affirmation Law. A draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights was expected to be discussed by the National Assembly with completion targeted for 2020 and never materialised; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of February 2026, and the implementing legislation promised for 2017 is still unimplemented. Obstacles to gender-affirming care and to changing the legal gender marker therefore persist.

No Vietnamese law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, according to Freedom House as cited by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada in June 2022. Amnesty International's 2025 report finds that LGBTI people's rights lack meaningful protection in both law and practice.

Same-sex couples may not be prosecuted: fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013, effective 11 November 2013, and same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts. Unions still confer no legal rights or recognition. Conversion therapy has been prohibited since 3 August 2022 under Ministry of Health Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into treatment.

Public assembly space narrowed in 2025. Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events; the Asia director of Human Rights Watch, Patricia Gossman, described this as a worrying sign of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long-standing reputation for tolerance in the region. Pride events had previously been held openly, with the first parade in Hanoi on 5 August 2012 and events in around 34 further cities and provinces by 2017.

Transgender visitors should expect document-related friction in healthcare settings. A United Nations feature of 30 November 2024 records transgender women being asked at medical encounters whether they are male or female and why their appearance does not match their identity card, together with heightened scrutiny and an economic- and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence, concentrated among transgender women in northern provinces and among ethnic minorities. A June 2023 report describes healthcare providers as respectful in person but says administrative red tape undoes that for four transgender Vietnamese whose cases it documents. Outright International's March 2026 overview frames accessible legal recognition as the unresolved barrier to non-discriminatory care.
VNM.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and border-document rules for transgender travellers are not covered by any source in this inventory, including whether passport gender markers that differ from presentation trigger additional screening at Vietnamese ports of entry. This is an unresolved gap, not a finding of permissive practice.

Whether the identity-card gender change permitted by the Law on Citizen Identification from 1 July 2024 can in fact be completed without a Gender Affirmation Law in force is not resolved in the sources; the statute's wording ties legal effect to that law's passage, while no source reports a documented case of the change being granted or refused.

Hate-crime provisions covering violence against transgender people are not sourced here. The 2024 United Nations account documents violence risk but does not establish whether aggravated penalties apply.

The availability and cost of gender-affirming care in Vietnam, as distinct from the administrative barriers to legal recognition, are not established by these sources; Outright International records obstacles to care without quantifying them.

Whether the 2025 Pride cancellations were an isolated permit decision or a standing policy is unresolved. Only Ho Chi Minh City and five unnamed 2025 events are identified, and no source reports a 2026 outcome.

sources.summary: DW (late Sept/Oct 2025): Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — HRW Asia director Patricia Gossman calls it worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long regional-tolerance reputation; notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions still without legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 still not implemented — obstacles to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change persist; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026. Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; LGBTIQ organisations operate openly though under government surveillance; Health Ministry declared (Aug 2022) same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders; no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

Amnesty International Viet Nam 2025 report: LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; sits alongside wider repression — vague Penal Code arts 109/116/117/331 used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, proposed press-law source-disclosure rules; Viet Nam re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council until 2028.

Lighthouse Vietnam study (Oct 2024): 'Exploring the lived experiences of conversion efforts (SOGICE) among LGBTIQ people in Vietnam' - documents experiences and forms of SOGICE in the Vietnamese context, with comprehensive data needs analysis.

UN Viet Nam feature (30 Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially northern-province and ethnic-minority trans women; framed as case for accessible legal recognition.

Saigoneer (June 2023): Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist, same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised; four trans Vietnamese describe respectful healthcare providers undone by administrative red tape.

IRB Canada Response to Information Request VNM201080.E (30 Jun 2022): Vietnamese law provides no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (Freedom House, 3 Mar 2021). The briefing draws on multiple sources and addresses treatment by society and authorities in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City across education, employment, housing and health care.

Viet Nam News (Nov 2018): National Assembly expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; per Outright (Feb 2026) a recognition draft law was still under consideration seven years later.

sources.title: Social News 16/1 — Separate jails proposed for transgender, gay prisoners
sources.summary: VietnamNet (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general prison population, to protect them from sexual harassment. The institute cited US California statistics that 67% of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered sexual harassment, and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. It stated that under Vietnam's then-current prison infrastructure transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, meaning no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity existed, and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is legal and has never been criminalized in Vietnamese history, and the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Historically, the 1812 Gia Long Code (Article 332) banned prostitution and illicit sexual activity including extra-marital sex, which in rare cases allowed homosexuality to be prosecuted under labels such as "extramarital sex" or "rape", though pre-colonial enforcement was so inconsistent that little to no known state action was taken. In 2002 the Ministry of Labour – Invalids and Social Affairs declared homosexuality a "social evil" comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and arrest same-sex couples; fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013 (effective 11 November 2013). Since 3 August 2022 conversion therapy has been outlawed via Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC from the Ministry of Health, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into "treatment". Wikipedia country coverage: Vietnam's first gay pride parade was held in Hanoi on 5 August 2012, and by 2017 pride events were held in around 34 other cities and provinces, with over 35 similar events held annually in cities including Haiphong, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City and Cần Thơ. Hanoi Pride ran for a fifth consecutive year from 18–24 September 2017 drawing thousands (versus about a hundred at the first parade), and its sixth edition in November 2018 saw more than 1,000 participants cycling to campaign for transgender rights and same-sex marriage; several events were aired on state channels VTV4, VTV6 and VTV9. Media coverage has shifted: in 2002 publications such as Thế Giới Phụ Nữ and Tiếp thị & Gia đình described homosexuality as a disease and "deviant behavior", while in September 2010 Tuoi Tre Online became the first major state media outlet to agree that "homosexuality is normal". The 2013 sitcom My Best Gay Friends was published on YouTube because Vietnamese broadcasters were reluctant to air it. VNM.blindSummary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised in the country and has not been criminalised in its history; the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. An 1812 code, Article 332, criminalised prostitution and illicit sexual activity such as extra-marital sex, and in rare cases prosecutions could be brought against homosexual conduct under those labels, but enforcement was inconsistent enough that little to no state action is recorded.

Article 37 of the 2015 Civil Code recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender. The amendment was passed by the national legislature on 24 November 2015 by 282 votes to 84 and took effect in January 2017, allowing people who have undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex; a November 2015 milestone separately allowed people who had changed gender to apply for a change of civil status. Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, which forced transgender people to travel to a neighbouring jurisdiction for the procedure. The implementing bill has never been enacted, so the statutory right has no operative procedure.

Under the Law on Citizen Identification, in force from 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their identity card when undergoing gender transition, but must present confirmation documents, and the change's legal effect depends on passage of a Gender Affirmation Law. A draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights was expected to be discussed by the national legislature with completion targeted for 2020 and never materialised; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of February 2026, and the implementing legislation promised for 2017 is still unimplemented. Obstacles to gender-affirming care and to changing the legal gender marker therefore persist.

No law of the country prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, according to a human rights monitoring organisation as cited by a national refugee documentation body in June 2022. An international human rights organisation's 2025 report finds that LGBTI people's rights lack meaningful protection in both law and practice.

Same-sex couples may not be prosecuted: fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013, effective 11 November 2013, and same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts. Unions still confer no legal rights or recognition. Conversion therapy has been prohibited since 3 August 2022 under a dispatch of the national health ministry, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into treatment.

Public assembly space narrowed in 2025. The largest city abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events; the regional director of an international human rights organisation described this as a worrying sign of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against the country's long-standing reputation for tolerance among neighbouring jurisdictions. Pride events had previously been held openly, with the first parade in the capital on 5 August 2012 and events in around 34 further cities and provinces by 2017.

Transgender visitors should expect document-related friction in healthcare settings. A United Nations feature of 30 November 2024 records transgender women being asked at medical encounters whether they are male or female and why their appearance does not match their identity card, together with heightened scrutiny and an economic- and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence, concentrated among transgender women in northern provinces of the country and among ethnic minorities. A June 2023 report describes healthcare providers as respectful in person but says administrative red tape undoes that for four transgender residents whose cases it documents. An international human rights organisation's March 2026 overview frames accessible legal recognition as the unresolved barrier to non-discriminatory care.
VNM.blindOutOfScope:
Entry, visa and border-document rules for transgender travellers are not covered by any source in this inventory, including whether passport gender markers that differ from presentation trigger additional screening at ports of entry. This is an unresolved gap, not a finding of permissive practice.

Whether the identity-card gender change permitted by the Law on Citizen Identification from 1 July 2024 can in fact be completed without a Gender Affirmation Law in force is not resolved in the sources; the statute's wording ties legal effect to that law's passage, while no source reports a documented case of the change being granted or refused.

Hate-crime provisions covering violence against transgender people are not sourced here. The 2024 United Nations account documents violence risk but does not establish whether aggravated penalties apply.

The availability and cost of gender-affirming care in the country, as distinct from the administrative barriers to legal recognition, are not established by these sources; an international human rights organisation records obstacles to care without quantifying them.

Whether the 2025 Pride cancellations were an isolated permit decision or a standing policy is unresolved. Only the largest city and five unnamed 2025 events are identified, and no source reports a 2026 outcome.

UGA.name: Uganda
UGA.summary:
Uganda is a destination trans and gender-nonconforming visitors should avoid. The Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023 provides the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," lengthy prison terms for the promotion of homosexuality, and penalties reaching 20 years for other offences under the Act. In April 2024 Uganda's Constitutional Court upheld the Act's core provisions, including the death penalty in certain circumstances, and dismissed challenges arguing that public participation requirements had not been met. The same court had previously voided a comparable 2013 statute on procedural grounds, leaving the 2023 Act fully in force.

The Act's offences are written around same-sex conduct and the promotion of homosexuality, but the enforcement climate treats gender nonconformity and perceived LGBT identity as grounds for suspicion, violence and detention. Human Rights Watch reported in May 2025 that the Act has unleashed arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings, with many LGBT Ugandans in hiding. In February 2026 Ugandan police arrested two women in Arua after neighbours reported them for allegedly kissing in public, one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Act.

Violence against gender-nonconforming people is documented and sometimes lethal. The Guardian reported in January 2024 that a transgender woman in Kampala was mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false TikTok allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a Kampala safe house. In June 2021 a raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala produced forty-four arrests, with several detainees alleging police performed invasive anal examinations. LGBTQ Ugandans face discrimination actively incited by conservative political, religious and community leaders, with violent attacks often carried out or incited by state officials.

Digital spaces carry acute risk. Access Now reported in May 2025 that digital entrapment via dating and social apps is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people, and that app companies do too little to protect users. Amnesty International's October 2024 report documented widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence, including doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation, and found the Act has fostered a climate of impunity forcing people to alter how they present themselves online. Visitors should assume device and app activity may be monitored or used as evidence.

Legal gender recognition is effectively unavailable. In October 2021 trans woman Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro was issued identification documents identifying her as female, the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised; no general process for document amendment is documented. Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally prohibited since 29 September 2005. A provision of the 2023 bill that would have criminalised merely identifying as gay or non-binary with ten years in prison was proposed but ultimately excluded from the enacted Act.

The Act imposes additional penalties relevant to long-stay or working visitors: people convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in childcare facilities even after release, minors convicted face three years imprisonment, and sexual intercourse with a person younger than 18 is classified as "aggravated homosexuality" punishable by death. Purporting to contract a same-sex marriage, or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony, carries ten years' imprisonment.

The US State Department's travel advisory for Uganda includes LGBT-specific warnings under its "Do Not Travel" advisory. Rights violations against Uganda's LGBTQ community were escalating as of June 2024 according to a pressure group cited by Reuters. Historical pattern reinforces the risk: in October 2010 the tabloid Rolling Stone published names, addresses and photographs of 100 allegedly gay Ugandans with a call for their execution, and activist David Kato was murdered in 2011 shortly after winning a lawsuit against the paper; Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest, and in June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality.
UGA.outOfScopeNotes:
The US State Department travel advisory page for Uganda returned HTTP 403 at research time and could not be retrieved directly; the LGBT-specific warning under the "Do Not Travel" advisory is asserted from the underlying advisory but the current wording and date of that advisory are unresolved.

The February 2026 AP report describes the Arua arrests as among the first known arrests under the 2023 Act; whether charges were brought, and their outcome, is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening procedures that might out a trans visitor, nor whether passport gender markers are checked against presentation at border control. The Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro case establishes that document change has occurred once but does not establish a general procedure; the availability of that procedure to a foreign visitor is not sourced.

Healthcare access for trans people, including access to hormone therapy or gender-affirming care, is not addressed by any source in the inventory. The HIV and stigma material cited is about cisgender LGB and sex-worker populations.

The Reuters June 2024 claim of escalating violations is attributed to an unnamed pressure group; the group's identity and the underlying data are unresolved.

UGA.tangentialFactors:
Public opinion data indicates the enforcement climate is not an isolated elite project. A 2013 Pew survey found 96 percent of Ugandans believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, while a 2017 ILGA poll showed 59 percent agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people. The gap between the two figures suggests some shift in attitudes, but the 2023 Act and its enforcement enjoy continued political support in parts of Africa, as The Guardian noted in January 2024, and international condemnation has not altered Uganda's domestic posture.

The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report for Uganda listed violence and discrimination against marginalized groups, including the LGBT community, among the three most important problems in the country, indicating that the pattern predates the 2023 Act by well over a decade.

Adjacent health and social factors compound risk for anyone perceived as LGBT. A 2018 article in African Health Sciences stated that Uganda's high HIV rate has roots in stigma against same-sex sexual behaviour and sex work, and Human Rights Watch reported in 2005 that abstinence-until-marriage programs discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, denying young LGBTQ people information that could save their lives. The sources do not address healthcare access barriers specifically for trans people.

Ugandan trans and gender-nonconforming residents live under a legal regime that criminalises same-sex conduct and its promotion while leaving identification as such formally uncriminalised. The exclusion of the proposed ten-year penalty for merely identifying as gay or non-binary means self-presentation, rather than identity itself, is the operative legal line, though in practice perceived identity attracts the same suspicion.

Document change is possible in principle but has been achieved once. Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro's October 2021 issuance of female identification documents is the only documented instance of legal gender recognition; no administrative pathway, court procedure or ministry process for general document amendment is described in the sources.

Employment and family consequences attach after conviction. A person convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in childcare facilities even after release, and minors convicted face three years imprisonment. Same-sex marriage has been prohibited by constitutional amendment since 29 September 2005, and purporting to contract or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony carries ten years' imprisonment.

Community-level organising has been repeatedly suppressed. Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest, and in June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality. A small group of Ugandan mothers has spoken publicly for their LGBT children, as Human Rights Watch documented in May 2025, but they operate against a backdrop of eviction, shelter raids and outing.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.summary:
Egypt presents a direct and documented entry risk to trans visitors. The Ministry of Interior holds broad powers under the immigration law to refuse entry to, or deport, anyone whose presence is said to disturb public order and morality, and those powers have been applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Cairo 52 study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) analyses that law and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents between 2018 and 2022. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights separately records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even where no charge is ever upheld. Removal therefore does not require any offence under Egyptian law.

Same-sex conduct is not expressly written into the penal statutes, but prosecutions are a routine outcome rather than a theoretical one. Economic Courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, and the resulting sentences are custodial. Court of Cassation interpretations from the 1970s had already removed the requirement of a financial exchange, so habitual conduct or multiple partners is sufficient to ground a charge.

Police obtain that evidence through entrapment. A BBC investigation, "How Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps", documents officers running fake profiles on dating applications, with victims describing blackmail and arrest; the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records the same pattern and notes that transgender women are a particular target. Arrests are obtained without any explicit prohibition on homosexuality being invoked.

Arrest carries physical risk. Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing documents rising arrests of gay and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations, and reports that authorities turn a blind eye; the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records continuing violations inside police stations. There is no anti-discrimination law or policy covering sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, so none of this conduct is met by a statutory protection.

Legal gender recognition is being actively closed. A Ministry of Interior directive issued to civil-registry heads nationwide in December 2024 shuts the loophole in Civil Status Law 143/1994 that had allowed transgender Egyptians to correct their gender marker through governorate committees.

Healthcare is a further documented barrier. TIMEP's 6 January 2025 submission for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle states that transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health, with barriers to equitable services persisting since the previous cycle and pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare settings.

Expression is constrained as well as conduct. Morality and public-order provisions criminalise "any behavior, or the expression of any idea" deemed immoral or offensive to religious teachings, giving police wide discretion over LGBTQ expression. The Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order in 2017 barring "the appearance of the homosexuals" or "promoting their slogans" in media, and legislation introduced in August 2018 places any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws.

Marriage and partnership offer no protection. Personal and family law follows the religious law of the person's recognised religion, none of which recognises same-sex relationships, so Egyptian law recognises marriage only between a man and a woman. If a same-sex relationship becomes public, police may use it as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.
EGY.outOfScopeNotes:
Several points remain unresolved in the sources available here. The December 2024 Ministry of Interior directive on civil-registry gender markers is reported by Cairo 52; whether it has been published in the official gazette, whether it is subject to challenge before the administrative courts, and whether any governorate has continued to process corrections after its issue are not established by the inventory.

No figure is available for the number of people prosecuted or convicted each year under the morality and debauchery provisions, nor for the number of foreign nationals deported on the grounds described. The 12 incidents analysed by Cairo 52 cover 2018 to 2022 and are documented cases, not a measure of total enforcement.

Whether coerced anal examinations continue after the reporting periods covered by Bedayaa and Human Rights Watch, and whether any official instruction prohibits them, is not sourced here. The current status of Egypt's UPR recommendations on the right to health for transgender and intersex people, referenced by TIMEP, is likewise not set out in the inventory.

A number of claims in this record rest on open-source country coverage rather than a primary legal instrument or a rights organisation's reporting, including the wording of the 2017 media order, the August 2018 social-network threshold, the 2013 and 2019 media prosecutions, the 2009 newspaper closure and the 2014 bathhouse raid. The underlying texts of the Penal Code articles and Article 9(C) of Law 10/1961 as applied by the Economic Courts are described secondhand and have not been read directly for this record.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Egypt's morality and public order provisions criminalize 'any behavior, or the expression of any idea' deemed immoral or offensive to religious teachings, giving police broad leeway to prosecute LGBTQ expression. In 2017 the Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order preventing 'the appearance of the homosexuals' or 'promoting their slogans' in media. In August 2018 the government introduced legislation placing any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws. In 2013 comedian Bassem Youssef was charged by the Morsi government with 'propagating and promoting homosexuality and obscenity.' State officials and police routinely harass, abuse and torture LGBTQ people, particularly trans people, leading to unfair arrests and abuse in custody. After the September 2017 rainbow flag incident, TV hosts Ahmed Moussa and Mohamed Al Gheity repeatedly incited violence against the community; Moussa shared personal information of flag-raisers, leading to at least 84 arrests between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many subjected to forced anal tests. In December 2014 TV presenter Mona Iraqi collaborated with police to raid a public bathhouse, arresting around 26 men, later acquitted. In January 2019 host Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his TV show. In 2009 newspaper Al Balagh Al Gadid was shut down and two reporters jailed for printing a story about actors' involvement in homosexual prostitution. Personal and family law is governed by the religious law of the person's recognized religion (Islam, Coptic Orthodox Christianity), none of which recognize homosexual relationships, so Egyptian law only recognizes marriage between a man and a woman. If a same-sex relationship becomes public, police may use it as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality. In 2004 a seventeen-year-old private university student received a 17-year prison sentence, including two years' hard labor, for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site. The September 2017 crackdown caused a state of trauma and despair among young Egyptian LGBTQ individuals, with many attempted suicides. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the incident, fled to Canada, was granted asylum and died by suicide in 2020. Many Egyptian LGBTQ youths and individuals left the country due to social and political threats. Pew Research Center found 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and polling suggests only a minority support LGBTQ rights, so Egyptian political parties and human rights NGOs do not express public support. The term 'khawalat', historically male cross-dressing dancers, has been stigmatized and used as a derogatory term for passive and gay men. Egyptian cinema has portrayed queer characters almost exclusively in a mode of stereotyping and defamation. After the 2011 revolution LGBTQ activists became more visible and online campaigns against homophobia and transphobia went viral on Twitter and Facebook by 2013, though this did not translate into legal reform. PER.name: Peru
PER.summary:
Peru does not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual activity, lawful since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to rape. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity itself is not an offence.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage. The repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree, following an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, a state-imposed limit on daily movement that can intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. The underlying bills, 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by legislators including Jorge Montoya and Muñante of Honor y Democracia, also ban inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; the committee approved the dictamen unanimously for plenary on 20 February 2025. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks, and it invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing in Peru with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
PER.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the Gender Identity Law introduced on 4 November 2016 is unresolved beyond March 2021; no source in this inventory confirms whether it has since been enacted, withdrawn or remains pending.

Whether Law 32331 of 13 May 2025 and the April 2025 sexual-integrity law have been challenged or suspended in court is unresolved here; the only litigation recorded is the July 2025 Lima constitutional court ruling against a separate anti-equality decree.

Whether Decree Nº 1323's Articles 46 and 323 were reinstated in any later Penal Code reform is not sourced; the inventory documents their removal and the resulting absence of coverage, not any subsequent restoration.

Hate-crime counts are drawn from a report whose authors state the figures are only a sub-registry, so no reliable national total or conviction rate for anti-trans violence is available from these sources.

sources.summary: Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Peru since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalized sodomy with penalties akin to rape. Age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation per a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, applicable to trans and cis youth. Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual orientation and gender identity were criminalized by governmental decree Nº 1323, in effect 7 January 2017, under Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip the provisions but Kuczynski's veto stood. Law 32331 (enacted 13 May 2025) prohibits trans people from using public restrooms, a state-imposed restriction on trans people's daily movements that could intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity; in 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a 21 October 2016 ruling published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' for health-insurance classification purposes. The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and 'not a voluntary choice'. Opinion polls show age-based variation: 18–24-year-olds (66%) were markedly more favourable toward homosexuals than the population overall (49%), and younger people showed higher approval of same-sex marriage (8.3% approval among Peruvians in 2010, higher among younger respondents). Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with specific relevance to trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

PER.blindSummary:
The country does not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual activity, lawful since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to rape. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 constitutional court decision, and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity itself is not an offence.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. A government decree criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through two articles of the Penal Code; the national legislature voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, the president's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. The country is one of only three in the subregion, with two neighbouring jurisdictions, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage. The repeal was carried by two right-wing legislative blocs arguing the president lacked authority to issue the decree, following an April committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, a nationally imposed limit on daily movement that can intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. The underlying bills, numbered 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, also ban inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; the committee approved the dictamen unanimously for plenary on 20 February 2025. A university human-rights institute finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks, and invokes an advisory opinion of the regional human rights court holding that gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by a legislator on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. An international human rights organisation reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably one on media and advertising and a further article, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. The organisation characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing with trans women most affected, and its trans co-author, a human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 university study found that 70% of trans women in the capital city and its neighbouring port city work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of a trans woman and LGBTI activist ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: three police officers received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the regional human rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the subregion's history, reaching that court through the regional human rights commission.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Trans people may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the constitutional court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, the national health ministry revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned for medical professionals, and in May 2024 the national health ministry reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a capital-city constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 a television presenter publicly harassed the country's first openly-lesbian legislator, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

URY.name: Uruguay
URY.summary:
Uruguay's trans-protection regime rests on the Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law No. 19684), promulgated by the Executive in October 2018, which establishes state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights and directs government to ensure that trans people are treated respectfully by authorities and are not denied health services.

Legal gender recognition is administrative and based on self-declaration. Since October 2018 no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis has been required to change legal gender on official documents; adults have been able to change name and legal gender since October 2009, and minors may do so with parental consent under the 2018 law. Documents carry only female and male markers, even though article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognises non-binary people in its definitions.

Crimes motivated by sexual orientation or sexual identity attract enhanced penalties under article 149ter of the Penal Code, and incitement to hatred on those grounds has been prohibited since 2003. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created a permanent honorary commission empowered to investigate unlawful discriminatory conduct, including on grounds of sexual orientation and sexual identity. Non-discrimination, a ban on conversion therapy and an equal age of consent of 15 are in force, and hate-crime rules cover sexual orientation and gender identity.

Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, same-sex marriage has been legal since August 2013, and Uruguay was the first country in Latin America to recognise same-sex civil unions, in legislation signed in December 2007 granting couples who had cohabited five years or more rights equivalent to marriage. Joint adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since September 2009, also a regional first.

Trans people in custody have the right to decide whether to be held in a men's or a women's prison. Official figures cited by the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System record 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 people deprived of liberty. The director of the National Rehabilitation Institute told a parliamentary hearing that trans women are currently placed in women's prisons but that cohabitation entails a process of adaptation, and that a new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population; a dedicated sector for trans people was announced in July 2023 as part of a new prison planned for Montevideo.

Lethal and everyday violence against trans people persists. Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder. Studies cited in country coverage report that about two-thirds of transgender Uruguayans have been victims of physical violence and that their life expectancy is around 45 years against a national average of 77.

Discrimination in services is documented in individual cases. In May 2024 a trans health-service user, Andreina Stuart, filed a criminal complaint alleging mistreatment and discrimination at San Carlos hospital in Maldonado, after which the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation and local officials pressed for health-system updates. Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued the state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage records the following. Incitement to hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation and sexual identity has been prohibited since 2003, and Penal Code article 149ter provides enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by those characteristics. Gay, lesbian and bisexual people have served openly in the military since May 2009 under a Defence Minister decree. The 2018 Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons stipulates the free development of personality according to chosen gender identity and calls on government to ensure trans people are treated respectfully by authorities. The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis being made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Since October 2018 no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis is required to change legal gender on official documents; name and legal gender changes have been possible for adults since October 2009, and for minors with parental consent since the October 2018 law. A non-binary marker does not exist, only female and male, even though Law 19,684 (article 4c) recognises non-binary people in its definitions. The 2018 law calls on government to ensure transgender people are included in housing programmes and are not denied health services, and in July 2019 the state water company Obras Sanitarias del Estado began offering jobs to transgender people in compliance with it. From 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men have been able to donate blood under the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending the previous 12-month abstinence requirement. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created an Honorary Commission to Combat Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and other forms of Discrimination to investigate allegations of unlawful discriminatory conduct, covering sexual orientation and sexual identity. The 2018 law passed 62-26 in the Chamber and 17-12 in the Senate, allows minors to change legal gender with parental consent, and mandates that transgender people receive 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships. Youth outcomes are severe: 25 percent of transgender Uruguayans left home before age 18 after family rejection, 87 percent did not finish secondary school, and other studies show about 75 percent expelled from the education system. Same-sex couples have been able to adopt jointly since September 2009, a first in Latin America, and same-sex marriage has been legal since August 2013; the age of consent has been equal at 15 regardless of orientation or gender since 1934. Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers. A 2014 poll found about 71 percent of Uruguayans supported same-sex marriage, the highest in South America, and in 2016 Americas Quarterly named Uruguay the most LGBT-friendly country in Latin America, calling it a model for social inclusion. Uruguay hosted the region's first international LGBT rights conference in July 2016, with hundreds of diplomats, politicians and activists attending. The Montevideo Pride parade has run annually since the 1990s and drew an estimated 120,000 people in 2018, alongside Punta Pride in Punta del Este each February, and Montevideo has several gay bars, restaurants and pubs. Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued the state bank over discriminatory handling by a private security guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; a public prosecutor compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

Law No. 19684 carries material entitlements for residents: a national employment quota for trans people, a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a mandate that trans people receive 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships.

The 2018 law also calls on government to ensure that transgender people are included in housing programmes and are not denied health services. In July 2019 the state water utility began offering jobs to transgender people in compliance with it.

The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis being made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Resident outcomes are weak despite the statutory framework. About 25 percent of transgender residents left home before the age of 18 following family rejection, 87 percent did not finish secondary school, and other studies indicate roughly 75 percent were expelled from the education system.

From 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men have been able to donate blood under the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending the previous 12-month abstinence requirement, and gay, lesbian and bisexual personnel have served openly in the military since May 2009 under a defence ministerial decree.

Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers.

QAT.name: Qatar
QAT.summary:
Qatar criminalises consensual same-sex relations. Article 296 of the Penal Code (Law 11/2004) punishes sodomy with one to three years' imprisonment, and the prohibition applies to Muslims and non-Muslims alike; sexual acts between men and between women are both covered. For Muslims convicted in sharia courts a capital sentence remains a theoretical possibility, though it has never been imposed. Article 296 replaced Article 201 of the 1971 Penal Code, which had carried up to five years, and before that Article 171 of the 1956 code, with the colonial-era Indian Penal Code imposed through Order in Council in 1938. The sources record no statute repealing or legalising this exposure.

Trans people face a distinct detention power: they may be held for up to six months without trial or charge on suspicion of "impersonating the opposite gender" or of violating "public morality" and "community protection" provisions. Human Rights Watch reported on 24 October 2022 that Qatar's security forces arrested and abused LGBT people between 2019 and 2022, documenting six cases of severe repeated beatings and five cases of sexual harassment in police custody. Arrests took place in public places on the sole basis of gender expression and were accompanied by unlawful searches. Mistreatment was recorded as recently as September 2022, during the period when Qatar was preparing to host the 2022 World Cup under international scrutiny.

Abuse by police and other authorities against LGBT people has included beatings, torture and forced "conversion therapy". A May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed, the first Qatari to publicly come out as gay, described LGBT people being held and physically abused, then promised safety from further torture if they agreed to become informants against others. BBC-sourced information states that trans detainees are required to undergo forced physical detransition, including surgical removal of breast tissue, while held, and must attend conversion "therapy" on release; Qatari authorities "categorically rejected" those allegations.

Detentions have targeted visitors as well as residents. On 4 February 2024 a dual British-Mexican citizen was arrested after police ran a fake Grindr profile; he was held 44 days, interrogated about other gay men, forced to sign documents in Arabic without a translator and denied a lawyer. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention raised concerns about his treatment, and detainees in that case were denied access to antiretroviral medicines needed to live with HIV, a denial the Working Group also flagged. In 2016 the Polish Instagram star King Luxy spent two months in custody on suspicion of being homosexual. In 1998 an American visitor was sentenced to six months in prison and 90 lashes for homosexual activity.

In May 2023 Gilbert Ignatius, a Qatar Airways employee, was detained by Qatar's Criminal Investigation Department over his appearance, with tinted moisturizer, designer clothing and a bag cited as evidence of prostitution; an officer told him "You have no rights. This is Qatar," and struck him when he asked to contact the Indonesian embassy. He was later deported, fired and banned from Qatar without official explanation. Ignatius reported that post-World Cup secret police crackdowns especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand.

The government does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and cohabitation is itself illegal. Because same-gender couples cannot marry, the local death penalty for same-gender sex is argued to apply only to Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions.

Entry and public conduct are framed by official statements rather than by a written visitor rule. In May 2022 the Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said LGBTQ visitors would be welcomed to the World Cup but must respect the nation's culture, and in 2013 bid chief Hassan Al-Thawadi said all were welcome provided they refrained from public displays of affection. In May 2022 some hotels on FIFA's official recommended accommodation list refused to serve same-sex couples outright, while others accepted them only if they hid their relationship in public; FIFA said it would remind hotels of non-discrimination requirements. Nasser Al Khater said in December 2021 that public display of affection "is frowned upon", and Major General al-Ansari warned that rainbow flags could be confiscated to "protect" fans. In 2013 Kuwait proposed banning gay foreigners from entering any Gulf Cooperation Council country and the GCC agreed to discuss it, then backtracked, possibly over concerns about the effect on Qatar's 2022 World Cup hosting.
QAT.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity-document markers for trans people, or whether a trans visitor's passport gender affects entry screening. That gap is unresolved here, not answered by the sources.

Whether Article 296 has been applied to women in practice, and how often it is enforced against residents rather than visitors, is not sourced. The inventory supplies individual cases and a 2019-2022 pattern of arrests but no prosecution statistics.

The claim that the sharia capital penalty applies to same-sex conduct is described in the sources as theoretical and never imposed; the argument that it reaches only Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions is presented as a legal reading rather than a settled holding, and no court decision resolving it is cited.

Qatari authorities "categorically rejected" the BBC-sourced allegations of forced surgical detransition and mandatory conversion therapy. The denial stands alongside the reporting and neither side is independently corroborated in this inventory.

The enforcement status of the hotel non-discrimination requirements FIFA said it would raise, and whether the 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council entry-ban proposal was ever adopted in any form, are unresolved: the sources record the proposal, the discussion and the backtrack only.

No source states whether hate-crime enhancements, anti-discrimination law, or partner/next-of-kin recognition of any kind exist in Qatar beyond the finding that marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised.
