KWT.name: Kuwait
KWT.summary:
Kuwait's National Assembly added Article 199 bis to Penal Code Article 198 in 2007, criminalising an indecent act in a public place or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex, with penalties of up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars (about US$3,500). Human Rights Watch found that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor obtain protection from the policing it authorised. The amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support.

Enforcement began immediately and violently. Within two weeks of the law taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, in coffee shops and in taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against transgender women pursued under the provision, and in 2017 a social-media personality known as King Luxy was detained for two weeks in Kuwait on suspicion of looking too feminine.

In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck the 2007 "imitating the opposite sex" provision down as unconstitutional, a ruling recorded by the Library of Congress and confirmed in HRW's World Report 2024. The challenge was brought by an individual targeted by police. HRW urged the National Assembly to repeal the provision outright, noting that the judgment removed criminal exposure but did not end the underlying dress-code policing practice; analysis by the Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute in July 2024 set out the steps still required after abolition.

Trans visitors remain exposed through other provisions. Penal Code Article 193 punishes consensual same-sex relations between men by up to seven years, adultery by up to five, and public morality laws are strictly enforced with regular prosecutions. In February 2023 DAWN reported that a year after the ruling transgender discrimination continued in practice, with social and employment discrimination persisting and no movement toward recognition of transgender rights. Officials continue to act on the presumption that gender non-conformity is suspect, whatever the constitutional position.

Entry and screening carry separate risks. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council states agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of testing to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners; officials later insisted it was only a proposal, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking. Foreign nationals found to be infected with HIV are deported, while Kuwaiti citizens are entitled to outpatient care through a specialised infectious disease hospital. No association or charity exists in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or to organise community events.

State censorship and official invisibility reinforce the risk. The communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information, no candidate stood for the National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation, and in August 2023 Kuwait banned the film "Barbie" on the stated grounds that it promoted homosexuality. Censors had also banned "The Danish Girl" among other films, and gender segregation and enforced dress codes across the region make gender-non-conforming visitors especially visible to scrutiny.
KWT.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the National Assembly has since deleted Article 199 bis from the Penal Code text, as distinct from the Constitutional Court's annulment of its application, is unresolved in the available sources; HRW's call for outright repeal is recorded but no legislative outcome is.

The practical enforcement picture after February 2022 is not sourced beyond DAWN's February 2023 assessment and the general statement that discrimination by officials persists. Arrest, stop-and-search and documentation-check data for transgender visitors since the ruling is not available here.

The procedure, fee and evidentiary requirements for changing gender markers on Kuwaiti identity or travel documents are not documented in this inventory, so the current documentary position for a trans visitor is stated only as the absence of any recognised route.

The 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council entry-testing proposal is recorded as a proposal that officials later disowned; whether any element of it was implemented, by Kuwait or by any other state in the council, is unresolved. The stated ground for the August 2023 "Barbie" ban comes from the authorities' own announcement and is reproduced as such rather than independently verified.

HRW (17 Feb 2022): Kuwait's Constitutional Court struck down the 2007 anti-transgender provision ('imitating the opposite sex') as unconstitutional; HRW urged parliament to repeal the law outright — the ruling removed criminal exposure but not the underlying dress-code policing practice.
A Library of Congress country entry records the Kuwait Constitutional Court ruling that struck down Article 198 of the Penal Code.

US State Dept 2023 Country Report on Kuwait (via ecoi): communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information; no candidate ran for National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation — documents censorship and invisibility of LGBT political participation.

HRW World Report 2024, Kuwait (events of 2023): penal code art. 193 still punishes consensual same-sex relations between men by up to 7 years and adultery by up to 5 years; positive step noted — Feb 2022 Constitutional Court ruling unconstitutional the 2007 art. 198 'imitating' provision.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute (11 Jul 2024): the 2007 amendment criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex' was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei with overwhelming parliamentary support, and abolished by the Constitutional Court in 2022 after an individual targeted by police challenged it — analysis of the steps still needed after abolition.

DAWN MENA (13 Feb 2023, Nora Noralla): a year after the Constitutional Court overturned the anti-transgender law, transgender discrimination continues in practice — the ruling was not a first step toward recognizing transgender rights, with social and employment discrimination persisting.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' (16 Apr 2018): regional study of LGBT activism in 22 MENA jurisdictions incl. Kuwait, based on interviews with 34 activists; six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or activism.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: In September 2013 it was announced that all Gulf Cooperation Council states had agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of 'testing' to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners; officials later insisted it was only a proposal, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking. Same-sex sexual activity between men is illegal under Kuwait's penal code with penalties of up to seven years in prison, and public morality laws are strictly enforced, leading to regular prosecutions of LGBTQ people. In 2017 Instagram star King Luxy was arrested in Kuwait for allegedly looking too feminine and spent two weeks in custody before release. A 2022 Constitutional Court ruling overturned the criminalisation of 'imitation of the opposite sex', though discrimination by officials persists. Foreigners found to be infected with HIV/AIDS are deported, whereas Kuwaiti citizens who are infected are entitled to outpatient medical care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence has remained under 0.1 percent through to the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25-49 making up 47 percent of those with HIV, and in 1992 the National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV; no youth-specific or minor-specific care access provisions are documented. No known association or charity exists in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or to organise educational and social events for the LGBTQ community. In 2007 a group of Kuwaitis applied to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form such an association and never received a formal reply, and in July 2019 they announced they would reapply after a Ministry of Commerce crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops. In August 2023 Kuwait banned the film 'Barbie', claiming it promoted homosexuality; no youth- or education-specific findings about minors are documented.

KWT.tangentialFactors:
Kuwait's regime does not operate in isolation. Regional norms of gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans visitors unusually legible to casual policing, and cross-dressing is a crime across a number of Middle Eastern jurisdictions, a pattern Brian Whitaker surveyed in 2016.

HRW's 2018 regional study "Audacity in Adversity" drew on interviews with 34 activists across 22 jurisdictions including Kuwait, and found that six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or activism. The pattern of outward movement is a signal about the durability of local protection.

Kuwait's HIV prevalence has remained below 0.1 percent through the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25 to 49 accounting for 47 percent of those living with HIV. The National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV in 1992. Deportation of infected foreign nationals is the practical consequence for a visitor, not care.
KWT.blindSummary:
The national assembly added Article 199 bis to the penal code in 2007, criminalising an indecent act in a public place or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex, with penalties of up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars (about US$3,500). A human rights organisation found that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor obtain protection from the policing it authorised. The amendment was proposed by a member of the national assembly and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support.

Enforcement began immediately and violently. Within two weeks of the law taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, in coffee shops and in taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as punishment. A 2012 report by the same organisation documented police violence against transgender women pursued under the provision, and in 2017 a social-media personality was detained for two weeks on suspicion of looking too feminine.

In February 2022 the constitutional court struck the 2007 "imitating the opposite sex" provision down as unconstitutional, a ruling also recorded by a national legal library and confirmed in the same organisation's 2024 world report. The challenge was brought by an individual targeted by police. The organisation urged the national assembly to repeal the provision outright, noting that the judgment removed criminal exposure but did not end the underlying dress-code policing practice; analysis by a regional legal research institute in July 2024 set out the steps still required after abolition.

Trans visitors remain exposed through other provisions. The penal code punishes consensual same-sex relations between men by up to seven years, adultery by up to five, and public morality laws are strictly enforced with regular prosecutions. In February 2023 a regional rights organisation reported that a year after the ruling transgender discrimination continued in practice, with social and employment discrimination persisting and no movement toward recognition of transgender rights. Officials continue to act on the presumption that gender non-conformity is suspect, whatever the constitutional position.

Entry and screening carry separate risks. In September 2013 the states of a regional council agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of testing to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners; officials later insisted it was only a proposal, with concern over hosting a major international sporting event in a neighbouring jurisdiction cited as a reason for backtracking. Foreign nationals found to be infected with HIV are deported, while citizens are entitled to outpatient care through a specialised infectious disease hospital. No association or charity exists in the country to campaign for LGBTQ rights or to organise community events.

State censorship and official invisibility reinforce the risk. The communications regulator blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information, no candidate stood for the national assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation, and in August 2023 the country banned a popular children's film on the stated grounds that it promoted homosexuality. Censors had also banned a well-known drama about a gender-non-conforming artist, and gender segregation and enforced dress codes across the region make gender-non-conforming visitors especially visible to scrutiny.
KWT.blindOutOfScope:
Whether the national assembly has since deleted Article 199 bis from the penal code text, as distinct from the constitutional court's annulment of its application, is unresolved in the available sources; the call for outright repeal is recorded but no legislative outcome is.

The practical enforcement picture after February 2022 is not sourced beyond the February 2023 assessment and the general statement that discrimination by officials persists. Arrest, stop-and-search and documentation-check data for transgender visitors since the ruling is not available here.

The procedure, fee and evidentiary requirements for changing gender markers on national identity or travel documents are not documented in this inventory, so the current documentary position for a trans visitor is stated only as the absence of any recognised route.

The 2013 regional entry-testing proposal is recorded as a proposal that officials later disowned; whether any element of it was implemented, here or in any neighbouring jurisdiction, is unresolved. The stated ground for the August 2023 film ban comes from the authorities' own announcement and is reproduced as such rather than independently verified.

BHR.name: Bahrain
BHR.summary:
Bahrain decriminalised same-sex sexual activity in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era statute, and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression. Under the 1976 penal code the age of adulthood for consensual same-sex acts is 21.

Decriminalisation has not removed exposure. Authorities continue to bring morality and indecency charges under Articles 324, 329 and 350 of the penal code, which carry three months to two years' imprisonment, fines up to 200 Bahraini dinars, and deportation for non-Bahrainis. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in Manama on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A man received a one-month sentence in 2009 for wearing an abaya and carrying a purse in public, and police raided a 2011 party described as a same-sex wedding. In February 2024 the Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation, extending the framework under which such charges are brought.

Entry is screened on gender presentation. The Interior Minister has stated that suspected effeminate homosexuals are barred from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and pending bills have proposed expressly banning LGBTQ foreigners from entry or from residency permits. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council agreed to discuss a proposal to test and exclude gay foreigners, though officials later backtracked.

Legal gender recognition is refused by the courts. In a May 2023 judgment a lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and refused his request for a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination. A 2023 ruling held sex-reassignment procedures contrary to Islamic law where a case is considered solely related to gender dysphoria, limiting eligibility to people with intersex traits. Courts require medical documentation of a sex change operation or of medical necessity before a legal marker is changed.

Gender-affirming medical care is heavily restricted. Article 330 of the penal code requires anyone charged with prostitution or fujoor to be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and permits relocation to a medical facility.

No law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and no hate-crime protection extends to gender and sexual minorities.
BHR.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved conflict in the sources. Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada response RIO BHR105575.E of August 2016 reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain', citing a Canadian government update of 14 July 2016 and Gulf News of 5 February 2011. That reading contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation position carried by Wikipedia, Outright International and the 2023 US State Department report, and the inventory does not reconcile the two.

Verification is constrained. Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade, including United Nations human-rights bodies and Amnesty International, so local media often serve as the only source for this jurisdiction.

The status of the pending bills is not sourced: whether the October 2021 promotion bill, the proposed entry and residency bans, and the teacher-instruction bills were enacted, lapsed or remain before the legislature is unresolved in the inventory.

sources.summary: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Bahrain' (continuously updated): legal status 'decriminalised since 1976' per ILGA-sourced infobox, with recognition limits and no SOGIESC discrimination protections. Orientation and recognition source, consistent with the Outright and State Department baseline. Wikipedia country coverage: The Interior Minister stated that 'suspected' (effeminate) homosexuals are banned from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and pending bills proposed to expressly ban LGBTQ foreigners from entering the kingdom or receiving residency permits. In September 2013, all Gulf Cooperation Countries agreed to discuss a proposal to establish testing to ban gay foreigners from entering, though officials later backtracked. Penalties under indecency provisions include deportation for non-Bahrainis. Wikipedia country coverage: In response to parliamentary questions about lesbianism in schools, the Assistant Under-Secretary for Educational Services stated the Education Ministry is not responsible for addressing sexuality and that 'The public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist,' adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined. Pending bills proposed to instruct children's teachers in warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children can be punished. In February 2024, the Ministry of Education referred a private school's administration and board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed students performing a scene with two male students pretending to propose to each other. Wikipedia country coverage: No LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters, or community organizations exist: the US Department of State reports there are no approved LGBTQ-related organizations, and ILGA concludes it is 'improbable' that any sexual- or gender-diversity group would be registered, since the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order. Gender-affirming medical care is heavily restricted: courts require medical documentation of a 'sex change operation' or medical necessity to change legal gender markers, and a 2023 court ruling held that sex-reassignment procedures are against Islamic law where cases are considered solely related to gender dysphoria, limiting eligibility to people with intersex traits. Article 330 of the penal code also mandates that anyone charged with prostitution or 'fujoor' be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and potentially relocated to a medical facility. Wikipedia country coverage: Bahrain has no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and hate speech against the LGBTQ+ community remains widespread with no legal consequences — partly because Article 309 protects religious groups but does not extend equivalent protection to LGBTQ+ people. Enforcement hits individuals through morality and indecency provisions (Articles 324, 329, 350), which carry 3 months to 2 years' imprisonment, fines up to 200 BHD, and deportation for non-Bahrainis; the government used these against people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of 'cross-dressing', including a 2009 one-month jail sentence for a man wearing an abaya and purse in public and a 2011 police raid on a party described as a same-sex wedding. False accusations of homosexuality are also used as a tool to discredit and bully government critics and protesters, including human rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and 2011 Pearl Square demonstrators. Media hostility compounds this: a widely-viewed August 3, 2024 Albilad caricature depicted a pride-flag roll of toilet paper captioned 'the correct place'. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth are a direct policy target: a bill proposed in October 2021 would have criminalized promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to 5 years' imprisonment, and other pending bills proposed instructing children's teachers to spot warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children could be punished. The Education Ministry disclaims responsibility for sexuality issues — Assistant Under-Secretary Khalid Al Alawi said it is parents' job and that 'the public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist', while adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined. On February 14, 2024, the Ministry referred a private school's administration and entire board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed two male students pretending to propose to each other in class; a 2022 incident in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality also triggered calls for stricter laws. Note also that the age of adulthood under the 1976 penal code is 21 for consensual same-sex acts, and the Gulf Daily News has published articles on female homosexuality in girls' high schools.

Cairo 52 (7 Feb 2024): in a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia — including refusal of a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he requested. For this record: the documented judicial-refusal practice blocking legal transition at first instance.

Cairo 52 country review: Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade, including UN human-rights bodies and Amnesty International, so local media often serve as the only source for this jurisdiction.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era law, and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy, but authorities still use 'indecency' and 'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people; the Feb 2024 Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation. Decriminalisation coexists with arrests under morality provisions.

Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada RIO BHR105575.E (Aug 2016, covering 2011-Jul 2016): reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain' (citing Canada 14 Jul 2016 and Gulf News 5 Feb 2011) plus societal-attitude and treatment-by-authorities research. This contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation reading of Wikipedia, Outright and the 2023 US State Department, and the conflict remains unresolved.

BHR.comparisons: Bahrain scores above Qatar, Oman, and the UAE because it lacks both a codified gender-expression statute and a documented pattern of systematic targeting.

OMN.name: Oman
OMN.summary:
Oman is a destination trans and gender-nonconforming travellers should avoid. The Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018) criminalises same-sex conduct with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, and its provisions on impersonation and gender non-conformity reach presentation as well as acts. The Public Prosecution has stated that any male who appears in female clothing or demeanour may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed for up to one year, with additional charges available for publishing such material on social media. These provisions are applied to foreign nationals.

The statute set is broad. Article 265 covers public indecency, punishable by 10 days to 3 months and a fine of OMR 100 to 300. Article 266 covers impersonation and entry into women-only venues while disguised, carrying 1 month to 1 year, and reaches gender non-conformity through Article 266(d). Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content held to violate public morals, offline and online, with penalties of up to one year and 10 days to one month respectively. The Cyber Crime Law 2011, Articles 17 and 31, is used against LGBT expression and carries 1 month to 3 years plus a fine of OMR 100 to 3,000.

Courts impose custody on this basis. In September 2018 the Public Prosecution reported that a Salalah preliminary court had sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and posting photographs of themselves in women's clothing on social media, and had sentenced two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video. The sentences were handed down under Article 22 of the July 2018 penal code. They followed arrests by the Royal Oman Police in January 2018 of a group of men for dressing as women after photographs circulated on social media.

Enforcement against gender expression is active and recent. In an open letter of 13 July 2020 Human Rights Watch addressed arrests and convictions under the 2018 code's 'imitating the opposite sex' provision: the Royal Oman Police announced the arrest of men in women's clothing after photographs from a private party in Salalah circulated on Snapchat, and an Asian expatriate wearing an abaya and niqab was detained during a women-only hour at a park in Al Buraimi. Human Rights Watch's April 2018 regional report records that Oman's 2018 penal code, effective that year, added a provision punishing any man who 'appears to dress in women's clothing', alongside the country's existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and barriers to LGBT organising.

Foreign nationals face removal in addition to imprisonment. Article 60 requires deportation of a foreign national convicted of a felony, permanently, and allows it after a misdemeanour conviction on a 3-to-15-year basis. Prosecution does not depend on a family complaint: cases are frequently opened on digital evidence surfaced during unrelated investigations, and Article 49's dual-criminality exception is recorded in that context. The state ISP Omantel enables surveillance, outing carries social as well as criminal risk, and the Civil Associations Law restricts assembly and advocacy.

Border treatment reaches visibly gender-nonconforming visitors. On 27 February 2023 a genderqueer, non-binary Indian model and activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa reported that her companions cleared immigration while she was held for separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers. This is first-hand evidence of how a visitor who does not present in line with sex expectations is handled at the primary port of entry.

Oman bans legal gender recognition and explicitly bans gender-affirming healthcare, and recent legislative developments have deepened the criminalisation of gender expression, according to a joint stakeholder submission by Cairo 52 and White Tent filed on 6 August 2025 for Oman's fourth-cycle Universal Periodic Review. The statute set is broad. Article 265 covers public indecency, punishable by 10 days to 3 months and a fine of OMR 100 to 300. Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content held to violate public morals, offline and online, with penalties of up to one year and 10 days to one month respectively. A cybercrime law of 2011, Articles 17 and 31, is used against LGBT expression and carries 1 month to 3 years plus a fine of OMR 100 to 3,000.

Courts impose custody on this basis. In September 2018 the public prosecution reported that a preliminary court in a southern city had sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and posting photographs of themselves in women's clothing on social media, and had sentenced two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video. BGR.name: Bulgaria
BGR.summary:
Bulgaria is an EU member state that imposes no traveller-facing restrictions on gender expression. There is no criminalisation of gender identity or presentation, no statute governing which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender, and no document, entry or border screening that turns on a visitor's gender marker. Same-sex relations have been decriminalised since 1968. Entry and visa rules are applied to foreign passports on ordinary terms, and a recorded gender raises no separate question at the border.

Legal gender recognition is effectively closed. The Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 holds that "the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one" and that the legal system rests on "the binary existence of humankind", which bars legal gender change; the Constitutional Court's verdict on the Istanbul Convention condemned the legislation permitting it. The European Court of Human Rights found in Y.T. v Bulgaria in 2020 that refusal of legal gender recognition violates Article 8, and in December 2024 the Court confirmed that those obligations were unaffected by the 2024 revision of the gender-recognition registry; Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic. In September 2025 an Advocate General of the Court of Justice of the European Union, Richard de la Tour, opined that EU law precludes national legislation such as Bulgaria's that refuses a trans person identity documents matching their presented gender, and the Court concurred with that reasoning. That line of pressure is unresolved at the level of a final judgment, and a visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with presentation should assume Bulgarian authorities will treat the document as issued.

Public visibility carries documented violence risk with weak state response. Hate crimes against LGBT people are frequently ignored and go uninvestigated, including the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to "cleanse" it of gay people, and the assault in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 on children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of Botev acting in an anti-LGBT "cleansing action". The first Sofia Pride in 2008, with about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles and more than 60 hooligans were arrested; the 2011 parade passed without incident only under heavy police guard; in 2017 Human Rights Watch warned that the group National Resistance was rallying counter-demonstrators to "cleanse Sofia from garbage". Order at Pride events is therefore police-dependent rather than structural.

Legislation now restricts discussion of gender identity directly. On 7 August 2024 Bulgaria's parliament amended the education law to prohibit "propaganda, promotion, or incitement" in the education system of ideas about non-traditional sexual orientation or gender identity other than the biological one; the amendment was introduced by the Revival party, backed by GERB, signed by President Rumen Radev, and in force from 16 August 2024. At municipal level the District Council of Pazardzhik voted in November 2009 to forbid the public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation; an administrative court struck it down in October 2010 on procedural grounds and upheld it on appeal in July 2011.

Anti-discrimination legislation in force since 1 January 2004 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment and bans hate speech based on sexual orientation; a 2015 amendment extended coverage to "sex" as including "sex change", though gender expression and gender identity are not named explicitly. A visitor refused a room, treatment or service on that ground has a statutory basis for complaint, but the enforcement pattern described below qualifies its practical weight. Health services fall within that ban, while same-sex couples are denied the right to make medical decisions for one another.
BGR.outOfScopeNotes:
Two court tracks are unresolved in the sources available. The Court of Justice of the European Union's reasoning in the Bulgarian identity-document case is dated to an Advocate General's opinion of September 2025 and the Court's concurrence with that reasoning, but no final judgment is recorded here; whether Bulgarian administrative practice has changed since is not sourced. The September 2023 European Court of Human Rights finding on non-recognition of same-sex couples is described as subject to appeals and awaiting a government response, with no outcome recorded.

Whether the July 2023 heavier penalties for sexual-orientation-based crimes have produced any measurable change in investigation or prosecution is not sourced. The most recent direct evidence of enforcement failure in the inventory remains the 2020 Plovdiv assault and the 2015 Amnesty International findings; a reader should treat the current investigation rate as unresolved rather than assume improvement or deterioration.

Practical police behaviour at Pride events after 2017, and any travel advisories issued by foreign ministries specifically addressing gender marker inconsistencies on passports at Bulgarian border points, are not covered by this inventory.

sources.summary: On 7 August 2024 Bulgaria's parliament passed an amendment to the education law banning 'propaganda, promotion, or incitement... directly or indirectly' of ideas about 'non-traditional sexual orientation and/or gender identity other than the biological one', signed by President Rumen Radev and in force from 16 August 2024, introduced by the Revival party and backed by GERB. In November 2009 the District Council of Pazardzhik voted to forbid the 'public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation'; the Administrative Court struck it down in October 2010 for procedural errors, and upheld it on appeal in July 2011. Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been banned since the Protection Against Discrimination Act took effect 1 January 2004, but gender expression and gender identity are not explicitly named in the 2015 revision. Billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in Varna and Burgas were vandalised in December 2018, and the Bulgarian Orthodox Church calls pride events a 'sinful demonstration'. Citing Coman and Others v General Inspectorate of Immigration, a Sofia court on 29 June 2018 granted an Australian woman and her French wife, married in France in 2016, the right to live in Bulgaria, after they had been denied residency a year earlier when they tried to move there. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights held that Bulgaria's refusal to recognise same-sex couples is an 'infringement of human rights'; that case is subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. Health services are covered by the anti-discrimination ban on sexual-orientation discrimination in force since 1 January 2004, and same-sex couples are denied the right to make medical decisions for each other. Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred from donating blood: the donor form, per a Ministry of Healthcare ordinance of 19 July 2004, does not ask orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV/STI-risk practices. Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the 'easier operation', with parents 'rarely informed' of later harm to the child's gender identity, and there are no laws concerning intersex people. Single Step Foundation launched Bulgaria's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies. State hostility is documented in law and courts: the 2024 education 'propaganda' amendment, the 2009 Pazardzhik council ban on public demonstration of orientation, the Constitutional Court's Istanbul Convention verdict condemning legislation for legal gender recognition, and the Supreme Court of Cassation's 20 February 2023 interpretative decision that 'the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one' and that the legal system rests on 'the binary existence of humankind', effectively barring legal gender change. Hate crimes against LGBT people 'are often ignored and go uninvestigated by authorities', including the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to 'cleanse' the park of gays, and the 27 September 2020 assault in Plovdiv on children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of Botev. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw such hate crimes was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections, though heavier penalties for sexual-orientation-based crimes were adopted on 28 July 2023. Media and political hostility includes the 1964 show trial of 26 men, including actor Georgi Partsalev and singer Emil Dimitrov, described by experts as 'a masquerade for the public' about 'decadent Western culture', the 2020–2021 rise in anti-LGBT rhetoric where 'gender became a slur', far-right National Resistance advocating brooms and shovels against pride attendees, and the Ataka party's protests. ILGA-Europe ranked Bulgaria 37 of 49 European countries for LGBT rights protection in 2020. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, explicitly banning same-sex marriage, and the Constitution does not ban civil unions, but none exist, so same-sex couples are denied inheritance, medical decision-making and joint property rights. A Bulgarian court recognised a same-sex marriage performed in France in 2019, and a Sofia court granted residency rights in June 2018 under the Coman ruling. A couple who married in the UK had their recognition claim rejected by the Sofia Administrative Court in January 2018, an appeal pursued by the LGBT organisation Deystvie. In September 2023 the ECtHR found Bulgaria's non-recognition an 'infringement of human rights', pending appeal. Same-sex couples are banned from adopting, and a 2021 ECJ ruling forced Bulgaria to issue an ID to a child of a lesbian couple after it refused a birth certificate. On 7 August 2024 parliament amended the education law to prohibit 'propaganda, promotion, or incitement... in the education system' of ideas about non-traditional sexual orientation or non-biological gender identity, defined as attraction 'contrary to Bulgaria's legal concept of... opposite sexes', in force 16 August 2024. The age of consent has been 14 regardless of sex since 2002, and since 2026 it is 16. A 2008 survey of 15 schools in Sofia, Varna and Plovdiv found 10.5% of students identified as bisexual and 1.8% as gay, with 29% saying they would refuse to sit next to a gay classmate, 5% saying they would bully gay classmates and 39% saying they would protect them. Children as young as 14 or 15 were assaulted in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 in an anti-LGBT 'cleansing action', and the first Sofia Pride in 2008, about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles with over 60 hooligans arrested. Single Step Foundation, founded 2016, works specifically with LGBTI youth on coming out and affirmation.

Institutional non-response to bias crime is long-standing rather than episodic. Amnesty International's February 2015 report "Missing the point" found that authorities consistently failed to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes: legislation existed, but bias attacks that spiked in 2013 according to the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee went unpursued, with the Sofia prosecution opening only some cases. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw hate crimes against LGBT people was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections. Heavier penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation were adopted on 28 July 2023, but the reporting that follows the 2020 Plovdiv assault continues to describe hate crimes as uninvestigated.

Beyond the National Resistance counter-demonstrations, the Ataka party has protested Pride, far-right groups have advocated using brooms and shovels against attendees, billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in Varna and Burgas were vandalised in December 2018, and the Bulgarian Orthodox Church describes Pride events as a "sinful demonstration". The 2020 to 2021 period saw a rise in anti-LGBT rhetoric in which gender became a slur. ILGA-Europe ranked Bulgaria 37th of 49 European countries for LGBT rights protection in 2020.

The legal regime for same-sex couples is relevant to any visitor arriving with a partner. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, and although the Constitution does not bar civil unions, none exist, so same-sex couples lack inheritance, joint property and medical decision-making rights, and are barred from adopting. A Sofia court granted residency in June 2018 to an Australian woman and her French wife on the basis of the Court of Justice's Coman ruling after residency had been denied a year earlier; a Bulgarian court recognised a French same-sex marriage in 2019; a couple who married in the United Kingdom had their recognition claim rejected by the Sofia Administrative Court in January 2018, with the appeal pursued by the organisation Deystvie. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights held that Bulgaria's non-recognition of same-sex couples is an infringement of human rights, subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. In 2021 a Court of Justice ruling forced Bulgaria to issue an identity document to a child of a lesbian couple after it had refused a birth certificate.

Blood donation is not restricted on orientation grounds. Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred; a Ministry of Healthcare ordinance of 19 July 2004 sets a donor form that does not ask about orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV or STI-risk practices.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 forecloses it on a biological reading of sex, and the Constitutional Court's Istanbul Convention verdict condemned the permitting legislation; the 2024 revision of the gender-recognition registry did not alter the European Court of Human Rights' Article 8 obligations arising from Y.T. v Bulgaria, and the Court of Justice's 2025 reasoning on identity documents remains to be applied in practice.

Young LGBT people have one dedicated national support channel: the Single Step Foundation, founded in 2016, launched Bulgaria's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies, and works specifically with young people on coming out and affirmation. Access to that support is being narrowed from the education side by the amendment in force since 16 August 2024, which bars promotion of ideas about non-biological gender identity in the education system and defines non-traditional orientation as attraction contrary to Bulgaria's legal concept of opposite sexes.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or enter a civil union, cannot adopt, and cannot make medical decisions for each other. Recognition of marriages performed abroad has been granted case by case and refused in others, so residency and property consequences for couples remain uncertain.
BGR.comparisons: Bulgaria scores below Romania (0.67, no propaganda law, less hostile FRA numbers) and level with Serbia (0.64, similar climate, no EU backstop but no propaganda law either).
BGR.blindSummary:
The country is a member of a supranational union that imposes no traveller-facing restrictions on gender expression. There is no criminalisation of gender identity or presentation, no statute governing which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender, and no document, entry or border screening that turns on a visitor's gender marker. Same-sex relations have been decriminalised since 1968. Entry and visa rules are applied to foreign passports on ordinary terms, and a recorded gender raises no separate question at the border.

Legal gender recognition is effectively closed. The highest civil court's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 holds that \"the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one\" and that the legal system rests on \"the binary existence of humankind\", which bars legal gender change; the constitutional court's verdict on a regional convention condemned the legislation permitting it. The regional human rights court found in 2020 that refusal of legal gender recognition violates Article 8, and in December 2024 confirmed that those obligations were unaffected by the revision of the gender-recognition registry that year; one judge dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic. In September 2025 the senior legal officer of the supranational union's top court opined that union law precludes national legislation such as this country's that refuses a trans person identity documents matching their presented gender, and the court concurred with that reasoning. That line of pressure is unresolved at the level of a final judgment, and a visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with presentation should assume local authorities will treat the document as issued.

Public visibility carries documented violence risk with weak national response. Hate crimes against LGBT people are frequently ignored and go uninvestigated, including the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a park in the capital by a group intending to \"cleanse\" it of gay people, and an assault in a second city on 27 September 2020 on children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of a football club acting in an anti-LGBT \"cleansing action\". The first Pride march in the capital in 2008, with about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles and more than 60 hooligans were arrested; the 2011 parade passed without incident only under heavy police guard; in 2017 a human rights organisation warned that a far-right group was rallying counter-demonstrators to \"cleanse the capital from garbage\". Order at Pride events is therefore police-dependent rather than structural.

Legislation now restricts discussion of gender identity directly. On 7 August 2024 the national parliament amended the education law to prohibit \"propaganda, promotion, or incitement\" in the education system of ideas about non-traditional sexual orientation or gender identity other than the biological one; the amendment was introduced by a nationalist party, backed by the governing party, signed by the head of state, and in force from 16 August 2024. At municipal level a district council voted in November 2009 to forbid the public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation; an administrative court struck it down in October 2010 on procedural grounds and upheld it on appeal in July 2011.

Anti-discrimination legislation in force since 1 January 2004 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment and bans hate speech based on sexual orientation; a 2015 amendment extended coverage to \"sex\" as including \"sex change\", though gender expression and gender identity are not named explicitly. A visitor refused a room, treatment or service on that ground has a statutory basis for complaint, but the enforcement pattern described below qualifies its practical weight. Health services fall within that ban, while same-sex couples are denied the right to make medical decisions for one another.
BGR.blindOutOfScope:
Two court tracks are unresolved in the sources available. The supranational union court's reasoning on the country's identity-document case is dated to a senior legal officer's opinion of September 2025 and the court's concurrence with that reasoning, but no final judgment is recorded here; whether administrative practice has changed since is not sourced. The September 2023 regional human rights court finding on non-recognition of same-sex couples is described as subject to appeals and awaiting a government response, with no outcome recorded.

Whether the July 2023 heavier penalties for sexual-orientation-based crimes have produced any measurable change in investigation or prosecution is not sourced. The most recent direct evidence of enforcement failure in the inventory remains the 2020 assault in the second city and the 2015 findings; a reader should treat the current investigation rate as unresolved rather than assume improvement or deterioration.

Practical police behaviour at Pride events after 2017, and any travel advisories issued by foreign ministries specifically addressing gender marker inconsistencies on passports at the country's border points, are not covered by this inventory.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: in August 2024 a law banning representation of LGBTI identities in schools was introduced (spearheaded by a nationalist party leader); the country continues rejecting asylum requests by LGBTI people from two other states and unlawfully detains LGBTI asylum-seekers from a conflict region in closed detention; a performer at the capital's Pride event received death threats; an LGBTI youth organisation faced institutional checks.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004, expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex change' under 'sex'. But a constitutional marriage-definition provision bans same-sex marriage, and there is no legal gender recognition. A 2023 regional human-rights court judgment (brought by two same-sex couples) found this country in violation of its obligations on non-recognition of same-sex relationships.

A regional union rights agency's LGBTIQ survey country sheet for this country (2024): 75% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (union-wide: 53%); 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (union-wide: 29%); only 27% are open about being LGBTIQ (union-wide: 51%); 28% felt discriminated against at work or looking for work. Indicates a strongly hostile day-to-day climate.

Foreign public broadcaster (Sept 2025): an advocate general of the regional union's court of justice issued a non-binding opinion that this country must not refuse a trans woman ID documents matching her presented sex ('lived gender identity') - the case concerns a trans woman on hormone therapy refused documents; such opinions are followed by the court in roughly two-thirds of cases.

Regional human-rights court analysis blog (Dec 2024) of a line of cases against this country: the original 2020 judgment found a violation of the convention's private-life article over refusal of legal gender recognition; on revision (July 2024) the application was declared inadmissible for abuse of process, but the court confirmed the country remains obliged (under a later judgment) to provide a framework for legal gender recognition - which it still lacks.

International human-rights organisation report (Feb 2015): the country's failure to adequately investigate and prosecute hate crimes fuels fear, discrimination and violence against asylum seekers, migrants, religious minorities and LGBT people; authorities consistently fail to identify bias motivation.
An international rights group (Jun 2017): urges this country's authorities to protect the capital's pride event and showcase a tolerant side of the country.

News outlet (June 2011): the 4th capital Pride march passed without incidents under heavy police guard - after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 parades; only a 'traditional family' NGO protested.
BGR.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition. The highest civil court's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 forecloses it on a biological reading of sex, and the constitutional court's convention verdict condemned the permitting legislation; the 2024 revision of the gender-recognition registry did not alter the regional human rights court's Article 8 obligations arising from its 2020 judgment, and the supranational union court's 2025 reasoning on identity documents remains to be applied in practice.

Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the easier operation, and parents are rarely informed of the later harm such surgery can cause to a child's gender identity. There are no laws concerning intersex people, and no framework governs consent, timing or disclosure.

Young LGBT people have one dedicated national support channel: a foundation founded in 2016, which launched the country's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies, and works specifically with young people on coming out and affirmation. Access to that support is being narrowed from the education side by the amendment in force since 16 August 2024, which bars promotion of ideas about non-biological gender identity in the education system and defines non-traditional orientation as attraction contrary to the country's legal concept of opposite sexes.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or enter a civil union, cannot adopt, and cannot make medical decisions for each other. Recognition of marriages performed abroad has been granted case by case and refused in others, so residency and property consequences for couples remain uncertain.
BGR.blindTangential:
Institutional non-response to bias crime is long-standing rather than episodic. A major international human rights organisation's February 2015 report found that authorities consistently failed to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes: legislation existed, but bias attacks that spiked in 2013 according to a national civil liberties committee went unpursued, with the capital's prosecution opening only some cases. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw hate crimes against LGBT people was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections. Heavier penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation were adopted on 28 July 2023, but reporting that follows the 2020 assault in the second city continues to describe hate crimes as uninvestigated.

Hostility to visible LGBT events is organised and recurrent. Beyond the far-right counter-demonstrations, a nationalist party has protested Pride, far-right groups have advocated using brooms and shovels against attendees, billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in two coastal cities were vandalised in December 2018, and the national Orthodox church describes Pride events as a \"sinful demonstration\". The 2020 to 2021 period saw a rise in anti-LGBT rhetoric in which gender became a slur. A pan-regional equality index ranked the country 37th of 49 jurisdictions in the region for LGBT rights protection in 2020.

The legal regime for same-sex couples is relevant to any visitor arriving with a partner. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, and although the Constitution does not bar civil unions, none exist, so same-sex couples lack inheritance, joint property and medical decision-making rights, and are barred from adopting. A court in the capital granted residency in June 2018 to a woman and her wife, married in a neighbouring jurisdiction, on the basis of the union's top court's ruling on free movement after residency had been denied a year earlier; a local court recognised a same-sex marriage performed abroad in 2019; a couple who married in another neighbouring jurisdiction had their recognition claim rejected by the capital's administrative court in January 2018, with the appeal pursued by a national LGBT organisation. In September 2023 the regional human rights court held that non-recognition of same-sex couples is an infringement of human rights, subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. In 2021 the union's top court forced the country to issue an identity document to a child of a lesbian couple after it had refused a birth certificate.

Blood donation is not restricted on orientation grounds. Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred; a national health ministry ordinance of 19 July 2004 sets a donor form that does not ask about orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV or STI-risk practices.

SVK.name: Slovakia
SVK.summary:
Slovakia poses no entry or documentation obstacle specific to a trans visitor. Legal gender recognition has been available for more than four decades, and no law restricts which toilets a person may use. Entry and residence fall under the free-movement rules of the European Union, and the Court of Justice of the European Union's Coman ruling of 5 June 2018 required the Slovak Interior Ministry to recognise the residence rights of same-sex couples married elsewhere in the union.

The recognition procedure itself is medicalised and restrictive. In force rules require surgical sterilisation before identity documents can be amended, registry offices are refusing to process gender-change applications pending new standards, and a Ministry of Health guideline that had permitted document change without surgery was revoked on 21 November 2023 on grounds of government coalition stability. A bill of 24 February 2023 would narrow recognition further to people whose sex was wrongly assigned at birth provable only by a karyotype test; it passed first reading with 87 votes, and the sources do not record its subsequent fate.

Legislative attempts to abolish legal gender recognition have so far failed. Bills tabled by ĽSNS on 12 February 2021 and by the Republic Movement on 23 September 2021 and again on 13 January 2023 sought to ban legal gender change, with the 2023 version also outlawing medical transition and carrying a prison sentence of at least four years; all failed, mostly through abstentions. In an April 2023 letter to the Slovak National Council, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović reported no discernible progress six months after the Tepláreň attack, judged the human rights of LGBTI people to be more at risk rather than less, and raised specific concern about regressive legislative proposals including a ban on legal gender recognition.

Trans-specific healthcare has been unstable. The Ministry of Health's standards of care were revoked on 18 May 2022 under pressure from the Conference of Slovak Bishops and MPs, after which no valid standards existed; by 18 November 2022 healthcare providers were refusing transgender care and individuals were being forced to seek treatment abroad. Standards were republished on 3 March 2023, but their implementation in care access and civil registries remains to be seen.

The security climate is the material concern. On 12 October 2022 a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger arrived in Bratislava at about 18:35, and at 19:11 fired eight shots at the LGBT bar Teplaren, killing two people and injuring one; the bar was his stated fallback target. The perpetrator died and the incident is treated as the country's first modern terrorist attack, met with terrorism charges and official condemnation. A 7 February 2023 assessment reports that rights groups regard the attack as having marked a new era for trans people in Slovakia, with the community's situation remaining precarious and fears about the future having intensified afterwards.

Protection machinery exists in part. The Anti-Discrimination Act, adopted in 2004 and broadened in 2008, outlaws discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity across employment, education, housing, social care and the provision of goods and services, and applies to the armed forces, where LGBT people serve openly. A Criminal Code amendment of May 2013 added sexual orientation as a hate-crime ground carrying harsher penalties and outlawed hate speech on that basis; the sources do not state that gender identity was added to that provision.

Any change of legal gender invalidates an existing marriage, and Slovakia recognises neither civil unions nor same-sex marriage, so a visitor in a same-sex partnership should not expect that relationship to be acknowledged. Hostile rhetoric from senior officials is documented: on 3 July 2024 the serving Minister of Culture, Martina Šimkovičová, publicly claimed that Europe is dying because of an excessive number of LGBT people.
SVK.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the bill making legal gender recognition impossible advanced, was amended or became law is not sourced in the material available here and remains unresolved.

Enforcement of hate-crime provisions, including any sentence or conviction arising from the July 2022 assault on two men perceived as gay, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The outcome of the terrorism proceedings arising from the 12 October 2022 shooting, including convictions and sentences, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Two of the supplied sources, an Amnesty International statement and a Pew Research Center survey, yielded no usable finding for this record.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D6, D7.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Same-sex sexual activity was legalised in Czechoslovakia in 1962, and the age of consent was equalised at 15 in 1990 after previously standing at 18 for same-sex activity. The Criminal Code amendment of May 2013 added sexual orientation as a hate-crime ground carrying harsher penalties and outlawed hate speech on that basis. The Anti-Discrimination Act, adopted in 2004 to meet EU requirements and broadened in 2008, outlaws discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity across employment, education, housing, social care and the provision of goods and services; Article 2 lists sexual orientation among protected grounds. The Act applies to the military, where LGBT people serve openly, though a 2005 Pravda report described a 'very homophobic environment' in the armed forces. Bills to criminalise trans lives were tabled by ĽSNS on 12 February 2021 and by the Republic Movement on 23 September 2021, and again on 13 January 2023; they sought to ban legal gender change and, in the 2023 version, to outlaw medical transition with a prison sentence of at least four years. All failed, mostly on abstentions. A bill of 24 February 2023 restricting legal gender change to people whose sex was 'wrongly assigned at birth', provable only by a karyotype test, passed first reading with 87 votes. Slovakia's first gay Pride, held in Bratislava on 22 May 2010, drew about a thousand attendees confronted by right-wing groups who threw stones at speakers, dispersed tear gas and infiltrated the march, forcing cancellation of the city-centre route; 29 people were arrested. On 3 July 2024 the serving Minister of Culture, Martina Šimkovičová, made a public homophobic and racist statement claiming Europe is dying because of 'an excessive number of LGBT people'. Transgender people in Slovakia have difficulty accessing healthcare. Following the revocation of the Ministry of Health's standards of care on 18 May 2022 under pressure from the Conference of Slovak Bishops and MPs, no valid standards existed, and as of 18 November 2022 healthcare providers were refusing transgender care, forcing trans people to seek treatment abroad. Standards were republished on 3 March 2023, but their implementation in care access and civil registries 'remains to be seen', and the guideline allowing document change without surgery was revoked on 21 November 2023 on grounds of 'government coalition stability'. In practice surgical sterilisation has usually been required for legal gender change, and registry offices refuse to process gender changes pending new standards. Gay and bisexual people are barred from donating blood if they had unprotected sex within one year, and any existing marriage is invalidated on change of legal gender. Slovakia recognises no civil unions or same-sex marriage. Bills introduced in 1997, 2000, 2012, 2018, 2021 and 2022 were all rejected (2012: 94 against to 14 for; 2018: 31 of 150 in support; 2021: 7 for, 67 against). Since 1964 the law recognises only a 'close person' (sibling or spouse) with limited rights, mainly inheritance. In June 2014 a constitutional amendment (Article 41) defining marriage as 'a unique union between a man and a woman' passed 102–18, potentially rendering future recognition laws unconstitutional. As of 2025 only married couples may adopt, barring same-sex couples, single people and unmarried partners. Under the ECJ's Coman ruling of 5 June 2018, same-sex couples resident in Slovakia who married in an EU state where one partner is an EU citizen enjoy full residency rights, and the Interior Ministry announced immediate compliance. The Alliance for the Family's 2014 petition demanded a ban on same-sex adoption, the prohibition of sex education in schools and a referendum question barring schools from requiring children to take sexual-behaviour education. The third question was ruled unconstitutional, and the referendum of 7 February 2015 on the rest was invalid at 21.07% turnout after opponents urged a boycott. In the 2017 Iniciatíva Inakosť survey nearly 40% of LGBT respondents had faced active discrimination (15.2% in the last year); many reported low self-esteem, anxiety, depression, alcohol abuse and suicidal feelings from homophobic persecution, and fewer than half were willing to hold a partner's hand in public. The same year's survey found family disclosure reactions mixed, with 54% of mothers, 42% of fathers and 49.5% of grandparents accepting, while 28.5% of fathers and 29% of grandparents were indifferent. The shooting outside Tepláren, a well-known Bratislava gay bar, on 12 October 2022 killed two people plus the perpetrator and wounded a third. Slovakia is described as having some of the worst LGBTQ rights in the EU and less supportive public opinion than the Czech Republic; support is volatile, from 66% acceptance in a 2007 Pew survey to 29–57% backing civil unions in 2019, falling to 40% after the 2022 attack, while the 2015 Eurobarometer put Slovakia fourth-lowest in the EU on same-sex marriage at 24% and PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked Slovakia 47th against Czechia 18th. The gay scene is small, consisting of a few bars and clubs in Bratislava.

Changing legal gender documents requires surgical sterilisation under the transition rules in force, a requirement that rights groups were already contesting before October 2022.

Residents faced a bill that would make legal gender recognition impossible; the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights raised it with the Slovak National Council in April 2023 as a regressive proposal.

Domestic LGBTI organisations described the Teplaren attack as marking a new era for trans people in the country, and reported heightened fear about the future in the months that followed.

Police provide protection at Pride events, and the state prosecuted the 2022 shooting as terrorism, so protection machinery exists and is used; the pressure sits in the political rhetoric and street hostility around it.
SVK.comparisons: Slovakia scores above Hungary (0.68 — LGR already banned there plus a propaganda law in force), below Poland (0.72 — no terrorist attack and larger protective infrastructure), and well below Czechia (0.74).
SVK.blindSummary:
The state carries no traveller-facing legal exposure for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has been available for more than forty years, though the procedure is medicalised and the rules in force require surgical sterilisation before identity documents can be amended. There is no bathroom law and no border obstacle under the free-movement rules of the national union to which the country belongs.

The security climate is the material concern. On 12 October 2022 a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was the sitting head of government arrived in the capital at about 18:35; at 19:11 he fired eight shots at a LGBT bar, killing two people and injuring a third. The bar was his stated fallback target. The incident is classified as the country first modern terrorist attack, and the national authorities responded with terrorism charges and official condemnation.

Rights groups assessed the shooting as marking a new era for trans people in the country. a February 2023 assessment found the trans community's position precarious: transition rules were already burdensome, and the aftermath deepened fears about what lay ahead.

Six months after the attack, a regional human rights commissioner wrote to the national legislature reporting no discernible progress and concluding that the human rights of LGBTI people appeared more at risk rather than less. She raised concern about regressive legislative proposals, including a bill that would make legal gender recognition impossible.

Street violence and political rhetoric compound the picture. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in the capital, and anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified after October 2022 rather than receding. Police protect Pride events, so the gap lies between functioning institutional protection and the street and political climate a visitor actually moves through.

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.summary:
Belarus presents an acute and documented risk to transgender visitors, and travel there should be avoided. In April 2024 the authorities widened the legal definition of pornography to encompass depictions of same-sex relationships and of transgender people, classing these alongside necrophilia and paedophilia as "non-traditional relationships". Production and distribution carry up to four years' imprisonment, rising to thirteen years for material involving children. Human Rights Watch described the change as an explicit attack on LGBT dignity. The charge attaches to visibility rather than to conduct: a trans person's own image or presence can be treated as pornographic material, and prosecution proceeds under Article 343 of the Criminal Code.

Enforcement followed quickly. In September 2024 the organisation TG House Belarus reported more than fifteen LGBTQ+ people detained within a single month, at least eight of them transgender. Most were charged with hooliganism and two with pornography. Detainees reported physical and psychological abuse in custody, and several left the country afterwards. Rights groups also report police beating LGBTQ+ people during arrests, extracting charges under duress, and expanding repression under "LGBT propaganda" framing.

In April 2026 the country enacted a law banning propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia, which critics have compared to Russia's 2013 statute. The Prosecutor General's Office has separately announced an administrative-penalty law against "LGBTI propaganda" that has not yet been tabled. A new National Security Concept adopted by the authorities emphasises "traditional values", and state television has equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and called them "a weapon in the hands of the West"; TG House recorded a rise in hate speech across state propaganda during 2024.

Protection machinery is effectively absent. Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE/ODIHR since 2015 and maintains no National Point of Contact, so no official statistics on anti-LGBT violence exist and monitoring rests on civil-society reporting from Human Constanta and others. There is no anti-discrimination protection and no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The country is not a member of the Council of Europe, so victims cannot appeal to the European Court of Human Rights.

Entry, status and exit exposure is significant. Sexual orientation and gender identity are not explicitly recognised as grounds for refugee status, and same-sex partners are not recognised for immigration purposes. At least ten transgender people left Belarus within a single year because of discrimination and repression. Foreigners openly participating in LGBT events have previously been threatened with immediate expulsion under the article on intervention in domestic affairs.

Care access compounds the risk. Qualified psychological help is generally unavailable, no trans-specific facilities are documented, and the psychology faculties of the country's universities do not address the needs of sexual minorities. Suicide rates are high among gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people, and being openly trans exposes a person to harassment, violence and physical abuse in a society where 84 percent of respondents told Pew Research Center in May 2017 that homosexuality should not be accepted.
BLR.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the April 2026 propaganda statute is sourced here only to a secondary encyclopaedic compilation rather than to the text of the law itself; the operative provisions, penalties and commencement date are not independently verified in this inventory.

Unresolved: the Prosecutor General's Office administrative-penalty measure on "LGBTI propaganda" is described as planned and not yet tabled, so its current legislative status is unknown.

Unresolved: the detention figures for September 2024 come from a single advocacy organisation, TG House Belarus, and no official confirmation or court record corroborates the count or the charges.

Unresolved: no official hate-crime statistics exist for Belarus after 2015, so the incidence of anti-trans violence can be assessed only from civil-society reporting and cannot be quantified.

Not sourced: conditions at border entry for transgender travellers, including passport and gender-marker inspection practice by border officers, are not covered by this inventory; nor is the current legal rule on legal gender recognition.

Explicitly aimed at LGBT dignity — a persecution vector for visitors and residents alike.

JURIST (28 Sep 2024): TG House Belarus reports 15+ LGBTQ people detained in one month, incl. 8 transgender — most charged with hooliganism, two with pornography; custody abuse (physical and psychological) reported and some fled the country.

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Belarus: Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since 2015 and has no National Point of Contact; civil-society reports for 2024 came from Human Constanta and others. No official data available.
AP: 'Activists say police in Belarus beat LGBTQ+ people while arresting and charging them' — rights groups report beatings, coerced charges and expanding 'LGBT propaganda' repression.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Belarus: state TV equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and called them 'a weapon in the hands of the West'; TG House recorded increased hate speech in state propaganda; the Prosecutor General's Office plans an administrative-penalty law against 'LGBTI propaganda' (not yet tabled); at least ten trans people left Belarus in a year due to discrimination and repression; a new National Security Concept emphasises 'traditional values'.
