sources.summary:
Persecution on the basis of sexual orientation is not explicitly recognised in Belarusian law as a ground for refugee status, and same-sex partners are not recognised for immigration purposes. After the fall of the communist regime many Belarusians sought and received political asylum abroad, most often citing formal or informal police harassment; Amnesty International and AILGBT-Belarus documented individuals granted asylum in the Czech Republic, France, the Netherlands and Sweden. Belarus is not a member of the Council of Europe, so activists cannot appeal to the European Court of Human Rights. In 2004, when an international gay and lesbian festival was targeted, authorities made threatening phone calls stating that foreigners attending workshops and discussions would be immediately expelled from the country under the article on intervention in domestic affairs.

Qualified psychological help is generally unavailable in Belarus, and no trans-specific facilities are documented; the three Minsk universities offering full psychology courses (Belarus State University, Belarus Pedagogical University, European Humanities University) do not address the problems of sexual minorities. Suicide rates are high among gays, lesbians, bisexuals and transgender people. LGBTQ venues have been shut or raided: the gay club Oskar was closed by authorities in February 2000 and its owner Ivan Suchinski was later killed, riot police raided a 1999 pride party, and police have conducted unprovoked actions in bars frequented by homosexuals in Gomel and Minsk. In prisons, homosexuality is subject to speculation, blackmail and extortion, gays and lesbians are largely unprotected, and turnkeys often encourage prisoners to abuse homosexuals. Police do not register brutality cases against sexual minorities or investigate homophobic motives; officers instead collect personal data, passport details and mugshots of gay people at known cruising areas, as reported by Vstrecha in Brest and Gomel. In September 2008 two transgender men raped in Minsk did not report to police because they were unsure police would help. No youth-specific access-to-care findings are recorded beyond this general pattern of concealment and unavailable support. Blood donation carries no particular limitations for gay and bisexual men; all procedures and requirements are the same for all donors.

In May 2003 the administration of the European Humanities University in Minsk banned a screening of the documentary Outlawed about discrimination of gays and lesbians, with staff saying the ban came under pressure of the Russian Orthodox Church. The April 2026 law bans propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia; in July 2001 the Organising Committee of the 1st Belarusian Youth Congress voted against admitting Lambda Belarus delegates; in March 2002 the youth organization Young Front published homophobic statements, with leader Paval Sieviaryniec calling homosexuality a death-worthy sin and perversion. Opinion among the young is comparatively less hostile but still largely negative: Pew's May 2017 poll found 22% of younger Belarusians favour legal gay marriage against 14% of elders, while a 2007 vote of Gomel region youth found 47.6% had negative feelings toward sexual and gender minorities and 10% wanted to criminalize homosexual relations.

Homosexuality remains highly stigmatized. A May 2017 Pew Research Center survey found 84% of Belarusians believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society and 81% opposed same-sex marriage with only 16% in favour; a 2002 Lambda Belarus survey found 47% of Belarusians think gays should be imprisoned, and many believe homosexuality is a psychiatric illness. Gay life is largely underground, most LGBTQ people hide their orientation in public, and those who are out face harassment, violence and physical abuse. State hostility is codified: the April 2026 law prohibits propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia, compared by critics to Russia's 2013 law, and a 2024 Ministry of Culture decree categorized homosexualism alongside paedophilia and necrophilia as pornography, enabling prosecution under Article 343 of the Criminal Code with up to four years in prison. Pride events from 1999 to 2010 were repeatedly banned, raided or forcibly prevented, no official organization represents gays and lesbians in Belarus with other initiatives working outside the legal framework, and there is no anti-discrimination protection and no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

BLR.blindSummary:
The country presents an acute and documented risk to transgender visitors, and travel there should be avoided. In April 2024 the authorities widened the legal definition of pornography to encompass depictions of same-sex relationships and of transgender people, classing these alongside necrophilia and paedophilia as "non-traditional relationships". Production and distribution carry up to four years' imprisonment, rising to thirteen years for material involving children. An international human rights organisation described the change as an explicit attack on LGBT dignity. The charge attaches to visibility rather than to conduct: a trans person's own image or presence can be treated as pornographic material, and prosecution proceeds under Article 343 of the Criminal Code.

Enforcement followed quickly. In September 2024 a national LGBTQ+ support organisation reported more than fifteen LGBTQ+ people detained within a single month, at least eight of them transgender. Most were charged with hooliganism and two with pornography. Detainees reported physical and psychological abuse in custody, and several left the country afterwards. Rights groups also report police beating LGBTQ+ people during arrests, extracting charges under duress, and expanding repression under "LGBT propaganda" framing.

In April 2026 the country enacted a law banning propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia, which critics have compared to a neighbouring jurisdiction's 2013 statute. The prosecutor general's office has separately announced an administrative-penalty law against "LGBTI propaganda" that has not yet been tabled. A new national security concept adopted by the authorities emphasises "traditional values", and state television has equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and called them "a weapon in the hands of the West"; the support organisation recorded a rise in hate speech across state propaganda during 2024.

Protection machinery is effectively absent. The country has not reported hate-crime data to a regional human-rights monitoring body since 2015 and maintains no national reporting contact, so no official statistics on anti-LGBT violence exist and monitoring rests on civil-society reporting. There is no anti-discrimination protection and no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The country is not a member of the main regional human-rights organisation, so victims cannot appeal to its court.

Entry, status and exit exposure is significant. Sexual orientation and gender identity are not explicitly recognised as grounds for refugee status, and same-sex partners are not recognised for immigration purposes. At least ten transgender people left the country within a single year because of discrimination and repression. Foreigners openly participating in LGBT events have previously been threatened with immediate expulsion under the article on intervention in domestic affairs.

Care access compounds the risk. Qualified psychological help is generally unavailable, no trans-specific facilities are documented, and the psychology faculties of the country's universities do not address the needs of sexual minorities. Suicide rates are high among gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people, and being openly trans exposes a person to harassment, violence and physical abuse in a society where 84 percent of respondents told a polling organisation in May 2017 that homosexuality should not be accepted.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.summary:
Nothing about being trans is criminalised in Ukraine. Legal gender recognition exists, but the procedure is medicalised: the 2016 protocol requires a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation before documents are amended. Against that requirement stands a concrete gain — a Ukrainian court ordered changes to passports and all other documents for two trans people without requiring sterilisation.

Obtaining the diagnosis that unlocks those documents has become harder. ZMINA reported on 28 July 2026 that trans women in Ukraine now face stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers when seeking a diagnosis, and that the difficulty is documentary as much as medical, affecting both the transition procedure and border crossing. Reporting from France 24 in June 2022 already placed Ukraine's trans community in the crosshairs of the war.

Wartime procedure carries the sharpest visitor-facing risk. Gender Stream documents that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service, and the organisation helps with processing or reissuing documents for transgender people, including those planning to cross the border legally. Human Rights Watch reported on 15 May 2024 that cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating Military Medical Commission confirmation; a Ukrainian activist described the commission's 8am to 8pm operating hours and gatekeeping that turns on a single doctor's statement.

Family recognition is now at risk in draft law. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would automatically annul marriages if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, directly targeting trans people's family status. Trans Forum 2026, held in Kyiv in early June 2026, discussed that draft's effect on the transition procedure and whether being trans should ground an exemption from mobilisation.

Protection machinery exists but is thin. Amnesty International reported on 16 May 2013 that Ukraine's government had to legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity amid a pervasive climate of homophobia, and that attacks were routinely used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people the right to expression and peaceful public events. The European Parliament put the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion on the record in written question E-002018/2022 in June 2022.
UKR.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the 2016 protocol's diagnostic requirements remain fully in force once the revised Civil Code draft, submitted on 22 January 2026, is debated or adopted. The inventory records the draft's submission, not its passage, and the Trans Forum discussion of its effect on transition procedure.

Unresolved: whether the State Border Guard Service stops of holders of male gender markers rest on a written order or on practice, and whether those stops continue at their reported frequency. The evidence sourced here is NGO documentation by Gender Stream; no official border directive is in the inventory.

Unresolved: whether being trans provides an exemption from mobilisation. The inventory records this as a question discussed at Trans Forum 2026, with no legislative or administrative outcome sourced.

Not sourced: the current enforcement record for the anti-discrimination and anti-violence protections Amnesty International called for in 2013, and the disposition of the 2012 attack investigation in which Human Rights Watch urged examination of a homophobic motive. The inventory carries those findings as dated reports without later outcomes.

sources.summary:
Ukraine's first LGBTQ rights group, Our World (Nash Svit), was created in 1998 as a community centre and human rights advocacy organization. In 2008, LGBTQ organizations formed the Union of Gay Organizations of Ukraine coalition, and the Gay Alliance of Ukraine was founded in 2009. The source text does not describe trans-specific facilities or shelters. Clause 211 of the Family Code of Ukraine explicitly bans same-sex couples from adopting children, while single Ukrainian citizens of any sexual orientation are permitted to adopt. Lesbian couples have greater parenting access than gay male couples because IVF and assisted insemination treatments are legal. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would automatically annul marriages if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, directly targeting trans people's family recognition. Foreign adopters must be married in a registered different-sex marriage.

Ukraine's path to partner recognition has been long and uneven: a 2015 government action plan promised a civil partnership bill by 2017, but the Ministry of Justice declared in 2018 it could not proceed due to pressure from religious organizations. A civil unions bill was introduced in Parliament in March 2023, and on 14 May 2025 the government's EU accession roadmap (p. 3.11) set a Q3 2025 deadline for a registered partnerships law. On 10 June 2025 the Desnianskyi District Court recognized actual marital relations between two Ukrainian men, the first such ruling in Ukraine, and on 22 January 2026 the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognizing same-sex couples as de facto family. A January 2023 NDI/KIIS poll found 56% of Ukrainians supported civil partnership registration for same-sex couples. A June 2024 KIIS poll found 28.7% supported civil partnerships without adoption, 35.7% opposed and 25.6% indifferent.

A summer 2015 British Council survey found one in five Ukrainian youth would be uncomfortable having lesbian and gay people as friends. Most Ukrainians grew up with little or no comprehensive, fact-based public education about human sexuality, sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap the source says promotes viewing homosexuals as dangerous and as sources of HIV/AIDS. The Ukrainian Council of Churches opposed the Istanbul Convention partly on grounds it could "distort" younger generations' sexual identity, framing anti-LGBTQ policy as youth protection. One source anecdote describes a 19-year-old confined indoors for over a year by parents after they discovered messages to his boyfriend. At a 14 November 2024 meeting with the Ukrainian Students Association, a student representative asked President Zelenskyy whether he would sign registered partnerships legislation and he replied "Yes!"

MDA.name: Moldova
MDA.summary:
Moldova's statutory framework is comparatively strong for the region. Anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes have been criminal offences since 2022 with sexual orientation and gender identity named explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover both grounds. A 2024 legislative analysis by ECOM, benchmarked against international standards and built on a survey of local partner organisations, still identifies gaps affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV in access to justice and in the operation of hate-crime and discrimination provisions.

Enforcement lags the statute. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious problem with no meaningful state response, a finding echoed in the European Commission's country report, and notes that political hate speech rose during the election period. Amnesty International's 2025 reporting states that discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and that freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted, with impunity persisting for past violations.

Document-related discrimination has been adjudicated. In 2023 the Equality Council confirmed that a trans woman had been denied bank service because her documents did not match her appearance, and recommended preventive measures; the case indicates that a mismatch between identity papers and presentation can be raised successfully before a national body, but that the underlying practice persists.

Hostility is measurable in social-distance data cited by GENDERDOC-M from the Equality Council's study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022", published in January 2023: 79% of respondents would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% would not accept them as work colleagues, and marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased during 2022.

Public assembly proceeds, with a documented record of state protection and of state failure. Moldova Pride 2024 in Chisinau was attended by participants of all ages and backgrounds and proceeded openly. In 2018 police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters attempting to disrupt the march in Chisinau, and activists at the time feared a repeat of earlier violent scenes. In 2013 the Balti Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February that the "gay propaganda" ban adopted by the northern city was unconstitutional and violated human rights, striking down church-led local bans introduced after protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.

Detention is the sharpest documented risk. Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man registered female at birth in 1972 whose documents were changed to male in 2007, served a four-year sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit, supposedly for his own safety. His request to be placed in sector 12, the unit for detainees requiring protection, was refused. He describes forced strip searches, gynaecology calls over the intercom, staff opening his bathroom door, and being addressed by a female name at roll-call, and states that only self-harm and hunger strikes caused him to be heard. The case amounts to de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system, prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option. The National Penitentiary Administration replied that he was held alone at his own written request, that no rights were violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. Ziarul de Gardă notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M of the case; Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR.

Reporting from Soroca district in April 2025 corroborates the same case: Brumarețchi, from Dubna village, spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The authorities acknowledged that homophobia persists in state institutions and said they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment.

One part of the country operates under a materially worse regime: in Russian-occupied Transnistria, new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".

LUX.name: Luxembourg
LUX.summary:
Luxembourg's legal gender recognition framework rests on self-determination. The Act of 10 August 2018 replaced the previous long and costly judicial procedure with a declaration-based route to change gender status and first name(s) in the civil register, administered through the official government portal Guichet.lu. The procedure is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Recognition is binary; no nonbinary gender marker is available.

The reform was presented in May 2017 by Justice Minister Félix Braz as a bill allowing trans and intersex people to alter civil status by declaration, and it was welcomed by LGBTI associations at the time. The Chamber of Deputies approved the simplified procedure in July 2018.

Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited in employment, goods and services, education and health, with complaints handled by the CET equality body. Gender expression and sex characteristics are not named as protected grounds. The Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale provides services to LGBTI people in the country and documents this framework in its human-rights reporting.

A national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018. In July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, which organisations criticised for omitting depathologisation and other elements they consider essential.

As of 2019 reporting, Luxembourgian criminal law lacked aggravating circumstances for LGBTphobic assault, and under-reporting by victims was documented. The justice minister signalled that the law would evolve following the 2017 intervention of a European anti-discrimination monitoring body.

Prison policy is protective rather than punitive. The prison administration places detainees who disclose or openly show LGBT or trans identity so that they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations assessed case by case on the information gathered about the individual; such placements are described as exceptional. Requests by LGBT detainees to be housed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the Justice Ministry has warned against measures that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff additionally honour a detainee's chosen form of address. The planned Uerschterhaff prison at Sanem was designed with multiple sections allowing separation by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, within those, sexual orientation. Placement therefore follows disclosed identity and need with no codified birth-sex rule, no documented special custody unit, and no solitary or administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners.

Marriage and adoption are available to same-sex couples. The country has no measures addressing conversion practices, and no measures regulating intersex medical interventions.
LUX.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2019 press report on the absence of LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances is the most recent hate-crime item in the available sources. Whether the promised aggravating circumstances were subsequently enacted is unresolved and not sourced here.

No source in the inventory documents a trans-specific violent incident in Luxembourg, its investigation, or its outcome; the violence picture rests on the under-reporting finding and on prison-placement policy rather than on case records.

The claim that no special custody unit or segregation practice exists for trans prisoners derives from a 2015 ministerial answer; whether this remains the case in the current prison estate, including the Uerschterhaff facility once opened, is not sourced.

Enforcement data for the discrimination prohibitions, including complaint volumes and outcomes before the CET, is not available in the inventory.

AND.name: Andorra
AND.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Andorra rests on the Law of the Person and Family of 21 July 2022, which allows trans people to update name and gender on legal documents through a simple process requiring no medical intervention. The same legislation unified civil marriage, so a trans visitor's marital status is recognised under the same regime as everyone else's.

Statutory non-discrimination protection covers gender identity and expression. Law 13/2019 of 15 February 2019 bars discrimination on grounds including gender identity and expression across employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments, and extends that protection specifically to education settings. Bias-motivated offences attract additional penalties. Law 14/2019 of 15 February 2019 on the rights of children and adolescents establishes that transgender children must be respected in their gender identity.

Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month during 2025. The association DiversAnd flagged further incidents across the June Pride celebrations and has called for a formal system to register and classify bias-motivated violence, so that such acts can be recognised and prosecuted as hate crime. No such registration system was in place during the year.

Access to gender-affirming care is a live question. In August 2023 DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health to press for protocols covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, and in some cases for 14-year-olds, following regulatory changes made in 2022. The sources in hand do not establish whether those protocols have since been issued, so a visitor seeking continuing care should confirm arrangements in advance.

Hostile media output occurs and is contested. A transphobic opinion piece in El Periòdic d'Andorra on 27 September 2023 was removed online with a public apology after DiversAnd requested it, though the piece had already run in print.

Public LGBT expression is lawful and has a visible history. The first LGBT demonstration was held on 6 September 2002 and the first gay pride parade followed on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som; DiversAnd was formed in 2019 after Som Com Som ended its work in 2018 and organised a pride parade that June.
AND.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether gender-affirming care protocols covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16- and 14-year-olds were actually adopted after the August 2023 meeting with the Ministry of Health is unresolved in the sources held here.

The formal system for registering and classify bias-motivated violence that DiversAnd called for in 2025 is not recorded as established; equally, the police figure of two to three bias-motivated incidents per month is not broken down by the type of bias involved, so the share attributable to trans victims is not sourced.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa screening, border questions about gender markers, or any risk of involuntary disclosure during immigration processing for Andorra; the Schengen-adjacent arrangements that would govern this are not covered by the materials assembled.

Nothing here is sourced on facilities access, health-care treatment of trans visitors, or recognition of foreign gender documents for short-term stays. GayLawNet's page on Andorra carries a 'limited information' flag, which limits its value for verification.

sources.summary: Andorra protects public LGBT expression and has a visible history: the first LGBT demonstration was held on 6 September 2002, and the first gay pride parade followed on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som. The LGBT group DiversAnd was formed in 2019, after Som Com Som ended its work in 2018, and organised a pride parade in June 2019; on 17 May 2019 the Department of Equality launched the short film "#lovingdiversity" to raise online awareness. Expression-related bias is penalised: hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation carry additional legal penalties, and Law 13/2019 of 15 February 2019 bars discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression across employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments. Law 14/2019 of 15 February 2019 on the rights of children and adolescents establishes that transgender children must be respected in their gender identity, and Law 13/2019 extends non-discrimination protection, including gender identity and expression, to education settings. The age of consent is 16 for both same-sex and heterosexual relationships under Penal Code Articles 162 and 163, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the prohibiting law was abolished in 1791. Preventing and addressing bullying and discrimination in schools is a stated focus of DiversAnd. Risks to LGBT youth are documented: in 2000 a 17-year-old gay man, Nuno Ribeiro, was murdered in the country because of his sexual orientation, prompting public outcry, and cases of parents expelling their children from home over their sexual orientation are also reported. Since the 2014 civil union law, adoption has been open to same-sex couples, and the Family Law passed 21 July 2022 lets trans people update name and gender on legal documents via a simple process without medical intervention. In September 2023 Prime Minister Xavier Espot Zamora publicly came out as homosexual.

MCO.name: Monaco
MCO.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has been legal in Monaco since the 18th century, and the age of consent is 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships alike. Hate-motivated conduct on the basis of sexual orientation is criminalised across several statutes. Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence on that ground.

Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 inserted sexual orientation into Civil Code articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (five years).

A Monegasque court applied this framework in July 2010, sentencing a man to five days' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. It is the only documented prosecution in the sources.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned by law; Outright International reports such discrimination as rare but describes protections as very limited. Monaco does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune, a cohabitation agreement signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry.

Transgender people cannot alter their legal gender in Monaco. LGBTIQ visibility is limited: roughly ten people are reported to dare to be openly out, no gay Pride is held anywhere in the principality, and there are no official gay bars, clubs or events. Visitors are directed to France or Italy for Pride.

Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it maintains close cultural and economic ties with France. France handles defence, and its armed forces allow openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve; Monaco itself maintains only a National Guard.
MCO.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports a prosecution under Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 or under Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019, so enforcement of those provisions beyond the July 2010 case is unresolved.

No source addresses entry, visa or border-screening practice, customs questioning, or the treatment of gender markers on foreign passports at Monegasque borders. Nothing in the inventory indicates whether a visitor's documents are inspected for sex or gender inconsistencies.

Facilities, healthcare access, and any rule on restroom or single-sex-space use for transgender visitors are not sourced here. Neither are hate-crime statistics, police reporting practices, or the operation of the protection machinery for LGBTIQ visitors.

Outright International's characterisation of discrimination as rare is self-reported and carries no underlying data in the inventory; the absence of a statutory ban means official statistics on complaints cannot exist.

The July 2010 judgment is described only in secondary coverage; the court, the exact provision applied and any appeal outcome are not available from these sources.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

The 2023 US State Department Human Rights Report recorded no significant changes for Monaco and limited its significant issues to libel and lèse-majesté laws, which it described as not enforced; no torture, arbitrary detention or similar abuses were reported.

Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which treats homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. SMR.name: San Marino
SMR.summary:
San Marino decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 1864. A residual provision, Article 274 of the Criminal Code, punished habitual homosexual acts causing public scandal with three months to one year of imprisonment; it was repealed in September 2004 and was never reported as applied. No criminal penalty attaches to gender identity, and no statute regulates which bathrooms or facilities a person may use.

Entry carries no documented friction. The border with Italy is open, and no identity screening that risks outing an arriving visitor is recorded.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The 2026 edition of the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map lists San Marino among the countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for changing a gender marker. The consequence falls on residents rather than travellers: a visitor's foreign documents govern throughout a stay, and no domestic procedure exists that could alter them.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited in primary law. A referendum held on 2 June 2019 carried with 71.46% in favour, inserting a prohibition on sexual-orientation discrimination into Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights. The Penal Code has outlawed discrimination and hate speech on sexual-orientation grounds since 3 May 2008 and provides penalty enhancements for hate crimes so motivated. In November 2019 San Marino accepted Universal Periodic Review recommendations to outlaw discrimination based on gender identity, the only protection machinery in the sources that speaks to trans people directly.

There are occasionally reports of violence and hate crimes against the LGBTI community. No pattern of anti-trans violence is documented in this small, tourism-dependent country.

Civil unions have been in force since 5 December 2018 and fully operational since 11 February 2019, granting couples rights over residency and citizenship, pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption. Sammarinese same-sex couples remain barred from marriage. A December 2017 budget-law amendment permitted foreign same-sex couples to marry in San Marino to encourage tourism, but as of 2024 the implementing legislation does not appear to have been drafted, so a visitor should not expect to complete a marriage here.
SMR.outOfScopeNotes:
The Legal Gender Recognition chapter of the ILGA Annual Review 2026, which sets out country-by-country findings for 2025, does not carry a San Marino entry; the documented cases in that chapter concern Albania's rejection of a self-ID recommendation at UPR, trans activist Luana Myrto's legal action in Albania, and Andorra's delayed hormone-treatment decree. Whether any Sammarinese development occurred in 2025 is therefore unresolved on these sources.

The scope of the gender-identity discrimination prohibition accepted at UPR in November 2019, and whether it has since been enacted in statute, is not sourced here.

No source in this inventory reports trans-specific violence, its perpetrators, or outcomes of prosecutions; the references to occasional violence and hate crimes concern the LGBTI community generally and are undated.

Whether the December 2017 amendment permitting foreign same-sex couples to marry has acquired implementing legislation after 2024 is unresolved. The absence of any statute on bathroom or facility access is stated as an absence of regulation, not as a judicial or administrative ruling on the point.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
San Marino decriminalised homosexuality in 1864. Article 274 of the Criminal Code, which had punished 'habitual' homosexual acts causing public scandal with 3 months to 1 year imprisonment, was repealed in September 2004 and was never reported as applied. In 2008 the Grand and General Council amended the Penal Code to outlaw discrimination and hate speech based on sexual orientation, effective 3 May 2008, with penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation.

Civil unions, in force 5 December 2018 and fully operational from 11 February 2019, grant same-sex and opposite-sex couples rights with respect to residency and citizenship as well as pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and Sammarinese same-sex couples are still banned from marrying. No other custody-specific provisions are recorded. In December 2017 the Grand and General Council approved a budget-law amendment allowing foreign same-sex couples to marry in San Marino to encourage tourism, but as of 2024 the implementing legislation does not appear to have been drafted. Gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned under 2019 constitutional amendments, and the Penal Code provides penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation was added to Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights after a 2 June 2019 referendum passed with 71.46% in favour; the March 2019 council vote fell short at 35 for, 8 against, 1 abstention, needing 39. There are occasionally reports of violence and hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. In November 2019 San Marino accepted UPR recommendations to outlaw gender identity discrimination.

The age of consent is 14 for both opposite-sex and same-sex sexual acts, and it is an offence to incite a minor under 18 to sexual corruption. San Marino's sex education programme, together with emotional education programmes, expressly provides for knowledge of LGBTQ rights, and the 'Curriculum of education to citizenship' also covers LGBTQ matters. Until recently LGBTQ people in San Marino went unnoticed, with very few public debates in media, society or politics, and in the early 2000s the government rejected LGBTQ groups' request to recognise 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. In 2022 Paolo Rondelli's election as Captain Regent made San Marino the first country in modern history with an openly homosexual head of state.

SMR.blindSummary:
The state is workable for trans visitors: safe in practice, thin in law. Consensual same-sex relations were decriminalised in 2004, no legal penalty attaches to gender identity, and no statute regulates which bathrooms or facilities a person may use. No pattern of anti-trans violence is documented in this small, tourism-dependent country, and entry carries no documented friction — the border with the surrounding country is open, with no recorded identity screening that risks outing an arriving visitor.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The 2026 edition of an international equality index lists the state among the countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for changing gender markers. The consequence falls on residents rather than travellers: a visitor's foreign documents govern throughout, and there is no domestic procedure that could alter them during a stay.

Constitutional anti-discrimination protection is anchored in sexual orientation. In a referendum held on 4 June 2019, citizens approved inserting a clause prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation into the constitution. The sources assembled here do not record a parallel clause covering gender identity or gender expression.

Relationship recognition is in place. The legislature approved a civil-union law in November 2018, reported at the time as leaner than the neighbouring country's equivalent statute, and legal recognition of gay couples is dated to 2016 in other reporting. Partner recognition therefore exists, though it is framed for same-sex couples rather than as a trans-specific protection.

The state has engaged international protection machinery. It was one of twelve states examined at the 34th session of an universal periodic review working group in November 2019, and an international LGBTI organisation has compiled the SOGIESC recommendations put to each state/province examined in that round, including this one, together with the responses. The individual recommendations are not reproduced in the material available here.

The overall picture for a visitor is very high de facto safety with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people. No legal exposure is documented for a traveller, and the gaps identified — the absent gender-recognition process and the orientation-only constitutional clause — are resident-facing rather than border-facing.

Unresolved: the dating of relationship recognition. One source places legal recognition of gay couples in 2016, another records legislative approval of the civil-union law in November 2018; whether these mark different stages of the same reform is not settled by the material available.

Not sourced: any data on enforcement of the constitutional clause, on hate-crime offences motivated by gender identity, or on access to trans-specific healthcare for short-term visitors. The absence of documented anti-trans violence reflects an absence of reporting rather than a verified count.

LIE.name: Liechtenstein
LIE.summary:
Same-sex relations are legal in Liechtenstein, and the country's anti-discrimination framework prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not covered by any anti-discrimination statute in force. No procedure exists for changing a legal gender marker in official documents, and no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities. Medical interventions on the genitals of intersex children are not prohibited by law.

Civil marriage and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since January 2025. The Landtag's motion of September 2022, 'Motion zur Öffnung der Ehe für alle', sought to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation and to remove the remaining legal differences, noting that registered partnerships were perceived as a second-class marriage. The motion also recorded that Prince Hans-Adam II had stated in 2021 that he had nothing against marriage equality other than adoption.

Official hostility is a live factor. In his New Year interview of January 2016 Prince Hans-Adam II called rainbow families 'irresponsible', asserted that children have 'a right to a normal family', and suggested that Liechtenstein could 'ignore' an adverse ruling of the European Court of Human Rights; the local LGBT organisation Flay responded that it was 'choqué' and the Freie Liste called the remarks contrary to the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. The state religion is Roman Catholicism, and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality.

Entry falls under the common border-free travel zone operated with Switzerland and Austria, and no source reports friction at that border for trans travellers. There is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in the country. Liechtenstein is very small, has very low crime, and is closely integrated with both neighbouring states; the first Pride was held in 2022.
LIE.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how border officers, document checks or security screening treat a traveller whose presentation does not match the marker in their passport; the absence of reported friction at the Swiss and Austrian borders is an absence of evidence, not a sourced assurance.

The inventory contains no information on legal gender recognition in neighbouring Switzerland or Austria, nor on how a Liechtenstein-issued document without a marker change would be read by either state.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, its cost, waiting times and the availability of prescribing clinicians, is not sourced here; nor is any provision on name change independent of a gender marker change.

The Reuters feature on small European states and LGBT equality returned HTTP 401 at research time, so its claims about Liechtenstein could not be verified.

VAT.name: Vatican City
VAT.summary:
Vatican City presents essentially no criminal-law exposure to a trans visitor. No documented criminal-law persecution of consensual homosexual conduct has occurred in the territory in modern times, and decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots. Nothing about being trans is criminalised.

No legal recognition of gender exists in Vatican City. No anti-discrimination protection, facilities rule, or document-amendment mechanism covers a visitor or a resident.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It holds only a few cells for pre-trial detention, and anyone sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serves the term in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. Because no domestic prison system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented trans-prisoner placement case for this jurisdiction.

The Holy See's institutional posture against homosexuality and gender theory drives policy even where the city-state's own law imposes nothing. The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document, Male and Female He Created Them, opposes what it calls gender theory, stating that it "denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman" and "eliminates the anthropological basis of the family." The legal baseline for a visitor is the city-state's own law, which is distinct from the Church's diplomatic and doctrinal positions.
VAT.outOfScopeNotes:
No separate United States State Department Holy See chapter for 2023 or 2024 was available for this record; parts of the assessment rest on last-resort encyclopedic sources, and the historical and prison-capacity claims are not corroborated by a primary government travel advisory.

No source in the inventory addresses gender markers on passports or identity documents, border or entry screening, restroom access, or access to gender-affirming care for a visitor. Whether any of these are governed by Italian practice at the point of entry is unresolved rather than established here.

No documented trans-specific prisoner placement case was found for this jurisdiction. The absence of documentation is not evidence that a policy exists or that none does; it is unresolved.

The 2008 diplomatic rejection is reported by a single outlet in the inventory and was not independently corroborated within this pass.

Whether any of these are governed by practice in a neighbouring jurisdiction at the point of entry is unresolved rather than established here.

No documented trans-specific prisoner placement case was found for this jurisdiction. The absence of documentation is not evidence that a policy exists or that none does; it is unresolved.

The 2008 diplomatic rejection is reported by a single outlet in the inventory and was not independently corroborated within this pass.
blindSourceSummaries: The nation operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment by the nation serve their time in another nation's prisons with costs covered by the nation; there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case. The sole prison-axis source is a general reference article on crime in the nation, used as a last resort.

The 2024 declaration condemned gender-affirming surgery and 'gender theory' as violations of human dignity; no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists; an educational document (2019) opposes 'gender theory' as denying natural difference.

A 2023 declaration permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage, with a January 2024 clarification reiterating that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Entry is via a neighbouring city with no border formality; the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression, there are no bathroom inspections and no morality police, and nothing about being trans is criminalised. No source addresses document checks or screening for visitors beyond the recorded absence of border formality.
VAT.tangentialFactors:
In 2008 Catholic officials rejected France's first-choice candidate as ambassador to the Holy See because he is gay, forcing Paris to name a different envoy. It is a documented instance of the Vatican government refusing an LGBT person in diplomatic relations, and it indicates the institutional climate a visibly LGBT person may encounter around the Holy See's own organs rather than any rule applied to visitors.

The current Holy See posture on blessing same-sex couples is set by the DDF declaration Fiducia Supplicans, issued under Pope Francis on 20 March 2023, which permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 DDF press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Both items concern sexual orientation and institutional diplomacy more directly than they concern trans visitors, but they establish the direction of official policy in a territory where doctrine and government are held by the same institution.

Residents of Vatican City have no mechanism to amend gender markers on identity documents, no route to legal recognition of gender, and no anti-discrimination remedy on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. CYP.name: Cyprus
CYP.summary:
Cyprus presents low legal risk to a trans visitor. There is no restriction on gender presentation, no facility or bathroom statute of the kind enacted elsewhere in the region, and no entry obstacle beyond the standard rules applying to any visitor arriving in an European Union member state. Tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to international arrivals.

The criminal law carries explicit gender-identity provisions. The Penal Code was amended in October 2013 to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment and/or a fine of €5,000; Law 87(I)/2015 extended this into a public hate-speech offence. Law 31(I)/2017 provides that prejudice-based motivation operates as an aggravating factor in sentencing. Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices.

Legal gender recognition remains unfinished. A gender-recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and received its first parliamentary reading in November 2022; it was still pending as of 2024. The reform had been promised earlier: in its 2019 universal periodic review national report, Cyprus stated that legislation to correct registered sex for adults and minors was in preparation, requiring only a Registrar's decision with no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports. Cyprus accepted all eight SOGIESC recommendations put to it at the 32nd UPR working group session in January 2019.

Gender identity is still absent from the statutory list of equal-treatment grounds, and no anti-homophobia action plan exists. The European Commission Network of Legal Experts country reports on non-discrimination (2020) and gender equality (2024) document how the EU equality directives are transposed into Cypriot law, including gender-identity-related aspects of the framework. ECRI has urged that gender identity be added as a prohibited discrimination ground. Workplace protections on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds date from 2004.

Prison conditions have drawn official attention: after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints were lodged with the Ombudswoman, prison guards received two days of LGBTI+ training in April 2023.

On the divided island, Queer Cyprus Association documents a gender-recognition framework built on self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping, and states that the northern part of Cyprus runs its own recognition process that explicitly includes recognition of non-binary identities. Queer Cyprus also operates a confidential psychosocial and legal support line seven days a week, covering identity, work, family, shelter, health and military-service issues. The organisation's UPR submission frames trans and gender-diverse rights as its first-order issue, recording that the hate-speech law was delivered while a gender-identity discrimination ground and trans-specific legislation were not. Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition as its 40th member in August 2018.
CYP.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the gender-recognition bill approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources, which stop at 2024. The current status of the statute should be verified against the legislature's own record before it is relied on.

The relationship between the self-determination recognition framework described in the Queer Cyprus booklet and the pending bill is not sourced. It is unclear whether the booklet describes existing administrative practice, a draft standard, or practice in the northern part only.

No enforcement data is available for the 2013/2015 incitement offence or the 2017 aggravating-factor provision: no case counts, charges or outcomes appear in the inventory. Whether the hate-crime provisions have been applied in reported incidents of anti-trans violence is not sourced.

The legal status and recognition practice of the northern part of Cyprus is described only from an advocacy source; the institutional basis of that recognition process, and whether its decisions are accepted for travel or civil purposes in the south, is not documented here.

There is no sourced information on post-2023 prison conditions, on the content and duration of the guard training beyond its two-day length, or on whether the Ombudswoman's complaints resulted in disciplinary findings.

CYP.tangentialFactors:
The pattern in Cyprus mirrors a wider regional sequence in which hate-speech offences land first and gender-identity recognition follows years later. Cyprus criminalised bias-motivated incitement in 2013 and aggravated sentencing in 2017, while the recognition statute promised to the UN peer-review process in 2019 was still before parliament in 2024.

Two European monitoring tracks run alongside the domestic record. The European Commission Network of Legal Experts publishes periodic country reports on non-discrimination and gender equality that track transposition of the EU equality directives, and ECRI has pressed for gender identity as a prohibited discrimination ground. Both sit outside the Cypriot legislature's direct control, so progress depends on domestic enactment rather than on the monitoring alone.

Advocacy documentation is unusually specific for this jurisdiction. Queer Cyprus Association and UPR-info publish itemised inventories of which commitments were met and which were not, which makes the gap between the delivered hate-speech provisions and the undelivered recognition and discrimination provisions unusually easy to date.

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity has never been criminalised in Cambodia; the country inherited no sodomy statute under the French protectorate and none was enacted after independence in 1953. The age of consent is 15 and applies regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans visitors have no route to legal recognition. Cambodian law does not permit changes to gender markers on official documents, and gender-affirming surgery is not legally available. The statutory framework contains no non-discrimination provisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

The state's formal posture is cooperative. At the 2019 Universal Periodic Review Cambodia accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage; at the 2024 review it accepted all 12 recommendations on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, covering marriage equality, legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures. The inventory contains no evidence that implementing legislation has been enacted. Cambodia also hosted the visit of the UN Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose report identified good practices, remaining challenges and recommendations to strengthen protection; an unofficial Khmer translation was produced for national stakeholders.

Lived conditions diverge sharply from that posture. A Cambodian Centre for Human Rights study documented harassment and abuse against more than 135 transgender women on the country's city streets, describing the level of abuse as shocking. It recorded a practice in Siem Reap in which police targeted transgender sex workers and forced them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water, sometimes naked, and to leave the area; cisgender sex workers were not documented as receiving the same treatment. The same 2016 study found about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested, with more than 90% of them stating the arrest was because they were transgender.

Family rejection is a principal exposure. A Rainbow Community Kampuchea study reported in 2019 found 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 had suffered emotional abuse by a family member, and 35% of participants under 35 had considered suicide because of family rejection, including a 27-year-old trans man forced by his mother into rehabilitation to 'fix his gender'.

Prison placement is decided administratively rather than by statute. In February 2025 the president of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee stated at a public handover ceremony that transgender offenders who had undergone sex-change surgery were transferred from Correctional Centre 1, the men's facility, to Correctional Centre 2, the women's facility at Prey Sar prison in Phnom Penh. The statement was made in praise of the centre and cites no published regulation or policy text.

Public visibility is real but concentrated. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have a visible LGBT bar and club scene, and Pride parades have run annually since 2003, with the first Siem Reap Pride in 2018. In 2017 the US State Department listed violence against LGBTI persons among Cambodia's most significant human rights issues, noting frequent harassment over appearance and work in entertainment and commercial sex sectors, with more than 100 incidents of violence or abuse reported by a local LGBTI organisation, while finding no official discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, citizenship, education or health care.
KHM.outOfScopeNotes:
The relationship between the accepted 2024 Universal Periodic Review recommendations and domestic legislation is unresolved in the inventory. Acceptance is recorded as a stated commitment; no source in the inventory confirms that implementing statutes on marriage equality, legal gender recognition or non-discrimination have been enacted, and the record states only the current absence of such provisions.

The February 2025 account of transferring post-surgical transgender prisoners between Correctional Centre 1 and Correctional Centre 2 rests on an official's remarks at an event. No statute, sub-decree or published regulation establishing this practice is cited, and it is unresolved whether the arrangement is written policy, an informal practice, or case-by-case.

A 2014 UNDP and USAID review of the legal and social environment for LGBT people in Cambodia, and a Frommer's travel guide section offering practical advice for gay and lesbian travellers, are in the inventory but were not relied on for specific legal or safety findings beyond their general scope.

sources.title: CHRC says transgender rights are observed in prison
sources.summary: Khmer Times (19 Feb 2025) reports Cambodian Human Rights Committee president Keo Remy saying, at the handover of an ambulance to Correctional Centre 2 at Prey Sar prison in Phnom Penh, that Cambodia observes transgender prisoners' rights: transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from Correctional Centre 1, the men's facility, to Correctional Centre 2, the women's facility. sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have a visible LGBT scene with bars and clubs catering to the community, and Pride parades have run annually since 2003 (first Siem Reap Pride in 2018). In February 2011 Cambodian tourism businesses launched a global 'Adore Cambodia!' campaign to signal welcome to LGBT tourists, which the Ministry of Tourism endorsed ('We have no policy to discriminate... We really support them'); a 2010 report described a concentration of poor and working-class LGBT people in Beoung Kak 2, dubbed 'Cambodia's first gay town'. Access to services is uneven: Cambodian law does not allow gender marker changes or gender-affirming surgeries, and trans sex workers in Siem Reap reported being forced to bathe in dirty river water, sometimes naked, and to leave the area, while cisgender sex workers were not documented as receiving the same treatment. State posture is officially non-hostile: the Ministry of Information sent a 2015 letter to media outlets asking them to stop mocking the LGBT community, citing the Constitution's protection of LGBT honour and rights, and in 2015 a Council of Ministers spokesman claimed existing law already protected LGBT people, a claim the Cambodian Center for Human Rights disputed. Hostility persists at official and societal level: Prime Minister Hun Sen publicly disowned and disinherited his adopted daughter in 2007 because she is a lesbian, and a 2016 CCHR report found about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested, with over 90% saying it was because they were transgender. The 2017 US State Department report listed violence against LGBTI persons among Cambodia's most significant human rights issues, noting LGBTI people were frequently harassed and bullied over their appearance and their work in entertainment and commercial sex sectors, with more than 100 incidents of violence or abuse reported by a local LGBTI organization; the same report noted increased government restrictions on speech, assembly and press freedom, while finding no official discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, citizenship, education or health care. In June 2017 the Khmer Government announced new life-skills courses covering sexual health, gender-based violence, gender identity and combating discrimination against the LGBT population, which became part of the curriculum in all Cambodian schools in 2018; before that rollout, LGBT activists working with the Ministry of Education trained more than 3,000 teachers in 20 schools across nine Cambodian provinces. Many LGBT Cambodians report bullying at school, and in January 2019 Cambodia received UN recommendations from Iceland, Mexico, Sweden and Uruguay to establish educational programmes and campaigns raising awareness of LGBT people and discrimination. The age of consent is 15 regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation, and in 2019 the director of the Cambodia Human Rights Committee reported rising HIV infections within the LGBT community, especially among people under 30.

In 2017 a foreign government's human rights reporting listed violence against LGBTI persons among the country's most significant human rights issues, noting frequent harassment over appearance and work in entertainment and commercial sex sectors, with more than 100 incidents of violence or abuse reported by a local LGBTI organisation, while finding no official discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, citizenship, education or health care.
KHM.blindOutOfScope:
The relationship between the accepted 2024 Universal Periodic Review recommendations and domestic legislation is unresolved in the inventory. Acceptance is recorded as a stated commitment; no source in the inventory confirms that implementing statutes on marriage equality, legal gender recognition or non-discrimination have been enacted, and the record states only the current absence of such provisions.

The February 2025 account of transferring post-surgical transgender prisoners between the men's and women's facilities rests on an official's remarks at an event. No statute, sub-decree or published regulation establishing this practice is cited, and it is unresolved whether the arrangement is written policy, an informal practice, or case-by-case.

A 2014 international development agency review of the legal and social environment for LGBT people in the country, and a commercial travel guide section offering practical advice for gay and lesbian travellers, are in the inventory but were not relied on for specific legal or safety findings beyond their general scope.
blindSourceSummaries: The country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression; the government accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 periodic human-rights review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted an independent international expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2023.
A human-rights organisation documents 'shocking' harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse).

The only placement finding is a February 2025 statement by the president of the national human-rights committee, made in praise of a women's correctional centre, that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility to the women's facility — a surgery-gated practice with no statute or formal policy text cited; nothing is documented on placement for trans prisoners who have not had surgery.

The same report flags that prison overcrowding has worsened because of gang-crackdown arrests; no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is on record, the placement statement is a human-rights-committee president's remark rather than a published regulation, and practice at other facilities is unverifiable here.
KHM.blindLocalsOnly:
Education policy was reworked toward LGBT inclusion. In June 2017 the government announced new life-skills courses covering sexual health, gender-based violence, gender identity and combating discrimination against the LGBT population; these became part of the curriculum in all schools nationally in 2018. Before the rollout, LGBT activists working with the education ministry trained more than 3,000 teachers in 20 schools across nine provinces. Many LGBT people in the country nonetheless report bullying at school, and in January 2019 the country received UN recommendations from four other governments to establish educational programmes and awareness campaigns on LGBT people and discrimination.

In 2019 the director of the national human rights committee reported rising HIV infections within the LGBT community, particularly among people under 30. A 2010 report described a concentration of poor and working-class LGBT people in one urban neighbourhood, which was dubbed the country's first gay town. Prison overcrowding has worsened because of arrests following a gang crackdown.
KHM.tangentialFactors:
A pattern of official welcome messaging exists alongside the enforcement record. In February 2011 Cambodian tourism businesses launched the 'Adore Cambodia!' campaign to signal welcome to LGBT tourists, and the Ministry of Tourism endorsed it, stating it had no policy to discriminate and supported the sector. In 2015 the Ministry of Information wrote to media outlets asking them to stop mocking the LGBT community, citing constitutional protection of LGBT honour and rights.

Statements by officials on the reach of existing law have been contested domestically. In 2015 a Council of Ministers spokesman claimed that existing law already protected LGBT people; the Cambodian Center for Human Rights disputed the claim. The 2017 State Department reporting also noted increased government restrictions on speech, assembly and press freedom in the country generally.

Official hostility at the highest level has been recorded: in 2007 Prime Minister Hun Sen publicly disowned and disinherited his adopted daughter because she is a lesbian.

NPL.name: Nepal
NPL.summary:
Nepal criminalises no conduct on the basis of gender identity or gender expression. Same-sex acts have been legal since the Supreme Court's December 2007 judgment in Sunil Babu Pant v. Nepal Government, which held that homosexuality is not 'unnatural'. The Criminal Codes Act 2017, which replaced the 1963 Muluki Ain, still lists 'unnatural sex' on its face and must be read in light of that ruling; the former Muluki Ain criminalised 'unnatural sexual intercourse' with up to one year's imprisonment, and LGBTQI+ Nepalis were arrested under it. The age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition rests on the 2007 Supreme Court ruling recognising the right to self-determined name and gender markers, and a third-gender category has been available on official documents by self-declaration. In August 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed more than 50 lawsuits from 2021 onward. Before that ruling, changing a marker to female or male had usually required surgery performed outside the country followed by in-country medical evaluations, including intrusive post-operative genital examinations.

The documentary pathway remained unclear at the level of ordinary administration. In February 2024 Human Rights Watch called on the government to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure for transgender and third-gender people to obtain official documents, indicating that no straightforward document-change process existed at that date. Reporting in February 2024 separately documented that officials limited marker changes to people identifying as 'third gender', while changes to male and female markers lagged behind the country's progressive reputation.

Visibly trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are frequently subjected to physical and sexual harassment, including in provincial cities such as Janakpur, according to reporting from November 2024. LGBT children encounter discrimination at school and leave education because of threats, bullying and neglect by fellow students and teachers, and trans Nepalis face severe gender-based violence and interrupted education, particularly in rural areas.

Partner recognition is partial and contested. On 28 June 2023 Justice Til Prasad Shrestha issued an interim order directing the government to 'temporarily register' marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities, and the full bench has yet to deliver a final verdict. In April 2024 the National ID and Civil Registration Department instructed local authorities to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register. Temporary registration confers no equal rights: same-sex couples cannot inherit property, receive tax subsidies, make spousal medical decisions or adopt children, and certificates label them 'groom and bride'. The first marriage of a trans woman and a cisgender man took place in November 2023, and as of June 2025 the Blue Diamond Society counted at least 17 documented queer marriages. Implementation is inconsistent: the Kathmandu District Court rejected a registration in July 2023, and compliance by local governments is unknown. Suman Pant's Supreme Court case set a precedent for same-sex spousal visas.

Gender-affirming care is newly established and thin. The first gender-affirming surgery in Nepal was performed in June 2025 at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, which has since established a Gender Affirming Clinic. Hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery remain hard to reach: a six-month hormone supply costs 4,500 rupees, providers are few, and many trans Nepalis take hormones without medical supervision because of stigma; some travel to India and Thailand for surgery. Conversion therapy is practised, including treatment in rehabilitation centres and traditional exorcism by family members, and lesbian couples are denied IVF.

Official hostility has surfaced alongside the protective rulings. On 30 October 2024 the Aamul Paribartan Nagarik Party held a protest rally opposing homosexuality and LGBTQ rights, and Mitini Nepal's executive director stated that anti-LGBTQ sentiments are gaining momentum in Nepal and South Asia. In April 2026 newly elected Prime Minister Balen Shah faced LGBTQ community criticism over a YouTube rap video containing derogatory and homophobic hate speech; after demands for an apology, his supporters markedly increased derogatory comments, hate speech and death threats against the community. The Communist Party of Nepal-Maoist made homophobic statements during the Civil War, describing homosexuality as 'a production of capitalism' and LGBT people as 'social pollutants'.

Two protective measures are on record but not verified as implemented: UNDP has recommended that transgender and intersex students be given access to safe toilets and bathroom facilities, and the Education Board has implemented information about sexual and gender diversity in the curriculum for grades 7–9 (ages 13–15), making Nepal the second Asian country after Mongolia to do so, with universities offering courses on LGBT issues.
NPL.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening rules for trans travellers, including whether passport or citizenship markers are checked on arrival. That layer is not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved rather than as absent.

Whether the August 2024 Supreme Court ruling in Rukshana Kapali's favour has been generalised into a standing administrative procedure for other applicants is not established by these sources; the February 2024 Human Rights Watch statement describes the position before that ruling, and no post-ruling assessment of routine practice is available.

The final verdict of the full bench on same-sex marriage registration remains pending, and compliance by local governments with the April 2024 instruction to maintain a separate register is unknown. Whether the temporary registration framework recognises marriages involving a trans spouse on the same terms as other couples is not sourced.

No source addresses hate-crime legislation covering gender identity or expression, the legality of conversion therapy, conditions of detention for trans people, or access to identification documents for non-citizens. These are unresolved, not confirmed absent.

The April 2026 account of Prime Minister Balen Shah's video and the subsequent online abuse rests on community criticism and reporting of that criticism; no official response or investigation is documented in this inventory.

For this record: official-observer statement on the documentary-recognition gap.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021; changing markers to 'female'/'male' has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams. For this record: the landmark ruling and the pre-ruling barrier path, dated.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns policy. For this record: documented doctrine-versus-implementation gap.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024) on trans life in Janakpur: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. For this record: ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities, dated 2024.

APTN (Asia Pacific Transgender Network) publication (Oct 2021, in Nepali): 'Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078: Civil Society Proposal' - by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi, produced through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship; a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition in Nepal.

The Record (Sept 25, 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: argues that despite the Constitution awarding the right to self-determine name and gender markers (2007 case), 'an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law' is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community. For this record: local-activist assessment of the gap between constitutional right and statute.

SIT Study Abroad ISP (Spring 2015) by Sophia Greene: 'Gender and Sexuality in Nepal: The Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minorities in a Rapidly Changing Social Climate' - despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.
