LKA.name: Sri Lanka
LKA.summary:
Sri Lanka criminalises same-sex activity under Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code. Section 365 covers "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and was applied to men; Section 365A covers "gross indecency" and was amended in 1995 to reach women as well, so both provisions now apply to men and women. The maximum penalty is ten years' imprisonment. Where an offence under these sections is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16, the aggravated penalty rises to ten to twenty years' rigorous imprisonment.

Formal prosecutions are rare. The Canada Immigration and Refugee Board's January 2012 research found no convictions under the articles, and Outright International's March 2026 overview describes prosecutions as limited. The provisions nonetheless structure everyday policing: the US State Department's country report documents police harassment of LGBT persons alongside the penal-code provisions, and Outright International records harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services as frequent. In an August 2023 opinion for the International Commission of Jurists, Mathuri Thamilmaran identified the Sri Lanka Police as the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals, noting that both the Police and the Human Rights Commission had acknowledged this in preceding months, and arguing that administrative circulars cannot substitute for legal reform. Advocacy groups report that police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, particularly those involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Section 365, and human-rights organisations have documented officers using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA people.

Authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence of same-sex conduct. Outright International records these examinations as widely condemned as torture. No comprehensive anti-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

Legal gender recognition is available through a certification process. The national Ministry of Health issued a circular in 2016 to health services and education institutions on issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the national human rights commission. A recognised identity card has been issued under that circular since June 2016. No surgical intervention is legally required, but obtaining the certification is described as bureaucratically onerous.

Prison placement for transgender detainees has no statutory rule. The national prisons department confirmed in October 2024 that current facilities cannot give transgender prisoners their own space, with separate accommodation planned only for prisons built in future. Placement is decided case by case: detainees holding the recognised identity card are accommodated according to their preferred gender where possible, while those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they can be considered transgender before placement, with the inmate's preference feeding the decision. Officials have stated concern about people accused of sex offences identifying as transgender to enter female housing, and placement by birth sex remains the practical default in the current male and female ward system.

Gender-affirming care is difficult to obtain. Hospitals lack the specialised surgical units and staff required, and a physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 report said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients. Patients report ignorance, curiosity and ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, raising treatment costs; hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught. The National Blood Transfusion Service bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as risky behaviour alongside drug use and multiple partners.

Family law recognises no same-sex marriage, no same-sex civil union and no equal rights for same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times. A March 2022 bill to ban conversion therapy was tabled by SJB MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna and remained unsupported by the government as of July 2024, though professional college ethics apply; families are reportedly still regularly seeking doctors to administer such treatment to LGBTQ family members.
LKA.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); its underlying content on criminalisation is assumed but not verified in this pass.

Several care-access, policing, public-opinion and family-law findings are carried from Wikipedia country coverage rather than primary documents, including the blood-donation rule, the 2023 opinion figures and the conversion-therapy bill status; these are unsourced at first hand here and would benefit from direct citation before publication.

The no-convictions finding dates from January 2012 and has not been reconfirmed by a later source in this inventory; whether prosecutions have been brought since then is unresolved.

The inventory contains no information on entry or visa rules, border screening, or whether gender markers on passports or other travel documents are recognised for arriving visitors; visitor-facing document and entry treatment is not sourced here.

No youth-specific care-access findings appear in the sources.

sources.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
sources.summary: Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing today: Media Spokesperson/Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake (Oct 2024) said current prison facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, and separate accommodation is only planned for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case-by-case: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender 'where possible', while those without it go through a doctor's assessment of whether they 'can be considered a transgender' before placement, weighing inmate preference. Officials explicitly worry about people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders, a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

sources.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
sources.summary: The Morning (original Daily Morning reporting, 4 Oct 2024) of the same Prisons Department statement: Commissioner Dissanayake said 'we always try to accommodate transgender prisoners who have the official identity card', and absent the ID a doctor assesses whether the inmate can be considered transgender, after which 'the preference of the particular inmate' feeds the accommodation decision. The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gender-affirming surgery is relatively inaccessible in Sri Lanka because many hospitals lack the highly specialised surgical units and staff required; a physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 'All Five Fingers are Not the Same' report said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients. The National Blood Transfusion Service also bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as 'risky behaviour' alongside drug use and having multiple partners. Wikipedia country coverage: Patients report meeting ignorance, curiosity and even ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, raising treatment costs; obtaining hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught. Legal gender recognition since 2016 requires bureaucratic certification that may be onerous to achieve, though no surgical intervention is legally required. Advocacy groups report police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, especially involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Article 365 as justification, and human rights organisations have documented police using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA individuals. No youth-specific care-access findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: Sri Lankan family law does not recognise same-sex marriages, same-sex civil unions, or provide equal rights to same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times and is based on European law. The Catholic Church in Sri Lanka does not recognise same-sex marriages, with Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith stating that same-sex marriages 'are not a human right'. A 2023 report found 69% of the population opposed legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2016 the Ministry of Health issued a circular to health services and education institutions about issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka. In August 2021 a video of a homophobic counsellor caused controversy; the College of Psychiatrists clarified that modern medicine does not consider homosexuality an illness and called for decriminalisation, noting that unlike psychiatrists, counsellors are not regulated and do not require degrees. In March 2022 SJB MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna tabled a bill to ban conversion therapy, which she said the government failed to support as of July 2024; despite professional college ethics, doctors are reportedly still regularly sought by families to administer 'treatment' to LGBTQ members. Sections 365 and 365A carry aggravated penalties of 10–20 years' rigorous imprisonment where an offence is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16. Wikipedia country coverage: Sri Lankan society is described as generally tolerant of homosexuality, with politicians from both major parties and across the spectrum expressing support for LGBTQ rights, and the influential Asgiriya Buddhist chapter backing rights extension and constitutional amendment. In March 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa tweeted that he was determined to secure everybody's right to live with dignity regardless of sexuality and gender, which the Financial Times called the first such public acknowledgement by a South Asian head of state. A 2021 Social Scientists Association poll found 72.5% believed LGBT people should not be punished for their sexual identity, 65% said an LGBT person can do a job as well as anyone else, and 51.4% would support rights legislation; a 2018 Equality Fund survey found 12% of respondents were LGBTQI. Community organisations include Companions on a Journey (1994, Sri Lanka's first LGBTQ support group), the Women's Support Group (1999) and Equal Ground, though Article 365 remains cited to justify police harassment and moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings.

LKA.localsOnly:
Community organisations with long operating histories include Companions on a Journey, founded 1994 as the country's first LGBTQ support group, the Women's Support Group founded 1999, and Equal Ground. These are the main points of contact for residents seeking support, documentation or referral.

Residents face the practical effect of Section 365 in dealings with the police regardless of whether charges are brought: moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings continues to cite the article, and complaints of sexual violence or blackmail may go unrecorded.

For a resident entering the prison system, accommodation follows the October 2024 departmental position: the recognised identity card issued under the 2016 circular is the strongest basis for placement by preferred gender, its absence triggers a medical assessment, and neither route guarantees a placement different from birth sex. Separate transgender housing exists only as a plan for future prison construction.

Transgender residents seeking medical care may encounter unfamiliarity or ridicule in public facilities, may need to use private providers, and are barred from blood donation if they are men who have sex with men. Conversion-therapy-style treatment remains available from unregulated practitioners despite the professional colleges' ethics positions, and the 2022 bill to ban it had no government backing as of July 2024.
LKA.comparisons: Pairwise: above Malaysia (0.28 — adds state-level Sharia “posing” laws with caning) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts and civil society). The police-as-perpetrator documentation keeps Sri Lanka in High Risk rather than Elevated.
LKA.blindSummary:
The country criminalises same-sex activity under Sections 365 and 365A of the national penal code. Section 365 covers "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and was applied to men; Section 365A covers "gross indecency" and was amended in 1995 to reach women as well, so both provisions now apply to men and women. The maximum penalty is ten years' imprisonment. Where an offence under these sections is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16, the aggravated penalty rises to ten to twenty years' rigorous imprisonment.

Formal prosecutions are rare. A refugee decision-making body in another country found no convictions under the articles in January 2012, and an international LGBTI rights organisation's March 2026 overview describes prosecutions as limited. The provisions nonetheless structure everyday policing: a foreign government's human-rights report documents police harassment of LGBT persons alongside the penal-code provisions, and the international organisation records harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services as frequent. In an August 2023 opinion, a legal advocacy practitioner identified the national police as the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals, noting that both the police and the national human rights commission had acknowledged this in preceding months, and arguing that administrative circulars cannot substitute for legal reform. Advocacy groups report that police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, particularly those involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Section 365, and human-rights organisations have documented officers using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA people.

Authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence of same-sex conduct. The international organisation records these examinations as widely condemned as torture. No comprehensive anti-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

Legal gender recognition is available through a certification process. The national health ministry issued a circular in 2016 to health services and education institutions on issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the national human rights commission. A recognised identity card has been issued under that circular since June 2016. No surgical intervention is legally required, but obtaining the certification is described as bureaucratically onerous.

Prison placement for transgender detainees has no statutory rule. The national prisons department confirmed in October 2024 that current facilities cannot give transgender prisoners their own space, with separate accommodation planned only for prisons built in future. Placement is decided case by case: detainees holding the recognised identity card are accommodated according to their preferred gender where possible, while those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they can be considered transgender before placement, with the inmate's preference feeding the decision. Officials have stated concern about people accused of sex offences identifying as transgender to enter female housing, and placement by birth sex remains the practical default in the current male and female ward system.

Gender-affirming care is difficult to obtain. Hospitals lack the specialised surgical units and staff required, and a physician interviewed for an international human-rights organisation's 2016 report said national doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients. Patients report ignorance, curiosity and ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, raising treatment costs; hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught. The national blood transfusion service bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as risky behaviour alongside drug use and multiple partners.

Family law recognises no same-sex marriage, no same-sex civil union and no equal rights for same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times. A March 2022 bill to ban conversion therapy was tabled by a member of parliament and remained unsupported by the government as of July 2024, though professional college ethics apply; families are reportedly still regularly seeking doctors to administer such treatment to LGBTQ family members.

MNG.name: Mongolia
MNG.summary:
Mongolia decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 1993. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, but the protections are fragmented and no comprehensive equality law is in place. The constitution bars marriage equality, and no form of union recognition is available to same-sex couples. LGBT organisations can register.

The Criminal Code in force from 2017 carries hate-crime provisions covering bias motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. A residual offence addressing "satisfaction of immoral sexual needs" remains in the statute book and can be invoked as a pretext against gender-nonconforming people, even though no provision specifically criminalises homosexuality.

Enforcement practice works in the visitor's favour. After a police officer was charged in 2019 for assaulting a detained transgender woman, the LGBT Centre trained more than 500 police officers, prosecutors and judges on the 2017 Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions. The force now has guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of what identity documents say.

Transition and visibility remain difficult in practice. An openly trans man, Anaraa Nyamdorj, co-founder and advisor of the LGBT Centre, came out publicly in 2004 and began transition in 2011; his account and the Centre's advocacy describe limited access to transition-related care and uneven social acceptance in Ulaanbaatar. Mongolia held its first Pride in 2018.
MNG.outOfScopeNotes:
The Asian Development Bank's legal-status survey carries no recorded finding for Mongolia, so no independent cross-check of the country's legal framework is available from that source.

Whether the 2019 assault prosecution resulted in conviction, and whether the police guidelines on transgender detainees are enforced beyond the capital, are unresolved in the sources on record.

Current access to transition-related medical care, including hormone therapy and surgical services, is not sourced here.

MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy is a criminal offence in Myanmar under Section 377 of the Penal Code, a colonial-era provision reported as carrying life imprisonment or up to 10 years' imprisonment. Police apply it alongside vague public-decency provisions, and authorities have used it to detain people who cannot satisfactorily account for their presence. The provision remained in active use as recently as 2018, when the HIV-positive LGBTI advocate Aung Myo Htut was charged under it.

Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has intensified. The National Unity Government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and two critically injured. Human Rights Myanmar's June 2024 submission to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killings counted 5 to 12 killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas, identified intensified Section 377 enforcement as an aggravating factor in those deaths, and described militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws as endangering the right to life. Torture and sexual violence in detention are reported.

Transgender visitors face a separate layer of exposure. Myanmar does not permit transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, so the state does not recognise their gender identity and no legal gender recognition procedure exists. Section 35(c) of the 1945 Police Act allows police to detain anyone they consider behaving suspiciously after sunset, criminalises face covering with up to three months' imprisonment, and is applied specifically against transgender people, who also report police harassment, sexual assault, mistreatment and extortion. A trans woman describing events in 2016 recounted arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night while police alleged sex work; in 2013 trans women in Mandalay were forced to strip and parade naked while photographed, an episode police called a public service.

There is no enforceable legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised: couples can cohabit and hold ceremonial marriages without legal action, but those ceremonies carry no legal standing.

Care access is constrained by the same regime. Section 377 was identified in 2013 as hampering the country's HIV response, and gay men, particularly those living with HIV or AIDS, face stigmatisation. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights names LGBTQ people as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law.
MMR.outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty attached to Section 377 is reported inconsistently across sources: several give up to 10 years' imprisonment, others give life imprisonment, and one gives both. Which sentence applies under which circumstances is not resolved by the available material.

Nothing in the available material addresses entry screening, visa rules, or checks on gender markers in passports or other travel documents at Myanmar's borders. Whether immigration authorities inspect documents for inconsistency with a traveller's presentation is not sourced.

Whether Section 377 has been charged against foreign visitors, or applied to conduct outside the country's territory, is not sourced. The same gap applies to the reach of the 2024 Conscription Law in respect of foreign nationals.

Enforcement frequency after 2024 is not sourced: the available counts of killings cover the period since February 2021, and no current figure for prosecutions under Section 377 or Section 35(c) is available. Practical access to legal representation, consular assistance, and HIV treatment for a non-resident is likewise not covered.

Verdict: avoid entirely.

DVB (Jan 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; the NUG recorded 17 LGBT killed and 2 critically injured since 1 Feb 2021; 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' found 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and 68%+ fear repercussions from abusers.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Myanmar does not allow transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, so the state does not recognise their gender identity. Transgender people are consequently subject to police harassment, sexual assault, mistreatment and extortion, and are frequently targeted using the 'shadow law' in section 35(c) of the Police Act (1945), which lets police detain anyone they consider behaving suspiciously after sunset. The source text describes no legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process for trans people in Myanmar. LGBTQ access to care is shaped by criminalisation and stigma: Section 377 of the Penal Code (up to 10 years' imprisonment for same-sex acts) was called out by Aung San Suu Kyi in 2013 as hampering the country's efforts to combat HIV, and gay men are stigmatised, especially if living with HIV/AIDS. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights includes LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law. On the youth side, the 2019 Child Rights Law contains a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation, but it applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms. Myanmar has no enforceable legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Existing measures are symbolic or non-binding: the 2019 Child Rights Law's non-discrimination clause covers sexual orientation but only for children and has no enforcement mechanisms; the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals but carry no legal penalties; and the 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights is a planning document, not law. Following the June 2019 death by suicide of young gay librarian Kyaw Zin Win after workplace harassment, the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission called for enactment of anti-discrimination provisions, and the same year's events prompted a national conversation on LGBT issues. Myanmar does not recognise same-sex marriages or civil unions. In 2014 a Burmese same-sex couple drew widespread media attention by holding an unofficial wedding ceremony after 10 years together, triggering a backlash from social conservatives who questioned why anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced against them. Same-sex couples can cohabit freely in Yangon and Mandalay and celebrate ceremonial marriages without legal persecution, but these carry no legal standing. Youth-specific findings centre on the June 2019 death by suicide of Kyaw Zin Win, a young gay man working as a librarian at Myanmar Imperial University in Yangon, after continuous harassment and bullying from colleagues; more than 600 people attended his funeral and a rainbow flag was wrapped around his coffin. The university opened an investigation and suspended three staff members, and the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission launched a separate investigation and called for anti-discrimination provisions. Legally, the 2019 Child Rights Law includes a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation, but it applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms; meanwhile same-sex conduct remains criminalised under Section 377 with up to 10 years' imprisonment regardless of consent or privacy.

MMR.tangentialFactors:
Expression around LGBT life is restricted. In January 2025 the junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as obscene and announced prosecutions against their publishers.

The civil-society infrastructure a visitor might rely on for support is under pressure. The Organization Registration Law of October 2022 provides for prison terms where organisations fail to comply with registration requirements, and compulsory military service announced in February 2024 compounds the pressure. Research from January 2025 found that the 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement.

Official hostility coexists with long-standing cultural visibility. Nat kadaws, traditional spirit mediums who are transgender women, have been publicly visible for decades, and same-sex couples have held ceremonies drawing national attention, including an unofficial wedding in 2014 that triggered a backlash from social conservatives demanding enforcement of the anti-homosexuality law. Visibility has not produced legal protection.

The June 2019 death by suicide of a young gay librarian, Kyaw Zin Win, after workplace harassment prompted the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission to call for enactment of anti-discrimination provisions, one of the few instances of the country's protection machinery responding to an anti-LGBT killing.
MMR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) only because Myanmar's persecution, while lethal, is part of generalised wartime violence rather than a codified anti-trans machine; below Uganda (0.17).
MMR.blindSummary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy is a criminal offence in the country under Section 377 of the Penal Code, a colonial-era provision reported as carrying life imprisonment or up to 10 years' imprisonment. Police apply it alongside vague public-decency provisions, and authorities have used it to detain people who cannot satisfactorily account for their presence. The provision remained in active use as recently as 2018, when an HIV-positive LGBTI advocate was charged under it.

Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has intensified. A parallel civilian government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and two critically injured. A national rights organisation's June 2024 submission to a UN special procedure on extrajudicial killings counted 5 to 12 killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas, identified intensified Section 377 enforcement as an aggravating factor in those deaths, and described militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws as endangering the right to life. Torture and sexual violence in detention are reported.

Transgender visitors face a separate layer of exposure. The country does not permit transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, so the state does not recognise their gender identity and no legal gender recognition procedure exists. Section 35(c) of the 1945 Police Act allows police to detain anyone they consider behaving suspiciously after sunset, criminalises face covering with up to three months' imprisonment, and is applied specifically against transgender people, who also report police harassment, sexual assault, mistreatment and extortion. A trans woman describing events in 2016 recounted arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night while police alleged sex work; in 2013 trans women in a central city were forced to strip and parade naked while photographed, an episode police called a public service.

There is no enforceable legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised: couples can cohabit and hold ceremonial marriages without legal action, but those ceremonies carry no legal standing.

Care access is constrained by the same regime. Section 377 was identified in 2013 as hampering the country's HIV response, and gay men, particularly those living with HIV or AIDS, face stigmatisation. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights names LGBTQ people as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law.

Nothing in the available material addresses entry screening, visa rules, or checks on gender markers in passports or other travel documents at the country's borders. Whether immigration authorities inspect documents for inconsistency with a traveller's presentation is not sourced.

Whether Section 377 has been charged against foreign visitors, or applied to conduct outside the country, is not sourced. The same gap applies to the reach of the 2024 Conscription Law in respect of foreign nationals.

Enforcement frequency after 2024 is not sourced: the available counts of killings cover the period since February 2021, and no current figure for prosecutions under Section 377 or Section 35(c) is available. Practical access to legal representation, consular assistance, and HIV treatment for a non-resident is likewise not covered.

CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.summary:
Cuba's constitutional framework names sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories. Article 42 of the 2019 Constitution was the first constitutional text anywhere to name both grounds expressly. Consensual same-sex relations were removed from the Penal Code in 1979, and the 2022 Family Code, approved by referendum on 25 September 2022 with 66.87% support, legalised same-sex marriage and adoption and confirmed that legal gender change does not require surgery.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than surgical or judicial. The July 2025 civil-registry reform removed the remaining bureaucratic obstacles to name changes, and the Family Code had already established that surgery is not a precondition. Since Resolution 126 of 2008, trans healthcare has been provided within the public health system rather than routed through separate or private channels.

Employment protection is narrower than the constitutional text. The Labor Code (Law 116) bars discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation, but article 2(b) covers orientation and does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground. A 2013 parliamentary amendment banning sexual-orientation discrimination in employment passed after sustained debate; CENESEX director Mariela Castro had proposed extending it to gender identity, disability and HIV status, and the sexual-orientation ban was the provision enacted.

The gap between statutory protection and daily experience is documented rather than denied by Cuban sources. Law and enforcement do not always meet: the Labor Code's identity omission, and the practical hurdles that remained until the 2025 registry reform, sit alongside state institutions that have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s. CENESEX has run a trans-rights programme, worked directly with the police and the supreme court, and pushed sexual-diversity education into schools.

Cuba's hostility is directed at emigration and dissent rather than at gender expression as such, but it bears on who is safe to arrive and leave. Authorities have used 'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who fled to seek asylum: Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years' imprisonment if they returned after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands in January 2018, a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018, and LGBTI activists including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation remained under monitoring.
CUB.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the gender-identity, disability and HIV-status extension to the 2013 employment amendment was ever enacted is not confirmed in the sources; only the sexual-orientation ban is confirmed as passed.

Not sourced: entry and visa rules, including whether passports or entry documents carry sex markers that do not match a visitor's presentation, and whether border or immigration screening can out a traveller. No information is available on airport or border practice.

Not sourced: rules on restroom and facility access, hate-crime penalties or their enforcement, recognition of a foreign spouse or partner, and how Article 42 has been applied by courts in individual cases.

Unresolved: the practical reliability of hormone supply is reported as degraded by the economic crisis, but no dated stock or availability data is in the inventory.

Not sourced: any sub-national variation in enforcement, since the sources describe national law and Havana-based institutions only.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D2, D3, D6, D9, D11.

sources.summary: LegalClarity overview (30 May 2026): documents Cuba's arc from the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, ~60 hrs/week cutting cane in Camagüey, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — 1979 Penal Code removal of consensual same-sex acts, Castro's public acceptance of blame (La Jornada, 2010), Resolution 126 (2008) trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 Constitution (Art 42, first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 Family Code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: Labor Code Law 116 bars SOGI discrimination but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, and the Labor Code's article 2(b) covers orientation, not identity.

Americas Quarterly (15 Sept 2022): previews Cuba's 25 Sept 2022 Family Code referendum, only the 4th national vote since 1959, which would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights. Opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (1,400+ arrestees) and record emigration. The equality settlement is contested rather than state-enforced.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (23 Dec 2011): sympathetic first-person account 'Rainbow Cuba' disputing claims of systematic state homophobia — documents the UMAP camps (conscripts paid seven pesos a day), the 1975 declaration-era turning point, and CENESEX's state-backed programme: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education. Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.

Washington Blade (21 Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; the trans-specific amendment drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, while passage of the sexual-orientation ban was the confirmed outcome. The measure predates the 2019 Constitution and the 2022 Family Code.

Washington Blade (26 May 2018): documents Cuba's use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned after filing Dutch asylum claims (Jan 2018); a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained (19 May 2018), and LGBTI activists (incl. Nelson Gandulla, Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation) remained monitored. Relevant to visitors: Cuba's hostility toward emigration/asylum, not toward gender expression as such.

CUB.tangentialFactors:
The historical baseline is severe and well documented. Between 1965 and 1968 the UMAP forced-labour camps held gay men, who cut cane in Camagüey roughly 60 hours a week for seven pesos a day and were subjected to electric-shock and injection experiments presented as cures. Consensual same-sex acts left the Penal Code in 1979, and Fidel Castro publicly accepted blame for the UMAP era in 2010.

Official institutions have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s, with CENESEX running trans-rights work and engaging the police and the supreme court, a baseline that predates the 2019 Constitution.

Cuba's hostility toward departure is documented and distinct from its stance on gender expression. In January 2018 Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years in prison for treason against the homeland after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands, a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018, and LGBTI activists including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation remained under monitoring. A trans visitor who sought asylum or fled could meet this machinery; a visitor who does not is unlikely to encounter it.

Compared with neighbouring jurisdictions, Cuba's constitutional and family-law settlement is among the most transformed in Latin America, though the employment-law gap on gender identity places it behind the standard its own constitution sets.
CUB.localsOnly:
Cuban workers are covered by Labor Code Law 116, which bars discrimination including on sexual orientation, but gender identity is not listed as a separate protected ground and article 2(b) addresses orientation only. Residents seeking redress therefore have a weaker statutory hook for identity-based workplace claims than for orientation-based ones.

Residents access trans healthcare through the public system under Resolution 126 (2008) and through CENESEX's official programme, which also conducts sexual-diversity education and works with police and courts. Supply-side reliability is constrained by the economic crisis.

The Family Code governs resident families directly, covering marriage, adoption, shared parental rights and codified domestic-violence penalties, and the July 2025 civil-registry reform governs name changes for people registered in Cuban civil records.

Citizens face the treason provisions if they leave to seek asylum, and independent LGBTI activists have been monitored. The absence of independent civil society means there is no organisation outside the state to which a resident can appeal.
CUB.comparisons: Pairwise: below Argentina (0.73 — democracy, independent NGOs, stronger recourse) and above Lithuania (0.66) and Vietnam (0.63 — Cuba's constitutional GI protection and official trans programme edge it).

ECU.name: Ecuador
ECU.summary:
Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution of Ecuador binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing, and gender, expressly including sexual orientation and gender identity. The provision sits within a secular, multinational constitutional order and forms the non-discrimination foundation on which LGBTI claims in Ecuador are brought.

Legal gender recognition has been available since 2016 on the basis of self-determination alone, without surgery or medical diagnosis, allowing a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents. The National Assembly's reforms of 12 December 2023 to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree issued by President Daniel Noboa on 11 June 2024, streamlined the civil-registry procedure through which the change is made; adults may change name and sex or gender marker directly at the civil registry, once, without a surgical requirement.

Constitutional Court rulings in 2024 and 2025 extended document changes to trans adolescents and publicly rebuked the National Assembly for stalling implementation of trans-rights legislation. An April 2026 report describes the adolescent ruling as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation. Conversion practices are criminalised as torture under Article 151 of the Penal Code, in force since 2014 and carrying 7 to 10 years' imprisonment, although as of 2023 hundreds of clinics were still promoting them.

Violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians rose amid the internal armed conflict, according to a January 2024 report. A 2011 United States State Department human-rights report found discrimination by public and private bodies against gay, lesbian and transgender people, and recorded LGBT group claims that police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals; the same report found the right to equal access to formal education frequently violated.

Detention is the sharpest documented harm. Trans women in Ecuador are held almost without exception in male prison spaces, where they report gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. Helen Maldonado, a trans woman, died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; in 2026 a 23-year-old trans woman died in state custody at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison, prompting calls for an independent investigation.

Family recognition is partial. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, and in 2018 the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of a same-sex couple, a precedent for state recognition of same-sex families. Adoption is constitutionally restricted to different-sex couples under Article 68, and legislation passed on 14 August 2026 by 118 votes to 0 explicitly prohibits single and same-sex couples from adopting.
ECU.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and border-screening rules for transgender visitors, including the treatment of gender markers on foreign passports, are not covered by any source in this inventory; no finding on entry screening can be made from the material available.

Facilities access, such as restroom and changing arrangements in schools, workplaces or public buildings, is not sourced. Nor is access to gender-affirming healthcare for a person visiting Ecuador, outside the documented refusal of medical care to a detained trans woman.

The inventory does not establish whether Ecuador's criminal law contains a hate-crime or aggravated-sentence provision for offences motivated by gender identity, beyond the conversion-practices provision and general constitutional non-discrimination. Nor does it source a specific anti-discrimination statute with a complaints mechanism.

The prison census figure of 73 trans women is contested by advocates who say the true number is far higher, so the scale of exposure remains unresolved. The 2026 death at El Encuentro was, at the time of the source, the subject of calls for an independent investigation rather than a completed one, and no outcome is recorded.

The sources do not state whether the 2024 and 2025 Constitutional Court rulings on adolescent document changes are final, appealable or contingent on implementing legislation, nor whether the June 2024 regulation has been amended since issuance.

sources.summary: Primicias (12 Jun 2024): President Noboa issued the reglamento on 11 Jun 2024 to the National Assembly's 12 Dec 2023 reforms of the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data. The reglamento streamlines civil-registry gender-marker changes, which is the operative procedure for legal gender recognition.
Los Angeles Blade (Jan 2024) reports that violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians is increasing amid the internal armed conflict.

AP (Apr 2026) reports that Constitutional Court rulings in Ecuador let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records, in a case described as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage legalised in 2019 but same-sex couples barred from adoption by constitutional ban; legal gender recognition possible since 2016 (not available to under-18s); conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.

The US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ecuador documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems in Ecuador, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption.

The 2008 Constitution of Ecuador (Georgetown/PDBA text): Article 11 principles bind the state to respect ethnic, national, social, generational and gender differences as well as sexual orientation and identity, forming the constitutional non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI rights in a secular, multinational state.

PinkNews (31 May 2018): the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of the same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon, the child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon. Lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said the refusal violated the child's rights, in a precedent ordering state recognition of same-sex families.

sources.title: Trans Women in Ecuador's Prisons | PrisioTrans Human Rights Program
sources.summary: Silueta X (leading Ecuadorian trans-rights organisation), PrisioTrans program, documents 2011-2026: trans women in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces and face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers. Key cases: trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; 2022 complaint over cruel/inhuman/degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast/body implants; 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman drew calls for an independent investigation at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison. The program explicitly does NOT push a one-size placement rule, instead advocating individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

ECU.blindSummary:
Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution of the country binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing, and gender, expressly including sexual orientation and gender identity. The provision sits within a secular, multinational constitutional order and forms the non-discrimination foundation on which LGBTI claims are brought.

Legal gender recognition has been available since 2016 on the basis of self-determination alone, without surgery or medical diagnosis, allowing a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents. The national legislature's reforms of 12 December 2023 to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree issued by the head of state on 11 June 2024, streamlined the civil-registry procedure through which the change is made; adults may change name and sex or gender marker directly at the civil registry, once, without a surgical requirement.

Constitutional Court rulings in 2024 and 2025 extended document changes to trans adolescents and publicly rebuked the national legislature for stalling implementation of trans-rights legislation. An April 2026 report describes the adolescent ruling as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made the country the first in its region to bar discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation. Conversion practices are criminalised as torture under Article 151 of the Penal Code, in force since 2014 and carrying 7 to 10 years' imprisonment, although as of 2023 hundreds of clinics were still promoting them.

Violence against LGBTQ people rose amid the internal armed conflict, according to a January 2024 report. A 2011 human-rights report issued by a foreign government found discrimination by public and private bodies against gay, lesbian and transgender people, and recorded LGBT group claims that police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals; the same report found the right to equal access to formal education frequently violated.

Detention is the sharpest documented harm. Trans women are held almost without exception in male prison spaces, where they report gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. A trans woman died during the November 2021 massacre at a major penitentiary while held in a male prison space; in 2026 a 23-year-old trans woman died in national custody at a maximum-security prison, prompting calls for an independent investigation.

Family recognition is partial. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, and in 2018 the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of a same-sex couple, a precedent for state recognition of same-sex families. Adoption is constitutionally restricted to different-sex couples under Article 68, and legislation passed on 14 August 2026 by 118 votes to 0 explicitly prohibits single and same-sex couples from adopting.
ECU.blindOutOfScope:
Entry, visa and border-screening rules for transgender visitors, including the treatment of gender markers on foreign passports, are not covered by any source in this inventory; no finding on entry screening can be made from the material available.

Facilities access, such as restroom and changing arrangements in schools, workplaces or public buildings, is not sourced. Nor is access to gender-affirming healthcare for a person visiting the country, outside the documented refusal of medical care to a detained trans woman.

The inventory does not establish whether the criminal law contains a hate-crime or aggravated-sentence provision for offences motivated by gender identity, beyond the conversion-practices provision and general constitutional non-discrimination. Nor does it source a specific anti-discrimination statute with a complaints mechanism.

The prison census figure of 73 trans women is contested by advocates who say the true number is far higher, so the scale of exposure remains unresolved. The 2026 death in national custody was, at the time of the source, the subject of calls for an independent investigation rather than a completed one, and no outcome is recorded.

The sources do not state whether the 2024 and 2025 Constitutional Court rulings on adolescent document changes are final, appealable or contingent on implementing legislation, nor whether the June 2024 regulation has been amended since issuance.

ECU.tangentialFactors:
Ecuador's framework is among the more developed in the region on paper: self-determination-based legal gender recognition dating from 2016, explicit constitutional protection of gender identity since 1998, and criminalisation of conversion practices as torture sit alongside marriage equality. The internal armed conflict and the associated rise in violence reported in January 2024 form the wider security background against which LGBTQ people move, and reportage links the deterioration in safety to that context rather than to any change in the legal position.

Public officials have faced legal consequences for anti-gay speech: presidential candidate Nelson Zavala was fined over $3,000 and barred from office for a year in 2013 for describing gay people as sinners and immoral. Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017.

JAM.name: Jamaica
JAM.summary:
Jamaica criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The Offences Against the Person Act makes buggery punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour, and the US State Department's 2023 country report confirms the provision remains in force. No statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the same report states that individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender. A trans visitor therefore has no legal gender recognition, no discrimination protection and no carve-out from the sexual-offences regime to rely on.

Violence against gender-nonconforming people is documented and, in the defining case, unpunished. In July 2013 a mob in St. James beat, stabbed and shot Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old, at a street party after he was identified; no arrests had been made and the case remained unsolved as of 2022. The matter is now before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights as Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica, and an amicus brief filed in February 2024 documents housing insecurity, and educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

The state's own machinery is recorded as a source of risk rather than remedy. A 2013 US Department of Justice country packet found that LGBT victims were reluctant to report offences because police leaked incident details, failed to investigate violence including murder, and did not intervene during attacks. Human Rights Watch's November 2004 documentation recorded police harassment of gay men and of HIV/AIDS outreach workers alongside community and family violence carried out with impunity and official indifference. Amnesty International's June 2006 urgent appeal described vigilante violence together with police ill-treatment of LGBT people, and recorded that lesbians had been raped and driven into exile abroad.

Corrections facilities are a documented site of identity-targeted violence with no gender-recognition framework to govern accommodation. A 2018 study by University of the West Indies lecturer Carla Moore found that people perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender were isolated in penal institutions, that their rehabilitation opportunities were effectively non-existent, and that other prisoners refused to touch objects or sit on seats they had used. The study estimated that roughly 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belonged to sexual or gender minorities, and reported prevalent corrective rape of lesbians. The 2023 US State Department report describes prisoner-on-prisoner violence as common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for perceived LGBTQI+ identity, and records a January 2023 video showing an inmate at a pre-trial police lockup beaten and scalded by other inmates accusing him of being gay. Tower Street cells hold three times their intended capacity.

Public hostility is measurable and long-standing. J-FLAG data recorded 68 reports of sexually motivated harassment or abuse in 2012, including 53 assault cases and at least two killings, with people aged 18 to 29 bearing the greatest share; a 2013 assessment found that the majority of LGBTQ people in the country reported facing homophobic violence in public. J-FLAG's co-founder Brian Williamson was stabbed to death in June 2004, with a crowd outside his home celebrating. Polling records 96% opposition to legalising homosexual relations in 2001, 85.2% opposition in a 2010 survey, 88% disapproval in a 2016 J-FLAG poll, and at least 60% opposition to acceptance of homosexuality in 2023 polling.

Marriage and partnership recognition are excluded by the constitution. The Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act 2011 explicitly bars recognition of same-sex marriage or any other same-sex union. In July 2019 Maurice Tomlinson petitioned the Inter-American Commission to rule that Section 18(2) of the Constitution contravenes the American Convention on Human Rights and to require Jamaica to recognise his Canadian marriage and to allow naturalisation of same-sex spouses of Jamaican citizens on the same terms as heterosexual spouses. Both Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Peter Phillips stated opposition to legalising same-sex marriage in 2019.

Official posture towards visitors is mixed. In January 2019 the Director of Tourism, Donovan White, stated that gay tourists are welcome and that Jamaicans harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors. In January 2018 Jamaica barred entry to Steven Anderson, a Holocaust-denying anti-gay pastor from Arizona, after activist objections. Statements of welcome have not translated into event-level protection: in September 2019 Montego Bay Mayor Omar Davis and Councilor Charles Sinclair blocked a local cultural centre's use by the local LGBT group, other venues cancelled reservations over fear of backlash, and October 2019 Pride events were forced to cancel after police said they could not provide protection.
JAM.outOfScopeNotes:
The Inter-American Commission proceedings are unresolved. Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica remains pending as a petition and the February 2024 amicus submissions are argument rather than finding; no Commission decision on the merits is sourced here. The Tomlinson petition on Section 18(2) and spousal naturalisation is likewise unresolved on the available sources.

The status of the Court of Appeal proceedings in Tomlinson's 2012 media-advertisement case is not sourced beyond the February 2016 hearing with judgment reserved.

No source in the inventory addresses how Jamaica treats a passport or identity document bearing a foreign-issued gender marker, or what a trans visitor would face at immigration beyond the documented bar on Steven Anderson's entry in January 2018. That entry screening question is unresolved on these sources.

Trans-specific access to health care is documented at the population level through UNDP's 2023 survey chapters, but no source addresses availability of hormone therapy, HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis continuity, or emergency care standards for a short-term visitor.

sources.summary: Amicus brief in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

US DOJ/EOIR Jamaica country packet (2013): Offences Against the Person Act makes 'buggery' punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour; LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks (documented via the CVC and local organisations).

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

Amnesty International urgent appeal (4 Jun 2006): reports vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people in Jamaica — gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once orientation known; lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad; concern that prominent musicians promote homophobia.

sources.title: Gays ostracised in prison – study
sources.summary: Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

sources.title: Jamaica 2023 Human Rights Report (US Department of State)
sources.summary: US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

sources.summary:
In 2012 Maurice Tomlinson sued Jamaican TV stations TVJ, PBCJ and CVM for refusing to air a 30-second advertisement, "Love and Respect," promoting recognition of LGBT people's humanity; the Constitutional Court ruled against him in November 2013, and the Court of Appeal heard the appeal in February 2016 with judgment reserved. The UN Human Rights Committee's 2011 review regretted virulent lyrics by musicians and entertainers that incite violence against homosexuals and urged Jamaica to investigate and sanction those responsible. Dancehall artists including Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Bounty Killer, Elephant Man, Sizzla and Shabba Ranks have written or performed songs advocating attacks on gay and lesbian people, and a 2005 agreement between dancehall labels and groups such as OutRage! and the Stop Murder Music Coalition sought to end anti-gay lyrics in live performance.

In January 2018 Jamaica barred entry to Steven Anderson, a Holocaust-denying anti-gay pastor from Arizona, after an outcry from activists; he said he was told at the airport he would not be allowed into the country.

LGBT Jamaicans have fled abroad for safety. Maurice Tomlinson moved to Toronto in 2011 after death threats, Gareth Henry sought asylum in Canada in 2008, and Simone Edwards was granted asylum in the Netherlands in 2008. Tomlinson's July 2019 IACHR petition asks that Jamaica allow naturalization of same-sex spouses of Jamaican citizens on the same terms as heterosexual spouses. In January 2019 the Director of Tourism, Donovan White, said gay tourists are welcome and that Jamaicans harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors.

In September 2019 Montego Bay Mayor Omar Davis and Councilor Charles Sinclair blocked the local cultural center's use by the local LGBT group to protect the building's "sacredness," and other venues then cancelled reservations over fear of backlash, forcing cancellation of the October 2019 Pride events; police said they could not provide protection to LGBT Jamaicans given the whipped-up hysteria. J-FLAG reported in 2012 harassment of gay and lesbian patients by hospital and prison staff and numerous reports of violence against gay inmates by wardens and other inmates, with few seeking recourse through the prison system. Quality of Citizenship Jamaica, founded in 2013, worked to create safe spaces for LGBT women, youth and transgender people before ending operations in 2018.

In 2011 Parliament passed the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act, explicitly banning same-sex marriage and any other kind of union from being recognized in Jamaica. In 2019 both Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Peter Phillips announced opposition to legalizing same-sex marriage, and in July 2019 Maurice Tomlinson petitioned the IACHR to rule that Section 18(2) of the Constitution contravenes the American Convention on Human Rights, seeking repeal and recognition of his Canadian marriage. Although lesbian civil ceremonies have taken place, including the 2012 celebration in Jamaica of Jamaican-born Nicole Y. Dennis-Benn and Emma Benn, legally married in New York, Jamaica recognizes no legal basis for partnerships between women.

J-FLAG data showed that young people aged 18 to 29 bore the brunt of violence based on sexual orientation, including 68 reports of sexually motivated harassment or abuse in 2012 with 53 assault cases and at least two killings. In July 2013 a mob in St. James stabbed to death Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old, and the case remained unsolved with no arrests as of 2022. University campuses have been sites of anti-LGBT violence. Students at UWI's Mona campus rioted in April 2006 while police protected a man chased across campus, and in November 2012 two campus security guards beat a reportedly gay student seeking refuge from a mob, after which the University of Technology established a working group on intolerance and bullying. Dr. J. Carolyn Gomes resigned as head of Jamaicans for Justice in 2013 after nationwide pushback on sexual-education leaflets for adolescents that mentioned anal sex.

Polls record deep hostility. 96% opposed legalizing homosexual relations in 2001; 70% said in 2008 that homosexuals are not entitled to the same basic rights; 85.2% opposed legalizing homosexuality among consenting adults in a 2010 survey; 88% disapproved of homosexuality in a 2016 J-Flag poll; and 2023 polling indicates at least 60% oppose acceptance of homosexuality. Time magazine labelled Jamaica "the most homophobic place on Earth" in 2006, and in 2013 the majority of LGBTQ people in the country said they faced homophobic violence in public. J-FLAG, founded December 1998, operates underground and anonymously as Jamaica's first LGBT human rights organization, and co-founder Brian Williamson was stabbed to death in June 2004 with a crowd outside his home celebrating and chanting slurs. In 2012 about a third of the population, over 900,000 Jamaicans, believed the government was not doing enough to protect LGBT people from violence and discrimination.

JAM.tangentialFactors:
Jamaica's violence problem is not confined to anti-LGBT conduct, which affects how the country's protection machinery functions generally. The Inter-American Commission's August 2012 report on the situation of human rights in Jamaica found the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject to be deplorable, while situating it within a broader record of police killings, including the May 2010 operation, and failures in the administration of justice. Civil-society input to that report came from Jamaicans for Justice and J-FLAG.

Cultural production has been identified by external bodies as a driver. The UN Human Rights Committee's 2011 review regretted virulent lyrics by musicians and entertainers that incite violence against homosexuals and urged Jamaica to investigate and sanction those responsible. Dancehall artists including Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Bounty Killer, Elephant Man, Sizzla and Shabba Ranks have written or performed songs advocating attacks on gay and lesbian people, and a 2005 agreement between dancehall labels and groups such as OutRage! and the Stop Murder Music Coalition sought to end anti-gay lyrics in live performance.

Maurice Tomlinson's litigation history illustrates the limits of judicial remedy. In 2012 he sued TVJ, PBCJ and CVM for refusing to air a 30-second advertisement promoting recognition of LGBT people's humanity; the Constitutional Court ruled against him in November 2013 and the Court of Appeal heard the appeal in February 2016 with judgment reserved. Separately, UNDP's March 2023 national survey, Being LGBT in Jamaica, quantifies lived experience of prejudice-based violence and of exclusion from health services under the criminalisation backdrop, giving a baseline for conditions a visitor would encounter in care settings.

Jamaican institutions have been sites of anti-LGBT violence in their own right. Students at the University of the West Indies' Mona campus rioted in April 2006 as police protected a man chased across campus, and in November 2012 two campus security guards beat a reportedly gay student who sought refuge from a mob, after which the University of the West Indies' sister technology university established a working group on intolerance and bullying. Dr. J. Carolyn Gomes resigned as head of Jamaicans for Justice in 2013 after nationwide pushback against adolescent sexual-education leaflets that mentioned anal sex.
