The country's oldest LGBT rights organisation recorded 68 reports of sexually motivated harassment or abuse in 2012, including 53 assault cases and at least two killings, with people aged 18 to 29 bearing the greatest share; a 2013 assessment found that the majority of LGBTQ people in the country reported facing homophobic violence in public. That organisation's co-founder Brian Williamson was stabbed to death in June 2004, with a crowd outside his home celebrating. Polling records 96% opposition to legalising homosexual relations in 2001, 85.2% opposition in a 2010 survey, 88% disapproval in a 2016 poll by the same organisation, and at least 60% opposition to acceptance of homosexuality in 2023 polling.

Marriage and partnership recognition are excluded by the constitution. The Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act 2011 explicitly bars recognition of same-sex marriage or any other same-sex union. In July 2019 a resident petitioned the inter-American commission to rule that the constitutional provision barring same-sex unions contravenes the regional human rights convention and to require the country to recognise his foreign marriage and to allow naturalisation of same-sex spouses of citizens on the same terms as heterosexual spouses. Both the prime minister and the opposition leader stated opposition to legalising same-sex marriage in 2019.

Official posture towards visitors is mixed. In January 2019 the director of tourism stated that gay tourists are welcome and that residents harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors. In January 2018 the country barred entry to a Holocaust-denying anti-gay pastor from a neighbouring continent after activist objections. Statements of welcome have not translated into event-level protection: in September 2019 the mayor and a councilor of a coastal city blocked a local cultural centre's use by the local LGBT group, other venues cancelled reservations over fear of backlash, and October 2019 Pride events were forced to cancel after police said they could not provide protection.
JAM.blindOutOfScope:
The inter-American Commission proceedings are unresolved. Dwayne Jones v. the state remains pending as a petition and the February 2024 amicus submissions are argument rather than finding; no Commission decision on the merits is sourced here. The 2019 petition on the constitutional bar to same-sex unions and spousal naturalisation is likewise unresolved on the available sources.

The status of the Court of Appeal proceedings in the 2012 media-advertisement case is not sourced beyond the February 2016 hearing with judgment reserved.

No source in the inventory addresses how the country treats a passport or identity document bearing a foreign-issued gender marker, or what a trans visitor would face at immigration beyond the documented bar on an anti-gay pastor's entry in January 2018. That entry screening question is unresolved on these sources.

Trans-specific access to health care is documented at the population level through a UN development programme survey published in 2023, but no source addresses availability of hormone therapy, HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis continuity, or emergency care standards for a short-term visitor.
blindSourceSummaries: The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books; the defining case is a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party, whose killing police failed to investigate — now before an international human-rights commission.

A 2018 academic study of the nation's prisons (about 300 of 1,800 prisoners at a major correctional centre belonging to sexual or gender minorities) reports that prisoners perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated', that rehabilitation opportunities are 'basically non-existent', that homophobia/transphobia is entrenched (other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners), and that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'.

A major foreign government's 2023 report confirms 'prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity', in facilities so overcrowded that a maximum-security centre's cells held three times capacity; a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay; the report records that the nation barred legal gender registration.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and community members report that violence against trans people is common but rarely reported; major tourist resort areas are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare.
JAM.blindTangential:
The country's violence problem is not confined to anti-LGBT conduct, which affects how its protection machinery functions generally. An inter-American commission's August 2012 country report found the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject to be deplorable, while situating it within a broader record of police killings, including a large 2010 security operation, and failures in the administration of justice. Civil-society input to that report came from a domestic human-rights litigation group and the country's oldest LGBT rights organisation.

Cultural production has been identified by external bodies as a driver. A UN treaty body's 2011 review regretted virulent lyrics by musicians and entertainers that incite violence against homosexuals and urged the country to investigate and sanction those responsible. Dancehall artists including Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Bounty Killer, Elephant Man, Sizzla and Shabba Ranks have written or performed songs advocating attacks on gay and lesbian people, and a 2005 agreement between dancehall labels and campaign groups sought to end anti-gay lyrics in live performance.

A resident activist's litigation history illustrates the limits of judicial remedy. In 2012 he sued the country's three main broadcasters for refusing to air a 30-second advertisement promoting recognition of LGBT people's humanity; the Constitutional Court ruled against him in November 2013 and the Court of Appeal heard the appeal in February 2016 with judgment reserved. Separately, a UN development programme survey published in March 2023 quantifies lived experience of prejudice-based violence and of exclusion from health services under the criminalisation backdrop, giving a baseline for conditions a visitor would encounter in care settings.

National institutions have been sites of anti-LGBT violence in their own right. Students at the national university's main campus rioted in April 2006 as police protected a man chased across campus, and in November 2012 two campus security guards beat a reportedly gay student who sought refuge from a mob, after which a technology university established a working group on intolerance and bullying. The then-head of the domestic human-rights litigation group resigned in 2013 after nationwide pushback against adolescent sexual-education leaflets that mentioned anal sex.
JAM.localsOnly:
Residents face the constitutional bar as well as the criminal law. The 2011 Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act removed any prospect of court-ordered recognition of same-sex unions, and both major party leaders publicly rejected legalisation in 2019. Lesbian civil ceremonies have taken place, including the 2012 celebration in Jamaica of Jamaican-born Nicole Y. Dennis-Benn and Emma Benn, who were legally married in New York, but the state recognises no legal basis for partnership between women.

Removal from the country has been the practical route to safety for several prominent activists. Maurice Tomlinson moved to Toronto in 2011 after death threats, Gareth Henry sought asylum in Canada in 2008, and Simone Edwards was granted asylum in the Netherlands in 2008.

Organisational space is narrow. J-FLAG, founded in December 1998 as the country's first LGBT human rights organisation, operates underground and anonymously. Quality of Citizenship Jamaica, founded in 2013 to create safe spaces for LGBT women, youth and transgender people, ended operations in 2018. J-FLAG reported in 2012 that hospital and prison staff harassed gay and lesbian patients and that wardens and other inmates committed numerous assaults on gay inmates, with few pursuing recourse through the prison system.

Age and setting shape exposure. J-FLAG's 2012 figures placed the heaviest burden of orientation-based violence on people aged 18 to 29, and the Moore study found that confinement inside penal institutions sharply curtails movement and access to resources for anyone identified as gay or transgender, with no specialised housing policy documented.

TTO.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TTO.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago's criminal law and its protective framework point in opposite directions. In Jones v Attorney General (2018) the High Court struck down the colonial same-sex criminal provisions, in a challenge brought by activist Jason Jones after he stated publicly that he faced up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner; the ruling was upheld on appeal. Decriminalisation removed exposure to prosecution but produced no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no mechanism for changing documents.

Entry rules have not caught up with the criminal-law ruling. Section 8 of the Immigration Act prohibits homosexual men and women who are not citizens from entering Trinidad and Tobago. The provision is not known to have been enforced. In 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice, ruling on Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson's case, held that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize had violated his freedom of movement, while clarifying that neither state may exclude gay nationals of other CARICOM states under the Treaty of Chaguaramas notwithstanding their domestic laws barring gay entry.

Trans visitors have no route to recognition of their documents or their gender. The director of the TT Transgender Coalition, Rae Alibey, stated in July 2024 that the trans community is the most marginalised group in the country and is not recognised at all, that gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation, and that institutional forms carry no gender-identity markers. She called for national discussion and attitudinal research as prerequisites for change.

There is no hate-crime category in the legislation. Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne identified that gap in June 2024 in connection with a spate of Grindr-related attacks numbering almost half a dozen in recent months. Police issued a further warning in November 2024 over criminals who create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings ending in armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault, with two separate incidents reported in a single week.

The constitutional route to protection was closed in 2024. The PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected adding sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution, with the decision announced at a special convention in August 2024. CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community had 'been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection'.

Family law offers nothing. Trinidad and Tobago does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions; households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible to the same rights and benefits as opposite-sex households; and same-sex couples are unable to adopt. In July 2018 Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property-dispute resolution between two gay partners, noting the unequal treatment under current law and warning that absent agreement the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law to divide property after the dissolution of a same-sex union.

Detention carries a specific and documented risk. The 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers, launched in November 2018, states plainly that there are no special facilities in the Trinidad and Tobago penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to make recommendations to prison authorities so that provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and it instructs courts to address intersex and transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and to permit court access irrespective of dress. Housing placement for trans prisoners therefore rests on a discretionary sentencing recommendation, with no facility of its own.
TTO.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Section 8 of the Immigration Act has been applied to any visitor since the 2018 decriminalisation ruling. No source in the inventory records an enforcement, a refusal of entry on that ground, or any court challenge to the section post-Jones; the only enforcement assessment available is that the law is not known to have been enforced.

Unresolved: whether the Caribbean Court of Justice's 2016 clarification on CARICOM free movement has been operationalised in border practice. The ruling's effect on non-CARICOM foreign visitors, as distinct from citizens of regional member states, is not addressed by any source here.

Unresolved: whether any prison housing incident involving a trans inmate has occurred under the 2018 Gender Equality Protocol. The protocol's own statement that no special facilities exist is sourced; no incident reports, complaints or litigation outcomes are available in the inventory.

Unresolved: whether the 2024 Grindr attack cases resulted in charges, convictions or sentences, and whether any were examined as bias-motivated despite the absence of a hate-crime category. The sources record the attacks and the police warnings only.

Not sourced: any post-2024 development in legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination legislation, or a fresh constitutional challenge following Jones. The most recent material in the inventory dates to November 2024 and records no change.

GHA.name: Ghana
GHA.summary:
Trans visitors to Ghana face imprisonment for identity itself. The Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by Ghana's Parliament on 29 May 2026 provides up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, with total prison terms of three to ten years and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Presidential assent by President John Mahama was still outstanding at the most recent reporting, and he had previously signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill.

The 2026 bill reaches beyond identity. Forming or funding an LGBTQ+ group carries up to five years; advocacy or intentional support of LGBTQ+ activities carries three to five years, with some proposals at five to ten; public displays of same-sex affection, crossdressing and disseminating information perceived as supporting LGBTQ people are also prohibited. A person who identifies publicly as an "ally" of LGBTQ people may also face prison.

A reporting duty compounds that exposure. The bill obliges anyone who becomes aware of prohibited acts to report them to the police, turning acquaintances, colleagues, landlords and hotel staff into potential informants and removing the ordinary discretion not to involve the authorities.

The bill's passage follows a cycle of failed enactment. A predecessor passed unanimously on third reading in February 2024, lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved before the 2024 election, and was reintroduced in March 2025 before passing again in May 2026. Ghana's Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two challenges to the 2024 bill, with Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson stating that until there is presidential assent there is no act and the review deferred until the president signs; the petitioners' lawyers said they would explore further options.

Colonial-era law remains the standing basis for prosecution. Section 104(1)(b) of the Criminal Code 1960 criminalises "unnatural carnal knowledge" as a misdemeanour carrying up to three years. Enforcement overwhelmingly targets LGBTQ people, while heterosexual couples performing the same acts are rarely or never prosecuted; CDD-Ghana describes the practice as moral policing rather than criminal justice. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2018 that the provision is seldom used formally while documenting mob violence, police abuse and extortion, including 2017 victim interviews in Kumasi and Tamale.

No procedure for legal gender recognition or document change for transgender people is documented in these sources. The 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and Ghanaian law contains no broad protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in education, health, housing or employment.

Venues that serve trans and LGBTQ visitors have been shut down rather than provided. The LGBTQ Centre in Accra was forced to close in February 2021 under pressure from religious and political leaders, and the office of LGBT+ Rights Ghana, opened in January 2021, was raided and closed by National Security in late February 2021. No publicly documented policy exists on housing trans prisoners, so the bill creates a pathway to imprisonment for identity alone without stating how such prisoners would be held.
GHA.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources contain no finding on legal gender recognition procedures or document-change rules for transgender people in Ghana. The nearest grounded items are the constitutional definition of marriage as between a man and a woman, Article 39's emphasis on traditional values, the 2017 ILGA poll figure of 55% support for legal gender change, and the bill's criminalisation of crossdressing and identifying as transgender. Whether any administrative route to a changed marker exists remains unresolved in this inventory.

Assent status is a live uncertainty. Reporting at the most recent dates states that President Mahama's signature was still required, but no source in this inventory confirms whether the bill has since been assented to, gazetted or brought into force, nor whether the deferred Supreme Court review has resumed.

No publicly documented policy exists in Ghana on housing trans prisoners, and the sources do not describe how an imprisoned trans person would in practice be classified or held.

No sources address entry, visa or border-screening questions for Ghana, including whether passport markers, arrival cards or immigration interviews could disclose a visitor's gender identity or trans status. Nothing here should be read as an assurance that such screening is absent.

No sources address availability of hormone therapy, gender-affirming care or prescription continuity for visitors, nor the treatment of imported medication at the border.

sources.title: Ghana parliament passes bill criminalising gay acts
sources.summary: BBC (30 May 2026): Ghana's parliament approved a new bill criminalising homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities. Identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer carries up to three years' imprisonment, and the bill adds a duty to report prohibited acts to police. It was passed under pressure from religious leaders on President Mahama, whose ratification is still required. The bill establishes the state pathway by which trans people in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone and contains no provision on how such prisoners would be housed.

sources.title: People 'panicking' as Ghana passes sweeping law criminalising LGBTQ+ activity
sources.summary: The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison terms of three to 10 years, with up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Community groups such as One Love Sisters Ghana report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. No publicly documented policy exists in Ghana on housing trans prisoners.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of speech, expression and assembly, but these rights are actively denied to LGBTQ people, and pro-LGBTQ activism is repeatedly thwarted by the government. In 2006 the government banned an LGBTQ rights conference at the Accra International Conference Centre, and in March 2020 President Akufo-Addo banned the Pan Africa ILGA conference planned for Accra as illegal. The Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by Parliament in February 2024 (reintroduced in March 2025 and passed again in May 2026) criminalises identifying as LGBTQ (up to three years), funding or forming an LGBTQ-related group (up to five years), advocacy or intentional support of LGBTQ activities (three to five years, with some proposals at 5–10 years), public displays of same-sex affection, crossdressing, and disseminating information perceived as supporting LGBTQ people. Those identifying as an 'ally' of LGBTQ people may also face prison.

No finding exists on legal gender recognition procedures or document-change rules for transgender Ghanaians. The closest grounded items are that the 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman (Article 39 emphasises traditional values), that a 2017 ILGA poll found 55% of Ghanaians believe transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender, and that the pending anti-LGBTQ bill would criminalise crossdressing and identifying as transgender.

Facilities for LGBTQ people in Ghana have been shut down rather than provided: in February 2021 religious and political leaders forced an LGBTQ Centre in Accra to close, and LGBT+ Rights Ghana's Accra office, opened in January 2021, was raided and closed by National Security in late February 2021 after opposition from locals, religious institutions and politicians. Most LGBTQ groups operate secretly or online, with FOTHA-Ghana members using the dark web for safety. No supported housing or shelter provision exists; instead young LGBTQ people are disowned and evicted from family homes, and the Solomon-supported Solace Initiative provides human-rights-trained paralegals to defend LGBTQ people in court.

Mental health and healthcare access are severely constrained: mental health professionals in Ghana are often not trained to work with LGBTQ populations and may hold prejudiced views, and the Ghana Mental Health Authority has not fully implemented inclusive policies under its 2012 Mental Health Act. Due to fear of persecution many LGBTQ people avoid seeking healthcare altogether, creating barriers to mental and sexual health support, and rates of anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and some deaths by suicide are linked to forced evictions, blackmail and violence. Conversion therapy, which families often seek from religious groups when a young person discloses same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity, is commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings; an August 2018 report documented conversion therapy programmes run by religious leaders, and a 2018 conference claimed about 400 people had registered for such programmes. A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana are at significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than their heterosexual peers, and government HIV/AIDS campaigns present the disease as an issue for straight people, leaving gay men unaware that HIV can be transmitted through anal sex even though the country receives HIV funding.

No broad legal protections exist for LGBT people against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Enforcement of the 'unnatural carnal knowledge' law (Section 104, Criminal Code 1960, a misdemeanour carrying up to three years under Article 296(4)) overwhelmingly targets LGBTQ people while heterosexual couples doing the same acts are rarely or never prosecuted, a disparity CDD-Ghana describes as moral policing rather than criminal justice. In a 2017 ILGA poll 59% of Ghanaians agreed LGBTQ people should be protected from workplace discrimination (62% for transgender people), while 89% reported disliking LGBTQ individuals and nearly 90% said they would report a relative or co-worker to police. The UN Human Rights Committee's October 2012 recommendation to eliminate 'unnatural sexual relations' and eradicate discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity was rejected by Ghana along with all other recommendations.

Ghana does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions: the 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and no provision of Ghanaian law allows legal recognition of same-sex relationships, leaving LGBTQ people in vulnerable legal positions around long-term relationships and shared property. Same-sex couples are explicitly excluded from the adoption process, since the system does not support joint applications from non-heterosexual partnerships. The pending Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill would additionally ban same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples outright.

Young LGBTQ Ghanaians are disowned by families and communities and evicted from their homes, and families often seek conversion therapy from religious groups when a same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity is disclosed, reported to be commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings, with medical bodies warning conversion therapy is ineffective and potentially harmful. A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana face significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than heterosexual peers. In January 2025 President John Mahama said he prefers teaching traditional family values through Ghana's school curriculum rather than passing anti-LGBTQ laws, and the National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education. The pending bill targets youth directly by criminalising identification as LGBTQ (three years), with Pan Africa ILGA's banned March 2020 Accra conference intended partly to protect queer youth in Africa.

GHA.tangentialFactors:
Constitutional guarantees of freedom of speech, expression and assembly exist on paper and are routinely denied to LGBTQ people in practice. In 2006 the government banned an LGBTQ rights conference at the Accra International Conference Centre, and in March 2020 President Akufo-Addo banned the Pan Africa ILGA conference planned for Accra as illegal.

Public opinion provides the political base for the legislation. In a 2017 ILGA poll, 89% of Ghanaians reported disliking LGBTQ individuals and nearly 90% said they would report a relative or co-worker to the police, though 59% agreed that LGBTQ people should be protected from workplace discrimination, rising to 62% for transgender people, and 55% believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

The UN Human Rights Committee's October 2012 recommendation to eliminate "unnatural sexual relations" and eradicate discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity was rejected by Ghana along with all of the Committee's other recommendations at that review.

Political signals have been mixed. In January 2025 President John Mahama said he preferred teaching traditional family values through the school curriculum rather than passing anti-LGBTQ laws, yet the 2026 bill was passed under pressure from religious leaders on a president whose ratification remained required. The National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education.

Community organisations describe the current climate as one of panic and withdrawal. One Love Sisters Ghana reports eviction risk and self-censorship among members following the 2026 vote. A 2017 survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland found most opposed decriminalisation on religio-cultural grounds and effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBTQ relatives but not blessing their marriages; that study measures diaspora opinion rather than conditions inside Ghana.
GHA.comparisons: Pairwise: above Nigeria (0.19 — SSMPA in force with mob lynching culture) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts). Ghana's near-passage of an identity-criminalising bill is what separates it from Elevated band: the legal floor is currently the old 3-year statute, but the demonstrated legislative intent is far harsher.
GHA.blindSummary:
Trans visitors to the country face a legal framework that, in its current form, criminalises identity itself. The Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by the national parliament on 29 May 2026 provides for up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, with total prison terms of three to ten years and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Presidential assent was still outstanding at the time of the most recent reporting, and the President had previously signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill after the earlier version failed to reach him.

The 2026 bill adds a reporting obligation: it establishes a duty on persons who become aware of prohibited acts to report them to the police. For a visitor, that converts acquaintances, colleagues, landlords and hotel staff into potential informants, and it removes the discretion that previously shielded people from formal complaint.

The 2026 law is not an isolated event. The national parliament unanimously passed the Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill in February 2024, carrying up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and up to five years for forming or funding LGBTQ+ groups. The national President declined to assent while legal challenges were pending; the national Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two of those challenges, with a justice observing that until there is presidential assent there is no act and deferring review until signature. The bill then lapsed unsigned when the outgoing parliament dissolved before the national election. Its unanimous passage, and its reintroduction, indicate the direction of travel rather than a stray piece of legislation.

Criminalisation predates both bills. Section 104(1)(b) of the national criminal code, a historic-era provision on 'unnatural carnal knowledge', remains on the books, though a human rights organisation reported in 2018 that it is rarely enforced through prosecution. That low formal enforcement rate did not make the country safe. The organisation documented mob violence against LGBT people, police abuse and extortion of suspected LGBT individuals, including victim interviews conducted in two inland cities in 2017, and published a report titled 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am: Violence and Discrimination against LGBT People' in January 2018.

The new bill enumerates transgender people explicitly alongside lesbian, gay, bisexual and queer people. It therefore supplies the national pathway by which a trans person can be imprisoned for identity alone, with no requirement of any act. The bill contains no provision on how such prisoners would be housed, and there is no publicly documented policy on the housing of trans prisoners, leaving placement to correctional discretion.

Community organisations describe the effect of the 2026 bill's passage in advance of assent. One community group reports panic among LGBT people, risk of eviction and widespread self-censorship. A 2017 survey of 113 diaspora nationals found that most respondents opposed decriminalisation or legalisation on religious and cultural grounds and concerns about effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBT relatives but not blessing their marriages. That diaspora sample is not representative of the population, but it is consistent with the political support the bill received.
GHA.blindOutOfScope:
Whether the national President has assented to the 29 May 2026 bill is unresolved in the source inventory. The most recent reporting states that ratification was still required and that the bill was expected to be signed. The legal status of the bill at the time a visitor reads this record should be verified against official national sources before travel.

Nothing in the inventory addresses gender-marker or identity-document rules for trans people, the treatment of foreign identity documents bearing conflicting markers at ports of entry, asylum or non-refoulement claims, or access to gender-affirming healthcare. These are not sourced and remain unaddressed here rather than assumed either way.

The Reuters report of the February 2024 parliamentary passage returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be read directly; the passage itself is corroborated by two other outlets in the inventory.

The inventory does not document any instance of a trans person actually being prosecuted or imprisoned for identity under section 104(1)(b) of the national criminal code, nor any data on the current population of LGBT detainees. The claim that the 2026 bill creates a pathway to imprisonment for identity alone is a statement about the statute's terms, not about documented enforcement.
blindSourceSummaries: In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed a bill on human sexual rights and family values (up to 3 years for simply identifying as LGBT, 5 years for 'promotion'); the president refused to assent pending legal challenges, the top court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when parliament dissolved.

In late May 2026 parliament passed a new bill on human sexual rights and family values: up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, longer terms for promotion/advocacy, and a 'duty to report' prohibited acts to police; the current president's ratification was still required and widely expected as of the reporting.

Under existing law, 'unnatural carnal knowledge' carries up to 3 years; mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection; the capital has a resilient underground community whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks.

Neither the 2024 nor the 2026 bill text, as reported, contains any provision on how trans prisoners would be housed; no national prison placement rule, trans special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record; the 2026 reports also describe panic, eviction risk and self-censorship among community groups.
GHA.blindTangential:
The country illustrates how a legislative instrument can matter without ever being law. The 2024 bill passed unanimously and was defeated only by the absence of presidential assent and the dissolution of the parliament, not by court judgment or popular rejection. a visitor assessing the country should therefore treat the 2026 bill's pending status as a question of timing rather than of outcome, given the President's stated willingness to sign.

The national Supreme Court's dismissal of the challenges to the 2024 bill did not clear the statute. The justice's reasoning was procedural: there was no act to challenge because no assent had been given, and review was deferred until the President signed. The petitioners' lawyers said they would explore further options. This sequencing means that constitutional challenge has so far operated at the threshold rather than on the merits of criminalisation.

The gap between the historic-era offence and the new statutory scheme is a gap in evidence rather than in law. Section 104(1)(b) survived unchanged for decades with little reported prosecution, while the violence documented in 2018 came largely from police and vigilante actors rather than from courts. The 2026 bill's reporting duty is designed to shift the enforcement burden toward third parties and formal complaint, which may change that pattern.

a human rights organisation has been the principal external documentation of LGBT conditions in the country since its 2018 report, and has consistently urged the President to veto the 2024 bill and opposes the 2026 legislation. Its reporting on the country forms part of its wider work on criminalisation in the wider national area, though the source inventory for this record does not extend to comparative data on other states in that area.

Conversion therapy is commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings, frequently sought by families from religious groups when a young person discloses same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity. Government HIV/AIDS campaigns present the disease as an issue for heterosexual people, leaving gay men unaware that HIV can be transmitted through anal sex even though the country receives HIV funding.

Organised LGBTQ life operates underground. Most groups meet secretly or online, with members of FOTHA-Ghana using the dark web for safety. GHA.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents, not only visitors, are caught by the reporting duty introduced in the 2026 bill. Members of households, landlords, employers and community members who learn of prohibited acts become obliged to report them to the police, which places LGBT residents in conflict with their own families and neighbours rather than only with the state.

Organisations working with LGBT people have been operating in a climate of documented police and vigilante violence well before the 2026 bill. The 2018 report recorded police abuse and extortion of suspected LGBT individuals alongside mob attacks, and its endnotes document interviews conducted in two inland cities in 2017. Residents of those areas have reported to such organisations that the principal threats come from vigilantes and from police, not from prosecution.

One community group reports that LGBT residents are experiencing panic, risk of eviction from housing and self-censorship following the 2026 bill's passage. Housing insecurity is a direct consequence where a landlord can report a tenant under the new duty to report.

Public opinion research touching on residents' own attitudes is limited to a small 2017 survey of 113 diaspora nationals, which found majority opposition to decriminalisation but majority support for familial acceptance of LGBT relatives short of marriage. No national polling data on attitudes to transgender people is available in this record.

MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.summary:
Morocco criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 489 of the penal code, which punishes "indecent acts" between persons of the same sex with six months to three years of imprisonment. Outright International reports that the provision is applied with wide police discretion and that arrests are arbitrary; 170 people were charged with same-sex relations in 2018. Human Rights Watch recorded Article 489 in its April 2018 report "Audacity in Adversity" among the statutes used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the wider region, and ILGA's State-Sponsored Homophobia survey lists Morocco among countries prohibiting same-sex activity between consenting adults.

Trans visitors face a further layer of exposure that the statute does not name. Cairo 52's country review finds no specific legal provisions governing transition, yet documents de facto criminalisation under Article 498, where morality charges follow gender-expression discrepancies and arrest produces involuntary outing. The Cairo 52 report "A Web of Violence" (January 2026), based on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans, documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility, and finds that Article 489 is weaponised to arrest trans people on the basis of gender expression.

There is no legal gender recognition pathway in Morocco. Cairo 52 records no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some Moroccans to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only. The Grand Mufti opposes transition. Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens.

Police conduct toward perceived trans people includes documented abuse. In November 2024 an Instagram model alleged that Moroccan police forced her to expose her genitals over suspicions that she was trans. In January 2019 El País reported that police in Marrakesh subjected a cross-dresser, Chafiq, to online humiliation after a minor traffic accident: he was handcuffed, filmed by bystanders and officers, his ID documents were photographed and posted online, and he subsequently sought asylum in Europe.

Public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment, and authorities block LGBTIQ organisations. Human Rights Watch documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; during that campaign some landlords ejected targeted tenants, and journalist Hicham Tahir reported receiving a hundred testimonies, with one person alleged to have died by suicide. A trans woman was violently beaten in Tangier in November 2022; three minors and an adult were arrested over the assault.

Morocco has no law against discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no political party has enacted LGBTQ rights legislation. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples. Police disproportionately target perceived LGBTQ people, and the names of arrested individuals are publicised before trial. In 2017 former Minister of Justice and Liberties Mustafa Ramid called homosexuals "trash" in an interview; local human rights associations petitioned Prime Minister Othmani to investigate what they termed his discriminatory and unconstitutional statements towards sexual minorities.

Enforcement has a documented record. In December 2007 a court in Ksar el-Kebir convicted six men under Article 489 after an online video of a private party, reported in the press as a "gay marriage", circulated; their lawyers said no evidence of prohibited conduct was presented, and the men were sentenced on 17 December 2007 to varying terms. Dozens then marched through the streets of Ksar el-Kebir calling for their punishment. In 2016 two girls in Marrakesh were arrested after a cousin photographed them kissing and their mother complained to police; both were acquitted in December 2016, provoking the #freethegirls outcry.

The government has banned books on homosexuality and requires schools to teach a curriculum that "emphasises ... the danger and depravity of unnatural acts". The 2018-19 Arab Barometer survey found 21% of Moroccan respondents said homosexuality is acceptable. The UN Human Rights Council adopted the SOGI resolution in September 2014, establishing an international human-rights scrutiny framework that applies to Morocco.
MAR.outOfScopeNotes:
No current trans-specific healthcare access, identity-document procedure, or shelter provision for trans visitors is recorded in the source inventory; the medical reference available is historical and describes clandestine, unregulated care rather than any documented public facility.

The scale of the April 2020 outing campaign rests on a single journalist's count of a hundred testimonies and one alleged suicide that is reported but not independently confirmed in the inventory.

The claim that Morocco enforces a de facto prohibition on gender-affirming surgery for its own citizens while permitting it for foreigners is asserted in the Cairo 52 report without a cited statutory or regulatory instrument in the inventory; the legal basis for the distinction is unresolved.

Whether Article 498 morality charges are routinely used against trans visitors specifically, as distinct from residents, is not separately quantified in the sources; the de facto criminalisation finding derives from Cairo 52's country review and interviews with Moroccan nationals.

DZA.name: Algeria
DZA.summary:
Algeria criminalises same-sex conduct under the Penal Code of 1966 (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966). ILGA records the offence as covering both male/male and female/female relations, punishable by 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500 to 2,000 Algerian dinars. The US State Department's 2023 country report gives the same custodial range, 2 months' to 2 years' plus fines, for undefined "homosexual acts". The UK Home Office country-of-origin information report of 26 July 2026, covering developments since May 2025, confirms that the 1966 Penal Code remains the operative framework, with same-sex activity prohibited as "acts of homosexuality" on the basis of a legal summary updated in June 2026.

Gender transition has no statutory route and is blocked in practice. Cairo 52 reports that Algeria has no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare and no legal gender-recognition route, so civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically blocked. The same source states that arts. 274 and 264 of the Penal Code could be used against providers of gender-affirming care, which it characterises as de facto criminalisation of that care. A fact-checking publication rated as TRUE, on 5 August 2024, the statement that Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and prohibits being transgender.

Arrests affecting the LGBT+ community are documented by NGOs, with little information recorded on the trans identity of those arrested, so the volume of trans-specific enforcement is not established by the available reporting. Enforcement against same-sex conduct itself is active and can be mass in scale. Human Rights Watch reports that a raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province on 24 July 2020 led to the arrest of 44 people, 9 women and 35 men, mostly university students, over an alleged "gay wedding". On 3 September 2020 a court sentenced 2 of them to prison and 42 to suspended terms, using party decorations and "gay appearance" as evidence.

Detention carries no trans-specific safeguard. The US State Department reports that prison authorities separate vulnerable persons, but that LGBTQI+ detainees have no specific legal protections, and that civil society has noted compounded discrimination faced by LGBTQI+ persons.

The UK Home Office assessment finds internal relocation viable for gay men, while lesbians and trans women face societal difficulties that make that option materially weaker for them.
DZA.outOfScopeNotes:
The fine range of 500 to 2,000 Algerian dinars comes from ILGA's State-Sponsored Homophobia 2008 table. The 1966 Penal Code itself is confirmed as still in force by the Home Office report of 26 July 2026, but no source in the inventory independently restates the monetary range as of 2026, so its current application is unresolved here.

No source gives a count or proportion of those arrested who are trans. Cairo 52 notes explicitly that little information is recorded on the trans identity of people arrested, so the frequency of trans-specific enforcement remains unresolved rather than low.

The claim that arts. 274 and 264 could be used against providers of gender-affirming care is presented by Cairo 52 as a risk of de facto criminalisation. Whether either article has in fact been applied against a provider is not sourced in this inventory.

The 2020 el-Kharoub case is reported as convictions for alleged homosexual conduct. No source links any defendant in that case to a trans identity, and the inventory contains no reported prosecution brought specifically for being transgender or for gender expression.

The Home Office relocation finding distinguishes gay men from lesbians and trans women but does not break the assessment down by region or city, so no locality-level variation is sourced.

TUN.name: Tunisia
TUN.summary:
Tunisia criminalises same-sex conduct under Penal Code Article 230, which carries up to three years' imprisonment, and enforcement is active rather than dormant. Article 226 bis on public indecency is applied to gender expression, and enforcement of both provisions falls disproportionately on transgender women. In October 2021 two transgender women were arrested under morality and debauchery provisions.

The scale of the current campaign is documented by Amnesty International on 11 February 2025: at least 84 people, mainly gay men and transgender women, were arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. The arrests took place in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, so the sweep is national in character rather than confined to one city. A mass conviction on 31 October 2024 imposed prison terms of up to four and a half years; the convictions were upheld on appeal on 5 February 2025, with four people released only after sentence reduction.

Human Rights Watch recorded at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months in 2016, all convicted under Article 230. Detainees interviewed in those cases reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police, which places physical abuse by the security services inside the ordinary arrest process rather than outside it.

Tunisia pledged to the United Nations in 2017 to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases while retaining the anti-gay law itself, so the commitment changed examination practice without decriminalising anything. A visitor should not read that pledge as a change in exposure to prosecution.

Legal gender recognition is unsettled and frequently refused. In April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man, weighing contradictory lower-court judgements, including case No. 12304/2018, and finding no consistent precedent; the question remains unresolved below the Court of Cassation, which makes recognition a court-by-court gamble. Cairo 52 records that gaps persist in legal gender recognition generally.

Custody carries documented identity risk. The Intersection Association reported in November 2024 that transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings, a systemic refusal of identity from the point of detention onward and a source of continuous suffering inside the prison system. A trans visitor who is detained should expect documents and hearings to use a name and gender marker they do not recognise.
TUN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry screening, visa conditions, airport document checks or border treatment of trans travellers, so exposure at the point of entry is unresolved rather than assessed.

The inventory does not establish whether Tunisia has hate-crime or anti-discrimination provisions covering gender identity, nor whether any such provision is enforced; protection machinery beyond the criminal law is not sourced here.

Whether Article 226 bis has been used against gender expression in any specific prosecution with a known sentence is not documented in these sources; its application to gender expression is asserted in the record without a cited case.

Current prison population figures for transgender detainees, and any post-2024 change to legal gender recognition practice, are not sourced and remain open.

CMR.name: Cameroon
CMR.summary:
Article 347-1 of the Cameroonian penal code criminalises same-sex conduct and carries a sentence of up to five years' imprisonment. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, replacing a colonial-era sodomy provision under which sentences ranged between six months and five years. Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise same-sex conduct, and a 2020 assessment described it as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. Reporting places Cameroon among the states in Africa with the highest prosecution rates.

Trans women have been prosecuted on the basis of clothing and gender presentation. In February 2021 a court in Douala convicted Shakiro, a trans woman with a Facebook and YouTube following, and her friend Patricia, charging them with attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification. Both received the maximum statutory term of five years plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs each. Defence lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu described the judgment as a political decision supported by no proof of any act, and an appeal was filed. The two women spent five months in prison before release pending appeal in 2021. Shakiro subsequently fled Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.

Appearance alone has served as the basis for prosecution. In November 2011 a Cameroonian court jailed Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome for five years after they were seen wearing women's clothes and ordering Baileys; the original judge cited their dress, speech and the drink as proof that they were gay. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013, with defence lawyer Alice Nkom arguing the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcoming the outcome. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance and served a three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison. In November 2011 three young men received five years for oral sex in a parked car.

Human Rights Watch documented a sharp rise in violence against LGBTI people in 2022. From 9 March of that year security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, over alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity; gendarmes beat two detainees. The organisation's researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi stated that the criminalisation law allows both civilians and security forces to abuse LGBTI people without consequence. Beatings of gay and trans people in public are reported as common.

The Law on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime (Law No. 2010/012, Article 83(1)) criminalises online same-sex sexual propositions with one to two years' imprisonment and fines of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, doubled where intercourse followed.

There is no legal gender recognition procedure and no documented name-change or identification and marker process; no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covers gender identity or sexual orientation. Failure to carry identification was itself charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts in the 2021 case against Shakiro and Patricia. A US State Department report noted harassment and extortion of gay and lesbian people by law enforcement and the use of false allegations to harass or extort.

Detention carries additional risk. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as hell, and Kondengui Central Prison held Jean-Claude Roger Mbede for three years. Few lawyers are willing to defend people accused in homosexuality cases. Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organisation, shut down after a police raid, removing a service base.

No Cameroonian visa policy, entry-refusal rule or border-admission procedure for LGBTQ travellers is described in the sources. The nearest material concerns outbound movement: in July 2010 the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities. In August 2011 a gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the UK Border Agency after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé. In May 2012 the UK Border Agency sought to return asylum seeker Ediage Valerie Ekwedde, finding no credible evidence that he was gay. In May 2005 the government threatened medical examinations to prove homosexual activity among eleven men arrested at a nightclub.

sources.summary:
Criminalisation and sentences: In February 2021 two Cameroonian transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in Douala for wearing women's clothing in a restaurant and convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification. Identification failure was therefore charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts, and both women received five years. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. No information on legal gender recognition, name change, or ID and marker procedures appears.

Entry and visa: No visa policy, entry-refusal, or border-admission procedure for Cameroon is described. The nearest material concerns outbound asylum. In July 2010 the UK granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities and that 'he is not the only gay person in Cameroon.' A link to UK government travel advice on Cameroonian laws and customs is listed; no Cameroonian entry rule for LGBTQ travelers is given.

Border and carriage screening: A gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the UK Border Agency in August 2011 after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé. In May 2012 the UK Border Agency sought to return asylum-seeker Ediage Valerie Ekwedde, finding 'no credible evidence' that he was gay, but held him in custody after he threatened to 'make a fuss' on the return flight. In May 2005 the government threatened medical examinations to 'prove' the homosexual activity of 11 men arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy. No Cameroonian border screening procedure is set out.

Facilities: Mbede served a three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as 'hell', and Shakiro and Patricia spent five months in prison before release pending appeal in 2021. Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organization, shut down after a police raid, removing a service base. Three young men were sentenced to five years in November 2011 for oral sex in a parked car, and two men received five years on the basis of appearance, women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor.

Care access: Healthcare, HIV, and medication access for transgender visitors is not described. The service findings are institutional: Alternatives-Cameroon was forced to shut down after a police raid, and few lawyers are willing to defend the accused in homosexuality cases. The 2005 threat of medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity among detained men represents coercive contact with health services rather than care.

State and media hostility: In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, boosting circulation and drawing criticism from the state communication council for privacy invasion, while President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy and continued prosecuting people accused of homosexual activity. In 1921 Günther Teonmann documented a same-sex custom among the Bafia people, where the 'kiembe' stage begins around age 15 and involves close male sexual friendships with a 'lexan', with consent symbolized by sharing earthnuts from a basketry plate, and where a father might later name his newborn after the lexan regardless of gender. Outcomes are not uniform. The 2013 appeals-court acquittal of Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, welcomed by Amnesty International, shows that convictions resting on appearance and stereotype can be reversed, while the Shakiro judgment shows the same evidence base producing the maximum statutory term. Adjacent background from US State Department reporting lists killings, torture, harsh prisons and arbitrary abuses by security forces alongside anti-gay discrimination, situating LGBTI mistreatment within a broader record of abuse rather than a distinct regime.

TZA.name: Tanzania
TZA.summary:
Same-sex activity is criminalised across Tanzania. Under the Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998, section 138A treats 'gross indecency' between men as an offence carrying one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of TSh 100,000 to 300,000, and the maximum penalty available for same-sex conduct between men is life imprisonment. Heterosexual oral and anal sex are also offences under the same framework.

The semi-autonomous island jurisdiction of Zanzibar operates its own criminal statute, the Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004, enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives, so a visitor may fall under two overlapping criminal-law regimes depending on location. Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934, as amended in 2004, outlaws sex between women with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine, and defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania. A partner cannot be sponsored for entry, inherited from, or recognised as next of kin on the basis of a relationship status, and adoption is restricted to a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly.

Enforcement has taken the form of organised persecution. In 2018 a 'witch hunt' against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam, where gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and were tortured; the Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner, Paul Makonda, announced a 17-strong committee of police, lawyers and doctors tasked with identifying and punishing homosexuals and scouring the internet for videos of supposedly LGBTQ people. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the basis of 'promoting homosexuality', directly disrupting services.

Amnesty International's January 2024 report, 'We Are Facing Extinction', documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people at national level, within a documented climate of discrimination that limits how far rights can be enjoyed in practice. Proposed legislation on same-sex relations was deferred after protests.

In June 2024 the UN Human Rights Office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on Mauzinde, a Tanzanian transgender activist from Rahaleo: she was abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut. The UN called for bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ+ people and flagged possible violations of ICCPR article 20 and the equality guarantees of Tanzania's Constitution under article 13.

OONI measurement data published in a 2024 report, 'Tanzania: Surge in online LGBTIQ censorship', documents state-directed blocking of LGBTIQ websites, social networks and rights sites, constraining access to information of direct use to LGBT visitors and residents.

A 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. A 2020 interview with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists records substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence and the denial of basic rights.

Health services carry formal non-discrimination duties: the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services regardless of 'age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference'; the Nursing and Midwifery (Practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation; and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. Tanzania's HIV/AIDS rate is high, with roughly one million people infected.
TZA.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Tanzania was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the criminalisation findings above are therefore sourced to other inventories, and the profile's own framing of penalties remains unverified for this pass.

Whether the mainland maximum of life imprisonment has been applied in a reported conviction in recent years is not established in the available sources; the inventory supplies the statutory maximum and the section 138A range but no case-level sentencing data.

The inventory states no youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family-planning counselling language, and does not resolve how Zanzibar's statute is enforced against visitors in practice or whether mainland authorities recognise island convictions.

Amnesty International's January 2024 report, 'We Are Facing Extinction', documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people at national level, within a documented climate of discrimination that limits how far rights can be enjoyed in practice. Proposed legislation on same-sex relations was deferred after protests.

In June 2024 a UN human rights office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on a transgender activist from a local LGBTI organisation: she was abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut. The UN called for bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ+ people and flagged possible violations of ICCPR article 20 and the equality guarantees of the national constitution under article 13.

Measurement data published in a 2024 report on online LGBTIQ censorship documents government-directed blocking of LGBTIQ websites, social networks and rights sites, constraining access to information of direct use to LGBT visitors and residents.

A 2013 Human Rights Watch and a local coalition's report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in a southern city who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. A 2020 interview with three pseudonymised LGBT activists records substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence and the denial of basic rights.

Health services carry formal non-discrimination duties: national family-planning guidelines from 2013 commit to services regardless of 'age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference'; nursing and midwifery practice regulations from 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation; and national guidelines from 2017 require non-discriminatory care. The national HIV/AIDS rate is high, with roughly one million people infected.

The inventory states no youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family-planning counselling language, and does not resolve how the state/province's statute is enforced against visitors in practice or whether national authorities recognise its convictions.

ETH.name: Ethiopia
ETH.summary:
Same-sex conduct between men and between women is a criminal offence in Ethiopia under Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code. Enforcement is comparatively rare, but the provision underpins pervasive stigma, harassment and violence against LGBTIQ+ people and drives near-total concealment of identity. Stakeholder submissions to Ethiopia's Universal Periodic Review report penalties of up to one year, with harsher terms under aggravating provisions, while a 2009 academic study of the same legal framework reports a maximum of three years for male homosexuality. Sources differ on the ceiling and the discrepancy is not resolved here.

The absence of any legal gender recognition mechanism compounds that exposure. Ethiopia has neither a surgical nor a psychiatric pathway for changing legal gender, so trans men remain legally women and trans women legally men. A trans person whose partner is of the sex recorded on their documents can therefore be treated as committing a same-sex offence, whatever the relationship looks like in practice. No hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covers gender identity, and there is no statutory protection from arbitrary arrest on grounds of gender identity or expression.

Enforcement is episodic and public. On 10 August 2023 security forces raided hospitality venues in Addis Ababa, shutting guest houses and arresting managers; the Addis Ababa Peace and Security Administration Bureau announced measures against hotels, restaurants, guest houses and entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts, and called on the public to report such incidents. Activists documented surveillance, entrapment and rising harassment and violence toward the end of 2023, alongside warrantless residential searches following neighbour complaints and physical abuse during detention.

Non-state actors carry much of the day-to-day risk. In August 2023 an online incitement campaign ended in physical attacks, including a 2 August video calling for gay men to be stabbed and a threat reading "We should find them and kill them." Being outed risks physical violence and ostracism, and ILGA World recorded a 2014 case in which a gay man was denied legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, with no trial records found. In January 2021 police disclosed the sexual orientation of two people released from detention to their families; one subsequently died by suicide.

Discrimination is documented across education, employment, housing and healthcare, with no statutory protection in any of them. LGBTI organisations cannot register: Article 69 of the Charities and Societies Proclamation bars them as contrary to public morality, and Pride events are not permitted, though national LGBTI organisations operate despite the ban. Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition. Christian and Muslim religious bodies campaign for harsher penalties, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church restating its position in June 2024.
ETH.outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty under Article 629 remains unresolved. The Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission gives up to one year with harsher terms under aggravation; a 2009 master's thesis gives up to three years for male homosexuality; Outright International describes the offence without a figure. The inventory contains no consolidated judicial reading that settles the ceiling.

No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening rules as they apply to trans visitors, including whether passport gender markers are examined on arrival, whether a visitor can be refused entry on gender-identity grounds, or which authority handles such decisions. Nothing here should be read as evidence that such screening does or does not occur.

Similarly unsourced: toilet and facility rules for visitors, availability of gender-affirming care to non-residents, recognition of foreign marriages or foreign gender markers, and any consular assistance pathway for a trans traveller detained in Ethiopia. Whether the conduct offence has ever been applied to a foreign visitor is also not documented in the inventory.

Several claims rest on a single tertiary compilation rather than primary documentation, including the 2008 petition interception, the 2012 conference cancellation, early-2010s media self-censorship, and the 2008 Sheraton Addis ceremony. F&M Global Barometers scores are an instrument's coding rather than a direct reading of statute, and its "no" on every axis from 2011 to 2024 should be read as such. The Outright International country overview carries an update date of 12 March 2026, later than other sources, and its description of the August 2023 crackdown as an official action against "homosexuality" is the organisation's characterisation.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Ethiopia: same-sex conduct is criminalised, and concealment of identity is the norm. In the early 2010s some Ethiopian media outlets, cooperating with the government, restricted discussion of "LGBTQ ideology" without enacting the policy into law. Internet censorship has limited LGBTQ organising; in 2008 a petition for equal rights signed by hundreds of gay people was blocked en route to Prime Minister Meles Zenawi's office, and a pro-gay conference scheduled for Addis Ababa in 2012 was cancelled after fundamentalist Christian and religious groups called organizers "missionaries of evil." In 2023 the House of Guramayle reported online harassment of self-identified gay, lesbian and transgender people on platforms including TikTok, citing an August 2 video calling for gay men to be stabbed and a threat reading "We should find them and kill them." In July 2021 German authorities ordered the deportation of a trans woman of Qatari origin holding Ethiopian citizenship. She testified that after someone discovered she was registered as male in her passport and attempted extortion, she was reported to Ethiopian authorities, held about a year in an Ethiopian men's prison and subjected to physical and sexual abuse by staff and inmates. German officials argued she would be safe because she could "pass" as cisgender, citing the absence of explicit laws regarding gender identity. On 10 August 2023 the government raided hospitality venues in Addis Ababa to crack down on alleged homosexual activity, shutting down guest houses and arresting managers, while the Addis Ababa Peace and Security Administration Bureau announced measures "against hotels, restaurants, guest houses, and other entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts" and called on the public to report such incidents. ILGA World recorded police residential searches without warrants following neighbour complaints, physical abuse during detention, and a 2014 case in which a gay man was denied legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, with no trial records found. In January 2021 police disclosed the sexual orientation of two people released from detention to their families, and one subsequently died by suicide. The AIDS Resource Center in Addis Ababa reported that the majority of self-identified gay and lesbian callers, mostly male, requested help changing their behavior to avoid discrimination, with many gay men reporting anxiety, confusion, identity crises, depression, self-ostracism, religious conflict and suicide attempts. Stigma and discrimination toward people living with HIV/AIDS affected residents' ability to receive an education, find employment and integrate into the community. In early December 2011 Christian and Muslim religious leaders tried to derail a sexual health seminar targeted at men who have sex with men; the government intervened and the seminar went ahead at a different location. Organizers of the 2014 anti-gay rally and religious figures publicly blamed gay people for the rape of children and young men, and an anonymous LGBTQ activist told the AP in 2019 of wide misconceptions that gay people may be culpable for rising rape incidence, a climate that deters young people from seeking services. The DANA Social Club, founded 2013 by Beki Abiy, campaigns for transgender people's rights to sex reassignment surgery. Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition. In 2008 an unofficial gay marriage took place at the Sheraton Addis in Addis Ababa, and in Nuer society researcher Brian MacDermot encountered a transgender woman, formerly a man who dressed as a woman, who received spiritual approval to change status and marry a husband, suggesting precolonial acceptance of gender fluidity. In December 2008 nearly a dozen Ethiopian religious figures, including the leader of Ethiopian Muslims and heads of the Orthodox, Protestant and Catholic churches, adopted a resolution urging lawmakers to ban homosexual activity in the constitution, and religious figures that month held homosexuality responsible for a rise in sexual attacks on children and young men. In March 2014 the Council of Ministers endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a "non-pardonable" offence, but the government later cancelled both that bill and a planned April 2014 anti-gay rally, with spokesman Redwan Hussien saying the current jail term was deemed sufficient. The Addis Ababa Youth Forum, together with a church group linked to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, had planned the rally for 26 April 2014 alongside debate on the proposed bill; group chairman Dereje Negash claimed "Children are being raped by gay people in this country." The US Department of State's 2011 Human Rights Report found that stigma and discrimination toward people living with HIV/AIDS impacted residents' ability to receive an education. Historically, David F. Greenberg reported that shepherd boys of the Amhara and Qemant developed homosexual relationships with one another until marriage.

ETH.tangentialFactors:
The LGBTIQ+ legal framework sits inside a wider pattern of constrained civic space. US State Department human rights reports for 2010 and 2011 document restrictions on civil society under the Charities and Societies Proclamation, anti-terrorism prosecutions, torture and harsh prison conditions, alongside their sections on the criminalisation of same-sex conduct; those general conditions bear on what happens to anyone detained in Ethiopia.

Periodic moves toward harsher punishment have been floated and withdrawn. In March 2014 the Council of Ministers endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a non-pardonable offence, but the government later cancelled both that bill and a planned April 2014 anti-gay rally, a spokesman saying the existing jail term was deemed sufficient. In December 2008 religious leaders, including the head of Ethiopian Muslims and leaders of the Orthodox, Protestant and Catholic churches, adopted a resolution urging lawmakers to ban homosexual activity in the constitution.

The F&M Global Barometers time series scores Ethiopia "no" on every protection axis in every year from 2011 to 2024, indicating no measurable movement in either direction over thirteen years. Parallel constraints on expression are documented too: some media outlets restricted discussion of "LGBTQ ideology" in the early 2010s, a 2008 petition for equal rights signed by hundreds of gay people was blocked before reaching the prime minister's office, and a 2012 conference in Addis Ababa was cancelled after religious groups called organisers "missionaries of evil."

Historical accounts suggest earlier, more fluid arrangements. Research on Amhara and Qemant shepherd boys records same-sex relationships before marriage, and a researcher's account from Nuer society describes a person who changed social status and married a husband with community approval. These are historical observations, not present legal protections.
ETH.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Ghana (0.24 — Ghana's near-passed bill signals worse trajectory; Ethiopia's steady-state is worse today), above Tanzania (0.18) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts, visible community, and a 2023 Supreme Court NGO-registration win).
