LBN.name: Lebanon
LBN.summary:
Lebanon penalises transgender expression both explicitly and through general morality provisions. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for "men disguising themselves as women", a provision that reaches trans feminine presentation directly. Article 534, which punishes "intercourse contrary to the order of nature" with up to one year of imprisonment, remains in force. A regional country review concludes that the state employs both de facto and explicit criminalisation, with transgender women bearing the greatest exposure.

Policing of trans and gender-nonconforming people is documented rather than theoretical. Human Rights Watch reported in April 2022 that trans people in Lebanon face policing and documentation barriers, and called on the state to guarantee access to legal gender recognition. Prosecutors have ordered intrusive anal examinations, including after a 2012 cinema raid in which 36 people were arrested, and Article 534 has been used to harass and persecute LGBT people through police arrests.

The article has nonetheless been refused application by a long run of courts. JOR.name: Jordan
JOR.summary:
Jordan does not criminalise same-sex relations. The historic-era ban was abolished by the 1951 Penal Code, which legalised private, adult, consensual same-sex acts with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or orientation. No statute on the books prohibits gender expression as such, and the 1951 reform left no anti-discrimination protection in its place.

That baseline does not translate into safety. Human Rights Watch reported on 6 June 2024 that authorities in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait substitute public-morality and debauchery provisions for formal criminalisation, using them to harass LGBT people. Vague morality provisions give security forces and private individuals licence to target LGBT people with impunity, and Human Rights Watch found Jordan's cybercrime and morality laws being used to persecute them.

Legal gender recognition has no clear pathway. Intersex people can change official gender markers; transgender people cannot. OutRight International records that marker changes are allowed in some cases without any defined procedure being published.

Gender-affirming surgery turns on intersex status. Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018 permits such procedures for intersex people and criminalises them for transgender people, with CAIRO 52 recording penalties of up to 10 years' imprisonment for sex reassignment except in intersex cases. The same 2018 law outlaws changing of sex while permitting correction of sex, wording that also exposes doctors who perform gender-affirming surgery to medical-liability penalties.

In Case No. 2092/2014 the Court of Cassation allowed a plaintiff born in 1977 to change name and gender from male to female in official records after hormone therapy and surgery undertaken in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically. The court justified the change by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex rather than transgender.

Speech and digital access are restricted. A cybercrime law promulgated in August 2023 can target digital content on gender and sexuality as well as activists advocating LGBT rights. Human Rights Watch reported on 11 January 2024 that the authorities limited civic space during 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online, with peaceful dissidents and journalists arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws and intrusive digital surveillance applied. The Press and Publication Law, amended in 1998 and 2004, replaced a ban on depicting sexual perversion with a requirement that the press respect the values of the Arab and Islamic nation.

Security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave. On 4 December 2023 Human Rights Watch reported that Jordanian authorities systematically targeted LGBT rights activists in a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality. Officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation, social-media users posted their photographs alongside messages inciting violence, and two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation; several organisations shut down, suspended activities or their staff fled.
JOR.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Case No. 2092/2014 establishes a binding precedent for transgender marker changes, or remains a one-off decision routed through an intersex reclassification, is unresolved in the sources available here.

The figure of up to 10 years' imprisonment for sex reassignment comes from CAIRO 52's analysis of the case; the operative statutory text and article number behind that penalty were not independently verified in this inventory, and the sources do not reconcile it with Article 8 of the 2018 medical-liability law.

OutRight International's statement that marker changes are allowed in some cases is not accompanied by a description of the procedure, the deciding authority, or the criteria applied.

The relationship between the cybercrime law promulgated in August 2023 and the new cybercrime law described by Human Rights Watch in January 2024 is not resolved here; they may be the same instrument or successive ones.

CAIRO 52 refers to new legislation curtailing LGBTQ speech and digital access without naming the instruments in the material supplied, so the specific statutes behind that claim remain unverified.

sources.summary: The Jordanian government tolerates a few cafés in Amman that are widely considered gay-friendly. Books@Cafe, opened in 1997, remains a popular bookstore and cafe for patrons supportive of creativity, diversity and tolerance. Homosexuality has not been criminal in Jordan since the 1951 penal code, which legalised private, adult, non-commercial, consensual same-sex acts with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or orientation. The 2018 Medical Responsibility Law vaguely outlawed changing of sex while legalising correction of sex, potentially criminalising doctors performing gender-affirming surgery. Honor killings as a legal justification for murder were made illegal under the 2013 revised Penal Code. In my country, most magazines rejected me and my ideas due to my young age at the time, and I felt like an outcast in my own society!" IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.summary:
Iraq is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a trans visitor. On 27 April 2024 the Council of Representatives passed an amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression. The President signed the legislation on 29 June 2024 and it has been in force since 1 July 2024. The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor, Human Rights Watch and ILGA Asia all record it as the operative legal baseline.

The penalties are severe. Consensual same-sex relations carry 10 to 15 years' imprisonment. Undergoing or performing a gender-affirming procedure carries 1 to 3 years, applied to both the transgender person and the doctor, which places transition itself beyond the law; court-ordered procedures on intersex people are excluded. VEN.name: Venezuela
VEN.summary:
Venezuela does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct: the age of consent is 16 and applies identically to same-sex relations, and homosexuality is legal. The country has no hate-crime statute and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, so conduct directed at trans people attracts no dedicated penalty. Visitors should note that legality on paper has not prevented police action: in May 2026 NGOs including the Observatorio Venezolano de Violencias LGBTIQ+, Caleidoscopio Humano and Movimiento SOMOS denounced the detention of around 30 people in a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto, Lara state, where officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, extorted detainees and accused them of 'committing the crime of homosexuality'.

There is no working legal gender recognition route. A 2017 constitutional action filed before the Supreme Justice Tribunal requires each case to be assessed individually against certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist certifying the veracity of the intended sexual identity, and the Tribunal has still not granted the requested name and gender changes. Identity documents are equally blocked: SAIME announced in September 2016 that transgender people may request an identity card matching their gender identity, but no administrative procedure or mechanism exists to enact the relevant article, leaving trans visitors and residents without a document that reflects their gender.

Conditions have deteriorated alongside the political crisis. The Washington Blade reported on 10 September 2024 that LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution following the disputed July 2024 election, with the persecution tied directly to the political upheaval; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 September 2024. The European Union Asylum Agency maintains a dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of Venezuela within its country-focus material covering the reference period through 2025, used in international protection decisions, and AFS and the Vance Center published an LGBTQ guide on Venezuela in October 2024.

The statute book offers trans and LGB visitors little protection elsewhere as well. The law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions. Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children, although lesbian couples are permitted to access IVF, and an equal-marriage bill was slated for introduction to the National Assembly in January 2014 with no later enactment recorded.
VEN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or border-document rules for trans travellers, including whether a passport or entry record may carry a gender marker that differs from presentation, or whether immigration screening risks disclosure. That layer remains unsourced here.

Whether the Supreme Justice Tribunal has granted any name or gender change since the 2017 constitutional action was filed is not resolved; the available material records only that none has been granted.

There is no reported outcome, prosecution or disciplinary follow-up for the May 2026 police raid in Barquisimeto, Lara state, beyond the NGOs' denunciation. The independence of the officers' conduct and any accountability measures are not documented in this inventory.

The status of the January 2014 equal-marriage bill after its reported introduction is unresolved, as is whether any anti-discrimination or hate-crime measure has been tabled since. Public-opinion figures cited are dated to 2013, 2023 and 2023 respectively and are not current.

BOL.name: Bolivia
BOL.summary:
Bolivia's 2016 Gender Identity Law grants legal recognition on the basis of self-declared identity through an administrative procedure, permitting a change of name and legal gender marker without surgery, sterilisation or a medical diagnosis. Gender identity is a protected ground in the country's anti-discrimination legislation.

The 2009 Constitution prohibits discrimination and protects bodily integrity: Article 15(II) addresses violence and Article 45(V) addresses maternity, while Title VIII of the Penal Code governs abortion. Formal protection has not produced equal treatment in practice. The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia recorded the constitutional guarantee against discrimination alongside persistent societal discrimination against LGBT people, and a first national virtual survey published by Agencia Presentes in December 2024 found severe exclusion of LGBTI people across Bolivian society.

PRY.name: Paraguay
PRY.summary:
Paraguay has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. Trans people are not allowed to change their name and gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

Amnesty International's 2025-26 report records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents, evidence that the documentary gap reaches administrative encounters rather than staying theoretical.

There is no general anti-discrimination law covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime statute is recorded in the sources. A November 2015 bill to ban discrimination on those grounds has not advanced since its introduction. Protections that do exist are narrow and sector-specific, addressing sexual orientation in dormitory placement, violence against women, stateless persons, personal data and the internal staffing rules of one public office. None supplies a general remedy to a trans visitor refused service, accommodation or police assistance.

Violence and discrimination against LGBT people remain frequent in Paraguay and are often ignored by the police. An Associated Press report of September 2025 found that discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into migration and sex work, a pattern that shapes the settings a trans visitor may move through.

Official hostility is documented at national and municipal level alike. The government banned discussion of LGBT issues in public schools in October 2017, and the Minister of Education said he might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March, per Amnesty International. Horacio Cartes, a senior ruling-party figure, said in 2017 that he would "shoot himself in the testicles" if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in Paraguayan law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights has held in an advisory opinion that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage; Paraguay is an OAS party and is bound by the ruling, while domestic law has not been brought into line. A trans visitor's partner therefore has no standing under local law.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Paraguay since 1990. The sources record an age of consent of 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct.

Healthcare carries one trans-specific entitlement. Resolution 695, approved by the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare in October 2016, requires that health service officials record and treat transgender patients under their identified social name on medical records, medical histories and forms. Law 7018 on Mental Health, enacted 15 November 2022, states that a mental health diagnosis cannot be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity.
PRY.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory gives an outcome, a hearing date or an expected timetable for the ten name-recognition lawsuits or for the communications before the UN Human Rights Committee; both are recorded as pending with no decision.

Hate-crime legislation is not addressed anywhere in the inventory. Whether Paraguay has a statute covering offences motivated by gender identity, or what penalties such a statute would carry, is not sourced here.

Whether Resolution 695 remains in force, and how consistently hospitals and clinics apply the social name requirement, is not documented in the sources available for this entry.

The age-of-consent difference of 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct rests on a secondary reference work rather than on a quoted provision of the Penal Code; the current statutory text is not reproduced in the inventory.

Amnesty International's count of identity-document refusals covers two trans migrants and no wider figure for refusals issued to trans people is available. The Asunción city council's ban on the commemorative event is reported without a date for the council decision, and the defender's death is given only as March.

Nothing in the inventory records whether the inter-American advisory opinion has been invoked in Paraguayan litigation to challenge the marriage bar, or how courts have responded.

Adoption-law reality check.

sources.summary: During the Stroessner dictatorship (1954-1989) LGBT people faced heavy persecution. In the 1959 Caso 108, police arrested and tortured 108 gay men in Asunción and made their names public, and the government publicly encouraged hatred and violence against LGBT people. Violence and discrimination against LGBT community members remain frequent in Paraguay today and are often ignored by the police. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Paraguay since 1990, though the age of consent is 16 for homosexuals and 14 for heterosexuals. There is no broad anti-discrimination law, and a November 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction. Limited protections exist in specific contexts: Law 5162/2014 requires that collective dormitory placement for adolescents take into account age, sexual orientation and degree of psychic development; Decree 6973 under Law 577/2016 protects women from violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation; Law 6149/2018 bars discrimination against stateless persons based on sexual orientation and gender identity; Law 6534/2020 treats sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data; Article 28 of the Ministry of Public Defense internal rules prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation against employees. In October 2017 the Government of Paraguay implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues within public schools, and the Minister of Education said it might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Transgender people are not allowed to legally change their name and gender on official documents, though in December 2016 two transgender women filed a lawsuit to change their names citing constitutional free expression and identity provisions. In October 2016 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved Resolution 695 requiring that all transgender people may use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms, and that health service officials must treat transgender patients using their identified social name. Law 7018 on Mental Health (enacted 15 November 2022) states that a mental health diagnosis cannot be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity.

The limited anti-discrimination provisions operate in separate compartments. Law 5162/2014 requires that collective dormitory placement for adolescents take account of age, sexual orientation and degree of psychic development. Decree 6973 issued under Law 577/2016 protects women from violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation. Law 6149/2018 bars discrimination against stateless persons on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Law 6534/2020 treats sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data. Article 28 of the Ministry of Public Defense's internal rules prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation against its own employees. The November 2015 bill that would have generalised these protections has not moved since introduction.

The October 2017 school policy constrains what residents can encounter in public education: discussion of LGBT issues is banned in public schools, and the education minister floated burning books that raise awareness about transgender people.

Resolution 695 of October 2016 governs everyday healthcare contact for trans residents, obliging health service officials to use the patient's social name across records, histories and forms. Law 7018 on Mental Health, of 15 November 2022, bars a mental health diagnosis resting exclusively on sexual choice or identity.

GTM.name: Guatemala
GTM.summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing in Guatemalan law criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 of the victims saying they intended to flee the country.

Guatemalan officials have excluded trans women from the protection of the country's femicide legislation, justifying the exclusion on the stated ground that trans women are not "biological women". Central American governments have long maintained that exclusion, and it underpins the documented violence context for trans people in Guatemala.

There is no legal gender recognition in Guatemalan law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' 2017 Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 requires states to provide legal gender recognition and marriage equality, and Guatemala was among the Latin American countries urged in January 2018 to abide by it. Compliance by Guatemala is not recorded in the available material.

Legislative activity runs against trans rights rather than toward them. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2022 on an anti-trans bill in Guatemala that threatened rights, including provisions that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

Detention carries a specific, documented risk. Human Rights Watch's October 2020 report, which examines violence and discrimination against LGBT people in El Salvador, includes a Guatemala chapter finding that trans women are held in men's prisons on the basis of birth sex, with no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on trans custody. Bárbara Herrarte, a trans activist with Redmmutrans (Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans), described her time in a men's prison: "Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him." Lambda also flags forced internal displacement arising from violence.
GTM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Guatemala has implemented Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 is unresolved in the sources available here; January 2018 coverage records that Guatemala was urged to abide by it, and no later compliance record is sourced.

The fate of the January 2022 anti-trans bill, including whether it was enacted, amended or defeated, is not sourced in this inventory.

Not sourced in this inventory: entry and visa rules for trans travellers, document and marker requirements at Guatemalan border control, airport or security screening practices, hate-crime protection and its enforcement, restroom and facility access, healthcare or hormone access, and recognition of partners or marriages. These remain open questions rather than findings.

The 2022 violence figures come from a civil-society observatory rather than Guatemalan state statistics, and no official counter-figure is available here.

Governments across the subregion have long maintained that exclusion, and it underpins the documented violence context for trans people in the country.

There is no legal gender recognition in national law. The regional human rights court's 2017 advisory opinion requires states to provide legal gender recognition and marriage equality, and the country was among several in the region urged in January 2018 to abide by it. Compliance by the country is not recorded in the available material.

Legislative activity runs against trans rights rather than toward them. A human rights organisation reported in January 2022 on an anti-trans bill in the country that threatened rights, including provisions that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

Detention carries a specific, documented risk. A human rights organisation's October 2020 report, which examines violence and discrimination against LGBT people in a neighbouring jurisdiction, includes a chapter on this country finding that trans women are held in men's prisons on the basis of birth sex, with no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on trans custody. A trans activist with a trans-led national network described her time in a men's prison: "Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him." A local LGBT organisation also flags forced internal displacement arising from violence.

HND.name: Honduras
HND.summary:
Nothing in Honduran law criminalises a person's gender identity. The Penal Code, amended by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility (Article 27); punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights, or refuses a professional service, on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages (Article 321); and punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on listed grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity with three to five years' imprisonment and fines of L.50,000 to L.300,000 (Article 321-A). LGBTI rights groups met Congress during the reform process to press for the wording of Articles 321 and 321-A to be retained, and the anti-discrimination provisions were kept. A name change for LGBTI persons is approved in Honduras.

The enforcement picture is severe. Honduras has one of the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, and trans women face the greatest obstacles to obtaining justice. The LAWG Education Fund attributes the resulting impunity to under-reporting, a lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and the intentional mishandling of cases, concluding that the institutions fail to effectively investigate and prosecute. The US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among the country's significant human rights issues. Human Rights Watch finds that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks, with officials in the region describing them as not biological women; Vicky Hernandez v Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case.

Police conduct carries specific risk for trans visitors and residents. Human Rights Watch's May 2009 report, Not Worth a Penny, documents police rape, assault and extortion of transgender people in Honduras. The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits police to raid streets, entrap sex workers under sanitation control, and arrest anyone who goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals; LGBTQ organisations document repeated use of that provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space. Early LGBTQ organisations also faced police harassment despite formal association rights under the Constitution, and initial attempts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays.

Detention is a documented danger. Transgender women are held in the men's prison system. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the La Isla module beside the mentally ill unit; trans women are forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women, and denied conjugal visits, with guards stating that they are men. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after intervention by the torture-prevention centre CPTRT was she isolated from male prisoners and her belongings returned. Placement follows birth sex with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad hoc protective isolation, and there is no placement-by-gender-identity policy. Human Rights Watch reported in October 2020 that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse; a Honduran judge described a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, told prosecutors, and saw no investigation, stating that there is no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.

Partner and family recognition is barred. The 2005 constitutional amendment expressly prohibits same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses to recognise same-sex marriages or unions performed lawfully abroad (Article 112), and bars same-sex couples from adopting (Article 116); same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are ineligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.

Trans visibility has grown alongside the security costs attached to it. A trans activist and co-founder of Asociacion Cozumel Trans ran for Congress in Francisco Morazan for the PINU party at the 26 November 2017 election, potentially becoming the first openly trans officeholder; she had won her party primary earlier that year, and Claudia Spellman had run for the LIBRE party in 2012. Victoria Gomez sought asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in San Pedro Sula in July 2017.

Public services are offered without formal exclusion but are constrained in practice. The government provides medical care to all citizens and has worked increasingly with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, yet the influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant churches has made comprehensive public programmes difficult to implement, and no youth-specific care or medication provisions appear. Police harassment and political hostility remain live factors: the two major parties have largely ignored LGBTQ rights, three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats, President Juan Orlando Hernández stated on 12 October 2018 that as a Christian he opposes same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association has urged President Xiomara Castro to stop immoral laws.

No procedure details are given for how an LGBTI person obtains a name change in Honduras, beyond the fact that it is approved and that church leaders have attacked it; the documentary requirements, processing time and whether the change extends to a passport or national identity card are unresolved.

No youth-specific care or medication provisions appear in the sources reviewed; whether gender-affirming healthcare is available, restricted or publicly funded is not sourced either way.

The 2017 congressional candidacy is described as potentially the first openly trans officeholder, and the sources do not confirm whether she won; the outcome of that election is unresolved here.

Case-level outcomes for the killings of LGBTI activists referenced in the GlobalGayz archive, and the current enforcement record for Articles 321 and 321-A since March 2017, are not sourced in this inventory.

Under the Constitution, citizens may establish and associate with political parties and interest groups, but initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met with government opposition or extended delays. The first organizations arose anyway, often in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing, and were essentially ignored by the Government apart from police harassment. In 2004 the Government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups despite organized protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula. Penal Code Article 321-A (Decree No. 23-2013) punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on listed grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity with three to five years' imprisonment and fines of L.50,000 to L.300,000.

Same-sex unions are not legally recognized. The 2005 constitutional amendment expressly bans same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses to recognize same-sex marriages or unions performed legally in other countries (Article 112), and prohibits same-sex couples from adopting (Article 116). Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A name change for LGBTI persons is approved, described by the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association as an 'aberration in God's eyes'; no procedure details are given.

The Government offers medical care to all citizens and has been increasingly working with non-governmental organizations to raise awareness on HIV/AIDS, but the socially conservative influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestants has made it difficult to implement any comprehensive public program. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups. In 2013 the National Congress adopted amendments to the Penal Code via Decree No. 23-2013. SLV.name: El Salvador
SLV.summary:
El Salvador has no Gender Identity Law and no legal recognition of gender identity. A trans visitor carrying documents issued in another country has no domestic mechanism through which those documents could be aligned or challenged, and Salvadoran citizens face the same absence: in 2022 the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court ordered the Name Law reformed so that individuals could change their names to match their gender identity, holding the existing regime unconstitutional because it discriminated on the basis of gender, after a case brought by a transgender activist in 2016. As of 2023 the Legislative Assembly had enacted nothing, so transgender Salvadorans still cannot update official papers.

The penal code carries an enhanced penalty for bias-motivated killing. In September 2015 the National Assembly approved reforms under which homicides motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender draw 30 to 60 years under Article 129. The same 2015 reforms added sexual orientation and gender identity provisions to the Criminal Code carrying three to six years' imprisonment for discriminatory acts.

The limits of that framework are illustrated by the killing of Camila Díaz Córdova, a transgender Salvadoran woman deported from the United States, who was killed in January 2019. On 28 July 2020 a San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of her murder and sentenced each to 20 years. The judgment was the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for the killing of a transgender person; Human Rights Watch called it pivotal for transgender Salvadorans' rights, and advocates had argued during the prosecution that it could produce the country's first hate-crime homicide conviction.

Enforcement remains thin. About 500 hate crimes against LGBTQ people were reported between 1998 and 2015, with many more unattributed, and police have shown open refusal to cooperate in LGBT death investigations. Human Rights Watch reported in October 2020 that El Salvador, alongside Guatemala and Honduras, fails to address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people effectively, driving asylum claims abroad, and documented obstacles to obtaining protection in a full report issued in January 2021 with recommendations to the president, attorney general, congress and ministries. The peer-reviewed longitudinal dataset on killings of LGBTI+ people covering 2000 to 2020 was published by researchers at the Fundação Oswaldo Cruz in 2024.

Since the state of exception began in March 2022, trans women captured in mass raids have been held within the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. One woman arrested in San Salvador on 14 April 2022 was held first in police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman for punishment drills in the sun while handcuffed and forced to squat, and denied her access to an HIV clinic. A judge released her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported; the other woman remained imprisoned. Human-rights organisations attribute the abuse directly to the absence of a Gender Identity Law, and trans detainees are placed by birth sex in the general prison population.

Prison conditions are explicitly hostile to gender nonconformity. Homosexual inmates are forbidden from dressing or behaving in an effeminate manner, and gender-nonconforming men are targeted by police officers, soldiers and prison guards through unwarranted searches, theft of property, sexual assault and other physical violence. In a 1999 investigation, two transvestite detainees were forced to wear men's clothing for their hearing.

Healthcare access carries its own risks. Hospital specialists frequently dismiss trans patients' complaints as a side effect of being transgender, and patients are sometimes made to wait longer or refused care, a pattern that can be applied discreetly. There are no protocols or programmes for hormone therapy or sex reassignment surgery, and studies record that many trans women avoid seeking medical help after surgical complications because they have learned not to trust the system. Psychological care, where LGBT people obtain it, often takes the form of conversion therapies. Against this, the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance issued guidelines in April 2009 banning discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services, and a 2009 national HIV/AIDS plan prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in healthcare.

Violence risk is reinforced by public attitudes. A 2013 study found that 62% of Salvadorans do not accept homosexuality and 85% believe it acceptable to attack a transgender individual on the basis of their identity. Gang violence includes targeting of LGBT people through physical and sexual assault, forced recruitment and extortion for protection, and police cooperation in investigating such attacks is unreliable.

There is no recognition of same-sex partnerships. Article 11 of the Family Code defines marriage as a heterosexual union, same-sex couples may not adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence does not apply to same-sex couples. Since 2006 there have been proposals to amend the Constitution to bar recognition even of same-sex couples married abroad. Two challenges to the marriage ban were dismissed on technical and procedural grounds, on 20 December 2016 and 17 January 2019, although the Constitutional Court declared a proposed marriage ban unlawful in January 2018 and admitted a recognition lawsuit for hearing in August 2019 following the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of January 2018.

CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.summary:
Costa Rica decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and adopted marriage equality in 2020, the first Central American country to do so. Outright International (updated 12 March 2026) and the ILGA World Database both record the resulting LGBTI legal framework, covering same-sex conduct, gender recognition and legal protections.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than judicial. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, permits a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. Since May 2018 name changes on official identification have been available through a simple, free procedure at the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones; before that, from 2013, transgender people could change their legal name only on a judicial order. A 2016 bill that would have allowed transgender people to change both name and gender without surgery or judicial permission did not pass.

The state health system funds gender-affirming care. The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal coverage and identified good practices in specific legislation while raising concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups, and recommending intersectional data collection.

The Legislative Assembly strengthened hate-crime penalties in 2020. Amendments to the Penal Code provide 20 to 35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation (article 112), one to three years for exclusion or segregation on that basis (article 380), and three to ten years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion or blackmail on that basis (article 386bis). The inventory does not state that gender identity is a listed motivating ground in these provisions.

No current visa or entry rule targets LGBTQ travellers. In December 2018 the President signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples. A 1990 instruction from the Minister of the Interior directing consulates to refuse visas to women travelling without a man, intended to block foreign lesbians from attending an international meeting, is decades old and is not described as current policy.

Prison placement for transgender detainees is governed by a stated policy that has not produced consistent results. In June 2017 the Justice Ministry, through Vice-Minister Marco Feoli, announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility, with relocation strictly voluntary, decided case by case with prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners and an exclusive module for trans people was under consideration, with Spain's system cited as the model and vulnerable-population protocols developed with a regional human-rights organisation since 2016. By June 2019 a trans woman was held at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility, having transitioned while incarcerated, and the Justice Ministry confirmed 23 transgender people in the national prison system at the time. She recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape with a broomstick-handle at La Reforma in Alajuela, witnessed by a custodian.

Rollback pressure is documented alongside these protections. A conversion-therapy bill has stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.
CRI.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether gender identity, as distinct from sexual orientation, is a statutory aggravating ground in the 2020 Penal Code amendments is not resolved by the inventory; every penalty listed is framed around sexual orientation.

The current operational status of the 2017 prison placement policy after 2019 is not sourced. The inventory does not establish whether the census and the proposed trans-only module were completed, or how many of the 23 transgender prisoners recorded in 2019 were held in facilities matching their gender identity.

The inventory does not say whether the December 2018 decrees on immigration rights for binational same-sex couples have been amended, narrowed or challenged since entry into force, nor whether the definition of binational couple covers unmarried partners.

The UN Special Rapporteur's recommendations on intersectional data collection and on a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts are recorded as recommendations; their implementation is not sourced.

The extension of survivor's pension rights to same-sex partners is documented through 2016 and 2018 announcements; whether trans spouses and partners are covered under the same plans, and whether the teachers' budget exclusion was later closed, is unresolved.

President Luis Guillermo Solis placed a rainbow flag in the Presidential House on 15 May 2014, and President Carlos Alvarado Quesada became the first Costa Rican President to march at the annual gay pride parade in San José in June 2019, an event that drew about 100,000 participants. In 2018, President Alvarado issued a public apology to the LGBT community for past state persecution, citing state "promoted and executed persecutions, raids, arbitrary arrests and beatings." The President designated 17 May as the National Day Against Homophobia by executive order in 2008. No explicit visa or entry policy targeting LGBTQ travelers appears in current law; in December 2018, President Alvarado signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples. The historical finding is the 1990 incident when the Minister of the Interior instructed Costa Rican consulates not to grant visas to women travelling unaccompanied by men, warning all such women would be stopped at the airport, in an attempt to block foreign lesbians from attending an international meeting; this policy is decades old and not described as current. The Supreme Court ruled in 2000 that a gay sauna must remain open, holding that "subjective criteria of morality and proper behaviour have no legal basis" and violate constitutional rights. In 2011, the Supreme Court reversed its 2008 ruling and now allows same-sex couples equal access to conjugal visits in prison. Police harassment and raids of LGBTQ people and private establishments were "formerly commonplace" while homosexuality was technically legal. In 2020, the Legislative Assembly strengthened hate crime penalties: up to 20–35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation (amending article 112 of the Penal Code), 1–3 years for exclusion or segregation based on sexual orientation (article 380), and 3–10 years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion, or blackmail based on sexual orientation (article 386bis). In 1993, Universidad Internacional de las Américas was found to have a policy of expelling LGBTQ students and firing LGBTQ faculty and staff; when the Ministry of Education was informed, it said the policy would likely violate constitutional articles 20, 33, and 70 if enforced. Comprehensive sex education campaigns are described as "almost nonexistent" in Costa Rican public high schools due to opposition from the Catholic Church and other religious groups. LGBTQ rights remain a major political flashpoint affecting young people: the 2018 general election was sharply divisive over same-sex marriage, and a 2012 poll found 60% of 18–34-year-olds supported equal rights for same-sex couples. A 2016 bill to allow transgender people to change name and gender without surgery or judicial permission was unsuccessful; since 2013 transgender people can change legal name with a judicial order, and since May 2018 name changes on official IDs are permitted through a simple, free procedure by the TSE.

The country decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and adopted marriage equality in 2020, the first country in the region to do so. An international LGBTI rights organisation (updated 12 March 2026) and a global LGBTI legal database both record the resulting framework, covering same-sex conduct, gender recognition and legal protections.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than judicial. An executive decree in force since 2018 permits a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. Since May 2018 name changes on official identification have been available through a simple, free procedure at the national electoral authority; before that, from 2013, transgender people could change their legal name only on a judicial order. A 2016 bill that would have allowed transgender people to change both name and gender without surgery or judicial permission did not pass.

The national health system funds gender-affirming care. The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal coverage and identified good practices in specific legislation while raising concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups, and recommending intersectional data collection.

She recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape with a broomstick-handle at another facility, witnessed by a custodian.

PAN.name: Panama
PAN.summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is legal; it was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. No traveller-facing restrictions are in force: there are no bathroom or facilities laws, no documented inspection of gender markers at the border, and no recorded pattern of police targeting trans visitors.

Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery, and no nonbinary recognition is available. A visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with presentation has no documented record of friction at Panamanian entry points, though the surgery requirement shapes which documents residents are able to obtain in the first place.

No statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. The National Assembly blocked an amendment to the general anti-discrimination law in 2024, on the stated basis that existing provisions cover such grounds implicitly, and a 2015 bill to bar discrimination on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds has not advanced. No acts are formally recognised as hate crimes, so violence against a trans visitor would not be charged or recorded under a hate-crime regime.

Partner recognition is restricted. Article 40 of the Code of Private International Law, approved 8 May 2014, states that same-sex marriages are strictly prohibited and that foreign same-sex marriages will not be recognised, which bears directly on a visitor travelling with a same-sex spouse. The Supreme Court ruled on 27 March 2023, after a seven-year delay, that there is no positive right to same-sex marriage under the constitution. A constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman was approved by the National Assembly on 29 October 2019 but withdrawn before referendum following public protests.

Litigation over marriage ran from 2017, when two suits were combined after oral arguments, through a draft ruling by Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega in October 2017 that the family code's same-sex marriage bars were not unconstitutional while leaving the legislature to consider civil unions; the justice withdrew that draft in February 2018. The government signalled it would comply with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision of 9 January 2018, but no implementing legislation followed.

At the 2025 UN Universal Periodic Review multiple states urged Panama to adopt explicit anti-discrimination protections, reform gender recognition and strengthen safeguards against violence. Those recommendations remain unimplemented and legal reform is stalled, leaving Panama behind much of the region.
PAN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records either friction or its absence at Panamanian border points for trans travellers presenting documents inconsistent with their appearance; the assessment rests on the absence of any recorded incident rather than on an affirmative official statement or published entry guidance.

Whether the Inter-American Court decision of 9 January 2018 has been implemented through any pending bill is unresolved here; the sources record the government's signal of compliance and the subsequent 2023 Supreme Court ruling, but no legislative outcome.

Outcomes for trans victims of violence, including police handling of complaints, are not sourced. The non-recognition of hate crimes is established, but no case data accompanies it.

Access to trans-specific healthcare, hormone prescriptions and入境 medical screening for visitors is not covered by the inventory. The blood-donation deferral is stated for gay and bisexual men and its application to trans travellers is not specified.

The Guna Yala account derives from a single 2018 travel feature and is not corroborated by a rights-monitoring source.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The Panamanian state has repeatedly acted against LGBT legal equality: the Code of Private International Law approved 8 May 2014 (Article 40) states that same-sex marriages are strictly prohibited and foreign same-sex marriages will not be recognized; the Supreme Court ruled on 27 March 2023 (after a seven-year delay) that there is no positive right to same-sex marriage under the constitution; and a constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman was approved by the National Assembly on 29 October 2019 but withdrawn before the referendum after public protests. Cultural context varies sharply by place. In the Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing third-gender community, the Omeggid, is described as accepted as completely normal, with matriarchal figures elevating the status of women, per a 2018 feature.

Adjacent health rules: gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood, with an indefinite deferral, and conversion therapy is not banned.

DOM.name: Dominican Republic
DOM.summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the surviving sodomy-law articles is resolved: the current criminal code contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct. Those articles reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no equivalent provision for heterosexual acts, and Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy.

Enforcement against same-sex couples has historically run through public-order offences rather than a sodomy statute. A former law criminalising acts that violated "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for displays of affection; it was repealed by a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code. In 2006 several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo were shut down as part of a police harassment programme. In 2012 police broke up the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride Parade and arrested marchers on the ground that they were improperly using the national flag. Reports indicate that visible, politically active LGBTQ community signs are often targets of government crackdowns, sometimes with the support of religious leaders.

Transgender people cannot change their legal gender and name to reflect their gender identity. In June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree granting 35 transgender Dominicans the possibility of changing their legal name to match their gender identity; television journalist Mía Cepeda was among the 35 and subsequently changed her name. The decree addressed names only, not legal gender recognition.

Family law statutes recognise no legal status between same-sex persons, neither marriage nor marriage-like relationships. The 2010 constitutional amendment added Article 55, under which the State shall promote and protect family organisation based on marriage between a man and a woman; same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. Article 41 of Law 544-14 (Private International Law) could justify recognition of a foreign same-sex marriage, since marriage is valid if considered such by the law of the place of celebration, national law or domicile of at least one spouse. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage; several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it, but no implementing legislation is sourced here.

Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in areas including health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services and public accommodations, so many LGBTQ people feel the need to remain in the closet. Since 2011, Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Citizens have a constitutional right to access health care services, but health care programmes for the LGBTQ community have generally focused on HIV/AIDS education, often run by non-governmental organisations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos.

The socially conservative mores of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations hold significant sway in both public policy and prevailing attitudes surrounding LGBTQ rights. Because most residents hold conservative views, the major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. A 2017 ILGA poll found 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals, and only a plurality of 5% believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

Organised opposition is visible and directed at visible LGBTQ figures. Former openly gay U.S. Ambassador Wally Brewster (2013-2017) was regularly insulted by religious leaders and some politicians, and evangelical groups started an unsuccessful petition asking the government to expel him, telling him to "go home and cook since he's married to a man." The backlash against him after his June 2015 presentation with his husband in Santo Domingo included attacks on LGBT Dominicans, showing organised domestic opposition; his departure in 2017 left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence, including speaking at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 July 2016, and his tenure exposed a polarised climate.

Advocacy infrastructure exists. COTRAVETD (Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers), co-founded in 2004, is led by executive director Nairovi Castillo, who has given first-hand accounts of trans struggles in the country. In April 2017 more than 300 activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT/intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo, where Dominican government officials spoke.

The Dominican Republic has accepted UPR recommendations on intersex persons' rights and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the accepted record carries no domestic implementation detail.
DOM.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Dominican Republic is a party to the American Convention on Human Rights and whether the Inter-American Court's 9 January 2018 advisory opinion is binding or persuasive there; the sources assert only that several Dominican legal experts say it must be implemented.

Unresolved: whether Article 41 of Law 544-14 has ever been applied to recognise a same-sex foreign marriage. The provision's text is sourced; no decision or registry practice is.

Unresolved: the scope of the June 2018 executive decree beyond the 35 named individuals, and whether any subsequent procedure for legal gender change has opened. The inventory records only the single decree.

Not sourced: any hate-crime statute covering offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity, and any independent complaint or oversight mechanism for police conduct against LGBTQ people. The 1997 repeal of the "decorum and good behaviour" offence and the 2011 anti-discrimination provision in the HIV/AIDS law are documented; a general hate-crime framework is not.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (30 Aug 2024): documented the Constitutional Court challenge to sodomy-law remnants reaching only police and military officers (no equivalent for heterosexual acts), with HRW's amicus brief arguing equality/privacy violations. sources.summary:
Wikipedia country coverage: A former law criminalising acts violating "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for public displays of affection; it was repealed by a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code. In 2006 several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo were shut down as part of a police harassment programme. In 2012 police crashed the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride Parade and arrested marchers on the ground they were improperly using the national flag. Reports indicate that visible, politically active LGBTQ community signs are often targets of government crackdowns, sometimes with support of religious leaders.

Transgender people in the Dominican Republic are not allowed to change their legal gender and name to reflect their gender identity. In June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree granting 35 transgender Dominicans the possibility to change their legal name to match their gender identity; television journalist Mía Cepeda was one of the 35 and subsequently changed her name. A 2017 ILGA poll found only a plurality of 5% of Dominicans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender. Family law statutes recognise no legal status between same-sex persons, neither marriage nor marriage-like relationships.

Citizens of the Dominican Republic have a constitutional right to access health care services, but health care programs for the LGBTQ community have generally focused on HIV/AIDS education, often run by non-governmental organizations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos. Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in areas including health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services and public accommodations, so many LGBTQ people feel the need to remain in the closet. Since 2011, Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The socially conservative mores of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations hold significant sway in both public policy and prevailing attitudes surrounding LGBTQ rights. Because most residents hold conservative views, the major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. Former openly gay U.S. Ambassador Wally Brewster (2013-2017) was regularly insulted by religious leaders and some politicians, and evangelical groups started an unsuccessful petition asking the government to expel him, telling him to "go home and cook since he's married to a man." A 2017 ILGA poll found 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals.

The family law statutes recognise no legal status between persons of the same sex: neither marriage nor civil or domestic partnerships. The 2010 constitutional amendment added Article 55 stating the State shall promote and protect family organization based on marriage between a man and a woman; same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. Article 41 of Law 544-14 (Private International Law) could justify recognition, since marriage is valid if considered such by the law of the place of celebration, national law or domicile of at least one spouse. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage, and several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it.

CAN.name: Canada
CAN.summary:
Canada is among the safer large destinations for trans visitors. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender; Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement and replaced it with a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. Federally, identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction.

Provincial human rights machinery is available to visitors and residents who face discrimination. The Ontario Human Rights Code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission's published policy sets out the legislation, case law and complaint route under the Code, giving an explicit official basis for lodging a discrimination complaint.

National crime data shows a mixed picture for sexual-minority hate crime. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, a 1% rise after a 34% jump between 2022 and 2023. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, down from a 2023 peak of 889, ending three consecutive years of increases. The release breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, so trans-specific hate-crime volume is not established by this dataset.

Sub-provincial policy turbulence is concentrated in schools and sport, and primarily affects minors and residents rather than visitors. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or their gender identity at school; human rights groups called for repeal and litigation followed. Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, the Education Amendment Act and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then shielded them from legal challenge through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause.

Conditions inside correctional institutions are the weakest point in the record. After Bill C-16, federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities according to their gender identity, and the prime minister committed to reviewing prison assignment so facilities match gender identity. Transgender prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Litigation has tested both placement and care: lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in a case over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns bear on transit visitors only if detained.
CAN.outOfScopeNotes:
The Statistics Canada release for 2024 breaks out hate crime by motivation including sexual orientation, but the sources do not show a separate gender-identity category, so trans-specific hate-crime volume and trend in Canada remain unresolved on this evidence. The Egale Canada analysis of the same 2024 data may contain that breakdown; its contents were not available for this assessment.

Whether the Prince Edward Island document pathway is representative of all provinces is unresolved. The sources establish that most provinces allow declaration-based gender-marker change and that Prince Edward Island's Vital Statistics Act was amended in 2016 to drop the surgery requirement, but province-by-province statutory detail was not sourced.

Enforcement of the federal prison placement policy, and actual access to sex-reassignment surgery for prisoners held beyond 12 months, are stated as policy rather than verified in practice. The 2022 CTV report alleging a pattern of abuse and sexual victimisation of gender-diverse prisoners was not corroborated against official correctional data in the sources used here.

The outcome of the litigation following Saskatchewan's 2023 school legislation is not established, nor is the precise scope of Alberta's 2024 statutes as applied in practice. The federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings were not summarised in the available sources, so no quantified measure of resident experience under the Action Plan is included.

CAN.localsOnly:
Residents of Ontario can invoke an express statutory ground: the Ontario Human Rights Code covers discrimination and harassment because of gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy material sets out the legal context, case law and legislation for bringing a complaint under the Code. That machinery is available to residents as well as visitors, and the Commission's guidance is published.

Residents with school-aged children face divergent rules by province. In Saskatchewan, students under 16 need parental consent before a school will use their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. In Alberta, the 2024 health, education and sport statutes operate under a notwithstanding-clause shield enacted in 2025, so they cannot be struck down on charter grounds. Most other provinces have anti-bullying statutes that name LGBTQ students as a protected category in school settings, including Quebec, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Yukon.

Residents held in the correctional system are covered by a federal identity-based placement rule and by a policy of considering sex-reassignment surgery for those imprisoned more than 12 continuous months. Access to that care has been contested in court, including in the Kavanagh litigation over gender-affirming treatment and placement in a women's institution. Conditions of confinement for gender-diverse prisoners have been disputed publicly, with a 2022 report alleging abuse, discrimination and elevated risk of sexual assault, and a 2022 Nova Scotia study finding correctional officers generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety while raising concerns about risk to other prisoners.

Residents can participate in national policy consultation: the federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan includes survey findings drawn from the community, and Egale Canada publishes periodic analysis of police-reported hate-crime data affecting 2SLGBTQI+ people, both of which feed into advocacy and federal programming.

Document changes for residents are low-barrier in the provinces addressed by the sources. Prince Edward Island allows the gender marker on official documents to be changed through a declaration of identified gender supported by a doctor's letter, with no surgery requirement. Federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker.

AUS.name: Australia
AUS.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member; Reuters reported the decision as a landmark for gender-identity discrimination.

Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 carries the same grounds and takes effect on 30 June 2026. Outside that federal layer, vilification coverage is uneven: New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also cover gender identity, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither.

State law has moved toward stronger protection. Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024, and New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. The underlying Queensland Human Rights Commission announcement is no longer reachable, and the NSW Parliament bill document would not load, so both rest on the record held here rather than on a live page.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere: no law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017 after a 61.6% Yes result in the national postal survey. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access is where official policy has tightened. Since November 2017 a transgender child could access puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where child, parents and doctors agree, with surgery generally unavailable until 18. In January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services, exempting existing patients; the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, and a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, with a legal challenge filed in December 2025. A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research.

Detention carries a stated rule with discretion attached. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 (fully in force from 2023), direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process. The 2009 Corrective Services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective.

The scope of the December 2025 challenge to the Queensland youth-gender-care directive, and any ruling on it, are not sourced.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Federal hate crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with up to 7 years' imprisonment, and Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 (effective 30 June 2026) covers the same grounds. Vilification laws in NSW, ACT and VIC cover only sexual orientation, those in SA, TAS and QLD also cover gender identity, and NT and WA cover neither. Public expression is protected and visible: Sydney hosts an annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras and has been named one of the most gay-friendly cities in the world.

Medicare covers many major sex reassignment surgeries, but the gap between the benefit and the surgeon's fee can run to thousands of dollars, and private hospital policies or insurers typically impose a waiting period of about 12 months before claims for SRS. Since November 2017 a transgender child can access puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where child, parents and doctors agree; puberty blockers are Stage 1 (from around age 10, reversible) and hormone therapy Stage 2 (usually from 16, irreversible), with sex reassignment surgery generally unavailable until 18. In January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services, existing patients exempted; the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, and a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, with a legal challenge filed in December 2025. A NSW independent review released September 2024 found puberty blockers 'safe, effective and reversible' but called for more long-term research. From 1 August 2013 religious aged care providers receiving Commonwealth funding can no longer exclude people based on LGBTI status or same-sex relationships. From April 2025 Medicare IVF rebates were extended to single individuals and same-sex couples, not surrogacy.

Same-sex marriage was legalized on 9 December 2017 under the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017, following a 61.6% 'Yes' postal survey result, making Australia the last of the Five Eyes countries to do so; overseas same-sex marriages are automatically recognized and couples could no longer be barred from divorcing. Federal law has recognized same-sex couples as de facto relationships since 2009, through reforms amending 85 federal laws across taxation, superannuation, health, social security, aged care, child support, immigration, citizenship and veterans' affairs, with Centrelink recognizing same-sex de facto partners from 1 July 2009. States and territories have offered domestic partnership or relationship recognition from 2003 onwards: civil partnerships in the ACT and Queensland, registered partnerships in NSW, Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia, while Western Australia and the Northern Territory lack such schemes, so couples often need judicial approval to prove a de facto relationship. De facto partners face higher eligibility periods and a burden of proof that married couples do not, differing under Centrelink, migration and family law, which can impede arranging a partner's funeral and is poorly understood by some government departments.

Since 2016 every jurisdiction has an equal age of consent of 16 for all sexual acts, except Tasmania and South Australia where it is 17; Queensland was the last to equalise in 2016, dropping anal intercourse from 18 to 16. Religious educational institutions may still discriminate against LGBT students and teachers under sections 37 and 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984, though discrimination against LGBT students is barred in Queensland, the Northern Territory and Tasmania, and Tasmania has the fewest exemptions overall. The Safe Schools Coalition Australia, begun in Victoria in 2010 and national from 2014, was curtailed under the Turnbull government (restricted to high schools, role plays removed, parental consent required) and lost federal funding after mid-2017, though Victoria, the ACT and South Australia fund it themselves; GaLTaS lobbied for LGBT students from 1991 to 1998. Tasmania's 2019 law lets a person change legal gender at 16 without parental permission and recognises non-binary genders. The 2021 Census counted 13,554 (17.3%) children in same-sex couple families, up from 6,915 (14.8%) in 2016.
