NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.summary:
New Zealand's framework for trans people rests on statutory self-declaration. The Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 2021 eased correction of sex markers on identity documents, and the Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022 makes conversion practices unlawful. Protection under the Human Rights Act 1993 remains an open question rather than a settled guarantee: the New Zealand Law Commission's Issues Paper 53, 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024), reviews the Act's coverage of transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics.

Reported hostility has risen sharply. Data released under the Official Information Act and reported by RNZ on 17 April 2024 records 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023, against 161 in 2022, an increase of 42%. Police say the figure likely understates the true level of anti-trans hate, and the dataset shows a spike in March 2023, the month anti-trans activist Posie Parker visited.

The Counting Ourselves survey, reported by RNZ on 27 February 2025, gives the first clear population picture of violence against these communities: almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders were threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the past four years, and 8% experienced deliberate physical violence.

A community-safety assessment published by The Spinoff on 2 July 2024 records a worsening street climate alongside those statutory wins, citing a spate of rainbow event cancellations and the 2023 Posie Parker protest, with calls for greater security provision for rainbow communities.

Trans people in New Zealand prisons are more likely to have prior experience of abuse and show a higher rate of incarceration, according to Dalzell, Pang and Broemdal (2024) in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry. The New Zealand government has declared support for gender-affirming healthcare and gender-affirming clothing for incarcerated persons.
NZL.outOfScopeNotes:
No prison housing placement rule for New Zealand is sourced here: whether placement follows birth sex or gender identity, and whether any special unit or segregation practice exists, is unresolved in the material available.

The scope of the Human Rights Act 1993 as it applies to transgender, non-binary and people with innate variations of sex characteristics is unresolved pending the Law Commission review; the issues paper is a consultation document, not a finding.

No entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to trans travellers are sourced for New Zealand in this inventory, and no passport or travel-document marker rules are stated. The Spartacus index material available gives no New Zealand score.

ALB.name: Albania
ALB.summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. Homosexuality carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995, and no equivalent provision has been reinstated since.

The operative instrument is the comprehensive anti-discrimination law in force from 4 February 2010, which covers sexual orientation in employment, goods and services, education, housing and health care, and which was expanded in October 2020 to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sex characteristics and HIV status.

Enforcement of that law is uneven. In December 2010 the Deputy Commissioner for Labour, Social Affairs and Health, Tritan Shehu, stated publicly that homosexuality should be treated by medical staff as a hormonal and psychological disorder; the Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination reprimanded him only on 30 September 2011, after a lengthy delay. LGBT groups had by then lost confidence in the body over slow and bureaucratically impeded investigations, with only one of nine LGBT-linked cases concluded by December 2012. A more recent test was the 2023 complaint over screenings of the film 'Strange World', which the Commissioner mediated with a ruling in favour of the complainant in one case.

Hate-motivated offences were placed on a statutory footing on 4 May 2013, when Parliament amended the criminal code to treat offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity on a par with offences motivated by race, ethnicity, religion or disability. The package adopted the same day also provides for a fine and up to two years' imprisonment for disseminating homophobic information through any means, including the internet.

The constitutional layer is weaker. In 2016, under pressure from faith-based leaders, members of parliament removed sexual orientation and gender identity from Article 18 of the Constitution at the last moment, contrary to earlier promises; PINK Embassy condemned the removal on 20 July 2016.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for same-sex marriage in July 2009, framing the question as part of EU integration, but no recognition followed.

Violence remains documented. For 2023, the ILGA-Europe Annual Review recorded ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people logged by the group Rainbowphilia. Community organisations ran support schemes in the same period, including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

Access to care is constrained by public attitudes as well as by the law. A 2022 nationwide questionnaire found that only 9.3% of Albanians would accept an LGBT person as a family doctor. Social hostility is also recorded in wider survey data: 56.1% of Albanians told Gallup's Balkan Monitor in 2010 that homosexuals should not show their preferences in public, and 56.2% said they should not hold public posts such as teacher; 55% of Albanians aged 16–27 said in 2015 that they would not want homosexual neighbours, and a 2016 study found homophobia among university students associated with being male, politically conservative and religious.

Official hostility surfaces in parliamentary speech. In October 2011 the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu for telling parliament that 'homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones', warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community. In July 2021, during a row over LGBT campaigning in high schools, MP Luçiano Boçi attacked the groups as extra-curricular organisations with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda', while MP Nard Ndoka used Facebook to brand the government 'LGBT' and accuse it of pushing LGBT values in schools.

Schools policy has been a site of contention: in June 2016 the government passed a National Action Plan for LGBTI addressing bullying and discrimination in primary and secondary education, which drew strong political opposition.

The international review baseline is the visit of the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity to Albania from 1 to 12 July 2024, whose end-of-mission statement assessed good practices and challenges and set out recommendations to the State. The full report, A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 of 17 June 2025 by Independent Expert Graeme Reid, evaluates Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on sexual orientation and gender identity, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit.
ALB.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Albania has a legal procedure for gender recognition, and how identity documents are handled after a gender change, is unresolved in the available material: the People's Advocate, Erinda Ballanca, pledged in April 2018 to support the right to legally change one's gender, but no source in this inventory states whether such a procedure exists, what it requires, or how markers are issued.

No sourced information covers airport or border screening practices, custody or detention placement by gender marker, or access to hormone therapy for visitors; these remain not sourced rather than established as absent.

Bathroom and facilities rules, and any trans-specific provisions in policing or hate-crime prosecution statistics beyond the ten cases logged by Rainbowphilia for 2023, are not sourced here.

The ten-year penalty that applied until 1995 and the 2013 homophobic-materials offence are described from secondary summaries; the operative wording of the current criminal code provisions is not directly quoted in this inventory.

MKD.name: North Macedonia
MKD.summary:
North Macedonia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1996 as a Council of Europe accession condition, and the anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and gender identity following the 2019 amendments to the Criminal Code, which explicitly list both grounds under the hate speech provisions. The Law on Primary Education adopted in July 2019 likewise introduced anti-discrimination language covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and the 2019 US Country Report found the government enforced such laws in access to government services including health care.

Legal gender recognition remains the central unresolved gap for a trans visitor carrying documents. ILGA-Europe and the ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024, working with the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia, identify Legal Gender Recognition as the top priority; the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the LGR chapter a day before Parliamentary Committee review. In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that requiring sex reassignment surgery before changing a gender marker violated human rights and awarded €9,000 in damages, but NGOs report the government still fails to recognise gender identity changes in identification documents. A visitor should therefore expect documents to reflect a marker that may not match presentation.

Public trans organising proceeds openly. TransFormA's March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2024 under the words "we march bravely", and the first Pride Parade took place in June 2019. A 2025 Pride Parade drew lower attendance after organisers declared it a protest, and foreign embassies pulled funding.

The protective machinery around such events is thin. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious and continuing problem with countless reports and no meaningful state response, a reading the European Commission's country report shares. The 2019 US Country Report deemed the Skopje public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases and found the LGBTQ community "still prejudiced and harassed by the society, media and the authorities", with hate speech on social media following the June 2019 Pride Parade. In September 2023 the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with sexual-orientation and gender-identity aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code, one documented instance of the aggravation working in practice.

Violence against LGBTI people is documented and under-reported. The 2019 US Country Report details fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student, breaking his nose; the student reported the incident to the principal but chose not to report it to police. The same report cites CSO Coalition Margini documenting 70 cases of violence against LGBTI individuals in 2019, including five discrimination cases and one verbal assault by a police officer, and notes most such violence goes unreported to police or institutions. It also states there are many reports about public humiliations, worker firings and even casting homosexual teenagers onto the streets due to revelation of their sexual orientations. Global Voices reported in March 2024 a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

Same-sex relationships carry no recognition. Family law defines marriage as "a union between a man and a woman", and a 2014 government motion sought a constitutional amendment to the same effect, requiring two-thirds of MPs. A 2015 constitutional amendment that would have barred legal recognition of same-sex relations absent a two-thirds majority passed committee 72-4 and was approved in Parliament on 20 January 2015. ECRI has called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

Support infrastructure exists in the capital. The LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, offers free legal aid, and EGAL is the oldest organisation working on gay and lesbian health issues.

Whether the 2023 Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentence on aggravating grounds has been appealed or has entered into force is not sourced here. The two-year figure is as reported by ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024.

The current status of the Draft Law on Civil Registry after its withdrawal is unresolved in this inventory; no later reintroduction is sourced.

Post-2019 polling on attitudes toward gender identity specifically, as distinct from sexual orientation, is not sourced. The 2002 Center for Civil and Human Rights figures concern homosexuality.

Whether any sub-national authority besides Strumica has moved against LGBTI organisations since June 2023 is not sourced.

The 2019 US country report deemed the capital's public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases and found the LGBTQ community "still prejudiced and harassed by the society, media and the authorities", with hate speech on social media following the June 2019 Pride Parade. In September 2023 the Basic Criminal Court of the capital sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with sexual-orientation and gender-identity aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code, one documented instance of the aggravation working in practice.

Violence against LGBTI people is documented and under-reported. The 2019 US country report details fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student, breaking his nose; the student reported the incident to the principal but chose not to report it to police. The same report cites a national CSO documenting 70 cases of violence against LGBTI individuals in 2019, including five discrimination cases and one verbal assault by a police officer, and notes most such violence goes unreported to police or institutions. It also states there are many reports about public humiliations, worker firings and even casting homosexual teenagers onto the streets due to revelation of their sexual orientations. A March 2024 report noted a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

Same-sex relationships carry no recognition. Family law defines marriage as "a union between a man and a woman", and a 2014 government motion sought a constitutional amendment to the same effect, requiring two-thirds of MPs. A 2015 constitutional amendment that would have barred legal recognition of same-sex relations absent a two-thirds majority passed committee 72-4 and was approved in Parliament on 20 January 2015. A regional human-rights body has called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

Support infrastructure exists in the capital. The LGBTI support centre, a subsidiary of the national human-rights committee, offers free legal aid, and the country's oldest gay and lesbian health organisation continues to operate.

MNE.name: Montenegro
MNE.summary:
Montenegro decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1977, in the same year as Croatia and Slovenia, and the prohibition has not returned. The current framework comprises an anti-discrimination law that expressly covers gender identity, hate-crime provisions that list sexual orientation and gender identity as motives, and a same-sex partnership law adopted in 2020 after parliament rejected an earlier version on 31 July 2019. A visitor has no legal exposure for being trans or for presenting gender non-conformingly in public.

Two gaps shape what that framework delivers. There is no legal gender recognition statute, so change of gender markers is handled through inconsistent administrative practice rather than a defined procedure. The European Commission has also found that prosecutors overuse misdemeanour charges in place of proper hate-crime proceedings, which blunts the sentencing uplift the hate-crime provisions are meant to provide.

Public hostility remains organised and documented. The first Podgorica Pride, scheduled for May 2011, was cancelled after two attacks on gay people in the capital. The first Pride eventually marched in October 2013: roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, with rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records continued anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric during 2023, alongside more than 222 reported online hate-speech incidents.

Trans-specific violence is documented. In 2023 a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on television was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks, with police response monitored. A visitor who is visibly gender non-conforming can expect verbal hostility and a realistic risk of physical confrontation at Pride or in visible public settings, even though the state deploys heavy police protection at such events.

The partnership law grants near marriage-equivalent rights through a registrar ceremony and explicitly excludes parenting, foster care and adoption. Hospital visitation and shared-benefit rights were absent before its adoption, which is why advocacy groups described LGBT people as living as second-class citizens in 2019; a 2018 study found 51% of LGBT Montenegrins were closeted.

BIH.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
BIH.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina removed it from its criminal code in 1996 and Republika Srpska followed in 1998, each through its own entity-level code, so a trans visitor carries no legal exposure on that basis. The age of consent is set at 14 years equally regardless of gender and sexual orientation, with sex below that age treated as statutory rape.

Statutory protection at state level is explicit. The amended Anti-Discrimination Law adopted in 2016 covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics in the terminology used locally; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination had covered sexual orientation and gender expression but omitted gender identity as originally intended. The Sarajevo Open Centre presented the 2016 amendments together with the Agency for Gender Equality after public consultations held in autumn 2015.

Hate-crime sentencing enhancement exists at entity level. In April 2016 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina amended its Criminal Code to name sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances, published 15 June 2016; Republika Srpska and Brčko District run their own separate regimes with similar provisions. The Federation's adoption followed sustained coalition advocacy, confirmed by Sarajevo Open Centre coordinator Vladana Vasić.

Public expression has repeatedly drawn violence. The Queer Sarajevo Festival in 2008 was stormed by football fans and religious extremists shouting death threats, leaving eight people including a policeman injured; in 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled that authorities had failed to protect participants' freedom of assembly. Organised anti-LGBT violence has occurred even with prior police coordination: staff of the Sarajevo Open Centre said they had arranged security with police about three weeks before the February 2014 attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers, and Human Rights Watch's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of the attackers. The first Pride march in Bosnia and Herzegovina was held in Sarajevo on 9 September 2019 with an estimated 2,000 marchers. In March 2023 police cancelled LGBTQ film screenings in Banja Luka over security concerns, and activists were chased and attacked afterwards.

The Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024, published 13 June 2024, records a number of negative events over the past year with significant impact and describes the long-visible worsening trend as becoming increasingly evident.

Legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice. The Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions document changes on completed medical transition, and Balkan Diskurs reported on 25 October 2024 that these constraints are described as discriminatory and degrading; legal gender change is available only after sex reassignment surgery and other medical treatments. This pathway is a resident-facing burden rather than a border issue, but it shapes what documents a trans person can present.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples at national or subnational level. The Constitution is silent on gender eligibility for marriage, both entities' family codes limit marriage to opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couple households are not eligible for the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples. On 19 October 2018 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a request to legalise civil unions; a working group was established in January 2020 but its start was postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Healthcare and social climate carry documented risk. A 2017 PLOS ONE qualitative study documents the stigma and discrimination men who have sex with men experience from healthcare professionals and the general community. A 2015 survey found 48% of Bosnians would try to 'cure' their child if the child came out as gay and 16% would stop communicating with that child; the same survey found 19% supported granting same-sex couples some marriage-associated rights, and a 2017 Pew poll found 13% support for same-sex marriage with 84% opposed. A 2021 study found the 2019 Sarajevo Pride parade increased support for LGBT activism only in Sarajevo, not nationwide.

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors, and the position has deteriorated sharply. In September 2024 the Parliament of Georgia adopted the law "On the Protection of Family Values and Minors", which bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, public LGBT assembly and the dissemination of "LGBT information". It is the harshest such legislative package in the region, and it closes both routes by which a trans visitor or resident would ordinarily deal with documents and care.

The document problem predates the ban and is now absolute. Legal activists had been pressing for gender recognition reform for more than a decade on the grounds that official paperwork failing to match a person's identity made job applications difficult and exposed them to disclosure; from 2024 no recognition procedure is available at all, so a trans visitor's passport or ID will carry whatever marker their home jurisdiction issued, with no legal mechanism to alter it in Georgia and no lawful route to transition-related care if it is needed during the stay.

One day after the law passed, Kesaria Abramidze, a trans model and influencer and one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in Tbilisi. AP reported in October 2024 that the killing, together with Russia-style "gay propaganda" measures, had raised fears of hate crimes in the country. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path.

Assembly rights were already constrained before the statutory ban. In June 2019 the Interior Ministry declared the country's first-ever Tbilisi Pride "impossible" in its planned city-centre locations on safety grounds, while organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march and far-right groups vowed to thwart it. Public LGBT assembly has since been prohibited outright.

The domestic protection machinery has been formally found wanting. A report submitted on 5 August 2024 by WISG and partner organisations to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on implementation of LGBTI-rights decisions calls for urgent action: effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of the proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.
GEO.outOfScopeNotes:
Several points are unresolved on the sources reviewed. The specific offences and penalties attached to the 2024 law's bans on gender recognition, transition-related healthcare and LGBT assembly are not stated in the inventory, so the exact sanction a visitor would face is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening, the acceptance of foreign-issued identity markers at the border, or any risk of being flagged during arrival processing. Nor does the inventory record the outcome of the investigation into the killing of Kesaria Abramidze, including any hate-crime charges or conviction, or the current enforcement posture toward public assembly since the ban took effect.

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.summary:
Armenia decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2003. There is no statute of the restrictive type operating in neighbouring Azerbaijan. In 2013 police proposed a bill criminalising "non-traditional sexual relationships" and LGBT "propaganda" directed at young people, modelled on Russian legislation; it failed to pass after Pink Armenia argued it functioned as a distraction tactic.

Same-sex marriage is prohibited. The legal framework offers trans visitors little affirmative protection: there is no discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence has been characterised as ambiguous since 2022.

Legal gender recognition exists as an administrative practice and has been available since 2006, but it requires surgery. Gender-affirming care is restricted, and there is no legal recognition of non-binary gender.

Enforcement of law and order provides thin protection in practice. In May 2012 the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan was firebombed with a Molotov cocktail by suspected neo-Nazis; police took twelve hours to respond, and two suspects were later detained through CCTV footage. In April 2019 Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered trans woman, became the first trans person to speak at the National Assembly, addressing LGBTI discrimination; she then received extensive death threats by Facebook and email, including from members of parliament who called for her to be burned alive. In February 2020 a member of a nationalist party burned incense over the same lectern, denouncing her speech as a desecration.

Official and private restriction of LGBT expression is recurrent. In 2017 organisers of the Yerevan International Film Festival cancelled the screening of two LGBT-themed films after negative public reaction. In November 2018 a Christian LGBT group was forced to cancel planned forums and events, citing constant threats and organised intimidation from political and religious leaders and what it described as insufficient police readiness to protect them. In 2014 the Iravunk newspaper published a list of dozens of Armenian LGBT Facebook accounts, describing them as "zombies"; the Court of Appeals ruled the newspaper had not offended anyone and ordered the plaintiffs to pay 50,000 dram (about US$120) to the newspaper.

Documented violence against LGBT people is severe and ongoing. Pink Armenia's 2024 annual report records discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, violations of private and family life, discrimination in education and work, and hate speech, including a chapter on pressure directed at a transgender individual who participated in a beauty pageant. The 2009 ILGA-Europe and COC fact-finding report "Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia" documented societal and institutional homophobia, harassment, violence and discrimination in education, work and services.

Public acceptance is very low: Equaldex scores Armenia at 5 out of 100, and a 2012 study found 55% of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out, while 70% described LGBT people as "strange".
ARM.outOfScopeNotes:
Hate-crime protection is characterised as "ambiguous" rather than absent or present; the underlying statutory wording and prosecutorial practice are not resolved in the sources consulted here.

The scope of restrictions on gender-affirming care is not specified in the sources: which treatments are restricted, by which regulation, and under what conditions is unresolved.

The 2024 findings in Pink Armenia's report are presented as documented allegations and organisational reporting; individual case outcomes, prosecutions and court dispositions are not sourced here.

The February 2020 incense-burning incident at the National Assembly lectern is described in reporting as a denunciation by a nationalist party member; any criminal or disciplinary follow-up is not sourced here.

No source in the current inventory addresses entry, visa or border screening questions for trans visitors, including how gender markers on passports are treated by Armenian border authorities. That layer of the assessment is not sourced.

AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.summary:
Police conduct is the clearest documented danger. In September 2017 national police in Baku detained at least 100 members of the LGBT community in raids conducted ostensibly against prostitution; beatings, forced medical examinations, interrogation and blackmail were documented, and a 2017 United States State Department report recorded threats of rape and the use of electric shocks. At least 60 people were imprisoned or fined, and the detentions formed part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games. Azerbaijan acknowledged the cases in 2019, and in April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the arrests and mistreatment.

KAZ.name: Kazakhstan
KAZ.summary:
Kazakhstan does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 104 of the Penal Code, which criminalised "buggery", was repealed in late 1997 and took effect in 1998, introducing a common age of consent of 16, and lesbianism was never a criminal offence. No statute restricts clothing according to gender presentation, and no bathroom or facilities restriction applies to a trans visitor.

A prohibition on LGBT "propaganda" is nonetheless in force. On 30 December 2025 President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a law banning "information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation" in public spaces and media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine; the Mäjilis had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025. The measure followed a petition titled "We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!", filed by the Union of Parents, which the Ministry of Culture and Information confirmed in June 2024 it was reviewing after the petition met the threshold for government consideration. Human Rights Watch warned on 10 July 2024 that such a ban would violate rights nationwide. Kazakhstan now prohibits LGBTQ propaganda by law alongside Russia, Hungary and Georgia, and public advocacy or visible campaigning should be treated as legally exposed.

Legal gender recognition is medicalised, expensive and in practice geographically concentrated. Since 2003 trans people may change the gender marker on identity documents, but only after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder" requiring medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission, at an applicant cost of around ₸100,000 tenge. Since 2023 commissions can in principle be convened in every region; in practice the only functioning one is in Almaty, because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. Since 2011 document changes have required gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation, and people under 21 cannot change gender on documents at all. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months, permitting medical transition to begin.

No law protects LGBTQ people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit. Kazakhstan does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.

Bias-motivated violence is documented but thinly investigated. The ILGA-Europe annual review covering January to December 2023 records an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation opened, alongside an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied registration of an employment site after listing its focus. Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE/ODIHR since its 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and is assessed as needing victim-support and awareness measures. ECOM's 2024 analysis identifies health-right barriers for LGBT people in the country alongside informal behavioural practices that formal policy analysis misses.

Social risk persists even where a legal remedy exists. On 24 September 2019 Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who had posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, upholding privacy rights over a "moral foundations" defence; the two women fled the country for eight months fearing for their safety. Police conduct toward trans people is described as unhelpful rather than predatory, with no recorded pattern of police targeting.

Adoption is closed to same-sex couples. As of 2020 same-sex couples could not legally adopt children, and in February 2024 the president signed a law prohibiting adoption of orphans by same-sex couples. A deputy education minister stated that a parent's sexual orientation would play a "key role" in approval, assessed through a "special psychological test".

Gender-marker change carries a medical and financial burden borne by residents rather than short-term visitors: a psychiatric commission evaluation lasting 30 days, medical tests, costs of roughly 100,000 in local currency, and, since 2011, proof of gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation. Regional commissions were authorised in 2023 but only the commission in the country's largest city functions in practice.

Registration refusals on the basis of LGBTQ focus are documented at the level of civil-society administration: an LGBTQI+ education NGO was denied employment-site registration after listing its focus, per the 2023 annual review.

Public opinion is strongly opposed to legal equality: 89% of people opposed same-sex marriage in a 2015-16 Pew survey. That figure predates the current legal regime and is offered as background to the social environment rather than as a current measurement.

UZB.name: Uzbekistan
UZB.summary:
Article 120 of Uzbekistan's 1994 Criminal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between men and carries a penalty of up to three years' imprisonment. Human Dignity Trust and the UK Home Office's country-policy note of July 2024 both record the offence as in force, and the Home Office documents Article 120 cases prosecuted between 2009 and 2023, so the provision is applied rather than dormant. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024, covering events of 2023, likewise states that same-sex conduct between men remains criminalised.

Trans visitors fall inside this exposure. Uzbekistan has no legal gender recognition, so a trans person remains legally their sex assigned at birth, and Human Dignity Trust notes that transgender people may be prosecuted under Article 120 on that basis. Human Rights Watch reports that police target gay and bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment.

Custodial abuse is documented. HRW's 2024 chapter records forced examinations that amount to torture under WHO standards, alongside persistent impunity for police ill-treatment. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records torture and ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in custody, with social stigma and violence against LGBT people operating under the criminalised framework.

Enforcement is entangled with extortion. The State Department's 2023 report states that LGBTQI+ people were arrested and then released, or threatened with arrest, unless they paid bribes, and that police coerced LGBTQI+ people to inform on others under threat of prison. Human Rights Watch's March 2021 reporting describes blackmail and extortion by both state and non-state actors, with almost no legal protections available to victims. The Home Office records police intimidation, violence and exploitation of gay men and trans people as routine.

The formal legal environment offers no counterweight. The Home Office states that LGBTI organisations cannot register and operate unofficially. In April 2023 the Constitution of Uzbekistan deliberately omitted sexual orientation while explicitly including gender, race, religion and nationality among the protected categories. In November 2024 Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish party, announced that he was drafting a law banning discussions of LGBTQ people, claiming it was inspired by statements about "LGBT propaganda" in schools by Ivanka Trump.

Societal hostility compounds the legal risk. The Home Office attributes much discrimination to a rural taboo, and the State Department's 2023 report records continuing societal harassment alongside self-censorship by websites and bloggers on LGBTQI+ issues.
UZB.outOfScopeNotes:
ECOM's 2024 national report is listed as examining legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination provisions and criminalisation of HIV transmission, but the specific findings of that report are not reproduced in the inventory and remain unresolved here.

The inventory does not resolve whether the anti-discussion bill announced in November 2024 has since been introduced or enacted, or what penalties it would carry.

Entry, visa and document-screening consequences for a trans traveller whose passport marker differs from their presentation are not sourced; nor are facility-access, healthcare-availability or hate-crime provisions specific to trans visitors.

Whether Article 120 prosecution rates are rising or falling after 2023 is not established by the sources, which provide a documented range rather than a trend.

NIC.name: Nicaragua
NIC.summary:
Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or trans identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, inserted by religious legislators into a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape and signed into law in July 1992, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner"; the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality challenge in March 1994. The provision's vagueness had also made it usable against LGBT-rights organising and sexual-health work. Its language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since.

Formal legality does not translate into protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Nicaragua documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived opponents of the government that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among the year's significant human rights violations. The official US assessment places anti-LGBTI abuse inside a broader climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International's May 2019 reporting places homophobia inside that same repression. The crackdown on protests that began in April 2018 left at least 325 people dead and more than 2,000 injured, according to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and journalist Miguel Mora described being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay.

Documented violence against LGBT people is persistent and under-recorded. A 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, among them 15 murders: 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with the true total expected to be higher. The NGO Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime or murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person in the first two quarters of 2024. Trans women are the most targeted group, and state police are among the aggressors, tied with family members in 2022. Attacks go largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes.

Family-law exclusion is explicit. The Family Code approved by the Nicaraguan Congress in June 2014, in force from 8 April 2015, limits marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples, and Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. Several organisations filed an action of unconstitutionality against the Code. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration rights including marriage, and no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.

Discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is barred in several settings, including health care. Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 bars discrimination in access to health services on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, which is the provision most directly relevant to a visitor seeking care.

Public opinion is largely opposed. A Pew survey conducted from 9 November to 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed to same-sex marriage, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support.
NIC.outOfScopeNotes:
One source in the inventory, the Franklin & Marshall Global Barometers country page for Nicaragua, records no documented finding for this jurisdiction; nothing in this record is drawn from it.

The outcome of the action of unconstitutionality filed against the 2015 Family Code is unresolved in the sources, as is any Nicaraguan implementation of the 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion.

No youth-specific care-access findings are recorded, and entry, visa and document or gender-marker rules for trans visitors are not sourced in this inventory.

GUY.name: Guyana
GUY.summary:
Guyana remains one of five countries in the Western Hemisphere that criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Sections 351 to 353 of the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, retained in force after independence, create an offence of gross indecency punishable by up to two years' imprisonment and an offence of buggery punishable by life imprisonment. Prosecutions are rare, but the provisions structure police encounters with LGBT people and anchor public stigma. A constitutional savings clause bars judicial review of laws inherited at independence, which limits the routes by which the remaining statutes can be attacked in court.

There is no legal gender recognition procedure in Guyana. The one direct anti-cross-dressing offence, section 153(1)(xlvii) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act, derived from an 1893 statute, was struck down by the Caribbean Court of Justice on 13 November 2018 in McEwan v Attorney General, which held it unconstitutionally vague, archaic and contrary to freedom of expression. The challenge had been filed in 2010 with SASOD after trans women were arrested in 2009 and held for three nights under the provision.

One 2017 case shows what the pre-2018 regime meant in practice. Trans woman Petronella Trotman was stabbed in Georgetown in January 2017, sustaining a neck wound. On 2 March 2017 magistrate Dylon Bess refused her entry to the Georgetown Magistrates Court and told her to dress like a man; the case against her attacker was dismissed. SASOD's Joel Simpson called the magistrate's conduct a dereliction of duty while arguing that Parliament, not the courts, must repeal the 1893 statute.

Rights groups document continuing police abuse of the surviving Summary Jurisdiction clauses. In May 2019 Simpson described officers threatening men found in compromising positions with arrest in order to extract bribes, and harassing same-sex couples at seawalls and parks. People who lodge formal complaints face secondary discrimination at police stations and end up giving watered-down accounts; loitering and vagrancy provisions remain usable against LGBT people, in practice mostly sex workers. Hate crimes often go unreported.

Trans women bear a documented share of the violence. A hearing at the 191st session of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in November 2024, requested by the Guyana Equality Forum on the impact of gender-based violence on migrant women, sex workers and transgender women, heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition. The Commission's chair, Roberta Clarke, called on Guyana to take urgent action; the record put to the Commission cited 69 documented cases of violence against trans women between 2018 and 2022.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist. Discrimination and violence at the hands of law enforcement, religious leaders and others are widespread, and most LGBT Guyanese hide their orientation as a result. A 2022 poll recorded 72% acceptance of LGBT people, with hostility 13 percentage points lower than in 2013.

Three questions remain unresolved in the sources assembled here. No figure is available for how often sections 351 to 353 are actually prosecuted; the available characterisation is that enforcement is rare. There is no sourced information on whether legal gender recognition reform has been drafted or tabled since the 2018 ruling removed the cross-dressing offence. It is also not established whether the constitutional savings clause blocks every challenge to the 1893 statutes or only some grounds of review.

Whether the cross-party backing for decriminalisation shown in the 2025 election has produced legislative action is not sourced beyond the March 2026 country overview, which still lists the offences as in force. The 69-case figure for violence against trans women comes from the record presented to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and its methodology is not documented in these sources. No youth-specific or minor-specific findings on health or social care were recorded.

sources.summary: Guyana retains colonial-era criminal provisions: Section 351 (gross indecency, up to 2 years' imprisonment) and Section 353 (buggery, life imprisonment) of the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, kept in force after independence, with a constitutional savings clause blocking judicial review of inherited laws. A 2013 CADRES survey found 14% support for legalising same-sex marriage.

SUR.name: Suriname
SUR.summary:
Suriname has not criminalised consensual same-sex conduct since 1869, and that position applies to men and women nationwide. Following the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the Penal Code was revised so that the age of consent is the same for same-sex and opposite-sex relations.

In March 2015 Articles 175, 175a and 176 of the Penal Code were revised to reach discrimination and hate speech grounded in sexual orientation. Whether those provisions extend to gender identity is not stated in the sources available here.

Protection otherwise rests on an implied reading rather than an express statute. Article 8.2 of the Constitution of Suriname lists 'any other status' among prohibited grounds, and the government treats that clause as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity. No statutory instrument enumerates sexual orientation or gender identity as protected grounds.

Legal gender recognition is not available. A trans visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with their presentation should expect document checks to be difficult rather than routine, and the sources available here do not describe how Surinamese border authorities handle such documents.

Formal protection has not produced safe conditions. A July 2024 civil-society report filed with the UN Human Rights Committee records that LGBTI people face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation despite constitutional protection, and the US State Department's 2015 human rights report documented discrimination against LGBTI persons and other minorities in Suriname.

Registration of LGBTI organisations is permitted. The Surinamese state told the Human Rights Committee in July 2024 that its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, with monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission in place; committee experts pressed the delegation on implementation of a regional court's judgment concerning transgender identity.
SUR.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans visitors are not covered by the source inventory and remain unresolved here, including any requirement to disclose gender identity or prior name on arrival documentation.

Whether the March 2015 Penal Code provisions on discrimination and hate speech have ever been applied in a prosecution, and with what outcome, is not sourced. Enforcement of the constitutional 'any other status' reading through the courts is likewise unresolved.

The precise content of the regional court judgment on transgender identity that experts pressed Suriname to implement in July 2024 is not described in the inventory; the deadline or status of implementation is not sourced.

Facilities access, healthcare restrictions and partner recognition for trans visitors are absent from the available sources. The inventory confirms only that legal gender recognition is not possible.

Civil-society report of July 2024 (Projekta Foundation with VIDS and LGBT Platform): Constitution Article 8 covers SOGI only implicitly through 'any other status', and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since 1869. The LGBT Platform Suriname, founded 29 August 2011, unites PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action; the report urges a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

The US State Department's 2015 Human Rights Report for Suriname records discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities. The same report also documents the Bouterse trial, police brutality and corruption.

Submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (115th session) from LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata: despite constitutional protection LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization. It records that in March 2015 Penal Code Articles 175, 175a and 176 were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

Human Rights Committee review of Suriname, July 2024: the State asserted its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while experts pressed on implementing the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity. The Committee welcomed abolition of the death penalty in the Penal Code (2015) and Military Code (2021).

The platform also reports it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.

KGZ.name: Kyrgyzstan
KGZ.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Kyrgyzstan since 1998, with the age of consent set at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The constitution has banned same-sex marriage explicitly since a 2016 amendment, and no same-sex union of any kind is recognised.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. A 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status removed the provision allowing trans people to change their legal gender markers, and ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that amendments to the Law on Civil Acts have left trans people unable to obtain legal recognition at all since 2021. TGEU's Trans Rights Index Map 2024 places Kyrgyzstan alongside Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia as states that removed the right to legal gender recognition, and scores Kyrgyzstan together with Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan at only the bare minimum of not banning recognition, the floor of trans legal status in their wider region.

Access to transition care has narrowed sharply. Clause 47 of the Law on the Protection of the Health of Citizens was amended from 2024 to bar trans people from accessing transition-related care before age 25, where previously the process could start at 18. A draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 and passed first reading on 4 June 2026 would prohibit transgender individuals from changing gender markers and from accessing gender-affirming care and surgeries, and would affect minors as well as adults.

Anti-LGBT legislative pushes have been accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from members of parliament, according to ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025. A 2014 bill criminalising expression creating a "positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations" through media or networks passed first reading by 79 votes to 7 in October 2014 but expired without a final vote. On 14 August 2023 the president signed amendments to the child protection law adding to Article 2-1 content that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations" among information deemed harmful to children; the law does not define its key terms and does not mention sexual orientation explicitly.

No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBT people is described in the sources. ECOM data cited in the ILGA-Europe review shows high stigma and discrimination against trans people, particularly at the hands of law enforcement. Police officials were reported in 2018 to be blackmailing LGBT people on social media and dating sites, demanding payments of between 5,000 and 30,000 soms, roughly 70 to 500 US dollars. After the government launched legal reforms including an anti-gay propaganda law in 2014, attacks against LGBT people rose by nearly 300 per cent.

Organised public LGBT life in the capital has contracted. Bishkek's only gay bar, London, closed in 2017, and reporting by RFE/RL and The Guardian on the closure of the city's last LGBT club, a car-wash venue reached through a derelict yard, described patrons entering furtively as the atmosphere worsened; no other gay venue remained. In March 2019, after a march of about 400 people in Bishkek described as Kyrgyzstan's first gay pride march, MP Jyldyz Musabekova publicly called for participants to be beaten, though other deputies condemned her remarks.
KGZ.outOfScopeNotes:
Human Rights Watch World Report 2025, Kyrgyzstan chapter, contains no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing; its only prison references concern journalists and opposition activists sentenced to terms for media repressions and freedom of expression. The placement and conditions of trans detainees therefore remain unresolved and not sourced here.

The 2020 Human Rights Watch country chapter yielded no usable finding for this record, so any change it may have documented is unresolved.

ECOM's 2024 study covers Kyrgyzstan and includes material for trans migrants, but country-level findings beyond the stigma data cited by ILGA-Europe have not been extracted, so the specific healthcare obstacles it records remain unresolved.

The status of the draft law after its first reading on 4 June 2026 is unresolved; whether it has been enacted, amended or dropped is not sourced.

Whether the August 2023 child protection amendments have been used in enforcement, and against whom, is not sourced.

sources.summary:
Wikipedia country coverage: Reports of discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people in Kyrgyzstan are frequent, and after the government launched legal reforms including an "anti-gay propaganda law" in 2014 there was a near 300% increase in attacks against LGBTQ people. Police officials were reported in 2018 to be blackmailing LGBTQ people on social media and dating sites, demanding between 5,000 and 30,000 soms (roughly 70 to 500 US dollars). In March 2019, after a march of about 400 people in Bishkek dubbed Kyrgyzstan's "first gay pride march," MP Jyldyz Musabekova publicly called for participants to be beaten, though other deputies condemned her remarks. LGBTQ people fear social ostracism from friends and family, especially in rural areas, and Bishkek's only gay bar, London, closed in 2017.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1998, with an age of consent of 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, but the constitution has explicitly banned same-sex marriage since 2016 and no same-sex unions are recognised. A 2014 bill criminalising expression creating a "positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations" via media or networks passed first reading 79–7 in October but expired without a final vote. On 14 August 2023 the president signed amendments to the child protection law (Article 2-1) expanding information deemed harmful to children to include content that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations"; the law does not define key terms or mention sexual orientation explicitly. No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBTQ people is described.

Youth are a specific target: the August 2023 child protection law restricts children's access to information that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations," and the 2014 anti-propaganda-style bill was framed around media accessible to minors, echoing Russia's 2013 law on "propaganda...to minors." On transition care, Clause 47 of the Law on the Protection of the Health of Citizens was amended from 2024 to bar trans people from accessing transition-related care before age 25, where previously the process could start at 18, directly affecting trans youth and young adults. A draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 and passed first reading on 4 June 2026 would prohibit transgender individuals from changing gender markers and accessing gender-affirming care and surgeries, affecting minors as well. The age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

TJK.name: Tajikistan
TJK.summary:
Consensual same-sex relations have been legal in Tajikistan since May 1998, and sexual relations between women were never criminalised. The age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The formal legality does not carry through into protection: no legislation in Tajikistan prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

The country's first anti-discrimination law, adopted in July 2022, dropped sexual orientation and gender identity as protected grounds and retains only "sex". A regional monitoring review covering 2024 finds the statute only partially aligned with international standards, and an earlier comparative legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners records legal barriers and gaps affecting gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, including cases where the written law protects but practice does not.

Authorities maintain a register of LGBT people. Police introduced it in 2016, and Outright International flags a 2017 government registry of "proven" LGBT persons. ILGA-Europe's annual review for 2024 reports that police lure LGBT people into fake meetings in order to register them in a database, harvest their social-media contacts and extort money, with more than ten such cases recorded in Sughd province.

Policing is the documented source of the acute risk. IPHR's report of February 2024 records police raids in 2022 and 2023 that brought forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges, together with documented ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by officers. ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people during 2024, including arbitrary arrest, blackmail and extortion. ILGA-Europe further reports that forced or sham marriages are used against LGBT people with police declining to intervene.

Legal gender recognition is blocked in practice. Tajik law permits reassignment on some documents, but medical institutions issue no official documents for that purpose. A diagnosis of transsexualism is required, surgery is required for transgender women but not for transgender men, and evaluation is carried out by commissions of three psychiatrists on an unregulated case-by-case basis in which activists say bribes are often necessary. Only three to six people are known to have completed a legal gender change.

Gender-affirming medical services are not available in Tajikistan, so trans people who medically transition must travel abroad, and most doctors have no expertise in the treatments required. Patients report disrespectful treatment from medical staff, and some Tajik psychologists and doctors offer pseudoscientific methods that present homosexuality as an addiction comparable to alcoholism or drug addiction.

The wider social climate constrains visibility. Public expression of support for LGBT people is effectively suppressed and public attitudes have been described as entirely negative, with homophobic and transphobic remarks from politicians forming part of everyday politics. The Supreme Mufti, Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has called same-sex relations a "disaster", condemned countries legalising same-sex marriage, and spoken against human-rights activists and anti-discrimination laws. Those who disclose their orientation become targets of physical and psychological abuse, including at the hands of police.

No relationship-recognition framework exists in Tajikistan, and same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to married heterosexual couples.
TJK.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records the placement or conditions of trans detainees in Tajikistan; Human Rights Watch's 2025 chapter does not cover them, so that question is unresolved rather than answered.

The inventory contains no findings on LGBT minors, education-sector policies or school environments in Tajikistan.

Entry, visa and border-document screening rules for trans travellers are not sourced here, so whether identity documents are checked for gender markers on arrival is unresolved. Whether the police registry is accessible to or applied against foreign visitors is also not established by these sources.

It is not sourced whether the July 2022 anti-discrimination law has been invoked in any proceeding, and no enforcement data on that statute appears in the inventory.

TKM.name: Turkmenistan
TKM.summary:
Turkmenistan criminalises consensual sex between men. Article 135 of the Criminal Code identifies consensual same-sex acts between adult men as an offence, with a sentence of up to two years' imprisonment and, in some readings of the provision, a further two to five years in a labour camp; Article 19 allows increased penalties for repeat convictions. The Criminal Code adopted in April 2022 retained the 'sodomy' provisions and increased both the severity and the scope of the punishments attached to them.

Enforcement was rare before 2006. Since then the reported consequences of an Article 135 investigation include state-sponsored violence and torture during criminal investigation, interrogation that witnesses describe as grossly humiliating, and vigilante attacks that are especially common in prison. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report on Turkmenistan lists the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct among the country's significant human rights issues, together with abuses committed by security-service officials who engage in corruption with impunity.

Detention carries a second risk. Repeat convictions under Article 135 can lead to compulsory psychiatric admission and involuntary conversion therapy, and homosexuality is institutionally treated as a form of mental disorder within those facilities. Attorneys who brought off asylum claims for Turkmen clients describe suspects subjected to interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 reports torture and inhumane treatment present throughout the country, with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them.

Two incidents show how the charge is deployed. In October 2019 a gay doctor was tortured by the state apparatus over a long span before temporarily disappearing. In May 2020 several well-known figures from the modelling industry were arrested on charges of homosexuality. The government has justified its discriminatory frameworks in UN dialogue by arguing that any deviations pose a potential threat to the fabric of Turkmen traditions and society.

No anti-discrimination legislation protects a visitor or a resident on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The government has rejected such legislation despite requests made through three Universal Periodic Reviews, and in February 2021 it told the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights that it intended to 'study the option of introducing anti-discrimination legislation'.

Flight abroad is an established route. EHPV's 2020 mid-term UPR stakeholder submission notes increasing flight and states that LGBT persons and people living with HIV in Turkmenistan have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights, identifying Article 135 as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination. Columbia Law School's Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured US asylum in May 2007 for an anonymous Turkmen woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions, believed to be the first-ever asylum granted to a lesbian from Turkmenistan, and Goldberg Kohn secured asylum in September 2019 for a lesbian couple from the country who feared imprisonment and torture.
TKM.outOfScopeNotes:
Sources disagree on the current maximum under Article 135. Coverage of the provision gives a penalty of up to two years' imprisonment while also recording that a 2019 amendment raised the two-year maximum carried by the 1997 code. The applicable figure for conduct today is unresolved from the material in hand.

The primary text of the Criminal Code adopted in April 2022 has not been read. Its retention of the 'sodomy' provisions and its increase in severity and scope are reported through ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 rather than verified against the statute, and the offence wording, the sentences and any aggravating categories as they now stand are not independently sourced.

No source states how often Article 135 is enforced under the 2022 code. The account of rare enforcement before 2006 and the documented incidents of October 2019 and May 2020 do not establish a current prosecution rate.

Entry and visa rules, passport and marker requirements, and any border screening that risks disclosing a visitor's orientation or gender identity are not sourced for Turkmenistan. Hate-crime provisions, and whether aggravating motives are recognised in sentencing, are likewise not sourced. No youth- or minor-specific care access findings appear in the material.

SYR.name: Syria
SYR.summary:
Syria is a country trans visitors should not enter. The fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 did not disturb the statutory framework that governs a visitor's exposure: Penal Code Article 520 prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" with up to three years' imprisonment, and Article 517 criminalises public indecency. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that both provisions are applied to women as well as men, so a trans visitor is reachable by the same articles irrespective of legal sex marker or presentation.

The same overview records that legal gender recognition is impossible in Syria and that LGBTI organisations cannot register. There is no anti-discrimination protection of any kind; the state's answer to same-sex conduct is criminalisation, which removes the complaint route a visitor would otherwise have after an incident.

The security position has worsened since December 2024. The Guardians of Equality Movement (GEM) worked through an on-the-ground reporter network and documented waves of violence against Syrian transgender women across the first two months of 2025, with non-state armed groups and security forces implicated in several cities. GEM also circulated video footage from February 2025 showing authorities detaining trans women. Any state actor or armed group operating today can act against a trans visitor under the provisions that remain in force.

Violence by armed groups is documented alongside state action. A Human Rights Watch report of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021) tallied at least 16 killings in Syria claimed by ISIS for alleged sodomy as of June 2016, against 23 in Iraq and 3 in Libya. A separate record in the same inventory states that ISIS reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in the areas it controlled, and that Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State carried out beatings and torture of LGBTQ people. The killings were reported to the UN Security Council in August 2015, in the Council's first-ever discussion of LGBTQ concerns.

State enforcement has precedent inside Syria itself. In June 2010 Syrian authorities raided a series of private parties over preceding weeks and arrested more than 25 men, most charged with "homosexual acts" and others with drug offences; the charges later listed also included encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Private gatherings are therefore not a safe setting.

Political actors across the spectrum have publicly endorsed harsher treatment. A Free Syrian Army member stated he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, and a secular leader said Syrian society would answer "no way" to gays claiming rights. Such statements from armed and political figures are not historical curiosities in a country where armed formations still hold coercive power.
SYR.outOfScopeNotes:
The casualty tallies for ISIS killings of men accused of sodomy in Syria are not reconciled in the sources: Human Rights Watch records at least 16 claimed killings as of June 2016, while another record states ISIS reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in its areas. The discrepancy is unresolved here and may reflect different counting periods or inclusion of pre-2016 events.

Whether the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 changed the text or penalties of Penal Code Articles 520 and 517 is not sourced in this inventory. The assessment treats the articles as operative on the strength of Outright International's overview updated 12 March 2026, but a current consolidated Penal Code has not been consulted.

No source in this inventory addresses entry and visa rules for trans visitors, airport or border screening that could expose a traveller's documents, the treatment of foreign versus Syrian citizenship at the border, or the availability of consular assistance. Those points are not sourced rather than confirmed as safe.

The inventory carries no trans-specific judicial decision, sentence or acquittal after December 2024, and no named case of a foreign national prosecuted under Article 520. Enforcement figures for the current period are likewise absent; the pre-2011 and civil-war-era incidents are the only quantified enforcement records available.

Sub-national variation is barely covered. GEM's early 2025 findings reference several cities, and a debunked claim centred on Homs is noted, but no source establishes which authorities currently control enforcement in which governorate.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Expression is criminalised and chilled: Article 520 of the 1949 penal code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" with up to three years' imprisonment, and a 2010 police crackdown arrested over 25 men on charges including homosexual acts, encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Public cultural expression has been squeezed since the civil war: the region's only gay tour (Damascus and Aleppo, run by Bertho) stopped operating, and the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus have been eradicated. Hammams in Aleppo and Damascus were the main venues of the pre-2011 tour, described by its organiser as "a paradise for gay people" where "we never had any problems," but the civil war ended that activity. Digital expression persists anonymously: the "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020, later moving to Twitter, with university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographing themselves by a faculty building under #oneofyou, most using fake accounts for fear of being identified; reactions ranged from defence to threats of blood before it faded amid COVID-19. Earlier literary expression includes Nizar Qabbani's 1971 poem "The Evil Poem," describing a relationship between two women.

Health care access is shaped by official stigma and under-provision: in 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected and offered free medicines, a figure NGOs estimated at least five times too low, and the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs, and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational program for youth in secondary schooling; comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist. Prevalence is low, under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987. Physical safety is also a care barrier: beatings and torture of LGBTQ people occur frequently, including attacks by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State, which reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in its areas, an issue reported to the UN Security Council in August 2015 in the Council's first-ever discussion of LGBTQ concerns.

There is no anti-discrimination protection; the state criminalises same-sex conduct instead. Violence comes from non-state armed actors as well, and political actors endorse harsher treatment: Free Syrian Army member Nasradeen Ahme said he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while secular leader Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would say "no way" to gays claiming rights. In the diaspora, Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees face discrimination and exclusion in host countries based on race, language, skin colour and religious background.

Youth are both a target and an organising force. Abdulrahman Akkad, a Syrian young man in Germany, came out publicly on Facebook in July 2017 while under family pressure to marry against his will, and his case was raised in the German Parliament's 2020 human rights session. The 2017 film Mr. Gay Syria follows two gay Syrian refugees rebuilding their lives.

That finding does not negate the documented pattern of attacks on trans women in early 2025; it does mean that viral allegations should not be taken as established fact in either direction.
