In 2005 a deputy minister of religious endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected and offered free medicines, a figure NGOs estimated at least five times too low, and the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs, and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational programme for youth in secondary schooling, but comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist.

Reported prevalence is low: under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 cases reported through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987. Physical safety is itself a barrier to care, with beatings and torture of LGBTQ people recorded frequently.

Expression remains chilled at home. In the capital, homosexuality and "public decency" offences are illegal, and a resident described living "only in whispers" when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes. Young people who campaigned publicly did so through fake accounts.

LBY.name: Libya
LBY.summary:
Libya's Penal Code penalises "illicit sexual intercourse" and "indecent acts", with the indecent-acts provisions carrying up to five years' imprisonment. Same-sex relations are not legal for men or women. No provision criminalising homosexuality by that name is identified in the sources; a regional guide published by The Guardian on 21 June 2016 lists Libya among states where imprisonment is the penalty, and notes that where no specific law exists other laws are used, with terms varying from country to country.

Cairo 52's country review records de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process itself, whether social, medical or surgical, enforced through the same indecent-acts and illicit-intercourse provisions. Recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible, which narrows the ground on which a trans person can seek care.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: official identity documents cannot be changed. A visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with their presentation has no domestic route to align documentation, and the criminalisation framework described above applies to public gender expression regardless of what any foreign document says.

Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, further records that there are no legal protections against discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, that same-sex relationships are not legally recognised, and that LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Violence against people perceived as gender-nonconforming or as same-sex-attracted has been documented as coming from both organised extremist control and militia activity. Human Rights Watch reported on 8 June 2015 that Islamic State killed men accused of homosexuality in the territory it controlled, including in Derna, where a young man was targeted by local Islamists for effeminate dress and "contemporary" clothes in a case dated from November 2014. D+C reported in June 2015 that Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in Derna in April 2015, that information in the city flowed only through the mosque, and that the situation for homosexuals in Libya was worsening as militias controlled territory. In November 2012, twelve men accused of being gay faced torture and threatened death at the hands of a militia, in the early post-revolutionary period.
LBY.outOfScopeNotes:

Entry and visa rules, border screening practice, airport treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers, and whether any screening could out a visitor are not covered by this inventory. Nothing in the record establishes an entry-level risk assessment for Libya.

Whether a court process for legal gender recognition exists in statute but is unavailable in practice, as distinct from having no legal basis at all, is unresolved; the sourced statement is that official identity documents cannot be changed.

The violence reports are dated between 2012 and 2015 and the legal overview to March 2026. Current militia and extremist control of territory, and whether Derna-specific killings continue, are not sourced and remain unresolved.

The 2010 asylum account gives no age, schooling or student status for the person concerned, so its scope cannot be fixed; it is retained as evidence of family and state response rather than as a dated incident record.

YEM.name: Yemen
YEM.summary:
Yemen's Penal Code 1994 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Article 264 defines homosexuality between men as anal penetration and, for participants who are not married, prescribes 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment; the article prescribes a different penalty where the participants are married. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 restates the same provision for events of 2025, and GayLawNet carries the statute as Yemen's canonical criminalisation citation.

The article reaches women as well: Article 268 prescribes up to three years' imprisonment for premeditated lesbianism. A visitor should therefore treat any same-sex conduct, not only conduct between men, as criminal.

Capital exposure is documented, not hypothetical. In January and February 2024, two courts administered by the Houthi authorities in Yemen sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or imprisonment over same-sex conduct. The Dhamar criminal court sentenced nine people to death on 23 January 2024, seven by stoning and two by crucifixion, and gave 23 further defendants terms of six months to ten years for homosexuality or spreading immorality; an Ibb court handed additional death sentences on 1 February 2024. Amnesty International called for an immediate halt to the executions and for the release of those facing LGBTI charges. Readings of Article 264 that treat the conduct itself as a capital offence also circulate, and Wikipedia's country coverage records death as the penalty for married men, so a visitor should treat execution as a live risk rather than a remote theoretical maximum.

The statute's territorial reach is contested by the conflict. Cairo 52's country review records that the penal provisions apply only in government-controlled regions, with other parts of the country under competing faction authorities, so legal exposure shifts at front lines and checkpoints. Human Rights Watch makes the same finding for 2025, describing Houthi and government factional control as determining where the law applies.

Formal enforcement is only one layer of exposure. Cairo 52 records that the erosion of the rule of law and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced by courts in some areas but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands, and IPS's reporting from Sana'a in 2013 describes a gay man hiding his appearance as still problematic in a conservative society with no place for people like him. Discretionary social enforcement thus sits alongside the statutory penalty.
YEM.outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty structure where the participants are married is not resolved across the sources. Article 264 as carried by GayLawNet and Human Rights Watch states 100 lashes and up to one year for unmarried participants and indicates only that the article prescribes differently for married participants; Wikipedia states death for married men, and current readings treating the conduct as a capital offence circulate without a cited statutory clause confirming that this is codified rather than applied. Whether the capital penalty derives from the statute, from Shariah application, or from discretionary sentencing in Houthi-administered courts is not sourced here.

No source in this inventory addresses entry and visa rules, passport gender markers, airport or border screening that could disclose a visitor's status, access to healthcare or gender-affirming care, facilities or bathroom rules, hate-crime provisions, or partner and marriage recognition. Those fields remain unsourced for Yemen rather than negative findings.

The practical scope of the Penal Code after February 2024 is unclear: the inventory documents sentences from two Houthi-run courts in January and February 2024 but does not record whether those death sentences were carried out, nor the enforcement position of government-controlled courts during the same period.

BTN.name: Bhutan
BTN.summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. The lower house of Parliament voted 43-1 in June 2019 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions carrying one month to one year of imprisonment, which had gone unenforced for at least 15 years. The upper house reinserted the ban, and a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, and no reversal has followed.

The repeal created no protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics. Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a domain where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Where markers can be changed at all, the process requires a medical note plus a supporting letter from a civil society organisation. A trans person's identity card therefore continues to display the sex assigned at birth, with direct consequences for how violence against them is treated.

Violence risk is elevated and reporting channels are effectively closed. Trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault. A 49-year-old trans woman interviewed in November 2024 described police dismissing her cases because her identity card reads male, on the reasoning that 'both parties are men'; families pressure victims to accept the assault as fate, and assistance routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. The result is practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

Entry and visa rules carry no trans-specific screening provisions in the sources reviewed. Bhutan provides no legal recognition of same-sex relationships, and partners of trans and other LGBTQ people cannot be recognised in any legal proceeding. A marriage bill using gender-neutral pronouns was discussed during the 2018 summer parliamentary session but deferred because of the 2018 parliamentary election.

Some protective instruments exist at sectoral level. The Bhutan Medical and Health Council's Code of Professional Fidelity, issued in 2021, protects sexual orientation. The 2020 Standard Operating Procedure for Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response requires healthcare providers to deliver age-appropriate, culturally sensitive, and sexual orientation and gender identity sensitive care, and requires case managers to provide tailored care for people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. The National Strategic Framework on Comprehensive Sexuality Education (2021) covers LGBTI issues.

Official engagement has increased without producing legislation. The 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, the Attorney General's Office and the Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians. Two consultation workshops convened community members with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.

The sources do not address entry, visa, or border-screening rules as they apply to trans travellers, and no finding on that question should be read from this record.

LAO.name: Laos
LAO.summary:
Laos has never criminalised consensual same-sex conduct. The penal code, modelled on the French system after independence in the 1950s, contains no sodomy offence, which distinguishes the country from neighbours that retained colonial-era prohibitions.

No law in force prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution addresses neither. At the 35th session of the Universal Periodic Review on 21 January 2020, Malta's ambassador recommended that Laos improve LGBTI rights and involve LGBTI representatives in decision-making, and Iceland's ambassador recommended comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity. In March 2025, National Assembly member Maifong Maixai proposed changing Article 36 of the 2025 revised Constitution to expand room for non-discrimination protections for gender-diverse people.

Official tolerance is conditional and easily withdrawn. The government generally tolerates or ignores LGBT people unless they campaign for LGBT rights or are judged too publicly immodest or indecent, and a 2014 decree prohibited criticism of all government policies. The government has blocked access to LGBTQ-themed webpages, and discussion of LGBTQ issues in the media is described as rare apart from transsexuals visible as entertainment. Reporting from October 2018 documented a social-media crackdown in which influential Facebook users known as net idols faced retribution for posts; Proud to be us Laos, the country's only LGBT advocacy group, was among those quoted.

Trans-feminine people are a visible presence. Activist Anan Bouapha reported seeing transgender people wearing traditional costumes to temples and ceremonies, alongside some gay students expressing their identity among peers and teachers. Beyond that visibility the scene is small, discreet and social: a first-person account from Vientiane in 2000 described a small circle of lesbians and gay men whose lives centred on a few restaurants and friendship networks. Gay foreigners reported in the 1990s that a taboo made interacting with Laotians difficult except discreetly at night, and the United States Department of State reported in 2013 that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and against persons with HIV/AIDS was prevalent. The age of consent is 15 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Protection machinery exists but is narrow. The European Union marked the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane, giving LGBT rights visible diplomatic backing. Health-sector partners involved in LGBT events include the Center for HIV/AIDS/STI at the Lao Ministry of Health, the Lao Positive Health Association and the Vientiane Youth Center for Health and Development, which was among the organisations that organised the first public LGBT Pride in Laos in June 2012, drawing about 100 participants on the United States embassy sports field in Vientiane. The Law on Electronic Data Protection (No. 25/NA, 12 May 2017) lists sexual behaviour among prohibited categories of data.
LAO.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this set addresses legal gender recognition, the amendment of sex markers on identity documents, or passport and visa screening of trans travellers. Whether officials can refuse or delay documents on presentation grounds is not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved rather than as absent.

Hate-crime provisions, marriage and partnership recognition, and any complaint or redress mechanism for a visitor denied a service are not covered by these sources. The claim that a visitor would have no documented recourse rests on the absence of anti-discrimination law, not on a sourced account of an incident.

It is unresolved whether the March 2025 proposal to alter Article 36 of the revised Constitution was adopted, and whether the two 2020 Universal Periodic Review recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity were accepted or implemented.

Two of the inventory's links, the UNAIDS joint analysis entry and the Asian Development Bank overview of the legal status of sexual and gender minorities, yielded no usable finding and support nothing in this record.

LAO.localsOnly:

The Vientiane Youth Center was among the organisers of the first public Pride in June 2012.

Legislative openings come from inside the National Assembly rather than from civil society. Maifong Maixai's March 2025 proposal to change Article 36 of the revised Constitution was aimed at widening the room for non-discrimination protection for gender-diverse residents, and the 2020 Universal Periodic Review recommendations from Malta and Iceland were addressed to the state as obligations it had not yet met.

Public campaigning for LGBT rights, or conduct judged immodest, is what draws official attention rather than identity as such, and the 2014 decree restricting criticism of government policy narrows the space for contesting that treatment. Discussion of LGBTQ issues in domestic media remains rare, with transsexuals appearing chiefly in an entertainment register.

TLS.name: Timor-Leste
TLS.summary:
Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex sexual conduct. Same-sex sexual acts have been legal since 1975, and no source records anti-trans legislation, arrest patterns, or police targeting of trans people in the country. No law restricting trans people from public facilities, health care, or employment is documented.

No legal gender recognition procedure exists in Timor-Leste. For a visitor, the operative document is therefore the passport or identity card issued in the home jurisdiction, including any gender marker changed there. There is no domestic route by which a foreign trans person could alter or regularise a marker while in the country.

Official signals run in a supportive direction at the highest level. The Prime Minister gave televised endorsement to the country's first Pride parade in 2017, and President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the 2019 march, stating that he is a president for all people. Day-to-day rejection is nonetheless documented alongside those statements, including hostile messages sent to the family of a Pride organiser, so public visibility attracts both state endorsement and social hostility.

Pride marches are held annually in Dili, in July. A visitor present during those weeks can expect a visible public event of a scale that has grown substantially since 2017.
TLS.outOfScopeNotes:
The current inventory does not address border or visa screening, airport document checks, or whether gender markers on foreign documents are inspected on arrival. Whether a visitor's presentation could prompt secondary questioning is unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

Hate-crime provisions, their penalties, and their enforcement are not sourced for Timor-Leste, as is the treatment of gender identity as distinct from sexual orientation under any offence. Marriage and partner recognition for trans and same-sex couples is likewise not addressed.

Coverage of Pride in the sources stops at July 2019. Whether the annual marches continued after that point, and whether any anti-trans legislative proposal has emerged since, is not sourced here.

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.summary:
Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Sex between men is criminalised, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the regime of stigma and violence around it applies visibly to transgender people. The Asian Development Bank's 2024 assessment of the legal status of sexual and gender minorities across 17 countries in Asia and the Pacific includes Papua New Guinea, with decriminalisation among the topics examined, confirming that the criminal-law position remains a live legal question rather than a settled matter.

Reporting on trans and gender-diverse people in Port Moresby documents direct targeting. ABC News reported in October 2014 that gay and transgender people in the capital are commonly raped or beaten, in some cases by police officers. A 24-year-old gay man recounted being pelted with stones and bottles. Transgender people who present as women face the same exposure to this violence.

One documented pocket of safety exists: Hanuabada, a village built over the sea on Port Moresby's outskirts, where residents live openly and transgender people wear women's clothing in the street without retaliation. This is an exception, not the national pattern.

The wider accountability climate compounds the risk. Human Rights Watch has recorded police abuse, including of children, continuing with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse, and has found that sorcery-related killings in the highlands provinces go largely unpunished, with police routinely taking no action. A visitor who is assaulted has little practical recourse.
PNG.outOfScopeNotes:
The precise statutory provision and current penalty for sex between men in Papua New Guinea are not stated in the sourced inventory beyond the figure of up to 14 years' imprisonment; the exact offence and any recent amendment are unresolved.

No sourced material in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, marker changes on documents, passport or visa rules for trans travellers, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or hate-crime provisions specific to gender identity in Papua New Guinea. These remain not sourced.

The inventory does not establish whether the Asian Development Bank's 2024 assessment recommends or records any change to Papua New Guinea's decriminalisation status; only that the topic was examined.

sources.summary: The ADB publication 'Assessment of the Legal Status of Sexual and Gender Minorities in 17 Countries in Asia and the Pacific', content dated 17 May 2024, lists Papua New Guinea among the 17 assessed countries. Its keywords include decriminalization and SOGIESC inclusion.

HRW commentary (27 Jan 2009): PNG violence-accountability climate — a mob stripped, beat with hot iron rods and burned a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station; provincial commanders recorded 50+ sorcery-related killings in two highlands provinces in 2008 with perpetrators rarely brought to justice; sorcery accusations (linked to HIV deaths) used to hide murders and mitigate sentences; police routinely take no action.

ABC News (8 Oct 2014): Hanuabada village on Port Moresby's outskirts is a safe haven for PNG's gay and transgender community — residents live openly, transgender people wear women's clothes in the street without retaliation, while in Port Moresby gay/trans people are commonly raped or beaten, sometimes by police (documentary maker Vlad Sokhin, who found the village while travelling).

The Guardian (13 Jan 2017) on HRW's annual world-report assessment of PNG: the government of Peter O'Neill has failed to protect women and children and to respond to corruption and police violence — 'police abuse, including of children, continues to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse'.

Guardian Nigeria (reprint): describes Hanuabada ('big village', built over the sea) as a pocket of tolerance where the gay community is accepted — set against PNG where sex between men is illegal and stigma/violence widespread (a 24-year-old gay man recounts being pelted with stones and bottles); campaigners say attitudes shift with exposure to the LGBT community.

PNG.tangentialFactors:
The violence documented against gay and transgender people in Port Moresby sits within a broader pattern of mob violence and police impunity that Human Rights Watch has recorded for years, including a 2009 case in which a mob stripped, beat and burned a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station.

Campaigners quoted in reporting say that attitudes toward LGBT people shift with direct exposure to the community, which is why a single village can function as a safe haven while the capital remains hostile.

Papua New Guinea's position is assessed alongside 16 other Asia-Pacific jurisdictions by the Asian Development Bank, placing its legal regime within a regional comparative framework rather than treating it as an isolated case.
PNG.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Cameroon (0.21 — both pair criminalisation with extreme ambient violence), above Nigeria (0.19) and below Egypt (0.22).

BWA.name: Botswana
BWA.summary:
Botswana decriminalised consensual sexual conduct between adults through its own courts. The High Court struck down Penal Code Section 164(a) and (c) on 11 June 2019 in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General, and the Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 29 November 2021, holding that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." The two paragraphs were formally deleted from the statute book in March 2026 by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026. Before that, the offence covered heterosexual and homosexual sodomy alike and carried up to seven years' imprisonment.

Prosecution was rare even while the offence stood. The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded that police "did not target same-sex activity" that year and found no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2011. Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC that during his ten years in office he instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people, while declining to change a law he said would cost him an election.

One provision remains unaddressed in the sources. Canada recommended at the 43rd session of the Universal Periodic Review in May 2023 that Botswana repeal Penal Code Section 167, which covers same-sex conduct between women; Botswana did not accept the recommendation, and no source in the inventory records a subsequent repeal of Section 167. Botswana likewise declined a recommendation to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition, with the review noting that "a clear administrative process ... was yet to be introduced" (para 570).

Legal gender recognition has nonetheless been won case by case. In September 2017 the High Court held that the Registrar of National Registration's refusal to change a transgender man's gender marker violated his constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. In December 2017 the same court ordered the government to recognise the gender of transgender woman and activist Tshepo Ricki Kgositau, who received a female identity card after a four-year legal battle and gender confirmation surgery in December 2016; she dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana." Human Rights Watch records the trans legal-gender right as confirmed across 2017 to 2022. Recognition therefore rests on litigation rather than on a standing administrative route.

The constitutional framework has moved in the same direction. In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation; legal commentator Carmel Rickard wrote that this gives LGBTQ Batswana "an even stronger, constitutionally-based argument" against discrimination.

Official rhetoric has been openly divided. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he held the power. President Ian Khama deported the American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson in September 2016, stating "we don't want hate speech in this country." In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and said they deserved protection. Afrobarometer recorded tolerance of a homosexual neighbour rising from 43% in 2016 to 50% in 2021, a level that still leaves roughly half the population unwelcoming.
BWA.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Penal Code Section 167 survived the March 2026 Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order is unresolved: the inventory records only the deletion of paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164, and records Canada's 2023 recommendation to repeal Section 167 as not accepted. No source consulted states its current status.

No source in the inventory establishes that an administrative gender-recognition procedure now exists; the 2023 Universal Periodic Review record states it was yet to be introduced, and later material does not revisit the point. Confirmation that the 2017 rulings remain operative in 2026 rests on Human Rights Watch's 2017 to 2022 window rather than on a more recent audit.

The 2011 Human Rights Report is fifteen years old and speaks to police conduct and reported violence at that date; no post-2021 enforcement statistics on police treatment of trans visitors appear in the inventory. The status of the draft constitutional amendment on intersex and disability discrimination is also unresolved, as is the scope of the wider review process that civic groups criticised.

sources.summary: SALC, Digashu & Mmolai-Chalmers (20 May 2024): Botswana's precedent wins — 2016 Court of Appeal ordered registration of LEGABIBO (freedom of association, expression, assembly), a 2017 High Court ordered the state to change a trans man's identity documents from female to male (dignity and humanity), and the 2021 Court of Appeal decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct — yet implementation across Botswana and Namibia 'has not been satisfactory so far'.

Alta Advisory (18 Jun 2024): Botswana's draft constitutional amendment would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities; in June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep 'intersex' and 'same-sex' distinct. Civic groups criticise the wider review process, but the intersex provision signals momentum toward broader LGBTQI+ protection.

UN UPR outcome, 43rd session (May 2023): Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendations to repeal Penal Code Section 167 (same-sex conduct between women) and to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition — 'a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced' (para 570); abortion-decriminalisation recommendation also declined.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Botswana: the LGBT section documents that same-sex conduct was then criminalised and records societal discrimination against LGBT people. The report's wider assessment covers violence against women, prison conditions and San discrimination.

LEGABIBO official site: Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation running advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health/HIV work (e.g., World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong), with Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources — a functioning, legally registered community infrastructure (registration won in the 2016 Court of Appeal order).

The Independent (19 Dec 2017): Botswana's High Court ordered the government to legally recognise a trans woman's gender for the first time — Tshepo Ricki Kgositau won a female identity card after a four-year legal battle (gender confirmation surgery December 2016), dedicating the victory to 'every single trans diverse person in Botswana'. A landmark for legal gender recognition in the country.

Human Rights Watch (24 Jan 2018): previewed the Botswana constitutional challenge to the colonial-era 'carnal knowledge' law, with the hearing set for March 2018. The law was struck down on 11 Jun 2019 and the judgment upheld on appeal on 29 Nov 2021; the trans legal-gender right was confirmed 2017-22.

NAM.name: Namibia
NAM.summary:
Namibia's Supreme Court ruled on 16 May 2023 that same-sex marriages performed abroad must be recognised under the Immigration Act, granting non-Namibian spouses the same residence rights as opposite-sex spouses. Compliance has failed: immigration officials tell litigant Daniel Digashu that the ruling covers only the couples who brought the case, and he is issued a visitor's visa on every exit. Gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than to "all persons".

Parliament answered the litigation with hostile marriage bills and, in late 2024, passed an act explicitly forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad, overriding the Supreme Court ruling. Reporting that amplified the non-implementation compounded the effect, according to an op-ed by Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre published by the Washington Blade on 22 May 2024.

On 21 June 2024 the High Court of Windhoek declared unconstitutional and invalid the references to sodomy and "unnatural sexual offences" in the Immigration Act; the government appealed in July 2024. The UNDP reports that Namibia's courts decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2024 and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested. The government told the UN it had no intention of repealing the colonial-era sodomy law, which has not been believed used since independence in 1990.

Gender-marker changes are available under section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and described as "not problematic" by the Legal Assistance Centre (2015). Article 10 of the Constitution omits gender identity and sexual orientation, though "other status" should encompass them per the UN Human Rights Committee.

Residence rights at the border have been contested for decades: in 2001 a Namibian woman's German wife Elisabeth Frank won a Supreme Court permanent residence permit without the court endorsing same-sex relationships, and in January 2018 Daniel Digashu won a court petition to enter Namibia while his case was reviewed.

Public displays of affection between two men can still be treated as "immoral" behaviour punishable under the Combating of Immoral Practices Act of 1980. Organised political hostility exists: a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters launched in 2014 with identical branding but an explicitly anti-gay stance, and the SWAPO Party Youth League is listed among parties opposing LGBTQ rights.

The Namibia's Broadcasting Code for Broadcasting Licensees 2018 (General Notice No. 602) bars licensees from broadcasting material advocating hatred based on gender or sexual orientation, sanctions violence or unlawful conduct on those grounds, and prohibits material likely to incite hatred or severe ridicule against persons because of sexual orientation where that constitutes incitement to harm.

MUS.name: Mauritius
MUS.summary:
Mauritius presents limited legal risk to trans visitors. Same-sex conduct ceased to be a criminal offence on 4 October 2023, when the Supreme Court struck down Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838, which had provided for penal servitude of up to five years, ruling that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. The US State Department's 2016 country report found that the provision had rarely reached same-sex couples in court: sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce proceedings as an aggravating factor, though a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy. No criminal provision in the sources targets gender expression, and no case is recorded in which a visitor was prosecuted or detained for presenting in clothing associated with another gender.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Mauritius. The AfricLaw analysis of 23 August 2024 identifies the Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database as the administrative framework under which trans Mauritians are denied recognition. Outright International's country overview, last updated 12 March 2026, states plainly that legal gender recognition is not possible. A trans visitor should expect identity and travel documents to carry a sex marker unchanged from birth, and no route exists locally for amending them. Whether consular or immigration screening at entry engages gender markers is not addressed in the sources.

The 2021 Civil Status Act permits intersex newborns to be registered as 'undetermined', but nonconsensual intersex medical procedures are not banned. The same overview records that no same-sex marriage or civil union is recognised.

The documented harm to trans people in Mauritius is social rather than statutory. The 2016 State Department report recorded the harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing, and noted that LGBTI people facing verbal abuse or violence within the family generally reported to local NGOs rather than police. Public events carry visible opposition: Pride has been held since 2005 and has drawn counter-protesters, and in 2018 the march was cancelled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, though police had earlier that year deployed to protect marchers and an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront proceeded with the Prime Minister's support. During the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and other candidates used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

Formal protection is partial. The Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 prohibit discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, but the sources do not identify equivalent statutory protection for gender identity. Outright International records that LGBTI organisations cannot register, which constrains the formal support infrastructure available to a visitor in difficulty. On healthcare, the government states that hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, while gender-affirming care is available only in limited form; LGBTQ people may face discrimination in public hospitals.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's Mauritius coverage reports that Collectif Arc-En-Ciel, founded in 2005, organised the country's first Pride and has done so for fifteen years, drawing more than 1,200 participants in 2016, when the march moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis. In 2018 the Pride march was annulled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, and a counter-protest was organised by Javed Meetoo, an Islamic extremist under state surveillance; a strong police force had been deployed earlier in 2018 to protect marchers, and an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support. AfriGay reports that gay life is fairly quiet, existing mainly online, in private and at occasional parties, though resorts are welcoming and non-discriminatory and no problems with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms have been recorded. LGBTQ people may face discrimination notably in public hospitals; according to the government, hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form. In 2014 the Ministry of Health amended blood donation policy to allow men who have sex with men to donate, although anecdotally LGBTQI persons have still been prevented from donating on occasion. Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838 provided for penal servitude of up to 5 years for sodomy, the law under which a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy; prosecutions under the law were rare, and on 4 October 2023 the Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional, ruling that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. In 2017 the government said it would not repeal Section 250, saying it would address the issue after further consideration, and former Attorney General Rama Valayden's decriminalisation bill failed to pass. Conservative attitudes remain commonplace and LGBTQ people still face discrimination; in 2018 religious extremists issued hundreds of death threats that cancelled Pride and organised a counter-protest, with Cardinal Maurice Piat and other religious leaders condemning the anti-LGBTQ protest and calling for tolerance. State actors have also shown support: police protected Pride marchers, Prime Minister Pravind Jugnauth backed an LGBTQ sit-in, and the Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights. LGBTQ people may face bullying in schools, while acceptance is growing particularly among the younger generation, with polls indicating Mauritius is one of Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries. In October 2019 a group of young people filed a constitutional challenge to Section 250, supported by the Young Queer Alliance and the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, alongside activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek, 29, backed by Collectif Arc-En-Ciel. The Young Queer Alliance was founded on 1 September 2014 for young LGBTQ Mauritians, engaging in support, advocacy and anti-discrimination campaigns; a 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour.

MUS.tangentialFactors:
Outright International's overview frames the 2023 decriminalisation as a measurable advance for lesbian, gay and bisexual people while recording that progress for trans and intersex people has been 'less evident', a distinction that matches the gap between the struck-down sodomy provision and the continuing absence of gender recognition.

Visibility has outpaced law. Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan became the first transgender woman to compete in Miss Universe Mauritius in 2024, and AfricLaw treats the participation as a milestone set against legal obstacles that remain inadequate. Advocacy by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G continues under those constraints; the Young Queer Alliance's July 2021 policy brief on administrative recognition cites the WHO's ICD-11 removal of trans categories from mental disorders in 2019 and calls on Mauritius to join the states recognising gender identity in law.

Societal attitudes are mixed rather than uniformly hostile. Polling cited in secondary coverage places Mauritius among the more LGBTQ-friendly countries in Africa, acceptance is reported as growing among younger Mauritians, and a 2016 poll found 49 per cent of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. Conservative religious opposition remains organised, as the 2018 threats to Pride and the 2024 election rhetoric show, while religious leaders including Cardinal Maurice Piat publicly condemned the anti-LGBTQ protest that year.

State actors have also supported LGBTI people in specific instances: police protected Pride marchers in 2018, the Prime Minister backed the subsequent sit-in, and the Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights.
MUS.localsOnly:
Residents hold employment protections on grounds of sexual orientation under the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019. The sources do not identify gender identity as a protected ground in that legislation.

Trans Mauritians cannot obtain legal gender recognition; the Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database define the administrative position. Intersex newborns may be registered as 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act, though nonconsensual intersex procedures remain lawful.

LGBTI organisations cannot register, which affects the operational status of groups such as the Young Queer Alliance, founded on 1 September 2014, and Collectif Arc-en-Ciel, founded in 2005, both of which run support, advocacy and anti-discrimination work and receive disclosures from LGBTI people experiencing family violence. LGBTI people may face discrimination in public hospitals and bullying in schools. Government statements indicate hormone therapy is available through public hospitals, with gender-affirming care limited in scope.

Public events carry visible opposition: Pride has been held since 2005 and has drawn counter-protesters, and in 2018 the march was cancelled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, though police had earlier that year deployed to protect marchers and an LGBTQ sit-in at a waterfront site proceeded with the prime minister's support. During the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and other candidates used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

Formal protection is partial. The Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 prohibit discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, but the sources do not identify equivalent statutory protection for gender identity. The regional organisation's overview records that LGBTI organisations cannot register, which constrains the formal support infrastructure available to a visitor in difficulty. On healthcare, the government states that hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, while gender-affirming care is available only in limited form; LGBTQ people may face discrimination in public hospitals.

Intersex newborns may be registered as 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act, though nonconsensual intersex procedures remain lawful.

LGBTI organisations cannot registered, which affects the operational status of two local groups, one founded in 2014 and one in 2005, that run support, advocacy and anti-discrimination work and receive disclosures from LGBTI people experiencing family violence. Visibility has outpaced law. A trans woman became the first transgender contestant in the country's national Miss Universe franchise in 2024, and the 2024 legal-academic analysis treats the participation as a milestone set against legal obstacles that remain inadequate. Polling cited in secondary coverage places the country among the more LGBTQ-friendly jurisdictions in its region, acceptance is reported as growing among younger Mauritians, and a 2016 poll found 49 per cent of residents would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. State actors have also supported LGBTI people in specific instances: police protected Pride marchers in 2018, the prime minister backed the subsequent sit-in, and the parliamentary opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights.

SYC.name: Seychelles
SYC.summary:
Seychelles decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2016 with the repeal of Penal Code Section 151, a colonial-era provision that had carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex intimacy.

The Constitution of Seychelles guarantees freedom from torture under Article 16 and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex under Article 27. The source text listing those grounds does not name gender identity expressly.

Section 5 of the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) adds sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status to the protected characteristics, creating an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences.

The revised law increases prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward a victim's sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability. The Human Dignity Trust describes Seychelles, after South Africa, as the second African country to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation.

Seychelles does not recognise same-sex marriage or same-sex civil unions. In June 2015 two men, one British and one Seychellois national, were married at the British High Commission in Seychelles by High Commissioner Lindsay Skoll, a ceremony performed under foreign mission authority rather than Seychellois law.

Legal and social conditions for visitors continue to vary from the statutory position; the statutory framework is protective, but the sources do not document enforcement practice or day-to-day experience for trans travellers.
SYC.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2024 enhanced-protection provisions have been applied in any reported prosecution is unresolved in the sources; no enforcement case is documented.

The sources do not address legal gender recognition, marker changes on identity documents, or any screening process that could expose a trans traveller's gender history at entry; these remain not sourced.

Facilities access, healthcare restrictions, and any documented incidents of violence against trans visitors in Seychelles are not covered by the inventory and remain unresolved.

SEN.name: Senegal
SEN.summary:
Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity under Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, which carries a maximum of five years' imprisonment. The provision is enforced: in September 2018 four LGBT people, two women and two men, were detained in Dakar on charges of "acts against the order of nature" after videos of them circulated, part of a wave of politically motivated detentions in the run-up to the 2019 elections.

A campaign to raise the maximum penalty to 15 years has run since 2020, with anti-LGBT forces pressing for the increase as of July 2024. The maximum sentence remains five years; the proposal has not been reported as enacted.

Official hostility extends to speech on the subject. A political activist and a preacher were jailed and fined 100,000 CFA francs each after posting a video attacking opposition leader Ousmane Sonko for allowing a visiting French politician to express support for same-sex marriage. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report on Senegal listed pre-electoral violence, torture, and violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the country's major human-rights problems.

Violence by non-state actors is documented at extreme scale. In November 2023 the body of a 31-year-old man, named locally as Cheikh Fall, was dug up from a cemetery and burned in the street after it became known that he was gay. Four men were arrested in connection with the incident; images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathered around the fire.
SEN.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced information on legal gender recognition or the change of sex markers on Senegalese identity documents, on hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, on recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriages, on entry or visa screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status, on access to gender-affirming medical care, or on facilities and restroom rules. These are unresolved rather than absent from Senegalese law.

Whether Article 319 has been applied specifically to transgender people, as distinct from cisgender men and women, is not sourced here; the 2018 detentions involved two women and two men but the reporting does not identify any of them as trans.

The legislative status of the proposed fifteen-year penalty is unresolved beyond July 2024, the date of the most recent source in the inventory. The US State Department human rights material dates from 2012 and does not establish current conditions on its own.

BBC News reports that a political activist and a preacher were jailed in Senegal for criticising opposition leader Ousmane Sonko and fined 100,000 CFA francs ($165, £130) each. They had been angered that Mr Sonko allowed a visiting French politician to express his support for same-sex marriage, and were arrested after posting a video attacking him for giving the politician a platform. Homosexual acts are banned in Senegal and are punishable by up to five years in prison.

SEN.tangentialFactors:
Enforcement in Senegal has a demonstrably political rhythm. The September 2018 detentions in Dakar came amid a wave of arrests ahead of the 2019 elections, and the US State Department's 2012 report identified pre-electoral violence as one of the country's major human-rights problems alongside anti-LGBT abuse. Travellers should expect the intensity of policing around LGBT people to rise during election periods rather than remain constant.

The Sonko affair shows that the sensitivity runs to association as well as conduct: the two men jailed were punished for criticising a politician for giving a platform to a foreign figure who voiced support for same-sex marriage, not for any sexual conduct of their own. Public discussion that appears to tolerate same-sex relations can itself draw criminal penalties.

The pending debate over raising the sentence from five to fifteen years keeps the legal environment unsettled. Abuses against LGBT people are described as commonplace in the country, and the November 2023 exhumation drew a crowd of hundreds, indicating that mob action can occur with broad public participation while arrests follow after the fact.
SEN.comparisons: Pairwise: below Malaysia (0.28 — comparable criminalisation-plus-mob climate) and above Pakistan (0.26) and Côte d'Ivoire (0.34 — CIV decriminalised but has the 2024 hunt-down violence wave; SEN has statutory criminalisation but no equivalent mob-hunt wave; net SEN slightly worse).

CIV.name: Côte d'Ivoire
CIV.summary:
Same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence in Côte d'Ivoire. The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices records that same-sex relations are not an offence, so a trans visitor carries no statutory exposure on that ground.

Violence against LGBTQ people by non-state actors is documented and has been lethal. The 2023 report counts three deaths within the community during that year. Police handling of such violence was described as sometimes slow and ineffective and often inclined to blame the victim, although authorities were dealing with complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

Trans and gender-nonconforming people face the sharper risk. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man.

Peer-reviewed research published in 2015 found that travestis, people born male who live as women, endure harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender presentation does not attract attention. The same study reports that Ivoirian rights groups distanced themselves from travestis and left them underserved, and examines the isolation they experienced after the post-election violence of 2010–11.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, alteration of sex markers on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a trans identity, access to gender-affirming care, facility or bathroom rules, or the recognition of partners. The absence of those rules from the record is a gap in sourcing rather than a finding that they are unrestricted.
CIV.outOfScopeNotes:
The placement of transgender detainees — whether they are held in units matching birth sex or gender identity, whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used — is not covered by any available publication. Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on this question for Côte d'Ivoire; on its country page, LGBT Rights appears only as a topic-facet link.

A UNDP report published in December 2024, reviewing ten years of African Commission Resolution 275, includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people. The specific findings of that overview are not stated in the available inventory and remain unresolved here.

Whether Côte d'Ivoire provides for legal gender recognition or amendment of sex markers on civil documents, and whether a visitor's entry documents are screened for such markers, is not sourced. Provisions on hate-crime aggravation, on partnership or marriage recognition, and on access to gender-affirming care are likewise not sourced from the inventory and should not be read as absent from the law.

MLI.name: Mali
MLI.summary:
Mali's penal code announced in October 2024 and in force from 13 December 2024 criminalises same-sex conduct, an escalation under the military junta that reverses the previous position in which same-sex relations were not a criminal offence. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 6 November 2024, describes the penalties as harsh.

The statute also bans the undefined offence of "promoting" homosexuality and reaches any citizen seen to encourage it. Because the term is not defined in the code, the provision widens the range of people who can be charged well beyond those accused of conduct itself, and Human Rights Watch states that the drafting is broad enough for expansive application.

Before the code took effect, same-sex conduct was legal in Mali, but the vague "public indecency" provisions of Article 225 were already used against LGBT people and against gender-nonconforming expression. Presentation rather than conduct has historically been what draws police attention, so a trans visitor's visible gender expression, not only any intimacy, is the surface on which enforcement has previously operated.

The change arrived alongside a wider clampdown on opposition and media under the military junta, in a security environment marked by armed-group violence and instability. Societal stigma toward LGBT people was already assessed as significant by the United States State Department in its 2021 human rights report, before decriminalisation ended.

No entry, visa, or gender-marker documentation rules for trans travellers are documented in the sources available for this record.
MLI.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile on Mali returned HTTP 403 and could not be retrieved at research time. It is understood to document the country's new criminalisation of same-sex conduct, but its content, including any stated penalty ranges, is not sourced here.

The exact penalties attached to the new offences are not specified in any source available for this record; sources describe them only as harsh.

Nothing in the available inventory addresses prison placement, special units, solitary confinement or segregation practice for trans detainees, nor visa rules, gender-marker requirements on travel or identity documents, access to gender-affirming care, hate-crime protection, or recognition of partners and marriages. These remain unresolved and unsourced rather than assessed as absent.

BFA.name: Burkina Faso
BFA.summary:
On 1 September 2025 the Transitional Legislative Assembly of Burkina Faso passed, unanimously, a law making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence. Penalties are two to five years' imprisonment plus fines. The criminal code in force from that date also prohibits the promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour, and the law took effect immediately on passage.

The prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code that the council of the military junta approved in July 2024 as part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law. The code entered into force on 1 September 2025 and is the instrument through which the ban operates as criminal law. Homosexuality had not previously been outlawed in Burkina Faso.

Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala stated that the penalty range of two to five years' imprisonment, together with fines, applies to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices", and that foreign nationals who violate the law will be deported. A trans or gender-nonconforming visitor convicted or accused under the provision therefore faces imprisonment followed by removal from the country.

As of 28 September 2025 no arrests under the law had been reported. France 24 and AFP coverage of 22 September 2025 described fears of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship among LGBTQ people in the country, which indicates heightened informal risk even where formal enforcement had not yet been recorded.

Article 23 of the Constitution defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman, describes the family as the basic unit of society owed state protection, and does not authorise same-sex marriage. Its list of prohibited grounds of discrimination in marriage covers race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin and wealth, and omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and on same-sex adoption remain in force.
BFA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory states whether the 2025 law's provisions or penalties apply differently to gender identity or gender expression as opposed to sexual conduct, and no trans-specific enforcement, arrest or prosecution has been reported. This is unresolved rather than established either way.

The conditions for the deportation of foreign nationals are not specified in the sources: the inventory does not indicate whether removal follows summary immigration action, criminal conviction, or both, and no visa or entry-screening practice for trans travellers is documented.

Whether the offence of promoting homosexuality or similar behaviour reaches possession of material, online expression or organised community activity is not set out in any source consulted here.

The 2011 Human Rights Report predates the 2025 criminalisation by fourteen years, and no current source restates protections in employment, housing, education or healthcare. Its findings should be read as historical baseline, not as the present state of affairs.

Access to gender-affirming care, availability of identity documents reflecting a trans person's gender, and any procedure for legal gender recognition are not covered by the sources; nothing should be inferred from their absence.

sources.summary:

The law passed unanimously in the unelected 71-member transitional parliament and took effect immediately. Foreign nationals who violate it will be deported. France 24–AFP coverage of 22 September 2025 described fears of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship in the LGBTQ community, and as of 28 September 2025 no arrests under the law had been reported.

Same-sex activity was legal before 2025, with an equal age of consent implemented in 1996 and overturned by the 2025 code. The Constitution's Article 23 defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman, describes the family as the basic unit of society owed state protection, and does not authorise same-sex marriage. That article bars discrimination in marriage based on race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin or wealth, a list that omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and same-sex adoption remain in force, and the July 2024 amended family code draft under the Traoré junta targeted consensual same-sex relations.

Under the U.S. Department of State, only married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married at least five years may adopt, and single applicants are almost never permitted to adopt.

The 2011 Human Rights Report found the law did not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation in employment and occupation, housing, statelessness, access to education or health care, while societal discrimination on those grounds persisted. LGBT persons were reported as occasional victims of verbal and physical abuse, religious and traditional beliefs did not accept homosexuality, and there were no reports that the government responded to societal violence and discrimination against them. LGBTQ organisations had no legal presence in the country but existed unofficially, with no reported violence against them.

National adult HIV prevalence stands at 0.80% of those aged 15 to 49. Of an estimated 94,000 adults living with HIV, 65% have antiretroviral drugs, and 28% of children aged 0 to 14 do, against all-ages coverage of 32% in 2010.

MOZ.name: Mozambique
MOZ.summary:
Mozambique's legal position on consensual same-sex conduct is among the more permissive in sub-Saharan Africa. The 2015 Penal Code erased the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision, and same-sex conduct has been legal since. A trans visitor faces no criminal exposure on the basis of identity or consensual conduct.

No procedure for legal gender recognition exists in Mozambican law. A visitor whose passport or other documents carry markers inconsistent with their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at checkpoints and in any interaction requiring identification. The sources describe no formal screening process, and they offer no assurance against one.

The Penal Code (Law 24/2019, in force from 2020) contains hate-crime and hate-speech provisions with direct bearing on trans visitors. Article 191 prohibits incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on grounds of gender identity, and also covers defamation, insults and threats directed at transgender people. Article 160 treats a victim's sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating factor in homicide. Enforcement of these provisions is not documented in the sources.

Protection machinery exists in limited form. Applications by Lambda Mozambique, the country's only LGBT organisation, were blocked from 2008 onward, prompting a UN appeal in 2010. In October 2017 the Constitutional Council struck down the 'moral order' clause of Article 1 of Law No. 8/91 that had been used to refuse registration, and on 28 November 2017 it ruled that the organisation's status did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in education, health, housing or employment. Employment protections that had been in place since 2007 were repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024. The Advertising Code of 2016 separately bars advertisements containing discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Mozambique does not recognise same-sex relationships; same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt. Reports from Lambda describe a community that is not subjected to the levels of targeted violence seen in some other African states but does face routine discrimination, family ostracisation and barriers in employment and education.
MOZ.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the instrument that removed employment non-discrimination protection: Outright International attributes the removal to a 2024 penal code, while other material attributes it to Labor Law No. 13/2023. Which instrument governs is unresolved here.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 chapter on Mozambique, published 11 January 2024, records general police detentions and election-related arrests but contains no transgender-specific content and no information on where trans prisoners are housed. Prison placement for trans detainees is not sourced.

No source in this inventory addresses border or immigration screening of gender markers, entry refusal on those grounds, access to gender-affirming healthcare for visitors, or facilities and restroom access. Whether enforcement bodies apply Articles 160 and 190 in practice, and how police handle an identity-document mismatch, are likewise not documented.

sources.summary: Outright International (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct legal since the 2015 penal code; no legal gender recognition procedure exists; societal attitudes broadly neutral but LGBTIQ people face family ostracisation and employment/education barriers; the 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations then disappointed. The 2024 penal code removed the employment non-discrimination protection that had existed.

GlobalGayz archive (2006-2011): dated milestones — first newspaper article arguing gay rights (Agencia de Informacao, 7 July 2006), Maputo men petitioning parliament, the LGBT group still unregistered as of March 2011, refugee deaths en route to South Africa; documents early organising under the colonial-era law.
Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2016) from Afrobarometer: Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant — 56% would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour (vs Uganda/Burkina Faso/Niger at 5%).

Global Voices (28 Nov 2017): after a decade of blocked applications (since 2008), the Constitutional Council — supreme court equivalent — ruled Lambda Mozambique's status did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration of the country's only LGBT organisation.

Guardian (30 June 2015): Mozambique's new penal code erased the colonial 'vices against nature' provision; Lambda (not yet officially registered at the time) pivoted to anti-discrimination lobbying; Lambda's Carina Capitine: the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination.

Mozambique does not recognise same-sex relationships, and same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt. Protests for same-sex marriage and common-law marriage have run since 2006. A 2017 survey found support for same-sex marriage at 47% in Maputo, 38% in Beira and 42% in Nampula, and a 2017 ILGA poll found 61% of Mozambicans agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people. The 2017 survey found most respondents would not accept a child who came out, with 28% of Beira respondents stating they would assault their child if he or she was gay; 85% opposed violence against LGBTQ people and would help if they were being physically assaulted, and about one-third of respondents personally knew an openly LGBTQ person. A 2013 survey found moderate support for parenting rights, and 55% of respondents in the 2017 ILGA poll believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

RWA.name: Rwanda
RWA.summary:
Rwanda does not criminalise same-sex intimacy, and the age of consent is 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. A trans visitor therefore faces no statute aimed at identity or consensual relationships. That baseline does not describe what happens on the street. A 2025 submission by the Human Rights First Rwanda Association to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuse directed at transgender people: harassment during identity checks and arbitrary arrests on vagrancy and public-order grounds, including during periodic round-ups in Kigali.

The detention record extends beyond that submission. In November 2020 Vice reported violent detentions of transgender people in Rwanda, describing how on Christmas Day 2018 a singer known as Bella, booked to perform at a hotel in Kigali, was stopped by police officers on the street after her show; her name was changed in the account over safety concerns. A 2016 United States State Department country report separately records LGBTQ Rwandans being harassed, blackmailed and arrested by police under public-order and morality laws, and LGBTI rights groups reporting occasional harassment by neighbours and police.

Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no domestic legal gender recognition path exists for a trans person. Article 26 of the Constitution, adopted in May 2003, recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman; same-sex marriages, civil unions and equivalent unions are not recognised, so a foreign trans marriage is not given effect under the constitutional text as reported.

Entry and protection machinery runs in the opposite direction to the street record. In 2024 the government issued immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. The 2024 Asylum and Humanitarian Protection Decision Making Standard Operating Procedures require interviews to be conducted so the applicant can present the grounds of the application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The 2014 Manual on Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures imposes a comparable requirement at appeal hearings.

Healthcare access is protected on paper. The Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy issued by the Ministry of Health in 2018 states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief or disability are equally entitled to receive health services, and applies across public, private and NGO sectors. Against that, there is no general anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity: Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution do not list either ground, with Article 16 naming ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability and others.
RWA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses Rwandan entry or visa screening, including whether border officials inspect passport gender markers or ask questions that could disclose a visitor's trans status. That question is unresolved here.

The inventory does not establish whether a legal gender recognition procedure exists in any administrative form, nor does it document hate-crime sentencing or any prosecution of police abuse reported by transgender detainees. Both remain unsourced rather than confirmed absent, except for the absence of anti-discrimination and recognition statutes stated above, which the sources do assert.

The Vice account relies on a pseudonymised source and the name used in it is a safety substitution; the underlying incident cannot be independently verified from this inventory.

President Kagame's 2016 remark is a public statement, not a legal instrument, and no source shows how it shapes present enforcement practice. The 2012 regional blog is historical and general, and its anthropological claims about pre-colonial same-sex relations are unverified here.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D6.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Homosexuality is a taboo topic in Rwanda with no significant public discussion, and LGBTQ people face stigmatization among the broader population. In September 2019 gospel singer Albert Nabonibo came out as gay on a Christian YouTube channel, causing shock in a country where such a public assertion is described as unheard of, with horrible reactions from family and friends, though the Minister of State for East African Community Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, publicly backed him. The Horizons Community Association of Rwanda has conducted public advocacy for LGBTQ rights since 2005, but its members have often been harassed by the government. The Anglican Church of Rwanda condemned non-biblical behaviors of Western churches in 2007 and refused to support ordination of LGBTQ clergy. In September 2016 President Paul Kagame said homosexuality hasn't been our problem and we don't intend to make it our problem. Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no legal gender recognition path exists for transgender people. The Constitution (adopted May 2003), Article 26, states only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman is recognized, so same-sex marriages, civil unions and similar unions are not recognized. Same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an age of consent of 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. In 2024 the Government issued immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. The Asylum and humanitarian protection decision making Standard Operating Procedures (2024) require that interviews be conducted so the individual can present the grounds of their application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The Manual on Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures (2014) similarly requires hearings to take account of the appellant's sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. Standard Operating Procedures on identifying and safeguarding vulnerable persons under the Migration and Economic Development Partnership (2024) define Vulnerable Persons to include individuals whose gender identity and/or sexual orientation place them at higher risk, expressly naming lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons. LGBTQ Rwandans have reported being harassed, blackmailed, and even arrested by police under various laws dealing with public order and morality, and LGBTI rights groups reported occasional harassment by neighbors and police (U.S. State Department 2016 report). The Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy (2018) issued by the Ministry of Health states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief, or disability are equally entitled to receive health services to promote and maintain good health, applying across public, private and NGO sectors. No youth-specific or minor-specific care access findings appear in the source text. There are no anti-discrimination laws afforded to LGBTQ citizens, and the Constitution's non-discrimination provisions (Articles 15 and 16) do not ban discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity; Article 16 lists ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability and other grounds but not SOGI. Limited protections exist: the Human Resource Management Policy (2015) of the Office of the Auditor General of State Finances lists sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for harassment; the Code of Conduct of the Public Private Partnership Guidelines (2018) bans discrimination against bidders on grounds of sexual orientation; and Law 058/2021 on Protection of Personal Data and Privacy protects a person's sexual life as sensitive personal data. The age of consent in Rwanda is 18, regardless of sexual orientation or gender. Historically, in the old Kingdom of Rwanda male homosexual relations were common among young Hutus and Tutsis: boys training as warriors and Tutsi boys training at court formed emotional and often sexual relationships, sometimes lasting into adulthood, and were sometimes made sexually available to guests; societal acceptance disappeared after the arrival of European colonialists and Christianity. No contemporary youth-, minor- or education-specific findings (school policy, bullying, medication carriage by minors) appear in the source text.
