AGO.name: Angola
AGO.summary:
Angola's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct took effect on 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era provision describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and, in the same instrument, made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment. A continental survey published in October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services.

The constitutional layer is thinner than the statutory one. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and expression are located across Title II of the same document. A visitor therefore has statutory protection against orientation-based discrimination without a constitutional guarantee expressly naming gender identity.

Angolan organisations submitted a shadow report on the country's compliance with the African Charter for the African Commission's 81st session in Banjul in October and November 2024, authored by Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA, Diversidade Masculina and others with ILGA and Synergia support, documenting human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. A separate submission by Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, ahead of the committee's 74th-session review of Angola, raises discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people.

No specific law allows transgender people to change their gender marker on official documents or passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states that, in general, there should be no alteration of details entered into registration records, while section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status. Transgender people could possibly rely on section 87 to change their legal gender, but no worked procedure or precedent is recorded. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

No entry or visa provisions are recorded for Angola. The only entry-adjacent material available is external: an asylumlaw.org information packet on sexual minorities and HIV status used for asylum purposes, and UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office travel advice on local laws and customs.

Legally, people living with HIV/AIDS in Angola are entitled to health care services and to protection from employment discrimination. No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded anywhere in the country. On relationship recognition, there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant; in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as 'shameless' and 'abominable' in national news magazines.
AGO.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not record whether any person has successfully used section 87 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 to alter a gender marker, so the practical availability of that route is not established here.

Unresolved: no entry, visa or border-screening provisions specific to trans visitors are sourced for Angola. The available material is limited to an asylum information packet and foreign-office travel advice, neither of which is an entry rule.

Not sourced: there are no youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education for Angola, and no recorded shelters, safe houses or gender-neutral facilities for LGBTQ people.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Two LGBT groups operate in Angola, and only one, Iris Angola Association, has received official and legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018. At that time it had about 200 members, based in Luanda with offices in Benguela and Lubango. The three major political parties have not formally addressed LGBT issues in their platforms. The government does allow non-governmental organisations to exist, and some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education. In 2010 the Angolan Government refused to receive openly gay Isi Yanouka as the new Israeli ambassador, allegedly due to his sexual orientation, a diplomatic reception decision rather than a visa rule.

No specific law allows transgender people in Angola to change their gender marker on official documents and passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states that, in general, there should be no alteration of details entered into registration records, but section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status, meaning transgender people could possibly use this section to change their legal gender. A 2017 ILGA poll found 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

No entry or visa provisions are recorded for Angola; the only entry-adjacent items are external reference links to 'Asylumlaw.org: Sexual Minorities & HIV Status (Angola)' with information packets used for asylum purposes and to Angola travel advice on local laws and customs from the UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office.

Legally, people living with HIV/AIDS in Angola are entitled to health care services and protection from employment discrimination. No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded. On relationship recognition, there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant; in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as 'shameless' and 'abominable' in national news magazines.

Education-focused work for LGBTQ Angolans is nascent and underfunded: the first association, Acção Humana (Human Action), launched in 2006 but has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programs specifically for LGBT people have struggled to get NGO funding. An HIV/AIDS educational program for LGBT people is only just beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International, and a 2007 study estimated roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men. No youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education are recorded.

The country's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct took effect on 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the historic-era provision describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and, in the same instrument, made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment. A subregional survey published in October 2019 rated the country as having gone furthest among reforms in one region of the continent during that period, both by removing the historic-era offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services.

The constitutional layer is thinner than the statutory one. A chapter on transgender rights produced by a regional litigation centre records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and expression are located across Title II of the same document. A visitor therefore has statutory protection against orientation-based discrimination without a constitutional guarantee expressly naming gender identity.

Organisations inside the country submitted a shadow report on the state's compliance with the regional human rights charter for that charter body's 81st session in October and November 2024, authored by several domestic LGBTQI+ collectives with support from an international LGBT organisation and a human-rights institute, documenting human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. A separate submission by domestic LGBTQI+ organisations to a UN committee on economic, social and cultural rights, ahead of that committee's 74th-session review of the state, raises discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people.

Section 78 of the national civil registration code of 2015 states that, in general, there should be no alteration of details entered into registration records, while section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status. Transgender people could possibly rely on section 87 to change their legal gender, but no worked procedure or precedent is recorded. A 2017 poll by an international LGBT research organisation found that 49% of residents believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

No entry or visa provisions are recorded for the country. The only entry-adjacent material available is external: an asylum information packet on sexual minorities and HIV status used for asylum purposes, and travel advice from a foreign government on local laws and customs.

Legally, people living with HIV/AIDS in the country are entitled to health care services and to protection from employment discrimination. No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded anywhere in the state. On relationship recognition, there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant; in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as 'shameless' and 'abominable' in national news magazines.

COD.name: DR Congo
COD.summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo does not criminalise same-sex conduct. Same-sex activity has never been outlawed, including during Belgian colonial rule, and the age of consent is equal for partners of any sex. A March 2024 stakeholder submission to the country's 5th-cycle Universal Periodic Review by Savie asbl and co-signatories records that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights, so the absence of a ban carries no statutory safeguard behind it.

Public same-sex affection remains prosecutable. Article 176 of the Penal Code punishes anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions, and local ordinances are applied against LGBTQ people on the same territory. Queer In The World reports that LGBT expression is censored and can expose individuals to imprisonment, and GayOut rates the country high risk for LGBTQ travellers despite the lack of an explicit national prohibition.

Trans visitors have no route to legal status change: the country provides no gender-identity recognition and no legal gender change, and no relationship recognition of any kind, with same-sex marriage constitutionally banned since 2006. Queer In The World reports violence, harassment and torture against LGBT people involving police, security forces and the army, and advises visitors to exercise discretion and keep a low profile.

Armed militia groups in the eastern part of the country have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity. Where state authority has collapsed, legal protections are theoretical in practice, and the exposure a visitor faces arises from police, administrative and armed-group action rather than from a written prohibition.
COD.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document how often Article 176 is used, the outcomes of any prosecution under it, or whether particular cities apply their local ordinances more aggressively than others. Frequency and severity of enforcement therefore remain unresolved.

No trans-specific incident with a date, location and legal outcome is sourced for the country. Reports of violence involving police, security forces and the army are recorded without individual case detail, so their scale and whether they fall under hate-crime provisions cannot be established here.

The Human Rights Watch findings of December 2017 concern the response to protests, not the targeting of LGBT people, and no later reporting in this inventory revisits that pattern. Whether security-force recruitment of ex-m23 fighters continues is not sourced.

The stakeholder submission dates to March 2024 and the Queer In The World entry to 3 December 2023; whether the state has since accepted or rejected any Universal Periodic Review recommendation on sexual orientation or gender identity is not sourced. One supporting entry is a mirror of a Wikipedia article, so its claims on constitutional and age-of-consent points rest on secondary compilation rather than primary legal text.

ZMB.name: Zambia
ZMB.summary:
Zambia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct and the prohibition is actively enforced. Amnesty International's campaign of 26 November 2024, "Madalitso's story", follows a 36-year-old Zambian medical professional who had served three years of his sentence by November 2024 for consensual same-sex acts; his imprisonment removed a trained clinician from a health system already short of workers. The case is presented by Amnesty as illustrative of the persecution of LGBTI people in the country.

Police are a documented source of risk rather than protection. The US State Department's 2021 country report records police perpetrating violence and verbal and physical harassment on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation, together with prolonged detentions, and advocacy groups reported that police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTI individuals, with on-the-spot fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha, roughly $30 to $900. The 2022 report adds that officers who detain LGBTQI+ members often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release. LGBTQI+ people also face societal violence driven by prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of the law.

Forced anal examinations have been used to gather evidence in same-sex conduct prosecutions. Human Rights Watch's 2016 report "Dignity Debased" documents the practice in at least eight countries including Zambia, where it is less frequent than in Egypt and Tunisia but where prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal examinations as court evidence, including in a mass trial of about 20 men. Victims treat such examinations as painful, degrading sexual violence; Amnesty International described a 2014 case as tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid, and the WHO and medical authorities have condemned the practice.

Public advocacy of LGBTQ rights is effectively barred. The US State Department's 2021 report concluded that freedom of expression or peaceful assembly on LGBTQI+ matters remained nonexistent, and the government does not permit advocacy of LGBTQ rights. In 1998 Vice President Christon Tembo called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona (2013), an activist arrested after calling for decriminalisation on a television talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court held that he was reasonably exercising his right to freedom of expression, with the High Court rejecting the soliciting, public place and immoral purposes charges, though the government contested the decision.

Official policy is hostile. The 2022 country report found no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons, and while it recorded no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, a 30 May statement by President Hichilema opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults.

Violence from the public is documented and can be communal. In May 2014 residents of Marapodi in Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest, and in January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Threats, stalking, vandalism and hate crimes including murders are reported with little recourse to police, and most LGBTQ people in Zambia remain closeted out of fear of targeting, with lesbians described as especially vulnerable within the country's patriarchal structure.

Discrimination in employment, housing, education and health care is documented, and there are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care. The 2021 report records LGBTQI+ persons facing an inability to access healthcare services, and societal discrimination in access to health care and education is reported by the US State Department and by Global Rights/IGLHRC.
ZMB.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, or entry and visa screening for trans travellers, so those questions remain unresolved here rather than answered in the negative.

There is no information on trans-specific healthcare or medication in Zambia, including whether hormone therapy is available, restricted or obtainable privately.

Whether forced anal examinations continue to be ordered in current prosecutions is not established by these sources; the Human Rights Watch documentation dates from 2016 and the Amnesty reference from 2014, and no later case is cited.

It is unresolved whether the Kasonkomona precedent has been applied in subsequent prosecutions of advocacy, and whether the 2022 report's finding of no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws still holds in the most recent reporting year, as no post-2022 government report appears in the inventory.

Figures on HIV counselling provision and prevalence are drawn from 2007 and 2010 reporting and may not reflect current service coverage.

sources.summary:

The internet and digitization are credited with reducing prejudice among growing youth, and in 2013 Christine Kaseba, wife of then-President Michael Sata, said silence around men who have sex with men should end and no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation.

Violence from the public is documented and can be communal. In May 2014 residents of a residential area of the capital apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest, and in January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Threats, stalking, vandalism and hate crimes including murders are reported with little recourse to police, and most LGBTQ people in the country remain closeted out of fear of targeting, with lesbians described as especially vulnerable within the country's patriarchal structure.

Discrimination in employment, housing, education and health care is documented, and there are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care. The 2021 report records LGBTQI+ persons facing an inability to access healthcare services, and societal discrimination in access to health care and education is reported by international rights monitors.

Whether forced anal examinations continue to be ordered in current prosecutions is not established by these sources; the documentation dates from 2016 and 2014, and no later case is cited.

ZMB.blindTangential:
Public opinion is overwhelmingly negative and organised opposition exists. A 2010 survey found that 2 percent of the population regard homosexuality as morally acceptable, nine points below the 11 percent recorded in a neighbouring jurisdiction, and social attitudes are coloured by perceptions that homosexuality is immoral and a form of insanity, reflecting evangelical religious influence and historic-era attitudes. An advocacy group formed in 1999 explicitly to combat homosexuality has operated in the country since.

ZMB.localsOnly:

There is no parallel offence for minors of the opposite sex, and the provision applies only to same-sex conduct between minors.

Residents have limited formal protections in health care. The Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management based on sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour. The National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy (2015) recognises sexual orientation and gender identities as central aspects of being human.

ZWE.name: Zimbabwe
ZWE.summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The offence covers sodomy and, per the Human Dignity Trust country profile, acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent, so conduct short of intercourse can still fall within the criminal law.

Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024), 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries', examines rising anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in the countries it covers, Zimbabwe among them. The report's finding of law being deployed as an instrument of hostility is the operative risk context for a visitor, alongside the statutory exposure itself.

Healthcare access is formally protected. In July 2018 the Zimbabwean health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender or non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, recording that nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups. It was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor this means formal policy guarantees health-service access, including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990 with more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, provides legal support explicitly covering arrests for 'sodomy', counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. Legal aid and counselling remain reachable for an LGBTI traveller despite criminalisation.
ZWE.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether the 2018 handbook remains the operative health-sector instruction, whether it has been revised, withdrawn or reissued under a later administration, or how widely its training has actually been delivered since.

No source here states the statutory penalty for the sodomy or indecent-contact offences, nor whether any prosecution has been brought in recent years; the Human Dignity Trust profile is cited only for the scope of the offence.

Whether GALZ's four resource centres and legal support are accessible to a foreign national rather than to residents is not stated in the inventory.

Entry, visa and document-marker rules for trans travellers to Zimbabwe are not covered by any source supplied.

MWI.name: Malawi
MWI.summary:
Malawi criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 remain in force, and the provisions reach gender identity directly through their application to people whose gender expression departs from expectations; Human Rights Watch reports that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are the most likely to be targeted. Under sections 153 and 156 men face up to fourteen years' imprisonment and women five years, and the sections were before the courts in 2024 as carrying up to fourteen years.

On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court rejected the challenge to those sections. The application had been brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. Faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage. The court left any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the decision a dark day and warned that it exposes LGBT people to heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence.

Enforcement has been intermittent and evasive rather than absent. A justice-ministerial moratorium on arrests announced in 2012 was reaffirmed in December 2015, then suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 following litigation by religious leaders, leaving its legality contested. In April 2018 police in Mzuzu arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, a choice that circumvented the six-year moratorium while both laws faced constitutional challenge; police spokespersons confirmed the custody.

Arbitrary detention and ill-treatment by police are documented. A 61-page Human Rights Watch report released on 26 October 2018, based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, found that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and at times assaulted them. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion, forced stripping, forced medical and HIV and sexually transmitted infection examinations, and distribution of photographs on social media by community police.

Care access is compromised on gender-expression grounds. The same 2018 report records a trans man beaten and then refused treatment, and nurses mocking people presenting for HIV tests. Detention itself carries risk: Malawi's prisons were described as harsh in a 2011 United States State Department human rights report, and that report documented the July 2011 protest killings in which 20 people died.

Marriage and legal recognition are closed. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions, states that gender is assigned at birth, and does not permit a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender. No process for legal gender recognition is described in the sources. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; since 2019 the only limited protection is against hate speech, through sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d) of the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019, which bar broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference.

Official hostility is documented at the highest levels. In April 2010 President Bingu wa Mutharika called same-sex marriage evil and bad before the eyes of God, and in July 2011 he threatened activists Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence, saying he would hunt them in their homes and smoke them out, forcing them into hiding amid treason threats. In January 2016 People's Party spokesperson Ken Msonda posted that gay people are worse than dogs and should be killed; the Malawi Law Society filed charges but the director of public prosecution took over the matter and discontinued it on 21 January. The Muslim Association of Malawi called for the death penalty for gay people in February 2014, and on 4 January 2017 thousands across 28 districts marched against legalising homosexuality in protests led by the Episcopal Conference of Malawi and the Evangelical Association of Malawi. Peter Sawali was arrested in 2010 and given a 60-day sentence for posting Gay rights are human rights posters in Blantyre.
MWI.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state whether parliament took any action on Penal Code sections 153, 154 or 156 after the Constitutional Court's 28 June 2024 ruling, nor whether the government has announced a policy on enforcement since that date. Enforcement frequency after the ruling is unresolved in this inventory.

Whether the 2012 moratorium on arrests is legally operative remains unresolved: the Mzuzu High Court suspended it in 2016 following religious leaders' litigation, and no later judicial or executive determination is sourced here. The distinction in penalty between men and women under sections 153 and 156 is reported by Human Rights Watch, but the underlying statutory text is not reproduced in the inventory and the treatment of trans defendants under those provisions is not sourced.

No source in the inventory describes an administrative procedure, statutory or otherwise, for legal gender recognition in Malawi, and the absence of such a process is stated only descriptively in country coverage rather than confirmed against primary legislation. Several claims, including the 2015 marriage law provisions, the 2019 broadcasting regulation sections and the details of the December 2015 arrests, rest on secondary or encyclopedic sourcing that has not been checked against gazetted texts.

Whether the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019 hate-speech provisions have been invoked in any enforcement action is not documented in the inventory, nor is the current status of the prosecutions or charges described for Ken Msonda and Peter Sawali.

In April 2018 police in that city arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, a choice that circumvented the six-year moratorium while both laws faced constitutional challenge; police spokespersons confirmed the custody.

Arbitrary detention and ill-treatment by police are documented. A 61-page report released on 26 October 2018, based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in the capital and the largest city alongside lawyers, activists and officials, found that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and at times assaulted them. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion, forced stripping, forced medical and HIV and sexually transmitted infection examinations, and distribution of photographs on social media by community police.

Care access is compromised on gender-expression grounds. The same 2018 report records a trans man beaten and then refused treatment, and nurses mocking people presenting for HIV tests. Detention itself carries risk: the country's prisons were described as harsh in a 2011 human rights report issued by a foreign government, which also documented protest killings in July 2011 in which 20 people died.

Marriage and legal recognition are closed. The national marriage law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions, states that gender is assigned at birth, and does not permit a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender. No process for legal gender recognition is described in the sources. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; since 2019 the only limited protection is against hate speech, through sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d) of the 2019 broadcasting regulations, which bar broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference.

Official hostility is documented at the highest levels. In April 2010 a sitting president called same-sex marriage evil and bad before the eyes of God, and in July 2011 he threatened two prominent activists, saying he would hunt them in their homes and smoke them out, forcing them into hiding amid treason threats. In January 2016 a governing-party spokesperson posted on social media that gay people are worse than dogs and should be killed; the national bar association filed charges but the director of public prosecution took over the matter and discontinued it on 21 January. A national religious body called for the death penalty for gay people in February 2014, and on 4 January 2017 thousands across 28 districts marched against legalising homosexuality in protests led by two major church bodies. An activist was arrested in 2010 and given a 60-day sentence for posting gay-rights posters in the largest city.

MWI.localsOnly:
Residents live under a legal framework that assigns gender at birth and offers no procedure for legal gender recognition, so a person's documents continue to reflect the sex assigned at birth regardless of transition. The 2015 Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law bars same-sex unions and bars marriage between a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery and someone of that person's prior gender, which constrains relationship recognition for trans residents as well as same-sex couples.

There is no general statutory protection against discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity for residents; the only codified protection is the hate-speech limitation in the 2019 broadcasting regulations, which applies to broadcast content rather than to employment, housing, healthcare or education. Residents therefore depend on prosecutorial discretion, which has been inconsistent: a moratorium on arrests has existed on paper since 2012, was reaffirmed in December 2015, was suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016, and was circumvented by at least one police charge in 2018.

Healthcare access on gender-expression grounds is documented as unreliable, including refusal of treatment after assault and mockery at HIV testing points, even as officials from 2009 onward have argued for inclusive HIV services and government Global Fund money funds LGBTI HIV programming. SDN.name: Sudan
SDN.summary:
Sudan is a jurisdiction in which gender nonconformity is itself a criminal offence. Article 152 of the Penal Code prohibits wearing clothing of the opposite sex, and the provision targets gender presentation rather than sexual conduct. A trans visitor whose appearance is read as incongruent with the sex recorded on their documents falls squarely within its scope, independent of any other behaviour.

Same-sex sexual activity between men and between women is also criminalised. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, with the death penalty historically available for a third offence. Following the amendment adopted by Sudan's Sovereign Council in July 2020, the death penalty for homosexuality was removed and the maximum penalty for a third offence set at life imprisonment; the 100 lashes previously imposed for same-sex intimacy were abolished and a first offence carries up to five years' imprisonment.

The 2010 US State Department human rights report for Sudan records the then-applicable Article 148 provisions, which carried flogging and the death penalty. The same report documents extrajudicial killings, torture and other abuses under the Bashir government.

Sudan provides no legal gender recognition. Gender-affirming healthcare is legally constrained, the ongoing conflict further restricts access to it, and state reliance on Sunni fatwas blocks transition. Cairo 52's Sudan profile reports no arrest statistics specific to trans people, but does document state violence against LGBTQIA+ individuals, including extrajudicial killings.

Documentation by Bedayaa, the LGBTQI organisation for the Nile Valley, records daily struggles, discrimination and violence against LGBTQI people in Sudan rooted in societal gender and sexual norms. Rainbow Sudan, a Sudanese community magazine, records an organised local community presence, including history and analysis of LGBTI rights in Sudan and profiles of Sudanese LGBTI organisations.
SDN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory states whether Article 152 survived the July 2020 amendment to the criminal code; the amendment is reported only in relation to same-sex conduct penalties. That question remains unresolved here.

Arrest statistics specific to trans people are unavailable in these sources. Cairo 52 states plainly that none exist, and no other source supplies them.

Whether courts have applied Article 152 to visitors, and with what frequency, is not sourced. The provision's text and the documented pattern of state violence are the available basis for the risk assessment.

Current enforcement practice under the post-2020 framework, including actual sentences imposed for a first or third offence, is not documented in the inventory.

SSD.name: South Sudan
SSD.summary:
South Sudan's Penal Code reaches gender presentation on its face: it criminalises "any male person who dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman", with a penalty of up to three months' imprisonment. For a trans visitor presenting female, that provision is the operative exposure. It requires no sexual conduct and no disclosure of identity.

The same law treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as "unnatural offenses", defined as carnal intercourse against the order of nature, punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual, the term rises to up to 14 years.

United States State Department country reports on human rights practices for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that there were no reports of authorities enforcing the same-sex conduct provision. Those reports describe no repeal, no moratorium and no prosecutorial policy behind the non-enforcement, so the statute remains in force.

The reported non-enforcement of the conduct provision does not describe the wider picture for a visible trans person. The same State Department reporting across 2018 to 2022 documents security forces routinely harassing LGBTQI+ persons and, in some cases, arresting, detaining, beating and torturing them. In 2017 security forces raided Access for All, a community-based LGBTQ-supportive organisation; its staff were detained for several months and released without charge, and the organisation was intimidated into closing, its executive director later leaving the country.

Official hostility is stated in explicit terms. In September 2017 the minister for Labour, Public Service and Human Resource Development, Gathoth Gatkuoth Hothnyang, said the government would order security forces to arrest LGBTQ persons and detain them until they procreate. No such arrests were reported by the end of that year. The State Department's 2022 report found that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled South Sudan because of actively hostile government rhetoric and action.

Protection machinery for a visitor who is targeted is absent. The country has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime legislation protecting LGBTQ persons from harassment or abuse on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, and same-sex marriage has been constitutionally banned since the Constitution was adopted in 2011.

Societal conditions raise the likelihood of non-state violence. LGBTQ people face widespread stigmatisation among the broader population, the 2011 State Department report found "widespread" societal discrimination against gay men and lesbians, and the country has no known LGBTQ-support organisations to which a traveller could turn after an incident.
SSD.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal recognition of gender markers on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a traveller's gender history, access to healthcare including HIV-related care, or facility and restroom rules. These remain unsourced for South Sudan.

The inventory does not establish whether the cross-dressing provision has been enforced at any point. The State Department non-enforcement finding attaches to the same-sex conduct provision; whether the dress provision has produced prosecutions is unresolved on these sources.

The three-month penalty for the cross-dressing offence is drawn from secondary country coverage rather than the Penal Code text, and is not corroborated by the State Department reports, which state the provision without giving a penalty.

Reported non-enforcement is not decriminalisation. No source indicates repeal, a moratorium or a stated prosecutorial policy, and non-enforcement recorded by one government's annual reporting cannot be read as a legal change.

The sourced coverage ends with the 2022 reporting year. No material in the inventory establishes the state of enforcement, official rhetoric or the security environment in later years, and no hate-crime or violence statistics are available.

SOM.name: Somalia
SOM.summary:
Somalia criminalises same-sex sexual activity, but the sources give irreconcilable penalties. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of life imprisonment under the penal code it dates to 1964, together with the death penalty under sharia in some regions. US State Department reporting for 2021 gives up to three years, and its 2022 report gives three months to three years for "carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex". The statutory text cited by Wikipedia is Article 409 of the Somali Penal Code, carrying three months to three years for intercourse and two months to two years for an "act of lust" other than intercourse; Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, intended to prevent re-offending.

Enforcement by the federal authorities is undocumented. The 2022 US State Department report states that no official reports of enforcement were available, and that impunity generally remained the norm for violence against sexual minorities. Reporting covering government-controlled areas nevertheless states that LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted, so the absence of reported cases should not be read as decriminalisation.

The lethal risk lies in territory outside federal administration. Under local interpretations of sharia in areas held by Al-Shabaab, and in Jubaland, homosexuality is punishable by death, with the sentence at a judge's discretion. ILGA records killings of people alleged to have engaged in same-sex conduct: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed by Al-Shabaab in 2024. The 2010 US State Department human rights report had already documented the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control. Al-Shabaab's leadership has publicly stated an intent to enforce harsh punishments, and senior figures claimed a "death chamber" for gay and lesbian people if they returned.

Non-refoulement is well supported. Benjamin Christman's February 2016 report on the treatment of gay persons in Somalia concluded that gay persons should not be returned to the country because of persecution risk, providing a basis for refugee status and for LGBT asylum claims. Reporting from 2013 records Somali refugees in Kenya facing death threats and racist discrimination while UN officials nonetheless pushed for return, and documents persecution as a driver of displacement. Human rights and LGBTQ activists, and people accused of homosexuality, have fled the country for fear of execution or assassination.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, as the US State Department reported in 2022. The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family, which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition.

Social stigma compounds the legal exposure. Sexual orientation is a taboo subject with no public discussion in any region of the country, according to US State Department reporting for 2010 and 2022, and severe societal stigma prevents LGBTQI+ individuals from disclosing sexual orientation or gender identity publicly. The population is around 99 percent Muslim and has lived through decades of civil war and unstable government.
SOM.outOfScopeNotes:
The identity of the governing statute is unresolved. One source dates the penal code to 1964 and another to 1973, and the two do not agree on the maximum penalty: life imprisonment against three months to three years. The inventory does not settle which text is currently in force or which figure a Somali court would apply.

Whether federal authorities have ever charged anyone under Article 409 is not sourced. The 2022 report's "no official reports of enforcement" may reflect absent reporting rather than absent prosecutions, and no case-level evidence is available here.

No source in the inventory addresses trans-specific questions: legal gender recognition, amendment of sex markers on identity or travel documents, access to gender-affirming care, or rules on gendered facilities. Any statement about these would be unsourced.

Entry, visa and border-screening requirements for Somalia are not covered by these sources, nor is the treatment of a trans visitor at ports of entry.

Named territorial control is dated to individual reports and may no longer describe the ground: Jubaland and Al-Shabaab-held areas are as characterised in the sources cited, without a current control assessment.

sources.summary: Under Article 409 of the Somali Penal Code (1973), sexual intercourse with a person of the same sex is punishable by three months to three years' imprisonment, and an 'act of lust' other than intercourse by two months to two years. Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, to prevent re-offending. The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as 'a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family,' which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition. In al-Shabaab-controlled areas and Jubaland, capital punishment is imposed for consensual same-sex sexual activity, with punishment at a judge's discretion. ILGA reported killings by al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups of alleged homosexual activity: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed by Al-Shabaab in 2024. In government-controlled areas, civil law specifies prison sentences of up to three years, and LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted. The law does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, as reported by the U.S. Department of State in 2022. Pervasive social stigma attaches to same-sex relationships, and sexual orientation is a taboo topic with no public discussion in any region of the country, per U.S. Department of State reports from 2010 and 2022; severe societal stigma prevents LGBTQI+ individuals from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly as of 2022. Stigmatisation and criminalisation occur where 99% of the population follows Islam amid decades of civil war and unstable government. Human rights and LGBTQ activists and those accused of homosexuality have been forced to flee the country for fear of execution or assassination. Family planning services and fact-based information on human sexuality are hard to access, and Islamic social mores often make it difficult to publicly discuss HIV transmission. Since 1999, much AIDS/HIV education and care has come from international organizations such as the United Nations. Somalia has one of the lowest HIV infection rates on the continent, with adult prevalence estimated at 0.5% in 2007. SOM.tangentialFactors:
The penalty range reported for the same conduct varies by a factor of more than twenty between sources, from three months under the 2022 US State Department account to life imprisonment in the Human Dignity Trust profile. A visitor cannot know in advance which figure a given court would apply.

Two enforcement accounts point in opposite directions: no official reports of enforcement alongside routine prosecution of LGBTQ people in government-controlled areas. Neither resolves whether charges are brought under Article 409 in practice.

The boundary between federal administration and insurgent-held territory determines whether the applicable penalty is a prison term or death, and control of that territory is fluid, so the governing regime at a given place and date is not fixed.

Somalia's pattern of criminalisation, non-state execution and non-refoulement recognition resembles that of other jurisdictions where a functioning asylum case rests on documented persecution rather than on statute alone.

ERI.name: Eritrea
ERI.summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's 2015 Penal Code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries up to seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained after independence and enhanced in the first post-independence penal code adopted in 2015. The UK Foreign Office records same-sex activity as a crime and confirms that no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people.

Exposure is not limited to prosecution. The US State Department's 2023 reporting states that openly LGBTQI+ persons risk imprisonment and for that reason did not participate in the political process, and that societal discrimination against them continues. The same report found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by heavy social stigma; in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programs detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality.

Foreign nationals are not shielded. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, a gay Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government called him a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local laws including the Penal Code's homosexuality provision. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one described as openly homosexual; Eritrea's ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the law prohibiting homosexual relations, and Italian diplomats condemned the action.

Detention and abuse accompany enforcement. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, known for housing political prisoners and journalists, where abuse, torture and beating of prisoners is commonplace. Gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have suffered severe physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers, on a 2002 UK refugee claimant account that is unconfirmed. The 2011 US State Department reporting records that the government labelled disloyal individuals "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles".

Criminalisation undermines health and care access: ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing it makes prevention programs directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern. There are no laws banning conversion therapy, and OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma; LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea and cannot adopt. The government has rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appeal to legalize same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people", with no major efforts to change or rescind existing laws, and in 2010 Eritrea, with other African states, rejected the Yogyakarta Principles. The UK raised these concerns bilaterally and via the EU.
ERI.outOfScopeNotes: The military abuse account rests on a single 2002 UK refugee claimant account and is unconfirmed. The current status of Article 310(1) as applied in practice, the actual frequency of prosecution, and whether the enhanced 2015 sentence has been imposed are not sourced in this inventory. No youth-specific care findings are recorded. The UK Foreign Office report carries a 2015 copyright date, so its currency relative to the 2023 US State Department reporting is unresolved.

ATG.name: Antigua and Barbuda
ATG.summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy between adults is not a criminal offence in Antigua and Barbuda. On 5 July 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Orden David et al v The Attorney General of Antigua and Barbuda, declared Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional and void. Before that ruling, adult-on-adult buggery carried up to fifteen years' imprisonment, five years where a minor committed the act, and life where an adult committed it against a minor; 'serious indecency' carried up to ten years where the target was a child under sixteen, and repeat offenders convicted of buggery were placed on the Sex Offenders Register for life.

The same judgment read the constitutional prohibition on sex discrimination as covering sexual orientation and gender identity. That interpretive holding does not function as a statutory protection regime: Antiguan law still does not address discrimination or harassment on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no explicit antidiscrimination protections exist in legislation.

Trans visitors have no route to legal recognition of gender identity. There is no mechanism to change a legal gender marker; only name changes are available. A passport or identification document showing a gender inconsistent with presentation will therefore stand unremedied for the duration of a visit, and there is no sourced pathway for a visitor to resolve that mismatch.

Same-sex unions are not recognised in any form. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights afforded to opposite-sex married couples, so a partner cannot rely on marriage-based entry, inheritance, hospital-visitation or next-of-kin standing.

Violence against LGBTQ people has been documented rather than merely alleged. Orden David, the Antiguan activist who brought the constitutional challenge, was bullied and physically attacked before the ruling, including being struck on the head and knocked out in daylight. Advocacy litigation in the region has argued that buggery and indecency laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence, and that framing remains the backdrop against which street-level hostility occurs despite decriminalisation.

Official hostility is part of the recorded record. At the May 2016 Universal Periodic Review, several governments urged Antigua and Barbuda to repeal the sodomy ban and guarantee full human rights to LGBTQ people; the government announced on 24 August 2016 that it had no intention of repealing the ban, while acknowledging that a lawsuit would most likely strike it down on the basis of the identical jurisprudence from Belize. Human Rights Watch reported the 2022 decriminalisation ruling, and Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, still records the absence of antidiscrimination protection and of legal gender recognition.
ATG.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the sources: whether the 2022 ruling is consistently applied by police and prosecutors in practice, and whether any charges under Sections 12 or 15 have been brought or dropped since July 2022. No enforcement data is available here.

Not sourced: whether any legislation on hate-crime enhancement, conversion-therapy prohibition or relationship recognition has been introduced or enacted after the March 2026 update of the Outright International overview.

Not sourced: any trans-specific provision on access to gender-affirming healthcare, on customs or border treatment of hormone medication, or on the evidentiary standard applied when a traveller's documents do not match their presentation.

Unresolved: the scope of the constitutional sex-discrimination reading in litigation. The sources record the interpretive holding but do not document a decided case applying it to a discrimination complaint.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Official positions rather than media reporting document state hostility toward LGBTQ people in Antigua and Barbuda. At the May 2016 Universal Periodic Review of the UN Human Rights Council, Argentina, Australia, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Nicaragua all urged the government to repeal its sodomy ban and guarantee full human rights to LGBTQ people. Minister of Social Transformation Samantha Marshall called the ban antiquated and said it should be repealed, while Parliamentary Secretary Maureen Payne-Hyman assured the Council that LGBTQ people are not persecuted in the country. On 24 August 2016 the government announced it had no intention of repealing the ban, while acknowledging that a lawsuit would most certainly strike it down given the identical jurisprudence in Belize. On 1 November 2019 the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality announced it would file a legal challenge by the end of 2019, which culminated in the 5 July 2022 ruling in Orden David et al v The Attorney General of Antigua and Barbuda, in which the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court declared Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional and void. Antiguan law does not address discrimination or harassment on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not recognize same-sex unions in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights given to opposite-sex married couples.

ATG.tangentialFactors:
Antigua and Barbuda sits within a region in transition. As of the 2023 reporting, six Caribbean countries still criminalise same-sex conduct, and a visitor crossing from a neighbouring jurisdiction may enter a materially different legal regime without any change in practical surroundings.

The litigation that produced the 2022 ruling was announced on 1 November 2019 by the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality, which had stated in December 2019 that it would file court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia. The regional character of that campaign means the Antiguan outcome is one data point in a wider judicial pattern rather than an isolated exception.

The Advocates for Human Rights lodged a submission to the UN Human Rights Committee in January 2025 listing the LGBTQ+ rights issues Antigua and Barbuda still faces ahead of its review, which indicates that decriminalisation left substantive questions open before international scrutiny.

Statements made to the UN Human Rights Council in 2016 were divided: the Minister of Social Transformation, Samantha Marshall, called the ban antiquated and said it should be repealed, while Parliamentary Secretary Maureen Payne-Hyman assured the Council that LGBTQ people are not persecuted in the country. ATG.localsOnly:

BRB.name: Barbados
BRB.summary:
Same-sex conduct between men was decriminalised in Barbados in December 2022, on the strength of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program. The Human Dignity Trust places the Barbados case within a series of constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-gay statutes across the Eastern Caribbean, and a High Court ruling on sodomy published in May 2023 found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is recent and specific. In February 2018 Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward, suffering serious injuries including to her throat. He was convicted in April 2019 and sentenced to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or serve three months in prison, with no jail time handed down. Hoffmann has written first-person about the visibility and danger trans people face on the island.

Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct category, and the state has questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration. In 2011 the government said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada. In 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean said such applications risked abusing the Canadian refugee system, noting that two of nine Canadian applications had been denied, and a Guyanese newspaper that year reported over 300 LGBT members in Barbados seeking asylum in Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States. On the entry side, the 'Welcome Stamp' remote-work visa introduced in July 2020 initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse before being changed to permit same-sex spouses.

Employment is the sharpest practical exposure for a trans visitor working locally. The Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars employment discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status. Hoffmann argues the Act excludes trans workers because gender identity and gender expression are not listed as protected grounds; reporting from August 2020 describes trans Barbadians being fired or denied jobs for 'dressing wrong'.

No same-sex relationship or union is recognised. The government ruled out same-sex marriage in June 2016, and in September 2020 announced only a plan to recognise 'some form' of civil union followed by a referendum on gay marriage; critics called the civil union proposal 'unnecessarily vague' and expected the referendum to fail, and neither had been enacted as of the source account. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging sections 9 and 12 of the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154), and the Commission gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019; failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision.
BRB.outOfScopeNotes:
Identity-document processes and legal gender recognition for trans Barbadians are not covered by any source assembled here, so the requirements, route and timeframe for changing gender markers on Barbadian documents remain unresolved.

No findings appear on access to transition-related healthcare, mental health or specialist care for trans residents; the only health provisions identified are the Barbados Fertility Centre's IVF and artificial insemination for lesbian couples, the illegal status of surrogacy, and UGLAAB's work on AIDS.

No findings appear on trans-specific custody or parental-rights outcomes. Family-law material reaches only adoption, surrogacy and family recognition, all of which concern same-sex couples as such rather than trans parents.

No findings appear on the treatment of LGBT minors, detention of unaccompanied youth, or school-based anti-bullying and gender-affirming education. The only youth-adjacent legal detail is that under the former Section 12 of the Sexual Offences Act, 'serious indecency' carried a maximum penalty of ten years where the act was committed on or towards a person aged 16 or older.

The current status of sections 9 and 12 of the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154) after the December 2022 decriminalisation, and the outcome of the Inter-American Commission petition filed in 2018, are not resolved in these sources. Whether any screening, declaration or health requirement applies specifically to trans entrants at Barbadian border control is likewise not sourced here.

The current status of sections 9 and 12 of the national sexual offences statute after the December 2022 decriminalisation, and the outcome of the regional commission petition filed in 2018, are not resolved in these sources. Whether any screening, declaration or health requirement applies specifically to trans entrants at the country's border control is likewise not sourced here.

Media report (Apr 2019): sentencing in a violent attack on a trans activist — no jail time handed down; reported via an advocate and a legal network — an impunity outcome visitors should weigh.

Commentary (Aug 2020): trans residents are frequently fired or denied jobs for 'dressing wrong'; an employment-protection bill does not cover them, and the country's remote-work visa markets openness while the anti-gay law stands.

BRB.blindLocalsOnly:
Family formation is restricted for resident same-sex couples. Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt, surrogacy is illegal although not explicitly prohibited or regulated by statute, and same-sex couples are not recognised as families. The only parenting-related service identified is a private fertility clinic, which offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.

The 2020 employment statute is the principal domestic protection, but its coverage of trans workers is contested. Parliament passed the national employment non-discrimination act in August 2020 with sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status as protected grounds; the trans claimant's position is that the omission of gender identity and gender expression leaves trans employees outside it, consistent with reports of trans residents being dismissed or refused work for how they dress.

Trans residents' contact with the state as migrants or asylum seekers has been treated as suspect rather than protected. The 2011 investigation into gay residents claiming refugee status abroad, the 2016 statements by the foreign minister, and the 2016 report of more than 300 LGBT members locally seeking asylum in three destination countries all frame such applications as an abuse risk; a local civil-society body said it would investigate the same allegations.
BRB.blindTangential:
Official hostility has been stated plainly and repeatedly. In 2016 the national justice department said the country would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage, and after a foreign head of government's 2011 summit warning linking aid to sodomy laws he said the country would not be dictated to by that government. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting an international human rights organisation to call the response a 'cheap political trick' because its report did not mention same-sex marriage.

Religious and media pressure runs alongside that official line. Fundamentalist groups including a major imported church have claimed sexual orientation is chosen and argued that discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, and human rights activists report that foreign evangelical ministers arriving locally have spread homophobic rhetoric more widely. A national newspaper's informal comment line drew opposition to a proposed gay tourism package. Set against this, the local Anglican bishop and the Catholic Church oppose the buggery law while respecting LGBT rights, and the prime minister, elected in May 2018, is reported as pro-LGBT.

The constitutional litigation is part of a regional pattern rather than a local exception: equivalent challenges are documented across the wider subregion, and the regional commission petition on the sexual offences statute remains an open channel for a binding outcome.

Community visibility exists despite the risk. A Trans Day of Remembrance vigil held locally in November 2018 was the second of its kind, organised with the national women's organisation, a local ally and veteran trans advocates. A national LGBT organisation founded in 2013 by two local women was set up to create an education mechanism and open public dialogue, and Pride events have served an awareness-raising function, from a small first event in November 2017 to a parade of about 120 people in the capital in July 2018.

KNA.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
KNA.summary:
Saint Kitts and Nevis no longer criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. On 29 August 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General, struck sections 56 (buggery) and 57 (indecent assault against men) of the Offences Against the Person Act as contrary to the constitutional rights to privacy and freedom of expression. The ruling took immediate effect and decriminalised consensual sexual intercourse between adult men in private across the country. Consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful since that judgment.

The decriminalisation came through a civil-society constitutional challenge rather than legislation, and the judgment was issued by a regional court whose rulings also affected neighbouring Eastern Caribbean states. Human Dignity Trust and 76 Crimes track the wider pattern of regional challenges to anti-sodomy laws, of which this case formed part.

Legal gender recognition is not available. No statute, court process or administrative route in Saint Kitts and Nevis allows a person to obtain official recognition of a changed gender marker, and the sources document no pending reform.

No provision of the penal code or of any other statute prohibits discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Discrimination in the workplace, in education and in accommodation remains lawful, as does hate speech directed at LGBT people. Same-sex unions are not recognised in any form, whether as marriage or as a registered partnership, and same-sex households receive none of the rights available to opposite-sex married couples.

Official hostility is on record. In 2011 the Government of Saint Kitts and Nevis stated that it had no mandate from the people to abolish criminalisation of homosexuality among consenting adults. In 2005 the port authority of Nevis barred a cruise ship carrying 110 passengers, most of them gay, from docking; a police boat intercepted the vessel and it was ordered to sail on, with port officials describing the exclusion as a decision that homosexuality was not to be part of the island's culture. Civil society reports that LGBT people in the country avoid law enforcement, which limits the practical value of the 2022 judgment as a protection mechanism.
KNA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory confirms whether any hate-crime sentencing enhancement exists or has been applied to offences against LGBT people; the sources address only the general absence of non-discrimination and harassment provisions, and this remains unresolved.

Procedures for amending gender markers on passports, national identification or birth records are not sourced. The inventory states that legal gender recognition is not possible but does not document the administrative practice of the passport office or the registry, and the position on secondary documents is unresolved.

No sourced information addresses whether the 2022 judgment altered police handling of complaints by LGBT complainants, or whether any training, guidance or oversight mechanism was issued after it. The claim that LGBT people avoid law enforcement rests on civil-society reporting and is not accompanied by incident-level data.

DMA.name: Dominica
DMA.summary:
Dominica's High Court of Justice in Roseau ruled on 23 April 2024 that sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act, which criminalised consensual same-sex activity, were unconstitutional. The case was brought by a gay man living in Dominica, and as a result consensual same-sex conduct between adults is no longer an offence under the statute.

The change came through constitutional litigation rather than an act of parliament: the High Court struck the sections down as unconstitutional, so decriminalisation rests on a judicial judgment rather than legislative repeal.

The provisions had been under challenge for years before the ruling. In July 2019 Daryl Phillip, founder of the Dominican LGBT organisation MiRiDom, announced at a news conference that a High Court challenge to the buggery and sexual-activity provisions had been filed.

Human Rights Watch reported the decision on 24 April 2024 and called on all Caribbean nations to repeal comparable criminal laws, placing the ruling against a regional pattern in which such statutes remain in force. Activists described the judgment as a significant milestone in the ongoing struggle for LGBT rights in the Caribbean.
DMA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition in Dominica, including change of name or gender marker on birth certificates, national identity documents or passports. That question is unresolved here.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of trans travellers is not sourced. Whether any documentary or medical screening at entry could disclose a traveller's gender history remains unresolved on this record.

The sources do not establish whether Dominican law provides hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, nor whether indecency, public-order or impersonation-type provisions continue to affect trans people after the 2024 judgment. Both points are unresolved.

Same-sex marriage and partner recognition, access to gender-affirming care, and rules governing restroom or other sex-segregated facilities are not covered by the available material and should be verified against primary Dominican sources before publication.

Local religious authority has also moved against criminalisation. In May 2013 Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica publicly called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and for an end to all forms of violence against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position.

Human Rights Watch's call for other Caribbean states to repeal comparable laws indicates that Dominica's decriminalisation is not regional: neighbouring jurisdictions retain sodomy statutes, so conduct lawful in Dominica may remain criminal elsewhere in the subregion.
DMA.localsOnly:
The litigation campaign was run by Dominican activists. The Catholic Church in Dominica has a documented public position against criminalisation: Bishop Gabriel Malzaire's May 2013 call covered both the repeal of criminal penalties and protection from violence for LGBT people, framed on the Holy See's teaching.

Decriminalisation was achieved through the domestic courts, so the protection available to residents rests on a constitutional judgment of the High Court of Justice rather than on a statutory amendment that parliament could readily reverse.

LCA.name: Saint Lucia
LCA.summary:
Saint Lucia's High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in July 2025, striking down the criminal provision as unconstitutional in Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia. Human Rights Watch reported the judgment on 31 July 2025 and the Associated Press carried it as well. The case was part of strategic constitutional litigation brought across the Eastern Caribbean rather than a legislative amendment, and the provision struck down was the colonial-era statute that had governed same-sex conduct.

For a visitor, the practical effect is direct: consensual same-sex conduct between adults no longer carries criminal exposure in Saint Lucia. Before the judgment, the statutory prohibition applied to anyone present on the island, residents and visitors alike, and that specific criminal risk ended with the court's declaration of unconstitutionality.

The judgment addressed criminal liability only. Matters such as legal gender recognition, relationship or marriage recognition, hate-crime protection and anti-discrimination coverage are not addressed by the sources available for this record, and a visitor should not read the decriminalisation ruling as settling them.

Official engagement with LGBTI rights is documented at the enforcement level. United and Strong St Lucia reported that a human-rights sensitisation session for law enforcement was held in Castries on 19 May 2015, bringing together officers of the Royal St Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and staff of the Bordelais Correctional Facility, alongside CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson. The session built on sensitisation work carried out in 2014.
LCA.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust case digest covering Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403). The ruling itself is corroborated by Human Rights Watch and the Associated Press, but the digest's fuller treatment of the court's reasoning remains unresolved for this record.

Rules on legal gender recognition and gender markers on documents are not sourced in the available material for Saint Lucia and are unresolved here. The same applies to recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriage, to hate-crime provisions covering gender identity or expression, and to statutory anti-discrimination protection. No source in this inventory speaks to entry, visa or customs screening practices that could expose a visitor's gender identity or expression.
