VCT.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
VCT.summary:
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults. Section 146 of the criminal code, the British-inherited buggery offence, carries up to 10 years' imprisonment; section 148, gross indecency, carries up to 5 years. These colonial-era provisions remain in force.

On 16 February 2024 the High Court dismissed a constitutional challenge and upheld the ban, holding that outlawing homosexual activity is lawful. Same-sex conduct therefore stays criminal in the country. On 19 February 2024 the Eastern Caribbean rights alliance ECADE condemned the ruling, stating that LGBTQ+ Vincentians face greater vulnerability as a result.

No visa, entry-screening or admission rule affecting LGBTQ travellers is recorded in the sources, and no law governing gender markers on travel or identity documents is sourced here. The sources likewise record no provision on restroom or facilities access and no prohibition on gender-affirming care for visitors. These gaps reflect the sourcing, not a finding of permissive rules.

Violence risk is documented. Human Rights Watch reported on 20 July 2023, in the 58-page report 'They Can Harass Us Because of the Laws', that LGBT people in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines face bias-motivated violence and discrimination in daily life. In April 2019 Leswan Stewart, a cross-dressing gay teenager, was assaulted in a transphobic attack and then prosecuted for fraud on the allegation that he had pretended to be a woman; the prosecutor withdrew the charge in May 2019 without stating a reason. In September 2018 three cross-dressing young men were physically attacked.

Protection machinery is thin. The legislation addresses neither discrimination nor harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so LGBTQ people have no statutory basis on which to claim protection when they speak out. No associations or organisations dedicated to LGBTQ people exist in the country, and no helpline or help centre for LGBTQ youth operates. The country does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples receive none of the rights given to married couples. The Prime Minister has said any change to the law would be an OECS-wide decision, because constitutional and legislative provisions are similar across member states.

The sources record no enforcement figures for these offences, so the practical exposure of a visitor to prosecution cannot be quantified from this inventory.
VCT.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory carries no enforcement data for sections 146 and 148: no arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction figures are recorded, so the practical likelihood that a visitor is charged for consensual private conduct is unresolved on these sources.

A Human Dignity Trust page documenting Eastern Caribbean constitutional challenges could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), so the comparative litigation record for the wider Eastern Caribbean, including outcomes in other member states, is unresolved here.

The inventory states that 'healthcare, medication, and HIV services are not covered' without identifying which coverage scheme or eligibility category is meant; the meaning of that claim for a visitor seeking treatment is unresolved and should be verified against current health-service rules before it is relied on.

No source in this inventory addresses gender markers on passports or other identity documents, entry or visa rules keyed to gender presentation, facilities or restroom access, or requirements applying to gender-affirming medication carried across the border. These are gaps in sourcing rather than confirmed absences of regulation.

The laws address neither discrimination nor harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, leaving LGBTQ people without legal protection when they speak out. No associations or organisations dedicated to LGBTQ people exist, and no helpline or help centre for LGBTQ youth operates, so dedicated support and care access is absent. Healthcare, medication, and HIV services are not covered, and no visa, entry-screening, or admission rules affecting LGBTQ travellers are recorded. LGBTQ life is invisible and stigmatised. In September 2011 a same-sex couple's article 'Not Easy Being Gay in St. Vincent and the Grenadines' in the Vinci Kallaloo drew over 3,400 hits in under a day and 50+ comments, several containing violent murderous threats. In September 2018 three cross-dressing young men were physically attacked; Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves condemned the attacks, called such homophobia unacceptable, and called for an open conversation on homosexuality. In April 2019 Leswan Stewart, a 'cross-dressing gay' teenager, was the victim of a transphobic assault and was then charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman; the prosecutor withdrew the charge in May 2019 without giving a reason. In 2011 three lecturers at the St. Vincent and the Grenadines Community College were targeted by the college's director in an orchestrated scheme accusing them of 'homosexual tendencies', allegedly to fire political opponents. Two men left the country because of the law. Javin Johnson, 22, successfully claimed asylum in the United Kingdom in 2017 after establishing he could not live as a gay man in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Sean Macleish, 53, a Vincentian resident of Chicago, publicly advocated to the Prime Minister for removal of the laws so he could return home with his partner, without effect. In their 2019 affidavits the two petitioners stated that the legislation had exiled them from the country due to its severely draconian and damaging effects. The country does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnerships, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the same rights given to married couples. In 2024 Saint Vincent and the Grenadines upheld its ban on same-sex sexual activity in its High Court, affirming it was legal to outlaw homosexual activity. The Prime Minister said any change would be an OECS-wide decision because constitutional and legislative provisions are similar across member states.

VCT.tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's July 2023 report, drawn from interviews with LGBT people in the country, recommends decriminalising gay sex and enacting non-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity. Its documentation of everyday harassment is the principal evidence base for the hostility a visibly LGBTQ visitor may encounter outside formal legal channels.

Public expression has drawn threats. In September 2011 an article titled 'Not Easy Being Gay in St. Vincent and the Grenadines', written by a same-sex couple and published in the local magazine Vinci Kallaloo, drew more than 3,400 hits and over 50 comments within a day, several of them violent and murderous threats. In 2011 three lecturers at the St. Vincent and the Grenadines Community College were targeted by the college's director in what was described as an orchestrated scheme accusing them of 'homosexual tendencies', allegedly to remove political opponents.

The law has produced exile. Two men left the country because of the legislation; in their 2019 affidavits the constitutional petitioners stated that the legislation had exiled them from the country through its severely draconian and damaging effects. Javin Johnson, 22, was granted asylum in the United Kingdom in 2017 after establishing that he could not live as a gay man in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Sean Macleish, 53, a Vincentian resident of Chicago, publicly urged the Prime Minister to remove the laws so that he could return home with his partner, without effect.

The September 2018 attacks on three cross-dressing young men drew a response from Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves, who condemned the violence, called such homophobia unacceptable and called for an open national conversation on homosexuality. Official condemnation of discrete incidents has not translated into legislative change, and the constitutional challenge was lost in February 2024.

GRD.name: Grenada
GRD.summary:
Grenada criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Section 431 of the Criminal Code, covering "unnatural crime," carries a maximum of ten years' imprisonment for male same-sex acts. Section 430 addresses "grossly indecent acts" between men, and a gender-neutral grossly indecent act provision reaches same-sex conduct committed willfully in public. Both provisions remain in force.

United States Department of State reporting for 2023 states that the criminalising laws are not enforced in practice, and records no arbitrary killings, torture or enforced disappearances in Grenada that year.

No legal gender recognition is available. A trans visitor's passport or other documents will carry the sex marker assigned at birth or by another jurisdiction, with no domestic procedure to amend it.

Neither the 1973 Constitution, which contains no equality or privacy clause, nor any statute prohibits discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTIQ people in Grenada face discrimination in housing, education, employment and access to public services.

Fear of prosecution under the criminal provisions inhibits LGBTIQ people from reporting crimes to the police, which reduces the practical protection police provide.

Grenada does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or registered partnership, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights granted to opposite-sex married couples.

In May 2013 the President of the Senate publicly called for reconsideration of the ban, stating that "the day is fast approaching" for repeal. No legislative repeal has followed.

GrenCHAP, a local civil-society organisation, has for more than fifteen years provided services to marginalised groups including LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth, as documented in a joint stakeholder report by The Advocates for Human Rights, Khaleem Ali and GrenCHAP submitted for the 2024 Universal Periodic Review.
GRD.outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty documented here applies to Section 431. The specific penalty range attached to Section 430, and to the gender-neutral grossly indecent act provision, is not sourced in the available inventory and remains unresolved.

No source in the inventory addresses how Grenada handles trans people in immigration screening, in detention, or in access to gender-affirming healthcare. Whether any such policy exists is unresolved rather than absent.

The claim that the criminalising laws are unenforced rests on a single reporting year (2023) from one government's human rights report. No prosecution or acquittal statistics covering other years are available here, and the durability of the non-enforcement pattern is unresolved.

The 2013 call by the President of the Senate for reconsideration of the ban is documented as a public statement; whether any bill, parliamentary motion or official review followed it is unresolved in this inventory.

No data is available on hate-motivated violence against trans people in Grenada, on police handling of complaints from LGBTIQ victims, or on whether GrenCHAP's services include trans-specific care beyond the categories listed in the stakeholder report.

Outright International profile (updated Mar 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised under Sections 430 ('grossly indecent act') and 431 ('unnatural crime'); no legal gender recognition; no anti-discrimination protections; LGBTIQ people face discrimination in housing, education, employment and public services, and fear of prosecution inhibits reporting to police.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ people in Grenada face social and legal challenges not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents. The criminal code punishes male same-sex acts with up to 10 years in prison (Grenada Criminal Code Section 431, 'unnatural crime'). Section 7's gender-neutral 'grossly indecent act' provision reaches same-sex conduct committed willfully in public. The 1973 Constitution contains no clause on equality or protection of privacy, and Grenadian law does not address discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity. In May 2013 the President of the Senate publicly called for reconsideration of the ban, saying 'the day is fast approaching' for repeal. Grenada does not recognize same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnerships, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights given to opposite-sex married couples.

GRD.tangentialFactors:
Grenada's legal framework is characteristic of a penal code retained from the colonial era, with the criminal provisions framed in terms of morality rather than age of consent or public order enforcement. The 2023 United States Department of State assessment that the laws are unenforced suggests the practical risk of prosecution is low, but the offences remain available for use.

The absence of any equality or privacy clause in the 1973 Constitution weakens the basis for constitutional challenge to the criminal provisions or to discrimination, since no explicit fundamental right is breached by them.

The May 2013 statement by the President of the Senate indicates that repeal has been raised at the level of the presiding officer of one chamber of Parliament, but this constitutes political signalling rather than legislative change.

Grenada participates in the United Nations Universal Periodic Review, and in October 2024 non-governmental stakeholders submitted a report documenting the country's LGBTIQ+ legal and social situation for that process, indicating an active, if small, domestic advocacy infrastructure.

Outright International's regional programme covering the Americas includes Grenada among the jurisdictions it monitors, placing the country within a Caribbean subregional group where decriminalisation litigation and reform have been contested in several neighbouring states, though specific outcomes elsewhere are not sourced here.
GRD.localsOnly:
Residents who have sex or intimacy that falls within Sections 430 or 431 remain technically exposed to prosecution, and the absence of legal gender recognition means Grenadian trans people live with the sex marker recorded on their birth documentation with no domestic route to change it.

Grenadian residents cannot enter a legally recognised same-sex partnership or marriage, and same-sex couples have no claim to the property, immigration, hospital-visitation or inheritance rights attached to opposite-sex marriage.

Workers, tenants, students and patients have no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no constitutional equality or privacy clause to invoke.

GrenCHAP operates locally with more than fifteen years of service history, providing support to LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth, and functions as a principal point of contact for community members needing assistance or referrals.

The social environment is reported as one in which LGBTIQ people face discrimination not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents, and in which the criminal code is a known deterrent to reporting victimisation to police.

BHS.name: Bahamas
BHS.summary:
The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991 through the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct.

Transgender and intersex people hold no statutory protection. Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign in April 2016 stating that no laws protect transgender and intersex Bahamians, and its member Torri Culmer has campaigned against the dismissal of trans and intersex workers from their jobs.

The constitutional guarantee against discrimination does not extend to sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving of protection, and proposals to include it in a draft constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition. A clause banning sexual-orientation discrimination in employment was removed from the 2001 Employment Bill shortly after passage. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 treats 'sexual life' as sensitive personal data, but no enacted non-discrimination provision covering gender identity appears anywhere in the sources.

There are no national hate-crime laws, and discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal. The sources record no HIV-specific and no trans-specific care provisions.

Documents and relationship recognition are restrictive. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. In 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated that a marriage is void if it is between persons of the same sex, describing this as a community standard. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people. The criminal code sets the age of consent at 16 for heterosexual acts and 18 for same-sex acts.

An official statement points the other way. In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced that the military, prison service and police do not discriminate, and the sources record no prohibition on LGBT citizens serving in those forces.

Official and political hostility is documented. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the 'Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas,' urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island and pledging $1,000 toward it. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 that he did not believe in same-sex marriage and said in 2016 that a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth.

Violence against LGBT visitors has occurred. On 8 May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, and said he wanted charges laid. BLZ.name: Belize
BLZ.summary:
Same-sex conduct is decriminalised in Belize. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, presided over by Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, declared the colonial-era Section 53 of the Criminal Code unconstitutional in the challenge filed in 2010 by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco and heard in Belize City in May 2013. The Human Dignity Trust carries the case in its documentation of constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy statutes, and Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn such a law.

The ruling was upheld on 30 December 2019 by the Court of Appeal, which confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation and that freedom of expression encompasses sexual expression. A visitor therefore faces no criminal exposure for consensual same-sex conduct.

Entry remains governed by Section 5(1)(e) of the Immigration Act, which lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson filed a challenge in 2013, obtained leave from the Caribbean Court of Justice in May 2014, and was joined by CARICOM as an interested party in October 2014; on 10 June 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice dismissed the case, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. Belize argued in that litigation that Section 5(1) reaches only persons offering sexual services for financial gain and is not applied as a blanket prohibition on homosexual immigrants. The court's 10 June 2016 judgment further clarified that neither Belize nor Trinidad and Tobago may bar homosexual nationals of CARICOM states from entering, given obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas.

Statutory protection against identity-based harm exists. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly covers sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity, and Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 makes bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance in sentencing, effective 27 April 2024.

Official protection machinery is stated in commitments accepted during Belize's 2018 Universal Periodic Review: police training to respond properly to violence, measures to counter discrimination, violence and hate crimes, educational campaigns against societal stigma, and steps toward universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people. Enforcement of these commitments by Belizean police and agencies is not documented in the sources at hand.

Public hostility has been organised and at times violent. The Supreme Court case was heard amid violence and death threats directed at LGBT activists, and religious bodies campaigned openly against decriminalisation. Visitors should expect visible social conservatism even though the law no longer criminalises same-sex conduct.
BLZ.outOfScopeNotes:
Prison conditions for LGBT and trans detainees remain unresolved. The encyclopedia source surveyed was fetched successfully but its only Belize content is a navigation link; it contains no Belize-specific practice on housing by birth sex versus gender identity, no trans special units, and no solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. No placement finding can be stated.

No youth- or minor-specific findings on care, medication or travel appear anywhere in the source inventory for Belize.

Whether the pledges accepted in the 2018 Universal Periodic Review, including anti-discrimination legislation and police training, have been enacted or funded is not sourced. The two recommendations noted rather than accepted are not identified in the inventory.

The sources do not document enforcement practice under Section 5(1)(e) of the Immigration Act against individual visitors since the 2016 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment, so the practical screening risk at the border is unverified.

HTI.name: Haiti
HTI.summary:
Haiti does not criminalise same-sex conduct; the prohibition has been off the books since 1791. The legal framework provides no recognition of gender identity, no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime enhancement. The judiciary does not function as a protection avenue in practice.

The legislature has twice moved to tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Haitian Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. Both measures awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies as of November 2017.

The certificate itself already operates against LGBT people: it lists homosexuality as a crime that can justify refusal, which directly affects students and job seekers, and the June 2017 bill was drafted to regulate who receives it. No procedure for legal gender recognition exists, so a visitor's documents will carry the sex marker assigned at issuance.

Visible trans and gender-nonconforming people face a documented hostile climate. The US State Department's 2018 report recorded that attitudes in Haiti "remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince." Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, the national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince on 25 November 2019; press reports cited unconfirmed poisoning, and ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. Transgender people have faced documented harassment in the post-earthquake displacement camps.

No prison-placement practice is documented for trans detainees: there is no known rule assigning housing by birth sex versus identity, no separate units, and no recorded solitary or segregation practice. That absence reflects a lack of documentation rather than a guaranteed placement outcome.

Constitutional guarantees of health care, housing, education, food and social security apply to all citizens, but LGBTQ people routinely conceal their orientation or gender identity for fear of discrimination, which impedes access. After the 2010 earthquake, gay and bisexual men reported adopting a more masculine demeanor to avoid harassment and to reduce the chances of being denied emergency housing, health care and food-for-work programs.

FJI.name: Fiji
FJI.summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct has been decriminalised in Fiji since the Crimes Act 2010 came into force on 1 February 2010, repealing the colonial-era Penal Code offence (Article 175) that carried a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment. Enforcement of that offence was documented into 2005: in April of that year two men, one of them an Australian tourist, received two-year prison sentences, and the presiding judge described the acts as "so disgusting... any decent person vomit". Human Rights Watch urged that the charges be dropped and the men released, citing Fiji's 1997 constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Arrests ended before the statute changed. In July 2006 the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested, four years before decriminalisation took legal effect. The practical end of enforcement did not follow from a court ruling but from executive policy.

Fiji was among the first countries in the world to write sexual-orientation non-discrimination into its constitution, in 1997, alongside South Africa. The 2013 Constitution reinstated that protection and expanded it to gender identity and gender expression, a formulation described in regional policy analysis as unique worldwide. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been prohibited since 2007, and health professionals are barred from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation.

The constitutional guarantee has produced no implementing mechanism for trans people. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker on official documents and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, and the resulting marginalisation and discrimination are documented in the 2023 Asia Pacific Alliance case study on legal gender recognition in Fiji. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

No same-sex marriage or civil union is available: the Marriage Act 2002 defines marriage as between one man and one woman. Intersex bodily autonomy is unprotected by law.

The political and religious climate behind the enforcement era remains part of the record. Days after the April 2005 sentences, Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in what he described as a conservative Christian nation. Public health bodies linked the criminalisation regime to the undergrounding of sex work and the spread of HIV.
FJI.outOfScopeNotes:

The inventory does not resolve which reflects the current position of that source's data, and the Crimes Act 2010 date is corroborated independently by Human Rights Watch, PinkNews and GlobalGayz.

Unresolved: the claim that LGBTI organisations cannot register appears only as an at-a-glance flag in one source, with no legal basis, ministry, or date given. Whether this restriction is current, and whether it applies to all civil-society registration or to a specific category, is not sourced.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory reports an enforcement mechanism, penalty, or decided case under the 2013 Constitution's gender-identity and gender-expression protection, or under the 2007 workplace protection. The absence of documented litigation is not evidence that none exists.

Unresolved: the GlobalGayz page is undated and pre-2013, and the Sydney Morning Herald and PinkNews items date from 2005 and 2006. Their value is as evidence of the enforcement era; none of them speaks to present-day conditions.

Not sourced: entry, visa and border-screening practice for travellers whose passport gender marker does not match their presentation, and any airport or immigration screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status. The inventory addresses domestic law only.

At a glance: same-sex relations illegal per overview flag, LGR No, orgs cannot register.

Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study, 'Legal Gender Recognition in Fiji' (2023): the 2013 Constitution's discrimination protection on gender identity and expression is described as unique worldwide, yet legislative/policy frameworks permit NO gender-marker change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities — headline constitutional protection with zero implementation for trans people, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.

Human Rights Watch (11 Apr 2005): two men (one an Australian tourist) received two-year prison sentences under colonial-era Penal Code Art 175 (up to 14 years) for consensual sex; HRW urged charges dropped and release, citing Fiji's 1997 constitutional ban on SO discrimination (Fiji one of first two countries worldwide, with South Africa); the judge called the acts 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Documents the enforcement era before the 2006 no-arrest policy and 2010 decriminalisation.

PinkNews (10 Jul 2006): the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex will no longer be arrested — the practical end of enforcement two years before the Crimes Act 2010 decriminalisation; NZ AIDS Foundation (Exec Dir Rachael Le Mesurier) linked criminalisation to undergrounding of sex and HIV spread.

GlobalGayz country page (pre-2013, undated): Fiji timeline — 1997 second country in the world to enshrine SO non-discrimination; 2006 no-arrest policy confirmed; 2007 state of emergency ousted PM; 2009 Constitution abolished; 1 Feb 2010 full decriminalisation under Crimes Act 2010; Marriage Act 2002 bars same-sex marriage; ~322-island archipelago. Legacy-era overview — its claim that SOGI discrimination was not banned predates the 2013 Constitution.

Sydney Morning Herald (14 Apr 2005): PM Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in 'the conservative Christian nation', days after an Australian tourist and a Fijian man received two-year sentences — the political/religious climate context behind the sodomy-law enforcement that HRW protested.

FJI.tangentialFactors:
Fiji's constitutional position is unusual in both directions: it was the second country in the world, after South Africa, to enshrine sexual-orientation non-discrimination, and its 2013 text carries gender identity and expression protection described as unique worldwide, yet neither protection has been converted into statutory procedure. The gap between headline constitutional text and lived implementation is the central turbulence in the record.

The traditional third-gender role of vaka sa lewa lewa is recognised in Fijian culture and has historical standing in the community, but it carries no legal status. Cultural recognition and legal recognition are separate questions here, and only the former exists.

Contemporary sources disagree about the basic criminal-law position. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states in its body text that same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2010, while its at-a-glance panel still flags same-sex relations as illegal. The GlobalGayz country page, which is undated and predates the 2013 Constitution, states that sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination was not banned; that claim has been overtaken by the 2013 Constitution.

Enforcement history is short and recent enough to matter to expectations: convictions were handed down in April 2005, a no-arrest policy was confirmed in July 2006, and the statutory repeal came only in February 2010. Prime Minister Qarase's 2005 statements show the domestic political reception of external pressure during that window.
FJI.localsOnly:
Residents have had statutory protection against sexual-orientation discrimination in the workplace since 2007, and health professionals are prohibited from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation. These are resident-facing entitlements with no evidence in the inventory of a complaints mechanism or enforcement record.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. No legislative or policy framework permits a change of gender marker, and traditional third-gender identities are not recognised in any official process, despite the 2013 Constitution's protection on gender identity and expression. The Asia Pacific Alliance case study records the resulting marginalisation and discrimination as a documented outcome rather than a projection.

LGBTI organisations cannot register, according to Outright International's country overview. The inventory does not indicate the legal basis or the date of that restriction.

Intersex people have no statutory bodily-autonomy protection, and the cultural standing of vaka sa lewa lewa does not translate into any legal status for people who occupy that role.

WSM.name: Samoa
WSM.summary:
Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 criminalises same-sex sexual activity, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment, as recorded in the Human Dignity Trust country profile. The offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, so it applies equally where one partner is transgender. A trans visitor in a same-sex relationship should treat Samoa as a jurisdiction where that conduct is a criminal offence carrying a custodial penalty.

The same statute removed the colonial-era offence of impersonating a woman, so no Samoan law targets gender expression itself. RNZ Pacific reported on 3 May 2013 that the new Crimes Act was in force that week and that Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief at the repeal. The same reporting records that the community was not at that time agitating for repeal of the sodomy provisions, so the decriminalisation position on that front remained unchanged.

Gender-diverse identity is culturally embedded in Samoa. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association's stakeholder report for Samoa's Universal Periodic Review at the 39th session in 2021, titled 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa', describes the third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the stated aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation. That report is an advocacy submission rather than a source of binding protection, and the inventory does not establish any statutory mechanism for changing gender markers.
WSM.outOfScopeNotes:
A Reuters feature on Samoa's third gender and the balance between sex and religion could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so its reporting is not carried into this record; the underlying subject matter remains unresolved rather than confirmed or denied.

The APTN socio-economic study covering Samoa is published as a scanned image document, so its contents could not be extracted in text form and none of its findings are reflected here.

The inventory does not address legal gender recognition or the procedure for changing gender markers on passports and identity documents, access to gender-affiliated facilities, hate-crime or hate-speech provisions, access to hormone therapy or transition-related care, or recognition of partners and marriages. These points are not sourced and should be verified independently before travel.

WSM.tangentialFactors:
A convening reported by APTN on 9 May 2024, held in Nadi, Fiji, brought together gender-diverse community members from Samoa, the Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua and Papua New Guinea. It documents the Pacific MVPFAFF+ spectrum of identities that Samoa's fa'afafine community belongs to, including fa'afafine in Samoa and American Samoa, fakaleiti in Tonga and fakafifine in Niue. Visitors crossing neighbouring jurisdictions will encounter parallel but differently named identities, and the legal position changes at each border.

The UN Free & Equal information sheet of August 2015 on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific lists the fa'afafine of Samoa, American Samoa and Tokelau among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities described as important parts of the cultural treasure of the region. Regional framing of these identities is therefore favourable even where the criminal law is not.
WSM.localsOnly:
Samoa Fa'afafine Association's 2021 Universal Periodic Review submission is the principal local vehicle for pressing non-discriminatory policy and legislation, setting out the culturally specific standing of fa'afafine and fa'atama in Samoan life and the community's lived experience of discrimination. It is a document for the human rights review process, not an instrument that alters duties owed to an individual.

Schmidt's 2001 study 'Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa', published in Intersections, glosses fa'afafine as 'in the manner of a woman' and argues that the identity is both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality and transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora operating as a contact zone. Locals and diaspora members may therefore use the term with different assumptions than a visitor expects.
WSM.comparisons: Calibration (Aug 2026, two rounds of pairwise challenge): on traveler-facing axes Samoa beats Slovakia (0.69) on public presence, outing violence, and state climate; beats Greece (0.75) on public presence, police predation, and documented violence; and beats Romania (0.67) on every axis. It sits level with Greece — its lack of EU-style institutional recourse (a resident-weighted factor) is the only axis where European comparators hold an edge, and Estonia (0.77) keeps a 0.02 edge on that basis alone.
WSM.blindSummary:
The country's Crimes Act 2013 criminalises same-sex sexual activity, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment, as recorded in the profile held by an international LGBT litigation NGO. The offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, so it applies equally where one partner is transgender. A trans visitor in a same-sex relationship should treat the country as a jurisdiction where that conduct is a criminal offence carrying a custodial penalty.

The same statute removed the colonial-era offence of impersonating a woman, so no national law targets gender expression itself. A regional news service reported on 3 May 2013 that the new Crimes Act was in force that week and that the national fa'afafine association's president, To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley, expressed relief at the repeal. The same reporting records that the community was not at that time agitating for repeal of the sodomy provisions, so the decriminalisation position on that front remained unchanged.

Gender-diverse identity is culturally embedded locally. The national fa'afafine association's stakeholder report for the country's Universal Periodic Review at the 39th session in 2021, on the protection of the rights of fa'afafine, fa'atama and LGBTIQ persons, describes the third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the stated aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation. That report is an advocacy submission rather than a source of binding protection, and the inventory does not establish any statutory mechanism for changing gender markers.

TON.name: Tonga
TON.summary:
Tonga's Criminal Offences Act criminalises same-sex activity between men and women, with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment. Outright International's overview, updated in March 2026, records no evidence of enforcement in recent years, and the US State Department's 2010 human rights report described enforcement of the sodomy provision as rare.

The same statute contains an offence aimed squarely at gender expression: a male who solicits in public "for an immoral purpose" with intent to deceive as to his true sex commits an offence. This is a trans-expression provision on the books, and unlike the sodomy provision it turns on visible presentation rather than private conduct, so it bears directly on how a trans visitor may appear and speak in public spaces.

Tonga provides no legal gender recognition. A visitor's documents will therefore carry the sex marker assigned at birth, with no domestic mechanism to alter it, and no source in the inventory describes any screening process, entry form or facility rule that would accommodate a marker that does not match presentation.

Tongan law does not address discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment or in the provision of goods and services. The Judicial Code of Conduct 2010 requires judges to be aware of diversity including sexual orientation and prohibits bias on irrelevant grounds, but it binds judges alone, not employers or service providers, so it offers a visitor no practical recourse.

Tonga does not recognise same-sex sexual relationships or unions in any form. No partnership, marriage or next-of-kin rights appear in the source material, which matters for hospital access, emergency contact and inheritance in a country where a visitor's partner has no standing.

Violence risk is documented rather than theoretical. Polikalepo Kefu, a noted LGBTQ activist, was murdered near his home at Muʻa in 2021. The source material describes a climate of fear, discrimination and homophobia attributed to conservative values, colonial-era laws, and rising fundamentalism and religious fanaticism that has increased hatred towards LGBTQ people and fakaleitis.

Community infrastructure for LGBTQ people is thin and has been damaged. In February 2018 Cyclone Gita tore off part of the roof of Tonga's LGBTI drop-in center and shelter on Tongatapu in Nuku'alofa, with winds over 120 mph, damaging bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans; the country's only such shelter.

Official posture offers little protection machinery. Tonga, along with Kiribati, is the only Polynesian country that has not signed or expressed support for the 2011 UN joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The 2010 US State Department report recorded no government abuses, while naming domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption as the most prevalent human rights problems.
TON.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the trans-expression offence has ever been charged or prosecuted is unresolved: no source in the inventory reports a conviction, a charge or a stated enforcement policy for that provision, and the enforcement-rarity finding rests on a 2010 government report plus a 2026 NGO overview rather than court records.

No source addresses entry or visa screening, airport document checks, or whether a mismatch between a visitor's gender marker and presentation would be questioned at the border; this remains not sourced rather than confirmed absent.

Availability of gender-affirming healthcare, prescription-hormone rules and any local clinical gatekeeping are not sourced here, as is the position on restroom and facility access for trans visitors.

Whether Tonga would recognise a same-sex marriage or civil partnership obtained abroad is not stated in the source material and should be treated as unresolved.

The inventory contains no Tongan court decision, ministry statement or police data on hate-crime treatment of offences against LGBTQ people, and no source on whether any legal gender recognition process exists in draft or before parliament.

KIR.name: Kiribati
KIR.summary:
Sections 153 to 155 of the Penal Code criminalise sex between men. Anal intercourse carries up to fourteen years' imprisonment; attempts and assault with intent to commit it carry up to seven years; acts of gross indecency between males carry up to five years. Sex between women is not a criminal offence.

The provisions are not enforced in practice. A 2015 US State Department human rights report recorded no prosecutions under them, and no prosecution of an LGBTQ person under these sections has been reported.

There is no statutory protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 15(3) of the Constitution prohibits discrimination by reference to race, place of origin, political opinions, colour and creed, and does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. As of the 2015 reporting cycle, no non-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity was in force.

The Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015 is reported to prohibit employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation under Article 107(2)(b). The 2015 US State Department report described the position differently, finding gender-based discrimination prohibited only in the field of employment and poorly enforced in practice.

The Marriage Act (Cap 54) does not expressly bar recognition of same-sex marriages; its drafting assumes the parties are of opposite sex, and its restrictions on marriage cover relatives, parties below the age of 16, and bigamy. No mechanism for legal recognition of a same-sex partnership is sourced.

At the 21st session of the Universal Periodic Review, in 2016, France, Slovenia and Chile each urged Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality. The Kiribati delegation made no response to those recommendations, but stated that it was considering advice, from Uruguay, to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation.

Kiribati voted at the UN General Assembly in November 2016 in favour of retaining the mandate of the Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the amendment to defund the mandate was rejected 84 to 77. Reporting on that vote identified Kiribati and Sri Lanka as the only two states that criminalised homosexuality yet supported the mandate's continuation, and also cited Kiribati, alongside Sri Lanka, among the states that still maintained anti-homosexuality laws at that date. No more recent status of the criminal provisions is sourced.
KIR.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources disagree on the scope of employment protection. A secondary reference attributes a sexual-orientation employment discrimination ban to Article 107(2)(b) of the Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015, while the 2015 US State Department report describes only gender-based employment discrimination and calls it poorly enforced. No primary text of the Code is in the inventory; this conflict is unresolved here.

No source addresses entry or visa screening, including whether passport or travel-document gender markers are checked, amended, or a cause of secondary screening. Nothing is sourced on legal gender recognition, on access to gender-affirming medical care, or on prison placement for a trans detainee.

No reporting covers violence against trans people specifically. The only violence-adjacent finding is a general note that lesbians may face violence and discrimination, without incident dates, perpetrators or outcomes.

The most recent dated evidence in the inventory is the November 2016 UN General Assembly vote and the 2016 Universal Periodic Review cycle. Whether sections 153 to 155 remain in force and unamended after that date is not sourced.

TUV.name: Tuvalu
TUV.summary:
Sections 153, 154 and 155 of Tuvalu's Penal Code make male homosexual intercourse, attempts to commit it, and gross indecency between males felonies carrying up to 14, 7 and 5 years' imprisonment respectively. ILGA World's jurisdiction database records the offence as in force and dates the provisions to the colonial era. The exposure is gendered: because the provisions define conduct by male persons, a transgender woman read by police as male falls within them.

The evidence on enforcement is thin and old. The US State Department's 2013 human rights report for Tuvalu describes criminalisation under the Penal Code with no prosecutions of consenting adults recorded, and reports no government abuses of LGBT people in that year. The same assessment attributes discrimination to traditional customs that perpetuate religious and social prejudice rather than to state action. Nothing in the inventory documents a conviction under these sections at any date, and nothing more recent than 2013 on enforcement practice is available here.

No detention-condition, strip-search or custody-treatment findings for transgender detainees appear anywhere in the sourced material. The inventory also contains no hate-crime incidents, hate-crime statistics or hate-crime legislation for Tuvalu, and no entry, visa or border-screening rules with any bearing on gender marker or trans status.

On the protective side, Tuvalu was among roughly 80 signatory states to the UN joint statement on human rights, sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011, recalling General Assembly resolutions on the subject. The Labour and Employment Relations Act 2017 bans workplace discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, alongside gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, HIV/AIDS status and disability. Constitutional protection is narrower: the freedom from discrimination in section 27 of the Constitution, as amended in 2023, lists sex but does not refer to sexual orientation, and no gender-identity or gender-expression protection is described in any source.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. The 2023 constitutional amendments prohibited same-sex marriage, and section 43(2)(b) of the Charter of Duties and Responsibilities defines a family unit as a marriage between a man and a woman to the exclusion of all others. The Marriage Act (Cap 29) does not expressly bar recognition of same-sex unions but assumes parties are male and female, and same-sex marriages do not appear in its restrictions on marriage; no partner-visa, next-of-kin or foreign-union recognition provisions are discussed in the sources.

The Penal Code's asymmetry matters for anyone assessing personal exposure: the age of consent is 15 for heterosexual vaginal intercourse and for lesbian sex, while the male homosexual provisions carry separate felony penalties regardless of that threshold, an arrangement that affects young men who have sex with men. A 2005 study found about 14 per cent of young Tuvaluan men aged 15 to 24 had had sex with a male partner at some point.
TUV.outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement evidence stops in 2013. The inventory contains no human rights report, court record or police data for Tuvalu after that year, so whether the Penal Code sections remain unprosecuted is unresolved rather than confirmed.

No entry, visa, passport or border-screening rules are sourced for Tuvalu, including any requirement to declare or disclose gender history on arrival. Absence of such rules in this inventory is not evidence that none exist.

Treatment of transgender detainees is unsourced: the material contains no detention conditions, strip-search practice, placement decisions or complaints data for trans people in custody. Likewise, no hate-crime legislation or incident record is available for Tuvalu, so the presence or absence of a hate-crime regime is unresolved.

The inventory does not state how a gender marker change on a passport or birth certificate is handled in Tuvalu, whether any legal recognition of gender identity exists, or how foreign same-sex marriages are treated by the Marriage Act. No source documents consular or immigration consequences of the 2023 constitutional amendment for foreign visitors.

The Tuvalu Ministry of Health's 2017 Global AIDS Progress Report sets out the national HIV response and draws on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations, a regional exercise covering men who have sex with men and transgender Tuvaluans. Scale shapes what can be observed. UNAIDS estimates for 2017 put the national population of men who have sex with men at about 300 and of pinapinaaine at about 40, so enforcement patterns, service coverage and incident reporting would be difficult to detect even if they existed.

SLB.name: Solomon Islands
SLB.summary:
Solomon Islands criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women under Penal Code provisions inherited from the colonial period, with a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. The ILGA World Database entry and the Human Dignity Trust country profile both record the offence, the historic-law basis and the same statutory maximum; a general reference summary repeats the figure of up to 14 years.

Enforcement is absent from the record. The United States State Department's annual human-rights reports for 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 record no arrests or prosecutions directed at LGBT people, the 2011 report records no LGBT-specific abuses, and the 2013 report records no abuses by security forces while noting the penal code provisions and no prosecutions under them. Human Dignity Trust documents no recorded prosecutions in recent years, and reference coverage states plainly that the law is not enforced. A visitor's exposure therefore rests on the statute remaining in force and on social and official responses, not on an active prosecution campaign.

Successive governments have refused reform. The Law Reform Commission proposed legalising gay and lesbian sexual activity in December 2008, and the proposal was strongly opposed. The government told the United Nations in 2011 that it had no intention of decriminalising homosexuality. Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare publicly opposed same-sex marriage in a 2017 speech to a local church group, and in June 2018 Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used his Queen's Birthday address to warn that same-sex marriage cannot populate the world, while also acknowledging in the same period that being gay or lesbian is said to be biological and beyond individual control yet citing both the criminal code and the Bible against any legal change.

No protective framework accompanies the offence. Same-sex couples have no relationship recognition, there is no non-discrimination shield covering sexual orientation, and no same-sex marriage law exists; Parliament has not legislated one. Constitutional reform has narrowed visibility of the issue: a 2009 draft constitution listed sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination, but the 2011, 2013 and 2014 drafts dropped it, with reform still ongoing as of 2019.
SLB.outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement data in the inventory stops at the 2013 reporting year. No source here covers arrests, police conduct or prosecutions after 2013, so the current enforcement position is unresolved rather than confirmed as unchanged.

The inventory contains nothing on gender identity specifically: no source addresses legal recognition of gender, identity-document or passport marker rules, screening at ports of entry, or the treatment of trans travellers as distinct from lesbians, gay men and bisexual people. Any trans-specific finding would be unsourced.

Also not sourced: hate-crime or bias-motivation provisions, hate-speech law, access to gender-affirming healthcare, prostitution or public-order offences that could be used against trans people, and rules on entry and visa refusal. The constitutional reform process is described only as ongoing as of 2019, with no later status in the record.

SLB.tangentialFactors:
Official hostility is rhetorical rather than prosecutorial. The strongest statements in the record come from the head of government and the head of state addressing church and national audiences, which points to a social and reputational risk for an openly visible trans visitor rather than a realistic prospect of criminal proceedings. No source in the inventory records an arrest, charge or conviction for same-sex conduct at any point in the periods covered.

The reform trajectory runs against the visitor's interest. A formal decriminalisation proposal from the Law Reform Commission in 2008 was met with strong opposition, the government ruled out decriminalisation in a United Nations communication in 2011, and the equality language present in the 2009 constitutional draft was removed from every subsequent draft. A visitor assessing prospects should treat the current legal position as stable rather than transitional.

The wider human-rights reporting in the State Department material covers matters that do not bear directly on trans visitors, including pretrial detention, corruption and violence against women; these are general country conditions rather than identity-specific risks.

VUT.name: Vanuatu
VUT.summary:
Vanuatu has never criminalised same-sex conduct, and the sources record no documented pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors. The operative risk for a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming traveller comes from official posture rather than from statute: in November 2024 the Ministry of Justice and Community Services was directed to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion. National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 had targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, with V-Pride framed as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values. That framing invites suspicion of advocacy or promotion rather than of private conduct, and a foreign visitor who is visibly gender-nonconforming has no standing as a resident to argue the distinction.

Parliament amended the Marriage Act in November 2024 to define marriage as the union of a male and a female. Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed that same-sex marriages cannot be registered and that pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law. The amendment removes any assumption that a partnered trans visitor's relationship would be recognised locally.

Country coverage describes Vanuatu as socially conservative, advises gay and lesbian travellers and citizens to avoid public displays of affection, and reports no active gay scene. There is no general legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no general prohibition of employment discrimination on that basis. Two narrow provisions exist: Section 18.2(f) of the Teaching Service Act 2013 bars the Vanuatu Teaching Service Commission from discriminating on the ground of "sexual preference" in recruitment, promotion, professional development, transfer and staff management, and Section 2(2)(j) of the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024 bars digital communications that denigrate a person by reason of, among other grounds, sexual orientation.

Prosecutorial practice runs against that hostility. The Office of the Public Prosecutor's Prosecution Policy 2003, the Prosecutors Code (Gazette no. 13 of 2017) and its General Principles on vulnerable witnesses in sexual and gender-based violence cases require prosecutors to disregard sexual preference and to treat discrimination or hostility based on sexual orientation or gender identity as factors weighing toward prosecution. Vanuatu signed the United Nations joint statement on ending violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011.
VUT.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources disagree on the VPride Foundation's founding year: Sista's 2016 report gives 2014, while the country coverage gives 2009. The discrepancy is unresolved and does not affect the risk assessment.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, the amendment of sex markers on passports or identity documents, or whether entry and immigration screening could disclose a visitor's gender history. Care access, including hormone supply and trans-specific medical services, is likewise not sourced here.

The November 2024 committee was tasked with drafting a national policy; whether that policy has since been issued, and how any resulting rule would be enforced against visitors rather than residents, is not documented in the available material. There is also no sourced data on trans-specific violence, so the absence of a documented pattern reflects an absence of reporting rather than a positive finding of safety.

sources.summary: Sista (Oct 2016): VPride Foundation and Vanuatu Women's Centre's first joint LGBTI human-rights workshop (SPC-funded) established that same-sex partners get no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes; USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted violence-against-lesbians case and near-invisible LGBTI court presence; VPride (est. 2014) faced church/official/chief opposition at founding.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Vanuatu is described as socially conservative: gay and lesbian travellers and citizens are advised to avoid public displays of affection, and there is no active gay scene. Section 2(2)(j) of the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024 bars digital communications that denigrate a person by reason of, among other grounds, sexual orientation. The Ni-Vanuatu group VPride Foundation (founded 2009) advocates LGBTQ rights and freedom of speech, has organised awareness events, and first marked the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia in Vanuatu in 2016. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal protection against all forms of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no general prohibition of employment discrimination on that basis. Narrow exceptions exist: Section 18.2(f) of the Teaching Service Act 2013 bars the Vanuatu Teaching Service Commission from discriminating on "sexual preference" in recruitment, promotion, professional development, transfer and staff management; the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024 (s.2(2)(j)) bars denigrating digital communications by sexual orientation. The Office of the Public Prosecutor's Prosecution Policy 2003, Prosecutors Code (Gazette no. 13 of 2017) and its General Principles on vulnerable witnesses in sexual and gender-based violence cases require prosecutors to disregard sexual preference and to treat discrimination or hostility based on sexual orientation or gender identity as factors weighing toward prosecution. Vanuatu signed the UN joint statement on ending violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011.

VUT.blindSummary:
The country has never criminalised same-sex conduct, and the sources record no documented pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors. The operative risk for a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming traveller comes from official posture rather than from statute: in November 2024 the national justice ministry was directed to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion. A national human rights coordinator said a cabinet decision earlier in 2024 had targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, with a national LGBTI advocacy organisation framed as contrary to constitutional, Christian and customary values. That framing invites suspicion of advocacy or promotion rather than of private conduct, and a foreign visitor who is visibly gender-nonconforming has no standing as a resident to argue the distinction.

Parliament amended the national marriage law in November 2024 to define marriage as the union of a male and a female. The internal affairs minister confirmed that same-sex marriages cannot be registered and that pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law. The amendment removes any assumption that a partnered trans visitor's relationship would be recognised locally.

Country coverage describes the country as socially conservative, advises gay and lesbian travellers and citizens to avoid public displays of affection, and reports no active gay scene. There is no general legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no general prohibition of employment discrimination on that basis. Two narrow provisions exist: a section of a 2013 teaching-service law bars the national teaching service commission from discriminating on the ground of "sexual preference" in recruitment, promotion, professional development, transfer and staff management, and a section of a 2024 digital-communications law bars digital communications that denigrate a person by reason of, among other grounds, sexual orientation.

Prosecutorial practice runs against that hostility. A 2003 prosecution policy, a prosecutors' code gazetted in 2017 and its General Principles on vulnerable witnesses in sexual and gender-based violence cases require prosecutors to disregard sexual preference and to treat discrimination or hostility based on sexual orientation or gender identity as factors weighing toward prosecution. The country signed a United Nations joint statement on ending violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011.
VUT.blindOutOfScope:
The sources disagree on the advocacy foundation's founding year: a 2016 regional report gives 2014, while the country coverage gives 2009. The discrepancy is unresolved and does not affect the risk assessment.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, the amendment of sex markers on passports or identity documents, or whether entry and immigration screening could disclose a visitor's gender history. Care access, including hormone supply and trans-specific medical services, is likewise not sourced here.

The November 2024 committee was tasked with drafting a national policy; whether that policy has since been issued, and how any resulting rule would be enforced against visitors rather than residents, is not documented in the available material. There is also no sourced data on trans-specific violence, so the absence of a documented pattern reflects an absence of reporting rather than a positive finding of safety.

NRU.name: Nauru
NRU.summary:
Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016. The provisions repealed were sections of a criminal code inherited from Queensland in 1899, and the repeal also covered the attempted-suicide offences that sat alongside them. A visitor should not expect prosecution for consensual same-sex intimacy under Nauruan law.

The legal position for trans and intersex visitors is markedly thinner. Kaleidoscope Trust's country assessment records that intersex and transgender people in Nauru have no explicit legal recognition or protection, that same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal, and that there is no employment-discrimination protection for lesbian, bisexual, trans and intersex people.

No source in this inventory documents how Nauru handles gender markers on passports or other identity documents. A visitor cannot assume that a Nauruan-issued document will reflect a stated identity, and no consular or immigration screening procedure for trans travellers is described anywhere in these sources.

The one gender-identity provision located for Nauru operates inside immigration detention. The Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, prohibit discrimination against any person on the basis of sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity within the regional processing facility. That protection is confined to the immigration-detention estate. It does not reach Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and it addresses non-discrimination rather than questions of housing by birth sex versus identity, special units or solitary confinement.

Nauru's diplomatic position has at points favoured protection. In 2011 it was among 84 countries signing a joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, delivered by Colombia, alongside Fiji, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others.
NRU.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in the inventory addresses gender markers on Nauruan passports or identity documents, nor any entry, visa or airport-screening practice that could disclose a trans traveller's status. The absence is a gap in these sources, not evidence that no rule exists.

Unresolved: whether the regional processing centre's gender-identity non-discrimination clause has ever been invoked, and how it is enforced in practice, is not sourced here. The same is true of any complaint mechanism available to a trans detainee.

Unresolved: no documentation was found on housing placement for transgender prisoners in Nauru's corrections system, and no trans-prisoner case or judicial ruling is recorded in these materials.

Unresolved: the inventory does not show whether Nauru maintains any statutory pathway for legal gender recognition, or whether the 2016 CEDAW report omission on LBTI matters was raised by the treaty committee.

PLW.name: Palau
PLW.summary:
Palau decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2014. The Penal Code signed by the President in April 2014 dropped the sodomy offence formerly at section 2803 of Chapter 28, "Sex Crimes", Title 17, which carried up to ten years' imprisonment. Palau's Attorney General confirmed the repeal to Human Dignity Trust, and no offence against consensual same-sex conduct is in force.

Before that repeal, Palau appeared on a list of more than 70 Pacific and global jurisdictions whose laws still criminalised same-sex relations, published around 2011 by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Palau and Nauru both accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts during their Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appearances, which documents a stated commitment to repeal rather than an unannounced change.

At its 2011 Universal Periodic Review, Palau also accepted recommendations to combat discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. On 22 March 2011 Palau was among the 84 countries on whose behalf Colombia delivered a joint statement to the Human Rights Council calling for an end to violence and human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. That statement is the earliest dated record of the government's position in the sources.
PLW.outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition is unresolved in the sources: the inventory contains no provision, procedure or refusal governing change of name or gender marker for Palau residents or visitors, and no statement that such a path exists or does not exist.

Hate-crime provisions, statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, bathroom and facilities rules, healthcare access rules, and recognition of partners or marriages are not sourced here. Their status in Palau is not established by this inventory and should not be read as either present or absent.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for transgender travellers are not covered by any source in this inventory.

The decriminalisation claim rests on a 2014 report by 76crimes citing Human Dignity Trust and the Attorney General's confirmation. The underlying Penal Code text and the current consolidated statute have not been checked directly, and no source post-dates 2014 to confirm that section 2803 has not been reinstated.

Erasing 76crimes (16 Oct 2014): Palau decriminalised homosexuality — per Human Dignity Trust, Palau's Attorney General confirmed the new Penal Code (signed by the President in April 2014) dropped the sodomy offence formerly at s.2803 Ch.28 'Sex Crimes' Title 17 (up to 10 years' imprisonment); at its 2011 UPR Palau had accepted recommendations to repeal criminalisation and combat LGBT discrimination; the move dropped the global anti-sodomy country count to 79.

Scoop/OHCHR Pacific piece (c. 2011): Palau appears among more than 70 Pacific and global jurisdictions with laws criminalising same-sex relations still on the books, and Palau and Nauru accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts during their Human Rights Council UPR appearances, documenting Palau's stated commitment to repeal.

PLW.tangentialFactors:
The 2014 repeal, taken together with São Tomé and Príncipe's, reduced the global count of countries criminalising anti-sodomy provisions to 79 at the time of reporting. Palau is therefore one of a small number of jurisdictions that legislated repeal rather than inheriting decriminalisation from a colonial-era reform.

Palau's record sits alongside Nauru's in the same Pacific review cycle, where both states accepted decriminalisation recommendations. The regional pattern in the sources is one of repeal and stated commitment rather than active prosecution, but the inventory contains no enforcement data, no reported prosecutions before or after 2014, and no evidence about how the repeal is applied in practice.

The 2011 joint statement Palau joined was delivered on its behalf by Colombia, so the position recorded is Palau's endorsement of a multilateral text rather than a domestic legislative act.

FSM.name: Micronesia (FSM)
FSM.summary:
The Federated States of Micronesia carries no legal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct. US State Department human rights reporting recorded no laws criminalising homosexuality in 2010 and again in 2015, and current legal overviews describe the same position.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been illegal since a 2018 constitutional equality reform adopted by the national Congress. The archived State Department reports from 2010 and 2015 predate that reform and describe only limited protection, so they should not be read as the current legal position.

The 2015 report also recorded societal stigma affecting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, without documenting instances of discrimination under the law.

No legal gender recognition procedure is documented for the Federated States of Micronesia, and no source in the current record describes an available route for a trans person to amend sex markers on official documents.
FSM.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in the inventory documents how the 2018 constitutional equality provision has been enforced, whether any complaint has been brought under it, or what remedies it provides.

Unresolved: no source addresses hate-crime or hate-speech provisions that might cover anti-trans conduct, and none addresses bathroom or facilities access, healthcare provision, or restrictions on gender-affirming care.

Unresolved: entry, visa and border-document screening for trans travellers is not sourced for the Federated States of Micronesia. No source describes how sex markers on foreign passports are treated at entry, and no source records trans-specific violence with a date or outcome.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no source on partner or marriage recognition, and no current (post-2018) human rights report for the country.

MHL.name: Marshall Islands
MHL.summary:
The Republic of the Marshall Islands has no criminalisation regime covering consensual same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust's record of the global history of criminalisation dates the country's decriminalisation to 2005, so a visitor faces no statutory offence for consensual same-sex relations.

The most recent official country reporting in the inventory is the United States Department of State's 2015 Human Rights Report on the Marshall Islands. It recorded no reports of torture, arbitrary killings, enforced disappearances or LGBT-specific abuses, and it listed prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence among the significant problems it identified.
MHL.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition in the Marshall Islands. Whether a resident or visitor can obtain a change of gender marker on a Marshallese passport or other national document, and by what procedure, remains unresolved here. What can be said is that border and screening officials will work from the marker on the document presented at entry, since no local amendment route is documented.

Entry and visa requirements are not covered by any source in the inventory, and no source addresses how Marshallese border officials treat a foreign passport carrying a gender marker changed in another country. That handling is not sourced.

Human Dignity Trust supplies the 2005 decriminalisation date, but no source in the inventory identifies the statute repealed or the body that repealed it.

The 2015 United States Department of State Human Rights Report is the most recent official country reporting available here. Anything after 2015, including later changes to law, policy or enforcement practice, is not sourced in this inventory.

sources.summary: The Marshall Islands decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2005 and has no criminalisation regime in force.
