sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Rock of Hope states that with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa. In April 2022 the High Court, while upholding refusal to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities, accepted that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. Officials refused to register ESGM in June 2019 on the grounds of morality. Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced. There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said people of the same sex cannot even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not even ready to consider it; in 2014 Press Secretary Percy Simelane said the government was closely monitoring the situation with a view to take a legal position. A 2019 survey found 59% of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities, with 30% denied healthcare services. In February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a move LGBTQ groups welcomed. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion. The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles. The 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation. A 2013 survey found 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Limited protections exist in policy: the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law, saying so few gays lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort; in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The BTI 2024 country report records that the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations within an oppressive environment in which 'Mswati must fall' has become a common protest slogan.

Media regulation carries a counterweight. The 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation.

Self-reported harm among LGBTQ Swazis is high. A 2013 survey found that 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances in order to feel normal.

External pressure has been persistent but ineffective. In May 2017 the United Nations Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
SWZ.blindSummary:
Same-sex relations are criminalised in the country for men and women throughout the country, as recorded on 12 March 2026. No legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor's passport and other documents are read exactly as issued, with no route to align them with lived gender.

LGBTI organisations cannot obtain official registration. The national registrar of companies refused to register a sexual and gender minorities group in June 2019 on grounds of morality, and in April 2022 the High Court upheld that refusal while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. A visitor should not expect to find a registered national advocacy body to contact for assistance.

Hostility from official figures is documented. A 2021 report by a foreign government's human rights bureau found that some traditional, religious and government officials publicly criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally local nor Christian. In June 2012 the prime minister stated that people of the same sex could not even go to regional offices to get married and that the state was not ready to consider the question, and in 2014 a government spokesperson said the government was monitoring the situation in order to take a legal position.

Public visibility has nonetheless been tolerated on several occasions. The first national Pride, held in July 2018, was reported as a great success, a virtual Pride celebration held in June 2021 passed without incident, and a church welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in December 2018 at a time when discrimination showed no let-up.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships. Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced.

Healthcare carries a documented outing and refusal risk. A 2019 survey found that 59% of LGBTQ residents had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities and 30% had been denied healthcare services.

Anti-LGBT violence has produced fatalities. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from a small town was murdered by a man who said he did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. A national advocacy group states that, with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and that most choose to remain in the closet or move to a neighbouring jurisdiction.

No broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity exist in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. A 2012 statement by the then foreign minister rejected a United Nations working group call for an LGBTQ protection law on the grounds that so few gay people lived in the country that drafting one was not worth the effort.

LSO.name: Lesotho
LSO.summary:
Lesotho does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The common-law crime of sodomy was struck down in 2012, the US State Department's 2016 human rights report for Lesotho records no criminalisation, and a joint stakeholder report to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho likewise confirms that same-sex conduct is lawful while noting that no anti-discrimination protections exist.

There is no legal gender recognition in Lesotho. No statute permits a change of the gender marker on official documents. A 2017 constitutional analysis by the Southern African Litigation Centre sets out the absence of any statutory route, and a October 2020 briefing by the same organisation with the People's Matrix Association and the Women and Law in Southern Africa Research and Education Project, 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho', assesses the country's law and policy against international best practice and finds no framework meeting it.

For a trans traveller the document problem is immediate. On the 2017 assessment, a person travelling on a passport whose marker does not match their presentation or stated identity could face a charge, because no statutory procedure exists to have the document recognised as consistent with the holder's gender.

The constitutional position remains an argument rather than enacted law. The 2017 analysis concludes that section 4(1) of the Constitution, through the grounds of sex and other status, should be read to cover gender identity on the authority of the UN Human Rights Committee. That interpretation has not been written into statute, and it has not been shown to have been applied by a court.

Violence and service exclusion are documented. The October 2024 joint UPR report records discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people in Lesotho, community-level discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics, and barriers to health and education services. The 2016 US State Department report separately documents societal stigma against LGBT people. Protection machinery is thin: the International Commission of Jurists' November 2024 UPR submission raised LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination as one of three key concerns for Lesotho.

Employment sits under the Labour Act 2024, which sets the current statutory framework covering unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, and forced and child labour prohibitions. The 2017 analysis records that the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omitted gender and sexual orientation.
LSO.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa requirements for trans travellers, including any screening of passport markers at border or airport, are not covered by the sources held, and no immigration rule on document presentation has been located.

Whether the Labour Act 2024's unfair discrimination clause names gender identity, gender expression or sexual orientation is unresolved on the material available; the sources give the Act's subject matter but not its protected-grounds list.

No hate-crime statute or aggravated-penalty provision addressing anti-trans or anti-LGBT violence is sourced for Lesotho, so the question of enhanced penalties for the assaults documented in the October 2024 report stays open.

The 2017 conclusion that a trans traveller could be charged over a non-matching passport is a legal analysis; no reported arrest, prosecution or judicial decision applying it has been found in the inventory.

CPV.name: Cabo Verde
CPV.summary:
Cabo Verde does not criminalise same-sex relations. The national employment discrimination prohibition covers sexual orientation but does not extend to gender identity, so a trans worker has no explicit statutory basis for a workplace complaint (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026).

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. In 2016 civil law blocked Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed trans woman in the country, from changing her legal name to a female one; the source inventory holds no later statute or administrative procedure permitting a legal gender change. A trans visitor whose passport marker differs from their presentation should therefore expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility.

Same-sex unions are not recognised. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva said on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, a statement made after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Trans-specific violence is documented at a personal level. Tchinda Andrade, who came out publicly in 1997 at the age of 19, reported verbal violence and two physical attacks while describing Cabo Verde as markedly freer for LGBT people than other African countries and the island of São Vicente as relaxed.

Public visibility is high and organised. LGBTIQ organisations register freely, the first public Pride was held in 2013, making Cabo Verde the second African country to do so, and the 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with NGO campaigns by the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law, with the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged in the programme.

Survey evidence points to broad public acceptance of LGBT people alongside a narrower margin on gender variance. Polling across 2019–21 found 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, and Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020) placed Cabo Verde among the particularly tolerant countries in Africa while recording that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

The state presents itself internationally as a protector: Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group and made anti-discrimination commitments under the 2024 Universal Periodic Review.
CPV.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory contains no source dated after 2016 on legal gender recognition, so whether any administrative procedure for changing a legal gender has since been introduced is not established either way.

Unresolved: the 2018 petition to the National Assembly for an anti-discrimination law is documented, but no source states whether such a law was subsequently enacted, and the current coverage beyond the employment-law sexual-orientation ground is unconfirmed.

Not sourced: the dossier has no material on hate-crime sentencing enhancements, on public-order or decency provisions that might be applied to trans people, or on their enforcement.

Not sourced: no entry, visa or border-screening rules are available, including whether passport gender markers are checked or whether trans travellers face additional questioning.

Not sourced: access to gender-affirming healthcare, locker-room and bathroom access rules, and school or institutional facility policies are absent from the inventory.

The public-opinion figures date from 2019–21 and May 2020 and have not been refreshed by the sources; they may not reflect current attitudes.

CPV.tangentialFactors:

Political opinion at the top has been restrained rather than hostile. In July 2017 the prime minister kept same-sex marriage off the agenda while publicly distancing himself from the opposition to it voiced by MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro.

On the ground, the country's most prominent trans woman rated São Vicente as relaxed even while recording two physical assaults and repeated verbal abuse, suggesting that tolerance measured in surveys does not eliminate targeted violence against visibly trans people.

STP.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
STP.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal since the Penal Code entered into force in November 2012, and the age of consent is set equally regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. The sources disagree on the figure: two record it at 16, while a third states that Law 15/2021 raised it to 18 for everyone in 2021. Travellers should treat 18 as the operative figure until confirmed, since the higher number, if correct, applies to visitors as well as residents.

São Tomé and Príncipe has no legal framework for gender-identity recognition. There is no procedure for amending sex or gender markers on identity documents, so a traveller whose passport, visa or other papers do not match their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible to border and hotel officials with no domestic remedy behind it.

No form of relationship recognition exists for same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, so a foreign partner arriving on a spouse-derived entitlement has no locally recognised status to rely on.

Crimes motivated by sexual-orientation hatred attract enhanced sentencing under Article 130(2)(d) of the Penal Code, which places sexual-orientation-motivated offending above the ordinary sentencing range. The inventory does not record equivalent treatment for gender-identity-motivated crimes.

The Labour Code of 2019, Article 16.2, bans workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that is the only codified anti-discrimination protection in the sources; no general protection across housing, services or public accommodation is recorded. São Tomé and Príncipe is listed among the signatories to an international joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity.
STP.outOfScopeNotes:
The current age of consent is unresolved: one source records 16 under the 2012 Penal Code and another records 18 following Law 15/2021, and the inventory contains no text of either provision to settle which is in force. Visitors should verify the figure against the current statute before relying on it.

Whether the enhanced-sentencing provision in Penal Code Article 130(2)(d) has ever been applied in practice, and whether it extends to offences motivated by gender identity rather than sexual orientation, is not sourced here. No enforcement statistics, complaint procedures or case outcomes are available in the inventory.

The sources record no information on prison or detention conditions, border-screening practices, or the treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers during security checks in São Tomé and Príncipe. Nothing is stated either way about availability of gender-affirming healthcare or HIV services for visitors.

MDV.name: Maldives
MDV.summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct under its 2014 Penal Code, which extended the offence beyond Muslims to everyone, and reporting on the statute notes that death-penalty provisions remain theoretically in reach.

Enforcement is documented rather than theoretical. Police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men, aged 56 and 27, on 29 August 2015 after they were found engaging in homosexual activity in a private home. Prosecution reached into a residence on a local island, so exposure is not confined to public space or to Maldivian nationals. Rainbow Warriors warned after the arrests that tourists could face similar threats.

The Maldives holds reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and the CRC. In review by the UN Human Rights Committee, the government was recommended to adopt anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and to take action against stigmatisation of homosexuals. No source in the inventory records such legislation in force.

Human-rights experts surveyed for HRMI's 2024 Maldives report most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people, alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers, as at risk of violations of empowerment rights. The same report scores political participation at 6.4/10 while other civil and political rights score considerably lower, so the channels that function best do not include the rights on which this group depends.
MDV.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no source addressing gender identity, legal gender recognition or trans-specific criminal provisions. The findings above rest on sexual-orientation sources, and their application to trans visitors specifically is not sourced here.

Whether the death-penalty provisions referenced in reporting on the 2014 Penal Code have ever been imposed in a same-sex conduct case is unresolved in these sources; the sourced claim is that they remain theoretically in reach.

No source in the inventory records the outcome of the Dhaandhoo prosecutions after the arrests of 29 August 2015.

Whether the Human Rights Committee's recommendation on anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation has been acted on is not recorded in the inventory.

PRK.name: North Korea
PRK.summary:
North Korea exposes trans visitors to unbounded official discretion rather than to a defined offence. The Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but Article 193 prohibits the import, possession and distribution of "decadent culture," including sexual recordings, and Article 262 punishes collective "obscene activities." Neither provision is defined in terms that constrain how the authorities apply it.

The US State Department's 2022 human rights report on North Korea reaches the same position: no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, and the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life. Its 2020 report states that reliable information on LGBT persons is unavailable and that repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality in the country.

Gender identity has no standing in the legal order. The Constitution, last revised in 2024, does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no provision of North Korean law prohibits such discrimination; the US State Department reports that the concepts do not appear in the country's legal texts. As of 2026 no law recognises same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Article 8 of the Family Law of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea states that marriage may be concluded only between one man and one woman.

Official hostility is documented on the state record even while the state denies the existence of homosexuality. A KCNA commentary of 22 April 2014 rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report on North Korean human rights as a political fabrication and personally attacked commissioner Michael Kirby as "a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality" in order to discredit the findings. KCNA had denied homosexuality's existence earlier the same year.

Violence against LGBT people is reported but thinly sourced. A 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report, the 584-page North Korean Human Rights Report, cites defector testimony alleging that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014. A 2011 Korea Times report, sourced to Free North Korea Radio, claimed that North Korea executed a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, for capitalist influence and "corruption of public morals." Outright International's country page records no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people, which reflects the absence of reporting channels rather than an absence of incidents.

Exit narratives form the main body of evidence. An openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017, and CNN's April 2017 account of that defector records both the place of homosexuality in North Korean society and the punishment it carries. Jang Young-jin, a novelist who fled in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, is documented by BBC Korean in October 2024 as the first publicly known gay defector; the same feature describes how a regime subordinating the individual to the collective forces sexual minorities into silent self-suppression.

The legislative environment has tightened. BBC Korean's 10 October 2024 feature, produced ten years after the UN Commission of Inquiry report, identifies new laws including the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act as extending state control over expression. Article 193's ban on decadent material and Article 262's ban on collective obscene activities sit within this framework, and neither carries a defined penalty range in the sources reviewed.
PRK.outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and border-screening practice for trans travellers, including how immigration officers treat foreign passport gender markers, is not addressed by any source in this inventory and remains unresolved here.

The claim that the Criminal Code contains no penalty for consensual same-sex acts is phrased in the source as an apparent absence rather than an affirmative verification; a definitive reading of the 2009 revised text is not available from these materials.

Whether Articles 193 and 262 have been applied to consensual same-sex conduct specifically is not sourced. Their use in any individual case is unresolved.

The execution allegations from 2011 and 2014 are unverified by any source in this inventory; no corroborating record, name or case file is available.

Access to legal redress for a foreign visitor who experiences violence is not covered by these sources. No consular, complaint or protection mechanism for trans visitors is documented here.

Official rhetoric is a risk factor in its own right. The state news agency's 2014 attack on a UN commissioner used homosexuality as an insult, which indicates that visible association with LGBT identity can be framed as disqualifying or politically hostile by the authorities, independently of any statute.

Outright International's position that no state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people is documented sits alongside the Ministry of Unification's execution allegations. PSE.name: Palestinian Territories
PSE.summary:
Trans visitors face a severe and divided risk environment. Two separate criminal-law regimes apply across the Palestinian territories, and the difference between them is decisive: consensual same-sex conduct is not an offence in the West Bank, while in Gaza the same conduct is punishable by up to ten years' imprisonment under a statute that has been enforced against LGBT people.

The West Bank operates under the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision of its own code dropped offences against consensual private sexual conduct and the 1960 code carried that position forward, so no provision criminalises consensual same-sex acts there. The Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality, and Israel stopped applying the older Mandate criminal code in 1977.

Gaza is governed by Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936, which remains in force. Section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex 'carnal knowledge' with up to ten years' imprisonment, and the same code sets out broader historic terms, including sodomy with up to fourteen years and an 'act against the law of nature' with up to ten years. Section 152(1)(c), the only youth-linked provision cited, carries up to fourteen years for sodomy with a child under sixteen. The Human Rights Watch and the Human Dignity Trust hold the 1936 ordinance to be in force in Gaza; its applicability is contested by other commentators, and Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there.

No provision of either regime expressly prohibits trans identity, but the 1936 code's public-morality provisions are broad enough to catch trans people in practice. No legal gender recognition provisions are set out for the territories, and Equaldex reports no broad legal protections against discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people.

Formal legality does not describe what is encountered on the ground. Social and family persecution makes daily reality harsher than the written law, and periodic transphobic threats and attacks are recorded. Palestinian police action against a planned event organised by al-Qaws drew a wave of hate messages that activists said posed a serious threat to the community, and rights groups condemned the police ban on LGBTQ activity. Palestinian Authority non-signatory status to key human rights treaties limits the protection machinery available to a visitor.

HIV prevention and care are inadequate. HIV-positive queer individuals often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and stigma is high, and epidemiological surveillance is lacking: only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered between 1988 and 2017, with the true figure believed to be far higher because taboos hinder data collection. In Gaza since October 2023, the collapse of the healthcare system together with Israeli blockades has made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult.

Entry runs through Israel. Around 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence, and since June 2022 Israel has issued work permits to gay Palestinians granted asylum and to those fleeing domestic violence. LGBTQ Palestinian asylum seekers in Israel are routinely excluded from basic healthcare programmes and shelter access available to other asylum seekers, and some have faced house arrest or deportation.
PSE.outOfScopeNotes:
The in-force status of the 1936 British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance in Gaza is unresolved in the sources: the Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force, Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there, and Anis F. Kassim has argued it could be read as permitting homosexuality. This record follows the Human Rights Watch and Human Dignity Trust position while noting the disagreement.

Whether the 2003 draft Palestinian penal code was implemented is not established in any source consulted.

The gap between officially registered HIV cases and actual prevalence is acknowledged but not quantified; the true number is described only as likely far higher.

Incident-level documentation of transphobic violence in the territories is thin: sources record periodic threats and attacks without dated case details or outcomes, and no named trans-specific killing or prosecution in either territory was located in this inventory.

No source consulted sets out an entry, visa or border-screening rule that turns on gender marker or trans status for visitors arriving via Israel or via the Jordanian and Egyptian crossings.

Kassim argues it could be read as permitting homosexuality. The 2003 draft Palestinian penal code criminalised adult consensual same-sex conduct, carrying up to five years for male-male sodomy, and it is unknown whether it was implemented. Equaldex reports no broad legal protections from discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people in Palestine, no legal gender recognition provisions are set out, Palestinian queer organisations operate from within Israel, and statelessness is cited as a structural condition of LGBTQ Palestinians.

Only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered in Palestine between 1988 and 2017 (79 AIDS, 19 HIV-positive), with the true number likely far higher because taboos hinder data collection. In Gaza since October 2023, collapse of the healthcare system plus Israeli blockades has made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult. In Israel, LGBTQ Palestinian asylum seekers are routinely excluded from basic healthcare programs and shelter access available to other asylum seekers, and some have faced house arrest or deportation; only in June 2022 did Israel begin issuing work permits to gay Palestinian refugees granted asylum and those fleeing domestic violence.

Section 152(1)(c) of the British Mandate Criminal Code is the only youth-linked legal provision cited, under which sodomy with a child under sixteen carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, alongside Section 152(2)(b) criminalizing 'carnal knowledge' against the law of nature with up to 10 years. SLE.name: Sierra Leone
SLE.summary:
Sexual activity between men is a criminal offence in Sierra Leone under the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act, which carries a penalty of up to life imprisonment; the Human Dignity Trust country profile records the statute as the basis of the country's criminalisation regime. Consensual sexual relations between women are not explicitly outlawed, per Amnesty International's 2025 country report, but the absence of an explicit prohibition does not translate into safety for a trans visitor.

Enforcement does not run through prosecution. The US Department of State's 2012 Human Rights Report records that the 1861 buggery law was not enforced, while police continued to harass, detain, beat and denounce persons perceived to be members of the LGBT community. Men dressed as women were singled out for detention, harassment and public humiliation, and were not formally charged with any crime or misdemeanor. For a trans woman, the practical exposure is a police encounter rather than a charge.

No non-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is documented. Amnesty International's 2025 report records no SOGI protection, so a visitor refused a hotel room, turned away from a clinic or met with inaction at a police station has no statutory complaint to make.

Violence against LGBT people has produced no reliable accountability. The November 2004 rape and murder of lesbian activist FannyAnn Eddy was followed by the January 2005 arrest of her killer; police refused to classify the killing as a hate crime, and the alleged murderer was reported to have escaped from custody in July 2005.

The US Department of State's 2012 report documents official and societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender individuals. A joint shadow report to the UN Human Rights Committee under the ICCPR, submitted in March 2014, records discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, hate speech by religious institutions, and hate crimes against LGBTI human-rights defenders.
SLE.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address entry and visa rules, airport or border screening on the basis of gender presentation, or the rules governing gender markers on passports and other identity documents. Nothing in the inventory indicates how Sierra Leonean authorities treat a foreign passport whose marker differs from the holder's presentation.

No sourced material covers access to gender-affirming healthcare, any restriction on such care, or bathroom and facilities rules applicable to visitors.

Recognition of marriages or partners of same-sex couples is not addressed, and no hate-crime sentencing provision covering gender identity is documented.

Enforcement data after 2012 is absent from the inventory: whether the 1861 Act has been used in prosecution since then, and whether the pattern of detention without charge recorded in 2012 continues, remain unresolved on these sources.

Whether the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act has ever been applied to women, and how its provision would be applied to a trans woman, is not resolved by the sources.

XKX.name: Kosovo
XKX.summary:
Article 24 of the Constitution of the Republic of Kosovo prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, and the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination extends that protection to gender identity. Outright International's March 2026 overview records that implementation of both provisions remains inconsistent in practice, so the guarantees a visitor can cite are stronger than what is reliably delivered.

Legal gender recognition runs through the courts rather than an administrative procedure. In January 2019 Blert Morina's application for a name and gender-marker change on Kosovo identity documents was before the Constitutional Court of Kosovo, and applicants in Kosovo followed closely the European Court of Human Rights ruling in X v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, which held that a surgical requirement for changing a gender marker violates private-life rights.

Partner recognition remains unadopted law. Parliament rejected a law recognising same-sex civil unions in March 2022. Prime Minister Albin Kurti pledged in April 2024 to legalise same-sex civil unions, and a Justice Ministry working group was drafting the relevant bill, but as of February 2026 Parliament had still not adopted the new Civil Code amid fierce opposition that included the ruling party. IntelliNews reports that the draft Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language would open the way to same-sex marriage if it enters into force.

Public LGBTI organising is visible in Prishtina, where the third annual Pride Parade was held alongside a week of exhibitions, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty. The CSGD annual report for 2022 documented intolerance and hatred, with hate speech by politicians common during the Civil Code debates, and an artist received death threats over a painting.
XKX.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border screening of trans visitors, including whether identity documents are inspected for gender markers on arrival; that question is unresolved here.

The outcome of Blert Morina's Constitutional Court case on name and gender-marker change is not sourced beyond its pending status in January 2019, and no source states the current evidentiary or medical requirements for legal gender recognition in Kosovo.

The inventory does not cover access to gender-appropriate facilities, healthcare or hormone treatment for visitors, nor the penalties attaching to hate crimes or the enforcement record of discrimination complaints brought under the 2015 law.

GIB.name: Gibraltar
GIB.summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, and the code on single-sex services issued in 2025, bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension appears in the sourced material.

No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender reassignment, alongside sexual orientation, has been in place since 2007 under Gibraltar's own equality provisions.

Hate-crime coverage now extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013, and in July 2026 passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy.

Partner and family recognition is established locally: civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016 after a bill passed unanimously, a Supreme Court ruling of 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and an Adoption Act 2023 in full effect from 18 April 2024 that expressly allows same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender is 16. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry into overseas territories recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories, and its Seventh Report of 2007-08 sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.
GIB.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or the 2025 single-sex-services code has ever been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council is unresolved in the sourced material; the sources record no extension, but they are not a register of Orders in Council.

The enforcement record of the gender-reassignment discrimination protection is not sourced. No material addresses complaints, tribunal or court outcomes, or penalties applied under that provision.

No sourced material covers border screening practice, document inspection of gender markers by Gibraltar or United Kingdom officers, visa conditions for trans travellers, prison placement, or access to transition-related healthcare for visitors.

Royal assent and commencement dates for the two bills passed in July 2026, covering transgender identity in hate crime and hate speech legislation and the conversion therapy offence, are not stated in the sources; only passage by Parliament is recorded.

Several legal-history claims rest on a single open-source chain: one of the cited pages is a mirror of the same Wikipedia article used elsewhere, so corroboration is weaker than the number of links suggests.

The Foreign Affairs Committee report's material on corruption concerns Turks and Caicos and has no bearing on Gibraltar; only its governance expectations and its 2008 recommendation on sexual orientation and gender status are used here.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity'. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

BMU.name: Bermuda
BMU.summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex services code do not automatically extend to Bermuda. Local legislation governs, and United Kingdom measures could be applied to Bermuda only by Order in Council.

The House of Assembly voted 22–16 on 14 May 1994 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, striking two sections of the Criminal Code. The debate divided the island at the time, with religious leaders split and the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change.

In July 2013 the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and, in the same instrument, on grounds of age. Same-sex marriage was not permitted at that point.

The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act in February 2018. It replaced same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships open to both same-sex and opposite-sex couples, making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. Partner recognition for a same-sex couple therefore rests on the partnership register rather than on marriage.

Whether the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex services code has been applied to Bermuda by Order in Council is unresolved here; no instrument extending it is cited, and the sources describe the position as one in which local legislation governs.

CYM.name: Cayman Islands
CYM.summary:
The Cayman Islands decriminalised same-sex intimacy in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

In August 2009 members of the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording citizens less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

Relationship recognition moved through the courts rather than the statute book. Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the prohibition on same-sex marriage in March 2019; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019, restoring the statutory ban.

Recognition then arrived through immigration administration. In December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. Overseas marriages therefore carry immigration effects in the Cayman Islands even though no local route to marriage exists.

Public visibility is high in the tourist-facing environment. Around 600 people, including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation. Organisers asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection as a condition of the public-space route.
CYM.outOfScopeNotes:
The current statutory age of consent in the Cayman Islands, and whether the inequality left by the 2001 reform has since been equalised, are not sourced in this inventory and remain unresolved here.

Whether any route to local same-sex marriage survives the August 2019 appellate ruling, whether further litigation was filed or is pending, and the precise scope of the Court of Appeal's December 2020 reasoning are unresolved on the available sources.

No sourced position is available on civil unions or registered partnerships, partner-based visa categories beyond the single 2020 immigration recognition, joint adoption, or partner inheritance and next-of-kin standing.

Whether the European Convention on Human Rights, or equivalent United Kingdom-level protections, extends directly to the Cayman Islands is not settled by these sources; the 2009 warning about Article 14 indicates the question was contested but does not resolve it.

Enforcement practice is unverified: no source addresses police guidance on public affection, whether the organisers' condition on displays of affection was enforced, or how the unequal age of consent is applied in practice.

VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws in the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded the position publicly, stating that "there is nothing we can do." The decriminalisation arrived by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly.

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, including its 2025 single-sex-services code, does not automatically apply in the British Virgin Islands. The territory stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume the Equality Act's discrimination and service-access protections are available there by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Family status remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under British Virgin Islands law was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not itself a ruling on whether such a marriage is recognised in the territory.
VGB.outOfScopeNotes:
No provision on legal gender recognition, or on amending gender markers on British Virgin Islands identity documents or on the British passport issued there, is sourced in this inventory. How an amended marker would be read at entry to the territory is not established here.

Nothing in the inventory covers gender identity within the territory's hate-crime or sentencing framework, nor any local anti-discrimination statute addressing gender identity in employment, housing, health care or public services. Whether a comparable local statute exists is not resolved by these sources.

Rules governing access to sex-segregated facilities, and any local code on single-sex services, are not sourced, nor is access to gender-affirming health care or the treatment of trans people by the territory's police and courts. Constitutional protections for trans residents under the territory's own constitution are likewise not addressed.

The validity of same-sex marriages celebrated outside the British Virgin Islands remains unresolved in this inventory. The only sourced ruling is the 29 July 2022 refusal of the BVI Christian Council's bid to appeal Justice Adrian Jack's case-management orders, not a determination of the underlying question.

AIA.name: Anguilla
AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory whose law is local law: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the island, and they can be applied there only by Order in Council.

Sex between men in private is legal, but the repeal was imposed from London rather than enacted by Anguilla's own legislature. On 5 January 2001 the Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands — acting unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Anguillian law provides no legislative protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution outlaws discrimination only on grounds of race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex or place of origin, leaving gender identity outside the protected categories.

The age of consent is set at 18 for homosexual conduct and 16 for heterosexual conduct, a differential that exposes same-sex couples to legal risk that different-sex couples do not face.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is one of the British overseas territories that has not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island confirms that same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so only symbolic, non-legal ceremonies are available to same-sex couples; non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place.

Public LGBT life is extremely constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy, and the island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs, and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to the small population of roughly 15,000 residents. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the source cautions that the situation for locals may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family likewise found gay sex legal through the British decriminalisation order but a muted, not out-and-proud scene, rooted in the imposed colonial legacy rather than local choice.
AIA.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not address document or gender-marker rules for passports and identity documents, entry or visa screening procedures that could expose a trans traveller's status, access to gender-affirming healthcare on the island, or facilities and bathroom rules. These remain unresolved and are not sourced here.

One travel account dates the British decriminalisation order to 2000, while the Associated Press report and other sources give 5 January 2001; the discrepancy is unresolved in the inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime provisions, official protection machinery for trans people, or whether any local enforcement action has tested the constitutional non-discrimination clause as it might apply to gender identity.

MSR.name: Montserrat
MSR.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been legal in Montserrat since 2001. The reform was effected retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. It formed part of a single British decision to scrap anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories, including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, on the stated ground that the laws violated signed international human rights agreements. The order reached Montserrat from London over the objections of local politicians and religious leaders rather than with their consent.

Residual criminal exposure remains and is defined by the sex of the partners. Lesbian activity was never an offence in Montserrat. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for everyone. The age of consent is set at 18 for homosexual activity against 16 for heterosexual activity, so conduct that would be lawful between opposite-sex partners of the same age can be an offence between same-sex partners.

Montserrat's constitutional and statutory framework prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code ban such discrimination, with 'discriminatory' defined as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. As a British Overseas Territory, Montserrat must also comply with international human rights instruments, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Relationship recognition does not extend to same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, stating that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family.

A visitor should expect almost no visible organised LGBT social infrastructure. Montserrat has no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues. Several hotels on the island welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.
MSR.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses legal gender recognition, change of gender markers on passports or identity documents, non-binary recognition, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or hate-crime provisions covering gender identity. Whether Montserrat's constitutional and Labour Code non-discrimination language is applied to gender identity, as distinct from sexual orientation, is not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved.

The inventory does not document enforcement of Article 16 or Article 79, any complaints brought under them, or any recorded incident of violence against a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The description of Montserrat's social scene derives from a single 2012 report and may not reflect the present position; the same applies to the claim that several hotels operate non-discrimination policies, whose terms for trans guests are not specified in the sources.

TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
TCA.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code on single-sex services do not automatically extend to the Turks and Caicos Islands. Local law governs the territory, and United Kingdom measures reach it only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2001, decriminalised through the United Kingdom-led reform programme across the Caribbean, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

The Court of Appeal ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar. Reading "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, the court held that a refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees, while leaving the statutory definition of marriage untouched. The ruling secures residence recognition for same-sex partners of residents; it does not establish a right to marry locally.

Transgender status is handled operationally through United Kingdom document channels rather than through a published local statute. The United Kingdom HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the territory, operational guidance covering nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor holding a United Kingdom passport with a changed gender marker can therefore expect that document to be treated as valid here; the underlying local legal instrument, if any, is not documented in the available sources.

The social climate favours discretion over visibility. A resident account from May 2009 described virtually no public information about gay life in the territory, no visible social scene, and privacy as the everyday norm, attributing this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands and full-citizen Belongers are a demographic minority. A visitor should read that account as dated and impressionistic rather than as a finding on violence risk.
TCA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses trans-specific hate-crime penalties, hate-speech provisions, or any criminal sanction for hostility motivated by gender identity in the Turks and Caicos Islands. That gap is unresolved, not an absence of risk.

The local legal instrument, if any, governing gender recognition on territory-issued documents is not sourced. The available evidence covers United Kingdom passport practice only, and says nothing about a birth certificate, national identity document or local statutory process.

The May 2009 resident account is a single impressionistic account, now more than fifteen years old, and is treated here as context on visibility and discretion rather than as an assessment of current conditions.

Whether a same-sex couple can marry or register a civil partnership within the Turks and Caicos Islands itself is not addressed by the sources; the Court of Appeal expressly left the definition of marriage in the Immigration Ordinance unchanged. The scope of the residence ruling beyond immigration decisions, for example in taxation, hospital visitation or inheritance, is also unresolved.

FLK.name: Falkland Islands
FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with its own Legislative Assembly, which makes law for the territory. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989, and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The sources identify sexual orientation only; no gender-identity ground is stated in the Constitution.

United Kingdom frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, so protection and recognition depend on the territory's own ordinances.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014. There is no self-identification route and no recognition of non-binary status, and holders of a UK Gender Recognition Certificate are recognised in their acquired gender under the CPE Ordinance 2014.

Three ordinances frame the criminal-justice treatment of bias. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 provides for hate-stirring on grounds of sexual orientation, the CPE Ordinance 2014 provides for sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and a Prisons Ordinance was enacted in 2017.
FLK.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not identify a gender-identity ground in the Constitution Order 2008; whether any local statute or ordinance supplies equivalent protection on that ground is unresolved in this inventory.

No sourced enforcement data exists here for the Crimes Ordinance 2014 hate-stirring provision or the CPE Ordinance 2014 aggravating-factor provision: no prosecutions, sentences or reported incidents are documented in the inventory.

The Prisons Ordinance 2017 is cited by name only; its treatment of trans detainees, including placement and healthcare, is not specified in the sources.

Nothing in the inventory addresses trans-specific healthcare access, gender-marker treatment at ports of entry, or facilities access on the Islands.

For South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands, only the absence of same-sex marriage is sourced; the remainder of that dependency's legal position for trans visitors is unresolved.

SHN.name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
SHN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Local law governs the territory, and those United Kingdom measures can apply only by Order in Council.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha.

The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.

Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0; it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 and commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017.

The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, with applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights recorded on that basis.

PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands stand under the United Kingdom's framework: defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures such as the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not apply here of their own force. Local law governs, and those measures could reach Pitcairn only by Order in Council. Military service is likewise a United Kingdom responsibility rather than a local one.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that guarantee has been in force since 2010.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. The Island Council approved the ordinance unanimously on 1 April 2015; Governor Jonathan Sinclair signed it on 5 May 2015 and it was published on 13 May 2015.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn. Adoption has been legal since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.

None of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship.
PCN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, marker changes on documents, screening or medical gatekeeping, or access to gender-affirming care in the Pitcairn Islands; the position on these matters is unresolved on the present record.

No source addresses hate-crime provisions, enforcement of the constitutional non-discrimination guarantee, or any documented incident of violence against trans or gender-nonconforming people; these remain not sourced.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for visitors are not covered by the inventory and are unresolved here.

GGY.name: Guernsey
GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Guernsey's criminal law has decriminalised same-sex sexual activity since before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom. The male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. The island nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law permits only the issue of a new birth certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document.

On 10 December 2015 the States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018. Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil-partnership legislation of its own, though United Kingdom civil partnerships have been recognised for succession purposes since 2 April 2012.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting; the States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay andbisexual men eligible after a twelve-month deferral from around 7 November 2011, ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era. Other donation restrictions were unchanged.

Discrimination protections were built up in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, by 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations. It took effect on 1 October 2023.
GGY.outOfScopeNotes:
No recorded rule governs whether Les Nicolles houses prisoners by birth sex or gender identity, and no source documents a separate unit, solitary confinement, or segregation practice for transgender prisoners there. This is an absence in the available material, not a finding of safety or of risk.

No source in this inventory addresses access to gender-affirming healthcare on the island, waiting times, or referral pathways to the United Kingdom.

No source documents hate-crime reporting rates, police recording practice, or prosecutions with a transgender victim in Guernsey.

Whether the residual offence on non-private homosexual conduct has been used in prosecution, or remains a dead-letter provision, is not sourced here.

The practical application of the 2023 anti-discrimination regime to gender identity in services beyond employment is not evidenced in this inventory.

IMN.name: Isle of Man
IMN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Isle of Man. Local law governs, with United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency whose parliament, Tynwald, frames these questions through its own bills. The Legislative Council's proceedings of 26 April 2016 record the Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016, which is the primary legislative record of the island's marriage-equality debate.

Same-sex marriage took effect on the island after Royal Assent of the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act, reported on 28 July 2016. The first conversion of a civil partnership into a marriage was completed within days of entry into force; civil partnerships, legal since 2011, convert without a second ceremony, which indicates a routine registration process rather than discretionary approval.

Employment protection preceded that debate by a decade. On 30 November 2005 the House of Keys adopted an amendment to the Employment Bill, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, barring dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligning the island with United Kingdom human-rights law.

The legislative sequence also had explicit political sponsorship. On 9 June 2015 Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, a commitment that preceded the 2016 Act.

Nothing in this inventory documents a gender-recognition procedure, identity-document marker rules, entry or visa screening that could disclose a trans visitor's status, hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, or facility access rules. Visitors should treat those questions as not evidenced here rather than as absent from Manx law.
IMN.outOfScopeNotes:
Prison housing is unresolved for trans people. The island's only functioning prison operates separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders, vulnerable prisoners and a segregation unit, but the available material documents no birth-sex-versus-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit, and no trans-specific solitary or segregation practice. No finding on the prison-housing axis can be drawn from this inventory.

No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, the process for changing sex markers on passports or driving licences, or whether a foreign gender-change certificate is accepted locally. Those questions are not sourced here.

Entry, border and visa screening procedures that could expose a trans visitor's documents, and any hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, are likewise not sourced in this inventory; their absence from these findings does not establish their absence in law.

GUF.name: French Guiana
GUF.summary:
French Guiana is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework. Identity documents, the criminal code, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here exactly as in metropolitan France, and there is no separate local legislation on gender identity.

Legal gender recognition has been available on a simplified administrative basis since 2017. The procedure is a declaration before a civil-status officer; no surgery, sterilisation or psychiatric diagnosis is required. A trans person living in French Guiana therefore uses the same prefectural and tribunal machinery as one in Bordeaux.

Nothing in French law criminalises trans status or gender expression. The anti-discrimination statute has covered gender identity since 2012, and hate-crime sentencing enhancement provisions were added in 2017. Same-sex relations and same-sex marriage are legal under the same French law, and Pride events are held in the territory.

The most serious documented risk is custodial. Reporting from January 2018 found that trans women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender occupy a legal gray area, with placement decided case by case and little consistent protection; that practice governs French Guiana's prisons. The French national body responsible for places of deprivation of liberty issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations in the treatment of transgender detainees persist across French places of detention, a finding that extends to the territory.

Access to specialised transgender healthcare is limited by French Guiana's remoteness from mainland treatment centres, which adds travel cost and delay to any medical step in transition. Socially, transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility and make reporting of abuse less likely, including reporting to police.

The visible scene is small and anchored in Cayenne, with no venues listed by the main travel guides. One LGBTQ+ travel guide rates the territory 'Very Safe for LGBTQ+', an assessment grounded in formal legality rather than in the detention and healthcare gaps described above.
GUF.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory gives French Guiana-specific figures on transgender detainees, on placement decisions in the territory's prisons, or on recorded offences against trans people. The detention material is national in scope and is applied here by jurisdiction, not by local measurement.

No named incident of violence against a trans person in French Guiana appears in these sources, and the absence is a gap in the record rather than evidence that none has occurred.

One country guide covering LGBTQIA+ data for the territory yielded no specific figures on equality indexing or gender-identity recognition that could be quoted here; a second guide produced no usable finding on trans visitor safety. Both remain unquantified.

The 'Very Safe for LGBTQ+' rating is a travel-guide assessment with no published methodology; how it treats detention risk and healthcare access is unresolved.
