GLP.name: Guadeloupe
GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe stands under the national framework of France. The French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply in the territory as they do in the metropole. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the 1810 Code, though public morality provisions were subsequently used against LGBTQ people. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Legal gender recognition follows the simplified French procedure, available since 1 January 2017 under a law signed on 18 November 2016. Surgery and medical diagnosis are not required, and both self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were dropped from the final bill. A change of first name is handled at the registry office; a change of the gender marker still requires an appearance before a court. In 2017 the Court of Cassation rejected a bid to have the law recognise a neutral sex classification.

Conversion therapy was banned in a statute that passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and a fine of up to €30,000. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, a serving member of parliament, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006; the Court of Cassation later cancelled that conviction. Civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders argued that the 2004 statute seriously infringes free speech.

Parental recognition has shifted in the trans-related families case law of the French courts. The Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father; the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised; and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change.

Detention carries documented risk. In French prisons, whose rules apply in Guadeloupe, placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not match gender presentation; in practice, assignment weighs the person's best interests through individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings. The CGLPL, France's oversight body for places of deprivation of liberty, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010.

Guadeloupe has its first LGBT+ centre. The Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion opened on 24 April 2024, run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations, and offers reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities. The visit of the minister Aurore Bergé for the opening was accompanied by announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted to overseas territories.
GLP.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Senate has voted on the March 2024 compensation bill for men arrested before 1980 is unresolved in the sources, as is any movement on the under-18 transition bill after 23 July 2024.

No source in this inventory reports Guadeloupe-specific enforcement data: there are no figures on prosecutions under the 2004 hate-speech law, the conversion therapy ban or the anti-discrimination statute as applied in the territory, and no territory-level breakdown of the CGLPL's roughly 40 detention referrals since 2010. Whether the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion is resourced on a permanent footing beyond the announced ministerial measures is not sourced.

Entry and visa requirements, customs screening and any territory-specific document checks are not covered by this inventory. The treatment of trans passengers on flights to and from Guadeloupe, and any local practice on identity document presentation at the border, remain not sourced here.

sources.summary: French law applicable in Guadeloupe decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained this in the 1810 Code, while public morality laws continued to be used against LGBTQ people; in Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. The law of December 2004, passed 31 December 2004, made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. It created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, about 10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities. Transgender people have changed legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but must still appear before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change, while a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness, removing gender identity disorder by decree, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

MTQ.name: Martinique
MTQ.summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815, the 2013 marriage-equality law applies, and gender-marker change is available through the simplified judicial route introduced by the 2016-17 reforms.

Discrimination protection rests on several instruments that reach the island directly. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. No Martinique-specific enforcement or litigation record for these provisions is documented in the sources available for this entry.

Hostile public speech is a criminal offence. A National Assembly amendment approved on 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comment illegal, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and up to 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 press-freedom law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. The first conviction under the provision, of MP Christian Vanneste in January 2006, was cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Penalties for physical assault or murder rise where the offence is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has operated as an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison.

Legal gender recognition operates on the island under the regime effective since 1 January 2017: no surgery and no medical diagnosis are required, but an application must still be made to a court to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be handled at the registry office. The bill was signed on 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly; the Constitutional Council ruled it constitutional on 17 November 2016 while dropping the original self-certification provision. Before that reform, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France.

Prison is the sharpest documented risk for trans visitors. Under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, placement follows the gender marker on the detainee's identity documents rather than anatomy, which puts most trans women into all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'). The department's establishments operate under this same framework. France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, found on 25 May 2021 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse; its recommendations cover placement, isolation, safety and staff training.

Healthcare is covered but uneven. Gender-affirming treatment is reimbursed by the Sécurité Sociale under the long-term-illness scheme ALD 31, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report nonetheless documented significant problems, including extended waiting times and access that varies with location. Trans youth care is contested nationally: a report commissioned in March 2024 by centre-right Republican senators fed legislation to ban medical transition under 18, which passed the Senate in May 2024, was opposed by the Macron government and has had no recorded movement since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine has characterised the rise in people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access.

Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published on 1 February 2022. Recorded anti-LGB(T) violence rose nationally by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018, according to a report released on 16 May 2020. Community infrastructure exists on the island: JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, with events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025, and the Rights in Exile (AsyLex) resource page lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts for the department.
MTQ.outOfScopeNotes:
Several points remain unresolved in the sources assembled for this entry. There is no Martinique-specific data on how the gender-marker court route is applied on the island, including filing costs, hearing schedules or refusal rates; the 2016-17 reform is documented at national level only.

The CGLPL findings on transgender detainees rest on referrals and inspections conducted at mainland establishments (Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Whether its recommendations have been implemented at the department's own prisons is not sourced here, and the departmental prison population figures for trans detainees are not documented.

Enforcement figures for the 2004 hate-speech offence and for homophobic and transphobic aggravated penalties are national; no island breakdown appears in the record. The 36% rise in recorded attacks and insults is a national 2019 statistic and cannot be attributed to Martinique.

The status of the under-18 medical-transition bill after 23 July 2024 is unresolved in the sources, as is any local waiting-time or access data for gender-affirming care in Martinique beyond the national ALD 31 coverage position.

REU.name: Réunion
REU.summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the metropolitan statute adopted in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, which made transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The provision is in force in Réunion.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. The government's three sub-amendments could limit the scope of that section.

Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. The placement rule is the framework that governs detainees in Réunion.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.
REU.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports on conditions for transgender detainees held in Réunion's own detention facilities. The CGLPL opinion is a national document and the Lille case is a mainland facility; conditions specific to Réunion are unresolved.

Whether the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282 has since been amended, narrowed by the three sub-amendments or supplemented by later legislation is not sourced here. The 2016 text is stated as adopted; its current wording after subsequent revisions is unverified.

No prosecution figures, sentence outcomes or case law applying article L225-1 to transphobic conduct in Réunion are available in the inventory. Enforcement in practice is not documented.

Whether French authorities now make placement decisions for transgender detainees case by case rather than strictly by identity-document sex is not resolved. Article D248 is stated as the governing rule and the CGLPL opinion documents violations, but no post-2021 guidance is sourced.

The inventory does not distinguish between a free-standing hate-crime enhancement for transphobic offences and the discrimination ground in article L225-1; any separate aggravated-sentencing provision is not sourced.

MYT.name: Mayotte
MYT.summary:
Mayotte stands under the national framework of France. Identity-document rules, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules governing places of deprivation of liberty apply on the island as French law, and the French prison framework binds Mayotte's establishments as French prisons.

Nothing in that framework criminalises trans people or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been lawful on the island since the 1975 vote to remain within the Republic, and Mayotte is one of few jurisdictions in Africa and in the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document rather than anatomy, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Reporting of 12 January 2018 documents that trans women incarcerated in France are accordingly held in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, and the French prison framework extends to local jails as French establishments.

France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL concluded in an opinion of 25 May 2021 that there is a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. That assessment rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections that interviewed eight trans women and one trans man at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse; the establishments it covers include those on Mayotte.

The simplification of legal gender change voted by the French National Assembly is French law and therefore applies on Mayotte, giving trans residents access to the simplified civil-status procedure.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A report of 23 May 2023 describes a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner, pseudonym Abdallah, completing a long and complicated path before marrying at Sada Town Hall, in a predominantly Muslim society where the rights the law confers are not matched by social acceptance.

NCL.name: New Caledonia
NCL.summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while the territory legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are therefore French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.

Sexual identity became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment legislation of 2012, which enabled prosecution of discrimination and of transphobia as discrimination; the provision was amended in 2016 to read gender identity. As French law, the provision reaches New Caledonia.

Placement of detainees follows the legal gender marker rather than anatomy: Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code assigns incarcerated trans people according to their recorded sex, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees (BuzzFeed News, 12 January 2018). The French prison framework governs the collectivity's establishments in the same way.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. Because French law applies here, the opinion extends to establishments in New Caledonia.
NCL.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records an instance of the gender-identity discrimination provision being invoked in New Caledonia, and no enforcement or prosecution data for the territory is available here.

Whether any detainee in New Caledonia has been placed according to the Article D248 rule, and how local facilities house trans detainees, is unresolved: the sources describe the French framework and mainland practice only.

There is no sourced information here on hate-crime sentencing enhancement as applied in the collectivity, on procedures for changing gender markers on identity documents, or on access to gender-affirming care for residents and visitors.

PYF.name: French Polynesia
PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France. French law governs matters of justice and civil status, so gender recognition, criminal procedure and the anti-discrimination framework that a trans visitor encounters are set by Paris, while the territorial institutions in Papeete administer daily life, health policy and policing resources.

Detention follows the gender marked on an identity document, and Article D248 of the French Code of criminal procedure requires separate men's and women's establishments. A trans woman holding a male marker is therefore held with men. BuzzFeed News, reporting on the situation in France in January 2018, treated this as a legal grey area rather than a settled outcome. France's Law 2016-1547 removed the requirement of medical transition or surgery for a legal change of civil-status gender, but no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly. The CGLPL, the national preventive mechanism for places of deprivation of liberty, concluded in an opinion of 25 May 2021 that serious violations against transgender detainees persist across French detention, a treatment that reaches the prisons of French Polynesia.

France's Penal Code has carried gender identity as a protected ground since 18 November 2016, when it replaced the earlier wording of sexual identity in article 225-1, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by imprisonment. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks during 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties.

The conversion-therapy ban passed the French Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022. The Académie Nationale de Médecine has described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an epidemic-like phenomenon and a primarily social problem, and a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a health scandal and youth transness a social contagion. A bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, with no National Assembly action recorded since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.

Access to transition-related care inside French Polynesia is constrained by limited local expertise. Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua's government tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment, progesterone and testosterone, on the same basis as mainland France, but after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. Some trans people, referred to locally as raerae, encounter family rejection and move to mainland France for specialised services.

The social environment is markedly more open than the legislative record suggests. The mahu is a traditional Polynesian social role in which a person embodies both male and female qualities and holds cultural standing, and mahu and rae-rae are visible in daily life across the 118 islands. OutTraveler, writing on 4 July 2025, described inclusivity as ingrained enough that Pride displays are absent, with a visiting couple reporting mainstream acceptance and no Pride flags.

Partner recognition follows the French civil-status framework: civil solidarity pacts date from 1999, same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, and assisted reproduction was extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Since March 2019 French higher education institutions are expected to use trans students' preferred names, a provision that governs the territorial university in Papeete as well.
PYF.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 has been applied to, or cited in, any specific inspection of a prison in French Polynesia is not sourced here; the inventory establishes only that the French framework is applicable in the territory's prisons. The BuzzFeed News treatment of Article D248 as a legal grey area is a characterisation made in January 2018 and no later French court ruling resolving it is present in the inventory.

Whether the Senate bill banning medical transition under 18 advanced after 23 July 2024 is unresolved, as is the current status of the March 2024 compensation bill for men arrested under the repealed 1960 indecent-exposure clause, for which the Senate had not voted as of the inventory.

Several items in the source coverage concern France nationally with no stated bearing on French Polynesia and should be read as background rather than territorial findings: the repeal of sodomy provisions by the Penal Code of 1791 and the silence retained by the Penal Code of 1810; the indecent-exposure clause of article 330, second alinea, inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment and repealed in 1980; the statute of 6 August 1942 setting consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982; and the internment of LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine after 1940. The conversion-therapy helpline estimate and the 2014 overseas-versus-metropolitan attitude figures derive from mainland or aggregated French data, and the Mayotte findings concern a different overseas collectivity.

The inventory contains no entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to trans travellers, no data on documentation changes at Papeete's airport, and no trans-specific violence statistics recorded inside French Polynesia itself. The Out Adventures source carries no trans-specific finding and was excluded on that basis. The hostile language attributed to the Académie Nationale de Médecine and to the commissioned March 2024 report is documented as French debate and no source in the inventory shows territorial officials adopting it.

The national penal code has carried gender identity as a protected ground since 18 November 2016, when it replaced the earlier wording of sexual identity in article 225-1, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by imprisonment. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks during 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties.

The conversion-therapy ban passed the national upper house on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022. The national academy of medicine has described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an epidemic-like phenomenon and a primarily social problem, and a March 2024 report commissioned from a national research institute called gender-affirming care a health scandal and youth transness a social contagion. A bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the upper house in May 2024, with no lower-house action recorded since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from a national paediatric endocrinology society recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.

Access to transition-related care inside the state/province is constrained by limited local expertise. The deputy head of the state/province government tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment, progesterone and testosterone, on the same basis as the parent nation, but after heated debate in the state/province legislature the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. Some trans people, referred to locally as raerae, encounter family rejection and move to the parent nation for specialised services.

The social environment is markedly more open than the legislative record suggests. The mahu is a traditional Polynesian social role in which a person embodies both male and female qualities and holds cultural standing, and mahu and rae-rae are visible in daily life across the 118 state/provinces. A travel publication writing on 4 July 2025 described inclusivity as ingrained enough that Pride displays are absent, with a visiting couple reporting mainstream acceptance and no Pride flags.

Partner recognition follows the parent nation's civil-status framework: civil solidarity pacts date from 1999, same-sex marriage passed the national lower house 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, and assisted reproduction was extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Since March 2019 national higher education institutions are expected to use trans students' preferred names, a provision that governs the state/province university in the capital as well.

Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, and the Labour Code covers sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training.

In 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France, and Mayotte, another overseas collectivity, reports frequent family rejection and discrimination. Le Refuge estimated that 3-4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy.

WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna
WLF.summary:
Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic and stands under the French national framework: the civil and criminal codes of France apply locally unless a local measure overrides them. No law in force criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since the 2012 statutory extension covering employment, housing and access to services.

Legal gender-marker change is available on the basis of the 2016-17 French reforms, which removed the requirement for surgery or a psychiatric diagnosis. A trans visitor whose documents already reflect their lived gender can present them without entering a separate local procedure. French law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained.

Nothing in the sources indicates trans-specific screening at entry or in local administrative processing. Practical exposure to harm is concentrated in two areas: detention and everyday social conditions. Under the French prison framework that applies here, trans women whose legal gender is marked male, largely those without reassignment surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a situation described in reporting as a documented legal grey area; one such transfer to a men's facility in Lille took place in 2014.

BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies.

Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is delivered in a jurisdiction of about 8 square miles and roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against Saint Barthélemy in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access; prescriptions and ongoing treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. French prison administration policy recognises only biological sex for placement, and trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex; a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention.

Socially the territory is discreet rather than permissive: it has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene, same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low and no hostility toward gay or trans visitors is noted in the sources.

No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted for the territory, so the practical guidance in the sources rests on general reporting about the French system and on travel-writing accounts of the island's social climate rather than on trans visitors' own accounts.

ABW.name: Aruba
ABW.summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and applies its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, as the instrument carrying its anti-discrimination provisions. Decisions of its Appeals Court in sexual-orientation cases have been reviewed by the Supreme Court of the Netherlands, which on 12 July 2024 upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Aruba for both male and female forms. The age of consent is 16 and is equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision.

Parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples on 8 September 2016 by 11 votes to 5, an Associated Press report of 9 September 2016 recording the same margin with four abstentions. The amendment extended civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions and conferred spousal pension rights and emergency medical decision rights. Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. Same-sex marriage itself was established by the 12 July 2024 Supreme Court ruling.

Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge. The Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.

Several gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly.
ABW.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses gender markers or identity-document rules, entry and visa requirements, border screening, healthcare access, hate-crime sentence enhancement, or facility and restroom rules. Whether any other Aruban or Kingdom-level instrument covers gender identity and gender expression is unresolved, since the Criminal Code grounds cover sexual orientation only.

The age of consent of 16 is the only youth-specific legal threshold supplied by the sources; findings on schools, education, or minors' access to services and documentation are not sourced here.

The 2016 vote is reported as 11 to 5 in one account and as 11 to 5 with four abstentions in another; the discrepancy is unresolved.

The tourism board's safety claims are the destination's own marketing copy and are not independent verification of conditions on the ground.

Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

sources.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Aruba for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold given; the text contains no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation. The Aruba Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including 'heterosexual or homosexual orientation'. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed. On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba.

Aruba is frequently called one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands. Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. CUW.name: Curaçao
CUW.summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here, and holds full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. The agreement commits the Kingdom's governments to equal treatment; it does not establish an immediately enforceable right that a visitor can invoke at a border or in a local court.

Senior Curaçao officials have publicly endorsed equal treatment. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano backed "equal rights for everyone" in the local press.

Enforcement practice has not consistently followed that rhetoric. Winifred Raveneau, a Pueblo Soberano party colleague of Wiels, opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. The episode indicates that public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.
CUW.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no trans-specific material. Nothing is sourced on legal gender recognition or marker-change procedures for Curaçao identity documents, on whether a visitor's home-country documents are accepted as presented, or on any screening at Queen Beatrix International Airport that could expose a trans traveller's status.

No statutory penalties are sourced for conduct criminalised under Netherlands criminal law as extended to Curaçao, nor is there sourced text on hate-crime enhancement, anti-discrimination complaint machinery, or access to gender-related healthcare for visitors or residents. Whether the rights package delivered to ministers in The Hague produced enacted Curaçao legislation after April 2015 is unresolved on this inventory.

The substantive reporting available dates from 2015 to 2017. Current enforcement conditions, the present status of permitting for public LGBT events, and any post-2017 violence or legal developments are not sourced here.

BES.name: Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba)
BES.summary:
Caribbean Netherlands comprises Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law on civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination extends to the islands, and the statutory framework operating in the European Netherlands applies here in the same form.

That protection covers visitors as well as residents. Travel-facing coverage of the region treats Bonaire as a destination where strict anti-discrimination statutes stand behind an equality-friendly welcome, and the island markets itself on that basis.

Same-sex unions have been registrable since 4 December 2012, when the Census Office in Saba recorded the Caribbean Netherlands' first: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on the island; both were visiting, which establishes a local record of performing same-sex unions for people who are only passing through.

Ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry. The official weddings page of Saba Tourism identifies the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony and documents registrar Julieta Woods as flexible with couples' wishes, alongside a full destination-wedding supply chain of caterers, florists and accommodation. No source in the current inventory addresses gender-marker rules on identity documents, entry screening practice, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and harassment exposure for trans visitors specifically; the findings above rest on marriage and anti-discrimination provisions rather than trans-specific legal text.
BES.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the current inventory: whether the Netherlands' rules on amending gender markers on passports and identity cards apply unchanged to residents of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, and whether Dutch travel documents reflecting a gender change are accepted without questioning at local entry points.

Unresolved: local availability and cost of gender-affirming healthcare, including whether hormone therapy can be prescribed or continued on-island or requires referral to the Netherlands. No sourced reporting on documented violence against trans visitors, on police handling of complaints, or on public facilities access for trans people was available for this pass.

FRO.name: Faroe Islands
FRO.summary:
The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Denmark's national criminal law and document rules extend to the territory; equality and family law are made locally beneath that framework.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when decriminalisation took effect across the Kingdom of Denmark. The territory set its age of consent for male same-sex relations at 18 and did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988.

Same-sex marriage was legalised in 2017, later than any other Nordic jurisdiction, after open friction between church and state.

The territory's anti-discrimination statute took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. The only criminal penalties in force that touch sexual-orientation hostility sit in that statute: anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or to imprisonment for up to two years.

Before that date a visitor or resident had no statutory recourse. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered roughly 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000 demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with neighbouring Nordic jurisdictions; the territory had neither at that date.

Violence against openly gay people was documented and, at the time, legally unaddressed. In 2006 the singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression aggravated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically attacking them in Tórshavn; the group had not been assaulted anywhere else on its tour.

Religiously motivated opposition remains prominent in Faroese public life. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic Prime Minister Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion. In July 2015 he demanded that Pride be banned, the event falling two days before the national holiday, and he has repeatedly compared the local LGBT organisation to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and urged that the Tórshavn parade be moved out of the town centre; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.
FRO.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address gender recognition, legal document or identity-marker changes for trans people, whether issued by the Faroe Islands or by Denmark, beyond the general statement that Denmark's national document rules extend here. Which specific authority a Faroese-issued document carries, and what a Danish passport issued to a resident shows, is unresolved in this record.

No sourced material covers restroom or facility access, healthcare provision or bans on care, entry and visa screening, or port-of-entry examination of gender presentation.

No data is available on the number of complaints, charges or convictions under the anti-discrimination provision that took effect on 1 January 2007, so its practical enforcement cannot be assessed from these sources.

The extent to which Danish hate-crime sentencing provisions, as distinct from the Faroese statement offence, apply in the territory is not resolved here, nor is partner, next-of-kin or inheritance recognition beyond the 2017 marriage law.

GRL.name: Greenland
GRL.summary:
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts handling domestic affairs. Danish legislation on marriage and on official identity documents has been adopted and applies here, so a visitor's legal position on those questions follows the Danish framework as received in Greenland.

The sources record no criminal penalty for same-sex relations. Since 2010 Article 100 of the Criminal Code has prohibited speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other protected categories, and the Code provides penalty enhancement for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. No reported cases of prosecution under these provisions appear in the inventory.

Same-sex marriage has been in effect since 1 April 2016, adopted from a Danish bill passed unanimously on two occasions after the first lapsed through elections. It replaced the registered partnership regime that had run from 1 July 1996 until that date, and the bishop of the established church supported the change.

Legal gender recognition operates on a self-determination basis. A law passed by decree in 2016 allows the sex designation on official identity documents to be changed without sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or a medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18, state that they want the change to their documentation, and observe a six-month reflection period before the request is confirmed. Greenlandic passports are available with an "X" sex descriptor alongside male and female.

Parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, in force from 1 July 2024, prohibiting discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics. The law establishes an Equal Treatment Board to handle discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination.

Public expression carries little risk on the record assembled here. Sources describe gay life as low-key, integrated and non-violent, with the first pride parade held in Nuuk on 15 May 2010 attended by about 1,000 people and a modest annual march since. There is virtually no organised gay scene, attributed to the small and scattered population, though some nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd.
GRL.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no reported prosecutions under Article 100 of the Criminal Code or under the hate-crime penalty enhancement, so their enforcement record is unresolved rather than established as unused.

Whether the "X" passport descriptor is accepted by foreign border authorities is not sourced here; the sources establish only that Greenlandic passports can be issued with it.

No source in the inventory addresses入境 or visa screening, entry refusals, or treatment of trans travellers by customs or immigration officials in Greenland, and none addresses access to transition-related healthcare for visitors.

The 2024 equal-treatment law took effect on 1 July 2024 and the sources give no case outcomes under it, so its practical operation is unverified.

No source documents violence against transgender people in Greenland, or the treatment of trans people in detention, policing or asylum procedures.

PRI.name: Puerto Rico
PRI.summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening at Puerto Rico's airports follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched. Prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary equipment rather than liquids: they are exempt from the three-liquid rule and are allowed through the checkpoint after screening. Guidance for trans travellers advises packing strategies that reduce the likelihood of invasive searches.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for that care, and set penalties of up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of medical licences for doctors who violate the ban. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The care law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment, but the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage remains partial. The 2013 law that passed (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered by it. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Under Executive Order 14168, which directs United States federal agencies to recognise only two sexes, the Bureau of Prisons houses transgender inmates by sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity, a rule that governs any federal custody in Puerto Rico. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment.
PRI.outOfScopeNotes:
No Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy on transgender-inmate housing, no special unit, and no judicial ruling on the point was located in the sources; the custody picture rests entirely on the federal order and on ACLU reporting.

The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced a legal challenge to the July 2025 care ban, but no filed case, ruling or injunction appears in the inventory, so the ban's litigation status is unresolved.

Restroom and facility access for trans people, and the procedure and fees for changing gender markers on Puerto Rico-issued identity documents, are not addressed by any source here; the document picture is limited to the federal travel-document position.

Whether the under-21 care ban applies to adults aged 18 to 20 who are visiting rather than residing in Puerto Rico is not stated in the sources reviewed, as is enforcement practice against non-residents.

Texas ruling in 2003 struck down state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

LGBT rights groups in Puerto Rico have repeatedly defeated religious-freedom pairings with conversion-therapy measures, and marriage equality reached the territory through federal rather than local litigation, the pattern by which several protections described here arrived.

Departmental campaigns against trans-affirming care are part of the enacted text.

Conversion-therapy regulation has been repeatedly blocked. In March 2019 the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors, despite Senate passage and governor support; Senator Zoe Laboy, a co-sponsor, publicly dissented. In April 2019 Governor Rossello announced a pairing of SB1253, framed as clarifying religious freedom principles, with SB1254, a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy; LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open doors to discrimination, arguing the religious-freedom carve-out licensed refusal of service on orientation and gender-identity grounds. GUM.name: Guam
GUM.summary:
Guam stands under the full United States federal framework as an unincorporated US territory. United States passports and other federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X gender marker was eliminated by a January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Screening at Guam's airport follows Transport Security Administration procedure, which applies in Guam as a US territory. The agency's body-scanner and pat-down protocols can disclose a trans traveller's status to officers. Travellers may request an alternative screening method and escalate problems on the spot, and most trans travellers pass screening without incident.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Guam, so access to that care during a visit can be constrained by federal policy rather than local practice.

A separate January 2025 executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly and directs the Secretary of Defense to submit an implementation plan within 30 days; the order frames trans identity as "radical gender ideology." It applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent United States military presence, and signals the federal posture a visitor can expect from official institutions on the island.

On partner recognition, Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage was struck down in June 2015, and the territory became the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage.
GUM.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not resolve whether Guam's local statutes provide hate-crime enhancement for offences motivated by gender identity, or whether any local non-discrimination ordinance covers gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. Those questions are not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses Guam-specific rules for changing a gender marker on a local birth certificate or driver's licence, nor whether a local facility policy governs restroom access; the federal document position is sourced, the local one is not.

Two listed sources, a Pacific sexual-identity research guide and a document-guide page for Guam, yielded no usable finding for this record, so they neither support nor contradict the claims above.

Enforcement practice at the airport is described only in general terms by a national know-your-rights guide; no Guam-specific complaint data or incident record is available in the inventory.

VIR.name: U.S. Virgin Islands
VIR.summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework sets what a trans visitor faces at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Airport screening follows federal procedure. Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and trigger secondary screening and pat-downs; travellers may request alternative screening and may decline the scanner. The agency's own know-your-rights guidance covers U.S. nationals travelling to and from the territory on the same terms as mainland travellers, including what may and may not be carried in hand baggage under the federal screening framework.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

Territorial law provides an additional layer of protection. The U.S. Virgin Islands human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending the protection explicitly into the education setting.

Relationship and marital status are settled. In 2015 the Superior Court of the U.S. Virgin Islands struck down the refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional, and later federal recognition settled the question nationwide; a married couple can rely on their marriage in the territory. The historic sodomy statute applied to the territory since 1957 has been replaced and is no longer in force.
VIR.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the U.S. Virgin Islands issues any territorial identity or driver-licence document carrying a gender marker that differs from the federal standard is not sourced here and remains unresolved; the sources reviewed address federal passports only.

The enforcement record of the territorial anti-discrimination law, including how complaints by transgender residents and visitors have been handled since the 2017 Attorney General interpretation, is not documented in the sources reviewed and remains unresolved.

Territorial health-insurance and Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming care, separate from the federal funding restrictions, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The practical implementation of the January 2025 federal funding order at named institutions in the territory, and whether any territorial programme fills resulting gaps, is not documented in the sources reviewed and remains unresolved.

The current wording of the territorial sodomy statute as replaced, and whether consent-in-private conduct is fully protected, is not reproduced in the sources reviewed and remains unresolved.

ASM.name: American Samoa
ASM.summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applicants. The policy is challenged in federal courts, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; trans and nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad.

Same-sex marriage remains formally contested in the territory. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it. In 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory whose attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it. In January 2016 a district court judge confirmed by the Senate told legislators he had not read Obergefell and that the district court did not deal with the ruling. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date; the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar, then the United States Department of the Interior. As of mid-2024 the local ban was still treated on-island as operative, with its constitutional durability an open question under academic study.

Trans-specific violence and protection machinery are documented. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case against the American Samoa Government over harassment of a transgender employee; a June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity; and in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local cultural context shapes daily expectations. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, frames fa'afafine as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture; reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and homosexuality is widely accepted within Samoan culture compared with neighbouring Pacific states.
ASM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Obergefell is operative in American Samoa is unresolved in practice: a 2026 law review article by local practitioners concludes it applies and that a marriage certificate would have to be issued, but no same-sex couple has applied to date and no territorial court has ruled. The on-island constitutional durability of the local ban was still an open research question as of mid-2024.

The scope of federal executive orders on sex classification as applied to territorial government facilities, territorial funding streams, and territorial schools is not sourced in this inventory; only the federal-agency channel of reach is documented.

Enforcement patterns for the passport and document rules among travelers departing from or arriving in Pago Pago specifically are not sourced; the reported confiscations and blocked applications are national-level reports.

The outcome of the February 2023 sexual-abuse charge involving a 16-year-old transgender teen is not sourced beyond the charge itself.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.summary: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

USA TODAY (7 Mar 2025): Trump executive order requires all US identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; ACLU sued the State Department for seven plaintiffs; trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

Lambda Legal's FAQ sets out passport and identity-document rules for TGNCNBI people under the current federal policy change: which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the current status of document updates.
