ASM.blindSummary:
The country is an unincorporated country of the parent nation and stands under the full national entry-and-documents regime. National executive orders reach the country through national agencies: an executive order on binary sex classification in documents, national facilities and care funding; a second executive order on gender-affirming care funding; and a third on athletic participation, the last paired with a foreign-ministry visa restriction carrying an internal marking.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all national identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The foreign ministry has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applicants. The policy is challenged in national courts, and a civil-liberties union has sued the foreign ministry on behalf of seven plaintiffs; trans and nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad.

Same-sex marriage remains formally contested in the country. The national legislature voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after a House judiciary committee recommended killing it. In 2015 the country was the only one under the parent nation whose national justice department said applicability of the national marriage ruling was still under review, while several other state/provinces moved to apply it. In January 2016 a district court judge confirmed by the Senate told legislators he had not read the national high court's marriage decision and that the district court did not deal with the ruling. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in the country concludes that the ruling does apply and that the country would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date; the litigation path runs through the country's High Court against the national registrar, then the national interior department. As of mid-2024 the local ban was still treated in the country as operative, with its constitutional durability an open question under academic study.

Trans-specific violence and protection machinery are documented. In September 2023 the national justice department settled an employment-discrimination case against the national government over harassment of a transgender employee; a June 2023 national civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the national government over her gender identity; and in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local cultural context shapes daily expectations. The country's fa'afafine association, formed in 2010, frames fa'afafine as a recognised and integral part of traditional local culture; reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and homosexuality is widely accepted within the local culture compared with neighbouring jurisdictions in the region.
ASM.blindOutOfScope:
Whether the 2015 national marriage ruling is operative in the country is unresolved in practice: a 2026 law review article by local practitioners concludes it applies and that a marriage certificate would have to be issued, but no same-sex couple has applied to date and no national court has ruled. The in-country constitutional durability of the local ban was still an open research question as of mid-2024.

The scope of national executive orders on sex classification as applied to national government facilities, national funding streams, and national schools is not sourced in this inventory; only the national-agency channel of reach is documented.

Enforcement patterns for the passport and document rules among travelers departing from or arriving in the country's main port specifically are not sourced; the reported confiscations and blocked applications are national-level reports.

The outcome of the February 2023 sexual-abuse charge involving a 16-year-old transgender teen is not sourced beyond the charge itself.

MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
MNP.summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth and stands under the national framework of the United States for travel documents, immigration and airport screening. United States passports and entry documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker option was eliminated by the January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents presents a gender marker that may not match presentation at the port of entry.

Screening at the airport follows federal procedure, and the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to such care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges; the first same-sex marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015.

Commonwealth law provides for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes: CNMI Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal commonwealth-level protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence.

Legal gender change is permitted in the Northern Mariana Islands provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process, which means identity documents can be brought into line with presentation, subject to that medical requirement.

Wider protection remains thin. As of 27 September 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scored the territory's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a Negative gender-identity score. There is no comprehensive commonwealth nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity; recourse beyond federal EEOC complaint channels is limited, and commonwealth-level protections extend to government employees only.
MNP.outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced: whether territory-issued identity documents, such as driver's licences, permit a gender-marker change independently of the federal passport process, or what evidentiary standard the specified medical process requires in practice.

Not sourced: any enforcement record for the enhanced-sentencing provisions of Public Law 22-32, including whether a gender-identity-motivated offence has been charged under it and what sentence was imposed.

Unresolved: whether the January 2025 order ending federal funding for gender-affirming care affects privately run, non-federally funded clinics in the Northern Mariana Islands, and whether any such care remains obtainable in the territory on a self-pay basis.

The Movement Advancement Project figures cited are stated as of 27 September 2026 and may not reflect subsequent legislative action; the current status of any proposed commonwealth nondiscrimination bill is unresolved in the available inventory.

COK.name: Cook Islands
COK.summary:
The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Cook Islanders, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male. Consent was explicitly not a defence. Reported maximum terms differ across sources: the 2017 coverage of the draft reform gives seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while later reporting on the repeal cites exposure of up to ten years for indecent acts between males. All sources agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited. The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so a foreign same-sex marriage is not recognised locally and a trans visitor in a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing.

The repeal followed a protracted legislative path. A 2017 select committee recommended removing sections 154 and 155, and the provisions were struck from the draft Crimes Bill, which was drafted with New Zealand assistance; MPs subsequently backtracked. In October 2020 deferral continued when members again pushed the bill's report back, this time by three months, before the 2023 passage.
COK.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources address sexual orientation offences and same-sex marriage. None provides sourced information on legal gender recognition, identity-document marker rules, or administrative procedures for changing gender on Cook Islands or New Zealand documents used locally; that layer of the record is unresolved.

No source identifies hate-crime legislation covering gender identity or expression, nor any provision restricting trans people from facilities, or any rule governing access to gender-affirming healthcare on the islands. Whether such rules exist under Cook Islands statute is unresolved rather than absent, and cannot be confirmed from the inventory.

The maximum penalty reported for the former sections 154 and 155 differs between sources (five, seven and ten years). The inventory does not resolve the correct statutory figures against the text of the 1969 Act.

Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

NIU.name: Niue
NIU.summary:
Criminal liability for sexual conduct in Niue is set by Niue's own statute law. Sections 43 and 44 of the Criminal Law Code criminalised male homosexual conduct: consensual sodomy carried up to ten years' imprisonment, attempted buggery and indecent assault on males fell under the same provisions, and indecency between males carried up to five years. The provisions were inherited from New Zealand through the 1901 annexation, retained when Niue achieved self-governance in 1974, and left untouched by New Zealand's own decriminalisation in 1986, which amended New Zealand law only (Human Dignity Trust; Wikipedia).

Those sections were repealed by the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act 2024, passed in May 2024 and in force from June 2024, decriminalising male homosexual activity (Human Dignity Trust). No source in the current inventory records criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct in Niue today, and none documents enforcement against queer people.

Relationship recognition runs the other way. Section 6 of the Family Relationships Act 2022 expressly prohibits same-sex marriage, and same-sex unions are not recognised in Niue even though they are recognised in New Zealand. Same-sex couples, and households headed by same-sex couples, are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples (Wikipedia).

New Zealand nationality and passport rules govern entry into Niue; the territory operates no independent citizenship or passport regime.
NIU.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no source on trans-specific legal questions in Niue: change of gender markers on identity documents, legal recognition of non-binary or third-gender status, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or prohibition of discrimination on grounds of gender identity. These remain unresolved and are not sourced here.

Sources disagree on the exact date of the 2024 repeal: Human Dignity Trust records passage in May and entry into force in June, while Wikipedia records enactment on 5 June 2024. The discrepancy is unresolved.

No source in the inventory documents enforcement practice, police conduct, hate-crime incidents, or violence against trans people in Niue, and none records entry screening, facility access, or healthcare availability for trans visitors. Absence of such records is not evidence of safety.

sources.summary: The Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May, in force in June, removing 'buggery', 'attempted buggery' and 'indecent assault on males' (Human Dignity Trust, Niue section). Those offences sat at ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code and carried up to 10 years. HKG.name: Hong Kong
HKG.summary:
Hong Kong is a special administrative region of the People's Republic of China running its own legal system under the Basic Law, and trans claims here have been settled by courts rather than by statute. No comprehensive gender recognition framework exists, and as of 2026 there are no laws against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity and no hate crime legislation.

The Court of Final Appeal ruled in February 2023, in the Henry Tse case, that full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card. This overturned the High Court's February 2019 judgment against trans men Henry Tse, Q and R, in which Judge Thomas Au's 59-page ruling had made full confirmation surgery the 'only objectively ascertainable criterion' and rejected self-ID as leading to 'uncertainty and arbitrariness'; the men had already changed legal gender in Britain, and counsel had called the requirement 'out of proportion'.

Since April 2024 a revised policy allows individuals who have undergone specific gender-affirming surgeries (mastectomy for trans men; penectomy and orchiectomy for trans women) to apply for an ID gender marker change, provided they supply medical proof, live as their identified gender for at least two years, and undergo continuous hormone therapy. Hong Kong law allows change of legal documents such as the ID card and passport but does not permit birth certificate changes. Cross-dressing per se is not illegal.

Same-sex conduct is not prohibited outright: the Crimes Ordinance set the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 against 16 for heterosexual acts, and the Court of Appeal's September 2006 judgment in Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (CACV317/2005), brought by a 21-year-old who had been in same-sex relationships since 16, examined whether that facially neutral disparity unjustifiably discriminated. The case is the landmark precedent on equal age of consent in Hong Kong. During the Legislative Council debate over the disparity, conservative lawmakers argued legal inequality was necessary 'to protect youth and preserve tradition'.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognized. The Court of Final Appeal in September 2023 directed the government to establish an alternative recognition framework within two years but also ruled that no constitutionally guaranteed right to marry exists. The Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill, introduced in July 2025, would have granted limited medical decision rights including hospital visits, shared medical information, organ donation, and dealing with remains; the legislature vetoed it on 19 September 2025 by 71 votes to 14, leaving same-sex partners without recognized medical decision-making rights. Around 80% of 10,775 written submissions on the bill were in opposition, and political opposition comes from social conservatives, often with evangelical Christian ties.

Same-sex couples have obtained a series of partial rights through litigation: spousal visa rights via the Court of Final Appeal ruling of 4 July 2018 (QT case), effective 19 September 2018 when the Director of Immigration announced favourable consideration of such applications; joint tax filing effective 19 September 2018; limited domestic violence protection since 2009; and equal public housing rights from the Court of Final Appeal on 26 November 2024. Since 2021, step-child adoption has been affirmed for same-sex couples in the Court of First Instance case AA v BB (S v KG), which granted a lesbian couple joint custody, shared care and guardianship over their two children after separation. Under Cap. 13 Guardianship of Minors Ordinance the Court of First Instance has full control over appointing or removing guardians. Many Hong Kong residents who are British Nationals (Overseas) can register civil partnerships at British consulates in 22 countries.

On 23 July 2025 the High Court ruled in K v Secretary for Environment and Ecology that government regulation prohibiting trans people from using public toilets matching their lived gender identity was unconstitutional under the Basic Law's right to equality. The ruling provides a legal basis for facility access, though implementation details are not described in the source. Trans people report being susceptible to verbal, physical and sexual abuse in public toilets.

Trans people face a high rate of rejection, victimization and discrimination, with social marginalization producing negative mental health effects: trans Hongkongers disproportionately experience moderate-to-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms. A 2013 case saw trans woman Eliana Rubashkyn discriminated against and sexually abused by Hong Kong airport customs officers, subjected to an invasive body search lasting more than nine hours, and left stateless pending UN and NGO assistance. A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion in domains including personal security, health and education.
HKG.outOfScopeNotes: The April 2024 ID-marker policy's implementation record, including approval rates and processing times, is not sourced here. The September 2023 Court of Final Appeal direction to build an alternative recognition framework within two years has no sourced follow-through after the September 2025 bill veto, so the current status of that directive is unresolved. Whether the July 2025 public-toilet ruling has been implemented across government facilities is not described in the available sources. The scale of enforcement of the 2013 airport customs abuse pattern against other trans travellers is not documented.

MAC.name: Macau
MAC.summary:
Macau is a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China, standing under the national framework of the Basic Law while administering its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1996, the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offences identically, and no provision criminalises gender expression. The general age of consent is 14 for both homosexual and heterosexual sex; Penal Code Article 166 separately prescribes 3 to 10 years' imprisonment for anal intercourse with a person under 14, and up to 4 years where a 14-to-16-year-old's inexperience is taken advantage of.

There is no legal pathway to gender recognition. The Identification Services Bureau maintains no policy for changing the sex marker on Macau identity cards, and the gender-marker-change study carried out in 2015 never produced legislation. Between 2004 and 28 February 2026 the Bureau received eight written requests to change the gender marker on identity documents and rejected all eight. On 7 April 2026 the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) stated that legal recognition of gender identity still requires "prudent study" of core societal values, civil law and family relations, and that there are "no plans to revise the framework"; a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents had not altered that position. Macau is the only area in China without either identity-card gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions, both of which are available in mainland China and in Hong Kong.

The document mismatch has direct border consequences: a trans man holding a Hong Kong identity card marked male remains registered female in Macau, producing confusion when crossing the boundary.

The Basic Law's Article 25 list of protected grounds omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Statutory non-discrimination protection is sectoral, extending to employment under Article 6(2) of Law No. 7/2008, with fines of up to MOP$50,000 per affected worker, and to personal data under Law No. 8/2005 and the ombudsman's mandate under Law No. 4/2012.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. A March 2013 bill tabled by Legislative Assembly member José Pereira Coutinho to grant same-sex civil unions the rights available to heterosexual couples was rejected 17 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions and expressly excluded the right to adopt. Same-sex couples, and households headed by same-sex couples, remain ineligible for some legal rights available to opposite-sex couples.

Domestic-violence protection excludes same-sex partners. A 2011 public consultation had included "same-sex cohabitants in an intimate relationship" in scope, but the government's 2012 concluding report removed the reference citing "a lack of social consensus", and the 2016 legislation insisted on the exclusion on the ground that same-sex partners were not considered family members. Rainbow of Macau lodged a complaint with the UN Committee against Torture in October 2015; the Committee's 2015 concluding observations urged Macau to protect all domestic-violence victims "without discrimination". The UN Human Rights Committee noted in 2017 that Macau still does not permit transgender people to change gender markers on birth records and identity documents.

Public expression around LGBT people is constrained by stigmatising coverage. On 9 June 2015 the newspaper Exmoo headlined a report on an alleged sexual offence with a slur against gay people, prompting Rainbow of Macau spokesperson Jason Chao to restate that the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offenders identically.
MAC.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Macau's Penal Code or other statutes contain hate-crime or hate-speech enhancement provisions covering offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity; the stigmatising press material cited here evidences public hostility but not a charging or sentencing rule.

No sourced material addresses access to gender-affirming care in Macau, including whether hormone therapy or surgery are available, lawful, or reimbursed, nor whether prescriptions issued abroad are honoured.

Facilities and screening questions are unresolved: nothing in the sources states how Macau handles gendered toilets, detention cells, airport or border screening, or security pat-downs for trans travellers, beyond the identity-card mismatch noted above.

Whether Macau recognises foreign same-sex marriages, foreign civil unions, or foreign court-ordered name and gender changes for residents or visitors is not sourced here.

The circumstances of the 2015 gender-marker-change study, including its authors and its actual recommendations, are not detailed in the available material; only its outcome, no enacted law, is established.

Enforcement practice under Law No. 7/2008 in cases alleging sexual-orientation or gender-identity discrimination is unverified: no complaint counts, outcomes, or penalty records appear in the inventory.

sources.title: Transgenders don't exist in the eyes of the law
sources.summary: Plataforma Media (8 Sep 2023): transgender residents cannot change sex on Macau ID cards — no data-change policy exists — causing border-crossing confusion (a trans man holding a Hong Kong card marked male is still registered female in Macau); activists press the long-promised legislative reform.

sources.title: Macau: legal recognition of gender identity requires 'prudent study'
sources.summary: Plataforma Media (7 Apr 2026): the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) says gender-identity legal recognition still needs 'prudent study' of core societal values, civil and family law, and states there are 'no plans to revise the framework' — Macau remains the only area in China without ID gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions (both possible in mainland China and Hong Kong), despite a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents.

MAC.blindSummary:
The country is an autonomous area standing under the national framework of the Basic Law of the country, while administering its own civil-law system of historic-era derivation. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1996, the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offences identically, and no provision criminalises gender expression. The general age of consent is 14 for both homosexual and heterosexual sex; Penal Code Article 166 separately prescribes 3 to 10 years' imprisonment for anal intercourse with a person under 14, and up to 4 years where a 14-to-16-year-old's inexperience is taken advantage of.

There is no legal pathway to gender recognition. The identification bureau maintains no policy for changing the sex marker on local identity cards, and the gender-marker-change study carried out in 2015 never produced legislation. Between 2004 and 28 February 2026 the bureau received eight written requests to change the gender marker on identity documents and rejected all eight. On 7 April 2026 the regional justice services office stated that legal recognition of gender identity still requires "prudent study" of core societal values, civil law and family relations, and that there are "no plans to revise the framework"; a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents had not altered that position. The country is the only area in the country without either identity-card gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions, both of which are available in other parts of the country.

The document mismatch has direct border consequences: a trans man holding an identity card issued elsewhere and marked male remains registered female locally, producing confusion when crossing the boundary.

The Basic Law's Article 25 list of protected grounds omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Statutory non-discrimination protection is sectoral, extending to employment under Article 6(2) of Law No. 7/2008, with fines of up to MOP$50,000 per affected worker, and to personal data under Law No. 8/2005 and the ombudsman's mandate under Law No. 4/2012.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. A March 2013 bill tabled by a member of the regional legislature to grant same-sex civil unions the rights available to heterosexual couples was rejected 17 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions and expressly excluded the right to adopt. Same-sex couples, and households headed by same-sex couples, remain ineligible for some legal rights available to opposite-sex couples.

Domestic-violence protection excludes same-sex partners. A 2011 public consultation had included "same-sex cohabitants in an intimate relationship" in scope, but the government's 2012 concluding report removed the reference citing "a lack of social consensus", and the 2016 legislation insisted on the exclusion on the ground that same-sex partners were not considered family members. A local rainbow organisation lodged a complaint with a UN treaty body in October 2015; the body's 2015 concluding observations urged the state/province to protect all domestic-violence victims "without discrimination". A second UN treaty body noted in 2017 that the country still does not permit transgender people to change gender markers on birth records and identity documents.

Public expression around LGBT people is constrained by stigmatising coverage. On 9 June 2015 a local newspaper headlined a report on an alleged sexual offence with a slur against gay people, prompting a spokesperson for the local rainbow organisation to restate that the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offenders identically.
MAC.blindOutOfScope:
The inventory does not resolve whether the Penal Code or other statutes contain hate-crime or hate-speech enhancement provisions covering offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity; the stigmatising press material cited here evidences public hostility but not a charging or sentencing rule.

No sourced material addresses access to gender-affirming care in the country, including whether hormone therapy or surgery are available, lawful, or reimbursed, nor whether prescriptions issued elsewhere are honoured.

Facilities and screening questions are unresolved: nothing in the sources states how the state/province handles gendered toilets, detention cells, border screening, or security pat-downs for trans travellers, beyond the identity-card mismatch noted above.

Whether the country recognises same-sex marriages, civil unions, or court-ordered name and gender changes granted elsewhere, for residents or visitors, is not sourced here.

The circumstances of the 2015 gender-marker-change study, including its authors and its actual recommendations, are not detailed in the available material; only its outcome, no enacted law, is established.

Enforcement practice under Law No. 7/2008 in cases alleging sexual-orientation or gender-identity discrimination is unverified: no complaint counts, outcomes, or penalty records appear in the inventory.

ESH.name: Western Sahara
ESH.summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory. Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate across the parts of it under Moroccan control, and a visitor there stands under Moroccan law wherever those institutions act. Human Rights Watch recorded that authority in a dispatch of 9 December 2005, covering the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; the organisation called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under that framework and carries six months to three years of imprisonment. The broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. Its own legal order is recorded by the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA as punishing same-sex sexual activity for both males and females with up to three years of imprisonment, and a global legality roundup published in July 2017 lists the state as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and illegal there for decades.

Protection machinery is absent on both sides of the dispute. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence, a conclusion it reaches in part from a 2010 statement by Ahmed Mulay Alli, the Sahrawi state's diplomatic representative in Mexico, that the constitution does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice and does not punish it. The statement resolves nothing for a visitor: the conduct is recorded as criminalised, while the protective text a traveller might rely on does not exist.

A visitor should expect screening, questioning and detention to be carried out by Moroccan officials in the controlled areas, under a morality provision whose wording leaves the decision to arrest largely with the officer on the street. No trans-specific entry rule, gender-marker rule or documented incident of trans-specific violence in the territory is recorded in the available sources.
ESH.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the available sources: no trans-specific rule on legal gender-marker change, passport or ID presentation at entry, bathroom and facility access, hate-crime enhancement, or access to hormone care is recorded for Western Sahara. Any statement about those questions would be unsourced.

The 2009 USCRI finding that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps were holding some prisoners on homosexuality charges, in cases where the alleged facts would more fittingly describe rape, concerns camps administered in Algeria. It does not describe conditions inside Western Sahara itself, and the sources do not establish whether comparable detention occurs within the territory.

The criminalisation figures reach the dossier through aggregation. The six-month-to-three-year range and the up-to-three-year Sahrawi figure come from secondary roundups and monitor entries rather than from primary text of the penal provisions, and no source quotes the operative statutory article for either framework. The current status of the constitution referred to in the 2010 statement, and whether any amendment has since added or removed protections, is not resolved here.

GMB.name: Gambia
GMB.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been criminalised in Gambia since the colonial era. The Criminal Code adopted in March 2025 removed the 2014 provision permitting life imprisonment for "aggravated homosexuality" and instead sets a five-year minimum sentence for "unnatural offences", defined in the statute as any homosexual act, with no stated maximum penalty; "gross indecency" carries three years. Regional reporting on the 2025 package confirms the five-year minimum for homosexual acts. The offence attaches to conduct rather than to stated identity or expression.

Gender expression is separately restricted. Since 2013, section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress "as women", punishable by up to five years in jail or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi. A visitor presenting outside conventional male dress should expect this provision to be the most readily invoked against them. On 10 April 2012 a court remanded 18 men, 16 Senegalese, one Gambian and one Nigerian, arrested at a bar in the Tourism Development Area for "indecent practice" after police said they were wearing women's clothes; all charges were dropped on 1 August 2012.

The government of President Adama Barrow has not typically enforced these provisions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the statute while documenting significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons, and the 2020 report recorded arrests together with societal discrimination. The Barrow government has promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, while stating that there are no plans for liberalisation of the homosexuality laws.

Enforcement was broad under the previous long-term ruler, Yahya Jammeh. On 15 May 2008 he gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the Gambia Immigration Department to conduct mass patrols to "weed bad elements in society", warning that any hotel, lodge or motel lodging such individuals would be closed down. In June 2008 two Spanish men in their 50s, alleged to be gay, were arrested and detained at Kotu police station after taxi drivers reported them, and were released reportedly after the Spanish government intervened. On 23 December 2008 Frank Boers, a 79-year-old Dutch national, was arrested at Banjul International Airport when officials found him in possession of pornography including nude photos of himself and Gambian men; he was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 dalasis in lieu of a two-year sentence. Arrests of gay people are believed to have been common during Jammeh's presidency, though data is lacking.

The 2014 Criminal Code (Amendment) Act defined "aggravated homosexuality" to include sexual acts with persons of the same gender under 18 years of age, carrying a mandatory life sentence, and imposed a mandatory life sentence specifically on gay or lesbian people living with HIV, a direct barrier to testing and treatment. In November 2014 state forces launched an investigation under that law producing at least eight arrests, including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women. Detainees were held at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly tortured to compel confessions. Human Rights Watch's September 2015 report "State of Fear" documents arbitrary arrests, torture and killings under Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Gambia, and the country prohibits LGBTQ people from adopting children. No law or regulation protects residents against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and citizens cannot change their legal gender. In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honour LGBTQ+ people's privacy, which has negatively impacted HIV care for LGBTQ+ Gambians. No incidents of conversion therapy or of surgeries on intersex children or non-consenting adults were reported.

Societal hostility is documented at high levels. A 2021-2023 survey found 93% of Gambians would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. No LGBTQ+ organisations exist in the country after 2016 because it is considered too dangerous, children are raised within strict male and female gender norms with non-conformity treated as deviant and taboo, and the country's media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ+ people.
GMB.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March 2025 Criminal Code retained section 167's restriction on men dressing "as women" is not resolved in the available sources; the provision is sourced to the 2013 code and its current text is not confirmed.

The maximum penalty for "unnatural offences" under the 2025 code is not stated in any source reviewed, only the five-year minimum. Whether the 2025 code altered gender recognition, adoption or anti-discrimination provisions is not sourced.

Enforcement data under the Barrow government is thin: the 2021 US State Department report records no prosecutions, but no source covers 2022 to 2026 prosecution figures, and the claim that arrests were common under Jammeh is stated by sources as a belief for which data is lacking.

The UK Home Office policy note's current certification and internal-relocation conclusions are summarised at the level of scope only; its detailed country findings are not reproduced here.

A visitor presenting outside conventional male dress should expect this provision to be the most readily invoked against them. In April 2012 a court remanded 18 men, 16 foreign nationals from a neighbouring jurisdiction, one citizen and one national of a second neighbouring jurisdiction, arrested at a bar in a tourist development area for "indecent practice" after police said they were wearing women's clothes; all charges were dropped four months later.

The government of the current president has not typically enforced these provisions. A foreign government's annual human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the statute in its most recent edition while documenting significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons, and the preceding year's report recorded arrests together with societal discrimination. The government has promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, while stating that there are no plans for liberalisation of the homosexuality laws.

Enforcement was broad under the previous long-term ruler. In May 2008 he gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the national immigration department to conduct mass patrols to "weed bad elements in society", warning that any hotel, lodge or motel lodging such individuals would be closed down. Two months later two foreign men in their 50s, alleged to be gay, were arrested and detained at a coastal police station after taxi drivers reported them, and were released reportedly after their government intervened. In December 2008 a 79-year-old foreign national was arrested at the international airport when officials found him in possession of pornography including nude photos of himself and local men; he was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 units of the national currency in lieu of a two-year sentence. Arrests of gay people are believed to have been common during that presidency, though data is lacking.

The 2014 Criminal Code (Amendment) Act defined "aggravated homosexuality" to include sexual acts with persons of the same gender under 18 years of age, carrying a mandatory life sentence, and imposed a mandatory life sentence specifically on gay or lesbian people living with HIV, a direct barrier to testing and treatment. In November 2014 national forces launched an investigation under that law producing at least eight arrests, including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women. Detainees were held at the national intelligence agency headquarters in the capital and allegedly tortured to compel confessions. An international human rights organisation's September 2015 report documents arbitrary arrests, torture and killings under that ruler, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, and the country prohibits LGBTQ people from adopting children. No law or regulation protects residents against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and citizens cannot change their legal gender. In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honour LGBTQ+ people's privacy, which has negatively impacted HIV care for LGBTQ+ residents. No incidents of conversion therapy or of surgeries on intersex children or non-consenting adults were reported.

Societal hostility is documented at high levels. A 2021-2023 survey found 93% of residents would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. No LGBTQ+ organisations exist in the country after 2016 because it is considered too dangerous, children are raised within strict male and female gender norms with non-conformity treated as deviant and taboo, and the country's media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ+ people.

The country was rated "Partly Free" with 50/100 by a comparative democracy monitor in 2024, which recorded improved political freedoms under the current president after 22 years of the previous ruler's rule while listing severe discrimination against LGBT+ people among ongoing concerns. The improvement in political space has not been matched by decriminalisation or by statutory protection against discrimination.

A foreign government's country information and policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity in the country (version 3.0, February 2023) assesses risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, and records country information on law and treatment. Its existence indicates that the country is treated by at least one foreign government as a place of origin where LGBT+ status carries well-documented risk.

The 2015 findings on arbitrary arrest, torture and killings concern the previous ruler's enforcement climate rather than the current government, and the shift in enforcement practice since 2017 is the main variable in what a visitor should expect on the ground.
